Economic and Market Commentary

Diversifying Globally Without Giving Up Yield

Bond yields have moved higher around the world. Portfolio Managers Pramol Dhawan and Sachin Gupta discuss how global fixed income can help investors diversify sources of return while uncovering opportunities across developed and emerging markets.

Pramol Dhawan, Sachin Gupta

10/26/2026

Text on screen: Why invest globally, and why now?
Text on screen: Sachin Gupta, Portfolio Manager, Global Bonds
Sachin: We think this is a very compelling environment for global diversification. For starters, the generational reset in bond yields that happened a few years ago was not just a U.S. phenomenon; it happened across the world.
Additionally, in the last few years in particular, we are seeing increasing divergence when it comes to policy settings, growth, inflation.
Text on screen: Diversify globally without giving up yield
Images on screen: Emerging Market countries
All of this means that when investors are looking to invest globally, not only are they not giving up on yields, but they are picking up on diversification benefits coming from all these drivers.
Pramol: The U.S. accounts for approximately
Text on screen: 25% of global output, 80% of portfolio allocations
25% of global economic output, yet it accounts for nearly 80% of all portfolio allocations. So the question that we hear the most from clients is, how can I sensibly diversify my portfolios?
Text on screen: Pramol Dhawan, Portfolio Manager, Emerging Markets
And interestingly enough, today, given the starting backdrop of yields not only in the U.S. but globally, you can actually get paid to diversify.
Text on screen: How does PIMCO turn global opportunity into alpha?
Sachin: Our approach to global investing is about finding value in what is a very vast and diverse opportunity set. In order to do that, we rely on teams of portfolio managers, or regional experts, who help us analyze individual countries, bond markets, and, in these pockets, and look for opportunities.
Text on screen: PIMCO frameworks uncover relative value
Images on screen: PIMCO trade floor and forum
The way we do that is to bring all of our homegrown frameworks to bear, analyze trends in growth and inflation, or other drivers, indeed, that could be driving relative value opportunities in all of these markets.
Text on screen: Where are you finding opportunities today?
Sachin: There are several opportunities that look really attractive for client portfolios.
Text on screen: TITLE – Where we see opportunities:, BULLETS: UK and Australia, Select Latin American markets
When you look internationally, for starters, bonds in the UK and Australia look just as attractive, if not even more so, than in the U.S.
At the same time, there are portions of global bond markets that actually look quite rich. An example would be Singapore, where the bond yields are substantially lower than any other comparable economy.
Pramol: We're particularly excited about strong balance sheets and conservative fiscal backdrops in Latin America. I think in Chile and in Peru in particular. Put together, we think you can build a very robust, high-yielding portfolio that offers true diversification away from U.S. assets whilst picking up incremental yield.

articles.title: First Meeting with a Financial Advisor | Wells Fargo Advisors
articles.text:
Day One With Your Financial Advisor

Preparing for your first meeting

Your first meeting with your Financial Advisor marks the beginning of an important professional relationship. Just as you rely on your doctor with your health and your mechanic with your car, you’ll be entrusting your Financial Advisor with something of great value too — your financial goals.

call out

Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client.

end call out

Our Financial Advisors work with many types of investors and value their diversity. Your Financial Advisor will want to know you as a person — not just as a client — so he or she can understand the best way to help you with your investment needs and life goals.

The right fit

Meeting with a Financial Advisor for the first time, you should expect a friendly, casual conversation — you’re just getting to know each other. There’s no obligation, no pressure, no judgment — and no cost for your first meeting. You should be candid about your level of investing experience, overall financial situation, and financial goals. You should also feel comfortable asking as many questions as you’d like.
It’s important you choose a Financial Advisor who listens to your concerns, understands your financial needs, and values your input. The relationship between you and your Financial Advisor is a critical one — through the years, you should have many sensitive, private conversations. The relationship may even expand to include friends and future generations of your family.

Getting ready

Before the meeting, your Financial Advisor should send you a checklist of items to bring. Your privacy is a top priority, and your Financial Advisor is committed to maintaining strict confidentiality.
A good Financial Advisor will want the right fit for you as much you seek the right fit in him or her. Before your first consultation, you’ll want to reflect on and be prepared to discuss:

Your values about money and your vision for your future
What life events are happening or could potentially happen
Short- and long-term life and financial goals
Investment questions
Your current financial situation
Preferred account management style

Remember, the more you share about your financial picture, investment goals, and risk tolerance, the better your Financial Advisor will be able to recommend strategies and create an investment plan. You’ll find the initial meeting with your Financial Advisor will set the stage for many conversations to come.

Next steps

Think about how you prefer to work with your advisor and what types of investments you’re interested in.
Gather the necessary documentation for your initial meeting and prepare answers to questions your advisor may ask.

articles.text:

Inflation

26 October, 2026

5 minutes

Dividends shine as tech cools

EDM

Weekly Market DirectionsENFR

Dividends shine as tech cools

5 minutes

EDM

Weekly Market DirectionsENFR

Summary

Markets are no longer convinced by AI spending alone. Investors now want evidence of cash flow and profitability. This is driving rotation into attractively priced, dividend-generating sectors that can also enhance diversification.

Technology stocks’ H2 performance underscores a clear market demand for greater visibility on capital expenditure. In this environment, companies that consistently return cash to shareholders are likely to stay in demand. While AI should deliver a productivity boost in the long term to the economy, markets will increasingly distinguish the winners from the losers in the sector.

Confidence in the artificial intelligence theme has weakened in recent weeks, with the MSCI World Technology Index giving back all of the previous month’s gains. This was likely driven by a combination of mixed corporate earnings and renewed concerns about AI-related capital expenditure. We think markets have now moved beyond the phase in which the mere mention of an AI roll-out could excite investors. Markets are now increasingly demanding clarity on cash generation from these sizeable AI investments. By contrast, the MSCI World High Dividend Yield Index gained 8% in the second half of the year as markets sought steadier ground, typically found in sectors such as consumer staples, healthcare and utilities — the traditional home of dividend-paying companies — which held up well as the broader market came under pressure. This suggests diversification* opportunities through more attractively valued sectors with strong, stable businesses.* Diversification does not guarantee a profit or protect against a loss.

This week at a glance

Global equity markets came under pressure, led by a reversal in technology stocks that spread more broadly. Bond yields in some countries, such as the US, declined amid safe-haven demand, whereas fiscal concerns in other countries pushed yields higher. In commodities, the oil price was affected by a flare-up in Middle East tensions. Gold prices declined amid concerns that persistent inflation could prompt central banks to raise interest rates.

Amundi Investment Institute Macro Focus

AmericasUS labour market holds firm, housing stays under pressureInitial jobless claims fell to 194,000 in the week ending 17 October, below expectations and consistent with a firm labour market. The housing sector, however, continues to struggle: September housing starts fell to an annualised 1.22 million units, sharply below forecasts and down from the prior month. The releases point to a divided economy, with elevated borrowing costs continuing to weigh on builders and buyers, leaving residential construction under pressure despite labour market resilience.EuropeEurozone growth momentum slows in OctoberThe EZ’s preliminary business activity reading for October came in below expectations, signalling a modest loss of momentum. The composite PMI index fell to 51.9 from 53.1 in September, as both services and manufacturing slowed. All three readings remain above the 50 threshold separating expansion from contraction, but the pace of growth is clearly decelerating. Weaker investor and consumer confidence also point to growing caution about the near-term economic outlook. AsiaJapan inflation risesJapan's inflation excluding fresh food and energy rose to 2.4% in September, above expectations and up from August, signalling renewed underlying price pressures. Meanwhile, the auction of 20-year government bonds drew record demand, while domestic investors increased purchases in the first half of the fiscal year, reflecting stronger appetite at elevated yields.

articles.title: Take Two: Market performance diverges - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
What do you need to know?

Stocks endured further volatility over the past week, as concerns over corporate spending on artificial intelligence and rising oil prices weighed on sentiment. The MSCI World NR and the US blue-chip S&P 500 indices each fell by 1% in the week to Thursday’s close, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped by a steeper 3%.* Elsewhere, the Dow Jones was up 1% while Europe’s Stoxx 600 was flat. Meanwhile, eurozone fixed income underperformed as US Treasuries rallied. The yield on French government bonds surpassed 5% for the first time since 2002 on uncertainty over the country’s finances – yields move inversely to prices.

*In US dollar terms. Source: FactSet, as of 22 October 2026

Around the world

China’s economy expanded at a faster pace than expected in the third quarter of this year. GDP grew by 4.5% on an annualised basis, up from Q2’s three-year low of 4.3%. Growth was boosted by artificial intelligence-related exports, despite domestic demand remaining subdued and an ongoing downturn in the property market. The quarterly data puts China on track to meet the lower end of the government’s official 4.5%-5% growth target for the year, analysts said.

Figure in focus: 18%

Greenhouse emissions must reduce by 18% by the end of the decade to limit global warming to 1.5°C, the United Nations warned. Current levels of emissions reductions show that under the “lowest possible” overshoot scenario, peak warming will reach 1.7°C to 1.8°C around the middle of the century. To meet the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C target, “immediate and aggressive cuts” to emissions are needed, of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, the UN said. If action is taken, including carbon capture and storage, global warming could return to below 1.5°C by 2100, it added.

Chart of the week

Technology hardware is dominant in driving corporate earnings growth and equity price appreciation. The information technology sector accounted for almost two-thirds of global earnings growth in the third quarter, at 60%, followed by energy at 20%. Expectations are high for technology companies globally, with the sector forecast to see a doubling of earnings compared to the same quarter a year ago, according to the market consensus. Earnings growth in other sectors of global stock markets is relatively low. Investors are keeping a sharp eye on earnings trends, reflecting concerns that stock markets may be overly dependent on the tech sector.

Words of wisdom: Small AI

Task-specific AI models which need less computing power and energy to run. The World Bank launched a new digital strategy to help developing countries improve digital access and services and create more jobs. It emphasised the potential benefits of small AI: tools that are adapted to specific tasks and local conditions, such as helping farmers identify crop disease, supporting health workers, or helping businesses manage inventory. However, substantial barriers remain, with only 23% of people in low-income countries using the internet, the World Bank said.

What’s coming up?

Central banks take centre stage this week. On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of Canada each meet to make their respective interest rate decisions. The European Central Bank follows on Thursday with its own rate-setting meeting while the Bank of Japan convenes on Friday. Elsewhere, the UK unveils its Autumn Budget on Wednesday. On Thursday, the US publishes its Q3 GDP growth rate, followed by the eurozone which reports Q3 growth data on Friday.

articles.title: Xi’s party: What to look for at the upcoming Chinese Communist Party plenum | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Xi’s party: What to look for at the upcoming Chinese Communist Party plenum

Jonathan A. Czin and

Jonathan A. Czin

Michael H. Armacost Chair in Foreign Policy Studies,

Fellow
- Foreign Policy, John L. Thornton China Center

Allie Matthias

Allie Matthias

Senior Research Assistant
- John L. Thornton China Center

October 23, 2026

From October 26 to 29, Chinese President Xi Jinping will convene a major annual Chinese Communist Party meeting focused on party governance. In the run-up, Xi has displayed dissatisfaction with the party’s leadership through speeches and purges across the Politburo, Central Military Commission (CMC), and Central Committee.
The purges have been most extensive in the People’s Liberation Army. The CMC only has two members left, including Xi. Only 17 of the Central Committee’s original 44 members nominally remain, and just two have appeared publicly in recent months. This plenum may be Xi’s last opportunity to repopulate and restructure the CMC before next year’s party congress.
Xi is almost certainly using this plenum to lay the groundwork for his fourth term, which will begin at next fall’s party congress. He will likely have to replace many of his remaining allies, but his third term’s extensive purges may make it harder to rebuild a team he can trust.

Attendants listen to Chinese President Xi Jinping's speech at the National Day reception on the eve of the 77th founding anniversary of the People's Republic of China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China September 30, 2026. REUTERS/Florence Lo/Pool

10 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

From October 26 to 29, Chinese President Xi Jinping will convene the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) for its fifth plenary session. This almost annual, closed-door meeting is a Marxist-Leninist party-state tradition for signaling major policy directions. The CCP’s 205 full members and 152 alternates will lay the groundwork for Xi’s likely fourth five-year term, which begins after next fall’s quinquennial party congress, when roughly 2,000 CCP delegates descend on Beijing. The plenum will focus on how the world’s largest party manages its 101 million members. Yet the most interesting developments will concern personnel movement, as Xi’s purges have swept through the party elite.
Since last year’s party plenum, Xi has continued his anti-corruption campaign against his own allies. Two more Politburo members were toppled, leaving 21 members. The purge of the 20th Central Committee’s Politburo has become the body’s most sweeping since the aftermath of the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown. Meanwhile, the party’s supreme military council, the Central Military Commission (CMC), has been almost entirely decapitated: shrinking from seven members at the start of Xi’s third term to just two—Xi and General Zhang Shengmin, who oversaw the purges of his peers. At the theater-command level, one grade below the CMC, as many as 33 officers have been removed. Since our February 2026 study with CSIS of the purges of the high command, only a few senior officers have been promoted—and there have been a few additional dismissals. The wide range of Xi’s military purges suggests that he may be dissatisfied with his 2016 restructuring of the high command and could yet again restructure the CMC, perhaps at this plenum or next fall’s party congress.
Only a Central Committee plenum can repopulate the CMC, making this Xi’s likely last opportunity to reconstitute his high command before next year’s party congress. It would be rather remarkable for Xi to pass on this opportunity and leave the CMC in its current rickety state—and could well signal his lack of confidence that the remaining senior officers are capable of running the world’s second most powerful military. But even if Xi were to repopulate his high command, he would still face a problem of trust: if he could not trust his own allies in the PLA’s high command, how can he trust any newly minted generals? Many of Xi’s closest remaining civilian allies are also expected to retire at next year’s party congress, raising questions about whether he can assemble a team that he can trust to govern effectively in his fourth five-year term.
Personnel
At last year’s plenum, only 168 of the Central Committee’s 205 full members actually showed up—the lowest attendance in the post-Mao era. The unexplained absences of so many colleagues must have been rather chilling to the attendees—many of whom serve in far-flung corners of the country, and all of whom operate in a secretive, highly stovepiped bureaucracy. In an authoritarian system like China’s, these absences are often indicative of a future expulsion or the complete disappearance of a political figure.

In the year since the last plenum, 16 of 205 full Central Committee members, and three of 152 alternate members, have been dismissed from their positions; another eight of 205 full Central Committee members and three of 152 alternates have been expelled from the party. An additional four Central Committee members and two alternate members are under investigation. The plenum will likely confirm the purges of those who have already been dispatched, per the CCP constitution, including two former Politburo members: former CMC Vice Chairman Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui.
The plenum is the only institution capable of appointing new Politburo members, but Xi did not replace previous Politburo members who were purged and may see little reason to do so now. He was loath to replace General He Weidong after expelling him at the last plenum, and he is even more unlikely to do so now with the party congress only one year away.
On the military side, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) started this term with 44 Central Committee members in 2022, but following dismissals and expulsions, only 17 are left standing. Of the 19 Central Committee members who have been dismissed from their positions since the last plenum, 12 are from the PLA. Of the 11 Central Committee members who have already been expelled from the party since the last plenum, two are from the PLA. Of the 23 alternate members from the PLA, one more officer has been removed, and an additional 18 are likely missing.
Remarkably, among the 17 PLA officers left on the Central Committee, the whereabouts of almost every general or lieutenant general remain unknown, as most have not been seen for several months and may have been dismissed themselves. The only clearly active Central Committee PLA officers who have weathered the purges are Admiral Dong Jun and General Zhang Shengmin—and even Zhang is rumored to face trouble, given that his former colleagues’ corruption occurred on his watch.
At the last plenum, Xi skipped over all the alternate Central Committee members from the PLA who should have been promoted to become full Central Committee members. Since the last plenum, only four PLA officers were promoted to general, none of whom are currently full or alternate members of the Central Committee. With the slow rate of promotions, there will likely be very few new generals and lieutenant generals promoted to the party congress next year—though it is still a question of who will continue to weather the storm of PLA purges in the remaining year before the party congress.

Meanwhile, as the plenum approaches and the purges continue, ministerial-level officials are jockeying to position themselves for promotion—including to the Politburo—at next year’s party congress.

Since last year, at least 13 Central Committee members have taken on new roles. Candidates for the next Politburo will likely need to be under 65 and usually have two ministerial positions under their belt to be eligible for promotion to the Politburo, though these requirements are increasingly flexible under Xi. Around 55 officials may currently meet those criteria.

Excluding the missing PLA officers, 15 more Central Committee members have retired, moved to a sinecure position, stepped down, or resigned since the last plenum, but remain on the Central Committee. Altogether, at least 28 individuals from this Central Committee have left their positions, likely due to age, but have not been purged.

Policy
The substantive focus of this year’s plenum will be party-building—and specifically “full and rigorous party self-governance”—as previewed at the Politburo’s September meeting. The concept of “full and rigorous party self-governance” (全面从严治党) entered the party vernacular at the 18th Party Congress when Xi came into power, marking a key focus for Xi throughout his rule. The Politburo’s pre-plenum announcement concentrated on broad, traditional concepts in Xi Jinping Thought, including an emphasis on the importance of party self-governance, rectification of prominent problems in the party, and further development of a favorable political situation.
Ahead of this plenum, Qiushi, the CCP’s leading theoretical journal, published a polemical speech by Xi on personnel management and cadre behavior—a theme consistent with his extensive pruning of the Central Committee’s ranks. He explicitly castigated politically opportunistic or self-interested behavior, as well as profligacy like “power-for-money, and power-for-sex transactions.” Prior to previous plenums on party building, corrupt behavior was named but not as extensively or descriptively as it was here. Likely aware of the upcoming party congress and questions over his own succession, Xi has taken a harsh tone with his underlings to warn against any sort of political jockeying and factionalism. These themes will likely be present throughout the communique and readouts of the plenum.
Other possible developments
Notably, during his first two terms, Xi has used the plenum the year before the party congress to establish his dominance within the party. This has sparked some rumors that Xi might make a bigger move like restoring the position of party chairman that Mao Zedong held—and which the party abolished in 1982—but the available evidence cannot substantiate these rumors. What we do know from his two previous plenums focused on party building is that Xi enjoys reasserting his centrality in the party today and in the course of the party’s history.

At the sixth plenum of the 19th Central Committee in November 2021, the party adopted the “Resolution on Major Achievements and Historical Experience of the Communist Party of China’s 100 Years of Endeavors,” which Xi used in part to elevate himself on par with Mao and Deng Xiaoping. This was only the third historical resolution in CCP history, after Mao’s 1945 resolution and Deng’s 1981 resolution.
In Xi’s first term, the sixth plenum of the 18th Central Committee emphasized Xi’s accomplishments in strengthening party discipline. Taking place early in Xi’s tenure in 2016, the plenum was used to substantiate Xi’s recent anti-corruption campaign by adopting new documents on party discipline.

Conclusion
Xi began his third term by stacking the leadership with longtime allies and associates but has since turned his own anti-corruption crusade against them. As a result, he has dredged deeper from the party’s well of cadres and delayed reconstituting the high command. As Xi gears up for his fourth term, he risks becoming even more isolated, as his remaining allies on the Politburo Standing Committee should retire next year if they abide by the party’s informal retirement rules. Xi will have to replace them with younger men who will likely seek to ingratiate themselves with Xi—in the hopes of replacing him one day. Xi can replace the men but not the trust. And in a conspiratorial system like China’s, trust is the rarest political commodity.

articles.title: What Should Investors Expect an Active Fixed Income Manager to Deliver? | PIMCO
articles.text:
Mohit Mittal

10/27/2026

| 3 min read

Share via Email

Share via Linkedin

Share via Twitter

What differentiates active fixed income investing in today’s markets? In this Q&A, Mohit Mittal, CIO of Core Strategies, discusses how PIMCO approaches portfolio construction and risk management as it seeks to generate outperformance, or alpha. Accompanying videos highlight current opportunities across credit, global markets, and mortgages.
Q: Investors have many ways to capture today’s higher bond yields, including passive index-tracking funds and building ladders out of individual bonds. Why consider actively managed bond funds?
A: Today’s attractive starting yields have restored bonds’ role as a potential source of income and return in a portfolio. But yield is only the starting point. An active manager can seek to add value through individual security selection, positioning across maturities, sector allocation, and relative-value decisions across markets.
Bond market structure can enhance active opportunities. For example, while equity indexes are often based on market capitalization, fixed income indexes generally assign greater weight to issuers with the most debt outstanding, so a passive approach may be exposed to the most indebted borrowers.
Certain bond market participants, including central banks, insurers, and pension funds, may have constraints and objectives beyond maximizing risk-adjusted returns. Their activity can create gaps between price and fundamental value that an active manager can seek to exploit, unlike a passive index or a mechanically constructed bond ladder.
Q: What is “alpha,” and how does PIMCO seek to generate it consistently?
A: Alpha is the excess return a manager seeks to generate above a relevant market benchmark. At PIMCO, our goal is for that excess return to be consistent, diversified, and repeatable. PIMCO organizes potential sources of alpha into three broad layers:

Structural opportunities: Persistent inefficiencies arising from market structure, index construction, investor constraints, liquidity needs, and access to transactions.
Thematic positioning: Views informed by macroeconomic, sector, and bottom-up research, expressed across interest rates, credit, mortgages, currencies, emerging markets, and other areas.
Opportunistic expressions: Positions taken when volatility, market events, or forced selling create temporary price dislocations.

Valuation is the common thread. We ask where investors are being adequately compensated for the risks, rather than beginning with a predetermined sector allocation.
Q: Where are you seeing opportunities to generate alpha today?
A: Today’s fixed income markets may offer attractive opportunities across several key areas.
Credit
An active approach does not require a broadly bullish or bearish view on credit. Dispersion across issuers, sectors, structures, and individual transactions can matter more than the overall market average.

In this video, Mohit Mittal and Sonali Pier discuss how bottom-up research, selectivity, discipline, and scenario analysis may help identify opportunities and risks amid the surge in AI-related investment.
Global opportunities
Market volatility and the broad repricing of yields across countries and maturities have created opportunities. For example, recent fiscal developments in France have started to create opportunities in European sovereign and credit markets.

In the accompanying video, Sachin Gupta and Pramol Dhawan discuss how global diversification may contribute both to alpha generation and portfolio resilience across developed and emerging markets.
Mortgages
Mortgages are a large and unique part of the high-quality fixed income universe. Their performance can vary materially by coupon, structure, prepayment behavior, and interest-rate scenario. That complexity creates room for active security selection and relative-value analysis that an index-level allocation may not capture.

In the accompanying video, Daniel Hyman discusses how PIMCO’s views on mortgages and securitized markets contribute to the pursuit of alpha.
Not every position will work. The aim is to diversify the sources of alpha, size positions deliberately, and prepare in advance for a wide range of outcomes.
Q: How does PIMCO turn research and market views into actual portfolio decisions?
A: Alpha generation starts with a team-based approach and scenario analysis. We consider how each position may behave both under the base case and under materially different economic and market outcomes.
Firmwide views are debated through the Investment Committee. Specialists bring sector-specific opportunities and market perspectives to the Investment Committee and CIOs. The process combines top-down macroeconomic and policy analysis, bottom-up security and issuer research, input from specialist portfolio managers and traders closest to individual markets, and a portfolio construction process that determines which ideas to use, how large they should be, and how they may interact with the rest of the portfolio.
Risk review is continuous, including formal monthly reviews and scenario analysis around potential tail outcomes outside the baseline. Liquidity is also a key part of portfolio construction. Maintaining liquidity may allow our team to provide liquidity when other investors are forced to sell.
Q: What should investors ultimately expect an active fixed income manager to deliver?
A: An active manager can build on the foundation of market conditions, including a competitive starting yield, and seek to generate incremental excess return from multiple, diversified sources.
An active fixed income manager can build a portfolio to navigate a range of outcomes, with disciplined risk management that considers downside scenarios and may preserve the flexibility to respond when markets move. An active manager can offer access to structural, thematic, and opportunistic ideas across sectors, countries, currencies, and public and private markets. An active approach treats volatility and dispersion as potential sources of relative value.
Active management is not about making one bold forecast. It is about repeatedly finding well-compensated risks, combining them thoughtfully, and building a portfolio that may remain resilient when economic and market conditions develop differently than expected.

Text on screen: What AI bond opportunities are worth owning?

Mohit Mittal: We are not looking for the top 2 or 3 companies that will win the race.
Text on screen: Debt investors seek resilience across scenarios
Images on screen: Data Centers, Chip Manufacturing
Instead, we are focusing on companies which will have most resilient cash flows across a range of scenarios and then looking to invest in them at attractive terms.
AI funding is creating huge investment needs across data centers, across chip financing, as well as across energy infrastructure. This is leading to widening in spreads and a move higher in yields, which creates this opportunities in the first place.
Text on screen: How do you assess AI credit opportunities?
Text on screen: Sonali Pier, Portfolio Manager, Multi-Sector Credit
Sonali Pier: There's significant amount of capital that needs to be raised across a wide number of asset classes, investment-grade, high-yield, structured products and direct lending.
So when we look at opportunities, we’ve seen, for perhaps every 100 deals we look at, we may only invest in two that meet the bar for what we're looking for from the perspective of cash flows, structure and protections.
Text on screen: TITLE – What we look for: BULLETS: Assets that outlast the debt, Diversified businesses, Resilient cash flows
So for example, do the assets outlast the debt? at the end, we don't want to be the ones bearing asset-lite refinancing risk. Similarly, we're looking for companies that are resilient.
Which of these companies will be completely disintermediated versus those that can actually have AI be a tailwind toward growth?
We want to make sure that the cash flows are going to outlast our lending. And by doing so, we're looking for robust cash flows, structure that's aligned as well as covenants to ensure downside protection as well.
Text on screen: What risks are AI investors overlooking?
Mohit Mittal: At the moment, everyone is focused on will AI change the world?
Text on screen: Can AI output justify today’s pace of investment?
Images on screen: Data Centers
I think what we are focused on is will AI change the world fast enough to justify the pace of investments?
Throughout history, when we look at big technological investments, be it railroads, be it telecom, be it the internet, all of these were very productive technologies in the end. But along the way, many investors lost a lot of money.
Images on screen: PIMCO forum
In our investment committees, in our forums, we are focused quite extensively on not just the AI boom scenario, but what if the cash flows don't materialize as fast as expected? What if demand doesn't show up? What if demand growth is slower than the pace of investments? All of these could lead to negative outcomes for investors.
Images on screen: PIMCO Trade floor
So that's what we are trying to do. Find companies which will have resilient cash flows across a range of scenarios, including the AI winter scenario.

Text on screen: What makes securitized markets attractive today?
Text on screen: Daniel Hyman, Portfolio Manager, Agency Mortgages
Agency mortgages, when you look at their returns across the full business cycle, have, one, delivered returns better than Treasuries across the full cycle. But importantly, they've delivered their best returns even in recessions. So when you think about that fixed income anchor in a portfolio, something that's supposed to be a diversifier, agency mortgages have been a true diversifier in portfolios.
Second, when we think about the opportunity set today, agency mortgages are historically cheap, or the spread is historically wide, presenting an opportunity for investors.
When you look at the market today,
Text on screen: Opportunities: quality, liquidity, and yield
Images on screen: Residential neighborhood
what we see is an opportunity for investors to go up in credit quality – government-backed Fannie, Freddie, Ginnie Mae securities – up in liquidity – this is one of the most liquid markets in the world, and pick up yield.
Text on screen: How do active managers pursue durable alpha in securitized markets?
Securitized markets have given investors opportunities year in and year out to add value, add alpha above and beyond benchmark returns. One of the things that is unique within the securitized markets is that when you look at, say, the agency market, a $10 trillion market, more than half of the participants in that market are not focused on the total return of bonds. They're investing in there for different reasons.
Images on screen: The Federal Reserve
So a great example would be the Federal Reserve. The Federal Reserve does not care about total return. They're utilizing the market to implement monetary policy. So thinking back to COVID, you had a big dislocation. You had liquidity problems in markets. And the Fed stepped in and said, "We're going to buy a lot of mortgages.”
That's also creating an opportunity today. This is a little bit nuanced, but if you look at how the Fed is engaged in quantitative tightening, what it is doing is creating another dislocation. It's cheapening newer issued mortgages and leaving older issued mortgages more expensive.
Text on screen: Agency MBS may provide attractive starting yields plus total return potential as spreads normalize
Images on screen: Residential neighborhoods
And so when we look at mortgage-backed securities, we see attractive starting yields plus total return potential, so making money from the normalization of those spreads. So great opportunity in mortgages today:
Images on screen: PIMCO trade floor
a chance for investors to go up in quality, increase liquidity and pick up yield.

How modern payments drive growth and resilience
[Music]
Max Neukirchen: Welcome to JP Morgan Making Sense. My name is Max Norkashan and I'm the co-head of our global payments business. I'm here with my friend and colleague, Umar Farouk, who is also the co-head of the global payments business. And together we will break down for you what's happening in payments, what's changing, and what we are doing about it. So Umar, looking forward to the conversation here.
Umar Farooq: And Max, I'm also really looking forward to it. I think it'll be a great conversation. So Max, you and I are partners in running the payments business at JP Morgan. Do you want to give our audience a little bit of an overview of our business?
Max Neukirchen: We serve businesses of all sizes, the largest companies all the way to small businesses around basically any of their payment needs. This could mean paying suppliers, paying their employees, doing M&A transaction, paying their taxes, but it could also mean taking money from consumers who do shopping or financing their supply chain. So we truly take care of our clients' payments needs end-to-end, and we do that in more than a hundred countries. Umar, why has the payments business become such an important strategic topic for our clients?
Umar Farooq: So Max, I think as you and I look back over the last decade or so, and we've been in this business for a few years now, payments has really evolved to become core to our client's own business. So when we think about our clients, for the longest time, I think you mentioned it many times, payments used to be something the treasurer did or the CFO did or the cash management part of the business did. But in reality, as you now look at the evolution, and by the way, the evolution is both in terms of payments infrastructure, but also how our clients do business. The experience of payments is core to their offering, to their end customers. So if you are in a ride-hailing service, when you get out of the car, the payments just happens. No one actually thinks about making the payment. It's actually transparent. Similarly, if you're on an e-commerce platform, you click a button and you buy the thing. And that experience is a core part of the value proposition to end customers. So for our clients, payments is a core part of how they design their product, and I think this has made payments a core part of their value proposition and their products.
Max Neukirchen: I love your examples around the ride-hailing app as well as the e-commerce platform, because as we often say, for the e-commerce platform, it matters big time if it's a one-click checkout as you described, or a five-click checkout. Because with the one-click checkout, their revenue lines are just so much higher. So payments is no longer just an expense item, but a true revenue enabler.
Umar Farooq: We move on average something like $12 trillion a day, and at one point we even hit 17 trillion as I think our highest record day this year, which means that in a little bit more than a week, maybe a week and a half or so at that level, we are managing to flow the entire world's GDP through our pipes.
Max Neukirchen: And I think no matter if it's 12 trillion, 13 trillion or 17 trillion, we sometimes try to illustrate what it actually means. What is also important, it comes with a huge responsibility for us running a business that is so important ultimately to the global economy that the things we care about, stability, resiliency and trust are really important given that we know how many companies, individuals, and even whole countries rely on that service.
Umar Farooq: So as I think about our time in this business, and Max, both you and I have been in this business for a number of years now, we've seen some significant shifts in the overall payments landscape. We have seen an increasing level of digitization, frankly, I would say over the last decade or two, you've seen multiple countries go from a very cash-heavy society to an extremely digitized money society. So if you think about China was probably one of the original pioneers more than a decade ago, but then you have India and Brazil, Mexico, other countries. We see increasing digitization. That's been one of the huge tailwinds for our business because we are not a sort of coin and cash operator in many of these countries. And the other thing from my point of view is also the evolution of rails, whether that means going from what used to be batch-based rails or overnight processing rails to real-time processing systems in most of the big countries in the world, and then now even other rails like crypto-based rails, DLT-based rails. I feel these have been some very interesting developments that have really come together to make our business even stronger and bigger than it used to be.
Max Neukirchen: I agree, Umar. And just to add a little bit to this, I do think payments have definitely gotten faster over the last decade or so where there's now a real expectation that money can move real time almost anywhere in the world. And it is a big change for how we run the business because you no longer have downtimes to upgrade your technologies, but you truly need to be on twenty four seven, 365. And you also need to provide different client service because money is literally moving all the time, including on the weekends and including at nights.
Umar Farooq: And Max, can I play back one of your quotes to you by the way, because I think I'll give you credit for this quote that with real-time payments comes real-time fraud. And so while we've seen a speeding up of payments and many of these trends, I think there are also some unfortunate negative trends, which is just like payments have become faster, more digitized, more real-time, fraud has also become faster, more digitized, more real-time. And I think that's also somewhere where players like JP Morgan payments come in, where the infrastructure we have built basically based on everything from what used to be machine learning and now much more AI driven that detects fraud and prevents fraud and actually saves our clients hundreds of millions of dollars a year. I think that's another big differentiating factor for our business.
Max Neukirchen: I would add maybe one more. That is also the increased global integration that we see in payments. Because over the last 10 years there's been a lot of discussions around what is the end of globalization, but we see tremendous growth even in cross-border flows, in new trade flows developing, which is exciting and is also a key foundation for some of the investments we are making in order to broaden our footprint and help our clients operate in even more countries.
Umar Farooq: In my mind, when you look at many of these shifts, I do think businesses are still not fully getting their minds around I think both the globalization point, the complexity point and how important it is to actually operate with a large player that can provide them services across the world, but then also coming back to the original sort of fraud prevention and other sorts of complexities that come with payments. And I think obviously it's a learning cycle, but I feel businesses are still on that journey and we are helping them understand it in many ways, including reaching out to them and helping them understand how to fight fraud in an age of AI.
Max Neukirchen: Another example is a benefit of ultimately broad reach. We see a few hundred million accounts every month, including also accounts where fraudulent activity happens. Now through such a broad network, we can then share that information with our clients and help them avoid being attacked by fraudsters. We already saw this year more fraud attempts on our clients' money than all of last year, and that is a trend that continues. I think a second big piece of feedback is still around operational processes. Think about onboarding, KYC, document management. These are all still important parts of our clients' day-to-day lives as they open accounts, move money, and it continues to be a pain point.
Umar Farooq: And I think Max, I would actually reemphasize one point you made, which is the scale and the reach. Payments is one of those businesses. I think the more scale you have, the more data you have, the better you can do for clients, whether it's fraud or money movement or other services, frankly. And I think we now are, as we embark on the next step of this journey, especially as AI becomes an evermore present tool at the backend, front end, middle office, our scale will enable us to actually optimize.
Max Neukirchen: And I think your point about AI is also well taken, and I wouldn't say that the industry is underestimating AI, but it's still very hard to grasp how payments and how the global financial infrastructure will change with AI because intelligent payments powered through AI ultimately mean that a lot of the tasks that treasurers, CFOs, payments professionals do today can be enhanced or improved with new AI tools. A lot of discussions happens around agentic treasury, agentic commerce, to really think about how do companies and individuals change their buying behavior and how do also payments flow differently as a result of that.
Umar Farooq: And I think one thing, Max, I would add is again to something we discuss all the time, the innovation in the space is another thing clients don't really struggle with, but they're trying to make sense of. There's a lot of real change. There's a lot of marketing around changes. There's a lot of people out there, especially smaller companies that are telling them there's different ways of doing things, whether that's based on distributor ledger rails or some AI system that someone has just created. So I think the clients are also sort of coming to us and asking us how should this separate signal from the noise? Because it does seem like noise is quite high.
Max Neukirchen: It's a great point, Umar. And I do think clients wonder what does it mean for them and what do they need to do versus where can they partner with us to take advantage of all these new technologies and capabilities?
Umar Farooq: I mean, as I've spoken to clients, I think over the last three to five years, clearly clients now see a lot more options in how they operate their businesses. Everything from core rails that have evolved to digitization of money, to frankly, offerings like embedded finance, which is again, a big product for us and how they can bring that into their platforms. These are all things that are top of mind for clients.
Max Neukirchen: To add to what you said, we have seen many clients now have payments as a topic for the CEO and the board, not only for the CFO and the treasurer, how it was historically. Why is that? Payments does drive revenues, payments creates new business opportunities. Umar, you mentioned embedded finance, embedded payments. A lot of clients look to create whole ecosystems by having their customers captive in their platform and payments is a critical part of it, driving key revenues and key client engagement. And I think we've really seen a big shift in terms of the level where payments is on the agenda for many of our clients. Real-time payments and instant money movement has definitely been a key trend in payments around the world for the last 10 years. We now have instant money schemes basically in almost every economy and it comes with real implications. Umar, you mentioned already fraud as a key concern in that space because every fraudster can also move money out real time. So the question about safety and resiliency is much more front end, but it also changes how we operate our business given that we are always on and need to have a infrastructure and technology platform that is actually able to process tremendous volumes and numbers of payments within a short period of time.
Umar Farooq: I fully agree, Max. And I think on top of that, it's not just a consumer question, but a lot of businesses we serve by definition interact with consumers as their end customers or as participants in their ecosystem. Let's say you're running an e-commerce platform, you ultimately have consumers in that e-commerce platform. So a lot of our even large business clients are coming to us to actually build solutions that enable real-time money movement for consumers within their platform or as they push out payments to sellers across the world, et cetera. And so there's a lot of emphasis on now a real-time money movement capability, both within their platform, outside their platform across geographies, and also doing so with full resiliency, stability, and fraud prevention as you talked about.
Max Neukirchen: And what I find interesting is that a lot of the innovation around real-time payments has also happened truly around the world. I think Pix in Brazil is a great example of a real-time payment scheme with tremendous growth that innovated and pioneered the QR codes. We have seen the same as UPI in India, real-time payments infrastructure, and that has created a tremendous round of adjacent industries as well. We have seen it in ASEAN, we've seen it in Europe and also in the US. It's really interesting to see how that has as a global trend reshaped the payments industry.
Umar Farooq: I think technologies generally try to solve the same problem, Max. They don't try to solve new problems. At the end of the day, if you really think about what customers want, they want faster, better, cheaper, almost in any product category. So even when it comes to new technologies like tokenization, like blockchain, ultimately they're trying to solve the very same kind of problems for our end clients. Can you move money in a smarter way? Can you move money instantly? Can you move money with instant settlement, for instance? So all these technologies are trying to really aim at that problem because if you really think about it, when we move money globally, and again, you and I both being practitioners in this space, we know there are cutoffs, there are country infrastructures. They don't really talk to each other very well, for instance, real-time payments infrastructures across many countries. So how do you enable a dollar or a euro or any currency to move from one country to another country instantly for effects to happen instantly, for delivery and settlement to happen instantly? And I think all of those are problems that tokenization, blockchain, other technologies are trying to solve. And then on top of that, they bring obviously unique capabilities like programmability or settlement of other assets in an atomic fashion. So I think it's both solving existing problems, but frankly, also solving problems of the future.
Max Neukirchen: I think you raised some great points there, Umar, and maybe to just add a few examples of client needs that blockchain solutions can help solve. Imagine you are a client in the Middle East and you want to move money on Sundays. Still not that easy today. Blockchain can help. Or imagine you want to move money after hours at 8:00 PM, 9:00 PM, you are a treasurer with operations in 20 countries, not so easy today, blockchain can help. So there's a bunch of really tangible use cases that can now be better addressed with the Kinnexus solutions that we have developed.
Umar Farooq: And I would even add, I think on top of that now, if you go into the securities world, and I know we are obviously on the payment side, but on every securities transaction, there's always a payments lag. So we always joke about how you can do payments by themselves, but you almost cannot transfer anything else without the payment involved. So if you think about securities transactions, what blockchain allows you to do with the infrastructure we have built is you can actually transact in securities that are tokenized because the two legs get executed at the same time. So there's these new capabilities that I think are still nascent. We've scaled them quite a bit, but they're still nascent compared to existing rails. And I think we are quite excited about the future of this technology. I think clients should be looking to their partners in payments to help them navigate a world that is much quicker, much more real time, much more intelligent, whether it's because of AI or other tools, and frankly has many more choices of rails and many more choices of infrastructure. And how can a player that they partner with, someone like JP Morgan Payments, bring them that entire globe, help them move their money, store their money, utilize their money in the most efficient and effective way, and frankly, be ready for any innovation that's going to come their way, whether that be distributed ledger technologies or AI to make their company ever more successful.
Max Neukirchen: I fully agree, Umar. And when it comes to the question, what should clients expect from their payments partner, I will always come back to the three areas that we look to deliver for our clients. One is global connectivity done easy. Supply chains and business is now global, and clients are looking for a partner who is truly making it easy for them to operate and have business in so many countries, which is one of the key things that we promise to our clients. The second one is around innovation. You said it earlier very well. Clients are thinking about what does the innovation mean for them? And they look for a partner who can help them navigate innovative new technologies such as blockchain, such as AI, such as biometrics, such as real-time payments and make it usable for them. And then the third thing is clients are looking for stability and resiliency with all the fraud activity, cyber attacks, and uncertainties out there. Also from a macroeconomic standpoint, they want a reliable, stable partner with a fortress balance sheet that can help them basically manage all these uncertainties.
Umar Farooq: Max, I think that's a great place for us to wrap up. Thank you so much for joining us.
Max Neukirchen: Umar, it was great to spend some time with you talking about payments.
[End of episode]

This podcast was recorded on August 24, 2026.

Payments decisions now influence growth, liquidity, and risk — often as much as traditional finance levers. In this episode of Making Sense, co-heads of J.P. Morgan Global Payments Max Neukirchen and Umar Farooq explain how payments became a revenue-enabling capability — and what “trust at scale” requires when clients expect instant, seamless experiences. They cover the move toward real-time rails, the operational demands of always-on infrastructure and the new fraud landscape where threats accelerate with speed. They also detail how data and AI-driven controls help safeguard transactions without adding friction. Looking forward, they discuss intelligent payments and embedded finance, and how blockchain and tokenization — including Kinexys — could modernize cross-border settlement and expand the window for global money movement beyond market hours.

The complexity and urgency of the world’s challenges require meaningful collaboration among members of the development community and other stakeholders if the goal of ending poverty on a livable planet is to be realized. With overlapping crises threatening global development and a growing global demand for a bold and coordinated response to these crises, the World Bank is working to strengthen partnerships and utilize every resource available to maximize development impact.The Bank works with a growing array of development partners, both traditional and non-traditional, formal, and informal, to help meet our shared goals. From the ongoing partnership with our sovereign donors, through engagement with foundations and civil society, to an increased focus on leveraging private capital, the Bank recognizes how transformative partnerships can be when new ideas, perspectives, and experiences are combined with the necessary financial resources.Development partners work with the Bank through trust funds, financial intermediary funds, and co-financing arrangements:to align and pool funding support with other development partners within agreed strategic frameworks.to benefit from the Bank’s convening power, at both the international and country level, to maximize coordinated action and achieve impact at scale.to benefit from the Bank's extensive technical expertise, country experience and supervision capacity, its financial control framework, and its ability to monitor and report on results.to provide grant funding in fragile, conflict-affected, and other complex situations enabling the Bank to engage and provide critical assistance in circumstances where traditional instruments are not well-suited.to support innovative or emerging policy areas, which the Bank and Partners view as a priority.Trust FundsThe World Bank uses trust funds, a financing arrangement set up with contributions from one or more development partners, to complement core funding from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), and the International Development Association (IDA) to help attain its institutional goals. Trust funds support the achievement of these goals by providing financial resources, contributing to the knowledge agenda, and leveraging the Bank’s convening power and global and local presence to contribute to country, regional, and global development. Trust funds allow the Bank to mobilize and direct concessional resources to strategic development priorities and to mobilize the resources and capabilities of other development actors through partnership programs.Financial Intermediary FundsFinancial Intermediary Funds (FIFs) are financial arrangements that leverage a variety of public and private resources in support of international initiatives, enabling the international community to provide a direct and coordinated response to global priorities. FIFs are a key financing arrangement for the World Bank, where the Bank acts as a trustee of large multilateral financial mechanism to support global development initiatives and partnerships. As a FIF trustee, the World Bank provides financial services, including receiving, holding, and investing contributed funds, and transferring them when instructed by the FIF governing body.Co-FinancingCo-financing is an important financing mechanism of the World Bank. The World Bank works with Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs), bilateral agencies, and other development partners to allow funds to flow directly from co-financers to the recipient client country and finance activities within the scope of a World Bank operation. Under these arrangements, World Bank resources and third-party resources are deployed in a coordinated manner to World Bank operations that are led by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) or the International Development Association (IDA).

articles.text:
ETF Corner series

The Next Frontier in ETF Technology: The Convergence of Servicing and Trading

As ETFs scale toward USD 30 trillion, the next advantage is the connected infrastructure behind them — not the wrapper itself.

alarm

6 minutes read

calendar_today

23 Oct, 2026

Note: Adapted from a recent BNY Consultant Webinar Series session, this article summarizes perspectives shared by BNY specialists from Asset Servicing and Markets on ETF market trends, growth opportunities and evolving operating models.

Key Takeaways

Global ETF assets are projected to exceed USD 30 trillion by 2030, driven by active ETFs and fund conversions1.The primary market — not the wrapper — is where the ETF operating model is now being tested.Cross-border growth demands multidimensional connectivity across settlement cycles, currencies, venues and counterparties.FX execution timing directly drives tracking quality; treating it as an afterthought compounds variance over time.

The global ETF market is growing rapidly and becoming more complex. Assets, flows, product launches and investor adoption continue to reach new milestones, while the product set expands beyond traditional passive exposures into active, options-based, fixed income, digital asset, alternatives and multi-asset strategies. In a recent BNY webinar, our experts highlighted that global ETF assets are expected to exceed USD 30 trillion by 2030, with active ETFs, fund conversions and precision portfolio construction among the key forces driving growth.

But as ETFs scale, the conversation is shifting. It is no longer enough to ask whether an investment strategy can be put into an ETF wrapper. The more important question is whether that ETF can operate efficiently in the market every day, across primary and secondary market activity, across currencies, venues, counterparties and settlement cycles.

That is where ETF technology and automation are becoming central to the next phase of market development. The ETF industry has long focused on the investor-facing benefits of the wrapper: transparency, liquidity, tax efficiency, access and cost. Less discussed is the technology infrastructure that underpins the primary market, where issuers, authorized participants (APs), market makers, service providers, trading desks and FX providers must connect efficiently.

Did You Know?
BNY’s ETF platform, ETX, supports more than 2,600 funds, more than 70 ETF issuers, over USD 4 trillion in ETF assets under administration and more than 4,400 daily baskets created2.
BNY also services hundreds of new ETFs annually, with more than 14 million trades originated and settled across the platform.
Read more about ETF

For BNY, this is an increasingly important area of investment and differentiation. “The main takeaway is that the ETF industry is hitting record highs across virtually every metric we track,” said Ben Slavin, ETF Global Industry Head at BNY. “We're seeing accelerating adoption globally, continued momentum in active ETFs, growing interest in ETF share class structures, and innovation across asset classes. Taken together, these trends point to an industry that is not only growing but entering a new phase of scale and maturity.”
The challenge now is how to make that scale work operationally.

The ETF Wrapper Is Evolving, and So Is the Operating Model

ETFs are often described as simple, transparent and efficient. For investors, that can be true. But behind the scenes, ETFs are operationally sophisticated market structure products.

As Bob Humbert, Global ETF Product Head at BNY, explained: "The best way to think about ETF servicing is that it sits at the intersection of capital markets, portfolio management and fund services." Increasingly, the industry's focus is shifting from individual functions to how those functions are connected. BNY’s ETX was designed around that principle, bringing together issuers, APs, market makers, exchanges and servicing providers in a single ecosystem that helps transform investment ideas into tradable ETF products.

That connectivity matters because ETF growth brings new operating demands. Active strategies may require more customized baskets. Options-based products can introduce additional trading and settlement complexity. Cross-border ETFs may involve multi-currency execution, multiple settlement cycles and fragmented liquidity. Emerging market exposures can create specific challenges around valuation windows, liquidity timing and FX benchmarking. Issuers are also exploring dual share classes, digital assets, alternatives and more complex multi-asset exposures.

ETX: Built for Scale, Built for ETFs
ETX is BNY's ETF technology platform, bringing together portfolio construction, basket management, AP and market maker connectivity, execution workflows and servicing capabilities in a single ecosystem. ETX helps issuers, APs and market makers operate more efficiently, with a focus on smoother execution, enhanced transparency and scalability across the ETF operating model.

“ETX’s goal is to remove friction and bring together the people, workflows and infrastructure required to support ETFs at scale,” said Humbert, adding that technology will increasingly be judged not by individual features, but by how effectively it connects the ETF ecosystem.

Primary Market Technology: The Less Visible Engine of ETF Efficiency
Technology that helps Authorized Participants operate more effectively can improve execution, support liquidity and enhance the investor experience. Innovations such as BNY’s ETF Directed Trading illustrate how continued advances in primary market infrastructure can help APs gain greater visibility into execution economics, streamline cash-order workflows and exercise more control over the creation/redemption process, ultimately supporting a more efficient and resilient ETF ecosystem.

From ETF Servicing to Connected Infrastructure

As ETFs evolve, success will increasingly depend on connecting servicing, trading, liquidity and distribution. The industry is moving beyond standalone servicing models toward more integrated platforms that connect portfolio construction, basket management, execution, AP workflows, FX and post-trade operations in a seamless manner
“A lot of friction is generated when ETF flow has to transition to traditional OMS/EMS stacks,” said Humbert. “It creates inefficiencies not only for issuers but also for APs and market makers.”
This is where ETX and BNY's broader ecosystem come into play. By connecting ETF servicing, markets, distribution via BNY Pershing, FX, transfer agency and execution capabilities through a common platform, the firm is focused on reducing friction across the ETF lifecycle and helping clients move more efficiently from investment concept to market execution.
“Our vision is centred on building the infrastructure needed to support the next phase of ETF growth,” added Slavin. “Helping issuers and liquidity providers scale more efficiently, improving connectivity across the ecosystem and supporting innovation as markets continue to evolve.”
As ETFs become more trading-intensive and liquidity-sensitive, servicing technology is increasingly expected to support front-office outcomes, linking operations, execution and liquidity in a more seamless way. It is not simply about launching more funds. It is about making them work efficiently at scale.

Buy-Side Trading Solutions: Execution Expertise Inside the ETF Workflow

"BTS brings institutional trading expertise into an ETF ecosystem where execution quality, liquidity access and market structure matter”, explains Dragan Skoko, Head of Buy-Side Trading Solutions at BNY.
For ETF issuers, that means helping connect portfolio implementation, AP engagement, market-maker interaction and execution workflows. Whether supporting newer entrants building ETF operating capabilities or established issuers expanding across jurisdictions, asset classes or more complex exposures, BTS can help market participants navigate liquidity and execution considerations while supporting each fund’s investment objective. Ultimately, ETF technology is not just about automation; it is about embedding market expertise into the workflow so issuers can scale efficiently and with greater control.

FX: The Hidden Lever in ETF Performance

FX is another area where ETF automation and market connectivity can have a meaningful impact. For issuers operating across multiple markets, currencies and liquidity pools, FX has become an important component of the ETF operating model. "The U.S. market is larger and more centralized, while European markets are more cross-border, multi-currency, multi-venue and operationally intensive”, Skoko noted.
Prashant Chandrashekar, FX Product Manager at BNY, described FX as becoming more instrumental within the investment process. “ETFs are becoming increasingly global, which then means FX plays a larger role in the overall global portfolio, performance of the ETF,” he said. He noted that investors and issuers are paying closer attention to performance attribution and currency impacts.
The timing of FX execution is particularly important. Where an ETF holds international securities, those securities may be valued at specific fixing windows. If the related FX trade is executed hours or days later at a different rate, the fund may carry unintended currency exposure. That slippage can compound into tracking variance over time.
Execution timing and workflow integration can directly affect tracking outcomes. It also reinforces why FX can no longer be treated as an operational afterthought. Chandrashekar describes BNY FX Plus’s slippage mitigation feature as a core benefit to address an on-going industry challenge and support more efficient currency execution
This is the practical value of ETF tech: making it easier to execute with a service provider by connecting servicing and markets capabilities in one workflow.

The Next Frontier: ETFs Built for Scale, Speed and Precision

The ETF market has always been shaped by innovation, but the next frontier may be less about the wrapper itself and more about the infrastructure behind it.
Tech and automation will be central to this next chapter. For issuers, the opportunity is to bring products to market with greater speed and control. For APs, it is to manage execution more efficiently. For market makers, it is to quote with better information. For investors, it is to access ETFs that trade and track more effectively.
As Skoko put it, what comes next is “tighter and tighter integration with the rest of the BNY ecosystem” to make it easier for issuers and APs to achieve efficiencies.

That integration is at the heart of the ETF technology story. It is not automation for its own sake. It is automation designed to connect the ETF ecosystem, from servicing to trading, from basket to execution, from FX to settlement, and from product idea to market outcome.
For an ETF industry scaling toward its next major milestone, that connected infrastructure may be one of the most important competitive advantages of all.

T+1 Raises the Stakes for Automation
As settlement windows shrink, firms have less tolerance for manual processes, fragmented systems and operational inefficiencies. The shift is reinforcing the importance of connected operating models that link execution, FX, settlement and fund operations seamlessly across the ETF ecosystem.
Read more: Europe's move to T+1: Implications for ETF servicing models

For more insights about ETFs, visit BNY’s ETF Corner, one destination for ETF market intelligence and expertise.
