Column 2 shows that Treasury coupon buybacks reduce dealer balance sheet constraints with respect to VaR usage. A $1 billion increase in Treasury buybacks implies a decrease of 0.5 percentage points on the same day and a decrease of 0.4 percentage points the following day (column 5). These magnitudes control for MOVE and are in addition to effects of Treasury issuance.

In column 3, we add in long (settled) positions as a control.12 Not surprisingly, the magnitude of the effect of Treasury issuance decreases somewhat after adding in Treasury positions, since the two are strongly related. However, the coefficient remains statistically significant at the 1 percent level, implying a 1.2 percentage point increase in mean VaR usage for every $100 billion increase in Treasury issuance (column 3). Adding in long positions also notably increases the magnitude of the effect of Treasury buybacks – every $1 billion increase in buybacks implies a 1.3 percentage point decrease in VaR usage.

Though not shown, the results are similar and robust when we use issuance dates for Treasury bills and coupons issuance instead of auction dates.

Overall, these results show a significant effect of Treasury issuance on VaR usage, a risk-based constraint that dealers face at the trading-desk level that can limit their intermediation capacity in the Treasury market.13

Implications for increased Treasury issuance

We find that dealer balance sheets expand around Treasury issuance, as demand for dealer market-making and repo intermediation rises. Although the immediate increases in dealer positions are typically quite short-lived, persisting for about 3-5 days on average, they have a measurable impact on dealers' risk-based constraints, as measured by VaR. These constraints become more binding during periods of elevated market volatility. Moreover, the effects of Treasury issuance on demand for financing appear more persistent, leading to a more sustained increase in dealer balance sheets. Overall, our findings suggest that upcoming increases in Treasury issuance will contribute to increased pressures on dealer balance sheets, which warrant monitoring.

This paper examines what's driving the current rearmament cycle, where capital is flowing, and what it means for the global economy.Download the ReportGlobal rearmament is reshaping industrial policies and drawing new sectors into the defense economy, with far-reaching implications for businesses and investors. Geopolitical competition, active conflict, technological innovation, and a widening definition of national security are driving a supercycle of investment.
This shift is about more than just increased military spending. Cheap unmanned systems are changing the economics of warfare, and capital is flowing to defense tech start-ups alongside established contractors. Governments and companies are turning to cross-border partnerships and industrial policy to expand production.
The focus on security is also lifting other segments of the industrial economy, such as advanced manufacturing and energy technology. Dual-use technologies are finding commercial applications beyond the battlefield, from drones for critical infrastructure inspection to distributed power systems for military and civilian users.
Going forward, defense is poised to become a pillar of industrial policy and economic strategy. As governments prioritize resilience, the strongest opportunities in the supercycle will capture a readiness premium, rewarding businesses whose scare capabilities deliver the assured capacity that customers must structurally maintain across cycles.
Learn more about how the security supercycle is reshaping global defense investment in our latest report.

articles.title: Understanding Trump's tariff reversals
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Understanding Trump's tariff reversals

Gary Clyde Hufbauer (PIIE) and

Katelyn Hetrick (PIIE)

Date
October 27, 2026 12:15 PM

Photo Credit: REUTERS/Carlos Barria

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
President Donald Trump has pitched tariffs to address varied US economic and national security concerns, while also generating revenues. And shortly after taking office in early 2025, he ordered a flurry of new tariffs on nearly all countries. But he also quickly eased or abandoned many of them. This process of imposing and reversing tariffs produced four major types of results, in rough chronological order: stabilization of financial markets, concessions from foreign governments, corporate investment pledges, and lower US consumer prices on some items.
The combined economic effects of reversals are unclear at this point, but to get a rough sense of their relative potential importance, we estimated the hypothetical annual tariff revenues the United States would have collected if each initial tariff threat had been implemented for a year. This measure provides a common basis for comparing the scale of tariff threats and the concessions or reversals that followed. By that measure, the biggest tariff threats served as negotiating leverage for foreign economic concessions, as seen in table 1 below.

Annualized revenue forgone is estimated by multiplying 2024 imports of the affected goods by the reduction in the tariff rate (peak rate minus the rate after the pause or deal). Revenue collected is estimated by dividing 2024 imports of the affected goods by 366 to get a daily import value, as there were 366 days in 2024. That figure is then multiplied by the number of days the additional tariff was in effect and by the difference between the original tariff rate and the peak rate under the collection window. Both figures are static estimates based on 2024 import values and do not account for changes in trade volumes, product exemptions, or the timing of duty payments.

Sources: PIIE calculations of United States International Trade Commission, UN Comtrade, US Census, US Bureau of Economic Analysis, Congressional Budget Office, and Federal Register data.

Financial turmoil
Soon after Trump announced(link is external) new tariffs on April 2, 2025—which he dubbed "Liberation Day"(link is external)—he backtracked on some, with the effect of arresting a stock market rout. On April 2, he had ordered a universal baseline 10 percent tariff on nearly all imports to take effect immediately, and he threatened additional "reciprocal" tariffs on individual trading partners to reflect their bilateral merchandise trade surpluses with the United States, to take effect April 9. During the week following that announcement, the S&P 500 plunged more than 12 percent(link is external) while yields on 10-year Treasury notes spiked about half of 1 percentage point.(link is external)
On April 9, Trump paused the "reciprocal" tariffs for 90 days (a period that was later extended) but kept the baseline 10 percent tariff. Stock and bond markets rallied. If all the threatened "reciprocal" tariffs had taken full effect, they would have generated annual US tariff revenue of $262.7 billion, assuming US import volumes and prices did not change in response (the same assumption applies to the subsequent calculations below).
Negotiating leverage
Tariffs are often withdrawn or lowered to press for concessions by a trading partner. Threatened tariffs on imports from China are exhibit A in the use of negotiating leverage. On April 9, 2025, after pausing the "reciprocal" tariffs announced on Liberation Day, Trump threatened an additional tariff of 125 percent on imports from China, worth an annualized $495.7 billion. Beijing quickly retaliated. The massive threatened tariffs jeopardized the global economy. Thus, on May 12, 2025, the United States and China agreed to reduce these tariffs for 90 days to 10 percent on the United States and to 30 percent on China but left in place other US tariffs on China.
On Liberation Day, Trump threatened a 27.5 percent "reciprocal" tariff on the United Kingdom. In June 2025, the United States agreed(link is external) to reduce this tariff to 10 percent on 100,000 auto imports annually. It also agreed to eliminate the baseline 10 percent tariff on civil aircraft and set a future most-favored-nation quota on steel and aluminum components. In turn, the United Kingdom enlarged market access for US meat and ethanol exports. Before they were withdrawn, the threatened US Liberation Day tariffs on UK autos and aircraft amounted to $1.7 billion.[1]
The United States threatened to impose a 20 percent "reciprocal tariff" on the European Union. On July 27, 2025, Trump met European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen at his golf course in Turnberry, Scotland, and agreed on a framework for US-EU trade and investment. He implemented the framework for the United States with a September 2025 executive order(link is external). EU implementation is working its way through the EU Parliament. Combined US tariffs on the European Union were capped at 15 percent. In turn, the European Union agreed to eliminate tariffs on US industrial exports; give US seafood and agricultural exports preferential access; procure US energy, artificial intelligence (AI), and semiconductor exports; and invest $600 billion in US projects over three years. Threatened US tariffs on autos before the Turnberry deal amounted to $6.3 billion annualized.
Late in July 2025, the United States and Japan reached a framework agreement, recorded in a September 2025 memorandum of understanding(link is external). The 24 percent US Liberation Day tariffs on Japan were generally capped at 15 percent, but separate tariffs of 50 percent on steel, aluminum, and copper remained in place. In turn, Japan agreed to invest $550 billion in US projects, buy 100 Boeing aircraft, increase its rice imports by 75 percent, and buy $8 billion of other US agricultural products. Before the July 2025 deal, threatened tariffs on auto imports from Japan amounted to $5.2 billion annualized.
Also late in July 2025, the United States and South Korea reached a framework agreement(link is external), finalized in October 2025. The threatened 25 percent US Liberation Day tariffs on Korea were capped at 15 percent, but other tariffs remained in place. Korea agreed to invest $350 billion in approved US projects. Threatened tariffs on imports from Korea amounted to $20.3 billion annualized.
Negotiating leverage with Canada remains a continuing saga. On an annualized basis, threatened US tariffs amount to $1.3 billion.
Industrial subsidies
The Global Trade Alert(link is external) recently uncovered a fresh avenue for tariff reversals: reduce or eliminate tariffs on imports by US firms that make approved commitments to invest in US plants. Between April and August 2026, executive orders authorized the secretary of commerce to negotiate company-specific tariffs to address what the Trump administration identified as national security threats under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. The administration imposed or threatened new duties on pharmaceuticals, aluminum, polysilicon derivatives, and drones. The government struck agreements with several companies under this authority but has not disclosed the terms. US imports of the specified items amounted to $264 billion in 2025. Threatened tariffs on aluminum, before the reversals, amounted to roughly $5.8 billion annualized.
Consumer prices
After more than five years of high inflation, Americans are sensitive to any policy that stretches household budgets. Serious research shows that tariffs are almost entirely paid by US households and business firms, not by foreign exporters.
Trump's executive order(link is external) issued November 14, 2025, exempted from all Liberation Day tariffs a range of tropical products plus beef, oranges, and tomatoes. The order did not mention consumer prices, but the accompanying White House fact sheet(link is external) did. On an annualized basis, the threatened tariffs amounted to $2.9 billion before they were reversed.
In August 2026, Trump announced(link is external) that, for the next three months, up to 100,000 tons per month of ground beef could enter the US tariff-free, a measure clearly intended(link is external) to provide relief from high prices at the meat counter. Threatened beef tariffs amounted to $2.1 billion annualized.
Summing up
According to these estimates, by far the biggest effect of these tariff threats and reversals was to deliver negotiating coin for concessions by foreign partners. Trump's biggest threatened tariff was on Chinese imports, worth some $496 billion on an annualized basis. Other reversals, with respect to the United Kingdom, European Union, and Japan, brought the total threats under this heading to $509 billion. Collectively, reversals with principal effects other than negotiating leverage addressed threats totaling just $274 billion annualized.
Note
1. Steel and aluminum tariffs are excluded from the estimate of the annualized threatened tariff amount because the US-UK Economic Prosperity Deal did not eliminate or reduce these duties. Rather, the agreement prevented an increase in these tariffs. These duties, therefore, are not counted as an additional tariff burden attributable to the agreement.

As investors reassess the AI trade, attention is shifting towards how the next phase of the cycle could play out across Asia. The region remains central to global AI investment, but changing sentiment is creating a more complex mix of opportunities and risks.
Recorded at the Barclays Asia Forum in Singapore, host Patrick Coffey was joined by JF Mastrangelo, Head of Markets, APAC, to discuss distinct investment cases across the region. They explore how Korea and Taiwan offer different forms of exposure to the AI investment cycle, and how the scale of the semiconductor sector can extend its effects into their wider economies. They also highlight how India’s domestic growth and banking sector could provide diversification beyond the AI infrastructure trade.
The conversation also covers China’s strength in exports, including green technology and AI-related products, and Japan’s combination of domestic growth and exposure to AI manufacturing.
For investors, the discussion highlights the importance of assessing Asia market by market, while remaining mindful of differences in valuation, volatility and sensitivity to the AI cycle.
Listeners can hear more related to this topic:​​

Trump-Xi: Stability without resolution
Pacing the Frontier: What’s next for AI?
Opportunities in Asian Equities
Japan: Why the world is watching

Clients can read more on Barclays Live:​​

Thinking Macro: SVB Redux?
AI in China: From AI investment to adoption​
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company: Confidence growing
Positioning for AI Disruption: The Next Phase of Enterprise Adoption

​

Transcript

Patrick Coffey 00:00
Think about what's driving your investments right now. AI, currencies, interest rates, geopolitics. At the centre of all of those stories is what's happening here in Asia. I'm Patrick Coffey. This is the Barclays Brief. It's Thursday, the 22nd of October and we're live from Singapore at the Barclays Asia Forum. I'm excited today to talk to JF Mastrangelo, our Head of APAC Markets. JF, thank you so much for being with me today and peeling yourself away from a very busy day at the forum.

JF Mastrangelo 00:30
Hey, Patrick, it's great to have you here in Singapore.

Patrick 00:32
Yeah, it's great. So very busy day. We've got over 1,000 investors and clients here today. What's the buzz? What are people talking to you about? What are investors worried about?

JF 00:40
Look, most of the Asian investors' questions revolved around three main themes. One is AI CapEx and revenues, second is oil prices and central bank policies, and third is fiscal deficits and long duration. And the reality is Asia sits at the centre of all those three themes. Why? Because Asia is the leading manufacturing hub of the world's AI CapEx. Secondly, the region imports a significant share of its energy. And thirdly, the region is mostly sensitive to changes in global liquidity. Now, today if you ask me, I would say that the main question is the AI CapEx. It's really the $1 trillion question that animates people's minds today.

Patrick 01:19
Yeah, definitely. I mean, that's what everyone's talking about here. Let's talk about the obvious trades. Korea and Taiwan are where I want to start because AI CapEx is on everyone's mind right now. Both markets have sold off a lot recently, but not the same as each other. Let's start with Korea. Is the sell-off enough to get investors interested? Are valuations attractive enough right now?

JF 01:40
Look, you're right to say Korea has been the epicentre of the sell-off. The largest two Korean stocks, SK Hynix and Samsung, have sold off 20 to 30% of their value since the start of October. Why is that? Their business is very cyclical based on memory prices, and they have suffered a lot from the negative AI CapEx sentiment since the start of the month. Also, we should look at the flows. The retail support has vanished since the collapse of the leverage ETF, and foreign investors have really sold throughout the year. So Korea trades on air pocket right now, leading to distressed valuations of the stocks, 3 to 4X forward P/Es, which leaves the investors interested by the value, but also wary of volatility. We have seen on some implementations through derivatives.

Patrick 02:25
OK, so derivatives are how people are playing it, but ultimately Korea is cheap, risky, and volatile. What about Taiwan?

JF 02:32
Look, Taiwan is a different story. The business model of the whole Taiwan ecosystem is to export semis that are much more tailored to end user needs compared to memory. So it's much more stable prices, and therefore much more stable investments. Now, TSMC remains the company everyone looks at because it is really the clearing house for AI CapEx. Its leading-edge manufacturing capacities of interest for everyone, you name it, Broadcom, AMD, NVIDIA, Apple, et cetera.

Patrick 03:01
OK. So let's move away from these obvious AI trades of Korea and Taiwan. Say I'm bearish on AI, and clients are becoming increasingly bearish on the AI infrastructure trade as we speak. Where in Asia should I be investing to diversify away from that risk?

JF 03:16
Many investors are going to name India here. First, the Indian IT services are obviously anti-correlated to AI growth, and typically since the start of the month, they've posted double-digit returns. Now, I tend to see India as a macro play. India has a strong population, strong demographics, and also a very high real GDP growth, more than 7% year-on-year recently. And if you want to play India growth, Indian banks are very attractive on a valuation point of view relative to history currently. They have posted large loans year-on-year growth, and some of them double digits. So somehow you don't trade India on chips, you do trade India on their domestic growth. And this is an interesting AI-agnostic investment to make.

Patrick 03:59
OK, so that's the AI-agnostic one. I always think about India through the lens of China and compare the growth rates, and the growth rates have decoupled in the last few years. As you say, very high growth in India, slower growth in China. When you look at China right now, what do you think? Because we've got low inflation, weak domestic consumption, low rates. It's a bit risky, isn't it? Is there any reason to be positive on China right now?

JF 04:22
First, you're absolutely right on the demographics. India and China currently have the same population, 1.4 billion, but one is growing, India, one is decreasing, China. So China has this ageing population problem, which explains why they are so much focussed on technology and productivity, and why they have become the leading force of robotics. China has a pattern that looks a little bit like Japan decades ago. They have this population issue, but also a large domestic savings rate, 40% of the GDP, which gets invested massively in domestic bonds. The Chinese rates are 1.6%. So what is there in China? Well, the reality while the world expects constantly Chinese consumer, the one that keeps surprising is the Chinese producer. China's exports are extremely strong. The latest print was 36% increase year-on-year, thanks to green tech and AI exports. So investors are really constructive about China exports, and therefore they are also constructive on the Yuan, maybe not against US Dollar because of hiking concerns on the US Dollar, but definitely against Euro for all the reasons we know in Europe.

Patrick 05:30
OK, so this idea that you're talking about with China reminding you of Japan a decade or so ago, that's interesting. We should talk about that another time. Let's switch to Japan because here at the Barclays Asia Forum, clients are pretty bullish on Japan, but there is of course, the potential for a lot of Japanese money to move back home. What would a meaningful repatriation of Japanese capital mean for Japanese assets?

JF 05:54
Look, first, you're right, Japan is a booming economy. It has found its way into the leading sector of AI manufacturing alongside Korea and Taiwan. And in a way, Japanese equities are really an investment on Japanese growth with an AI kicker, which is very interesting. Now to your question. This repatriation of assets is driven by one large national pension fund called GPIF, which is actually the biggest in the world. It owns $2 trillion of assets. And it is now quite consensual that they are somehow changing their allocations from US assets into Japanese assets. Japan bonds have rallied significantly on the basis of that expectation. Now to your question, what does it mean for US assets? Let's have some simple maths here. $2 trillion of assets, if you change your allocation by 5%, it's $100 billion of potential outflows from the US. If you compare that to the US Treasury buyback, for instance, it's significant. The buyback is $10 billion of buybacks per month roughly.

Patrick 06:57
OK. So finally, I've got you here. There's a big trade rotation happening in the market. What's your view in Asia? What's happening on the AI CapEx trade? What's your big picture take on how to play that as an investor?

JF 07:09
So look, first, why is AI CapEx, so important for Asia? For me, AI CapEx doesn't only create market leaders on the stock market, it creates national economic growth and wealth effect.

Patrick 07:21
Give me some examples of that.

JF 07:22
Taiwan is a $1 trillion economy, and TSMC as a company is meant to have a 2026 earning of $100 billion, 10% of the GDP. Korea is a $2 trillion economy, and its two largest corporates that we mentioned before will deliver $400 billion of earnings. That's 20% of the GDP. Those are massive numbers that influence not only those companies, but the whole country, the whole society, and the whole macro of those countries.

Patrick 07:51
OK, so those wealth effects will benefit the companies. How should we kind of end this in terms of thinking about the big picture on the AI CapEx trade from here then?

JF 07:58
Look, at the moment, there are the optimistic and the pessimistic on AI CapEx. I tend to sit on the optimistic side. Why? Those are the large picture numbers that help me think about it. The world has more than $100 trillion GDP per year. Corporates returned revenues of more than $30 trillion per year. Is the world going to find a way to pay for AI CapEx for $1 or $2 trillion per year? I would tend to think so. We've discussed about AI CapEx today, but there is so much more to Asia than the, the CapEx. And typically, let's all remember, Asia hosts 60% of the world's growth and also 60% of the population. So there will be many more opportunities across equities, rates and credit, but for that you have to come back next year.

Patrick 08:43
Well, I'll very happily come back. This is an amazing, amazing conference, and it's been great to catch up. JF, thanks for your time.

JF 08:48
Thank you, Patrick.

Patrick 08:49
So it's been great to talk to JF today, and we're in the midst of an AI rotation in markets right now. But standing here in Singapore at the Barclays Asia Forum, we're reminded that markets like Taiwan, Korea, Japan, offer different variations on the AI theme. Of course, many people out there will be bearish on AI. I thought JF's insights on India were particularly interesting around diversifying risk away from the typical AI markets. And finally, when considering investing in Asia, it's just so important to remember how nuanced this market is. So for global investors, they can't keep their eyes away from Asia. Thanks a lot for listening to the Barclays Brief. We'll be back next week with a very special episode, and until then, do hit subscribe.

About the experts

Jean-Francois Mastrangelo

Head of Markets, APAC

Jean-Francois Mastrangelo is Head of Markets, Asia Pacific at Barclays. Based in Hong Kong, he joined Barclays in November 2025, and is responsible for driving growth, fostering innovation, and deepening client engagement across the region. He chairs the APAC Markets Management Team and is a member of the Asia Pacific Executive Forum, Global Markets Management Team, and Global Equities Management Committee.

Jean-Francois brings nearly two decades of experience in global markets, most recently as Head of Equities APAC at Société Générale. His career spans senior leadership roles in Paris and Hong Kong across structuring, trading, and platform development.

articles.title: Lazard’s Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+)
articles.text:
Lazard’s Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+)

Lazard's Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+) analysis was originally developed in 2007 to bring clarity to the evolving cost dynamics of various generation technologies at a time when no industry standard approach existed. It remains a widely cited resource grounded in Lazard's extensive industry expertise and client relationships. This year's report explores key aspects of energy generation, energy storage and system-level considerations while reflecting on developments over the past 12 months.

Access the 2026 LCOE+ Report
Lazard's 2026 LCOE+ report highlights that, despite rising and inflationary cost pressures across all generation technologies, renewables remain the most cost-competitive form of new-build generation on an unsubsidized basis (i.e., without tax subsidies). The report also emphasizes that meeting unprecedented power demand will require both a diverse generation fleet and a thoughtful acceleration of permitting and approval processes. At the same time, rising new-build costs and execution challenges have made replacement capacity more expensive and harder to deliver while load growth drives increased utilization of existing assets, improving their marginal cost relative to new-build LCOEs. Storage costs have also risen this year, reversing recent declines.

Access Lazard's 2026 LCOE+ Report

In today's energy landscape, the relevance of data-driven cost analysis has never been greater. The LCOE+ captures a market defined by unprecedented demand growth, rising costs across every generation technology and an intensifying focus on reliability — making objective, real-world benchmarking more critical than ever for the stakeholders, policymakers and investors shaping the industry's future.

George Bilicic
Managing Director

We’ve entered a speed-to-power era—demand is outpacing supply, costs are climbing across every technology, and value is shifting to whoever can deliver capacity the fastest, renewables remain the lowest-cost and quickest to deploy resource, but meeting this moment will require a diverse generation fleet.

Samuel Scroggins
Managing Director

Ready to talk?

×

The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, and the Bank of Japan are all due to make policy decisions, but the ongoing earnings season is still the key focus this week, says Christian Nolting, the Private Bank’s Global Chief Investment Officer.

Energy prices are also getting plenty of attention, with crude oil climbing above $100 a barrel as the Iran conflict goes on. And though natural-gas costs are a concern as the northern hemisphere nears winter, Christian says it is unlikely that countries will face a risk to their supply. “If it's a very cold winter, then I think the next year will be a bit more tricky on gas prices.”

articles.title: Year-End Charitable Giving: Understanding the New Tax Rules | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
As year-end approaches, charitable giving presents an opportunity to align philanthropic goals with broader wealth and tax planning strategies. Beginning this year, several new tax law changes may affect the tax benefits of charitable contributions. Understanding these changes may help evaluate giving strategies and identify opportunities to optimize tax planning before year-end.

A Charitable Giving Benefit for More Taxpayers

Starting this year, taxpayers who claim the standard deduction can also take advantage of a new deduction for charitable contributions. The annual limit is $1,000 for single taxpayers and $2,000 for married couples filing a joint return. Because most taxpayers do not itemize deductions on their return, this provision creates an opportunity for many households to realize modest tax savings from their charitable giving. Note that only cash contributions to eligible charitable organizations qualify for this deduction. Contributions to supporting organizations, private foundations or donor-advised funds are excluded. Donations of non-cash assets, such as stocks or real property, also do not qualify.

Action step: To benefit from this new deduction, donations still need to be documented. Make sure to keep records and receipts of cash contributions during the year for tax filing purposes, including:

Name of the charitable organization
Date and amount of contribution
Other records such as a bank statement or receipt
For any single contribution of $250 or more, taxpayers must obtain a written acknowledgment from the charitable organization indicating whether any goods or services were provided in exchange for the contribution. If goods or services were provided, the deductible amount generally must be reduced by their value.

A New Hurdle for Charitable Giving Tax Benefits

While the new tax law creates a charitable deduction opportunity for non-itemizers, it also introduces a limitation that may reduce the tax benefits of charitable giving for taxpayers who itemize deductions. Beginning in 2026, taxpayers who itemize charitable contributions can claim a deduction only to the extent their total donations exceed 0.5% of their adjusted gross income (AGI). Consider this example:

Action steps: Taxpayers subject to this new limit may want to consider the following potential options:

For taxpayers age 70 1⁄2 or older, a qualified charitable distribution (QCD) may be a tax-efficient giving strategy. This allows eligible taxpayers to transfer funds directly from an IRA to a qualified charity, excluding donor-advised funds and most private foundations. Rather than claiming an itemized charitable deduction which may be subject to the AGI reduction, the taxpayer generally excludes the distribution from taxable income. This may be especially attractive to those subject to required minimum distributions (RMDs) who are not relying on those withdrawals to meet current income needs.
Lumping charitable contributions into a single tax year may help some taxpayers exceed the 0.5% of AGI threshold and maximize their itemized charitable deduction. If the AGI threshold is not met, an itemized deduction is not allowed. A donor-advised fund can be a useful tool for implementing this strategy while allowing grants to be distributed to charities over time.

articles.title: Daily: Build resilience as tech volatility rises
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Video: Why China's equity markets have lagged (6 mins)Thought of the dayMarket sentiment came under pressure on Friday as tech earnings raised fresh concerns about capital expenditure. Stocks in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan fell after a tech-led selloff on Wall Street, while Nasdaq futures were pointing 2% lower ahead of the US market open on Friday. Signs that the US may resume military strikes against Iran also pushed oil prices higher, with Brent crude trading at around USD 117/bbl at the time of writing.But further volatility does not make retreating from markets an effective way to protect portfolios from potential drawdowns, in our view. We continue to see scope for equity gains overall and believe investors should focus on building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech.AI demand remains robust, but we see a rising risk of mid-cycle capex indigestion. Weaker-than-expected growth in megacap tech companies’ core businesses was at the center of investors’ concerns, as markets questioned how the next phase of AI capex would be funded amid continued signals of higher spending from hyperscalers. We are seeing a shift in the funding mix for AI investment after four years of relying on hyperscalers’ cash flows, with incremental capex increasingly drawing on debt, equity, leases, and supplier-backed financing. In our view, the health of underlying demand remains a key metric to watch. Latest results showing accelerating cloud revenue growth and expanding advanced orders for cloud computing capacity point to still-robust demand for AI infrastructure, but we acknowledge the rising risk of mid-cycle capex indigestion, as financing and execution risks are emerging in the more capital-intensive areas of the AI buildout.Resilient growth underpins opportunities beyond US tech. The US economy expanded at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, ahead of the 3.1% estimate and up from 2.2% in the second quarter. This growth has helped keep inflation elevated, but the economy’s resilience also supports the outlook for sectors beyond tech. In fact, the equal-weighted S&P 500 has outperformed its market capitalization-weighted counterpart year to date, suggesting that an improving cyclical backdrop, healthy consumer spending, and structural trends—such as the growing longevity industry—are also supporting market performance. Outside the US, robust earnings growth across the Eurozone and Asia gives investors a broader range of opportunities to participate in potential further equity gains.Quality bonds can help stabilize portfolios. As equities have come under pressure, bonds have rallied, with the 10-year US Treasury yield falling by 37 basis points in October. This shows that quality fixed income is once again serving as a portfolio stabilizer, and we believe still-elevated yields provide sufficient income to compensate for the risk of potential yield volatility. Bonds could also benefit if inflation moderates or economic growth weakens, adding valuable diversification to portfolios.So, with cash unlikely to overcome the combined portfolio challenges of inflation, taxes, longer lifespans, and withdrawals, staying invested remains critical for the long term. Within tech, we continue to like leading megacaps, defensive names in payment networks and consumer electronics, as well as quality semis and hardware companies. But those with an outsized allocation to US tech should diversify across sectors and regions. We also believe investors should maintain a well-diversified portfolio that includes exposure to quality fixed income. Those willing and able to tolerate relevant risks can consider broad commodities and hedge funds to access additional return drivers.

By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

Away from European bond markets, the major story for equity markets has been renewed volatility in emerging market (EM) semiconductor and technology hardware stocks. An index of these companies has dropped back towards the lows of late July, though they are still 1.8% above that level. This leaves them 28% below the July peak but with a year-to-date gain of 47%.

Listen to the article

Play00:0003:19Volume

While the declines from the highs are unfortunate, this level of volatility should not be surprising. Estimates of the impact of the artificial intelligence phenomenon on the economy and on corporate profits range widely. This can be seen in the rising standard deviation of estimates for EM tech hardware stocks, which has jumped from 10 at the beginning of the year to 82 today. By contrast, the variation for non-tech stocks has stayed constant at around five (see Exhibit 1).

The consequence of the current high degree of uncertainty is that any marginal information can lead to a big change in the forecast for corporate profits, which can then lead to a big change in the stock price.

The key factor for investors with a longer-term time horizon is that the earnings growth in the years ahead should nonetheless be significantly positive; current forecasts for the next two years are near 90%. If in the end it turns out to be some (modest) percentage greater or less than those forecasts is secondary.

The Hutchins Center Fiscal Impact Measure shows how much local, state, and federal tax and spending policy adds to or subtracts from overall economic growth, and provides a near-term forecast of fiscal policies’ effects on economic activity.

FEDERAL, STATE AND LOCAL FISCAL POLICY AND THE ECONOMY
By Chase Parry, Zixun Tan, and Louise Sheiner
Fiscal policy added 0.4 percentage points to U.S. GDP growth in the third quarter of 2026, according to the Hutchins Center Fiscal Impact Measure (FIM). The FIM translates changes in taxes and spending at the federal, state, and local levels into changes in aggregate demand, showing the effect of fiscal policy on real GDP growth. Real GDP rose at an annual rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, according to the latest government estimate.
Real federal spending—adjusted for the effects of sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve—added 0.5 percentage points to GDP growth in the third quarter while state and local spending subtracted 0.2 percentage points.[1] The combined effect of all other factors—including underlying taxes and tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), transfers, tariffs, and supply side factors—boosted GDP by about 0.1 percentage points. (See the Fiscal Impact Breakdown spreadsheet in the Downloads section.)
We expect fiscal policy to be moderately restrictive over the remainder of 2026, as continuing weakness in government purchases and the effects of tariffs are partially offset by the stimulative effects of the tax cuts in the OBBBA.
In 2027, we project the FIM will become more restrictive as purchases continue to be weak and supply side effects—notably the equipment purchases we assume had been spurred by the CHIPS and Inflation Reduction Acts—turn negative. (Excluding the supply side effects, the FIM would show fiscal policy subtracting about .4 percentage points from GDP growth in 2027, rather than the .7 percentage points shown in our topline number.)
Our forecast assumes current law and does not anticipate new tax or spending legislation. We also assume that tariff rates remain near their second-quarter levels over the forecast horizon. This reflects our expectation that Section 232, 301, and 338 tariffs (invoked against Canada over alleged discrimination against U.S. commerce) will almost fully replace the revenue collected under the IEEPA tariffs.
The FIM tracks the influence of fiscal policy on GDP growth rates. It measures the direct impacts of fiscal policy on demand (including both discretionary fiscal policy and automatic stabilizers) and includes our estimates of the supply-side effects of legislation and uncertainty as well. It does not include fiscal multipliers. For further analysis on the effects of fiscal policy, read our explainer on the impact of federal, state, and local tax and spending policy on the level of GDP since the onset of the pandemic. For more on the FIM, see our methodology ». You can also read our Guide to the FIM »
[1] Oil sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) are recorded as “sales to other sectors” in the GDP accounts, reducing measured federal purchases. However, because these sales do not represent current production, they do not affect GDP and are offset elsewhere in the accounts. SPR sales were lower in Q3 than in Q2, boosting growth in real federal purchases. We did not adjust for these sales in our previous Q2 FIM publication. We now make this adjustment and have revised our Q2 FIM upward.

articles.title: View from the markets: The earnings season has been good, but is it good enough? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

At first blush, there is little to complain about regarding the third-quarter earnings results so far (about half of the companies in the S&P 500 and MSCI Europe have reported). Compared to the third quarter in 2025, profits have risen by 26% for the S&P 500 and by 40%(!) for Europe, with double-digit figures for other major indices, based on data from FactSet (see Exhibit 1). This is well above historical norms.

The worry is that those values are not far off what was expected by analysts, and in one case it was below. Earnings have come in only 2% better than expected for the S&P 500. Typically, earnings surprises (how much better or worse results are versus consensus) run in the 3-4% range. Over the previous few quarters, they were even higher. This quarter few indices have matched that.

The chart shows clearly what the source of the disappointment has been: technology. The surprise for the Nasdaq 100 index is -3% and for emerging market (EM) tech stocks it is -8%. The disappointments in emerging markets were almost entirely driven by tech stocks; results for the other sectors were 1% better.

There are two questions: Are these disappointments surprising and how much do they matter?

Given not only how high expectations have been for technology stocks, and how rapidly the artificial intelligence theme is developing, it is not surprising that companies have reported results that are further off the mark than is typically the case.

Though there has been some disappointment in the short term (which will drive the short-term performance of the stock), the more important consideration for investors is the medium-term outlook (which will determine the stock’s medium-term path).

It is worth recalling that consensus estimates for Nasdaq 100 earnings growth in 2027 is 35% and for emerging market technology stocks it is 39%. Even if actual results are a few percentage points lower, and if valuations do not change significantly, indices would typically appreciate in line with earnings.

Sector drivers

It is not only the tech sector that has boosted EPS (earnings-per-share) growth rates. Higher energy prices have contributed to strong results for indices like MSCI Europe and Russell Value. Excluding the energy sector, earnings growth for MSCI Europe is a (still good) 17%. But even setting aside the gains from tech and higher oil prices, results across other sectors are robust. The automobile industry continues to be a drag on the consumer discretionary sector, but most of the others are seeing high single or double-digit earnings growth (see Exhibit 2).

Whether this broadening in earnings continues, or even accelerates, will partly depend on the rate of adoption of AI technologies. There is already significant anecdotal evidence of companies finding meaningful productivity improvements through AI. One example is insurance companies reducing their claims review times and credit losses by using micro-expression recognition technology.

Stories of CFOs becoming alarmed by high AI bills also suggests adoption is accelerating. This will be critical not only for the future rate of non-tech company earnings growth, but also for the hyperscalers, as they look for the return on their massive capital expenditure.

Performance data/data sources: FactSet, BNP Paribas AM, as of 30 October 2026, unless otherwise stated. Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

articles.title: US Affordability challenges cut across every state and local election
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

30 Oct 2026

US Affordability challenges cut across every state and local election

The rising cost of living has emerged as the primary issue in the upcoming midterms.

The central driver of this has been higher oil prices, which have rippled across consumer categories such as groceries, electricity, and housing vis-a-vis elevated interest rates. Higher living costs have been exacerbated by cuts to ACA insurance subsidies, which have forced many to drop health insurance; the surge in data centers, which has heightened electricity prices; and tariffs, which have hurt Midwestern economies.

The US-Israel war with Iran has pushed up the cost of gasoline, utilities, and food, three non-discretionary categories. Low-income consumers are especially affected by rising costs as they spend a larger share of their disposable income on non-discretionary categories. Southern states and metros have been the most exposed, as they have the highest share of low-income households burdened by the high cost of necessities.

The rising interest rates that have accompanied these cost pressures have eroded housing affordability more than it had declined in prior years. Although coastal metros are most cost-burdened, no metro has escaped the material deterioration in affordability. The average household needed to earn $115,600 in income to afford median housing costs in Q3 2026, up from $111,500 in Q3 2025, and 75% more than the $66,200 needed five years ago.

Ballooning healthcare costs, data center-driven electricity price increases, and tariffs all add further cost pressures to consumers and businesses across the US. Southern states have weathered the steepest drops in ACA enrollment due to insurance subsidies cuts. Northeastern states are bearing the brunt of higher electricity costs, while manufacturing-heavy Midwestern metros are most exposed to tariffs.

articles.title: The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland
articles.text:
The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland

Speech at the Intergraf Currency & Identity Conference, Denmark

Published on
15 October 2026

Maintaining trust in banknotes is crucial to their continued demand and relevance. This requires more than robust security features and resilient infrastructure. Victoria Cleland explores how communications and public engagement can help build and maintain confidence and trust in cash.

Speech
Trust is essential to everything the Bank of England (the Bank) does. It underpins all our activities, from setting Bank Rate to operating payment settlement systems and much in between. And banknotes are among the most visible manifestations of that trust.
The Bank is the second oldest central bank in the world and issuing banknotes (originally promissory notes) was one of its earliest functions. Historically, confidence in banknotes was linked to their convertibility into gold. You can still see the words ‘I promise to pay the bearer on demand’ on our banknotes. While the nature of that promise has evolved over time and our notes are now indirectly backed by UK government bonds,footnote [1] the principle remains the same: banknotes derive their value from trust, and that trust must be maintained.
Every time someone accepts a banknote, they trust that it is authentic and worth the value stated. They have to be confident that it can be used again in the future: whether to spend it, save it or bank it. Without that trust, a banknote is simply an object, albeit with a beautiful design. With it, households spend, businesses trade and economies function.
Central banks play a crucial role in maintaining this trust in banknotes. We do so by ensuring banknotes are available, that the cash industry remains effective, resilient and sustainable, and that banknotes remain a secure method of payment.
Communicating openly with businesses and the public so that they can recognise and easily authenticate banknotes is also an essential part of maintaining this security. The Bank has engaged extensively with the UK public on the imagery for our next series of banknotes to ensure our banknotes remain recognisable as national symbols. This culminated in last week’s announcement that the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will feature as the central imagery on our next series of banknotes.
I will now dive deeper into the Bank’s work to ensure this essential trust in our banknotes through availability, secure design and public engagement.
Ensuring trust through availability
The public need to trust that banknotes will be available when required. The Bank does not, and cannot, do this in isolation. Just as a beehive depends on its community of different bees performing complementary roles, maintaining trust in banknotes requires organisations across the cash ecosystem to work together.
Central banks, printers, cash centre operators, cash-in-transit companies, financial institutions and retailers are all important members of this ecosystem. They all play crucial and complementary roles in ensuring that the public can continue to access and use banknotes so that cash remains a trusted source of payments. At the Banknote Conference earlier this year,footnote [2] I spoke about the importance of preserving choice in payments and the role of cash in preserving choice. Ensuring that choice remains requires the whole industry to work together like an efficient beehive.
For the Bank, this includes issuing banknotes to meet public demand. The use of cash for transactions has declined over recent years, accounting for 8% of all transactions in the UK in 2025, down from 45% a decade earlier.footnote [3] But according to our research, cash is still the preferred payment method for one in seven people and, is used at least once a week by almost a quarter of the public. It is essential for some people and is seen as an important contingency by many.
And the value of Bank of England notes in circulation has continued to increase, reaching £91.5 billion at the end of February 2026. This demonstrates the enduring importance of cash to our economy and our society.
We are committed to meet the demand for our banknotes and to ensure that the right banknotes are available, in the right places at the right time. It is important to us that people and businesses who want to use cash can continue to do so. We do this by monitoring payment trends and a range of economic factors to inform demand forecasts and contingency requirements, and to help us decide how many banknotes we need our printer De La Rue to produce.
Authorities and industry must work closely together to ensure the cash cycle as a whole remains effective, resilient and sustainable. The wholesale cash distribution market is the underlying “plumbing” that gets cash to where it is needed, via cash centres through to ATMs and retailers. Last year, the Bank took on a new role to supervise firms in the wholesale cash industry who operate cash centres and their backing FIs.footnote [4] In addition, the Financial Conduct Authority has powers to protect retail access to cash for consumers. Together, these regimes will help ensure that cash will be available and accessible.
Ensuring trust through design
Another key component of trust in banknotes is counterfeit resilience: the public and businesses must be confident that the banknotes they receive are genuine. We do this by incorporating sophisticated security features into the design: these need to be both hard to counterfeit and easy to authenticate. For trust in the security of banknotes to endure, it is important that central banks change the design from time to time to incorporate the latest security features. This requires suppliers and manufacturers to innovate and invest in developing new technology and more resilient features. To maintain trust in banknotes, it is essential that this innovation continues.
When you picture a puffin, you may think of its distinct colouring including its bright orange beak. Did you know their beaks glow under UV light, just like our banknotes? These markings and photoluminescence are not purely about aesthetic appeal but also serve a functional purpose in helping puffins lure prey, deter predators and attract mates. Similarly, at the Bank, we need to design banknotes that are not only attractive but also designed with function, particularly security, at their heart.
Our next series of banknotes (Series H) is currently being designed. The driver, as with any new series, is to further enhance counterfeit resilience. And following public consultation, the new notes will celebrate UK wildlife. Images of wildlife will also support resilience, enabling us to incorporate intuitive movements into the security features which are engaging and easy for the public to recognise and distinguish.
Trust also stems from our notes being accessible to all. We are continuing to invest in banknote accessibility, running research on how people with disabilities use cash today and including tactile features to help people with visual impairments differentiate between denominations.
Ensuring trust through communication and engagement
Trust in banknotes is founded on availability and effective design, but sustaining it requires engagement – with businesses, law enforcement and the public. Even the most sophisticated security feature is only effective if people know how to use it to verify a banknote. And so public engagement and communication are a pivotal part of our anticounterfeiting strategy.
The Bank provides free educational materials, such as booklets and posters to help businesses and the public to authenticate banknotes. We also provide online training and run a free Banknote Checking Scheme to help businesses keep a watchful eye out for counterfeits: a vigilance one could compare to the barn owl which will feature on our next series. This Scheme has grown considerably, now covering over 50,000 business locations.
Recently, we have supplemented this by launching a communications campaign aimed at businesses. This campaign shows business owners talking about their own experiences and how using best practice banknote checking has enhanced their trust in banknotes. We also engage closely with law enforcement, including the National Crime Agency and local police forces, to help them investigate and prosecute potential counterfeiters.
Incorporating images that resonate strongly with the public and which they can easily recognise is also a key part of banknote authentication and maintaining trust. So last year, we launched a two-stage process to engage the public in the choice of imagery for the next series of banknotes.
In July 2025, we announced that we would introduce a new series of banknotes with even more robust security features. A new series necessitates changes to the imagery, so we launched a consultation asking the UK public which theme they wanted to see featured in the design. The Bank has been celebrating historic figures on our banknotes since 1970. However there are many ways to represent the UK so we wanted to hear the views of the public, the users of our banknotes.
Around 60% of respondents chose nature as one of the themes they wanted to see featured with many nominating specific native animals. And this March, we announced that in the light of feedback from the consultation, images of UK wildlife would feature on the next series of our banknotes. We worked closely with a panel of wildlife experts to create a shortlist of native UK animals and in June we launched a second consultation asking the public to help us choose which of the shortlisted animals to feature as the central imagery on the next series. We were delighted by the scale of the response, with almost half a million people participating.
The Bank’s overarching objective is to increase counterfeit resilience through secure design, and for this to be effective, it is also important that the new series represents the UK and resonates with the users. After all, banknotes are not just a means of payment, but also a shared symbol of national identity. This helps to promote trust and security, as familiar imagery which resonates with the public will mean they look more closely at their banknotes.
The importance of awareness and familiarity is not new. In 1797, when the Bank rushed to issue new £1 and £2 banknotes following gold shortages, counterfeiting surged as counterfeiters took advantage of people’s unfamiliarity with new banknotes. The lesson remains relevant today: when introducing a new series, issuers must bring the public along on the journey to ensure they can recognise and authenticate the notes.
To do this successfully and inclusively, central banks need to engage people through different methods including the platforms they use every day. To help publicise our most recent consultation, the Bank used an integrated communication strategy which included press, social media, engagement with schools and visiting local communities around the UK. We also collaborated with influencers to help us reach young people and audiences who may not have engaged with the Bank’s work in the past.
We opened the consultation with a launch event at the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) London Wetland Centre to celebrate the shortlisted animals and give journalists an opportunity to ask questions – both to me and the wildlife Expert Panel who helped us develop the shortlist of animals. This provided an engaging backdrop to create content about wildlife to help raise awareness and encourage participation in the consultation.
To sustain momentum, we produced a variety of engaging and accessible content with the aim to appeal to different audience groups and help convey our broader message. This included factsheets on each of the animals and educational posts showing how banknotes have evolved over time, as well as some more fun posts.
Alongside the formal consultation, we also visited schools and ran a design challenge for children across the country to give young people a voice in shaping our next generation of banknotes. And we held a number of in-person Youth and Citizens’ panels in communities including Llandudno and Devon. These were a great opportunity for the Bank to learn directly from people about the role that cash continues to play in society as well as their views on the shortlisted wildlife.
Conclusion
Trust in banknotes begins with secure design but only endures if banknotes are available and recognised. Keeping banknotes trusted and relevant requires innovation and strong collaboration across the whole of the cash industry. And this must be coupled with communication and engagement to enable businesses and the public to understand, recognise and trust the banknotes they use.
Our recent consultation gave people a voice, helping them connect with the banknotes they use and have a meaningful say about their future design. There will now be a quieter period in our communications about the next series, while our design work continues in the background, with security at its heart. Like the hedgehog emerging after its winter retreat, we will return when we are ready to unveil the first denomination.
I would like to thank Elijah Lee, Zahra Damji, Nick McLaren, Ellen Caswell, Stuart Cooper, Lauren Murphy, Kiran Keer, Millie Rettie and Lisa Young.

“The fund’s return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments. Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell,” says Deputy CEO Trond Grande of Norges Bank Investment Management.
The fund’s value fell by 670 billion kroner in the third quarter. The accounting return was -278 billion kroner. The krone strengthened during the quarter, which reduced the fund’s value by 472 billion kroner. In the third quarter, 80 billion kroner was added to the fund after management costs.
The fund was valued at 22,014 billion kroner on 30 September 2026. Of this, 72.1 percent was invested in equities, 25.8 percent in fixed income, 1.6 percent in unlisted real estate and 0.5 percent in unlisted renewable energy infrastructure.

The current AI boom might be the first chapter of a much broader economic story, with investment and capital deepening as the main drivers for now. Over time, productivity gains could become increasingly important, broadening the benefits across the economy and equity markets.

articles.title: Emerging Market Debt: Navigating the Disconnect - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
By Alaa Bushehri, Head of Emerging Market Fixed Income

Emerging market debt benefits from resilient fundamentals despite a challenging global backdrop, impacting sentiment

Yields remains attractive while supportive policy and strong balance sheets are creating scope for positive returns beyond broader market movements

We see potential opportunities for active, selective investors in both hard currency and local currency emerging market bonds

Emerging market fixed income entered the fourth quarter of 2026 with an attractive combination of resilient fundamentals and scope for selective growth opportunities. However, the global backdrop remains challenging, with geopolitical uncertainty, elevated energy prices, higher US Treasury yields and a stronger dollar impacting sentiment.

Yet these pressures are not represented uniformly across all emerging markets. Through much of 2026, the asset class’s resilience highlights the disconnect between difficult external conditions and improving country-specific stories.

Our outlook is constructive but selective: attractive levels of interest income remain pivotal for returns, while credible policy frameworks and stronger balance sheets create potential opportunities beyond broad market movements.

Greater clarity on monetary policy, stabilising energy prices or an easing of geopolitical tensions could provide additional support, although none should be assumed in the short term. Rather than relying on a return to benign global conditions, our investment case rests on identifying markets where starting yields and durable fundamental progress could provide credible compensation for risk.

Potential opportunities for active investors

In the current environment, the breadth of the investment universe is a particular strength, with hard and local currency markets offering distinct sources of income and diversification, allowing opportunities to be assessed on their own merits.

Supportive demand complements generally robust fundamentals, but the most persuasive stories are those underpinned by credible fiscal trajectories, improving external balances, adequate reserves and sustainable financing requirements.

Underlying differences between issuers creates room for those who are able to be active, particularly where improving policy credibility can translate into better credit outcomes. In such cases diversification is more conditional than guaranteed in the near-term.

The simultaneous rise in Treasury yields, dollar strength and risk aversion will continue to pressure investors and is unlikely to dissipate meaningfully until there is meaningful progress towards an end to the conflict in the Middle East. Nevertheless, the ability to distinguish idiosyncrasies among countries, industries and balance sheets remain a potential advantage for active investors and supports a differentiated assessment rather than a single directional view of emerging markets.

Hard currency debt – balancing yield and quality

For hard-currency debt – emerging market bonds that are issued in major currencies such as US dollars – we retain a neutral stance overall, while recognising an attractive all-in yield proposition and compelling selective opportunities.

Resilient fundamentals and supportive technicals balance elevated Treasury yields and persistent inflation risks. With the relative valuation advantage over developed-market credit, higher levels of interest income and issuer differentiation offer a more credible return foundation than indiscriminate spread compression.

Investment-grade sovereign bonds continue to provide comparatively strong credit quality, although their typically longer duration profile increases sensitivity to rising US Treasury yields. High-yield sovereign bonds typically offer greater income and upside from improving fundamentals, but refinancing conditions, debt sustainability and risk aversion considerations require careful assessment.

Corporate debt broadens the opportunity set further. Issuers with strong liquidity, stable cash flows, manageable maturities and hard-currency revenues may demonstrate resilience even when domestic sovereign conditions are challenging.

Shorter-duration corporate securities may reduce interest rate sensitivity, although they remain exposed to credit deterioration. Across sovereign and corporate bonds, the emphasis is on quality interest income and identifiable balance-sheet improvement, not simply on maximising spread.

Stability in the Treasury markets would allow these strengths to contribute more visibly to returns; however, an adverse interest rate move could still outweigh positive credit developments.

Local currency debt: Selective optimism

Local currency debt offers a particularly differentiated source of potential upside, with markets continuing to offer attractive real interest rates, anchored inflation expectations and potential easing (although likely on hold for now). All of these aspects provide an appealing starting point.

The strongest cases also feature resilient external accounts, adequate reserves and offer investors a strong source of interest income. Currency exposure remains integral: favourable domestic bond performance can be offset by a stronger dollar, while income alone may not absorb adverse currency moves.

We therefore maintain selective near-term optimism alongside a positive medium and longer-term currency view, recognising that divergence between developed- and emerging-market growth could support emerging market currencies.

Fiscal expansion, political pressure on monetary policy and renewed energy inflation remain important constraints on local-market opportunities.

Across the asset class, the principal risk remains a sustained inflation shock that keeps policy restrictive and pushes global yields higher (for longer). However, weaker global growth could instead pressure commodity revenues and lower-rated credit.

The upside lies in easing geopolitical tensions, steadier energy prices and moderating developed-market yields, potentially supporting currencies, selective rate cuts and credit performance.

EM debt: More than just income

Overall, emerging-market debt offers more than an interest income story: improving fundamentals and selective appreciation potential support a positive fourth quarter assessment. Disciplined country and issuer selection remains essential to capture potential opportunities while managing duration, currency and credit risks.

Rather than a positive outlook across the board, we see potential opportunities for disciplined active investors who have the scale and the expertise to differentiate between idiosyncratic opportunities and the broader environment.

This article is part of the Fixed Income Quarterly Outlook for Q4 2026, covering US Treasury Bonds, Euro Government Bonds, Emerging Market Debt, Global Credit, and UK Government Debt.

articles.title: The Global Economy’s Tenuous Balance: Resilience Amid Uncertainty
articles.text:
Skip to main content
Global Markets and EconomyThe Global Economy’s Tenuous Balance: Resilience Amid UncertaintyGlobal Economics Outlook & StrategyArticle • October 30, 2026ResearchKEY TAKEAWAYSGlobal growth remains resilient with GDP expected to grow 2.7% this year and 2.8% next year despite geopolitical tensions fiscal concerns and uncertainty surrounding AIInflation risks have intensified driven by higher energy prices and supply-chain pressures prompting many central banks to adopt a more hawkish stanceAI remains a major global growth driver but financial excesses weakening political support and rising cyber risks represent important challenges to the sustainability of the investment boomA new Citi Research report from a team led by Global Chief Economist Nathan Sheets explores the global economy’s remarkable resilience despite mounting challenges, from the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom to geopolitical tensions. The number of such challenges in growing. The U.S.-Iran conflict has pushed Brent crude to $115 a barrel, close to this year’s high. Concerns about the AI boom have intensified, while renewed worries over French fiscal performance have added to broader sovereign debt pressures. Consumer and business confidence indicators remain subdued, with households particularly pessimistic.Yet despite notable and apparently increasing headwinds, we now expect global gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 2.7% this year, slightly stronger than last month’s forecast and broadly in line with our expectations at the start of the year. Developed markets are performing somewhat better than we anticipated in December, largely because of continued U.S. strength. Meanwhile, emerging markets remain slightly softer overall, as stronger growth in Asia is nearly offset by weaker outcomes in the Middle East and Africa. We expect global growth to climb to 2.8% next year.Recent Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) readings reinforce this picture. Global manufacturing activity has continued to strengthen, supported by the electronics sector and AI-related investment. Sharply rising U.S. investment has boosted production and technology exports across other regions, especially in Asia. Economies with significant exposure to AI, including Taiwan and South Korea, have posted strong growth despite their vulnerability to higher oil prices.The services sector has also remained resilient. After weakening during the early phase of the U.S.-Iran conflict, the global services PMI has rebounded. Labor markets remain firm, hiring has held up, and consumption continues to grow. Despite consumers’ caution, spending hasn’t materially slowed. Citi’s global Surprise Index similarly suggests that economic data continue to exceed expectations, while China has improved modestly and euro-area data have moderated.The key takeaway is that it will likely require a substantially larger shock to derail global growth. For now, businesses continue to adapt effectively to changing conditions, helping sustain expansion despite mounting risks.Inflation, however, has become a more significant concern. Since February, oil prices have risen roughly 60%, while jet fuel prices are up 100% and diesel prices 110%. As a result, we expect global headline inflation to reach 3.4% this year, compared with 2.8% last year, before easing to 3.0% next year provided that oil prices moderate.Core inflation pressures have also intensified. Higher transportation costs and disruptions to supply chains — particularly in aluminum, petrochemicals and fertilizers — are gradually feeding through to consumer prices. We now expect core inflation this year to be at least 0.5 percentage point higher than we projected in February for economies including Brazil, Australia, South Korea, the euro area and Thailand. Central banks are increasingly moving toward tighter policy stances.A notable consequence of this environment has been rising sovereign bond yields. Since the U.S.-Iran conflict began, 10-year yields have increased by 175 basis points (bp) in France, more than 100 bp in both the U.S. and the UK, and 75 bp in Japan, Germany and Canada. Several emerging markets have also experienced rising yields, including the Philippines, Indonesia and India.We attribute these moves partly to growing competition for global savings. U.S. Treasury issuance is likely to remain at $2 trillion or more annually, financing needs elsewhere are substantial, and AI investment is emerging as another major consumer of capital. Global AI-related capital expenditures are projected to exceed $3.5 trillion by 2030. At the same time, investors are demanding greater compensation for geopolitical uncertainty, fiscal risks, inflation volatility and governance concerns, contributing to higher term and risk premiums. We also see oil-market volatility as playing a role.France remains a particular source of concern. Even under relatively favorable assumptions, rising interest costs are likely to keep budget deficits near 4% of GDP, while government debt approaches 120% of GDP. Political uncertainty ahead of next spring’s presidential election has further undermined confidence. Encouragingly, pressures have largely remained contained, though Belgium and Italy have shown some sensitivity to French developments, and we continue to monitor potential spillovers to the UK.On AI, we remain constructive. We view the current investment cycle as being driven by businesses seeking productivity gains and competitive advantage. For many firms, AI investment has become an imperative for survival. We expect this spending wave to persist well into the next decade, with meaningful productivity benefits beginning to emerge over the next two to three years.That said, three risks warrant close attention. First, financial disruptions remain possible. As with the internet boom of the late 1990s, a transformative technology can generate bubbles, mispricing and failures. However, investors today appear highly alert to these risks, and periodic corrections may be reducing the likelihood of a broader speculative bubble.Second, political support for AI appears to be weakening, particularly in the U.S. Concerns about electricity demand, power-grid capacity and job displacement have become increasingly prominent, raising the possibility of more-restrictive policies toward data-center construction and AI deployment.Third, cyber risks are increasing alongside AI capabilities. More sophisticated cyberattacks or failures involving advanced AI systems could have significant economic and political consequences, potentially triggering stricter regulation.Against this backdrop of resilient growth and elevated inflation, central banks have pivoted toward tighter policy. Across 27 major central banks, we now expect 16 to raise rates this year, six to remain on hold, and only five to ease policy. This marks a sharp departure from expectations earlier in the year, and we note that in contrast to the period after the pandemic, central banks have generally refused to “look through” the supply shock.Looking ahead, we see a more mixed picture, with monetary policy remaining heavily dependent on oil prices and the trajectory of the U.S.-Iran conflict. We expect additional tightening from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of England, and Bank of Japan, although the outlook for 2027 appears more balanced. For now, central banks remain focused on preventing inflation from becoming entrenched, even as growth continues to prove more resilient than many expected.Our new report, Global Economic Outlook & Strategy: The Global Economy’s Tenuous Balance — Resilience Amid Uncertainty, also offers region-by-region economic discussions. Despite the challenges, strategic planners should give due attention to the ‘advantaged resources’ at scale offered by deepwater oil and gas
