With many oil and gas companies facing large production declines from existing assets over the next decade, portfolio renewal is high on the agenda for the upstream sector. Geopolitical volatility is increasing the pressure, highlighting concentration risk and pushing firms towards new growth areas.
For most, the deepwater thematic presents significant operational, technical and capital hurdles, but also attractive rewards. So how can E&P firms identify and evaluate the best deepwater opportunities for their own risk profile?
Drawing on data from our Lens Upstream platform, our analysts have created a strategic planners guidebook setting out in detail the global deepwater opportunities - in exploration, M&A and strategic partnerships - and how best to access them. Fill in the form to download a selection of complementary slides from the report, or read on for the answers to five key questions about how to grow in deepwater.
1. Why should E&P firms be interested in deepwater’s rapidly expanding opportunities?
For the Majors and many national oil companies (NOCs), deepwater represents the potential to access advantaged resources at scale. The right deepwater assets offer high margins, prolific reservoirs, large fields, low emissions intensity, and huge potential upside. For all the Majors peer group the scale and profitability of deepwater is critical to hitting cashflow and investment targets.
Wood Mackenzie’s Lens Subsurface platform holds data on over 130 ready-to-drill deepwater prospects, including chance of success, resource and valuation estimates. Find out more in the complementary report extract.
2. Why is it difficult to build a deepwater portfolio?
High technical, risk and capital thresholds make breaking into deepwater a challenge for many companies. The IOCs and NOCs leading near-term deepwater growth have either partnered with the right Major in the right basins, or built up their expertise on domestic assets before expanding abroad. Others have acquired their deepwater expertise through the corporate acquisition of a company already active in deepwater. In summary, there is more than one way to build a deepwater growth portfolio.
There are also some clear winners in terms of deepwater value creation over the last decade. Download the free slides to find out more.
3. What is the best way to grow in deepwater?
Exploration is the key catalyst driving upstream growth. However, many companies lack either the means or the desire to commit to high-risk frontier exploration campaigns. Most firms therefore lean heavily on M&A or bid on Discovered Resource Opportunities (DROs) offered by governments and NOCs. This reduces some risks but can also impact potential returns.
For firms willing and able to take the risk, however, the rewards from material deepwater exploration success can be significant. For example, ExxonMobil’s portfolio was transformed by discoveries in Guyana and will see it overtake Shell as the leading Major in deepwater in the early 2030s. You can learn more in the report extract.
4. How are operators using M&A to accelerate growth?
Deepwater is a rich hunting ground for firms with cash on the balance sheet, with a range of M&A opportunities offering access to deepwater assets in every major deepwater basin. Current pricing for some assets is attractive, with a few recent deals being completed at significant discounts, partly due to subsurface risks. However, as more firms focus on portfolio renewal and diversification, low prices may not last.
Want to know which factors could be driving the deepwater value discount? Download the complimentary slides to find out more.
5. Why are there increasing opportunities in exploration?
The need to renew ageing portfolios has led the Majors to pursue a massive acreage grab. These firms are building pipelines of drill-ready prospects of varying size and potential. Farm-in opportunities are plentiful, but E&P firms need to be careful to select the right basin and the right partner — specifically, those with the best track record in deepwater value creation.
Deepwater opportunity screening: want to identify the right basins with the best prospectivity and terms? Find out more by downloading the report extract.
This extract explores ready-to-drill deepwater and ultra-deepwater prospects by region, resource size, valuation and company. It also draws on Wood Mackenzie’s Exploration Service and Exploration Company Performance analysis to reveal the leading deepwater E&A value creators and well spenders of the past decade.

articles.title: Palestinian tech goes to Silicon Valley
articles.text:
Published on
Perspectives: MENA, Afghanistan, and Pakistan

Palestinian tech goes to Silicon Valley

Zackaria Sabella

Kaliza Karuretwa

Karen Grigorian

October 29, 2026

This page in:

English

English

The Palestinian tech delegation in San Francisco. Photo: Oaday Awadalla

This was not a charity evening. It was a business meeting. The room had founders, investors, tech executives, and ecosystem builders from the Silicon Valley and the Arab world.
The event was the centerpiece of a week-long mission organized by the World Bank's Technology for Youth and Jobs project – TechStart – co-financed by the EU, Switzerland, and the Kingdom of the Netherlands, which brought a Palestinian tech delegation to Silicon Valley in mid-September. The delegation included representatives from the Palestine Techno Park, Ibtikar Fund, the project implementing agency DAI, and nine startups supported by another World Bank initiative, the Innovative Private Sector Development II project – IPSD II. Together, they spent a week meeting with Google, Apple, NVIDIA, Amazon Web Services, Salesforce, Broadcom, and Plug and Play. They also participated in a dedicated panel on the Palestinian tech ecosystem at TechWadi's annual forum, one of the most prominent gatherings of Arab-American tech professionals in the United States.
Across every meeting, the message was clear: these were businesses seeking investment, not sympathy. Palestinian engineers are technically competitive, bilingual, and experienced working with international clients. The cost-quality proposition is strong. Companies supported by TechStart and IPSD II have been delivering for global customers through conditions that would have shut down most startups anywhere else in the world. What Palestinian entrepreneurs need is access: to platforms, to contracts, to the kind of commercial relationships that turn a promising company into a global one. The World Bank’s TechStart and IPSD II projects have together mobilized over $62 million in private capital for the Palestinian tech ecosystem. These are not donor grants, but rather commercial market bets made by investors who see the potential for Palestinian companies to compete and grow in global markets.
Iyad Zimmo, CEO of Damodi, said the week in San Francisco "put us in the rooms that matter" and helped move investor conversations forward. Hussam Irsheid of PalAID said he arrived focused on growing a local service and left thinking about how to build a global company. For Ibrahim Sana of Farabio, the value was the direct feedback from Silicon Valley practitioners, which helped him see international expansion from a more “practical and actionable” perspective.
The meetings with major technology companies were candid, thoughtful, and focused on concrete business opportunities. Conversations moved past awareness into practical possibilities: talent pipelines, developer certification, outsourcing pilots, and startup program integration. One global startup support program, open to companies at any stage, had no Palestinian members before the week began. By the end of the meetings, there was shared interest in changing that. The World Bank's role as a trusted intermediary, identifying firms, assessing capabilities, and facilitating introductions, emerged as a clear value proposition that resonated with several counterparts. Some conversations also pointed to the Gulf as an underexplored pathway into global markets through regional investment channels, data centers, and strategic partnerships that could complement the relationships being built in Silicon Valley.
The TechWadi annual forum added another dimension to the week. Representatives from leading venture funds, tech parks, and startups made the case for Palestinian tech to an audience of Arab-American investors and diaspora professionals at the heart of Silicon Valley. What stood out was not the message itself, which was familiar to the panelists, but how it resonated with the audience. Many in the room had not previously viewed the Palestinian tech sector as a commercial destination. By the end of the discussion, they did. A wave of social media posts followed, from people who said the panel changed how they thought about where to invest, where to hire, and where to look for the next generation of technical talent from the Arab world.
None of this turns automatically into contracts or investments. The less visible work begins now: developing pilots and partnerships, connecting startups to global programs, and advancing the investor conversations that started during the week. Several opportunities are already under discussion, and the World Bank's TechStart and IPSD II are following up on each.
Still, something shifted in San Francisco. Founders walked into rooms where their market was little known and their capabilities were often seen through the lens of crisis. Their sector operates under conditions most ecosystems never face. Yet by the end of the week, the conversations had shifted to business: talent, investment, outsourcing, and global expansion.
Whether pitching in San Francisco or from Ramallah, these entrepreneurs were not seeking validation. They came to challenge perceptions and demonstrate the strength of their businesses. The gap between what the Palestinian technology sector is and what much of the world thinks of it remains significant. But it is narrowing, and the work ahead will determine how fast.

articles.title: Here We Go Again: Binance Loses $6.3b in Largest Robbery in History
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Here We Go Again: Binance Loses $6.3b in Largest Robbery in History 

Written by:

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Topics

Bitcoin

Cryptocurrency

Ethereum

research • October 30, 2026

Here We Go Again: Binance Loses $6.3b in Largest Robbery in History 

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, was drained of roughly $6.3b across 10 blockchains on Thursday night. TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s Lazarus-linked unit. As of writing, the exchange has not yet re-enabled withdrawals. Start with scale. The benchmark for the largest robbery ever has long been the roughly $1b Saddam Hussein’s regime took from the Central Bank of Iraq on the eve of the 2003 invasion, about $1.8b in today’s dollars. Bybit beat that in nominal terms but not after inflation. Binance beats it on any measure. Even after roughly $2.5–3bn in freezes, this is the biggest heist of all time. Binance’s BTC outflows yesterday were 11 standard deviations higher than their 30-day average.

Then the method. On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702 to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper contract that took orders only from the attacker. It was backed by 50 pre-signed authorizations, one for each upcoming transaction number (nonce), so whichever one came up next would work. The code was rehearsed on three test wallets hours beforehand. Within minutes of each other, nine more chains were emptied, each with different key types and signing schemes. That is someone with intimate knowledge of how Binance’s withdrawal systems work. This is Binance’s preliminary finding: a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop gave access to a service container, with “no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”

Our take We believe our previous thesis from Bitget is consistent here. Nobody attacks the private-key math. They attack whoever, or whatever, tells the math what to do. The biggest mitigating factor of this exploit was stablecoin issuers. Tether froze about $1.77b in USDT, Circle about $825m in USDC, Ripple about $40m in RLUSD, and World Liberty about $28m in USD1. That’s a big part of why this appears to be a painful week rather than an existential one, and we believe Tether deserves credit for moving fast and at scale. We also believe Circle deserves credit for the freeze. Circle has long said it freezes only when directed by law enforcement or a court, not in real time during an active hack. After April's $285m Drift exploit, CEO Jeremy Allaire went further, saying a private company deciding "what is the right path or not" would be a "moral quandary." During the Drift exploit, about $232m in stolen USDC moved through Circle's own cross-chain transfer protocol over roughly six hours without being frozen. But, on Thursday, Circle froze $823m about 40 minutes after the Ethereum sweep, "in coordination with law enforcement." Does Binance have enough to cover the hole? The SAFU fund, about $1b in BTC, does not come close to covering it, so Binance says it will cover all losses from its own corporate funds. Last year’s 10/10 liquidation event cost Binance about $283m in depeg compensation plus its $400m “Together Initiative” ($300m in user vouchers and $100m in low-interest loans to institutions). That’s under $700m; this hack is roughly nine times that. A better yardstick is the BNB burn. 2026’s three quarterly burns so far have retired about $3.2bn of BNB. Net of freezes, the hole is roughly one year of burns, or about 4% of the ~$144bn in assets Binance held before the attack. It is a staggering amount of money, but Binance does appear to have it, or at least the ability to earn its way out of a hole based on our own calculations of their revenue-funded BNB burns. While we can’t independently verify Binance’s whole financial condition, and we don’t know exactly what Binance plans to do, Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said plainly: “Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and company funds.” What’s left: when will withdrawals reopen, where will the roughly $2.4b in ETH and BTC still in the attacker’s hands go next (THORChain, Tornado Cash, etc.), and how did an outsider come to know Binance’s systems this well? These are among the key specific questions we will be following in the coming days and weeks. But how the market reacts to the event broadly is also top of mind. Bitcoin and other crypto assets are trading lower on the news. Alex Thorn’s piece from Monday (Why Now Is the Time to Add and Hold BTC) relies heavily on the 50-week moving average as a key level to maintain a bullish trend, with a break below that is not retaken within 1 month cited as invalidating the paper’s thesis. That 50w MA currently sits at $76,103, and at the time of writing BTCUSD is trading at $77,000. So far, the 50w MA has held, with BTC trading as low as $76,301 overnight on Coinbase. Whether the 50w can hold this weekend is a key test that could be consequential for the next several months of Bitcoin’s technical market structure.

RESEARCH BRIEFING

27 Oct 2026

GCC recovery tracker shows initial rebound has stalled

The GCC economy faces challenges with a fragile recovery, varying regional performances, and resilient oil revenues amid ongoing disruptions. Discover more.

The GCC recovery tracker indicates a notable stall in economic rebound, with a forecasted GDP contraction of 5.7% for this year, followed by a gradual recovery to 5.5% growth in 2027. This trend reflects a decline in the diffusion index, which fell by 5.4 points to 51.0 in September, signalling a fragile recovery environment.

Flight disruptions and declining equity prices have contributed to this slowdown, particularly in Saudi Arabia, where ongoing attacks on civilian infrastructure have undermined confidence. Conversely, shipping activities have shown some resilience, with Saudi Arabia restarting exports, although oil production remains at only 77% of pre-conflict levels.

The outlook varies across the region, with Oman performing relatively well due to stable energy production, while Kuwait and Qatar continue to lag behind. Despite a drop in tourist arrivals and uneven fiscal impacts, Saudi Arabia’s oil and gas revenues have exceeded pre-conflict levels, demonstrating some resilience in the face of adversity.

articles.title: Spending it faster: What a 10,000-agent proof means for AI's borrowed expertise | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Spending it faster: What a 10,000-agent proof means for AI’s borrowed expertise

Niam Yaraghi

Niam Yaraghi

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Governance Studies, Center for Technology Innovation (CTI)

October 29, 2026

OpenAI’s unverified Navier-Stokes proof, produced by 10,000 AI agents in 88 hours, shows that AI excels at “normal science” inside frames humans built long ago.
The real problem is that AI can produce results at industrial scale, but understanding them still happens one trained person at a time, so the shortage of qualified evaluators is now the limit on what science delivers.
Congress should reverse the proposed 40% cut to National Science Foundation graduate fellowships and fund paid verification teams, because no institution exists to check machine-generated science outside pure mathematics.

Georgina Leeuwendal / https://betterimagesofai.org / https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

14 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Editor's note:
This piece builds upon two prior pieces published on the TechTank blog: “Borrowed expertise: Why AI’s productivity boom may not survive the generation that built it” (July 10, 2026) and “Repaying the inheritance: How education and research policy can address AI’s borrowed expertise” (July 20, 2026).

On Sept. 8, OpenAI announced that an unreleased internal model had produced a proposed solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems—a set of complex, unsolved problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000 that offer a $1 million prize for the first correct solution for each.
Roughly 10,000 agents ran in parallel for 88 hours. The compute bill ran millions of dollars, which OpenAI’s Sébastien Bubeck described in the press briefing as roughly a thousand times what the company had previously spent on a single problem.
The proof is not verified. Mathematicians are reading it now, and under Clay’s rules a proposed solution must appear in a qualifying publication, wait two years, and win general acceptance in the field before the prize is considered at all. OpenAI says it does not intend to claim it.
That was five weeks ago, and it is already the smaller story. On Oct. 6, OpenAI released 722 manuscripts in a single GitHub drop, claiming progress on 372 open problems across algebra, geometry, number theory, and theoretical computer science, all produced by the same unreleased internal model. The company estimates the average result cost roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro compute. Only 162 of the manuscripts arrived with the machine-checkable Lean formalizations that let a computer confirm a proof, and mathematicians pushed back immediately: A group calling itself the Association for Human Mathematics described the release as “not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power.” A day later, OpenAI withdrew three of the manuscripts after an internal audit caught a sign error that invalidated one argument and the constructions in two papers that depended on it.
Assume the Navier-Stokes proof holds. What it demonstrates is the pattern I described in July 2026: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is exceptionally well-suited to normal science, the puzzle-solving work inside a frame that people have already built. In this case, the frame was built by other people a long time ago.
What is new is the scale, and the scale changes the problem. Ten thousand agents working on well-posed questions for four days is a different kind of instrument. So is a model that can mint 700 papers at three hours of compute apiece. Together they move the binding constraint on science from the production of results to the absorption of them, and the policy agenda I set out in July is missing the instrument that matters most for that. The important part is not the proof. It is the mismatch the proof exposes: We are about to have far more machine-generated science than people qualified to evaluate it, there is no institution for verifying machine-generated claims outside pure mathematics, and the training pipeline that produces qualified evaluators is being cut at exactly the wrong moment.

Back to top

This is normal science, performed at a scale no one has seen

Nothing in that agent swarm decided that fluid singularities were worth 90 years of attention. The problem came to the swarm already framed, with a clean statement and an unambiguous success criterion. This is the most favorable possible terrain for a system that excels at search inside a well-specified frame.
Bubeck said OpenAI began working on the Millennium problems because of viral Twitter rumors that Anthropic had resolved two of them. The agenda was set by competitive anxiety about a rival lab. Whatever else that is, it is not a machine identifying an important question.
The telescope reading
When Galileo pointed a telescope at Jupiter in 1610 and found four moons, the instrument did not settle the questions astronomers already had. It generated new ones faster than anyone could work through them, and the number of working astronomers went up.
An agent swarm that can spend $10 million on inference for a single conjecture is an instrument of that kind. It reaches places unaided human cognition cannot, and it will return results nobody asked for and that nobody yet understands. The optimistic reading of this week is that we have acquired a very powerful telescope.
The pessimistic reading is that we have acquired it at a moment when we are cutting the number of astronomers.

Back to top

Production scales, absorption does not

Here is the asymmetry that should organize the policy response.
The production of new results is now a scalable industrial process: add agents, add compute, add hours, get more output. The unit cost falls every year, and the parallelism has no obvious ceiling. Bubeck framed the implication as a question for the audience: What happens when organizations can spend that kind of compute on problems they actually care about? The October release was a preview of the answer: 722 manuscripts in one day, most of them without formal verification.
Absorption does not scale. Understanding a result is a change in a person. It happens one person at a time, at a rate bounded by human cognition and by years of prior training. The internet made information nearly free and did not make doctorates meaningfully shorter. AI tutoring helps, and I have cited a Harvard physics trial before as the best causal evidence we have: Students with a purpose-built tutor learned roughly twice as much as students in an active-learning classroom, in less time. Twice is a real gain; it is not 10,000 agents in parallel.
The ratio of results produced to results understood therefore rises with every capability improvement. This is ordinary economics. When one input becomes abundant, the marginal value of its complement rises. AI substitutes for research labor and complements absorption labor, and absorption is becoming the binding constraint on what science actually delivers.

Back to top

What the mathematicians did next

In July, I leaned on Fabrizio Dell’Acqua and colleagues’ field experiment, which found that consultants using AI on a task outside its capability frontier performed about 19 percentage points worse because the model produced confident-sounding answers and the users lacked the expertise to detect them. The diagnostic point was that the user generally cannot tell which side of the frontier a task falls on. That problem has now arrived at the top of the skill distribution, and mathematicians have started saying so themselves.
The clearest evidence is from May, when an internal OpenAI model disproved Paul Erdős’ unit distance conjecture, an 80-year-old problem in discrete geometry. The company did not publish the proof alone. Nine mathematicians checked it and published a companion paper alongside it, which they describe in their own abstract as a short, digested, human-verified version of the machine’s argument, together with individually signed reflections on what it means.
Read that paper and the division of labor is unmistakable. The proof did not need rescuing. Thomas Bloom applied the test that matters for my argument, asking whether the result taught the field anything new and answering with a qualified yes: Number-theoretic constructions have more to say about these questions than anyone suspected, though the proof introduces no new geometric tools of the kind a proof of the conjecture would have required. Bloom then makes the point directly. The original AI proof was completely valid, and humans improved it substantially anyway, because the work of discussing, digesting, and improving a proof and drawing out its consequences remains theirs.
Two of the reflections should worry anyone assuming this layer will hold. Victor Wang noted that verification went smoothly because the digested argument ran only a few pages, and that a longer one might have gone differently, since the participants may have been less willing to spend the time. The check held because nine busy people volunteered and the reading was short. Melanie Matchett Wood put the jagged frontier in its sharpest form: In many cases it will be easier for AI to convince mathematicians it has a proof than to produce a correct argument, and she does not think the profession is prepared for that.
The Navier-Stokes episode shows the same layer operating under worse conditions. There is no companion paper. It was Tristan Buckmaster at New York University who recognized, from one word in a text message, that the smooth-forcing route was the obscure path he and Levent Alpöge had been walking, and who published a careful statement that stopped short of alleging anything. I take no position on that dispute. My point is narrower: The people positioned to notice there was anything to examine were two mathematicians who happened to be working on the same problem.
William Thurston made the underlying case in a 1994 essay that mathematicians still argue about. The discipline’s output, he wrote, is not a stock of proven statements but ways for people to understand and think about mathematics. The nine authors of that companion paper were doing exactly what he described, and they had to be assembled by hand to do it.

Back to top

Understanding is also what converts a result into something useful

The second reason to care about absorption is that knowledge sitting unread does very little.
Lawrence Craven, a general practitioner in Glendale, California, noticed around 1950 that his tonsillectomy patients who chewed aspirin gum bled more, reasoned that aspirin might therefore prevent the clots behind heart attacks, put several thousand of his male patients on a daily dose, and reported that none of them had one. He published in obscure journals, was ignored because he had no randomized evidence, and died of a heart attack in 1957. The finding sat for 20 years. Then John Vane showed in 1971 that aspirin blocks prostaglandin synthesis. The mechanism explained which patients would benefit and at what dose, and that understanding is what launched the trials that turned an ignored observation into one of the cheapest effective interventions in medicine.
Institutions reinforce this. Licensure, liability, regulatory approval, and peer review all run through a person who can be questioned and held responsible. A Food and Drug Administration reviewer signs. A licensed engineer stamps the drawing. You cannot operate those mechanisms on outputs that no accountable human comprehends, and rebuilding them so no human understanding is required would be a far larger undertaking than anything currently under discussion.

Back to top

The pipeline problem in its scientific form

The July argument returns here in its sharpest form.
The people who can check frontier work are produced by doing frontier work. There is no consumption-only path to that competence. It comes through apprenticeship: proof search, literature review, replication, reconstruction of other people’s arguments. Graduate training manufactures absorptive capacity as a byproduct of doing the research yourself.
That apprenticeship work is precisely what agents now perform faster and cheaper. The seniority-biased hiring I documented in firms has a direct analogue in the laboratory, and the logic is identical: Paying a graduate student to do work an agent completes in an afternoon will start to look indefensible to a department chair long before anyone notices what has been lost. In July, I called this spending an inheritance. The Navier-Stokes result means we are now spending it faster, because the volume of machine-generated science requiring human evaluation is rising at the same time that the number of qualified evaluators is falling.
The economics do not self-correct. Verification is a public good. It is nonrival, and a department that trains a competent skeptic captures almost none of the value that person later creates by catching someone else’s error. The private incentive to produce absorbers is weakest exactly when their social value is highest.

Back to top

The instrument the policy agenda is missing

In July, I proposed four things: sequencing in K-12 education, AI-free assessment at credentialing stages, research funding instruments that can distinguish novelty from recombination, and procurement standards for pedagogical AI. I would now add a fifth, and I would put it first.
We have no institution for verifying machine-generated scientific claims outside of pure mathematics.
Mathematics is the fortunate case. Programs provide mechanical checking, and Clay’s two-year publication-and-acceptance requirement is an explicit, deliberately slow human verification process. Nothing equivalent exists in biology, materials science, or clinical research, where AI systems are already generating candidate results at volume and where there is no formal verifier at all. The check in those fields is peer review, which is unpaid, already overloaded, and staffed by exactly the senior cohort that is aging out. OpenAI itself appears to see the gap: alongside the October release, it said it will fund workshops, conferences, and special programs “around the understanding of major results produced by AI.” A lab paying for the absorption of its own output is welcome. It is also the clearest statement available that no public institution exists to do the job.
The general principle is that verification should be treated as a first-class research activity rather than as unpaid service, and that federal training support should be justified by the evaluative capacity it produces rather than by the papers the trainees will write. The papers are about to be cheap. The evaluative capacity is not.
That last point cuts against how the case is currently made and how it is currently being decided. The National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Graduate Research Fellowship Program collapsed in 2025, rebounded to nearly 2,600 awards in April 2026, and the agency’s own solicitation now expects 1,500 next year, with the fiscal year 2027 request proposing just over a 40% cut. Defenders of that program have generally argued that the fellows produce valuable research. That argument is genuinely weaker this month than it was last month, and we should stop making it.
The concrete version of the alternative is not complicated. Congress should reverse the FY 2027 reduction and restore the fellowship program to at least its 2026 level. Additionally, the NSF should attach an evaluative track to a share of the awards, in which fellows spend part of their training independently reproducing and digesting machine-generated results in their field, with the digested version counting as a funded deliverable rather than as service. The NSF and the National Institutes of Health should stand up paid verification teams on the model those nine mathematicians improvised in May and should require any federally funded project that builds on AI-generated findings to budget for independent checking of them. The mathematicians wrote their companion paper because they were willing to spend the time. Willingness is not a policy instrument.
The magnitudes here are worth holding side by side. One laboratory spent millions of dollars on compute for a single conjecture in September, a thousand times what it had spent on any problem before. Keeping in existence the small number of people who can tell the rest of us whether that answer means anything costs a rounding error against the price of generating it, and it is the only part of the enterprise that money cannot buy back quickly.
The argument that survives is that we are about to have far more machine-generated science than we have people qualified to evaluate it. The pipeline that produces those people takes a decade to refill. It takes about three years to break.

articles.title: Main findings from the ECB’s recent contacts with non-financial companies
articles.text: Main findings from the ECB’s recent contacts with non-financial companiesPrepared by Davide Fantino, Alex Melemenidis, Richard Morris, Zsuzsanna Riedel and Moreno RomaThis box summarises the main findings from recent contacts between ECB staff and representatives of 64 leading non-financial companies operating in the euro area.[1] For further information on the nature and purpose of these contacts, see Elding, Morris and Slavík (2021). The exchanges mainly took place between 28 September and 7 October 2026.Reports from contacts pointed to ongoing moderate growth in activity in the third quarter and towards unchanged momentum in the fourth quarter (Chart A and Chart B). Activity in the manufacturing sector was uneven with a very strong rise in demand for high value-added electronics, electrical equipment and related machinery. Meanwhile, many other industries continued to struggle with low, flat or declining volumes amid intensifying import competition. Construction and real estate activity were also losing momentum. The hot and dry summer weighed on agricultural output and food production, but it increased the demand for air conditioning and thereby raised energy output. Retail trade and related transport services remained relatively subdued, but most other business and consumer services experienced good growth.Chart ASummary of views on activity, employment, prices and costs(averages of ECB staff scores)Source: ECB.Notes: The scores reflect the average of scores given by ECB staff in their assessment of what contacts said about quarter-on-quarter developments in activity (sales, production and orders), input costs (material, energy, transport, etc.) and selling prices, and about year-on-year wage developments. Scores range from -2 (significant decrease) to +2 (significant increase). A score of 0 denotes no change. For the current round, previous quarter and next quarter refer to the third and fourth quarters of 2026 respectively, while for the previous round these refer to the second and third quarters of 2026. Discussions with contacts in January and in March/April regarding wage developments normally focus on the outlook for the current year compared with the previous year, while discussions in June/July and September/October focus on the outlook for the next year compared with the current year. The historical average is an average of scores compiled using summaries of past contacts extending back to 2008.Chart BViews on developments in and the outlook for activity(averages of ECB staff scores)Source: ECB.Notes: The scores reflect the average of scores given by ECB staff in their assessment of what contacts said about quarter-on-quarter developments in activity (sales, production and orders). Scores range from -2 (significant decrease) to +2 (significant increase). A score of 0 denotes no change. The dot refers to expectations for the next quarter.Contacts painted a mixed but still mostly subdued picture of consumer spending. Retailers continued to perceive consumers’ price sensitivity and resulting downtrading as a major determinant of consumption dynamics, especially in Germany and France where consumer sentiment was particularly low. Contacts in – or supplying – the consumer durable goods sector reported weak or falling demand for furniture and household appliances, attributed in part to subdued housing investment. However, they noted rising demand for consumer electronics (in anticipation of rising prices) and passenger cars. In the case of passenger cars, this was reflected in surging demand for battery electric vehicles owing to high fuel prices and rapidly growing purchases of hybrid vehicles imported from China. Growth in spending on consumer services was said to be relatively robust, especially for digital services (mobile data etc.). Despite being negatively affected by the conflict in the Middle East, tourism-related spending was proving resilient as destinations in the euro area benefited from the diversion of tourism away from destinations closer to conflict areas.Growth in business investment and spending was increasingly driven by AI, electrification, defence and aerospace, although activity and investment in many sectors remained subdued. Contacts in the software and IT consulting industries reported ongoing, exceptional growth as customers accelerated their digital transformation, modernised legacy infrastructure, adopted cloud solutions and increasingly integrated AI into their processes. Such demand was particularly strong in the public, defence, health, life sciences, technology and utility sectors. Geopolitical independence was an important consideration with firms increasingly seeking to keep data within sovereign frameworks. Euro area engineering exports were already benefiting from the global data centre construction boom and data centre construction was also gathering pace in the euro area. Geopolitical concerns underpinned surging demand for defence and aerospace equipment, while high oil and gas prices, as well as data centre construction, were generating increasing demand for renewable energy infrastructure. Activity and investment in the steel industry was starting to benefit from recent policy changes – most notably, the application of stricter import quotas and tariffs since 1 July 2026. However, other process industries, such as food, chemicals, textiles, pulp and paper, continued to face weak demand amid high energy, labour and regulatory costs and intense international competition, causing them to scale back investment. Concerns about rising government bond yields and upcoming elections in some countries also weighed on the business outlook.Employment dynamics remained subdued. On balance, contacts reported declining headcounts in both the manufacturing sector and, albeit to a lesser extent, the services sector. Reductions in employment remained strong in manufacturing industries undergoing structural cost-cutting to regain international competitiveness. However, this was partly offset by growth in sectors such as IT, aerospace, defence and energy, as well as in firms supplying those sectors. In services, many contacts reported a stable employment outlook as a rise in demand could be met through productivity gains, with AI increasingly cited as a facilitator. Meanwhile, recruitment agencies pointed to moderating declines or modest increases in staffing, although this was mainly driven by temporary placements rather than permanent hiring.Contacts reported stronger increases in selling prices in the third quarter, amid higher than anticipated cost pressures, with some moderation expected in the fourth quarter (Chart C). Strong price increases were observed in energy and transport and logistics owing to the elevated price of oil and gas products resulting from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Strong price increases were also seen in much of the capital goods sector, partly reflecting strong demand and partly reflecting the surging prices of memory chips caused by the AI boom and related data centre construction. Despite stronger aggregate price dynamics than anticipated a few months ago, the pass-through of cost increases resulting from the conflict in the Middle East was becoming increasingly challenging, with costs rising further or remaining elevated as hedges expired and contracts were renewed. This pass-through was particularly difficult – and more limited – in consumer-facing sectors. Around 90% of contacts from consumer-facing firms said that the pass-through to selling prices was only partial or limited, compared with less than half of those from business-facing firms (Chart D). The main reasons were cited as weak demand and competitiveness pressures. Consistent with this, selling price growth was expected to moderate somewhat in the coming months. However, contacts expected that cost pressure would continue to be felt by many into 2027 as hedges would continue to expire, agricultural commodity prices would rise and supplier price increases would continue to feed through.Chart CViews on developments in and the outlook for prices(averages of ECB staff scores)Source: ECB.Notes: The scores reflect the average of scores given by ECB staff in their assessment of what contacts said about quarter-on-quarter developments in selling prices. Scores range from -2 (significant decrease) to +2 (significant increase). A score of 0 denotes no change. The dot refers to expectations for the next quarter.Chart DAssessment of the pass-through of higher costs resulting from the Middle East conflict to selling prices(percentage of responses)Source: ECB.Expectations for decelerating wage growth have moderated somewhat (Chart E). On average, the quantitative indications provided by contacts imply that wage growth is expected to slow from 3.2% in 2025 to 3.0% in 2026 and 2.9% in 2027. This is a milder deceleration than in previous survey rounds. Consistent with this, around 40% of contacts thought that the uptick in inflation caused by the conflict in the Middle East would result – or risked resulting in – higher wage demands (up from 20% during the previous survey round). Most, however, still did not anticipate any notable impact on wage growth, citing the subdued economic conditions and employment outlook.Chart EQuantitative assessment of wage growth(percentages)Source: ECB.Notes: Averages of perceptions of wage growth of contacts in their sector in 2025 and their expectations for 2026 and 2027. The averages for 2025, 2026 and 2027 are based on indications provided by 50, 55 and 51 respondents respectively.Contacts had been negatively surprised by the duration of the conflict in the Middle East but positively surprised by how firms had adapted to it. This round, we asked our contacts how they assessed the impact of the conflict in the Middle East on business conditions in their sector and how this compared with their expectations at the onset of the conflict. Around 40% said that activity in their sector had decreased as a consequence, while 20% said it had increased. Most, however, emphasised the impact on costs with almost 80% saying that costs had risen. Views were rather equally split between those saying that the impact on their business had been “worse than” or “better than” expected. Those that thought the impact had been worse than expected tended to point to the duration of the conflict, which contrasted with prior expectations for a more rapid resolution. Those that thought the impact had been better than expected instead pointed to the surprising resilience and adaptability of businesses and their supply chains. Some attributed this to what firms had learned and how they had adapted, as well as the information systems they had put in place, following a series of shocks (tariffs, pandemic and war) over the past decade.ReferencesElding, C., Morris, R. and Slavík, M. (2021), “The ECB’s dialogue with non-financial companies”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 1, ECB. For further information on the nature and purpose of these contacts, see Elding, Morris and Slavík (2021).

articles.title: What 100 Economies Have Taught Us About Climate and Development
articles.text:
Published on
Voices

What 100 economies have taught us about climate and development

Paschal Donohoe

October 28, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Credit: Isaura Martins, Amend

The current El Niño is a reminder of how quickly climate shocks can become development challenges. Drought can wither crops and drain the reservoirs that power homes and factories. Heavy rainfall can wash away schools, roads, and other infrastructure. The effects vary from place to place, but the lesson is widely shared: countries need to build resilience through smart development that protects livelihoods, creates jobs, and drives growth.
That is the thinking behind the World Bank Group’s Country Climate and Development Reports (CCDRs). Driven by national development priorities, the series now covers 100 economies, with São Tomé and Príncipe the latest addition. Each CCDR supports countries with a practical roadmap for resilient, low-carbon growth that advances their wider development priorities, from jobs and energy security to better health. They are complemented by annual summary reports that highlight the key global insights, with four reports published so far on infrastructure and the macroeconomy, the interplay with nature and role of forestry, the vulnerability and agency of people, and the implications for jobs.
Reaching 100 economies is a milestone and a good moment to ask what we have learned. I see four lessons and two priorities for the road ahead.
Start with countries’ development priorities
Countries make progress when investments serve their priorities: better jobs, more reliable energy, cleaner air, better infrastructure, or greater resilience. That means listening to what countries identify as their most pressing development challenges and where they see opportunities for action. That principle, set out in the first CCDR for Türkiye in 2022, has guided the series ever since.
Many investments serve multiple goals at once. Resilient infrastructure costs less to maintain and provides a stronger foundation for growth. Affordable renewable power lowers energy costs while reducing exposure to global price shocks and emissions. Public transport eases congestion, improves air quality, and connects people to jobs. Financial inclusion helps households manage climate shocks and invest in their livelihoods.
Where countries see opportunities to pursue these goals, they can leapfrog to technologies that support growth and expand access to essential services. To highlight a few examples. In Niger, off-grid solar is a cost-effective way to expand rural energy access and a low-carbon solution. In Fiji, renewable power and energy efficiency reduce dependency on expensive imported fuels. In Morocco, low-carbon manufacturing can strengthen access to and competitiveness in European markets. In Thailand, flood management is essential to protecting the country’s position in global manufacturing value chains.
Boost job creation by helping workers and businesses adapt to change
Climate change is reshaping labor markets alongside demographic shifts, digitalization, artificial intelligence, and migration. Putting people at the center of development also means helping countries adapting to these changes and adopting reforms that remove barriers to opportunity, from skills gaps and limited mobility to exclusion, and gender barriers.
Tajikistan will need 65,000 temporary workers for rooftop solar installations. As demand for this work tapers off, there is a risk of workforce oversupply. The CCDR identifies policy options to support reskilling, training, and lifelong learning as demand changes. In Brazil, 88 percent of formal job switches occur within the same state, suggesting that regional development strategies could support areas with high concentrations of at-risk jobs.
Link investment decisions to economic policy
Experts often know how to use water more efficiently, improve energy efficiency, and better manage floods and extreme temperatures. But this knowledge is often stuck in silos, lacks political commitment to implement or has insufficient resources.
Linking decisions on energy, transport, agriculture, and water to growth, jobs, poverty reduction, and financial stability can help translate countries’ ambition into action. CCDRs have helped bring these issues from line ministries into discussions with finance and planning ministries, where priorities are set, budgets allocated, and implementation decisions are made. For example, in Côte d’Ivoire, the Council of Ministers endorsed the CCDR as a government-owned document and charged the Prime Minister’s office with taking it forward.
Turn insights into action
These diagnostics help countries identify opportunities they want to take forward, including by mobilizing development finance and World Bank Group operations. Today, 42 percent of CCDR opportunities are being addressed through World Bank Group financing.
Turning opportunities into action means choosing priorities carefully based on development gains, feasibility, and urgency. When these factors align with national priorities, progress comes quickly. A few years ago, the growth of solar power in Pakistan or electric mobility in Nepal might have seemed unrealistic. Both advanced because they aligned with national priorities and had strong leadership behind them.
Bring private-sector knowledge and finance to the table
Moving forward, closer engagement with the private sector can make recommendations more practical, investable, and responsive to market realities. Businesses and financial institutions know best what prevents firms from investing and innovating, and which reforms would help. The next generation of reports will draw more systematically on this private sector expertise to assess risks and help countries prioritize interventions.
Put nature on the balance sheet
The reports for Cambodia, Peru, Ethiopia, and Fiji show how natural assets support jobs, resilience, and growth. Future diagnostics will better integrate ecosystem services, nature-related financial risks and natural capital into economic analysis to inform country policy and investment choices.
Taken together, these lessons point to a clear role for the World Bank Group: start with country demand. Our role is to support countries with the best development knowledge, financing, and partnerships to turn their priorities into action and investment for climate-smart development.

articles.title: Margins matter in US midterm elections | RBCCM
articles.text:
The U.S. military escalation against Iran appears increasingly likely despite growing pre-election pressure, with both Washington and Tehran maintaining entrenched negotiating positions. The conflict has proven impervious to pre-election off-ramps, expanding in scope with Houthi entry into the war. Regional talks in Tehran and Vice President Vance's reported outreach to Iran's hardline Supreme National Security Council secretary suggest the administration is calibrating rather than reversing course.
The critical strategic question is whether U.S. military action will constitute a final strike before withdrawal, or will be a more extensive operation designed to finish the job and orchestrate regime change. Some regional actors warn that a brief escalation followed by hasty exit would essentially amount to an Iranian victory despite reconstruction costs. Others caution that a sweeping military campaign dramatically increases the risk of Iranian retaliatory strikes on critical civilian infrastructure, including desalination facilities, alongside expanded proxy attacks on U.S. allies throughout the region.
While Congress cannot force an end to the war, Democratic control of either or both chambers will likely intensify efforts to control the purse strings. Even if the administration maintains veto authority over broad policy reversals, Democratic gains could embolden Republicans to challenge the administration's authority on Iran war funding through year-end defense legislation. With the size of Tuesday's Democratic victory determining the degree of Republican defections likely, the midterm results will substantially influence congressional leverage over military spending and escalation decisions heading into 2027.
A Democratic House victory would trigger a wave of hearings and investigations on energy deals involving administration insiders and military actions affecting major global producers. Venezuela will face intense scrutiny, with lawmakers seeking to determine whether oil companies had advance knowledge of the January military operation against Nicolás Maduro. Inquiries could expand to examine whether companies received privileged information or benefited from the operation, and challenge the Pentagon's authority to take a 35 percent stake in North American Blue Energy Partners.

"Even if the [Democratic] party only captures the House of Representatives, we anticipate a wave of hearings and investigations on energy deals involving administration insiders, as well as military actions/foreign policy decisions involving key global producers."
Helima Croft, Head of Global Commodity Strategy and MENA Research, RBC Capital Markets

Russia sanctions waivers and the recent diesel deal will draw bipartisan criticism, particularly from GOP Russia critics including Senators Susan Collins, Mitch McConnell, and Lisa Murkowski. Democratic-led committees will review the administration's suspension of sanctions measures mandated by the Graham Act, which authorizes 100 percent secondary tariffs on imports from Russia oil purchasers and imposes further restrictions on Russian banks and energy investment.
The scale of a Democratic victory could influence whether Republicans defect to challenge the administration's waiver authority through defense legislation. Beyond Venezuela and Russia, congressional reviews will likely examine government equity stakes in critical mineral firms and CFTC investigations into large energy trades around Iran war developments.
Growing concerns over electricity affordability could reshape the administration's data center acceleration initiative, despite likely bipartisan backing for AI and data center infrastructure expansion. The House's bipartisan passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act signals growing support for requiring data centers to shoulder their own costs. Democratic control would pursue stricter oversight, with House Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin already investigating major hyperscalers over nondisclosure agreements with local governments regarding data center projects.

View detailed data

Figure 2, titled "Iran War Tops Midterm Voter Priorities*," is a horizontal bar chart ranking nine political, economic, and geopolitical issues by their mean importance rating from voters on a 1-to-5 scale, with the x-axis displaying a truncated range from 3.0 to 4.0. From highest to lowest, the issues and their approximate mean scores are: Iran War at approximately 3.87 (highlighted in yellow), Jobs at approximately 3.80, Tariff Policy at approximately 3.72, Immigration at approximately 3.69, Gas Prices at approximately 3.69 (highlighted in yellow), AI Regulation at approximately 3.66, Interest Rates at approximately 3.55, Israel-Gaza at approximately 3.32, and Data Centers at approximately 3.21 (highlighted in yellow). The remaining bars are dark navy blue. The footer notes the sources as Emerson College and RBC Capital Markets, based on a National Poll conducted September 21–22, 2026, where respondents rated each issue from 1 (least important) to 5 (most important), with scores representing mean ratings and a sample size of n=1000.

Democratic congressional control could complicate broader efforts to expand conventional energy production and roll back environmental regulations. New majorities could investigate federal leasing decisions, environmental deregulation, and DOE funding allocations. Clean energy developers could benefit from heightened oversight of restrictions on offshore wind and solar approvals, though presidential veto authority and existing executive powers would limit Democrats' ability to reverse policies or reinstate repealed incentives.
Bipartisan permitting reform offers the clearest avenue for legislative cooperation, yet skepticism remains that this historical nonstarter could succeed post-election. The recently introduced American Affordability and Jobs Act seeks to accelerate energy infrastructure development across conventional and renewable technologies, though Democrats increasingly demand assurances against discriminatory treatment of clean energy projects. A sizable Democratic victory could strengthen their leverage, potentially complicating passage in the lame-duck session.
Ultimately, Democratic gains could constrain the administration's energy agenda through congressional oversight and legislative leverage, even as the administration pursues priorities through executive and regulatory authority.

Helima Croft authored "Washington Strategy: Margins Matter," published on October 28, 2026. For more information on the full report, please contact your RBC representative.

Fed Pauses as Rate Recalibration Continues

The U.S. Federal Reserve held its policy rate steady at 3.75%–4.0% at its October meeting, pausing after September’s 25-basis-point (bp) hike while maintaining a clear tightening bias. We expect another 25-bp hike in December and see a risk of one additional increase in early 2027, followed by an extended hold. In our view, this remains a recalibration of policy rather than the start of a prolonged rate-hiking cycle.
Going into Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference, the central question was why the Fed would wait to hike again when growth remains strong and inflation elevated. Warsh’s explanation was that policymakers want more time to assess how September’s hike and tighter financial conditions are affecting the economy. A majority of the committee, he suggested, believes “the medicine is starting to work.”

A pause to assess tightening already underway

The case for holding rested partly on financial conditions. Longer-term U.S. Treasury yields have risen meaningfully in 2026, increasing borrowing costs and offsetting some of the growth support from strong equity markets. (Learn more in our 30 September 2026 Macro Signposts.)
In addition, credit spreads have recently widened for lower-quality borrowers (mainly CCC rated issues) and certain parts of the AI value chain whose business models are particularly dependent on high initial investment and uncertain amounts of ongoing maintenance investment. This is consistent with Warsh’s comments that tech investment is sensitive to interest rates and provides policymakers with room to wait and assess the effects of higher rates rather than moving at consecutive meetings.
Still, a pause does not mean the Fed has finished adjusting policy. Domestic spending remains resilient, capital investment is robust, and inflation has moved sideways. Those conditions leave policymakers wary of allowing above-target inflation to persist, whether because demand remains stronger than expected or because renewed supply shocks add to price pressures.
The statement said that the “accumulation of more information” would help determine the policy stance needed to ensure a timely return to 2% inflation. We interpret that language as preserving flexibility over the timing and extent of further tightening, rather than signaling that September’s hike was sufficient.
The committee’s voting pattern also points to a debate about pace. The October decision passed 10–2, with Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack preferring another 25-bp hike. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari, who had dissented in favor of a hike in July, supported the hold in October. Their support is consistent with a willingness to proceed gradually, and it aligns with many Fed policymakers who (in recent comments as well as the September meeting minutes) have continued to frame further tightening as a risk management exercise in case of stronger-than-expected demand or renewed supply-side inflation pressure.
Importantly, Warsh did not endorse the view that the economy is clearly overheating. He indicated that most of his colleagues do not judge the economy to be running too hot and highlighted that inflation expectations have been stable.

A recalibration, not a prolonged hiking cycle

Warsh also outlined changes to the Fed’s meeting schedule. It will continue to meet eight times annually, but beginning in the fall of 2027, one meeting will be devoted to monetary policy strategy rather than a policy vote. In 2028, that structure will shift to six policy meetings and two strategy meetings without policy votes. Which meeting will first move to the strategy format has not yet been determined.
The distinction creates more dedicated space for strategic discussion, but it does not itself signal a different destination for interest rates. As we argued after the September meeting (see our 16 September 2026 Macro Signposts), the Fed’s adjustment may be more than insurance against an unfavorable inflation outcome. It also reflects dissatisfaction with the speed of inflation’s return to target. October’s pause does not change that underlying motivation.
Nevertheless, this is not 2022. Moderating wage growth and unit labor costs, alongside strong productivity, support a more measured response than a broad-based, labor-driven overheating episode would require.
Our baseline remains a December hike, with a risk of one further increase in early 2027 before an extended hold. Importantly, higher expected policy rates – not rising term premia – have driven much of the increase in longer-term yields. Over the next few meetings, preserving that tightening depends on the Fed delivering the hikes markets have priced in; otherwise, financial conditions could ease, helping to keep inflation elevated. As we move into 2027, however, clearer signs of disinflation and a larger drag from higher borrowing costs could reduce the need for further rate hikes. The medicine may be starting to work, but the Fed has not yet declared the treatment complete.

articles.text:
Webinar

AI winners and losers: a global sector view

Register Now

12 November 20262 sessions:12 November 2026 – 1.00pm HKT (Hong Kong/ 4pm Sydney)12 November 2026 – 2.00pm GMT (London / 10am New York)

online

AI is already changing the shape of the global economy, but the gains are far from evenly spread. Indeed, AI investment is concentrated on a narrow set of products, mainly chips, servers, software, and data centres, and much of the hardware is made in a handful of tech-focused economies.

Consequently, a continuation of the boom or a sharp bust would impact some industries and economies much more significantly than others. Over the longer term, our research shows differences in AI exposure and levels of adoption could open large gaps in productivity and output across sectors. In this webinar, Makoto Tsuchiya and Charlie Muir will present the global sector level results of our AI scenarios, covering:

Short-term boom and bust: changes in data centre demand affects tech-exporting economies the most, with impacts concentrated in electronic components and semiconductors. In a tech downturn, a stock market correction would also drag on consumer spending, spreading to household-facing and other non-AI sectors.

Long-term productivity: how exposed each industry is to AI in production, and how widely AI is adopted, drives differences in productivity gains, with implications for economic activity across sectors and economies.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Charlie Muir

Charlie is a Senior Economist in the industry team, based in London. He works on the global industry service, where his main focus is improving the service through model development and research alongside the regular forecast updates. He also runs the industry climate service and works on AI strategy for the team. Previously, he coordinated the forecast updates for the global industry service and was responsible for forecasting the consumer goods sectors.He achieved a first-class degree in Economics at the University of Bath and joined Oxford Economics in July 2021.

Senior Economist, Industry

Makoto Tsuchiya

Makoto Tsuchiya is an Economist at Oxford Economics. He oversees the forecast and analysis of the electronics sector, including semiconductors. He also works on a wide range of client projects, by way of producing bespoke forecasts as well as written reports. Makoto has a Bachelor’s degree from Temple University Japan where he majored in Economics with a minor in Business Studies. He also has sophisticated knowledge in the corporate accounting field.

articles.title: Crypto and Blockchain Venture Capital – Q3 2026
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Crypto and Blockchain Venture Capital – Q3 2026

Research • October 28, 2026 • 10 mins
Crypto and Blockchain Venture Capital – Q3 2026
Activity cooled in Q3, led by a pullback in later-stage financing, while the number of new funds raised fell to just three.

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

Cryptocurrency

Ventures

Introduction Cryptocurrency venture capital activity cooled in Q3 2026 after rebounding in Q2. In total, VCs deployed ~$4.5 billion into privately held crypto and blockchain-related companies across 296 deals. Capital invested fell 20% quarter-over-quarter, while deal count decreased 24%, with the decline in capital driven primarily by later-stage financing. Raising new venture funds remains difficult, and Q3 saw three new crypto venture funds raised, the fewest in any quarter since Q3 2019. Still, crypto venture activity remains healthy overall. Trading, exchange, investing, and lending businesses again attracted the most dollars, while payments/rewards led deal count and DeFi, privacy/security, tokenization, AI, infrastructure, Web3/NFT/DAO/metaverse/gaming, and enterprise blockchain also drew meaningful activity. Later-stage companies captured 76.5% of capital invested, while pre-seed and seed rounds accounted for 44.9% of completed deals. U.S.-headquartered startups accounted for 74.9% of capital invested and 44.6% of the 296 deals.
Key Takeaways Crypto VC activity declined in Q3 2026, with $4.5 billion invested across 296 deals. The 2026 year-to-date run rate annualizes to roughly $19.383 billion, slightly below 2025’s $20.3 billion total but above the pace seen during most of the 2023-2024 downturn. Later-stage deals captured roughly 76% of the capital invested in Q3, while earlier-stage deals accounted for 18% and seed/pre-seed made up the remaining 6%. Among startup categories tracked by Galaxy Research, Trading/Exchange/Investing/Lending received the most venture capital (roughly $2.370 billion), while Payments/Rewards led deal count with 38 deals. The U.S. continues to dominate capital invested and deal count, capturing 74.9% of dollars and 44.6% of transactions. Investors allocated roughly $1.3 billion to three new crypto venture funds in Q3.
Venture Investing
Deal Count and Capital Invested In Q3, venture capitalists invested $4.519 billion (-20% QoQ) into crypto and blockchain-focused startups and private companies across 296 deals (-24% QoQ).

The decrease from Q2 was driven primarily by a decline in later-stage financing. Capital invested decreased less than deal count, indicating that larger financings held up relatively well. For the year to date, VCs have invested $14.537 billion in crypto across 1,040 deals. Annualizing the first three quarters would imply roughly $19.383 billion of capital invested this year, slightly below 2025’s total but above the pace set during much of 2023 and 2024.

Capital Invested and Bitcoin Price The correlation between the bitcoin price and capital invested into crypto startups seen during prior cycles remains weaker than it was in 2017 and 2021. Bitcoin reached new highs in late 2025 while venture activity was uneven, and in Q3 2026 bitcoin rallied while capital invested fell.

Investment by Stage In Q3, 76% of capital invested went to later-stage startups, while 24% went to younger companies.

By deal count, pre-seed deals’ share of the total grew to 25%, while later-stage investments slipped to 24% of completed transactions. We track pre-seed transactions’ share to gauge entrepreneurial behavior and investor risk appetite. Later-stage deals’ share of the total remained elevated compared to the historical norm, reflecting the market's growing maturity.

Valuation and Deal Size VC-backed crypto company valuations (bars, left-hand vertical axis in the chart below) climbed to new all-time highs in Q4 2025, exceeding 2021’s then-record levels. Valuations in Q1 and Q2 2026 declined sharply from that high water mark before rebounding to a new all-time high of roughly $90m in Q3 2026, while valuations across the broader VC complex outside of crypto also rose to a new high in Q3. In Q3 2026, the median crypto deal size (fever line, right-hand axis) fell sharply from Q2’s all-time high of $5.0m to roughly $3.0m. (Note: Valuation data is sparse compared to the total universe of deals. For example, we only have valuation data for 12% of deals completed in Q3 2026 and the valuations that are available skew heavily to later-stage transactions.)

Investments by Category Companies in our Trading/Exchange/Investing/Lending category raised the most capital from crypto VCs, retaining the top spot by pulling in roughly $2.370 billion, or about half of Q3 capital invested. Privacy/Security was second at roughly $467 million, followed by Payments/Rewards, Data, Enterprise Blockchain, Banking, Infrastructure, Web3/NFT/DAO/Metaverse/Gaming, and DeFi.

Looking at the share of venture capital invested by category over time, the dollars deployed in recent quarters, including Q3, were unusually concentrated in Trading/Exchange/Investing/Lending compared to the historical norm. Outside that category, dollars were led by Privacy/Security and Payments/Rewards, followed by Data, Enterprise Blockchain, Banking, Infrastructure, Web3/NFT/DAO/Metaverse/Gaming, DeFi, and Tokenization.

The market was much more diverse than the dollar totals suggest. By deal count, Payments/Rewards led with 38 deals, followed by Trading/Exchange/Investing/Lending with 34 and DeFi with 31, then Enterprise Blockchain with 30, Tokenization and Web3/NFT/DAO/Metaverse/Gaming with 25 each, and Privacy/Security with 21.

The deal-count picture remains diverse when viewed over time. Payments/Rewards represented roughly 13% of Q3 deals.

Investment by Stage and Category Breaking down capital invested and deal count by category and stage gives a clearer picture of what types of companies in each category are raising funds. In Q3 2026, more than nine-tenths of capital invested in Trading/Exchange/Investing/Lending went to later-stage companies. Layer 1, Infrastructure, Privacy/Security, and Enterprise Blockchain also skewed heavily toward later-stage capital.

Analyzing the distribution of invested capital across different stages in each category reveals the relative maturity of various investment opportunities.

As in prior quarters, Q3 featured deals across a healthy dispersion of stages and categories.

Examining the share of deals done by stage in each category offers insight into the maturity of each investable category. Enterprise Blockchain, DeFi, Tokenization, Infrastructure, Banking, and Payments/Rewards all showed meaningful pre-seed or seed-stage activity, while Trading/Exchange/Investing/Lending and Layer 1 skewed more mature.

Investment by Cohort Startups founded in 2020 received the most venture capital in Q3 2026 at roughly $1.3 billion. Startups founded in 2022 captured the second-largest amount at roughly $500 million, followed by the 2016 and 2014 cohorts. Younger companies, led by the 2025, 2024, and 2022 vintages, dominated deal count.

Investment by Geographic Location In Q3 2026, 74.9% of capital represented went to companies headquartered in the United States, the most for any country by a wide margin, followed by Singapore with 12.7% and the United Kingdom with 2.9%.

The story was similar by deal count, though more geographically dispersed. Among the 296 deals represented, companies headquartered in the United States accounted for 44.6%, followed by the United Kingdom with 6.4% and Singapore with 5.1%.

Venture Fundraising Fundraising for crypto venture funds remains challenging. The macro environment and the turmoil in the crypto market from 2022-2023 have continued to dissuade some allocators from making the same level of commitments to crypto venture investments that they did in early 2021 and 2022. More recently, increased interest in artificial intelligence has also commanded some attention previously paid to crypto investing, while spot ETFs and digital asset treasury companies are also competing for institutional investment. In Q3 2026, the total capital allocated to crypto-focused venture funds was approximately $1.3 billion across three new funds, the fewest number of new funds in a quarter since Q3 2019.

On an annualized basis, year-to-date fundraising would imply roughly $8.2 billion for 2026, slightly below the $8.75 billion raised in 2025.

The year-to-date average fund size rose to roughly $386 million, while the median fund size fell slightly to $71 million.

Summary Activity pulled back in Q3 after Q2’s rebound but remains healthier than prior bear-market lows. Prior bull runs in 2017 and 2021 featured a high correlation between VC activity and liquid crypto asset prices, but that relationship has weakened. Q3 2026 saw bitcoin rally while venture activity fell, with capital invested decreasing less than deal count. Later-stage deals continued to lead capital raised. In Q3 2026, later-stage companies captured roughly 76% of invested capital, reflecting the industry’s maturity and the presence of larger, revenue-generating companies. Most completed deals were still earlier-stage rounds, while pre-seed firms accounted for roughly 25% of deal count. Venture dollars are consolidating around crypto’s financial plumbing. Trading/Exchange/Investing/Lending companies have captured a majority of capital invested for four straight quarters, after never exceeding a third of quarterly capital from 2022 through 2024. With seed-stage capital at its lowest level since Q4 2020, investors appear to favor companies that trade, move, and settle money onchain over earlier-stage consumer applications and new crypto primitives. Fund managers still face a difficult environment. Q3 2026 fundraising fell to $1.3 billion across three funds, the lowest new fund count since Q3 2019. Macroeconomic factors continue to present headwinds. With the CLARITY Act pushed back (maybe indefinitely), sovereign rates rising, continued conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, and upcoming mega IPOs from frontier AI labs, the landscape for raises looks tough in the short term. The United States continues to dominate the crypto startup ecosystem. Companies and projects headquartered in the United States accounted for most capital invested and the largest share of deals completed. That trend strengthened in Q3 2026, when U.S.-headquartered companies captured 74.9% of capital represented and 44.6% of the 296 deals represented.
