articles.title: Global responsible tax: How complicated is simplification?
articles.text:
KPMG International hosted a virtual roundtable discussion in July 2026, as part of the Global Responsible Tax Program, to explore what it would really take to simplify tax systems and what might be lost, gained or exposed in the process.Everyone wants tax to be simpler. It is a perennial challenge, with questions of certainty, compliance burden and basic comprehensibility consistently raised. A simpler system, many argue, would support growth, improve investment confidence and make it easier for taxpayers, businesses and revenue authorities to ‘do the right thing’. But the harder question is, what trade-offs are organizations prepared to make to get there?Tax systems are asked to do many things at once: raise revenue, support growth, redistribute fairly, encourage certain behaviors, deter others, provide certainty, prevent avoidance and remain administratively workable for taxpayers, advisers and revenue authorities alike. Complexity is often the result not simply of bad design, but of competing political, economic and social objectives being layered into the system over time.But how complicated can simplification be? Removing a relief may broaden the base and reduce distortion, but it may also remove targeted support. Fewer rules may make a system easier to understand, but they also may create more discretion, uncertainty or perceived unfairness. Harmonization across borders may help businesses and tax authorities operate more consistently, but it may also reduce national flexibility. Strong anti-avoidance rules may protect revenue and public trust, but it can also add complexity for those simply trying to comply.Technology and AI add a further dimension. Digital administration, data analytics, real-time reporting and automation may offer ways to make tax easier to navigate and administer. But if tax rules become more automated, who is responsible for interpretation and how can taxpayers understand and challenge decisions? If systems become easier to comply with but harder to see, has tax really become simpler? Held under the Chatham House Rule, the discussion brought together academics, policymakers, business representatives and civil society voices. The write-up below summarizes the personal views expressed and does not necessarily represent the position of any organization, including KPMG International Limited or any KPMG member firm.

Executive summary

Complexity is increasingly experienced as uncertainty
Discussion moved beyond the volume of legislation toward legal, administrative and policy uncertainty. Predictability, including confidence that rules, incentives and interpretations will endure, may matter as much as formal simplicity.

Process and design require different responses
Technology, pre-filled returns and better data can streamline administration, but they cannot resolve unclear policy choices or subjective rule design. Digitalizing a complex system may make compliance easier without making the underlying tax system simpler.

Shorter legislation is not necessarily simple
Detailed rules may provide certainty, while concise and principles-based laws may transfer complexity to guidance, tax officials and disputes. Legislative length is therefore an unreliable measure of practical simplicity.

Incremental reform may be more credible than wholesale redesign
Comprehensive reform could create disruption, implementation risk and an ‘economic freeze’ while businesses await clarity. Periodic pruning, improved data use, clearer thresholds and targeted procedural changes may offer a more practical route.

Rules should produce clearer outcomes
Regardless of legislative length, rules should generate yes or no answers wherever possible. This would improve certainty and remove cognitive burden for taxpayers and revenue authorities while making greater automation possible.

Small businesses bear disproportionate costs
Compliance costs, uncertainty and administrative friction are often regressive. Rules designed around large organizations, followed by exemptions or accommodations for smaller firms, may fail to reflect the limited financial and internal capacity of small and medium enterprises.

The economic case for simplicity remains central but can be complex to quantify
Some participants suggested that complexity can discourage hiring, investment and use of incentives, particularly among smaller businesses. However, further evidence quantifying these effects may be needed before simplification gains sustained political traction.

Tax may be carrying too many objectives
Some participants questioned whether redistribution and other equity goals should be pursued primarily through tax design or more directly through public expenditure and services. This raised a wider question about whether layering multiple social objectives into taxation contributes to unnecessary complexity.

Beyond the length of the law

Is complexity about how much legislation exists, or how effectively people use it?

It was agreed by many in the discussion that legislative length (or indeed number of taxes) is a poor proxy for the practical difficulty of a tax system. The length of the UK’s tax code is often cited in exasperation, but a lengthy provision may be relevant only to a narrow group and provide those taxpayers with valuable clarity. Conversely, a short or principles-based rule may create considerable uncertainty if it leaves important questions to interpretation.It is therefore important to distinguish between the volume of law and its effectiveness.The relevant test may not be how many people ultimately claim a relief or fall within a provision, but how many must spend time determining whether it applies to them. A narrowly used rule need not create widespread complexity if its intended users can identify and apply it easily.Clear drafting was seen as particularly important. Terms such as ‘reasonable,’ ‘normal’ or ‘just’ may permit flexibility, but they can also create blurred lines. Several participants favored rules that allow taxpayers to reach a clear yes or no answer in as many circumstances as possible.Periodic pruning of obsolete or duplicative provisions was supported, but not as a substitute for improving the usability of the law.

From complexity to uncertainty

Is the deeper economic problem unpredictability rather than complication?

As the discussion developed, many participants increasingly framed the challenge as one of uncertainty. Complexity and uncertainty are related, but they are not identical. A technically detailed system can still be relatively predictable, while a shorter and more discretionary system may produce divergent outcomes across regions, officials or taxpayers.Different forms of uncertainty were identified. Legal uncertainty concerns whether legislation provides an intelligible answer. Administrative uncertainty arises when the interpretation or behavior of a revenue authority is difficult to anticipate. Policy uncertainty reflects the frequency of rule changes and the possibility that taxes, reliefs or thresholds may be altered with limited notice.Long-term predictability was considered particularly important for investment. A business may be able to comply with a complicated incentive, but it may still decide not to invest if it cannot be confident that the relief will apply, that its claim will be accepted or that the policy will remain in place.One participant also raised the cognitive burden created by uncertainty. Businesses must devote management attention to interpreting rules and anticipating challenges, while governments and tax authorities must understand the interaction of numerous provisions before making further changes.Greater access to binding clearances was also suggested as a means of reducing the cost and risk associated with uncertainty over difficult legal interpretation and boundary questions.

Separating rule design from administrative process

Technology can streamline compliance, but can it simplify the underlying policy?

A central distinction emerged between the design of a tax and the process used to administer it. Either can be simple or complex independently of the other.Process simplification may offer the most immediate opportunities. Third-party reporting, pre-populated returns, integrated data systems and faster digital filing can reduce the information taxpayers must gather and submit themselves. Better use of third-party data may also narrow the tax gap by reducing non-reporting. However, some participants cautioned that the burden does not disappear; it may be transferred to banks, platforms, employers or other institutions required to provide the information. Where businesses are required to provide more third-party data, this should be considered holistically alongside opportunities to streamline or remove other tax or wider regulatory reporting requirements.It was also suggested that administrative complexity can also arise from limitations in revenue authority systems, particularly where these are fragmented or have not been upgraded for a significant period, requiring businesses to devote substantial time and resources to resolving issues that are not caused by the underlying tax rules.Several participants argued that machine-readable rules will increasingly require more structured conditions and clearer decision points. AI may assist by summarizing legislation, navigating guidance and identifying relevant provisions. However, one participant was wary that AI was the right way forward for tax legislation as its simplistic style can leave things out and hallucinate.

Designing for the smallest taxpayer

What would change if tax rules were built around small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) rather than adapted for them afterward?

The burden of tax complexity was described by one contributor as highly regressive. Large organizations can draw upon in-house tax teams, established relationships with revenue authorities and external advisers. Small and microbusinesses often lack comparable resources, making the same rule considerably more expensive for them to understand and administer. One contributor argued that tax jargon makes life harder and that language should be recognizable and understandable to taxpayers.Some participants argued that governments frequently ‘think large first’: rules are designed around the structures and capabilities of major organizations, with exemptions or simplified treatments added later for SMEs. This can produce a patchwork of thresholds, elections and special regimes that itself becomes difficult to navigate.The discussion of research and development incentives illustrated the problem. Some smaller businesses were said to be withdrawing from claims because the process, uncertainty or risk of challenge outweighed the expected benefit.Ideas included allowing microbusinesses to base tax more closely on their financial accounts, with reduced access to bespoke reliefs in exchange for lower compliance costs. Such approaches would involve trade-offs. Taxpayers might gain simplicity but lose opportunities to optimize their position.

International models

What can jurisdictions learn from one another without assuming that systems are inherently transferable?

International examples demonstrated that simplicity takes different forms.Singapore was cited as an example of a highly streamlined filing process supported by employer reporting and a relatively narrow range of taxable personal income. An individual with straightforward circumstances may be able to complete a return in minutes.At the same time, it was noted that this administrative simplicity is connected to wider choices about the tax base, redistribution and the role of government. A process cannot be separated entirely from the policy system it administers.India was mentioned as an example of technology and third-party data being used to pre-populate income information, facilitate electronic filing and accelerate processing. This illustrated how administrative reform can generate significant practical benefits even within a large and complex economy.The European Union (EU)’s emerging tax simplification agenda was discussed as an example of reform focused less on wholesale redesign than on cleaning up an increasingly layered body of rules. Participants pointed to the proposed tax simplification omnibus and the recast of the Directive on Administrative Cooperation as attempts to consolidate successive amendments, remove obsolete provisions and reduce overlaps between reporting regimes.Some proposals were seen as relatively straightforward administrative improvements, while others were more ambitious, including reducing withholding tax frictions on certain cross-border payments and reconsidering whether some anti-avoidance rules remain necessary where newer regimes, such as Pillar Two, already address similar risks.The central constraint is that EU tax measures generally require unanimous agreement among member states. This makes simplification both legally and politically demanding. The likely outcome is that the most pragmatic measures may progress, while more ambitious proposals are diluted, delayed or removed. The EU case therefore illustrates a broader lesson from the discussion: simplification is often easiest where it involves consolidation and duplication, but much harder where it requires governments to surrender discretion or accept a different balance between competitiveness, enforcement and national autonomy.

Incrementalism over wholesale reform

Can tax systems be improved without destabilizing economic activity?

Some participants were skeptical that wholesale reform could be implemented safely or sustainably. Rewriting numerous elements simultaneously would place significant demands on legislative drafters, revenue authorities, software providers, advisers and businesses. It could also create an ‘economic freeze’ as taxpayers delay decisions while waiting to understand the new system.The discussion therefore pointed toward incremental reform. Better use of third-party data, removal of duplicative reporting, clearer language, periodic review of thresholds and targeted improvements to areas of disproportionate burden may be more achievable than a single comprehensive redesign.Incrementalism is not without risks. Repeated small changes can themselves add complexity if they are not guided by a coherent direction. Participants’ comments therefore suggested a need for an enduring framework: reforms should be assessed against accessibility, certainty, administrative cost and economic impact, even when introduced separately.

Conclusions

Some participants were skeptical that wholesale reform could be implemented safely or sustainably. Rewriting numerous elements simultaneously would place significant demands on legislative drafters, revenue authorities, software providers, advisers and businesses. It could also create an ‘economic freeze’ as taxpayers delay decisions while waiting to understand the new system.The discussion therefore pointed toward incremental reform. Better use of third-party data, removal of duplicative reporting, clearer language, periodic review of thresholds and targeted improvements to areas of disproportionate burden may be more achievable than a single comprehensive redesign.Incrementalism is not without risks. Repeated small changes can themselves add complexity if they are not guided by a coherent direction. Participants’ comments therefore suggested a need for an enduring framework: reforms should be assessed against accessibility, certainty, administrative cost and economic impact, even when introduced separately.

articles.title: OFAC Sanctions North Korean IT Worker Fraud Scheme
articles.text:
Summary
OFAC sanctioned Russian and DPRK nationals that targeted U.S. businesses with fraudulent IT workers, generating cryptocurrency proceeds to fund the North Korean regime and its weapons programs.
Russian nationals Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov and Vitold Viktorovich Obertas converted millions of dollars in cryptocurrency on behalf of IT agencies that facilitated the placement of DPRK IT workers at target companies under false pretenses, enabling them to earn income.
DPRK nationals Kim Ki Hyok and Kim Hyo Dong managed groups of IT workers based in Russia, monitoring their work at victim companies and collecting the cryptocurrency income they generated.
On October 28, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity for their roles in North Korean government-run IT worker schemes that generate hundreds of millions in revenue for DPRK’s weapons programs.The action is the latest strike against a sprawling network of state sponsored North Korean agents who secretly seek employment in legitimate businesses, earn income, and pass that income along to fund the North Korean regime. This network has been growing in scope for years, posing a greater risk to corporations duped into hiring the agents, as well as providing Pyongyang with a steady flow of cash. In this instance, the DPRK workers and their facilitators leveraged Russian nationals to convert the crypto into cash.North Korean IT worker operations now span dozens of countries and generate an estimated $250 to $600 million in annual revenue for the DPRK regime, according to the United Nations panel of Experts. The threat has drawn a coordinated response from U.S. authorities: In May 2022, the FBI, State Department, and Treasury issued a joint advisory detailing how DPRK IT workers use VPNs, stolen identities, and proxy infrastructure to pass themselves off as non-North Korean freelancers or applicants.Since then, the U.S. Department of Justice has brought indictments against U.S.-based facilitators who operated laptop farms, forwarding equipment that helped DPRK IT workers fake a domestic presence during their employment at American companies. Today’s OFAC action targets the financial side of that same pipeline, the individuals and entities that convert the workers’ crypto earnings into usable funds for Pyongyang.The latest action targets a handful of individuals who helped that network convert their crypto into cash. Russians Vitold Viktorovich Obertas and Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov converted millions of dollars for front companies that provided a cover for DPRK IT workers, including Alis and Amnokang, both of which have been previously sanctioned. Our research into the Russians finds their relationships to these illicit networks stretches back years.The action also targets two DPRK nationals, Kim Ki Hyok and Kim Hyo Dong, who directly managed DPRK IT workers based in Russia. Both report to an umbrella company called Chinyong Information Technology Cooperation Company that OFAC designated in 2023 for its role in DPRK IT worker schemes. Our past research examines how groups like Chinyong launder crypto for the regime.Sanctioned actors facilitated crypto transactions for Chinyong, a North Korean state-run IT worker front companySince early 2025, Obertas has converted $2 million worth of cryptocurrency for DPRK officials, according to OFAC. But our research into his on-chain activity finds the relationship stretches back to early 2023.The below Reactor graph showcases the flow of funds that directly link crypto generated by DPRK IT workers to Obertas. On the left side is a DPRK worker who built code for blockchains and DeFi protocols, according to our research. The wallet’s inbound transaction history resembles that of a salaried worker: it received bi-weekly transfers of stablecoins for a period of months from late 2022 to early 2023.The IT worker wallet converted its stablecoins to ETH and passed it along to consolidation addresses that we track as sanctioned entities. From there the funds flow to Boykov, who sent the crypto along to Garantex, a now-sanctioned Russian exchange, for cashout. This on-chain relationship illustrates one instance of a financial fraud chain that adds up to millions of dollars.Amnokgang-linked facilitators and financial intermediaries were also designatedRussian national Vitold Viktorovich Obertas (Obertas) was also sanctioned for serving as an intermediary for illicit DPRK financial transactions, including those involving Amnokgang Technology Development Company (Amnokgang), which was itself designated in March for managing DPRK IT worker delegations.As the below Reactor chart shows, Obertas’ wallet received funds from Amnokgang. It also made deposits into accounts at both mainstream and sanctioned exchanges. Obertas has allegedly converted nearly $2 million in cryptocurrency into fiat for DPRK officials, according to OFAC.OFAC also designated FFTDC, a DPRK-controlled entity operating in Russia that deploys overseas IT workersAnother DPRK-controlled entity linked to today’s designations is the Russian-based First Financial and Technical Development Center (FFTDC), which has deployed IT workers who generate millions of dollars for North Korea. FFTDC was sanctioned today.These workers use AI tools and sophisticated money laundering techniques, including complex cryptocurrency transfers, to facilitate revenue generation. Since 2025, six Russia-based DPRK IT workers — Kim Kyong Ju, Ri Thae Chol, So Hyon Jin, Han Yu Song, Kim Sung Gwan, and Hyon Se Il — have collectively generated more than $750,000 for FFTDC. All six workers have been sanctioned.The use of AI marks a meaningful evolution in the IT worker threat. DPRK operatives have been observed using generative AI to fabricate resumes tailored to specific job postings, draft convincing cover letters, and prepare and conduct technical interviews. In some cases, workers have used AI-generated profile photos and deepfake video during hiring calls to conceal their identities. These tools lower the bar for less-skilled operatives to pass corporate screening processes, expanding the pool of workers the regime can deploy and making detection more difficult for employers who rely on interviews and document review as their primary safeguards.Pattern of DPRK cryptocurrency exploitationToday’s action is part of the Treasury’s sustained effort to counter North Korea’s abuse of cryptocurrency and digital assets for sanctions evasion. The DPRK has increasingly turned to cryptocurrency-related schemes to generate revenue, including IT worker fraud, state-sponsored cyber heists, and ransomware attacks demanding cryptocurrency payments. Chainalysis research has documented the DPRK’s growing sophistication in cryptocurrency theft and laundering, with North Korean hackers responsible for some of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record.We have labeled the designated cryptocurrency addresses in our product suite and have updated our screening solutions to include all designated individuals and entities from today’s action. Sending and receiving exposure to these addresses will trigger sanctions alerts for KYT customers, per their configured alert rules.If you’d like to learn more about how Chainalysis products can help protect your organization from sanctions risk and detect DPRK-related activity, request a demo. FAQWhat did OFAC announce on October 28, 2026?OFAC sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity for supporting North Korean government-run IT worker schemes that defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for the DPRK’s unlawful weapons programs.How do North Korean IT worker schemes operate?DPRK IT workers use fraudulent documents, stolen identities, and fabricated personas to obtain jobs at legitimate companies. The regime appropriates most of their earnings, while workers may also exploit corporate network access to steal sensitive data, deploy malware, and compromise business systems.How are cryptocurrency and financial intermediaries involved?DPRK-linked networks use cryptocurrency transactions, conversions, and money laundering techniques to move illicit proceeds. OFAC designated financial facilitators, including Russian national Vitold Viktorovich Obertas, who conducted nearly $2 million in cryptocurrency conversions and at least $1.25 million in other currency transactions for DPRK officials since January 2025.What role did Boykov, Kim Ki Hyok, and Kim Hyo Dong play?Russian national Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov supported Alis through cryptocurrency transactions, monitoring, and logistical assistance. DPRK national Kim Ki Hyok led an Alis IT worker delegation and transferred nearly $500,000 in cryptocurrency for the group. Kim Hyo Dong led a separate Chinyong-subordinate delegation, provided logistical assistance, engaged in sanctions evasion, and facilitated more than $100,000 in financial assets.What is FFTDC, and why was it sanctioned?The First Financial and Technical Development Center (FFTDC) is a DPRK-controlled entity located in Russia that deploys North Korean IT workers to generate revenue for the regime. OFAC sanctioned FFTDC and six DPRK IT workers who collectively generated more than $750,000 on its behalf since 2025.How can businesses detect DPRK-related sanctions exposure?Businesses can screen designated individuals, entities, and cryptocurrency addresses; monitor transaction exposure; and investigate suspicious activity involving overseas IT workers, cryptocurrency transfers, and potential sanctions evasion. Chainalysis customers can use updated screening and KYT alerts to identify exposure to addresses designated in this action. articles.title: Investment Accounting for Private Markets & AI | BNY
articles.text:
Data Management & AI

Using AI to Adapt Investment Accounting for Private Market Holdings

The Investment Accounting Shift for Private Markets & AI

calendar_today

26 Oct, 2026

Key Takeaways

Investment accounting is evolving from a recordkeeping function into a strategic data layer for portfolio-wide decision-making.The convergence of public and private markets requires a unified accounting foundation capable of supporting a total portfolio view.Modern accounting architectures can help firms simplify multi-basis reporting across regulatory, tax and financial reporting requirements.Added value from AI may not come from efficiency gains alone, but from generating new insights from unified investment data.

With unprecedented growth of private markets in recent years, the need to unify investment data to achieve a total portfolio view across public and private holdings has become paramount for heads of investment operations at asset managers and asset owners. Chief operating officers are rearchitecting their accounting foundation to build a data-centric strategic decision layer able to be leveraged by AI and convert accounting insights into competitive advantage.
Nearly 70% of asset managers cite data quality as the primary barrier to AI adoption, making achieving a unified ledger the critical enabler of AI insights.1 Additionally, the challenges firms must address regarding opaque and unstructured private markets reporting data, fragmented accounting systems and expanding global regulations continue to strain traditional investment workflows designed for liquid, publicly traded instruments.
The barriers are well known: entrenched organizational silos that resist data sharing across teams; technical debt from legacy systems that were never designed for real-time, multi-asset accounting; leadership misalignment on investment priorities and cultural resistance to change that keep firms anchored to familiar processes.

Unifying the Books of Record: IBOR and ABOR

Why a single multicurrency, multibasis ledger matters

Firms operating siloed investment book of record (IBOR) and accounting book of record (ABOR) systems are trapped managing reconciliation overhead and data gaps that lead to delayed decision-making. Unifying books of record on a single multicurrency, multi-basis ledger is the prerequisite for a true total portfolio view and real-time decision-making, because it eliminates the reconciliation lag between what the front office sees and what the official books record. The unification is a technical consolidation that creates the foundation making downstream capabilities such as multi-basis reporting, AI-driven insights and regulatory readiness possible.

Enlarge

Private Markets and Limited Partnership Lifecycle Accounting

Tracking the LP lifecycle

As private market holdings grow, firms are also grappling with tracking LP lifecycle events — commitments, capital calls, distributions — in the same system as public markets accounting, creating fragmented total portfolio views and manual workarounds. The solution is to integrate limited partnership lifecycle accounting into the same ledger as public-markets accounting, tracking initial commitment, funded and unfunded commitments, capital calls and distributions as first-class data objects on a unified platform. This integration approach can help decrease the amount of manual reconciliation between private and public holdings while also providing operations leaders with a single, authoritative view of committed and funded capital across the entire portfolio.

Multibasis Regulatory Reporting on a Single Ledger

GAAP, IFRS, statutory and tax in one transaction

The expanding and varied global regulatory landscape for private markets presents another common challenge for firms. Requirements such as the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive (AIFMD II) and Annex IV reporting in the European Union, the Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) Form PF reporting in the United States, Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) reporting requirements in the United Kingdom and Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) requirements in Singapore create complex and often overlapping data demands across jurisdictions.
Meeting these requirements can require firms to aggregate information across portfolio, investor, risk and fund accounting systems. Maintaining separate data sets and reporting processes across regulatory regimes can also increase duplication, inconsistency and operational and audit risk.
The solution: a single transaction that can support Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP), International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), statutory and tax bases simultaneously on one ledger. Each transaction would theoretically be tagged once at the source, and the platform would generate reports across all required bases without duplication or reconciliation between parallel ledgers while allowing for alternate accounting treatment and valuation. This approach potentially reduces regulatory risk, maintains consistency across filings and transforms compliance from a reactive, labor-intensive process into a byproduct of a well-architected accounting foundation.

AI-Enabled Accounting: From Efficiency to Insight

Intelligent document processing for private markets data

Once the fragmented data silos have been addressed in the accounting foundation, optical recognition technology can be utilized to extract structured data from the unstructured PDFs that private markets investors receive from general partners. Automated metadata classification further streamlines document ingestion. These capabilities directly address the data-quality barrier most asset managers identify as their primary obstacle to AI adoption. The unified accounting ledger is the critical enabler, because AI insights are only as reliable as the data foundation beneath them.

Enlarge

It’s not enough to say we’re using AI to improve efficiencies. It is important, and efficiency gains matter. But really, the next focus is to be able to generate novel insights, on-demand, for our clients by combining their data with ours.

Jay Hinton

Global Head of Product for Data and Analytics, BNY

The Case for Acting Now

Regulatory and market-structure changes are increasing data and operational demands. AIFMD II requirements are now being implemented across the EU, with further supervisory reporting changes applying from April 2027. With T+1 already in effect in the United States and European markets preparing to transition in October 2027, firms face increasing pressure to modernize and automate post-trade processes. Private markets growth continues to accelerate and the data-architecture work most firms need to be doing is not a next-year problem because 2027’s filings will depend on data captured from April 2026 onward.
Firms that delay rearchitecting their accounting foundation risk compounding reconciliation debt, missed regulatory deadlines and an AI-readiness gap that becomes harder to close. By contrast, establishing a unified accounting layer can provide the connective tissue between investment decisions and operational execution.
Content within this article was originally discussed on the December 2025 @RelationalAI podcast “From Data to Decisions: How BNY Is Operationalizing AI Responsibly,” featuring Jay Hinton, BNY Global Head of Products for Data & Analytics.

We take a deeper dive into the scenario assumptions, exploring a possible future in which geopolitical tensions continue to rise, populists gain political power, and the world fragments into trading blocs.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Paul Moroz

Paul Moroz holds an undergraduate degree in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE) from the University of Oxford and an MSc in Economics from Birkbeck, University of London. Paul contributes to the Global Climate Service, the Global Scenarios Service, and bespoke client scenarios.

Senior Economist - Scenarios and Macro Modelling

Harry Murphy Cruise

Harry Murphy Cruise is the Head of Economic Research and Global Trade at Oxford Economics Australia. He leads the Australian Macroeconomic Service and global trade initiatives, including TradePrism. Harry frequently provides insights to major media outlets, including CNBC, BBC, Reuters, and the Wall Street Journal. His research primarily focuses on global trade and investment flows, with particular interest in the challenges and opportunities of economic decoupling.

Harry holds a master’s degree in international and development economics from the Australian National University and a bachelor’s degree in arts and commerce from Monash University. He is a PhD candidate at ANU, exploring the role of China’s diverse households and firms in the country’s economic transition.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Harry was the Head of China and Australia Economics at Moody’s Analytics. He was previously responsible for Australian state and territory analysis at Deloitte Access Economics.

articles.title: The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick
articles.text:
The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick

Given at Mansion House

Published on
22 October 2026

In her first Mansion House speech as Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), Katharine Braddick sets out her vision for the PRA's second decade. She outlines plans for a new five-year strategy centred on four priorities: resilience, growth, innovation and transparency, alongside a series of reforms to strengthen operational resilience, streamline regulation and improve regulatory processes for firms.

Speech
Lady Mayor, thank you for inviting me to speak this evening. It is an honour to address you and your guests and a pleasure to be speaking alongside Nikhil, who I have known for many years and who I look forward to working with in this new role.
When I joined the PRA in July I joined an organisation that in a little over a decade had succeeded decisively in its initial core mission, a mission that is vital to the success of the United Kingdom and its economy: to restore the resilience of the financial sector, so that it can properly support businesses and households across the nation.
Thanks to the work of the PRA, and significant effort by industry, that resilience has not only been restored but significantly strengthened. This hard-won stability is a source of advantage for our financial sector and this country, and it underpins our position as a leading and trusted financial centre. It is also the principal legacy of my predecessor Sam Woods: we might all wish to say we had achieved such a thing in our careers.
In that decade or so the world has also, of course, changed. Security threats increase, exacerbated by a more fractured geopolitical landscape. Interconnected financial vulnerabilities are arising from stretched sectoral valuations, rising sovereign debt levels and increased market leverage. Technology presents extraordinary opportunities and material and novel risks. And society demands accountability and transparency from its public institutions to maintain their legitimacy.
A new long-term PRA strategy
In this context, then, our task is to determine what the PRA must deliver in its second decade and how to create the regulator the UK will need for the future. Next year I will publish for the first time a five-year strategy for the PRA. The strategy will set out how we intend to deliver four priorities I believe are central for the PRA’s future success:
Resilience
The first priority is resilience. Maintaining the resilience of the UK’s banking and insurance sectors is the foundation of our mission; the PRA identified early on that the need to address operational resilience as well as financial resilience is a prudential matter. Addressing non-financial resilience is an ever wider and more complex task, not least as the frequency and materiality of cyber incidents grows. Firms need to continue to invest in their capabilities, not only to prevent incidents, but to ensure they can respond to and recover from severe disruption.
The PRA similarly needs to evolve. We will significantly increase our focus on firms’ operational and cyber resilience. The cyber challenge, in particular, is an area where we can and do partner effectively with industry and our international counterparts to progress our understanding of both risks and mitigants. We will create a new PRA directorate, reporting directly to me, to act as a centre of excellence for operational and cyber resilience. We will also consult jointly with the FCA on a new supervisory statement by the end of the year, clarifying our expectations of firms as we develop our experience and understanding.
Growth
Our second theme is growth. Achieving sustained and sustainable growth is the key economic policy question of this moment and regulation has its part to play, even if it is rarely the determinative factor.
In the coming period we will further develop our framework for the secondary competitiveness and growth objective. It will address not only the costs and benefits of regulation, but how our work influences the investment environment, the availability of capital for the firms we regulate and the pricing of the services they provide. We will set out how that framework is embedded in our day-to-day decision-making, and how we will track the effect our work is having on the growth and international competitiveness of the UK.
This framework will help ensure our regime remains relevant, effective, and proportionate. We will engage industry and Parliament as we shape, use and learn from it. It will enable us to be clear and confident about our role, and articulate a well-founded understanding of our contribution to the economy. This is not just a means to deliver against the secondary objective but is ultimately a foundation for good regulation.
Of course, the PRA has already taken steps to keep our regime up to date, most recently working with our FCA colleagues to devise a new captive insurance regime to enable innovation and growth in the insurance market. And to remove barriers to growth and provide predictability, we consulted earlier this month on a framework to automatically index our regulatory thresholds with nominal growth, a first among major financial regulators.
As a next step, we have today set out with the FCA a second set of significant reforms to streamline the Senior Managers and Certification Regime. These proposals reduce the number of senior management functions requiring pre-approval and remove requirements relating to the certification regime, halving its regulatory burden on firms whilst retaining clear accountability of their senior leaders.
Innovation
Our third priority is innovation. The PRA is a world-class regulator. To continue to be so, we must become a world leading technologically enabled regulator. Working with industry, we will go further in refining the data we collect and how we collect it to ensure we can react to emerging issues and risks in a timely manner, while shrinking the need for ad hoc collections and removing collections whose benefits are not justified. We will take feedback from you on this as we go, refining our approach and prioritising the changes that add the most value.
We will accelerate our deployment of data analytics and new technologies, enabling supervisors to rapidly identify emerging themes and trends in risks. Working with industry, we will make it easier and more efficient to work with us by taking innovative approaches to data collection and enhancing the clarity and accessibility of our rulebook and supervisory guidance, streamlining communications so that firms can quickly and easily understand what we expect.
Transparency
And our fourth priority is transparency. A sound understanding of the intentions and priorities of the regulator is crucial for firms to be able to effectively plan and manage their risks. And a stable and predictable business environment is essential to enable investors to deploy capital in the UK economy. So we will provide a clear and transparent line of sight to firms, Parliament and society about our plans and priorities, not least through the publication of and reporting on the new strategy. That will provide the means for us to be held accountable for meeting our commitments and demonstrate that we are a listening and learning organisation.
As an early example of this approach, we will take decisive steps to improve the experience of banks and building societies in relation to internal models for residential mortgages. This has been a source of particular difficulty for many firms, and we need to learn the lessons of this experience.
The PRA has already improved the approval process for firms, and we will go further by providing additional transparency about our operational performance. We will consult in Spring next year on material policy changes to improve firms’ access to a modelled approach. These proposals will be subject to challenge by an independent panel of industry and regulatory experts to ensure their feasibility, learning the lessons of the past to ensure our future policy is grounded in operational realities. Working with our colleagues in the wider Bank, we will also examine the interactions between hybrid mortgage models and stressed buffer requirements.
And we will conduct an independent review of the UK’s implementation of hybrid mortgage model requirements to identify tangible ways to assist firms as they maintain and develop their models. The work of that review will be sequenced to ensure it does not jeopardise the delivery of ongoing model approval and policy work.
Delivering the strategy
The delivery of our strategy will rely on the considerable strengths that characterise the PRA: our deeply expert and purpose-driven people; our comprehensive knowledge of the firms we regulate; and our established approach to supervision – judgement-led, forward-looking and focussed on key risks to safety and soundness. That work has underpinned the success of the PRA’s first twelve years and must never be taken for granted.
As we take the PRA into its second decade, we will build on our strengths and track record by evolving our approach to meet the challenges of today and of tomorrow. We will ensure the financial sector remains resilient to the increasingly volatile environment we now face. We will set out clearly and confidently how we contribute to growth. We will exploit technology to retain our position as a world-leading regulator and supervisor. And we will operate transparently to underpin confidence in our work and thereby in our financial sector and economy.
The PRA in 2032 will be a forward-looking regulator that is respected and trusted. A regulator that is recognised for its work supporting a resilient, competitive and innovative financial system that in turn supports a thriving UK economy. I look forward to working with my PRA colleagues, and importantly also with you all, to deliver that vision.
Now, would you please join me in raising a toast to the Lady Mayor and the Mayoral Consort.

Katharine Braddick
Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation and Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority

Anatole Kaletsky

Gavekal Research | 30 Oct 2026

Sometimes a non-event is a great event. This can obviously be true in geopolitics, when a war or terrorist attack is avoided. But it can also apply to economic policy. A good example is Britain’s annual budget charade, which inflicts on the country a curse of fiscal fundamentalism unknown in any other mature democracy by twinning the crazy tradition of “budget secrecy,” which turns any discussion of fiscal plans into a crime worse than treason, with the even crazier convention of “parliamentary confidence,” which demands immediate resignation of any government that loses a budget vote.Between them, these two absurdities of Britain’s “unwritten constitution” exempt tax legislation from the rational debate and technocratic scrutiny taken for granted before any new legislation on infinitely less consequential issues like the regulation of bus routes or the protection of newts.

articles.title: Can the courts end Trump's illegal tariffs?
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Can the courts end Trump's illegal tariffs?

Alan Wm. Wolff (PIIE)

Date
October 26, 2026 9:00 AM

Photo Credit: Sipa via Reuters/Samuel Corum

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
There was rejoicing in the anti-tariff world, including among American consumers and businesses relying on imported inputs on February 20, when the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs of 10 percent or higher that President Donald Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
That said, the basic 10 percent blanket tariff stayed in place as if nothing had happened. The president invoked another tariff statute, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, for, the president said, balance of payments reasons. Customs and Border Protection(link is external) (CBP), a division of the Department of Homeland Security, immediately imposed this new tariff taking effect simultaneously with the end of the now illegal IEEPA tariff. That made the IEEPA victory seem somewhat hollow. Yes, there would be refunds, billions of dollars of them, but the new 10 percent tariff stayed in place.
This second blanket tariff, for supposed balance of payments reasons under Section 122, was declared illegal by the Court of International Trade on May 7. But as the balance of payments authority is limited to 150 days, when it expired on July 24 the administration was ready yet again with a new basis for a presidentially imposed blanket tariff.
The US Trade Representative (USTR), using Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, declared retaliation immediately against almost all exporting countries, which account for almost all of US trade, on the ground that these trading partners engaged in acts, policies, or practices that burden US commerce. How did so many countries merit this treatment? They were found by USTR to have fallen short of a newly-created standard none could meet: the vigor with which they could and did act against imports of goods into their own countries that might have been tainted by the use of forced labor. USTR's retaliatory "forced labor" tariffs were set again at a rate of at least 10 percent and took effect at 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on July 24, 2026, seamlessly, at the same moment that the balance of payments tariff ended.
That latest blanket tariff is still in place. The challenge to its legality is under consideration by the Court of International Trade, with a ruling expected any day.
Why haven't the courts been more effectual in eliminating the tariffs?
First, the administration has been skillful at shifting the basis for its presidential fiat tariff, pivoting from a nonexistent emergency to a nonexistent balance of payments problem to a supposed need for retaliation for an alleged unfair trade practice. There was no precedent for blanket tariffs imposed by presidential fiat in the 250-year history of the country until the second Trump administration took office.
The courts are a co-equal branch of government along with the executive and legislative. Each operates within constraints. The constraints on the Congress are plain to see. The Republican majority does not question this president's acts. The minority may be opposed but it has no effect. The Supreme Court has immunized the president against responsibility, either civil or criminal, for his acts done in the name of official business. He appears to be unconstrained, including by norms, the practices of all prior presidents.
There are certain basic constraints on the courts. There must be a case or controversy (Article III, Section 2, Clause 1 of the US Constitution). The courts cannot take issue with a policy judges do not like absent a case coming before them. But once a court has taken a case, it has wide latitude as to what it will decide, subject only to the norms it usually follows on how courts usually approach a solution. Could the courts have been more effective?
The Supreme Court could have struck down the emergency (IEEPA) tariffs as an unconstitutional invasion of Congress's prerogatives. Instead, perhaps to obtain a basis on which a majority of the justices could agree, it chose to rule against the emergency tariff on a technical reading of the text of the statute, arguing that it did not authorize the use of tariffs. This, however opened a door for the administration to try again to usurp Congress's power to tax.
The legitimacy of the five-month Section 122 balance of payments tariff is now being litigated on appeal. The Court of International Trade, a specialized court established by Congress, refrained from declaring that second tariff power grab unconstitutional. Rather it delved into the mysteries of the nation's international monetary accounts and determined that the statutory tests of what constituted a "balance of payments problem" were not met.
This is what courts do. They do not lightly find constitutional questions to resolve but see if the text of the statute itself serves as a basis for declaring a presidential action illegal, as being ultra vires, beyond the president's powers.
I assume the president will ultimately lose his Section 301 forced labor case, Burlap and Barrel, Inc. v. United States, No. 1:26-cv-03345(link is external). I have joined with two other veterans of the Office of the US Trade Representative—former USTR Carla Hills and former USTR General Counsel and White House official Warren Maruyama—to file an amicus(link is external) brief in the current court case, taking the side of the small importers. We argue that Section 301 is only for use against individual countries' practices, not a global measure like Section 122. We state that no prior administration and no Congress in its drafting of the provision, or subsequently in is amendments of the statute, ever indicated that Section 301 conferred global tariff authority. We argue that Section 301 could not do so under the Constitution and that USTR's forced labor Section 301 cases were arbitrary and capricious, and not authorized by law.
Oral argument(link is external) was held on September 30 before a three-judge panel of the Court of International Trade (CIT). The two-and-a-half hours of questions from the judges did not address the constitutionality of the forced labor tariff. The judges seemed unwilling to question whether the purpose of bundling 60 notionally separate Section 301 investigations was spurious in its entirety or that USTR was motivated primarily by a desire to deliver for the president a continuation of his invalidated broad tariffs. Rather, the CIT judges focused on the definitions that the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988 (Public Law 100-418) added to Section 301 and expressed surprise that the administration had not investigated provisions that specifically referred to forced labor. We did not address that Section 301 language in our amicus brief. Indeed, the assistant attorney general arguing the case for the government admitted that USTR did not see this language as particularly relevant. That admission could undermine USTR's use of Section 301 to punish countries over dealing with foreign forced labor practices affecting their own imports.
Whether the CIT could remand the case back to USTR to address any shortcomings of its investigation is not clear. If the court does rule against the government, an appeal is likely, during which the court is unlikely to enjoin collection of tariffs, which has not been considered irremediable harm justifying an injunction.
If the administration loses the forced labor cases, the result will not be the complete elimination of tariffs imposed by this president and his executive branch. Pending are 16 "excess capacity" Section 301 cases1 and that is just a current example; other Section 301 cases can be formulated. Tariffs will not be eliminated until a court, and ultimately the Supreme Court, states that the fundamental issue is that under the Constitution, it is solely the Congress that has the power to tax; it cannot be delegated to the extent that the president sets the tariff of the United States in its entirety or anything approaching that, which he did with IEEPA, with the balance of payments authority, and by bringing multiple claims of unfair trade practices against the United States' more important trading partners.
What we have seen to date is that the executive branch, with its ability to move instantly, has been able to find the means to impose tariffs far faster than the courts can review their legitimacy.
The fundamental question is whether any court, and perhaps finally the Supreme Court, will choose to use the forced labor Section 301 case to bring to an end to Trump's serial attempts to illegally usurp the Congress's power over tariffs. Findings that statutes were misapplied or investigations were inadequate—the normal outcomes in judicial review of executive branch actions—are not enough. No matter how many cases the administration loses, tariffs will likely remain in place for the duration of the Trump administration, absent a finding that there is no broad tariff authority delegated to the president nor can there be.
The court under Chief Justice John Roberts has repeatedly reached for a sweeping result when a majority sees that doing so is warranted. It did so by ending judicial deference to executive agencies' interpretation of their own authority (ending the Chevron doctrine, Loper Bright v. Raimondo(link is external)) as opposed to deferring to the office of the president.
The challenge to the Section 301 forced labor tariff case is an opportune time and place for the Supreme Court to defend the constitutional division of powers over imposing tariffs. Whether it will do so is far from guaranteed, but there is no evidence that Trump will cease imposing whatever broad tariffs he wishes independently of Congress until it does so.
Note
1. The 16 major US trading partners are: China, the European Union, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, India, Switzerland, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Cambodia, Norway, and Bangladesh. The inquiry spans at least 21 manufacturing and industrial sectors—including steel, aluminum, automobiles, semiconductors, chemicals, machinery, and solar modules, according to reports(link is external). The countries being investigated account for 60 to 70 percent of US imports.

Data Disclosure

This publication does not include a replication package.

articles.title: US Data centers are on the ballot
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

29 Oct 2026

US Data centers are on the ballot

How the midterm elections could reshape data center regulation, investment, and the future of AI-driven growth.

A Democratic sweep in the midterms would raise the prospects of federal legislation to ensure data centers contribute more to grid costs and improve environmental reporting. Federal action would be more limited in a split Congress. Regardless, the data center debate will intensify into the 2028 presidential election.

The outcome of gubernatorial races matters much more for the data center buildout, especially in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio. Simultaneous tightening of policy toward data centers across the South and Midwest is the main downside risk, though local opposition mostly relocates projects rather than stopping them.

Data center opposition softens appreciably when projects deliver local benefits or supply their own power. National security concerns and bipartisan lobbying should limit the bite of future regulation, which justifies not changing the baseline despite the rising political backlash.

The threat of moratoriums and tougher rules may be pulling data center construction forward into this year. Even if they materialize after the midterms, they wouldn’t immediately spell the end of AI capex’s GDP boost. Longer term, a slower buildout wouldn’t necessarily be a bad outcome for the macroeconomy.

articles.title: France's fiscal crisis is unlikely to prompt ECB action
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

28 Oct 2026

France’s fiscal crisis is unlikely to prompt ECB action

Political deadlock ahead of April’s presidential election could push French bond spreads higher, but an outright debt crisis would likely be averted.

France’s fiscal crisis might get worse before it gets better. Spreads could rise well above the 200bps peak in our baseline ahead of the April presidential election without triggering an outright debt crisis. Even if market pressure propels spreads to 300bps, political constraints would leave little scope for substantial fiscal action before the vote, while ECB bond purchases remain unlikely unless financial stability is at risk.

Risks that could trigger a further surge in spreads include sustained large-scale protests, a government collapse over the budget, a narrowing of Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s polling deficit against Marine Le Pen in the most likely election runoff, and further doubts about the fiscal credibility of Le Pen’s Rassemblement National (RN). A Le Pen presidential victory without an RN plurality in the subsequent legislative election could extend the fiscal deadlock.

In this higher-spread scenario, we think an outright crisis would likely be averted, given banks’ limited domestic sovereign exposure, broader financial resilience, and the absence of signs of systemic market stress so far, despite the rapid surge in spreads. However, France would still face high economic and fiscal costs.

In a full-blown crisis involving market-access difficulties or systemic financial instability, the ECB would be forced to act. However, pre-election posturing would make it difficult for French parties to agree on the credible fiscal consolidation commitments it would seek. These political constraints would raise the bar for early intervention, but the urgency of a crisis would weaken the ECB’s bargaining position.

articles.title: Policy Options Are Available Now to Lower U.S. Mortgage Rates | PIMCO
articles.text:
Libby Cantrill, Daniel Hyman, Munish Gupta

10/29/2026

| 5 min read

Share via Email

Share via Linkedin

Share via Twitter

Rising U.S. Treasury yields have added fresh strain to the U.S. housing market. The average 30-year mortgage rate, which generally tracks the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield plus a mortgage spread, rose to 7.5% in October 2026, according to Mortgage Bankers Association data, worsening an affordability crunch that remains a top concern among U.S. households.
Last week, President Donald Trump signed an executive order intended to reduce housing costs and expand access to homeownership. Among other measures, the order directs the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to cancel mortgage insurance premiums under certain conditions and establishes a task force aimed at lowering homebuilding costs.
While reducing costs is positive for borrowers, we believe several of the order’s changes could ultimately increase mortgage rates if applied too broadly. As we describe below, any changes should be targeted toward new purchases only, in our view, not refinancings. Otherwise, the market could price in more compensation for the increased risk of refinancing (or callability), potentially pushing mortgage rates higher. We believe policymakers can avoid this unintended consequence by limiting these changes to new mortgages, not existing ones.
Beyond the executive order, we believe there are several available tools that policymakers could use to lower mortgage rates in the near term. Doing so could deliver meaningful relief, as a 1-percentage-point drop in the mortgage rate lowers a buyer’s monthly payment by roughly as much as a 10% house-price cut (for more, see our September 2026 commentary, “The U.S. Housing Market Becomes a More Local Story.”)
We outline three policy options, all achievable under existing authorities, that we estimate could collectively lower mortgage rates by about 65-90 basis points (bps), or 0.65-0.9 percentage point.
1) Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could actively buy more mortgage bonds
Congress created government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac with a mandate to improve housing affordability and reduce risks to capital markets. The GSEs do this largely by buying mortgages from lenders and packaging them into agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS), a form of mortgage bonds, which they either sell to investors or purchase to hold on their own balance sheets.
Increasing mortgage bond purchases is within the GSEs’ existing authority and aligns with their Congressional mandate – and, importantly, it is what President Trump directed the GSEs to do in January 2026. The goal of increasing GSE purchases is to boost demand for mortgage bonds, which typically raises bond prices and lowers yields, thereby helping to reduce mortgage rates (for more, see our April 2026 commentary, “How Policymakers Can Lower Mortgage Costs and Increase Housing Affordability.”)
Fannie and Freddie have been slow to implement President Trump’s January instruction to buy an additional $200 billion of mortgage bonds, with Freddie Mac reporting that it had sold about $1 billion as of August and Fannie reporting that it had only purchased about $40 billion. If Fannie and Freddie were to simply follow through on this directive, we believe mortgage rates could be substantially lower.
Nor is a $200 billion increase necessarily the limit. Fannie and Freddie could potentially expand their purchases even further, though doing so may require their regulator, the FHFA, to increase the GSEs’ existing $450 billion investment cap. Raising the cap would involve amending the Preferred Share Purchase Agreement (PSPA) from 2008, a step the FHFA and the U.S. Treasury have taken several times, most recently in 2025.
To put it in perspective, the GSEs held about $310 billion of mortgages as of August 2026, according to Haver Analytics data, far below the roughly $1.6 trillion they held before 2008, despite the mortgage market doubling in size in that time. While there are good reasons not to return to pre-financial-crisis levels, Fannie and Freddie still have substantial firepower.
We estimate additional GSE mortgage-bond purchases could lower mortgage rates by 20–30 basis points, depending on the size of the program.
2) Regulators could cut fees for new home loans only, not refinancings
On 30 September, the FHFA released new mortgage pricing based on an alternative credit scoring approach, a change that could reduce mortgage rates for new homebuyers. We think this is a positive step, provided it applies only to new home loans and not to existing ones. Clarifying this distinction could be helpful for the market.
Measures that lower costs only for new-purchase loans may improve affordability without materially affecting mortgage investors. Extending those fee cuts to refinancings, however, would likely increase prepayment risk, prompting mortgage investors to demand more compensation and potentially pushing rates higher for all borrowers.
The clearest illustration of this dynamic is in the contrast between multifamily and single-family lending. Currently, JPMorgan data show that single-family mortgage borrowers pay a premium nearly 70 basis points, or 0.7 percentage point, higher than the premium paid by multifamily borrowers – mainly landlords – because multifamily loans are less refinanceable (or in mortgage-speak, less callable).
The broader lesson is that policies that reduce the callability of mortgages may lower mortgage rates for home purchases, in our view, while measures that make mortgages easier to refinance could potentially backfire and raise mortgage rates. We estimate that cutting fees for new borrowers only could lower mortgage rates by approximately 25-30 bps.
Similarly, some measures in President Trump’s latest executive order would apply the same changes to refinancing as to home purchases, which could widen mortgages spreads if fully implemented without adjustment. We continue to recommend a purchase only approach, which could lower mortgage rates for buyers without disrupting the mortgage market or putting upward pressure on rates and spreads.
3) The Federal Reserve could stop selling mortgage-backed securities
Another potential action is for the Fed to stop allowing its mortgage bond portfolio to “roll off” its balance sheet, which in practical terms is akin to selling mortgages and buying Treasury bonds. If the Fed simply stopped this (i.e., retained its mortgage portfolio at current levels), it could potentially bring down mortgage rates for homeowners – by about 20-30 bps, in our view. (For more, see our September 2025 PIMCO Perspectives, “A Fed Housing Fix That’s Hiding in Plain Sight.”) Ultimately, the Fed makes decisions about the size and composition of its balance sheet in accordance with its dual mandate of price stability and maximum employment.
Conclusion
For many households, the most immediate obstacle to homeownership is the cost of financing a home today. While policymakers have devoted considerable effort to expanding U.S. housing supply – a longer-term objective – policy choices that affect mortgage rates themselves could provide a more near-term path toward affordability.
The debate over mortgage affordability also sits at the center of renewed discussions about the future of the GSEs. In comments last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated that the U.S. may not look to remove the GSEs from their longstanding government conservatorship until 2027 or 2028 and only if it could be done without pushing mortgage rates higher (for more, see our May 2025 commentary, “The Future of the GSEs: Do No Harm.”)
For investors, the flip side of mortgage rates being high is that mortgage bond yields are also high. PIMCO continues to see value in mortgage-backed securities at today’s historically wide spreads and high all in yields. If policymakers succeed at lowering mortgage rates, investors in agency mortgages could potentially benefit from spread compression and price appreciation. If policymakers take no action, investors may continue to compound returns at today's attractive yields.

articles.title: View from the markets: Why have emerging market tech stocks been so volatile? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

Away from European bond markets, the major story for equity markets has been renewed volatility in emerging market (EM) semiconductor and technology hardware stocks. An index of these companies has dropped back towards the lows of late July, though they are still 1.8% above that level. This leaves them 28% below the July peak but with a year-to-date gain of 47%.

Listen to the article

Play00:0003:19Volume

While the declines from the highs are unfortunate, this level of volatility should not be surprising. Estimates of the impact of the artificial intelligence phenomenon on the economy and on corporate profits range widely. This can be seen in the rising standard deviation of estimates for EM tech hardware stocks, which has jumped from 10 at the beginning of the year to 82 today. By contrast, the variation for non-tech stocks has stayed constant at around five (see Exhibit 1).

The consequence of the current high degree of uncertainty is that any marginal information can lead to a big change in the forecast for corporate profits, which can then lead to a big change in the stock price.

The key factor for investors with a longer-term time horizon is that the earnings growth in the years ahead should nonetheless be significantly positive; current forecasts for the next two years are near 90%. If in the end it turns out to be some (modest) percentage greater or less than those forecasts is secondary.
