(Photo by Diego Radames/Anadolu via Getty Images)CommentaryEmissaryCan America First Be Exported to Europe?The illusion of reproducing the ideology would come at the cost of the continent’s prosperity.Link CopiedBy Giovanna De MaioPublished on Oct 28, 2026As student protests have raged through France, with some hijacked by looters, headlines proclaimed that the disorder was a gift to far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen. Le Pen’s bread and butter has always been law and order, and she quickly seized the moment, noting that “In six months, the French people will be able to choose a different path—one of authority and restored security.”Watching from across the Atlantic, U.S. President Donald Trump has not missed the opportunity to blame the unrest on “out of control mass migration,” echoing Le Pen. Trump continues to make Europe a favored target, repeating his administration’s warnings about “civilizational erasure” in Europe and excoriating it for being a mirror of exactly what he does not want the United States to be: heavily regulated, multicultural, and pluralist. Le Pen rarely mentions the American president these days, but she shares with him—and other rising European far-right parties—an openly hostile approach toward the European Union.Trump and his team have repeatedly said that Europe needs “tough love,” and they continue to prod and provoke Europe back to its ancient greatness, taking inspiration from Trump’s “America First” policies. Nominally, Trump administration officials seem to want to build a fraternity of national chauvinist illiberal governments—encouraging Europeans to adopt a similar every-country-for-itself approach to Trump’s own.But can America First actually be replicated outside America, and can far-right forces in Europe advance a collective America First–like agenda? Although the U.S. administration strategy to influence European politics is a threat to European democracy, the risk for Europeans is to get wrapped up in ideological debates about illiberalism without recognizing the nefarious power play of an external actor seeking to divide them.A Plan to Divide and Conquer The Trump administration’s ideological battle goes far beyond campaign slogans highlighting the state of European economies and societies. It is a deliberate playbook with three overlapping goals: getting favored European ideological politicians and parties into power, pushing European governments and the EU to adopt policies aligned with the America First agenda, and weakening the EU’s normative and economic power by supporting anti-European forces. Here’s the part that some Europeans, including the far right itself, don’t seem to have caught on to: All three of these goals add up to pushing Europe toward a new reality where, whether by intent or effect, the United States can maximize its leverage over individual member states. The playbook’s tools include denigration of the EU, funding opportunities for nationalist and anti-establishment organizations through State Department grants, public endorsements of politicians and parties, and economic and administrative pressure (such as a visa restriction policy for people responsible for what the administration views as censorship of Americans). Some European far-right parties’ agendas fit neatly into this playbook. For example, the fight against illegal immigration, the rejection of identity politics, and the anti-regulation agenda closely align with Trump’s political priorities and attacks on the European Union, whose regulations are perceived by the U.S. administration as discriminatory toward U.S. companies. In her recent interview with the Economist, far-right German leader Alice Weidel leaned into her skepticism toward supranational institutions, and her support for economic nationalism, and stricter border control and expulsion of illegal migrants. The Trump administration’s messages diffused through its playbook have been seen by many in Europe as a moral threat to the core principles of the EU, as they empower far-right parties that directly threaten European democratic foundations. But the threat is also a strategic one, because there’s no viable way for Poland or Germany or France to go it alone in 2026.Many of the far-right parties’ agendas are nationally focused and rarely include proactive cooperation with other entities, as that often implies compromise on sovereignty. But the reality is that their countries are not superpowers, and their bandwidth to act unilaterally for self-interest is substantially more limited than that of the United States—because of their size, geographic positions, and the collective institutions they are part of.To implement an analogue of the America First agenda in their own countries, these parties have to work together, including through EU institutions. They cannot do this unilaterally because no country has a sustainable upper hand on others, and existing interconnections between economies does not allow decoupling. For example, European countries cannot impose tariffs on one another, nor can they face common challenges such as illegal immigration without some coordination. Domestically, they can promote an illiberal agenda, but when it comes to economic and security issues, their individual capabilities and leverage are insignificant compared both to America’s and to the EU as a whole. The example of the UK—as one of the largest economies in Europe—provides a cautionary tale: The economic fallout began almost as soon as Brexit went into effect, and the UK public now widely regards the move as a mistake. If the UK can’t go it alone, smaller countries should be skeptical of their own abilities to do so.Indeed, previously, many European far-right parties’ goals included leaving the EU or NATO. In recent years, some have renounced this goal, instead shifting to changing the institutions from within. They may have realized these limitations but also understood how the European Union can allow them to amplify their power and advocate for their interests. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni did just this by siding with Brussels when Washington threatened tariffs on EU products—despite her ideological affinity with American conservatives on some social issues.So far, some of these parties have been able to work together in the European Parliament through the so-called Venezuela majority, but only by cozying up with the center-right coalition on issues such as toughening migration rules and undercutting green and deforestation regulations. But an EU in which right-wing nationalism is seen as a legitimate formula for member-state policies is bound to be entangled in divisions, including among those on the right. Divisions persist on several issues: On budget, France’s far right is at odds with Poland and Romania, and economic protectionism (a tenet of America First) may hinder a coordinated European strategy. EU enlargement is an even more heated battleground, with certain countries’ far-right parties favoring accession in some cases and opposing others, while other countries reject enlargement in all cases.Other key issues, such as Russia and immigration, could eventually widen gaps between far-right leaders emerging in Europe. Trump and several European populist parties from both the left and the right have signaled their desire to “reengage” with Moscow and lift sanctions, while for Eastern Europeans, Russia remains an existential threat. While countering illegal immigration in the EU is a strong common trend, clashes may occur between frontline countries on how to distribute the burden of repatriation. Signs of BackfiringDespite the continued rise of the far right in Europe, the America First playbook has been facing greater pushback. Much of this backlash has stemmed from perceptions of threats to sovereignty, therefore producing the opposite effect.In Hungary, far-right Prime Minister Viktor Orbán did not win reelection, despite U.S. Vice President JD Vance’s direct endorsement in Budapest. In Romania, the Trump-loving far-right candidate George Simion lost to the centrist Nicușor Dan. And the far right is not keen to advertise its ties to Trump, often seeking to distance itself from the unpopular American president. After the U.S. capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Le Pen was among the first European leaders to condemn Washington for violating international law, invoking a sovereignty that is “never negotiable.” Her protégé, Jordan Bardella, rarely mentions Trump at all these days, instead preferring to cite American culture war figures such as Charlie Kirk.Official pushback from governing parties also leaned into the sovereignty argument. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz openly warned “the American government or institutions close to the government” not to interfere in German elections. French Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noël Barrot posted on social media that “France will not tolerate any attempt at foreign interference in their electoral processes, regardless of where it comes from.” Recently, the State Department officially backpedaled on supporting parties in France amid concerns of conflict with a French legislative proposal that would harden penalties for online disinformation and foreign interference in democratic processes. The Trap of SovereigntyAmerica First has played an undeniable role in energizing European nationalist parties. For example, in Poland, Trump endorsed conservative presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki and later linked Nawrocki’s victory to the announcement of 5,000 more U.S. troops to be stationed in Poland. In Germany, Elon Musk’s endorsement of Weidel massively amplified the party’s outreach on social media. As the French elections approach, and protests spread to other countries such as Italy and Spain, anti-establishment sentiment and political polarization create a fertile ground for the spread of America First–like messages, fueling destruction and isolation rather than complicated collective solutions.Contradictions in the practical implications of an America First–style approach for European countries also contribute to a scattered agenda. In other words, these movements can hold pro-life rallies, rant about “woke decadence,” and proclaim a shared civilizational mission, just as Trump does. But the illusion of more sovereignty inspired by America First will instead bring much-weakened leverage, a more isolated continent, and ultimately leave each country’s self-interest severely compromised. If Europe wanted to take a real lesson from Trump’s hardball approach to international politics, the goal would not be to foster an “illiberal international” bouquet made up of movements and governments committed to Germany First, Slovakia First, Poland First, France First, Netherlands First, and so on—that would operate under the illusion of reproducing what Trump did in the United States. Although reforms addressing voters’ concerns—including those of the far-right—ought to be taken into account, responding individually will further undermine prosperity.Instead, all parties in Europe should see this as an opportunity to use the continent’s collective weight to push back and impose costs on aggressive behaviors, including from the United States, that threaten its sovereignty—putting Europe, not America, first.The author wishes to thank Zoe Raptis for research assistance.About the AuthorGiovanna De MaioVisiting Scholar, Europe ProgramGiovanna De Maio is a visiting scholar in the Europe Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. articles.title: Sustainability as a driver of long-term investment outcomes - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
How can investors navigate a world reshaped by environmental pressures, technological disruption and geopolitical uncertainty? For BNP Paribas Asset Management, sustainability is central to answering that question.

Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer, discusses BNPP AM’s updated Global Sustainability Strategy, which sets out its priorities through to 2030. Building on the recent merger with AXA Investment Managers, the strategy embeds sustainability expertise across asset classes, using ESG research, due diligence and stewardship to achieve better-informed investment decisions.

Jane explains how integrating sustainability considerations with financial analysis can help investors identify material risks and opportunities, while recognising that clients have different objectives and preferences. From net zero alignment and carbon footprint reduction to positive contributions towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the approach aims to deliver tailored solutions and better client outcomes. “Our underlying ambition is to connect sustainable investment practices with long-term returns to help clients navigate a rapidly changing world.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into solutions across many asset classes can help investors achieve their sustainability ambitions.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Andrew Craig: Hello and welcome to this week’s BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis through the lens of sustainability on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing our new revised edition of the Global Sustainability Strategy. This provides the framework for action on the environmental, social and governance considerations that are embedded in our investment processes and are grounded in the conviction that traditional financial analysis alone is insufficient to capture all the risks and opportunities in today’s global economy.

I’m Andy Craig, Co-Head of the Investment Insights Centre, and I’m joined today by Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management. Welcome, Jane. Thank you for joining me today.

Jane Ambachtsheer: Thanks, Andy. It’s a pleasure to be here.

AC: Can you explain why we need [a] Global Sustainability Strategy?

JA: Well, sustainability, is a core part of how we invest and how we operate as an entity, so it’s important to have a strategy which really articulates how we go about doing that and what our objectives are.

Our previous sustainability strategy took us to 2026, so it was time for us to launch our new one, which we’ve recently done, which takes us out to 2030. The other important component of our new strategy is that it reflects our new entity having evolved and completed the integration of AXA Investment Managers, which now results in BNP Paribas Asset Management being one of the world’s 10 largest investors, with over €1.7 trillion in AUM (assets under management) across liquid and alternative asset classes and a local presence in 35 countries.

So given our new size and scale, it was also certainly time for an evolved approach to our global sustainability strategy.

AC: How does the sustainability strategy fit with the new corporate strategy for the combined entity? What are the key components and how has it evolved?

JA: When we launched at the beginning of 2026 ‘AMplify 2030’, the overall strategy for the new entity, we identified sustainability as one of the core enablers of how we’ll achieve that strategy. That then opened the door for us to publish this new specialised strategy really focused on sustainability.

As a long-term investor, we believe our client outcomes and real economy outcomes are closely connected. Resilient companies, well-functioning markets and sustainable economic growth are really fundamental to the long-term returns our clients seek.

Our strategy sets out our forward-looking priorities and milestones through [to] 2030 and is organised around the pillars of how we achieve that. So, a focus on the future and identifying system level risks around how we do ESG research and due diligence stewardship. Our approach around articulating responsible business conduct expectations which can lead to different exclusions. Our approach to sustainable products and solutions and also around leading by example – our approach to our own culture, sustainability education and the corporate responsibility practices that we’re adopting for our own entity.

AC: How does this new strategy enable us to deliver the best outcomes for our clients?

JA: That’s at the core of everything we do. Our strategy is built for clients, informed by our clients’ expectations and what we believe best practice to be in the global market.

The first [thing] is around making sure we’re helping our clients navigate a changing world. We know that the world is being reshaped by a number of powerful forces:

Environmental pressures: reshaping industries, supply chains, capital allocation, presenting both risks and opportunities

Technology and innovation: creating new technologies, disrupting business models, creating different opportunities

Demographic shifts: transforming labour markets, changes to inequality around the world, consumption patterns and ageing

Geopolitical developments: influencing trade, energy security, energy systems, our approach to climate in nature and access to resources around the world in this changing geopolitical framework.

These megatrends are inter-connected and we try and take a forward-looking lens to help our clients navigate them through understanding the risks and the opportunities that they present. So that’s the broader macro perspective.

We also believe that by integrating ESG considerations alongside financial analysis from a bottom-up asset class perspective, we can have better insights and make better decisions on behalf of our clients.

So sustainability is not a separate investment decision. It’s an important component of informed decision-making from an asset class basis. One of the new evolutions in terms of our overall framework is that we now embed sustainability expertise across the different asset classes.

We have a central team which I lead, which is really responsible for driving the overall strategy and ambition, with our global leadership team overseeing stewardship, supporting our clients, supporting our overall external commitments and reporting stewardship and CSR (corporate social responsibility).

Then we have a number of sustainability experts embedded across the organisation within the different asset classes, reporting up to the different CIOs to make sure we have best quality ESG data, tools, research capabilities embedded into our investment decisions.

That takes me to this final point – the fact that the strategy is built for clients. We have clients from all around the world. They have different objectives, regulatory environments and sustainability preferences. To be able to cater to those different clients, we offer a range of investment approaches and have the opportunity to build structured, custom[ised] sustainability portfolios for our clients.

We have clients optimising around their own preferences or the preferences of their beneficiaries, whether that’s measuring a positive contribution to some of the specific sustainable development goals, achieving certain net zero alignment outcomes, measuring and achieving a certain carbon footprint reduction target.

Different clients have different preferences. A big part of our strategy and our new size and scale is that we have the ability to bring the firm in terms of helping our clients to achieve the best outcomes for them, tapping into the resources across BNP Paribas Asset Management, but also often working in partnership with our colleagues and the broader resources across BNP Paribas Group.

AC: Of course, there are implications for us, BNP Paribas Asset Management as a firm and our own practices. Can you talk us through those?

JA: At the end of the day, we’re a people business. Our people, the intellectual capital that they bring, their relationships with clients, are the greatest opportunity for embedding sustainability into who we are, how we deliver investment outcomes and how we’re operating as an entity.

So we have a strong focus on integrating sustainability into our culture and our own corporate practices. This is one of the unique differentiators for the way we’re approaching sustainability as an organisation.

In terms of our own corporate reporting, we seek to meet and exceed the standards and expectations we’re setting for the companies we’re investing in. That’s really important to our credibility as an asset manager – to live up to those expectations where we’re asking others to do the same.

We have a strong focus on sustainability education and we’ve developed different training pathways for different portions of our population, depending on their existing levels of expertise and focus areas – whether it’s investment teams or legal teams or client-facing teams – to make sure they have the right opportunities around internal training, but also the opportunity to pursue external certifications or training programmes.

We also have a strong focus on being active in the communities where we’re operating –volunteering, philanthropy and developing partnerships with organisations in different communities. Also our annual Community Impact Week, where we have a volunteering fair that we set up around our offices around the world, which is really a chance to engage in some of those organisations, but also to further enhance our internal community, give employees an opportunity to spend time together and spend time giving back.

So there’s a rich ecosystem of things we’re doing internally around creating awareness, providing educational opportunities and volunteering engagement opportunities for colleagues across the different offices around the world in BNP Paribas Asset Management.

AC: Can you talk [to] us about the key upcoming milestones and how you’ll be measuring success as we go forward?

JA: The first and most important measure of success is that we’re able to deliver the outcomes that our clients are engaging us to deliver. That’s front and centre for what we’re doing around our overall sustainability strategy.

But we will also continue to provide our annual sustainability report, which includes progress across all of the different six pillars of our sustainability strategy, including stewardship, which is an area of significant interest for many of our clients. We’re happy to be able to continue to evolve the level of detail around our different approaches for stewardship, be it statistics across the whole platform, a rich range of different examples of company engagement, as well as public policy advocacy.

Later this year, we’ll also be updating our new Net Zero commitment as a combined entity. That’s something we’ve committed to publish and we’ll be sharing in the coming months. We’ll also be introducing our new progress monitor in our next annual report, where we share a number of key indicators that [we] will be measuring and reporting on every year.

We view communication on sustainability as an ongoing opportunity, both at a portfolio and at a firm level, and it’s something that we’ll continue to share updates on with clients as we go.

AC: Jane, thank you. We’ll be looking forward to joining you to talk about those updates as the months go by. Thank you very much for joining me today.

JA: Thanks so much for having me. It was a pleasure to be here.

AC: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you’d like to learn more about our Global Sustainability Strategy, please reach out to your BNP Paribas Asset Management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings you commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Andy Craig and Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

Please do join us again next time. Until then, take care.

articles.title: Daily: AI delivers despite volatility
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Video: Why China's equity markets have lagged (6 mins)Thought of the dayNasdaq futures are pointing 1.2% lower ahead of the US market open on Thursday, after Alphabet shares fell almost 10% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and Samsung Electronics slid over 4% following their respective results. Alphabet’s September-quarter sales from most of its core businesses came in below market expectations, while Samsung’s chip operations missed estimates and capital expenditure expanded. The South Korean company also delayed the details of a new shareholder return plan until the end of January.But Alphabet’s cloud revenue growth accelerated, and Samsung’s record quarterly profits were nearly nine times higher than a year ago. Microsoft’s Azure Cloud also exceeded expectations, while Oracle beat estimates on both its top and bottom lines.The market reaction to the latest set of tech results underscores the elevated expectations going into the reporting season and a sharpening investor focus on AI monetization. Amazon’s results due later today are another catalyst to watch.Without commenting on individual companies, we think recent tech results reinforce our view that AI fundamentals remain robust overall and support our constructive outlook on the AI trade.The acceleration in cloud growth demonstrates hyperscalers’ ability to generate returns on their AI investment. With investors increasingly demanding evidence on AI monetization, the acceleration in cloud revenue growth is one of the key highlights in recent results. Alphabet’s Google Cloud posted a year-over-year revenue jump of 103%, up from 82% in the prior quarter, and 34% in the March quarter. Microsoft’s Azure grew 48% for the three months to September, compared with 43% for the June quarter, while Oracle’s growth also quickened to 62%, from 47%. All three companies offered a positive outlook for further cloud growth, saying that additional capacity could support the strong demand they are seeing in the pipeline.Monetization of AI products also showed encouraging trends. While cloud growth is a key metric in assessing the return on AI investment, there are increasing signs of monetization across AI products as well. Microsoft reported an eight-fold increase in large Copilot accounts, while Alphabet said its Gemini reached 1 billion users. A leading AI lab recently reported that compute costs are now less than 60% of its revenues, and that AI spending from its large enterprise customers only account for less than 1% of their total expenses.Robust capex should continue to support the compute complex amid robust demand. Microsoft reduced its 2026 capex guidance slightly, from USD 175bn to USD 170bn, but stated that investment will accelerate in the coming year. Alongside Meta’s recent equity raise and Alphabet’s signal of significant capex increase in 2027, we believe the robust growth in overall AI capex should continue to benefit quality semiconductor and hardware names, driving the industry’s earnings growth. While funding pressures and execution risks at specialized AI cloud providers warrant caution, rising GPU rental prices point to still robust demand for AI compute capacity amid supply constraints.So, we think AI remains a key growth engine for markets, and we continue to see opportunities in hyperscalers as well as high-quality semiconductor and hardware companies. Investors, however, should manage overly concentrated positions by considering exposure to more defensive areas of tech and diversifying across sectors and regions. Those willing and able to tolerate associated risks can use structured strategies with capital preservation or yield generating features to manage potential volatility.

articles.title: Higher Rates. Higher Bar. Managers Matter. | KKR
articles.text:
Investment Insights

Higher Rates. Higher Bar. Managers Matter.

October 2026

5 minute read

Alisa Amarosa Wood

Justin Park

Pat Nelson

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

Higher rates raise the bar for managers to grow and improve businesses, and put more weight on who is doing it.
Private equity has delivered strong returns across very different rate environments.1 Rates shift where returns come from, not whether they come. When borrowing costs are low, leverage and rising valuations do much of the work. When they are higher, returns depend more on a manager’s ability to grow and improve businesses.
Investors are now confronting that reality. Henry McVey and the Global Macro & Asset Allocation team have been in the “higher for longer” camp for some time, as laid out in The Divergence Conundrum. Experienced investors aren't counting on interest rates to fall; they're asking a more practical question: what actually drives returns, and how do we position for an environment where rates stay higher for longer?
Four ideas frame our view: today’s rates are closer to normal than they appear; rates influence company value but don’t create it; higher rates put more weight on earnings growth; and that makes the choice of manager matter more.

Sign up to subscribe to the latest insights from KKR

Email Address

Please enter your business email.

Please enter a valid email address.
Please enter a professional email address.

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

1. Today’s rates are closer to normal than they appear

Higher rates are a part of private equity’s history, not a departure from it.
KKR was founded in 1976, and in the decades since we have invested through surging inflation, multiple financial crises, a long stretch of near-zero rates, and the sharp reset that followed. Against that history, the unusual period was the decade of near-zero rates, low inflation and expanding multiples. Today's rates look less like an outlier and more like a return to the long-run norm. Each period tested something different. When inflation was high, pricing discipline set investors apart. When financing was nearly free, the challenge was resisting the urge to overpay.
EXHIBIT 1: Where Today’s Rates Sit, Fed Funds Rate 1976-2026

Data as of September 30, 2026. Source: Federal Reserve. The Federal Reserve defines the effective fed funds rate as, “the interest rate at which depository institutions trade federal funds (balances held at Federal Reserve Banks) with each other overnight”. When a depository institution has surplus balances in its reserve account, it lends to other banks in need of larger balances. In simpler terms, a bank with excess cash, which is often referred to as liquidity, will lend to another bank that needs to quickly raise liquidity. The rate that the borrowing institution pays to the lending institution is determined between the two banks; the weighted average rate for all of these types of negotiations is called the effective federal funds rate. The effective federal funds rate is essentially determined by the market but is influenced by the Federal Reserve through open market operations to reach the federal funds rate target.”

2. Rates influence value, but they don’t create it
Private equity returns come from three main sources: earnings growth, expansion of valuation multiples (i.e., selling at a higher valuation than was paid), and the capital structure.

Growing the company's profits (typically measured as EBITDA) by growing the top line, expanding margins, and improving how the business runs. Common levers include expansion into new markets, procurement, supply chain management, top-grading talent, M&A, and harnessing the power of human capital. The business is worth more because it earns more. This is the driver an owner has the most direct control over.

Selling the company at a higher valuation relative to its earnings than what was paid at purchase. If you buy at 10x EBITDA and sell at 12x, the extra two turns add value even if earnings stay flat. Market conditions play a large role, but so does strategic repositioning. A business that has moved into faster-growing segments, shifted its revenue mix to higher-margin offerings, or built scale and a better growth profile can earn a higher multiple than the one that was acquired.

The mix of debt and equity used to fund the purchase. Like buying a home with a mortgage, more debt means less cash invested up front, so gains are spread over a smaller equity check. Leverage magnifies returns, both up and down, and it is the driver most directly affected by interest rates. More isn't automatically better. The right structure leaves the owner with meaningful equity at stake, keeps enough cash flow to reinvest in growth, and is built for the rate environment.

Despite concern about rising rates, private equity has not depended on falling rates to deliver results. As the exhibit below shows, private equity has delivered strong returns when rates were rising, and the strongest when economic growth was rising alongside them.
EXHIBIT 2: PE Has Delivered Strong Returns When Nominal GDP Growth and Rates Rise Together

Data as of June 30, 2026. Source: Bloomberg, Burgiss, Cambridge Associates, KKR Macro & Asset Allocation Analysis. Past performance is no guarantee of future results. Indexes are unmanaged. It is not possible to invest directly in an index. GDP Growth and Interest Rate environments are defined by U.S. nominal GDP growth (YoY, SA) and 10-Year Treasury yields being above or below their levels four quarters prior. Returns shown are internal rates of return (IRR) for the periods falling within each environment.

3. Higher rates put more weight on earnings growth
With cheap leverage no longer a reliable driver of returns, managers must focus on creating value through operational improvements and earnings growth.
Lower rates made leverage cheaper. In a higher-rate world, that tailwind fades. Instead, managers must be able to grow earnings in their portfolio companies to make up for the role leverage used to play. Building better businesses is what carries a return when rates stop helping. Managers that are only now focusing on earnings growth are arriving late. A cycle-tested playbook and the resources to execute it take years to build.
Experience matters here. Approximately 60% of today's buyout managers were founded after the global financial crisis, so most built their track records largely in the decade of low rates.2 The years ahead will look very different and will reveal which managers can deliver resilient performance by helping their portfolio companies grow earnings.
When financing was cheap, capital structures were simple: more debt, less equity, and the math worked. Today the structure itself is a decision. Higher borrowing costs mean less debt capacity, more equity in each deal, and more of the company's cash flow going to interest rather than growth. Getting the structure right takes real expertise: how much debt, in what form and tenor, with what flexibility, and when to refinance or return to the markets. Managers with in-house capital markets teams can arrange financing, adjust structures as conditions change, and even help take companies public when the window opens. Rate risk can also be managed directly, through tools like fixed-rate debt and hedging, which limit how much a move in rates reaches a company's cash flow.
Higher borrowing costs also shape the exit, but not for every buyer. Sponsors that rely on leverage may be able to pay less for the same business. Strategic acquirers have a different cost of capital and in some cases are unlevered cash buyers. IPO investors tend to favor lower leverage and higher growth. So the exit that gets harder is mainly the sale to another sponsor, and it is hardest for managers that over-levered and didn't make the company attractive to other buyers. Multiples can still expand for businesses that are stronger and growing faster. What investors can't do is underwrite that expansion or count on market momentum.
Impact of Higher Rates

Earnings growth
MORE IMPORTANT

Multiple expansion
CAN'T BE UNDERWRITTEN

Capital structure
MUST BE BUILT FOR THE ENVIRONMENT

4. Higher rates make the manager matter more

When rates were low and financing was cheap, a rising tide tended to lift most boats, and differences between managers were easier to overlook. As those tailwinds fade, those differences have more room to show. Higher rates raise the bar, and clearing it depends on the manager. It takes a repeatable playbook for improving businesses, the resources to carry it out, and a real partnership with management teams, who ultimately deliver the results.
This is where scale matters. The resources that drive value are most useful when a manager owns them rather than rents them. A manager that relies on outside consultants and banks pays for that help deal by deal and has a harder time building deep institutional knowledge across companies. A manager with in-house operating teams, capital markets capabilities, and deep sector expertise can apply them across many companies and cycles, and can move quickly when markets shift. Those capabilities take years and real scale to build, which is why they are hard to replicate quickly. Experience across several rate cycles is how you tell whether a manager has them.
Conclusion: Three questions investors should ask
Rates shift where returns come from, not whether they come. Higher rates put more weight on a manager's ability to grow and improve businesses, which makes the choice of manager more important. When evaluating a private equity manager today, investors should ask:
Experience: Has the manager invested through more than one rate environment? How did they perform across those environments?
Value creation: Does the return depend on the business improving, or on conditions improving?
Resources: Does the manager own the capabilities it relies on, or rent them?
Managers who can answer these well are positioned for the market as it is, whatever the Fed and other central banks do next.

1 Data as of September 2026. Source: Cambridge Associates, KKR Global Macro & Asset Allocation analysis.
2 Data as of October 2026. Source: Preqin Fund Managers database, Private Equity – Buyout. Reflects the share of managers with a reported founding year of 2010 or later, used here to represent managers founded after the global financial crisis.

articles.title: Chainalysis Security Incident Information - Chainalysis
articles.text:
Chainalysis was recently the target of a cybersecurity incident, similar to many other tech platforms in recent weeks. Based on the investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens.Our team is working with leading cybersecurity experts to investigate this activity and harden our systems. We’ve proactively notified all of our customers and will keep them updated as our work progresses. This security incident is not related to the recent crypto theft at Binance. Below, you can find the full text of the email that was sent to impacted customers.
Chainalysis is committed to the security of our platform and the protection of our customers’ data. We are seeing an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks, and we are taking a whole-of-company approach to make sure our security posture meets the evolving environment and our customers’ expectations. In keeping with our commitment to transparency, we are writing to inform you of a security incident affecting your organization. Some of you have been previously notified and we want to provide an update on our work. Please note that this security incident is unrelated to the recent crypto theft involving Binance. What happenedThis month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems. Customer data impactBased on the evidence available to date, we have found no indication that these incidents resulted in the unauthorized access of investigation content (such as graphs, notes, or cases), transaction or query results, passwords in clear text, MFA secrets, or user session tokens.Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users. We are in the process of determining the records for your organization that were accessed and will provide a detailed breakdown as soon as that analysis is complete.What we have doneWe have engaged world-class third-party cybersecurity experts and are using sophisticated large language models to support a broader review of our platform’s security and strengthen our defenses. This work extends beyond the exploited vulnerabilities to enhance our security posture across the platform. What you can doChainalysis users should continue to be hyper-vigilant of unexpected password reset requests or authentication prompts. If your organization has not yet enabled two-factor authentication, we strongly recommend doing so. Your Chainalysis account manager can help you complete that process.What happens nextWe will provide you with updates relevant to your organization as our investigation progresses. We take the security of your data seriously and regret that this incident occurred.Respectfully,Your Chainalysis Team

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesReal Estate & HousingThe Outlook for US Housing in 2027 amid Rising Mortgage RatesOct 30, 2026Share Mortgage rates have risen to such a degree this year that affordability challenges are outweighing the impact of the longstanding US housing shortage. An expected decline in mortgage rates next year is likely to fuel a rebound in housing activity by the second half of 2027. Existing home sales are likely to slip in 2027 as many homeowners face the prospect of paying much higher borrowing costs if they move to another home. Home prices are likely to keep growing in the year ahead, but at an “anemic” rate of less than 1%. Rising mortgage rates are likely to outweigh a longstanding housing shortage in the US next year, leading to a drop in both the sales of existing homes and the construction of new ones, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
“In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity,” economists Ronnie Walker and David Mericle write in a report.
They project that existing home sales will total just 3.9 million in 2027, modestly below their forecast of 4 million for 2026 but 26% below 2019 levels. Against the backdrop of slower home sales, they forecast another year of “anemic” home price growth: 0.8% December-over-December in 2027 after 1.1% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2025.

Borrowing costs are a key component of housing affordability. This year’s jump in mortgage rates—in response to the Iran War, higher oil prices, and the prospect of rate hikes by the Federal Reserve—has reduced incentives for homeowners to sell. More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have interest rates below current market rates, and 65% have rates two percentage points below market rates, creating a “lock-in” effect that is slowing sales. In order to purchase a new home, such homebuyers would need to prepay their current mortgage and take out a new mortgage at a higher rate.
“The combination of mortgage borrowers refinancing at low rates en masse in 2020 and 2021 and the high current level of mortgage rates has created a significant financial cost to moving,” Walker and Mericle write.
Rates for 30-year mortgages in the US have climbed to 7.32% (as of October 22). Goldman Sachs Research’s credit strategists expect mortgage rates to decline in 2027 but remain elevated at 6.4%. Even if that decline is realized, affordability will remain at historically poor levels.
When is US housing market activity likely to improve?

Beyond next year, Goldman Sachs Research expects existing home sales to gradually edge higher, reflecting the natural decay of the lock-in effect that comes from, for example, borrowers paying down their mortgages.
The renewed popularity of adjustable-rate mortgages in the post-pandemic period could theoretically accelerate this process as well. As rates on such mortgages reset, they tend to erode the impact of the lock-in effect, as seen in other countries where adjustable-rate mortgages are more prevalent. But that impact is likely to be modest in the US, especially over the next couple of years. Adjustable-rate mortgages represent less than 10% of all outstanding mortgages in the US, and only a small share of them will begin to reset in the coming years.
Housing activity as measured by residential fixed investment (RFI)—a component of gross domestic product that includes new home construction—is likely to begin recovering by next summer after an expected decline in the months ahead.
After posting an estimated 3.1% annualized increase in this year’s third quarter, RFI is forecast to contract by 2.5%, 4%, and 1% annualized in the three quarters that follow, respectively. Thereafter, our researchers expect activity to rebound to a 1-2% growth pace starting in the second half of next year, reflecting the impact of declining mortgage rates. If rates remain at current levels instead, that would lower their RFI growth forecasts by one to two percentage points through the end of 2027.

How higher mortgage rates are forecast to impact US homebuilding in 2027

The longstanding housing shortage has kept single-family homebuilding resistant to higher interest rates. Single-family starts have averaged 3% higher than above 2019 levels despite mortgage rates that are three-and-a-half percentage points higher today. This year, however, they have declined by 3% compared with last year, and the slippage is likely to continue. Goldman Sachs Research expects single-family starts to total 0.87 million in 2027 compared to an estimated 0.90 million in 2026.
Our economists point to the increase in the available supply of housing, as well as the corresponding compression of margins for homebuilders back to pre-pandemic levels. The elevated pace of homebuilding in recent years has eased historically tight supply-and-demand balances. When the available supply of housing improves, it tends to increase homebuilders’ sensitivity to affordability constraints. Prior analysis by Goldman Sachs Research shows that the higher the vacancy rate was the year before, the more sensitive housing starts are to mortgage rate increases.
The combination of still-solid supply growth and slightly weaker demand should push the homeowner vacancy rate higher in the months ahead, from 1.2% in this year’s second quarter to 1.4% by the fourth quarter of 2027.
Housing demand is being buoyed by domestic demographic trends that remain supportive, along with real income growth that is likely to accelerate next year, and “build-to-rent” housing, which typically involves a partnership between single-family rental companies and homebuilders to construct rental homes. But on the negative side, survey-based measures of purchase intentions have declined in recent months. Our economists also expect that reduced immigration will continue to weigh on household formation.
“We expect housing demand to remain tepid,” Walker and Mericle write.

New power supply continues to lag soaring demand

How best to measure the breakneck pace of US AI and data centre roll-out? Well, there’s hyperscaler capital expenditure, which has increased four-fold since 2023 and is set to exceed US$750 billion this year, more than either the global spend in renewable power or upstream oil and gas.
Hyperscaler electricity consumption is another metric, skipping along at 23% a year so far this decade – way ahead of total US power demand, which did not grow from 2006 to 2024. Perhaps best is the 201 GW of new data centre capacity that US utilities have committed to connect to their grids, which would increase electricity demand by 30% if it’s all built.
Speed to power is the buzz phrase. All hyperscalers want their data centres plugged into reliable power supply as soon as it is ready to run their large language models and satisfy consumers’ growing reliance on them. The problem is that the US electricity industry, regulators and the entire supply chain alike are not yet capable of moving at the pace, or scale, required.
Chris Seiple, Vice Chair Power and Renewables, and I spent last week in New York talking with power sector investors and financiers about the challenges and opportunities ahead.
What are the biggest challenges for the power sector?
Among multiple challenges there are three big ones. First, the timetable for getting a data centre connected to the grid keeps getting longer. It varies by state but in Virginia, a hot spot for data centre location, the wait is 54 months at best. In Ohio, it’s 84 months – that is, no power supply until 2033 for a project going ahead today.
Second, public opposition to data centre development is growing. Lawmakers have called 400 moratoriums on data centre proposals. One-fifth of projects under development have been delayed by a moratorium, some by more than one.
Third, there’s an acute lack of essential components in the supply chain. Gas-fired power plants will dominate data centre power supply and the waitlist for the heavy frame gas turbines has stretched out to 278 weeks – roughly early 2032. Not much use if you want your data centre up and running before 2030 and weren’t early in the queue to order. Wire infrastructure is not much better with waitlists for transformers coming in at 162 weeks and circuit breakers at 137 weeks. Skilled labourers are also emerging as a bottleneck – not an easy problem to solve quickly.
Is it easier to build generation in regulated or unregulated markets?
Unregulated markets are easier in some ways in that the data centres are free to choose their power supplier and often have more flexibility in developing behind-the-meter generation (BTM) solutions. The main challenge is the disconnect between the planning for large loads and the planning for generation interconnections, and connecting the two.
In short, there are numerous independent decisions being made in unregulated markets that can get in the way of building out the grid in the most cost-effective way and that makes sure supply growth keeps up with demand growth. Regulated markets can mitigate some of the planning uncertainty and grid inefficiency.
What’s the timetable to deliver the power?
Realistically, there are no solutions that deliver new supply at any scale in 2027 or 2028 beyond what has already been committed. The task for regulators, the electricity industry and hyperscalers is to ensure that supply is connected by the time that demand ramps up beyond 2028. And the focus should be on delivering the 201 GW capacity already committed – adding more capacity to the pipeline before the current logjam gets moving will only hinder progress.
What solutions are there for power supply challenges?
First, BTM projects – which account for 15% of the pipeline by project count and 40% of planned capacity – skip the need for grid connection and the regulatory hurdles that go with it. Most BTM plans will be gas-fired capacity, backed increasingly by new high-discharge batteries. These projects will be expensive, complicated from an engineering perspective, and few data centres view the BTM solutions as a long-term plan, preferring to connect to the grid at some point.
The ‘ERCOT solution’ could be a pragmatic way forward for unregulated markets. The Texas system operator analyses the planned locations and scale of large load demand in the market, then makes assumptions where developers are likely to build generation. It can then make an ‘80/20’ decision on investment in transmission and connection and hope it all works out.
Interruptibility of demand is emerging as another solution. Data centre developers are trying to figure out how dedicated BTM resources, such as generators or batteries, might offer more flexibility to the grid. At the same ime, regulated utilities are working to communicate to data centre developers what type of flexibility will best optimise getting new load connected faster. Lastly, deregulated market rules are evolving to accommodate flexible interconnect.
Is AI-driven demand changing utilities?
Yes. For one thing, hyperscalers are currently price-insensitive. That’s a new experience for regulated utilities, which can leverage that price insensitivity to deal with affordability concerns and to find innovative ways to get load connected faster or to pursue new generation technologies, such as advanced geothermal or long-duration energy storage.
After operating in a low-growth bubble for decades, utilities are coming up with solutions for a new breed of customers with large loads in grids that are already constrained.

Protein has become one of the defining trends in food and beverage. Consumers are prioritising it, brands are reformulating around it, and companies are investing heavily to capture the opportunity. But as protein goes mainstream, an important question is emerging: are investors confusing protein demand with protein profits?​
​In this episode of The Flip Side, Brad Rogoff, Global Head of Research at Barclays, and Warren Ackerman, Head of European Consumer Staples Research, debate whether the protein boom still has significant room to run or whether expectations for growth, pricing power and profitability have become too optimistic.​
​They discuss whether brands can continue to command a premium, how private label could reshape the category, and whether supply constraints may support or undermine future returns. At its core, the debate asks whether protein's growing importance in consumers' diets will translate into durable profits for the industry, or whether capturing that opportunity is becoming increasingly difficult.​
​Listeners can learn more about this topic:

Barclays Brief #54: The US consumer won't quit​
Barclays Brief #36: The rise of the consumer health economy​
The Flip Side #79: Will the US consumer hold up in 2026?​

Clients of Barclays Investment Bank can read our latest reports by logging in to Barclays Live:​

Whey Too Cheap ​
This El Nino looks set to break records, but at what cost? ​
Protein Boom: Be prepared ​
Key takeaways from expert call on dairy protein​

Important content disclosures

Transcript

Brad: Welcome to The Flip Side. I'm Brad Rogoff, Head of Global Research, and I'm delighted to be joined today by Warren Ackerman, who is our Head of European Consumer Staples Research.
Warren: Thanks, Brad. Great to be here.
Brad: All right. Warren. So you're sitting in Europe, but we are going to talk about very much a global topic. And so the reason I wanted to have you on is, is all the time your team has spent in the last year researching what's certainly been one of the biggest trends in food and beverage. And I'm going to call that the protein boom. Consumers are clearly prioritizing protein manufacturers their products around it, and your research suggests the opportunity, it still has significant room to run.
Warren: Yeah. That's right. We've done a lot of work on this. Our research estimates that the global protein market is already worth around $1.7 trillion, and our work suggests that demand could increase by more than a third if consumption moves towards what we describe as health-focused levels.
Brad: All right. Well, $1.7 trillion is a big number, a third more than that's an even bigger number. But whenever I kind of see consumer trends that become this pervasive, I do start to wonder a little bit whether we're looking at the start of a long-term shift, which is kind of what you're suggesting here, or the point where expectations maybe have become a bit too optimistic. And protein, it's already everywhere. Yogurt shakes, bars and protein bread we're seeing now. Right. So, your research shows company references to protein. They've increased twelvefold I think you guys said over the last 25 years. But I'm just not convinced that consumer behavior has changed quite as much as that. Much of the apparent opportunity. It looks like to me, really effective marketing rather than a structural shift in demand to consumers, that they may care more about protein, but that doesn't automatically mean consumption keeps accelerating from here.
The big number that you already mentioned. So, I can see a scenario where the marketing campaign worked for call it the low hanging fruit. And now companies might be overestimating how much growth, pricing, power and premium remains.
Warren: Actually, Brad, I don't think so. I think what we're looking at here is a fundamental long-term shift in consumer behavior. If it were just marketing, we'd expect awareness to rise without much changing consumer habits. But we're not seeing that, consumers are becoming more health conscious. They're much more focused on nutrition and increasingly see protein as a central part of their diets. And really the behavior is driven by a few factors. Firstly, mainstream health and fitness culture, healthy aging, weight loss, drugs, and the wider availability of protein across food categories. And then you think about social media. If you look at Ocado, they're saying that 47% of Gen Z consumers use Instagram and TikTok for protein inspiration. So yes, protein is being marketed aggressively, but I think the marketing is succeeding because it's tapping into that genuine change in consumer priorities.
Brad: All right. Well, I'm certainly not the demographic they're looking at on Instagram and TikTok for protein inspiration, but thankfully they have enough protein already. But what I want to talk about here a little bit more is the difference between a trend becoming mainstream, which clearly, yeah, I think I'm not going to push back on you too much on that. And that trend actually continuing to accelerate. So, if consumers, not just me, already have protein across breakfast, lunch, dinner and even snacking. You think about U.S. household awareness of protein that's already close to 80%. My concern is that the markets it's approaching saturation, and the industry can overestimate the room for growth from here.
Warren: Yeah. Look, that's a fair challenge. But look, awareness doesn't always equal consumption. I don't want to throw too many stats at you, but I'm going to give you one, which is the IFIC survey shows that 70% of Americans want to consume more protein, but actually only 35% of them are doing that. So, the next leg isn't about teaching Americans that protein matters, it's about converting awareness into consumption. And if I look at one of the biggest sports nutrition players in the US, Optimum Nutrition, they were saying recently that 60% of their buyers are actually new to protein powder altogether. So yes, we're looking at this through a US lens, but globally the trend is far less mature.
Brad: That's fair to criticize me a little bit for getting to US centric there. So, but let's talk about the international story, and I do think it's a bit more complicated though. So if we think about some of the largest emerging markets, they're already consuming proteins at levels that are kind of comparable or maybe even above in some examples to develop markets which, look, when I was doing some research ahead of this, quite frankly, that surprised me. And I know you said you didn't want to throw out too many stats, but the stat that I was looking at was if you look at the FAO data, it shows China consuming a little bit more in terms of protein at 132g per day relative to the U.S., at 123g per day, and Brazil, for example, just behind the US.
Warren: Okay, I can see you got to be there, Brad. Look, you're right. China, Brazil. But that's not the real opportunity. It's actually the smaller emerging markets where consumption is much lower and the next wave of growth may not come from protein powder but will come from consumers maybe incorporating more protein into their everyday diets. The question for me isn't whether demand grows, but what form it takes.
Brad: Okay, that may be true, but even if you're right and demand does continue to grow, we got to talk about the economics and whether it can work here. Right. So, I think that's where it really tests the story. If you think about markets where protein is most established. Like let's go back to the US for a second here. You're also facing pressure from higher food bills, mortgage costs, tighter budgets and the US savings rate is falling, mortgage costs above 7%. Consumers are trading down. I mean, that's certainly a narrative we've been talking about a lot. And if you're faced with $7 protein yogurt, I think there are people going to choose cheaper alternatives. Manufacturers, they could be underestimating the pressure that consumers are facing. And if I look are U.S. food research team, they're seeing price increase, particularly among middle- and low-income consumers, which suggests further price increases could put volumes under pressure.
Warren: Yeah. Look, I think the jury is out on that. You know, we don't really know yet how much the elasticities are changing and how much brand loyalty is really being tested. So, our research shows that consumers are becoming more selective, true, but are not becoming less health conscious. Protein sits closer to health and functionality than discretionary indulgence, which makes it one of the last categories that consumers cut. I think you're treating protein perhaps more as a commodity than consumers do. Or think about it, than egg a chicken breast they're ready to drink shake may all provide protein, but consumers don't see it that way. They're not really direct substitutes. They're also buying at the same time convenience and functionality.
Brad: Look, I agree. Convenience may justify some premium, but affordability does determine the size of that premium. I think consumers, they don't need to abandon protein for the economics of the category to change. They can prioritize health while maybe trading down to like private label cheaper brands or just lower cost protein sources. And I think in the research, you've shown that only 2% of new protein products make a value for money claim, which suggests the industry; it's really focused more on that premium than affordability.
Warren: So, I guess that's one area where we're going to have to agree to disagree. I mean, I think consumers are becoming more price conscious, but that doesn't mean they're automatically trade down in this area. They aren't just buying grams of protein. Those brands earn a premium through convenience, through taste, trust and consistency and CivicService, they did a survey in January this year where they found that health and wellness is the only category, and that includes protein, where consumers intend to increase spending led by these categories. So maybe look, there is a squeeze, but that's spend on protein from the data we can see looks to be pretty protected.
Brad: So, look consumers might remain committed to protein. But what we're seeing here going on in the market means that we really need to see some premium in the protein product. I mean, one of the biggest ingredients players in the world recently said at their investor day that they'd seen a 133% increase in new product launches with higher protein claims just in the last 12 months. I mean, that doesn't sound like just looking for a small untapped opportunity. It's almost like a gold rush at this point. And if every brand is launching another high protein product and consumers are becoming at least somewhat more price conscious, doesn't that make it easier for private label to gain share? And private label, it doesn't need to be better, it just needs to be good enough and less expensive?
Warren: Yeah, I mean, that is a big number. And, you know, that's a fair challenge. But what we're seeing out there is what we call repertoire behavior. And that's where consumers rotate between 2 or 3 brands depending on price and promotion. So I think you're underestimating the barriers to entry here. Private label faces many of the same cost pressures as the branded manufacturers, and often they have less ability to secure those specialist ingredients. And you know where supply tightens, scale, procurement, formulation, expertise all of these things matter more, not less.
Brad: So, you just said the word supply. Let's move to supply. Industry promotes protein demand takes off, specialist ingredients become scarce, costs rise. And companies what they need to do next is higher pricing. It looks to me a little bit like protein has become a victim maybe of its own success.
Warren: I don't think it has become a victim of his own success. I think it's really more a category experience, how best to put this, growing pains. I think demand is growing faster than supply, which is supporting higher prices today. And if you look at whey that's probably the clearest example. Whey is a byproduct of cheese, so you can't simply decide to materially produce more whey in the way you might increase output on existing packaged goods. You need greater milk supply, cheese processing capacity, specialist filtration to turn that whey into higher value protein ingredients. And all of that takes time. And that explains why the key whey ingredient has gone up 3X in four years. But that's not evidence that the protein trend is broken. What that's evidence of is that supply is still catching up with demand.
Brad: Okay. But what it means practically is the industry wants consumers to pay a premium because proteins desirable. Okay, maybe that happens, but then they want them to pay another premium because the industry cannot produce enough of it. At some point, that's where this elasticity has to appear.
Warren: Look, it may I you know, I'd be surprised if there was no volume response to sustain price increases. But I think you're also assuming that supply pressures are permanent. They're not. There was a really interesting study recently from the International Dairy Foods Association. And what they said was that U.S. dairy processors are investing $15 billion in expanding manufacturing capacity across 23 states in the US, out to 2030. So supply constraints don't affect everybody equally. In some cases, what we're seeing is they can reinforce the advantages of the larger players. And, you know, companies with long term contracts scaling, procurement, multiple formulations, they may be able to secure those ingredients or reformulate more effectively actually, than those smaller guys.
Brad: But doesn't that not necessarily protect the category. It more protects the largest companies within the category, which I know are a lot of the companies that you follow. And even for them, though, higher sales I mean, doesn't automatically mean higher profits. So if I look at your research, which I did a lot of preparing for this, it noted that high protein yogurt can require around three times the culture content of standard yogurt. So protein cultures and formulation all cost more. How much of the retail premium reaches actually the bottom line? It seems to me that costs keep going up and prices keep going up, but many of the players in the industry are going to struggle. I mean, probably to even reach something like a 10% operating margin.
Warren: Yeah. Look, I spent a lot of time looking at operating margins, and I would be a bit careful with that, Brad. You know, because on margins it's quite hard to isolate individual high protein brand margins. You know, the margins depend on a lot of factors: market share, volume leverage, cost competitiveness. Yes. Costs are going up. These will all dairy proteins. And that pricing reflects that more than anything else.
Brad: I guess that brings us back to affordability, right. So, a manufacturer can protect margin by using cheaper proteins, for example. But if the taste suffers, the consumer may leave. Or it can protect taste, you know, your example maybe keeping whey as a protein and passing on the cost. And then the consumer could leave because of the price though.
Warren: Yeah, they could. I mean that's the tension. I mean that is the judgment call. The protein industry has to grapple with. Higher costs in real dairy are already constrained by more than factory capacity. You know, milk production depends on herd sizes, feed water, weather, farmer economics. In Europe as well, you've got environmental limits, which makes herd expansion more difficult. Beef supply has similarly long biological cycles. You can't just switch these supply chains on and off.
Brad: That's a good point. But there's one other big trend that everyone is certainly concerned about right now in the food world and in the cost part of it. And that's El Nino weather patterns. So, most of what I've read through does not make it clear cut, that El Nino will have a direct cost implication for the protein industry. Is that fair?
Warren: I think it's fair. I mean, you know, we don't really know yet the full impact of El Nino. We're watching it pretty carefully. The exact impacts are still far from clear and could be lagged. But what we have seen in the past from El Ninos is that big dairy regions around the world, I'm thinking Australia and New Zealand, they could face severe droughts and there could be a knock on impact to how much milk powder is then exported, which then could in turn drive up whey powder costs again, which the manufacturers will then need to reflect in their cost base. So, the reality is that the long-term climate volatility is here to stay, and consumers, unfortunately, will need to accept that dairy proteins are going to get more expensive.
Brad: But it seems more to me from what you're just saying, there's likely like kind of a 12-month lag from El Nino event on the impact to dairy, livestock, for example. And so, I wouldn't think this was like more of an immediate risk. And it almost feels like a bit of a scare story that allows you to take even more pricing to an already stressed consumer that's facing what I would consider pretty darn high protein prices already.
Warren: Now listen, Brad, this is real. This has been certified as being the most potent El Nino since records began in 1950. And it shouldn't be underestimated. Protein players will really need to think ahead and be savvy with the supply chain. And look, the obvious point is milk is perishable. It can't be stored for any period of time. So, if there are droughts, cows have to stay indoors where costs are just much higher. Plus, there are other environmental factors that may not be obvious but are real. I'm thinking the methane cap in Europe, which means that other countries just can't breed or buy more livestock.
Brad: All right. So, we've gotten probably a little bit technical here. Hopefully, people still enjoy that part of the discussion. But let's finish out with what might change either of our minds. But just to be clear, like my thesis is that consumers, they'll continue to eat protein, but the industry is probably overestimating how much growth, pricing power and premium remains for the industry. I mean, I might change my mind if we continue to see strong volume growth despite higher prices, without greater promotion, without a material shift towards private label, and without consumers switching into cheaper protein sources. What would change your mind, Warren?
Warren: Well, I've got to say that's a lot of caveats. It really is. Look, three things I think would change my mind. Firstly, if protein consumption starts flattening rather than just product launches, that's important, I think. Second, if consumers react to higher prices by eating less protein rather than switching formats. And third and final with supply catches up. But growth stalls, that would also suggest that perhaps we've been overestimating demand.
Brad: All right. Well, I deserve that because you were very succinct in your three points. But let me ask you a follow up. What about margins? I know you said to me earlier, I gotta be careful about operating margins, but would weaker margins in general change your view, even if category volumes remain fairly strong?
Warren: It wouldn't necessarily change my view of who the winners would be. At the end of the day, we're looking at the top line as well as the margin. I think protein can remain a structural consumer priority while some companies struggle, and others make acceptable returns. Our job is to try and pick which ones are which, and that's why, you know, stock selection really matters. You know, from my point of view, a company with secure supply, strong demand, strong brands, differentiated formulations, good price pack architecture, they're going to be the companies that will win and the company paying spot prices for whey and putting big price on undifferentiated claims on front of pack You know they're going to suffer. So, I think you're going to see bifurcation between the winners and losers.
Brad: All right. So, you look like you have your own long list of requirements too, Warren. Just to be clear here. And my argument, it was just it wasn't that protein is going to disappear. It's that expectations now require almost everything to go right.
Warren: Yeah, I guess true. But my argument is that protein has become so embedded in structural consumer priorities. You know, think about fitness, healthy aging, weight management, functional nutrition. Growth rates will normalize. Some products will fail, but affordability will matter and so will supply chain, but none of that means that the underlying shift and interest in protein has peaked.
Brad: Well, look, maybe I've got too much of my financial analyst had on, and I just think the industry might be confusing protein demand with protein profits. The consumer can maintain or even increase protein consumption while trading down private label, switching from steak to chicken, moving from shakes to eggs, or refusing to pay for protein where it's simply been bolted onto an existing product, the boom can continue nutritionally, while disappointing commercially.
Warren: Yeah, and I think you're confusing how deeply protein has moved into the mainstream health behavior. I mean, consumers are becoming more selective, but they are unlikely to stop prioritizing it. I think the opportunity shifts from putting protein everywhere. So offering better protein propositions at the right price. And look, that is the more difficult phase. But it's not the end of the boom.
Brad: Well, look, even though I feel strong on my side, I have to say that I might be helping you out here because I feel inclined to go have a nice protein packed lunch after this conversation. You know, so maybe the marketing is all working. But thank you for joining me today, Warren.
Warren: Thanks so much, Brad.
Brad: Clients at Barclays Investment Bank can read our recent reports on the protein trend on Barclays Live. Thanks, everyone for listening to The Flip Side. Please do subscribe wherever you get your podcasts, so you don't miss the next debate.

About the experts

Brad Rogoff

Global Head of Research

Brad Rogoff is the Global Head of Research at Barclays, based in New York. He is also a member of the Barclays’ Investment Bank Management Team and serves on the US Executive Committee. In addition to his leadership role, Brad focuses his research on the US high yield, leveraged loan, CLO and private credit markets. Since 2009, Brad and his team have consistently been ranked in the top three by Extel in the High Yield Credit strategy category. Under Brad’s leadership, Barclays ranked #3 in the Extel Global Fixed Income Research survey in 2022, 2023 and 2024. Since joining Barclays in 2008, Brad has held a number of leadership roles across Research, including Head of FICC Research, Head of Credit Research and Head of Credit Strategy.

Warren Ackerman

Equity Analyst, European Consumer Staples

Warren Ackerman heads our top-ranked European Consumer Staples team. He has been #1 ranked analyst in his sector in the Institutional Investor survey for past 3 years. This year he was also voted #1 individual analyst in Europe across all equity sectors. His team are top-ranked in Food Producers, Beverages, HPC and Tobacco. Warren provides broad sector knowledge, with a wealth of industry contacts. He focuses on deep dive research. He is also a columnist for the influential Grocer magazine. Warren has 25 years’ experience in the sector. He studied Economics at Exeter University.

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
Across the industry, we are seeing an increase in bad actors impersonating and misusing corporate brands to get access to personal information and funds from unsuspecting individuals. These activities may involve individuals acting as company representatives and may include fake websites, social media inquiries, or communications that closely resemble official channels.
Please read the below for important reminders that can help protect you from potentially fraudulent activity.
We strongly caution against providing personal data or transferring funds in response to unsolicited requests. For your safety, always verify the authenticity of communications claiming to be from Lazard by contacting us through our official website or known contact points.
Specifically, Lazard will never engage in the following activities:

Sending unsolicited investment proposals or requests for personal information from nonverified persons.
Requesting payments to bank accounts in the names of individuals, third parties, unknown company names, or through payment intermediaries.
Offering unrealistically attractive returns that seem too good to be true.
Expressing urgency to complete an investment or make a payment.
Requesting additional payments to release investments that have already been made.
Requesting money to be sent via social media messaging apps and/or platforms.
