articles.title: How Middle Powers Can Survive the AI Race
articles.text: World leaders and representatives at the 2026 AI Impact Summit in New Delhi.ArticleHow Middle Powers Can Survive the AI RaceFour scenarios for an uncertain future.Link CopiedBy Alasdair Phillips-Robins, Teddy Tawil, Sam Winter-LevyPublished on Oct 28, 2026U.S. allies may have breathed a sigh of relief earlier this year when AI developer Anthropic announced that it was extending access to Mythos, its most advanced AI model, to governments and institutions in fifteen partner countries. Any relief, however, was short-lived. Less than two weeks later, the U.S. government directed Anthropic to cut off all foreign access to Mythos and Fable, a more limited public version of the model. The administration also appeared to strong-arm OpenAI into limiting access to its newest model, before lifting restrictions on both companies.The episode provided a stark reminder that much of the world depends on the whims of the U.S. government for access to frontier AI. American companies produce the most powerful models, and the United States and China command a large share of the world’s top AI researchers, computing power, and investment. Foreign governments, fearful of missing out on the benefits of advanced AI while still bearing the brunt of its harms, are scrambling to respond.The right strategy will depend on each country’s current position and on the trajectory of AI progress. Some middle powers are deeply embedded in frontier AI supply chains, while others are primarily exposed to its effects. On the technological front, two variables should drive middle power choices: the speed of frontier progress and what we call the “frontier premium,” the gap between the best systems and open-source or other cheap alternatives. Together, these create four possible worlds for middle powers, each with its own best strategy (see figure 1).Of course, the variables are not fully independent—compute-intensive scaling may produce both rapid progress and advantages for the leading country—and the world may move between quadrants over time. But the matrix provides a guide to the range of possibilities. Outlining each scenario illustrates how it might arise, who would win and lose, and what governments can do to improve their position before knowing which outcome will appear.Two variables should drive middle power choices: the speed of frontier progress and what we call the “frontier premium.”So far, governments and analysts have advocated many potential strategies, but few are considering the full range of possible futures (see figure 2). Some governments want to build sovereign models. Some argue they should pool their resources to build frontier models and hardware together. Some believe countries can gain advantage by finding a chokepoint in the AI supply chain. For others, faster adoption will bring the biggest returns. Still others are betting on new technological directions entirely. Many have yet to make serious moves of any kind.Even in the face of uncertainty, governments can find strategies that remain robust across multiple scenarios. In particular, finding sources of leverage at supply chain chokepoints is valuable in almost every technological future—and most valuable in scenarios where AI poses the largest risks to middle powers’ economic and political standing. Where the right choice isn’t clear, policymakers can preserve optionality, gather information, and hedge against the most dangerous futures. Getting big bets right can pay off handsomely: If Taiwan had not invested in semiconductors in the early 1980s, or China had not built out its infrastructure for electric vehicles in the 2010s, each would be worse off today. Countries that wait for total clarity may find it too late to take advantage of the world that emerges.Scenario 1: Chokepoint World (fast progress, large gap)This is the world of the artificial general intelligence bulls: One company or a small group develops advanced AI systems that are not easily copied or recreated. Access to large quantities of compute drives dramatic performance gains, and labs figure out how to bar techniques like distillation, which involves training a less capable model on the outputs of a stronger one, and secure their algorithmic and data insights from competitors. The United States maintains a lead in chip production, in part by continuing to enforce its export control regime. As a result, the gap between U.S. and Chinese systems grows rapidly.In this scenario, the United States has both the incentives and the capacity to restrict access to the best systems. The beginnings of such a regime are already visible: In June 2026, the U.S. government revoked foreign access to Claude Mythos and Fable and barred OpenAI from publicly releasing GPT-5.6. (It later removed both restrictions.) If AI progress accelerates, restrictions will become more aggressive. Companies will develop models with cyber and military capabilities far exceeding those of Mythos, and national security agencies will push to limit distribution. U.S. allies and companies may lobby for a tiered access model, in particular for government agencies, but public access to the most powerful systems will be sharply restricted. The world will divide into AI haves and have-nots. For some middle powers, the best bet may be to find a position in the frontier AI supply chain that can be leveraged to ensure continued access, or some other point of interdependence that will make the United States reluctant to cut it off. Theoretical leverage will not be enough; governments will also need the political will to use it.Finding a true chokepoint—like TSMC and ASML, key companies in the semiconductor supply chain—is a heavy lift. But there are other ways for countries to gain influential positions. If the AI hardware landscape becomes more varied, for example, specialized chip firms may win by betting on a particular type of model or workload. The United Kingdom has embraced this approach, attempting to retain promising companies by offering public funding and expedited visa processing for employees. Or countries may be able to specialize elsewhere, such as in advanced testing and packaging (where chip firms compete heavily on cost) or semiconductor manufacturing equipment (an area of success for Malaysia, where tool maker Lam Research opened its largest global plant in 2021). Countries may also develop expertise in AI safety and evaluation, as the United Kingdom has done, or band together to offer market access, a potential strategy for the EU.Theoretical leverage will not be enough; governments will also need the political will to use it.Compute offers another possibility. Countries with readily available energy and fast-track permitting processes may be able to attract large data center investments; countries that serve as regional or global compute hubs will be in a stronger negotiating position relative to both the U.S. AI industry and the U.S. government. American firms are eager to build new compute capacity, and countries that can provide it will be able to negotiate for concessions, from tax revenue to frontier model access.In this world, countries that control critical chokepoints in the AI supply chain hold the strongest cards. Germany, Japan, the Netherlands, South Korea, and Taiwan are the obvious examples today. Those that can successfully develop new footholds may be able to bargain for access, though likely with less leverage than current players. Compute hosts, possibly including Australia, France, India, Malaysia, the Nordics, and the UAE, would hold leverage roughly proportional to the share of global compute they control. Important U.S. security partners, like the other Five Eyes countries, would also have a claim based on the broader value of their contributions to U.S. national security policy.Scenario 2: Transform or Die (fast progress, small gap)In this scenario, highly advanced AI exists, but can be copied or developed relatively easily by countries with access to compute and talent. The United States and China are locked in a close race, and the task for middle powers is to help preserve stability, build resilience, and promote productive adoption. A large edge in AI capabilities could be hard to defend, giving rise to this situation, if techniques like distillation continue to work on powerful models, security lapses allow the theft of model weights, or new techniques reduce the importance of additional computing power. Many observers contemplated such a scenario in early 2025, after the Chinese company DeepSeek released its R1 model, which some claimed reflected greater training and processing efficiencies than contemporary U.S. models. Such concerns have resurfaced more recently in the wake of Kimi K3, an efficient and highly capable open-weight model published in July 2026.In this scenario, the bottleneck is not access to AI but the speed at which institutions can adopt it. AI developers may struggle to capture returns, as profits are competed away, and strategic and economic value will flow to other bottlenecks: militaries with the strongest hardware and AI orchestration, compute providers capable of turning energy into tokens, and businesses that best convert tokens into economic value. That would make adoption capacity—the ability to reorganize institutions and workflows around abundant AI—critical.To that end, countries may strive to attract highly skilled immigrants and boost top educational programs. Risk-taking entrepreneurs, power users with domain expertise, and skilled engineers will be critical to turning cheap, capable models into productivity gains. And even if powerful AI models are broadly available, compute may not be. Governments may want to provide public computing infrastructure, perhaps with subsidized access for researchers or startups, since early and widespread use will build the knowledge to adopt AI effectively. Just as the internet made Amazon possible and the smartphone created Instagram, powerful and broadly available AI will generate new business models and powerful companies; the countries that enable them will have a significant advantage.Flexibility will come with difficult tradeoffs, however. The same lax regulations that could facilitate growth may also make it more difficult to block AI-enabled cyberattacks and manipulation campaigns. Disruption will drive political backlash. Permissive rules for the use of AI in government and critical infrastructure could embed unsafe technologies in essential systems, and inadequate social safety nets could lead to runaway inequality.The same lax regulations that could facilitate growth may also make it more difficult to block AI-enabled cyberattacks.Countries may also lean into the relational or the physical economy. The Google economist Alex Imas has argued that in a world where powerful AI systems can produce many goods cheaply, the gains will flow toward high-touch service sectors like arts, care, education, hospitality, therapy, and craftsmanship. These areas are harder to automate because human involvement is a fundamental part of the product. Countries that have existing advantages in these sectors may choose to lean in further, particularly where the products are exportable—handcrafted goods, for example, rather than live theater.Countries will also likely want to build industrial capacity along the AI supply chain, producing actuators for humanoid robots, for example, or semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Other physical industries may provide advantages, particularly if jobs require dexterity, benefit from tacit process knowledge, and need costly hardware to automate. And even in largely automated sectors, countries can reap economic benefits if they rely on scarce natural resources or can develop an early lead.China’s vast physical production capacity and ability to turn economic forces at central direction may position it well. Fast followers rich with talent, like Canada, Singapore, and the United Kingdom, could prove adaptable, although service-heavy economies might see their current profit centers eroded. Industrial powers like Germany, Japan, and South Korea would benefit from their manufacturing bases. Countries with economies heavily reliant on low value–added services—India and the Philippines, for example—could be badly exposed as AI replicates the skills on which their export sectors depend.Scenario 3: Adopt for Advantage (slow progress, small gap)In this scenario, AI is useful but its capabilities remain jagged. The gains seen in coding and mathematics—where solutions are verifiable and there is less uncodified process knowledge—fail to replicate in other sectors, and coding tools do not themselves reshape the economy. World models prove difficult, AI systems struggle to learn from real-world experience, and capabilities remain jagged and domain-specific. As the researcher Tom Reed puts it, “there is no GitHub for closing a Series B, winning a knife fight, or negotiating with Houthis.”If progress slows, governments and companies will have less reason to lock down the most advanced systems—which, in this scenario, won’t be much better than the second-best. AI company valuations might collapse if investors decide that transformative results will take longer than expected, and frontier AI model developers would likely operate on thin margins. Gains would instead flow to sectors where AI tools are most directly productive, such as finance and consumer tech, and to the companies doing the hands-on work of integrating AI into industries like law and healthcare, building bespoke tools, and reshaping internal systems around new AI products.This is the world in which sovereign AI efforts like open models fine-tuned for expertise in local languages are most likely to succeed. Second-best and open-source models would follow closely behind the frontier; customization and integration will be the hard part. Efforts to create national databases and develop models trained on local language data might add significant value, and national AI champions could compete effectively in particular markets by building on open models through fine-tuning, model harnesses, and other custom infrastructure. Sovereign programs could offer greater security and control, help spark AI startup ecosystems, and improve leverage in negotiations with American providers if they can offer a realistic alternative. Yet precisely because progress would have slowed in this scenario, pursuing sovereign AI would not be an overriding national priority.If progress slows, governments and companies will have less reason to lock down the most advanced systems.Governments would still want to promote adoption, but doing so would be less of an imperative than in worlds where progress is rapid. The technology would resemble other general-purpose technologies, where adoption boosts growth and could gradually reshape the world order, but without necessarily creating a narrow window for decisive government action. India’s huge IT services sector and domestic market, as well as its large pool of engineers, would position it well in this world. China’s ability to mobilize to promote mass AI diffusion could also pay off, though markets might beat mandates in promoting adoption. Moving slowly—Europe’s great sin—would be far less costly here than in a rapid-progress world.Scenario 4: Tiered Access (slow progress, large gap)In this scenario, AI progress plateaus, but a few clear leaders maintain a durable edge. This could happen if the strongest talent concentrates in one or two companies, or the frontier labs collect so much data from implementation that they can parlay early leads into a lasting advantage. Partnerships with other industries may also help build moats. Or producing and running frontier models may require so much computing power that only a handful of companies in rich countries can afford to build and access them. Frontier developers and the U.S. government would likely restrict access to the best systems, but not as aggressively as they would in a world with faster progress, because the range of dangerous capabilities (in areas like cyber and military operations) would be narrower. Both frontier developers and skilled AI users would capture economic value.In these circumstances, adoption and leverage to bargain for access may both help countries secure their economic and national security positions, though less urgently than in other scenarios. One significant difference between this scenario and those in which the frontier premium shrinks, though, is that the most ambitious sovereign AI model efforts that involve attempts to build independent frontier-model capabilities from the ground up would be particularly inadvisable. If well-funded American and Chinese companies struggle to catch up to the leaders, international competitors will find doing so even harder, perhaps wasting public funds and technical talent in the process.Middle-income countries with large technology and service sectors, like India, might be better positioned here than in faster-moving scenarios. They are likely not sufficiently close to the United States to gain full access in a fast-moving world, but if progress were slower and restrictions less widespread, their scale would let them play an important role in providing AI services like model customization, systems integration, and AI-driven process transformation. Countries without supply chain leverage, large domestic markets, or strong adoption capacity might find themselves in a slow squeeze, falling steadily behind in relative terms.If well-funded American and Chinese companies struggle to catch up to the leaders, international competitors will find doing so even harder.Implications for Middle PowersIf the right strategy depends on which scenario emerges, what should countries do now, while the future remains unclear? Countries enter the AI transition in a wide range of economic and strategic positions (see figure 3). Taiwan’s problem is how to convert hardware leverage into software access. India’s is how to capture implementation upside while managing exposure in tradable services. The UAE’s is how to convert its capital and energy into durable strategic relevance. But some principles apply broadly, and governments should not wait for one of these worlds to fully materialize before they act.Certainty won’t be possible, but there are some indicators to watch for. If distillation continues to help competitors quickly mimic the performance of frontier models, that will point toward a small-gap world. If unit economics at the top firms remain strong, that will suggest the opposite. If the United States formalizes its nascent ad hoc access regime, that could indicate it expects a large-gap, restriction-prone future. And if major labs begin reporting diminishing performance returns on new training runs, spending more compute for smaller capability gains, that might suggest progress is slowing. These indicators will not point cleanly to a single one of the four scenarios outlined here, but they can help governments figure out how urgently they need to move.Building leverage with supply chain chokepoints or scarce resources is valuable in most scenarios—and most valuable in the worlds where middle powers have the most to lose. If AI progress continues apace and the frontier pulls away from cheap alternatives, middle powers risk watching as AI winners race ahead. It is in this scenario that cornering the market on part of the supply chain will pay the highest dividends. In scenarios where progress is slow, or the frontier is easy to replicate, advantage in AI will be both easier to obtain and less significant. Countries will have more time to figure out their strategies, and mistakes today will be less likely to harden into permanence.Promoting adoption capacity also pays off in most scenarios, though it is far harder for governments to do well. Industrial policy is often ill-suited to encouraging businesses to use new technologies, and centralized programs risk subsidizing unproductive or inevitable applications. A few levers, however, make general sense. High-skilled immigration, investments in education, flexible labor markets, and openness to startups create conditions in which new organizational structures can emerge that take advantage of AI without requiring governments to predict which applications will matter.In scenarios where frontier access matters most, attempts to replicate the frontier through sovereign model development will be the hardest to pull off. If the leaders open up a large gap with second-best alternatives, developing powerful sovereign options will be difficult and expensive, perhaps costing as much as $900 billion, largely because of compute and talent needs.The track record of such moonshots is not promising. A few years ago, the UAE hoped that its national champions would rival the best U.S. offerings. In 2024, presidential adviser Faisal Al Bannai declared that the country’s new Falcon model showed the UAE could “compete with the best players globally.” But as the AI race has accelerated, Emirati companies have lagged. Sovereign efforts are most likely to succeed in scenarios where frontier progress is slow, and the gap between the best and second-best models is small—precisely the worlds where frontier access will be less important. More limited efforts to build domestic models—local language models, small models designed to fit specific use cases, and open-source platforms on which local developers can build—may attract talent and make adoption easier. But none of them will solve the economic and strategic problems that stem from a lack of frontier access.The best path across all scenarios demands smart engagement, not autarky.Establishing a stronger position at supply-chain chokepoints may help middle powers secure that access, but once a country has accumulated leverage, it needs the will to use it. This requires an ability to stomach pain. For example, if the Netherlands’ frontier access is cut off, the country could threaten to restrict access to ASML’s advanced lithography machines, but actually doing so would risk economic damage and harsh retaliation. Countries may do better by banding together (although the track record of the EU is mixed on this front) and focusing on their highest-priority asks—ones with enough domestic support that their political systems can endure a sustained effort.The best path across all scenarios demands smart engagement, not autarky. Adopting cutting-edge AI, innovating on top of it, and carving out a place in the value chain all involve various forms of industrial learning. The way to accomplish that learning is through partnerships that disseminate know-how from firms on the bleeding edge, not by trying to recreate it from scratch. This is the playbook that successful companies have followed in the past. South Korea’s Hyundai didn’t attempt “sovereign” auto manufacturing; it licensed access to engines from Japan’s Mitsubishi, visited as many international car makers as it could, and embraced foreign consultants. The playbook for AI is likely to be similar.Middle powers do not control the rate of progress or the size of the frontier gap. Pricing Europe’s Winter Demand For Natural Gas

Cedric Gemehl

Gavekal Research | 27 Oct 2026

Almost eight months since the start of the Iran war inflicted an energy shock on the world, the impact has hit European economies mainly through higher oil prices rather than through steeper gas and electricity prices. In September, European Union HICP inflation rose to 3.8% year-on-year, up from 2.1% in February, largely because of higher energy prices. But while higher prices for oil products contributed 1.3pp to September’s headline rate of inflation, the rise in natural gas and electricity prices added just 0.3pp.

articles.title: The State of Crypto Leverage – Q4 2025: Surviving a Stress Test
articles.text:
Insights / Research / The State of Crypto Leverage – Q4 2025: Surviving a Stress Test 

Research • March 06, 2026 • 20 mins
The State of Crypto Leverage – Q4 2025: Surviving a Stress Test 
Onchain lending slid with market prices and yields, but CeFi lenders held strong in the wake of a historic liquidation event.

Zack Pokorny
Research Associate

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

Bitcoin

Cryptocurrency

DeFi

Ethereum

Lending

Introduction  Crypto-collateralized lending dropped 9.81% in Q4 2025 from the all-time high set the previous quarter, a decline entirely due to a drawdown in onchain borrows. Onchain borrow activity, and borrow activity generally, is reflexive to prices and market activity. However, the introduction of looping strategies bound to market yields (e.g. funding rates) has brought onchain a new cohort of borrow activity that is sensitive to downturns in price, trading activity, and yield compression. Onchain borrows have continued to decline through the first quarter of 2026, falling 40% from the daily all-time high of $47.12 billion on Sept. 19, 2025. The bigger story in Q4 is the divergence between onchain reflexivity and offchain resilience. This is something we noted could happen in a market downturn on the Galaxy Brains podcast and in an interview with Market Watch. Despite the largest onchain liquidation event in history happening in October, there are few visible signs of stress in centralized finance (CeFi) loanbooks across the fourth quarter. That outcome is consistent with the structural shift we highlighted in our report on Q3 2025, when outstanding loan balances pushed to new highs: borrowed-funds use cases have generally de-risked, un(der)collateralized credit and rehypothecated collateral have been largely self-regulated out of common practice (and was effectively never an option onchain), and collateral asset quality has improved, leaving lenders and borrowers better positioned to absorb volatility without forced deleveraging or loss of funds. Coinbase’s quarterly filings are a testament to this. Despite negative price action through the quarter and the largest liquidation event in crypto history, Coinbase reported that “no cumulative realized gains or losses occurred during the period presented as no Crypto assets held as collateral were sold or rehypothecated." At the same time, onchain borrowing remains more rate-, yield-, and price-sensitive, particularly among the looping cohort tied to funding rates and market yields. As price, market activity, and yields compress, these positions can become uneconomical quickly, leading to sharper drawdowns in onchain borrows even when offchain loanbooks appear stable. The one caveat here is timing. The lack of observable CeFi stress in Q4 does not preclude pressure emerging with a lag, and a sustained price drawdown and the dust from Oct. 10 settling in Q1 could still translate into slower deterioration in CeFi credit metrics and risk appetite in subsequent quarters. Nonetheless, a major player like Coinbase growing its book and improving its collateralization ratio is a positive signal. Even in a downside scenario where CeFi credit metrics deteriorate with a lag, a gradual unwinding of loan books is a fundamentally different risk profile than what played out in 2022, when opaque, undercollateralized lending by the likes of Genesis, BlockFi, and Celsius led to overnight insolvencies, permanent loss of customer funds, and cascading contagion. In the background, the crypto futures market saw a significant drawdown in open interest and is showing few signs of recovery. After the largest liquidation event in perps market history taking place on Oct. 10, futures open interest has collapsed below $100 billion for the first time since April 2025 and is 33% lower than it was on the day President Trump was inaugurated for his second term. Still, perps are proving to be a valuable product. Hyperliquid’s HIP-3 has brought equity, commodity, and forex perps onchain, allowing users to trade these markets 24/7. These products have gained meaningful mindshare and adoption amid the Q4 2025/Q1 2026 geopolitical and market volatility, offering onchain users a way to express macro views without relying on traditional exchange hours or intermediaries. Traditional markets have proven (yet again) that they can't efficiently price events that break on weekends or overnight, while onchain perps can. Recent events have made that structural advantage tangible. In a world where information flows endlessly at the speed of light, we should have markets that never close. Onchain perps make this possible. As crypto lending and leverage markets mature and add step function improvements to traditional markets, their evolution is increasingly likely to mirror traditional credit infrastructure: tranched debt, fixed-rate loans, termed facilities, and more structured risk segmentation. Institutional entrants will accelerate this shift, bringing demand profiles distinct from the more cyclical and price-reflexive strategies that historically dominated onchain activity. On the derivatives side, synthetic perps are demonstrating the value of always-on markets, but they're ultimately limited by the traditional rails they reference. As onchain adoption deepens, the pressure on legacy markets to extend trading hours and modernize infrastructure will become harder to ignore. The result is a market that could look fundamentally different in the coming quarters, one that is less reflexive to crypto-native cycles and more integrated with broader capital markets. Taking this possibility into consideration, the next chapter of onchain-native leverage is being written now even as apathy and emotional despair plague the crypto community.
Key Takeaways  All told, crypto-collateralized lending contracted by $7.55 billion (-9.81%) in Q4 2025 to $69.55 billion. This is 6.79% lower than the Q4 2021 high of $74.62 billion. The dollar-denominated value of outstanding loans on DeFi fell meaningfully in Q4, contracting by $10.66 billion (-24.15%) to $33.5 billion. Galaxy Research is tracking more than $14 billion in debt outstanding used to directly buy or supplement the treasury strategies of digital asset treasury companies (DATs). The debt outstanding stagnated through the fourth quarter. Futures open interest (OI), including perpetual futures (perps), declined 39.09% QoQ from $197.18 billion to $120.11 billion at the end of the quarter. This decline was due, in part, to the largest perps liquidation event ever occurring on Oct. 10, just 10 days into the start of the quarter.
Crypto-Collateralized Lending  The market map below highlights some of the major past and present players in the CeFi and DeFi crypto lending markets. Some of the largest CeFi lenders by loan book size crumbled in 2022 and 2023 as crypto asset prices tanked and liquidity dried up. These lenders are flagged with red caution dots in the map below. Since Galaxy’s last crypto leverage report, we have added one new DeFi app and six new instances of DeFi apps already covered in past reports. We also added one new CeFi lender.   The additional DeFi apps are:    Loopscale on Solana. Miscellaneous Ethereum-based applications found on DeFiLlama The additional CeFi lender is: Milo - Founded in 2019, Milo describes itself as "a licensed digital lending company pioneering the intersection of crypto and real estate finance. Milo created the crypto mortgage category in 2022 and has remained the category leader ever since. The company has raised $24 million from leading venture investors and offers crypto mortgages, allowing borrowers to use their digital assets as collateral to purchase property as well as crypto-backed loans. To date, Milo has originated over $300 million in total loans, including more than $100 million in crypto mortgages, reflecting strong and growing demand for crypto-native financial products.”

CeFi  The table below compares the CeFi crypto lenders in our market analysis. Some of the companies offer multiple services to investors. Coinbase, for example, primarily operates as an exchange but also extends credit to investors through over-the-counter cryptocurrency loans and margin financing. The analysis shows only the size of their crypto-collateralized loan books, however.

As of Dec. 31, Galaxy Research tracked $27.56 billion of open CeFi borrows. This represents quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) growth of 11.66%, or $2.88 billion, and $20.23 billion (+282.37%) growth since the bear market trough of $7.21 billion in Q4 2023. Still, CeFi borrows outstanding are 25.58% below their Q1 2022 all-time high of $37.08 billion. Even so, CeFi loans outstanding grew for the eighth straight quarter in Q4 2025. The fourth quarter saw most non-stablecoin issuer lenders’ books remain flat to slightly down. However, Coinbase posted its largest quarter of loanbook growth by absolute change. Through Q4, Coinbase added $438.69 million in net new loans outstanding, representing +47.89% change.

Tether is the dominant lender in our analysis, commanding a 61.84% share (up 267 basis points from last quarter) of the CeFi lending market. Add in Maple, which entered the top three in the fourth quarter (6.62% market share, up 33 basis points from the third quarter), and Galaxy (6.51% market share, down 78 basis points), and the top three tracked CeFi lenders control 74.98% of the market (down 18 basis points). When comparing market shares, it’s important to note the distinctions between CeFi lenders. Some lenders only offer certain types of loans (e.g., BTC-collateralized only, altcoin-collateralized products, and cash loans that do not include stablecoins), only service certain types of clients (e.g., institutional vs. retail), and only operate in certain jurisdictions. The combination of these factors allows some lenders to scale more easily than others. 

The table below details the sources of Galaxy Research’s data about each CeFi lender and the logic we used to calculate the size of their books. While DeFi and onchain CeFi lending figures are retrievable from onchain data, which is transparent and easily accessible, retrieving CeFi data is tricky. This is due to inconsistencies in how CeFi lenders account for their outstanding loans and how often they make the information public, as well as the general difficulty of obtaining this information.  Note: Galaxy Research has not formally vetted the values supplied by private third-party lenders. 

CeFi and DeFi Lending The dollar-denominated value of outstanding loans on DeFi fell meaningfully in Q4, contracting by $10.66 billion (-24.15%) to $33.5 billion. Combining DeFi apps with CeFi lending venues, there were $61.06 billion of outstanding crypto-collateralized borrows at quarter end. This represents a reduction of $7.79 billion (-11.31%) QoQ, predominantly driven by compression of onchain borrows. On a combined basis, DeFi lending app and CeFi loans outstanding are still above the 2020-2021 cycle high of $58.69 billion. Galaxy Research sees a few contributing factors to the contraction in DeFi lending against the growth in CeFi lending: Looping becoming less economical: As market yields compressed and funding rates normalized after Oct. 10, the spread between borrow costs and yield earned on looped positions narrowed meaningfully. Ethena’s sUSDe (commonly used as collateral for looping strategies and in Pendle PT token collateral) yield fell from the 5%-7% range to 3.5% while USDC and USDT borrow costs sit between 3.75% to 4.15%. This dynamic flipped looping strategies on their heads, incentivizing users to close out their positions. Negative price action: The Oct. 10 liquidation event and subsequent price drawdown mechanically reduced DeFi borrowing in two ways: falling collateral values forced borrowers to repay or be liquidated, and risk appetite for new leveraged positions dried up in the aftermath. Historically low CeFi borrow costs: CeFi proxy rates used in our analysis fell below onchain borrow rates during Q4. This is an uncommon inversion of the typical dynamic where CeFi rates are higher or about equal to those of DeFi. Historically low absolute rates created an opportunistic borrowing window for CeFi counterparties, and the fact that offchain rates were cheaper than onchain only underscored how attractive the environment was for CeFi borrowers. Note: There is potential for double-counting between total CeFi loan book size and DeFi borrows. This is because some CeFi entities rely on DeFi applications to lend to offchain clients. For example, a hypothetical CeFi lender may pledge its idle BTC to borrow USDC onchain, then lend that USDC to a borrower offchain. In this scenario, the CeFi lender’s onchain borrow will be present in the DeFi open borrows and in the lender’s financial statements as an outstanding loan to its client. The lack of disclosures or onchain attribution makes filtering for this dynamic difficult. 

As a result of the quarter-over-quarter decline in outstanding borrows on DeFi lending applications, their relative lead over CeFi lending venues collapsed to Q1 2025 levels. At the end of Q4 2025, DeFi lending app dominance over CeFi lending venues stood at 54.86%, down from 64.24% at the end of Q3 2025.

The third leg of the stool, the crypto-collateralized portions of collateral debt position (CDP) stablecoin supply, increased by $262 million (+3.18%) QoQ. Again, there is potential for double-counting between total CeFi loan book size and CDP stablecoin supply, because some CeFi entities might rely on minting CDP stablecoins with crypto collateral to fund loans to offchain clients. All told, crypto-collateralized lending contracted by $7.55 billion (-9.81%) in Q4 2025 to $69.55 billion. This is 6.79% lower than the Q4 2021 high of $74.62 billion.

At the end of Q3 2025, DeFi lending applications represented 48.17% (-920 basis points from Q3 2025 share) of the crypto collateralized lending market, CeFi venues captured 39.62% (+768 basis points from Q3 2025 share) of the market, and the crypto-collateralized portion of CDP stablecoin supplies held 12.21% (+152 basis points from Q3 2025 share). Combining DeFi lending apps and CDP stablecoins, onchain lending venues held a 60.38% dominance (-768 basis points from Q3 2025 share) over the market.

Additional Views of DeFi Lending   Outstanding borrows on DeFi lending applications have seen material deterioration since reaching an all-time high of $47.12 billion on Sept. 19, 2025. Sitting at $28.17 billion as of February 16, 2026, onchain lending has collapsed by $18.94 billion, or 40.2%. Ethereum has seen a $16.02 billion decline in open loans on the chain since reaching its all-time high of $37.52 billion.

Stablecoins  The weighted average stablecoin borrow rate remained largely flat over the quarter, declining 28 basis points between Oct. 1, 2025 and Dec. 21, 2025. This is in line with our expectation that stablecoin interest rate volatility will remain tame and borrow costs will not exceed 10% through DeFi applications in 2026. This figure is calculated by blending the costs of borrowing from lending protocols and CDP stablecoin mint fees, weighted by outstanding borrows.

The following breaks out the costs of borrowing stablecoins through lending applications and minting CDP stablecoins with crypto collateral. The two rates track each other closely, although CDP stablecoin mint rates are typically less volatile because they are manually set periodically and do not move in lockstep with the market. Both rates have used the Fed Funds Rate as a floor for the last 18-plus months.

Benchmark over-the-counter (OTC) interest rates for USDC decreased 300 points through the quarter, falling from 6.5% to 3.5%. Since then, however, the rate has remained flat. For the first time in nearly two years offchain stablecoin borrow rates trended below that of onchain, presenting a unique opportunity to offchain borrowers. OTC interest rates are often quoted in bands depending on collateral or borrower creditworthiness. The middle band is the market rate while the top and bottom bands mark the range interest rates are quoted between. This is also true for all OTC rates shown in the following sections.

The chart below tracks the same rates as above, but for USDT lending. The onchain rate for USDT has been more in line with the OTC mid-rate than that of USDC.

Bitcoin  The chart below shows the weighted borrow rate for wrapped bitcoin (WBTC) on lending apps across several applications and chains. The cost of borrowing WBTC onchain is often low because wrapped bitcoin tokens are primarily used for collateral in onchain markets and are not in high demand for borrowing. In contrast to stablecoins, the cost of borrowing BTC onchain remains stable, because users borrow and repay it less frequently. The rate to borrow BTC onchain increased from 0.22% at the end of Q3 to 0.44% at the end of Q4.

The historical divergence between onchain and offchain (over-the-counter) borrow rates for BTC persisted throughout the fourth quarter, though offchain BTC borrow rates came down slightly and onchain rates increased slightly. In the OTC market, BTC borrowing demand is driven primarily by two factors: 1) the need to short BTC and 2) the use of BTC as collateral for stablecoin and cash loans. The former is a source of demand not commonly found in onchain lending markets, hence the spread between onchain and over-the-counter BTC borrow costs.  OTC rates for BTC declined 25 basis points over the quarter from 1.25% to 1%.

ETH and StETH  The chart below shows the weighted borrow rate for ETH and stETH (staked ether on the Lido protocol) on lending apps across several applications and chains. The cost to borrow ETH has historically been higher than for stETH because the former is in greater demand. Users repeatedly borrow ETH to fuel looping strategies to gain leveraged exposure to the Ethereum network staking APY – using stETH, the token they receive for staking ETH through Lido, as collateral. As a consequence, the cost of borrowing ETH fluctuates within 50 basis points of the Ethereum network staking APY on average. This strategy becomes uneconomical when the cost to borrow exceeds the staking yield, so it is uncommon for the borrow APR to clear the staking APY for extended periods of time. As with WBTC, the cost of borrowing stETH is often low because the asset is primarily used as collateral and not much else. 

By using liquid staking tokens (LSTs) or liquid restaking tokens (LRTs), both of which earn yield, as collateral, users borrow ETH at low, often negative, net interest rates. This cost efficiency fuels a looping strategy where users repeatedly use LSTs and LRTs as collateral to borrow unstaked ETH, stake it, and then recycle the fresh LSTs and LRTs to borrow even more ETH, thereby amplifying their exposure to the ETH staking APY. This strategy only works so long as the borrow cost for ETH is below the staking APY achieved on the LSTs and LRTs. Most of the time, users have been able to conduct this strategy without a hitch outside of a few notable periods.

ETH Over-the-Counter Rates  As with bitcoin, borrowing ETH through onchain lending apps has been historically cheaper than borrowing it over the counter. This is driven by two factors: 1) as with BTC, there is demand from short sellers through offchain venues that is not as common onchain and 2) the Ethereum staking APY serves as a floor rate for offchain borrowing because there is little incentive for suppliers to deposit assets with offchain venues, or for offchain venues to lend assets out, at rates below the staking APY. So, with ETH, the floor rate for offchain lending is often the staking APY while onchain the staking APY is often the ceiling rate.   

Corporate Debt Strategies  Since the last report we have made some amendments to the logic defining what a DAT is. To get the most accurate representation, we now define DAT as publicly traded companies whose main business may or may not be crypto-related but either way have a strategy to put crypto assets on the balance sheet. Given this amendment and greater access to public company data, the company mix used in the analysis may look different from previous reports. In addition, this quarter we started tracking Strategy’s preferred debt issuances. As a result, the amount of outstanding debt in this report is elevated compared to past ones. We are now tracking more than $14 billion in debt outstanding used to directly buy or supplement the treasury strategies of DATs. The debt outstanding stagnante through the fourth quarter.

The following timeline details the earliest maturity, call, or put date of DAT-issued debt looking forward from January 2026. Even with the expanded data set, most of the DAT debt is due, at the earliest, between June 2027 and October 2028.

The following details the effective quarterly interest due on DAT-issued debt. These values changed only marginally quarter-over-quarter and VFH Parent LLC (a subsidiary of Nasdaq-listed Virtu Financial) still holds the largest quarterly interest burden.

Total crypto-related debt outstanding, including the debt taken on by DATs, came down slightly quarter-over-quarter. After reaching an all-time high in Q3 of $91.6 billion, total outstanding debt through onchain and offchain channels sits at $84.37 billion (an 7.89% decline quarter-over-quarter).

Futures Market  Futures open interest (OI), including perpetual futures (perps), declined 39.09% QoQ from $197.18 billion to $120.11 billion. This decline was due, in part, to the largest perps liquidation event in history occurring on Oct. 10, just 10 days into the start of the quarter. Over the course of Q4: Bitcoin futures open interest decreased $27.44 billion (-34.2%) to $52.8 billion and stood at $43.97 billion as of Feb. 22. Ether futures open interest decreased $18.18 billion (-34.22%) to $34.95 billion and stood at $23.21 billion as of Feb. 22. SOL futures open interest decreased $5.28 billion (-46.42%) to $6.1 billion and stood at $4.26 billion as of Feb. 22. The futures open interest of all other crypto assets decreased $26.16 billion to $26.26 billion (-49.91%) and stood at $24.24 billion as of Feb. 22. It’s important to note that the entirety of the futures open interest figure does not constitute an absolute amount of leverage. This is due to the fact that some portion of the open interest figure can be offset by long spot positions, giving traders delta-neutral exposure to the underlying asset, and the total leverage ratio of the market is not directly observable from open interest alone.

CME’s share of open interest, including perps and non-perps, stood at 13.9% on Dec. 31, down 91 basis points QoQ. CME’s share of total ether OI (calculated as CME ETH OI divided by total market OI) stood at 15.44% as of Dec. 31 (down 210 basis points QoQ), and CME’s share of total bitcoin OI stood at 17.52% as of Dec. 31 (down 345 basis points QoQ).

Binance occupied the largest share of the perps market measured by OI with a 20.22% share on Dec 31. It was followed by CME with a 13.04% share and Gate with a 10.49% share. At the end of Q4, Hyperliquid held $7.47 billion in OI and commanded 6.22% of the total futures market (a 48-basis-point decrease from the end of Q3).

Perpetual Futures  Perps OI stood at $96.56 billion as of Dec. 31, declining by $61.75 billion (-39%) from the end of Q3. As of Feb. 22, perps OI was stood at $75.7 billion, representing a 56.91% decline from the all-time high reached in early October.

Perps OI dominance was 80.4% as of Dec. 31 and has increased 11 basis points from the end of Q3.

Conclusion Q4 2025 stress-tested the structural improvements in crypto credit markets, and the results were encouraging. CeFi loanbooks absorbed the largest liquidation event in crypto history without visible signs of contagion, while onchain lending behaved as expected, contracting reflexively with prices and yields. The divergence between the two lending markets validates the de-risking that has taken place since 2022. Looking ahead, the infrastructure for the next phase of growth is taking shape with talk of more structured credit products, institutional demand profiles, and real-world asset derivatives markets that never close. The next chapter of crypto leverage is being written now, even if sentiment hasn't caught up.

Speed to power: solutions to US data centres’ challenges
New power supply continues to lag soaring demand

5 minute read

Simon Flowers

How best to measure the breakneck pace of US AI and data centre roll-out? Well, there’s hyperscaler capital expenditure, which has increased four-fold since 2023 and is set to exceed US$750 billion this year, more than either the global spend in renewable power or upstream oil and gas.
Hyperscaler electricity consumption is another metric, skipping along at 23% a year so far this decade – way ahead of total US power demand, which did not grow from 2006 to 2024. Perhaps best is the 201 GW of new data centre capacity that US utilities have committed to connect to their grids, which would increase electricity demand by 30% if it’s all built.
Speed to power is the buzz phrase. All hyperscalers want their data centres plugged into reliable power supply as soon as it is ready to run their large language models and satisfy consumers’ growing reliance on them. The problem is that the US electricity industry, regulators and the entire supply chain alike are not yet capable of moving at the pace, or scale, required.
Chris Seiple, Vice Chair Power and Renewables, and I spent last week in New York talking with power sector investors and financiers about the challenges and opportunities ahead.
What are the biggest challenges for the power sector?
Among multiple challenges there are three big ones. First, the timetable for getting a data centre connected to the grid keeps getting longer. It varies by state but in Virginia, a hot spot for data centre location, the wait is 54 months at best. In Ohio, it’s 84 months – that is, no power supply until 2033 for a project going ahead today.
Second, public opposition to data centre development is growing. Lawmakers have called 400 moratoriums on data centre proposals. One-fifth of projects under development have been delayed by a moratorium, some by more than one.
Third, there’s an acute lack of essential components in the supply chain. Gas-fired power plants will dominate data centre power supply and the waitlist for the heavy frame gas turbines has stretched out to 278 weeks – roughly early 2032. Not much use if you want your data centre up and running before 2030 and weren’t early in the queue to order. Wire infrastructure is not much better with waitlists for transformers coming in at 162 weeks and circuit breakers at 137 weeks. Skilled labourers are also emerging as a bottleneck – not an easy problem to solve quickly.
Is it easier to build generation in regulated or unregulated markets?
Unregulated markets are easier in some ways in that the data centres are free to choose their power supplier and often have more flexibility in developing behind-the-meter generation (BTM) solutions. The main challenge is the disconnect between the planning for large loads and the planning for generation interconnections, and connecting the two.
In short, there are numerous independent decisions being made in unregulated markets that can get in the way of building out the grid in the most cost-effective way and that makes sure supply growth keeps up with demand growth. Regulated markets can mitigate some of the planning uncertainty and grid inefficiency.
What’s the timetable to deliver the power?
Realistically, there are no solutions that deliver new supply at any scale in 2027 or 2028 beyond what has already been committed. The task for regulators, the electricity industry and hyperscalers is to ensure that supply is connected by the time that demand ramps up beyond 2028. And the focus should be on delivering the 201 GW capacity already committed – adding more capacity to the pipeline before the current logjam gets moving will only hinder progress.
What solutions are there for power supply challenges?
First, BTM projects – which account for 15% of the pipeline by project count and 40% of planned capacity – skip the need for grid connection and the regulatory hurdles that go with it. Most BTM plans will be gas-fired capacity, backed increasingly by new high-discharge batteries. These projects will be expensive, complicated from an engineering perspective, and few data centres view the BTM solutions as a long-term plan, preferring to connect to the grid at some point.
The ‘ERCOT solution’ could be a pragmatic way forward for unregulated markets. The Texas system operator analyses the planned locations and scale of large load demand in the market, then makes assumptions where developers are likely to build generation. It can then make an ‘80/20’ decision on investment in transmission and connection and hope it all works out.
Interruptibility of demand is emerging as another solution. Data centre developers are trying to figure out how dedicated BTM resources, such as generators or batteries, might offer more flexibility to the grid. At the same ime, regulated utilities are working to communicate to data centre developers what type of flexibility will best optimise getting new load connected faster. Lastly, deregulated market rules are evolving to accommodate flexible interconnect.
Is AI-driven demand changing utilities?
Yes. For one thing, hyperscalers are currently price-insensitive. That’s a new experience for regulated utilities, which can leverage that price insensitivity to deal with affordability concerns and to find innovative ways to get load connected faster or to pursue new generation technologies, such as advanced geothermal or long-duration energy storage.
After operating in a low-growth bubble for decades, utilities are coming up with solutions for a new breed of customers with large loads in grids that are already constrained.

articles.title: European strategic autonomy: a €1.8 trillion investment opportunity - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
Europe is embarking on a far-reaching drive to strengthen its strategic autonomy, reducing dependence on external partners across critical areas including defence, energy, technology, healthcare, food security and industry.

For investors, the scale of this transformation could be significant. As Lazare Hounhouayenou, Portfolio Manager, tells Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, around €1.8 trillion of investment is expected to be deployed by 2035 under major European and national initiatives.

The spending could create powerful long-term opportunities for European companies exposed to these strategic sectors, potentially supporting growth and corporate profitability. Defence is already seeing increased investment, while measures to protect strategic industries and accelerate investment in space and technology point to a broader industrial policy shift.

Progress, however, is unlikely to be linear. Differing national priorities, regulatory hurdles and Europe’s complex decision-making processes could generate short-term volatility. “Yet the direction of travel is becoming clearer: Europe is recognising its vulnerabilities and taking concrete steps to address them.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast to discover how European strategic autonomy is opening new horizons for investors.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Lazare Hounhouayenou

Daniel Morris: Hello and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode will be discussing European strategic autonomy. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Lazare Hounhouayenou, Portfolio Manager. Welcome, Lazare, and thanks for joining me.

LH: Happy to be here.

DM: We’re all aware of the capex that’s being devoted to the development of artificial intelligence technologies – trillions in the US but significant amounts of money elsewhere, certainly in Europe. But we may not be quite so aware of what is going on in Europe around strategic autonomy initiatives. I hear that there’s supposed to be about €1.8 trillion devoted to this theme in the years ahead. Let’s get back to basics. To begin with, could you give us a simple and concise definition of strategic autonomy?

LH: Strategic autonomy refers to the ability of a state – or a group of states such as the EU – to act independently on the international stage and defend its interests against the world’s major power[s] in areas considered essential.

The means used to achieve these objectives, as well as the assessments criteria for sovereignty, evolve over time. In the ’60s, a state’s sovereignty was measured by its industrial and military power. Today, with the rise of AI, it is also determined by data centres, AI models.

This evolution raises new questions such as ‘has the control of [micro]chips and data centres replace[d] the control of physical borders?’ Or ‘does the state still maintain its cultural and political sovereignty when its citizens access information, communicate and form opinion[s] through AI algorithm[s] developed under a different jurisdiction?

In this polarised world, what is Europe’s position and where the region can create value according to its strengths in the long term? We think that regaining sovereignty is an absolute necessity for Europe, which must reposition itself within this new geopolitical landscape.

This requires reducing its dependence on partners and former partners across a number of sectors. Defence is one of them, but energy resources, industry, technology, healthcare and food security must also be mentioned.

DM: That sounds quite comprehensive. Can you make the connection, though, between these initiatives, and why Europe undergoing this shift to greater strategic autonomy is important for investors?

LH: Since 2022, the European Union and several European countries have launched a number of major initiatives involving significant level of investments aimed at strengthening Europe’s autonomy in sectors consider strategic and essential. Looking at the main programmes alone, we estimate that nearly 1.8 trillion of investment will be deployed by 2035.

Naturally, European industrial companies with exposure to these sectors are expected to benefit from this powerful long-term investment trend. In this context, investors have an opportunity to position themselves for the long term by investing in sectors with strong growth prospects while at the same time supporting Europe’s strategic autonomy agenda.

DM: When you look at these initiatives, are you seeing practical consequences from Europe’s decisions? That is, are you seeing progress or, conversely, obstacles, delays, rivalries that justif[y] some people’s scepticism and arguably could generate volatility in the short term?

LH: Europe is moving in the right direction, even if progress is never fast enough. Given the urgency of the situation, Europe is reconsidering its governance framework and recognises that its decision-making process[es] are not sufficiently agile.

Recently, Germany and France proposed to create a new cooperation format bringing together the European Union’s six largest economies. This is intended to overcome the slow pace of decision-making within the EU and allow the core group of countries to make faster progress on economic and strategic priorities.

At the same time, Europe has taken concrete measures in defence. For instance, we are seeing EU member states accelerating spending to meet NATO targets of three and a half [per cent] of GDP for core defence expenditure by 2035. The NATO summit held in Turkey last June just confirmed this trajectory.

Europe protected its steel industry through a protectionist steel action plan, reflected in a 50% increase in tariffs and a 47% reduction in import quotas.

And in the crucial space sector, the European Space agency has approved €22 billion for [20]26 to 20. This is an increase of nearly 30%. The objective is to strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy in space technology and mission[s].

This non-exhaustive list of proposals and decisions clearly show that Europe is advancing its thinking and governance and taking concrete action. However, Europe has still many challenges to overcome as interest[s] and priority[ies] differ from one country to the other, which is only natural when 27 countries are involved. These disagreements will create volatility around strategic autonomy themes.

But we believe it is important to take a step back and focus on the medium and long-term trajectory, which appear[s] to be moving in the right direction.

DM: Lazare, if I can summarise some of the key points that you shared with us? You explained that simply, European strategic autonomy is a group of policies/initiatives that enable Europe to act more independently on the international stage, with a focus on many sectors – industrial policy, defence, AI, to cite just a few. You highlighted that we’re talking about €1.8 trillion planned to be invested in the years ahead.

The significance of this for investors is simply that a lot of that money will flow to companies and ultimately should drive corporate profits. You acknowledge that it’s not as smooth or quick as we might like, but the important thing to keep in mind is that Europe is moving in the right direction. It does recognise the problems it’s facing and is working to tackle those problems. Well, Lazare, thank you very much for joining me.

LH: Thank you, Daniel. It was a pleasure to have the discussion with you.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities around European strategic autonomy, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com.

We recommend subscribing to Talking Heads on your favourite podcast channel, such as YouTube or Spotify. You’ll receive your podcast episodes every week. If you like Talking Heads, leave us a positive review and a nice rating.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, and Lazare Hounhouayenou.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

articles.title: ETF tax benefits: Why ETFs can be efficient investments
articles.text:
ETF education

ETF tax benefits: Why ETFs can be efficient investments

October 23, 2026

Key takeaways

ETF creation:

In-kind ETF creation and redemption may be facilitated by authorized participants in large quantities.

Tax efficiency:

ETFs typically generate fewer capital gains than mutual funds given how they’re structured and traded.

ETF events:

Portfolio rebalancing, stock splits, shareholder redemptions, and other events often don’t lead to more taxes.

Many investors may turn to exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for more transparency1 or lower costs.2 But ETFs are also tax efficient.3 They typically generate fewer capital gains than mutual funds due to how they’re structured and traded in the marketplace. Fewer capital gains to tax means investors potentially get to keep more of their returns.
How are ETFs created?
ETF creation and redemption typically avoid the cash transactions that may trigger capital gains distributions. Generally, an ETF issuer creates and redeems ETF shares through an “in-kind” process involving large institutional investors and market makers called authorized participants (APs). The APs have an agreement with the ETF manager that lets them create or redeem ETF shares in large blocks known as creation units. A creation unit typically consists of 10,000, 20,000, 25,000, 50,000, 80,000, 100,000, or 150,000 shares.
During the creation process, when demand for the ETF exceeds supply, the AP delivers a basket of securities held in the ETF to the issuer in exchange for a creation unit. In a redemption, however, the process is reversed. The AP receives a basket of securities while the ETF manager takes back a creation unit. ETF shares can be quickly created or redeemed elastically without cash transactions to help meet supply and demand in the marketplace.
Why do ETFs have fewer tax implications?
Since these transactions happen in shares (in-kind) and not in cash, there are typically no capital gains. What’s more, current tax law states that capital gains are not recognized at the time of the transaction and thereby not considered a taxable sale. The ETF creation and redemption structure may create meaningfully different after-tax returns between an ETF and an index-tracking mutual fund — even if both track the same index.
With ETFs, capital gains and taxes are generally recognized only when investors sell their own shares. On the other hand, mutual fund investors can see gains and taxes impacted by the selling activity of the fund’s other shareholders.
How do common ETF events affect taxes?
Portfolio rebalancing
Rebalancing a portfolio is typically handled in-kind with transactions and generally not taxable for the ETF and its shareholders. If the ETF must sell securities no longer in the index and buy additional securities, though, this may be a cash transaction and a taxable event for the ETF.
Corporate events
Stock splits, mergers, acquisitions, and other corporate events are also typically handled in-kind. But if the ETF must sell or buy securities for cash, there may be a taxable event for the ETF.
Shareholder redemption
When APs redeem their shares, this is usually handled with in-kind transactions rather than cash, which helps prevent distributions and taxes for shareholders.

articles.text:
Lotfi Karoui

10/26/2026

| 6 min read

Share via Email

All the presented audio appears as text.

PIMCO Pod
The Credit Market Lens: The Other Side of Higher Yields

0:00
/
10:30

Seek

Volume

Playback Speed

Key takeaways

Bonds’ renewed appeal comes with uneven economic costs. Higher starting yields offer income and potential downside mitigation, while exposing borrowers with weak balance sheets and significant refinancing needs.
Credit decompression should deepen (i.e., low quality borrowers will likely underperform the broader market). CCC rated companies, fiscally vulnerable sovereign issuers, and leveraged AI borrowers face distinct pressures from higher funding costs, with growing AI debt supply adding competition for capital.
Housing faces a prolonged adjustment, not necessarily a new crisis. Higher mortgage rates should extend residential housing weakness in the U.S., but despite higher real yields pressuring commercial property valuations, there hasn’t yet been a broad contraction in credit availability.

We have been arguing that the reset higher in yields has restored the dual role of bonds in multi-asset portfolios: providing attractive income while once again offering the potential for meaningful risk mitigation. This month’s tech market turbulence has provided a clear example: As equities came under pressure, U.S. Treasury yields fell amid a flight to safety, allowing duration to behave like a diversifier again.
One episode does not prove that the stock/bond hedge has been fully restored, but the starting point looks considerably better than it has for years. Investors are once again being paid to hold a potential hedge. (Learn more in our recent article, “Welcome Back, Balanced Portfolio.”)
But the same reset that has made bonds more attractive in portfolios also raises a familiar question for markets and the economy: Where will the higher cost of capital start to bite?
So far, the aggregate picture remains remarkably resilient. But higher borrowing costs are exposing greater differentiation. Rate sensitivity is becoming more visible where leverage is high, refinancing needs are significant, balance sheets are weak, or long-duration assets leave less room for error.
Five areas stand out to us.

1. Pressure on lower-quality credit could persist even without a meaningful deterioration in the macro fundamentals

Higher-quality companies can generally absorb a higher risk-free interest rate because leverage remains manageable, interest coverage is healthy, and market access remains available. CCC rated borrowers have far less financial flexibility, and the market has taken notice, as evidenced by the significant recent decompression within the U.S. high yield (HY) market – meaning spreads above Treasuries of lower-rated issues have widened more than those of the broader HY market.
The pressure works from both directions. With attractive all-in yields available higher in the quality spectrum, investors have less incentive to reach for incremental spread in CCCs. At the same time, the weakest borrowers face materially higher costs when they refinance. Figure 1 illustrates this pressure through the gap between secondary market index yields and existing coupons across HY rating buckets – a rough proxy for the increase in borrowing costs upon refinancing, rather than a direct estimate.

Figure 1: CCC capital structures face the largest increase in refinancing costs

Source: Bloomberg and PIMCO as of 22 October 2026. BB credit is represented by the Bloomberg Ba US High Yield TR Index; B credit is represented by the Bloomberg B US High Yield TR Index; CCC credit is represented by the Bloomberg Caa US High Yield TR Index.

2. European fiscal vulnerabilities should remain in focus

We’re closely monitoring developments in Europe, particularly in jurisdictions where weak growth and difficult fiscal arithmetic leave little room to absorb higher borrowing costs.
While yields have backed up on both sides of the Atlantic, the drivers have been different. In the U.S., the move has been overwhelmingly a real yield story (see Figure 2). In Europe, breakeven inflation has played a much larger role in the backup in nominal yields (see Figure 3). Put differently, the U.S. bond sell-off has looked like a growth repricing; Europe’s has not.

Figure 2: In the U.S., the move higher in rates has been almost entirely driven by the real yield component …

Source: Bloomberg and PIMCO as of 22 October 2026. The start date of 27 February 2026 represents the local trough in yields (following the onset of the U.S.–Iran war on 28 February, yields began increasing).

Figure 3: … while in Europe, breakeven inflation has played a much larger role

Source: Bloomberg and PIMCO as of 22 October 2026

The composition of the yield move has important implications for how easily it can be absorbed by the economy. Higher real yields are easier to absorb when they come alongside stronger nominal growth and healthier fiscal revenues. Rising borrowing costs driven more by inflation compensation are less helpful, particularly for sovereigns already facing weak growth and challenging fiscal dynamics.
France sits squarely in the latter camp: The global reset higher in yields has compounded an already fragile growth and fiscal backdrop. Spreads of French sovereign bonds (Obligation assimilables du Trésor, or OATs) have widened materially, and the bar for sustained normalization remains high (see Figure 4). A calmer global duration backdrop can help contain the widening, but weak growth, elevated funding costs, and a long political calendar support a more persistent, and elevated, rebuild of risk premium.

Figure 4: Eurozone sovereign spreads have widened, especially in France

Source: Haver Analytics as of 22 October 2026. Data shown are spreads over like-maturity German Bunds of 10-year Italian sovereign bonds or BTPs (Buono del Tesoro Poliennale), 10-year Spanish sovereign bonds or Bonos, and 10-year French sovereign bonds or OATs (Obligation assimilables du Trésor).

3. AI debt: Higher yields and more supply should accelerate decompression

The recent sharp underperformance of low-quality borrowers in the AI financing chain is not a reflection of weak compute fundamentals, in our view. Compute remains scarce and demand strong. What markets are repricing is the sustainability of leveraged financing models amid a higher-yield environment, accelerating debt supply, and increasingly attractive higher-quality alternatives.
The AI financing debate is often framed around whether investors have enough capacity to absorb the coming supply. But the more relevant question surrounds the price at which the debt clears the market. The next financing wave will likely be larger and more varied, forcing lower-quality borrowers to compete with hyperscalers, investment-grade-tenanted data centers, and better-protected asset-level structures. With all-in yields already elevated, investors have less reason to reach for incremental credit risk.
As the capex cycle matures, another challenge will emerge: The debate will shift from building capacity to monetizing it. Returns depend on utilization, compute pricing, technological obsolescence, and whether falling token costs generate enough additional usage.
Even if AI adoption ultimately validates today’s investment, where the value eventually accrues remains uncertain. Newer hardware could capture much of the upside while eroding the utilization, rental income, and residual value of legacy equipment. That wide distribution of outcomes leaves highly leveraged borrowers with little room for error.

4. U.S. housing: Higher rates should prolong rather than deepen the downturn

The latest increase in mortgage rates is unlikely to create a new housing downturn; instead, it should extend the weakness already in place. Housing remains one of the most rate-sensitive parts of the real economy, and conditions today are already deeply impaired.
Since 2022, higher home prices, mortgage rates, and insurance costs have pushed housing expenses far ahead of household incomes. Affordability is severely constrained, transaction volumes are depressed, the lock-in effect remains firmly in place, and residential investment remains near rock-bottom levels (see Figure 5).

Figure 5: Residential investment as a share of U.S. GDP remains at its cycle lows

Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis and PIMCO as of 20 October 2026. SAAR = seasonally adjusted annual rate.

Therefore, housing is not so much entering a new downturn as extending the existing one. Higher rates keep prospective buyers constrained while giving homeowners with low-rate mortgages little incentive to move, perpetuating weakness in turnover, brokers’ commissions, and transaction-related residential investment.

5. Commercial real estate: valuation pressure without a broad credit event

Higher yields leave commercial real estate (CRE) valuations vulnerable, but we do not yet see the ingredients for a repeat of the broad credit stress of 2023. The recent sell-off in public real estate investment trusts (REITs) looks more like a valuation reset than a renewed CRE crisis.
Higher real yields put upward pressure on capitalization rates, or the yield investors require on a property’s operating income. If the required cap rate rises while income is unchanged, then property values must fall, all else equal. With cap-rate spreads over real yields near historical lows (according to Green Street data), valuations therefore remain vulnerable.
Credit markets, however, are sending a more reassuring signal. REIT bond spreads have broadly tracked their benchmarks, commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) spreads remain resilient (see Figure 6), and financing markets remain open despite softer origination volumes. Unlike in 2023, higher yields have not coincided with a comparable contraction in credit availability.

Figure 6: Unlike in 2023, higher all-in yields haven’t resulted in a credit contraction in the real estate sector

Source: Bloomberg and PIMCO as of 22 October 2026. Investment grade real estate investment trusts (IG REITs) are represented by the Bloomberg Investment Grade US REIT Index; BBB commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) are represented by the BBB component within the Bloomberg US CMBS Investment Grade Index.

There are also important differences in the starting point. Borrowing costs are already elevated, reducing the incremental debt service shock from another move higher. Transactions completed since 2022 generally reflect lower leverage and stronger debt service coverage. Policy appears to be moving toward easing bank lending constraints, while most property sectors lack the structural demand deterioration that compounded office market stress in 2023.
Michael Puempel and Gabriel Cazaubieilh contributed to this report.
