CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesThe MarketsWhy Investors Are Reducing AI ExposureOct 23, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptMarkets are scrutinizing the crowded AI trade as investors reassess technology infrastructure spending plans and factor in rising capital costs, says Rich Privorotsky, head of European Equities Trading within Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. Third-quarter earnings from mega-cap tech will be critical, Privorotsky says on The Markets podcast. Investors are not only watching hyperscaler investment plans but looking for evidence that the spending is translating into revenue growth. He also describes a “seismic shift” from a savings glut to a spending glut, which along with high energy prices is lowering investor risk appetite.
Transcript:
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, October 22nd. And I'm joined from the Goldman Sachs trading floor in London by Rich Privorotsky, who is head of European Equities Trading within FICC and Equities.
Privo, thanks so much for joining us.
Rich Privorotsky: Thanks for having me, Hussey.
Chris Hussey: All right. Let's jump into it because I've been reading everything you've been writing about, and you made a great point, which was that earlier this summer, the pain trade, the trade that people were having to chase was long AI, short everything else.
It had become a little bit of one big trade. Now that seems to be unwinding as we go into third quarter earnings season. What's going on? How do you see it playing out from here?
Rich Privorotsky: There's just been an immense amount of concentration in the equity market, and I got to say that the past few weeks have been particularly painful for those types of consensual trades.
People were very concentrated within AI, within semis, within hyperscalers. And I would say that there are probably three different issues the market is kind of grappling with right now. One is obviously we've had a spillover in terms of the cost of capital, and I think we're seeing that pretty much everywhere. Whether it's triple C spreads, sovereign spreads in Europe, but also at the very pointy end within some of these more levered parts of the AI trade and the neoclouds really stand out.
And so that's become a question of supply. You know, will those corporates have struggle to find financing to deliver all this AI spend? The second point being on supply, that we've had questions about the ability to actually energize and deliver gigawatts, and the spread is kind of 20 at 40, 50 gigawatts for next year.
So if you can't get the power to actually energize a data center, will you actually be able to consume the chips you've already forward ordered? So those are concerns that are floating around the market. And then on top of that, you have more competition at the model layer and all of that is just compounded to a point where people have been in a de-risking mentality. And the nature of that has been taking growth expectations down via the AI trade and AI CapEx trade. And on the flip side of that, bonds have been rallying as growth expectations come down and that was on no one's bingo card.
Chris Hussey: Okay, a lot to unpack there. Let's focus though on the immediate future and actually the present, which is the third quarter earnings season. We're in the middle of it already. We've had some of the big mega cap tech stocks report, but we got a lot more to go. What are you watching for most carefully out of the third quarter earnings season?
Rich Privorotsky: Yeah, I think we're going to head into the meat of the hyperscaler numbers, and I think it's going to be really important to see not only that the CapEx is sustaining at the high levels and the market is kind of at $1.1 trillion for next year, but most importantly see continued cloud growth and monetization.
So, it's not enough just to say that you're spending a lot of money, but you also need to demonstrate that backlog is converting into revenues in a meaningful capacity. And so, I think that's going to be really critical for the market. I think the nature of how quickly their bridge to free cash flow break even occurs relative to market expectations could have a big implication on the credit markets, which have become acutely sensitive.
And so, really for me, there's a lot to look for I would say from the rest of the economy, but I think that the market's focus is really going to be on hyperscalers and then really the quality of the delivery, not just the spend.
Chris Hussey: It's a heck of a bar to have to scale for these companies. They have to keep pushing CapEx at the same time as they show you returns on that CapEx. It's not an easy setup, is it?
Rich Privorotsky: No, it's not. But, but look, I mean, the backdrop is one such that you see compute prices literally making new highs every day in the spot market. There is insatiable demand for what they have for sale. And so, I would say with a bit of a glass half full view, they should have a pretty good story to tell.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Rich, it's been a minute actually since we've had you on the call. You last joined us way back in January, but throughout the year you've been one of the guys with the mantra, "As goes oil, so goes everything else." Is that still the mantra?
Rich Privorotsky: Yeah. I think we've had a immensely problematic backdrop in energy. And I think the market, the equity market I think has done its best to really ignore and compartmentalize the rise in energy.
But that's not really fair because the S&P has done a great job compartmentalizing, but the median equity has in fact gone down well in excess of 10%. And so that has had an impact on rates. It has an impact on FCI. In fact, we've had a massive FCI tightening, and that has in a sense also pushed the Fed to do more, and we've repriced an entire hiking cycle.
So I think energy has been a big part of that. I think we still have a lot of risk premium because of energy and obviously now the next couple of weeks of how these things are going to play out is going to be really critical for broader risk, and I think my optimistic view is that we'll get some sort of resolution in the next few weeks. But, I have to admit, I've been kind of a little bit wrong thinking that would've happened a month or two ago.
Chris Hussey: I think we all have. And by FCI, of course, you're referring to the Financial Conditions Index, which is kind of a measure of tightening or loosening of the economy, of all the economic impulses. It's not just about rates. Sometimes it could be oil, sometimes it could be stocks as well when you're looking at an FCI. All right, good point on the oil side.
Also tied to that oil trade, though, was a comment you made back at the beginning of the year, which is, "I want to be long nominal assets. In an expanding world where GDP growth is strong, and GDP growth is looking still very strong, and inflation is high, I just want to be long those types of thing," which is a lot of commodities.
Where do you see that nominal asset trade today? Is it still a place to be?
Rich Privorotsky: I think in order to answer that question, I have to kind of answer the trillion-dollar question, which is what's going to happen with AI spending and how sustainable is it relevant to market expectations? Because the reality is that as we reprice that, we've repriced everything, including commodities, including nominal assets.
My gut is that we've kind of thrown the baby out with the bathwater, and we've certainly begun to worry about every dimensionality. And to kind of put that in context, I met investors this week who said, "I'm worried about the inability to deliver compute, and that scares me." And then I met another set of investors that said, "I'm worried we're going to over-deliver compute, and that scares me."
And it's somehow we've had two mutually exclusive outcomes that are both the summation of the market's worries. So, I think nominal assets are big picture where you want to be, unless we go into a disinflationary bust, right? Which is CapEx slows, everyone has to retrench, we have a proper credit cycle. And I would've said three months ago the risk of that was low, and now certainly it's a lot higher.
But my gut is that's still where you want to be over the medium and long term. But I think now perhaps a bit more of a barbell in the portfolio would be a bit more sensible.
Chris Hussey: So, it sounds like what you are saying is, whereas before it may have been as goes oil, so goes everything else, it's now as goes AI, so goes everything else. Is that right?
Rich Privorotsky: I think at the risk of being overly reductionist, that's probably about right.
Chris Hussey: Rich, thanks for being overly reductionist. I am Mr. Overly Reductionist, so I love that you were able to go there.
All right. You also mentioned that part of this, of course, would be a big credit cycle.
And that three months ago you weren't worried about a credit cycle, now you are a little bit more. Talk to us about that. Are you seeing credit cracks? Are you referring to the issues that are going on with sovereign bonds in Europe, or are you referring more to the credit issues that we see at the corporate side?
Rich Privorotsky: I've spent my entire career in what you could probably describe as a savings glut. We had more money in the system than we knew what to do with and really in the last year we're projecting to spend in excess of a trillion dollars on AI CapEx. Most governments around the world are running fiscal deficits.
We are in a spending glut, and this is a really big seismic change in terms of the way things work and what the cost of capital becomes. And so I think that is naturally pushing out borrowers who are at the fringe, who are not the highest of quality. I think you've seen it in CCC spreads, which is, in fairness, a bit idiosyncratic given the composition of what's occurred there, but they have moved a lot and that's spilled over a little bit into broader parts of credit.
And then obviously you have French sovereign concerns, which as a sovereign with a large fiscal deficit in this environment, they all get pushed out. So I think all these things are kind of having an impact and we go back to the oil trade simultaneously, as long as energy prices are high, it just kind of lowers the risk appetite and I think it is kind of a buyer's market for those types of assets.
Chris Hussey: Yeah, what a great way to crystallize it. From a savings glut to a spending glut. It's so true, and that savings glut was only five years ago. It's amazing how we've shifted. All right. A lot going on. You just told us. Let's put a bow on it. What's the trade?
Rich Privorotsky: It's a bit messy, and I would say conviction is not super high. But I think that there are pockets of electrification that we think look really interesting. They've derated a ton, and I still think there's plenty of visibility into 2027 that gives you a big margin of safety. I think there's lots of aerospace assets that have come off that, particularly on the civil side, again, equally incredibly attractive to us.
And then even parts of transports, quite frankly. If you do get any kind of energy resolution, there's a lot of, I would say, convexity in that trade given how low nets have become, how much selling we have seen in the past few week. I mean, for context, it was the biggest selling of tech we've ever seen in our prime book last week.
So, I think there are plenty of reasons to worry and I don't want to be too dismissive, but I kind of like try to be cautiously optimistic at this point.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Rich, let's fast-forward to next week. What are you watching for that's going to impact the markets in the week ahead?
Rich Privorotsky: I think it's going to be at numbers, hyperscaler numbers as we discussed. I think let's see the monetization. Let's see the CapEx figures. I think this is going to be really critical for the tape.
I think how that progresses will shape how people feel about the credit, how people feel about the underlying demand and whatever else we get, you know, in terms of data points coming from all the labs and all the providers.
Chris Hussey: Rich, always a wealth of information. Thanks so much for joining us today.
Rich Privorotsky: All right. Thanks, Chris. Thanks for having me.
Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening.This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, October 22nd. And I'm joined from the Goldman Sachs trading floor in London by Rich Privorotsky, who is head of European Equities Trading within FICC and Equities.
Privo, thanks so much for joining us.
Rich Privorotsky: Thanks for having me, Hussey.
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, October 22nd. And I'm joined from the Goldman Sachs trading floor in London by Rich Privorotsky, who is head of European Equities Trading within FICC and Equities.

articles.title: AI, the future of work and what it means for investors
articles.text:
Better Vantage podcast

AI, the future of work and what it means for investors

October 28, 2026

Video length: 18 minutes 1 second

Read the transcript

Christine Kashkari: Will AI truly transform the economy and the job market, or will it be just another automation tool? The answer has profound consequences shaping the direction of the economy and your portfolio. Welcome to season three of Better Vantage by Vanguard, a podcast series hosted by Custom Content from WSJ and Vanguard. I'm Christine Kashkari, editorial director at WSJ custom Programming. With me, as always, is my cohost and our resident expert, Joe Davis, global chief economist at Vanguard. Back in season one, Joe pulled double duty as both cohost and guest to explore what AI might mean for investors. But this debate moves fast, so today he's back in the guest chair. Joe is, of course, the author of Coming into View, how AI and other megatrends will shape your investments. Joe, welcome to the hot seat.
Joe Davis: It’s great to be back. I tell you, AI is moving fast. I mean, it's in every conversation I have with clients, with friends, family, my children.
Christine Kashkari: Where are you with your projections?
Joe Davis: I've been working as an economist, investment strategist for over 20 years. And you know, we started looking at AI in the future of work, what it could do to the workforce, our jobs included, Christine, believe it or not, ten years ago. So it's been increasing part of my focus, my team's focus. But four years ago, we took it even more seriously, and we collected the most data in the world to my knowledge on technology, the labor market, what AI could do, look at past technologies and throw them into the soup with everything else that's going on in the world. We got high debt levels, we got aging of society to really get a handle. Can we get a handle on where the risk, the opportunities, what the implications are of how AI could evolve and what it could do to growth, interest rates, and our personal lives too? And I can tell you that the diagnosis, the data-driven framework we created when I first started seeing the results three or four years ago, Christine, they were eye opening to me and so much so that we felt compelled to bring that to a broad audience. But the diagnosis, the heart of the diagnosis stands and that is one with increasing odds AI was going to prove to be the most disruptive and transformative technology in over two generations. So, at least as important impacts as the personal computer, but they will look different and we'll get into that. Secondly, is that it won't be a mass automation loss for all jobs, but there will be pockets clearly of disruption. And I think that's on a lot of people's minds. I have children of college ages on their mind. And so I think we'll talk about that.
And you know, thirdly, is that just as I openly what we diagnosed in our rich, you know, sort of analysis, Christine, and it's something I didn't see coming, is that there is risk and opportunities that emerge in the investment landscape that evolve over the course of the technology cycle. We're still what I would say is in phase one. So, you see some winners in the markets, but that will gravitate or pivot to phase two. So, I think there's risks and opportunities for listeners and we'll get into that. That's a diagnosis I didn't see coming. But when we look at in the past, it actually makes a lot of sense once you understand what's going on. So, I hopefully we'll talk about them today.
Christine Kashkari: Now, last year, I mean, economists were still debating abstract theoretical protections. Now we have the data, corporate earnings, capex spending, labor metrics. What are they telling you?
Joe Davis: We will see both continued acceleration in AI investment that ultimately over the next three or four years will start to translate into productivity. Some listeners will hear an efficiency which sounds like job loss and all make sure we're going to go there today. But ultimately, it'll have as important impact on the economy from a macro perspective as a personal computer, but it'll happen twice as fast. And so that's generally the good news. But I want to say it's disruption and disruption sounds negative, but there will be winners and losers during this transition. Over the course of the next two or three years, if we're right, AI will start to move from just potential way to invest in data centers and chips. This is the, you know, the the picks and shovels and some automation save time, sounds like job loss. You will also see augmentation. So, I get better at my job or I can do more with the same amount of time. That's what's being missed in the dialogue. And we will see three times as many occupations see that effect as the job loss. And finally, what we have not yet seen and there's still risk to never seeing. And that is what we saw with the Internet and with electricity. And that is it creates new industries. It's a platform. The great example would be with the rise of the Internet, there was companies that started to sell, I don't know, books online. They started to transform more other sectors. And so things such as online shopping, we take for granted today where the movie industry would not have occurred without electricity. These are things I talk about in the book that has still yet to be seen, which is why are the odds of us entering that higher growth trend world for the next three or four years? It's become our baseline. But why the odds are certainly not 100%. And where we could be wrong is that we don't see that augmentative. Hey, Joe, I want this as a copilot for my work, not just as a substitute or what are the new industries. But there's ways that we can navigate this as workers as well as investors.
Your job in five years
Christine Kashkari: Joe, I've heard you talk about this before that the AI does transform and lead to just enormous productivity that would be equivalent to, is it 17,000,000 baby boomers not retiring.
Joe Davis: Not retiring. Well, that's the unlock, yes, 17,000,000 that's both were a combination of saving some time as well as where it's more efficient and productive in the work that we do. So it's a combination, but again, it's overcoming effectively the demographic headwind that many societies have through the disruption that you're able to get those effects. I would say AI would come at is coming at the right time given some of the demographic challenges. But I do not want to sugarcoat it. Eighty percent of the occupations in the world will see a meaningful shift in how they do our work, mine included. And I believe yours as well, Christine, over the next three to five years. And when you hear disruption, when I hear that the human being in me says that's bad, that's what it I'm telling you there's change. And there are roughly by our best estimates, one in five occupations because they are exposed to what AI can do really well. There's not much leftover and you can start to see a stalling in the job market. And so our assessment was we're going to have this profound automation anxiety I feel with my friends. I have two college age children who are entering the work world. I know the concerns and I'm not dismissing them out of hand. They are there and they're legitimate. But what I'm trying to balance is for those that say mass law job loss, by our assessment, it is quite honestly, it is incorrect. They are not looking at the job descriptions because AI can also lead to more throughput. And there's a lot of tasks in the jobs that I have that I have to do, which is why net, net I'm changing what I do. But I'm going to see at the end of the day, more the need for my job, not less. So, I'd say for the average listener, the way to think about this is think about the percentage of the time at work that you use the computer. So for me, it's roughly 70-80%. So, Christine, is it the same? So, that's the likelihood of AI materially changing how you and I do our jobs in the next three to five years. That's high. The personal computer, by the way, was 30 to 40%. Now divide that number 70-80% by two. That is how you're going to spend your time differently on average three to four years from now. So if it's 80%, I just divide it by two. That's 40%. That's two out of five working days. I'm going to be doing things differently than what I am doing four years ago. So, what I tell individuals, use AI as much as humanly possible in your job. So, I'll be bold enough to say this, Christine, let's try to automate our jobs away. Odds are you actually won't be able to do it, but you will learn two things. One, you will say you know what, I'll become much more proficient what AI can do. I'm learning. That's good because I am now more productive, and I will either help my coworkers or I will get ahead of them. I'm going to be honest in a competitive world. Secondly, I may find I am in one of the the 20% of occupations that three or four years from now, we'll start to see a little bit of it, can do a lot of it. All I will say is we have a better indication now rather than avoiding AI. I will have a better sense and better assessment to start thinking about what I could do three or four years from now because it's not there, but there is some writing on the wall. With the benefit of hindsight, you could have told in 1990 you're going to have some job pressures in telecom. And so I'm not sugar coating this, but it would give you some time because we have identified and most of those affected occupations, there's a 70 or 80% chance that you can migrate with similar skills to a different field. We've taken this really seriously. It's not 100%, but you can and start getting a little bit ahead of that.
Portfolios and the great rotation
Christine Kashkari: What does this mean for investors?
Joe Davis: With all the research we did, the thing that I found pretty striking which I did not know was that on average when great technologies emerge over a seven or 10 year period, there actually tends to be what I would call two phases to the investment landscape in the investing cycle. And that the winners and losers, the asset classes, stocks, bonds, sectors of the market, countries within the equity market, the winners and losers actually changes over the course of that cycle in pretty profound ways. And loosely speaking, I think we're still in what's called phase one. It's the emergent. It's not, it's the production of the technology and one starts using it, right. It's what the economist called fusion. That's a fancy way for saying it's just, it's deploying through the economy, right? It's with the picks and shovels. So it's the today, it's the chips, it's the data centers, the computer and Internet. It was bandwidth, it's fiber optics. It's software and, personal computer hard drives. Who do you think is having the highest earnings growth in stock returns? Well, it's the producers of the technology. We saw this without exception in every past investment cycle, and that is what has carried the S&P 500, quite frankly. It's been a lot of the large technology companies and they're you know, they're being rewarded for a lot of the innovation and that they're doing. What I was shocked to find is that at some point in the second-half of the technology cycle, the investment opportunity shifts and pretty profoundly. But there's a rationale for it and for three reasons. The leadership changes significantly between the technology producers and the users of the technology. Because remember if this is a transformational technology, it's changing the profitability, the revenue, the efficiency of the companies that are now using it. So, which means it's outside the technology field. And it also is because the technology disrupts its own industry the most.
Christine Kaskari: What's the most important action an investor must take and a mistake that they should absolutely avoid?
Joe Davis: What is clear is investors the most high, the highest conviction sort of portfolio exercises to start deploying new capital or rebalancing your existing portfolio actually away from the technology field. Not because we're pessimistic on a, but quite the contrary, we're actually optimistic on some of its transformative ability because we are likely entering or starting to enter an extended period where AI will not just be picks and shovels just start to benefit the profitability and the new revenue for companies outside the technology space. And so that's the highest conviction. You know, we could talk about, you know, small cap versus large or other countries, but that is by far the biggest one. It's the simplest thing. The technology in the mag 7 have dominated returns for the S&P for some time. There's a rationale technology base that starts to deploy capital to other parts of the market. It's what I would call the great rotation, and it has happened in the six previous tech cycles. It's happened in every single one of them.
Christine Kashkari: What about for the mistakes?
Joe Davis: Well, the mistakes I think is, being too is being overly confident in that the AI momentum will continue to solely accrue to the technology producers. That's similar to what my previous comment is. I think the other thing is I'm trying to keep a dose of humility. I'm so close to this exercise. And so you know, hedging the conviction, the data says don't make drastic changes in the portfolio. We have a frothy equity market, but it's not in bubble territory. We have compelling fixed income yields. So I think it's around deploying new capital. Let's add some resilience here. It gets a little bit away from some of the concentration in the S&P and it's done in the thoughtful way that doesn't lead to radical changes in the portfolio.
Christine Kashkari: You talked a lot about equities. What about fixed income?
Joe Davis: Well, I think we're talking about resilience of an entire multi asset portfolio. So, I'd say, you know, if AI is transformational, like we think in the baseline value is the first deploy, you know, strategy if you're actively minded in the equity side. The second one is actually just harnessing fixed income and we have real yields or risk premiums, Christine, that are higher even from last year, but it's been a theme of ours. It provides some resilience if we have an equity market correction and you're not giving up as nearly as much. So that's a default. I think if AI is a sort of overrated, it'll push you even more in the fixed income there. You may have concerns of fiscal pressures and long-term Treasuries. You can make a case for a little bit shorter duration. But I think the headline though is you would actually deploy even more fixed income. So, you can see where I'm going here is either world pushes you within equity to deploy capital more into value. And certainly, it's a rich fixed income allocation in either scenario. And you would go up at actually if AI disappoints. And so that's what our analysts continue to push. That's where I would say deploying capital. So, pretty exciting.
What if AI disappoints?
Christine Kashkari: So, Joe, you lay out a compelling argument for AI as a transformative technology that we'll see sometime in their lifetime. But I'd love to do this exercise with you. The pre mortems. Not the post mortems, but the pre mortems. So basically, we'll lay out a scenario in the future where you are wrong.
Joe Davis: Yeah, sure. It's a healthy exercise. Yeah.
Christine Kashkari: Let's do this pre mortem. It's 2030. Yep. And AI has not delivered the economic and economic promise that we thought and had also at the same time delivered a lot of social implications.
Joe Davis: Yeah.
Christine Kashkari: Why do you think it failed?
Joe Davis: Why? I'd say it didn't evolve as we most likely thought. That's a world 2030. AI has not become a general purpose technology. The most likely thing what happened though, is that AI only automated. It's what our second most likely scenario is. It's a 20%. So I got some of the negative effects. Okay, so companies are more efficient, but we have job loss and you get the wealth effects of new industries. Christine or, or me being better. I'm getting a bigger paycheck because I'm more productive. And, and so, you know, you got the assembly line for the office. It would be very disappointing. There would be some social impacts because we have higher unemployment. Yeah, we don't have the higher growth to go with it. And the stock market is definitely not prepared for that. Society would that would be disruptive for sure. And we're keeping a close eye on that because 20% is certainly not a zero odds.
Christine Kashkari: What signal should people be watching out for?
Joe Davis: Well, I'll tell you once we are monitoring right now, Christine, if we're going down that path or we're not, three things we will see over the next two years. One is in the markets themselves. We're already starting to see it and that is the max 7 start trailing the 493. That's where it's actually where the concept came from is this dynamic that's one. Secondly, in the labor market, we see less of the automation concerns. We actually continue to see positive even though lower job growth. But here's the thing, you start to see the hiring rate of college age graduates start to strengthen again, why AI is now a complement of more jobs than a substitute. And then the third one, you would start to see investment rates and new company formation outside of AI companies. And so you start to see new healthcare companies, you start to see new financial service companies, that's the creative destruction and the green shoots, knowing that you have a technological transformation coming. And so those would be the three, I think in those order, we're seeing the first one, second one I think we could see, but time remains. And then the third one could be 2027 and beyond.
Christine Kashkari: Thank you so much, Joe.
Joe Davis: Oh, you're welcome.
Christine Kashkari: Well, that's it for today's episode. Next time, we're tackling one of the biggest challenges in personal finance, turning a lifetime of savings into income. Join us for that conversation and all upcoming episodes. If you enjoyed this episode and found it helpful, subscribe and share.

In the first episode of season three of Better Vantage, Joe Davis, global chief economist at Vanguard, explains why artificial intelligence could be as transformative as any innovation in two generations, but that transformation will look different from what many expect.
Rather than wholesale job loss, AI could reshape how 80% of occupations function while creating opportunities for those who adapt. One in five occupations may face pressure as AI takes on tasks traditionally requiring human judgment. Yet, three times as many will see workers becoming more productive with AI as a tool rather than replaced by it.
In addition to offering workers practical recommendations for adapting to this new technology, Davis says he sees AI’s investment impact as a shift from a market that favors companies producing this technology to one that rewards companies that use AI to transform their operations and create new revenue streams.
The key takeaway: AI represents genuine transformation, but navigating it successfully requires understanding its potential and people’s capacity to adapt. Do your homework, stay engaged with the technology, and think beyond the hype.

articles.title: Growth and regulation - speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
Growth and regulation - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at The Financial and Professional Services Dinner, Mansion House

Published on
14 July 2026

In his speech, Andrew Bailey argues that well-designed regulation can support sustainable economic growth by providing stability, enabling innovation and protecting financial stability. He sets out why the UK needs stronger long-term growth, explains the role of bank capital in supporting a resilient banking system, highlights the potential of modern payments and tokenisation, and discusses the opportunities and risks posed by artificial intelligence. This includes the need for proactive public policy and international coordination on frontier AI and cyber resilience.

Speech
Back in early February I was foolish enough to remark to a colleague that on the economic front things were looking more settled, and of course that was a good thing. We seemed to be in more stable times. I was expecting inflation to return to its 2.0% target in around April or May, and then we would need to assess what level of interest rate would keep it there.
Well, that jinxed it. Shortly afterwards, the Middle East conflict broke out. Since then, energy prices have gone up and then returned to levels a bit above where they were before it started, although we are now seeing renewed volatility. Inflation hasn’t returned to target, though the evidence we have seen over recent months has tended to reinforce my view that it would otherwise have done so. Moreover, we are operating in a fairly soft economic setting activity-wise.
We will ensure inflation returns to target and the context is currently encouraging, although uncertainty remains a feature of the situation. But, it will take longer.
I want to step back this evening and consider the longer-term context for the UK economy. Two things stand out for me in terms of the economic context here in the UK. First, we have had lower growth in the economy for the last fifteen years or so. Second, the economy has been hit by a sequence of negative supply shocks which have contributed to the lower growth rate – we can think of Covid, the Ukraine war, the impact of Brexit, etc.
When we think about sustainable growth we have in mind an upper limit that can be achieved without over-heating the economy - something we call the growth of potential supply. This is a speed limit on sustainable growth, and it is influenced by the amount of labour in an economy and how productive it is. For around fifteen years before the financial crisis, the average annual rate of growth of potential supply in the UK economy was around 2.8%. Productivity contributed 2.4pp and labour supply 0.4pp. For the roughly fifteen years since the financial crisis, the potential growth rate has fallen to 1.3% pa, of which productivity contributed 0.4pp and labour supply 0.8pp.
This has had a direct effect on living standards in the UK. Between 1990 and the financial crisis, the average annual growth rate of national income per head was 2.0%, whereas post-crisis it has been 0.6%.
It must therefore be a priority to raise the potential and actual growth rates. Macroeconomic policy provides an important backdrop to doing that. And the best thing we can do on this front is to create and maintain stability – and here I am talking about monetary and fiscal policy. My strongly held view is that, notwithstanding the sequence of adverse shocks, including the latest one from the Middle East, we have the policy frameworks, and policies themselves, in place to provide that stability.
Longer-term growth – the sort we need more of – comes from the supply side. As well as being impacted by negative supply shocks, growth can also be spurred by positive developments that allow us to take leaps forwards.
In this context, what are the longer-run causes of growth in an economy? The list is quite long: physical capital accumulation; technological progress; human capital including education and skills; trade; financial development; markets and competition; infrastructure; and institutional development, both public and private, including public policy and regulation.
Tonight, I want to focus mainly on the role of the final item on that list, regulation.
There is a lot of commentary that regulation is having an excessive negative effect on growth. We shouldn’t ignore this. Well-designed regulation should support economic growth, not hinder it. It can correct market failures; reduce transaction costs; lower entry barriers; and support competition and innovation. In our world, regulation has lowered the probability and severity of financial crises, thereby supporting sustainable growth by safeguarding the supply of finance – in other words, allowing companies and households to plan with confidence for the long term.
Of course, if regulation isn’t well designed and executed, this will not be true. And, to be clear, this would be a real issue across the whole economy.
What do we mean by well-designed and executed? Regulation should always be defined in terms of a positive purpose. In other words, we want to achieve an objective and regulation should help to do that. We should then design the precise regulatory regime that achieves this positive objective as quickly and effectively as possible whilst minimising any undesirable side effects.
This framing should lead to a better debate on the principle and practice of regulation. Are we achieving our objective or not? This is a much better way of framing the issue than simply a too much / too little debate about regulation which is divorced from the objective. Yet too much of the debate on regulation is precisely of this too much / too little sort, in abstract from the outcomes we want to see.
Much of our regulation has the objective of maintaining financial stability. We strongly believe that financial stability is a prerequisite of economic growth. However, we should never say that therefore every one of our rules and regulations is perfectly formed. That will not be the case. But, likewise, to simply argue for less regulation is unhelpfully reductive.
With that in mind, let me move on to look at three highly relevant current policy issues that we face, which are important in their own right but which also bring out the role of the regulation in public policy and the sort of issues we can face. The three current issues are: the level of capital held by banks; payments; and artificial intelligence, particularly so-called Frontier AI.
I will start with bank capital and go right back to basics to make the point that simply arguing for “more” or “less” are not sensible positions in and of themselves.
The main reason for regulating banks is to protect deposits. This begs the question, what is special about deposits? They constitute for all of us the main stock of money that we hold. Regulation exists to ensure confidence in the nominal value of that money. We could achieve this by requiring all the assets of banks to be risk free. But this is neither practical nor helpful from the point of view of supporting activity in the economy, where a degree of risk-taking is of course essential to support growth.
We have, therefore, a banking system that combines deposits as money with lending in the form of credit creation, also known as fractional reserve banking.
This puts banks at the centre of the financial and economic system. It also means that as well as wanting an assured nominal value for deposits, as policymakers we want banks to be able to extend credit across a wide range of activities at all times, thereby supporting the economy right through the business cycle. Striking this balance is the basis of macroprudential regulation and the work of the PRA and the Bank’s Financial Policy Committee in deciding how much capital banks must hold.
Capital is there to absorb losses and thus preserve the nominal value of deposits. It provides assurance to a bank’s customers and counterparties that they can go about their business with confidence. This means that capital instruments are performing the essential function of backing up the assured value of money. They bear the risk, and the return they earn must exceed the amount of loss providers of capital might expect to bear. This gets to the heart of why calibrating capital sensibly – not simply seeking more or less of it – is critical.
This is an important point, because for much of the post-financial crisis period major UK banks earned returns below 10 per cent, a lower-end estimate of the return required by equity investors over the longer term. Aggregate returns rose above 10 per cent in 2023 and reached 15.4% earlier this year. These banks’ price to book ratios are also now around 1.7 times, indicating that equity investors expect future returns to exceed the cost of capital.
There should not, to be clear, be a cap on returns set by regulators. That is a matter of commercial strategy for firms and good regulation should help markets to flush out supranormal profits by reducing barriers to entry. But conditions of financial stability do require that the return earned by investors is above the cost of capital, else capital will simply not be supplied. Regulation must therefore strike the right balance.
That leaves the important question of how much capital should be required. That is a debate that we can have, and are having, but it must be set within the context of maintaining financial stability. We announced changes to the capital regime last week to remove some anomalies, set within the positive objective of financial stability. We are very much open to simplifying and adjusting regulations where needed. But, doing so must contribute to sustaining a healthy banking system which can support and foster stronger growth in the economy.
What does this mean in practice? Sometimes, I hear arguments made which bear some resemblance to the old lump of labour fallacy – except that here it would be a lump of capital. Just as the lump of labour argument assumed a finite amount of labour input could be used in an economy, there is also I fear assumed to be an invariant amount of bank capital, and therefore lightening regulatory rules is necessary to allow that sum of capital to support more lending.
But capital is not invariant. The health of the banking system, and thus the support it can provide to the economy, are in good part interlinked with the returns it earns relative to the opportunity cost of supplying that capital. Banks that earn healthy returns which exceed the cost of capital will be in a stronger position to justify retaining earnings – building capital - to support more lending.
Regulation can support this outcome. Effective regulation which is proportionate will support a lower cost of capital, while weak and ineffective regulation will tend to raise the cost of capital.
I would contend that the position of UK banks today is one of good health and resilience, and this is supported by returns that exceed the cost of capital. The lump of bank capital is therefore not fixed. The system is competitive. This is a positive state of affairs, to which regulation contributes.
Let me move on to the second case, payments, something I spoke about at the end of my remarks here at the Mansion House last year. I am going to talk about regulation in a very broad sense, including the operational role of the Bank of England.
The are two critical positive objectives in the regulation of payments. One is to achieve the so-called singleness of money – which is the assured nominal value of money across all its forms. The second is so-called finality of settlement – the knowledge that payments, once made can be relied on. Together, these anchor confidence in the role of money as a means of payment.
Let me give a simple illustration of why these anchors are important. If we make a payment to each other, we want to know – and not have to spend our time worrying about - two things. First, that the pound in my account and in your account are the same – the nominal value point. And, second, that the payment will be finalised both operationally and legally, so a payment gets made and stays made. Regulation and public policy can help these outcomes happen, while also supporting innovation and competition.
As I said last year, we want to modernise payment systems. We think doing so will enhance their efficiency and functionality and support confidence in the role of money in the economy, thus supporting growth in the economy. We must also continue to enhance the operational resilience of payments, notably to protect against fraud and cyber attacks.
These more modern systems bring the potential benefits of digital technology to payments, for instance so-called programmable payments – “money with instructions” if you like. We think there is scope for important progress in tackling fraud, reducing payment delays, and benefitting trade by increasing the speed of cross-border payments. Innovation can also reduce contracting costs and increase transaction scope in a more digital economy, for instance by allowing small firms to participate better in ecommerce and thereby support growth in the economy.
Last year, we implemented a key part of the infrastructure to achieve this through the renewal of the RTGS system. This will enable innovation – something the Bank is doing jointly with the private sector through our Synchronisation lab.
And in our Digital Securities Sandbox we are supporting the issuance of tokenised assets. The first DSS participant was approved for live activity yesterday. This development will help support the issuance of a UK digital gilt, known as DIGIT. We will work with HMT to enable DIGIT’s eligibility as collateral in the Bank’s market operations.
We are now working with the banks to design and implement the introduction of so-called tokenised money. This will create the ability to tokenise bank deposits and allow the exchange of money to happen on digital tokenised ledgers, in turn enabling programmable payments.
Tokenisation sounds gimmicky and nerdy I admit. Put simply, it is another enabling step, in this case enabling things like faster, more assured payments or the contingent performance of contracts through smart contracts and programmability – i.e. payments that will only be made conditional on the other party first delivering. What might that deliver in the real world? It could be formally making a payment linked to the delivery of goods. It could be formally making a payment dependent on the recipient delivering proof of identity. The first could reduce late payments, the second could reduce fraud. Critically, it changes the point of review or audit of the payment from ex-post to ex-ante. These benefits are worth having, but need a policy framework to enable them to be exploited in an orderly fashion.footnote [1]
We are also moving to enable competition in this field. Recently, we issued proposed rules for so-called systemic sterling stablecoins, to enable these to come into existence as a means of payment beyond the crypto world. These rules will put into effect the key principles of assured nominal value and settlement finality.
This is all about making innovation happen, something that as a public authority and regulator we also do by working closely with industry. In the field of payments innovation using commercial bank money we now have the Bank chaired Retail Payments Infrastructure Board up and running to drive forward work on the design of the next generation retail payments infrastructure. It issued a consultation document on 25 June covering what types of retail payments are likely to be demanded by end-users in the future, and the resulting design issues and principles. The next stage will be to produce a Blueprint and Requirements which will be handed over to an industry owned Delivery Company to build. We are looking for feedback on this consultation by 11 September.
In turn, this kind of regulation supports outcomes that can spur growth in the economy, a positive outcome that we can do best by defining the public good outcomes that we want – these include setting the conditions for assured nominal value of money and settlement finality – and then getting on with them.
This brings me to the third case that we are dealing with, the impact of artificial intelligence. Obviously, it’s a big subject on which much can be said, so in no sense do I pretend to be comprehensive here. On a modest scale, I will make some more general comments relevant to the issues around economic growth and some big public policy and regulatory issues, and then I will add some thoughts on so-called Frontier AI.
I think that General Purpose Technology (GPT) innovation has been, and will continue to be, a major source of longer-run growth in the economy. A GPT is a technology with broad, economy-wide applications that advances over time and enables complementary innovations across many sectors of the economy. Looking back, I would say the following qualify as GPTs: the steam engine; the internal combustion engine; electricity; and information processing and the internet. GPTs come in long cycles, but there can be gaps between them which demonstrate lower growth.
Is this a reasonable description of the last fifteen years or so? Yes. The internet is everywhere but, as it has become so, its contribution to growth will have diminished. You can only get so much of it – honestly. One clue for this as a characterisation of the last fifteen years or so is declining productivity growth.
The obvious question is what will be the next GPT? It’s most likely to be AI, though I would add that AI – like most GPTs – will act to support advances elsewhere: in diagnostics, in research, or with robotics. This underscores that GPTs are enabling technologies – they make other things happen which support growth. The first invention often triggers a sequence of secondary innovations which spread its reach.
But timing is everything, and I think we are between two major cycles of technological innovation showing up in the productivity and growth statistics – between the internet and AI if you like. And innovation can take time to show up in productivity and growth at the economy-wide level. In 1987, the economist Robert Solow commented that “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics”.
A similar thing could be said about James Watt and the steam engine and Thomas Edison and electricity. This is not so surprising. Change can be gradual, and it often requires complementary innovations – as well as trial and error -to get the economic benefit of the GPT, and those take time. And, for now, we are really experimenting with the new technology before we get the economic benefits, which is certainly true of me and AI.
This does not detract from the view that AI is likely to be the next GPT and is likely to raise growth levels in the economy.
But, in doing so, it will raise very big public policy and regulatory issues which we will need to solve, and I would argue we should do so positively and promptly. In other words, we should be regulating for the positive outcome of safe, productive use of AI.
I could set out quite a few big questions of this sort which AI prompts. I am going to stick to two, to provide illustration. These are not questions for the Bank of England to answer, but certainly ones in which we all have a great interest.
First, there are questions on resource allocation. It is said to me by people in the AI industry that there is not enough foreseeable clean power supply (here I mean “clean” in the technical sense of high quality, uninterrupted supply) needed by datacentres to meet all the likely demand from AI. This ultimately, creates the need to make trade-offs. So, should we prioritise medical research (which has great potential), drone technology, finance, entertainment, etc? Markets can always answer that question, but they may well not do so in ways that capture the public interest. This is a big issue, at least potentially.
Second, the rise of AI creates problems of law. Consider so-called agentic AI where we can create AI agents to act on our behalf – say, to buy or trade things. But a feature of AI, including AI created agents, is learning from its own experience, and this learning capacity is growing rapidly. And they can develop bad habits of their own – like lying, or covering up gaps in knowledge in an attempt to please us. These are not new issues.
But, typically, in law a principal becomes responsible for an agent while the agent operates within the remit given to it by the principal. If the agent goes beyond that remit, or acts improperly, it becomes responsible. Traditionally that had depended on the agent having a legal persona, i.e. being a human or a company etc.
But when the agent has no legal persona does that leave the principal responsible at all times? If so, principals may need to constrain agents in ways that cut against the direction of innovation in AI models.
Put another way, is agentic AI in this context more a tool of the principal rather than strictly an agent, with the principal fully liable for all that is done and not done? Does this apply when real money is spent in ways that are final and binding, as and when agentic AI is allowed to hold the purse strings? This removes questions around the boundary of authority but should leave principals wondering how their governance frameworks can effectively operate with this technology. We must think about these things now: and I use this case study to illustrate why we must take a positive and pro-active approach to solving problems which are critical to ensuring effective innovation.
These are very big questions, on which there will need to be public policy input, and probably a mixture of law and regulation. My general argument is that we should tackle them pro-actively and positively, and not get stuck in a negative debate on regulation.
Let me turn to another aspect of AI, namely frontier AI and the risk it poses to the security of IT systems and the potential for cyber attacks. Suffice to say, it appears to have moved on very rapidly, and represents a major threat to the security of systems and thus in our world to financial stability.
To cut the story short, the ability of cutting-edge models to find, and potentially to exploit, vulnerabilities in systems poses some very important public policy and regulatory challenges, as well as challenges for all of us in relation to the systems we use ourselves. Here there are two big challenges relevant to the world of financial stability.
First, we need much stronger co-ordination of testing of frontier models before they go into wide circulation. This needs to be co-ordinated internationally because no country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today. Such co-ordinated testing needs to start at the level of public authorities. Here, the UK is in a strong position because the AI Security Institute is world leading. And, new models need to go on to testing across the Critical National Infrastructure. Again, the UK is well placed because of the strengths of the National Cyber Security Centre. We at the Bank are working very closely with firms we regulate, including establishing forums to share and improve the efficiency of work on patching systems where needed.
Second, we need to move to much more robust approaches to allow us to recover when things do go wrong. This is often described as Bare Metal recovery – think of it as restoring systems from scratch to a fully operational state. A bigger and more immediate threat means we simply must have the right capabilities. Again, these are big issues, and ones where the best sort of regulation involves working together to facilitate an agreed positive outcome.
To conclude. Economic growth is hugely important and regulation – done right - can play a hugely important role. Growth will come from innovation on the supply side of the economy. I believe technology is a source of growth, and AI is the most likely next big contributor. Inevitably, very big issues come with such change, ones that must be solved with a strong input from public policy and regulation.
But, as in other aspects of regulation, we must do this in a positive way – define what we want to achieve, by when, and then work out how to achieve it in the most effective way. We have to roll our sleeves up and get on with it. Yes, we must question existing regulation, but we must do so in a positive spirit of what we want to achieve.
I would like to thank David Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Victoria Cleland, George Johnston, Karen Jude, Tom Mutton, Nicola O’Keefe, Rhys Phillips, Rob Price and Francine Robb their assistance in preparing these remarks

There are other benefits of Tokenisation. Atomic Settlement – whereby all legs of a financial transaction either complete together or not at all, thus simultaneous settlement - can enable greater efficiency and less risk in wholesale markets.

articles.title: Commodity Prices Set to Increase by 23% in 2026 as Global Shocks Mount
articles.text:
PRESS RELEASE October 28, 2026Commodity Prices Set to Increase by 23% in 2026 as Global Shocks Mount

SharePrint

Energy prices to rise 32% in 2026; food commodity prices to climb 18% in 2026–27
WASHINGTON, October 28, 2026—Commodity prices are set to rise 23% in 2026 as global shocks mount, according to the World Bank Group’s latest Commodity Markets Outlook, released today. The conflict in the Middle East has drawn down oil inventories and is set to push energy prices to a four-year high. Meanwhile, disrupted grain shipments and El Niño threaten harvests and food affordability. With oil stocks depleted, the world is more exposed to further supply shocks. As countries respond to these challenges, the World Bank Group is making financing and support available through its existing instruments, while scaling up its ability to mobilize private capital alongside its own resources.
Energy prices are projected to rise 32% in 2026, reversing three years of declines, before moderating in 2027. Brent is forecast to average $91 per barrel in 2026, up from $69 in 2025, then ease to $79 in 2027. Food commodity prices are expected to rise about 10% in 2026 and another 7% in 2027—a cumulative increase of 18%—as conflict disrupts grain shipments, El Niño threatens harvests, and high fuel and fertilizer prices increase agricultural costs. Overall commodity prices are forecast to rise 23% this year before declining by 7% in 2027.
The forecasts assume no major intensification of conflicts affecting global commodity supplies. However, energy prices could rise further if the conflict in the Middle East escalates and damage to Russia’s oil infrastructure persists. At the same time, higher-than-expected energy prices, attacks on Black Sea grain shipments, and a very strong El Niño could combine to produce a food crisis that pushes more people into extreme poverty, similar to the situation during the early 2010s. In an adverse scenario in which these risks materialize together, Brent could average $105 a barrel in 2027 and food commodity prices could be 12% higher than expected in the baseline forecast, surpassing their level in 2022.
“Commodity markets are being hit by several major shocks at once,” said Ayhan Kose, the World Bank’s Deputy Chief Economist and Director of the Prospects Group. “Higher energy costs and trade disruptions are driving up prices across a broad range of commodities, threatening to worsen inflation, food insecurity, and economic growth. The priority must be to protect the poorest people and support low-income countries already struggling with heavy debt burdens.”
To support countries as they manage the fallout from higher prices, the World Bank Group has made $50 billion to $60 billion available through existing instruments, including $25 billion in pre-arranged financing. This can support social safety nets for the most vulnerable people, boost fiscal capacity, and provide working capital and liquidity support for firms and farms. At the same time, the institution has made substantial progress on accelerating and simplifying its ability to mobilize private capital alongside its own financing and knowledge services. As a result, the World Bank Group is well positioned to invest in the next generation of youth in developing countries—most importantly, by improving the conditions for job creation.
The conflict is forcing adjustments in how the world produces and consumes energy. Global oil supply is projected to fall 5.2% in 2026—the largest drop in more than four decades outside the 2020 global recession. Meanwhile, consumption is expected to decline 2.5%, the third-largest annual contraction on record, after 2020 and 1980. High prices amid supply shortages are curbing demand, while electrification is also reducing oil use, particularly in China. Even so, production remains below consumption, forcing further withdrawals from oil stocks and leaving markets more exposed to renewed disruption.
Fertilizer prices are set to rise 14% in 2026, after a surge in urea prices early in the year that has since eased, before returning to 2025 levels in 2027.
Metals prices are set to reach a new high in 2026, rising 25% as prices of aluminum, copper, and tin all hit record highs. These gains reflect strong demand from investments in renewable energy, electric vehicles, and data centers, together with supply disruptions this year. Prices are expected to decline by 3% in 2027. Precious metals prices are forecast to increase by 40% in 2026 as demand for safe-haven assets remains elevated amid geopolitical and policy uncertainty. They are expected to moderate somewhat in 2027 but remain more than three times their 2015–19 average.
The report’s special focus examines the interconnectedness of commodity markets, as in the degree to which variation in one commodity’s price can be explained by shocks to other commodity prices. It finds that links between commodity-price volatility become more pronounced during periods of economic or market stress, including since the start of the current conflict in the Middle East. Industrial metals transmit the most volatility to other commodity groups on average, although the role of oil prices rose markedly after the onset of the Middle East conflict.
