articles.title: 2026 MENA Crypto Adoption: $443.3B, UAE Up 32%
articles.text:
Summary
MENA’s crypto economy was essentially flat at $443.3 billion in the 2026 reporting period, a 1.4% decline that tracks the global rate.
The UAE’s crypto economy grew 32% to $104.8 billion, closing to 73% of Türkiye’s size and positioning the UAE to overtake Türkiye as MENA’s largest crypto economy as early as the 2027 period.
Türkiye’s $144.5 billion crypto economy contracted modestly as its licensing transition reshaped the service side, while domestic peer-to-peer stablecoin volume grew fivefold to $3.56 billion.
Iran’s crypto activity was shaped by two internet blackouts and the second Iran conflict, with bitcoin transactions falling as much as 90% during the acute phases but climbing back as users adapted.

The 2026 Geography of Crypto Report

Reserve your copy
The Middle East and North Africa spent the reporting period (July 2025 to June 2026) under a regional cloud of uncertainty, and crypto adoption reflects it in different ways. The Iran conflict that began on February 28, 2026, created cross-border pressure that touched every market we studied. On top of that sat market-specific stresses: an internet shutdown and crackdown in Iran and a licensing transition in Türkiye.As our intro chapter showed, the 2026 bear market cut crypto’s total market cap in half but barely dented on-chain economic activity worldwide. MENA followed the same pattern. The region’s crypto economy slipped from $449.6 billion to $443.3 billion, a decline of 1.4% that tracks the global rate. Sixteen of 24 MENA markets with measurable data grew. The regional total was essentially flat because Türkiye and the UAE, which together make up 56% of the regional economy, moved in opposite directions and largely cancelled each other out. What shaped MENA was not the bear market itself but the regional disruptions layered on top of it.What ties the regional story together is the encompassing pressure of geopolitical and economic uncertainty. When institutional capital looks for a durable regulated hub, it has concentrated in the UAE. When Türkiye’s exchange sector pauses to meet new licensing requirements, retail users bypass it and transact wallet-to-wallet. Each of these responses is specific to its market, but they are all responses to the same regional condition.Türkiye’s $144.5 billion crypto economy is shifting from exchange-dominated to institutionalTürkiye was MENA’s largest crypto economy in the 2026 period at $144.5 billion, roughly a third of the entire region. Our overall measure captures value received across service inflows, domestic peer-to-peer, cross-border peer-to-peer, and cross-border business-to-person transfers. Türkiye’s total contracted modestly year over year, but the decline reflects a market in transition, not one in retreat. Activity moved off licensed services onto wallet-to-wallet rails, and institutional engagement from banks and licensed platforms deepened. The net effect is a smaller but structurally stronger market.Right at the end of our study period, Türkiye began enforcing a new crypto industry regulatory regime that requires all Crypto Asset Service Providers (CASPs) in the country to hold licenses issued by the financial regulator SPK. Functionally, the country now requires CASPs to follow the same compliance protocols as financial institutions. The law “raised the operational bar for the whole industry,” said Burcu Küçükünal, CEO of Stablex, a Turkish exchange.“Crypto in Türkiye is becoming part of traditional finance rather than a parallel system,” Küçükünal said.Compliant exchanges are better-positioned to serve institutional demands under the new system, according to the experts we spoke to. For one, Turkish licensing criteria, operational rules, and capital requirements place the country’s crypto businesses in line with international standards, said Fatih Günaydın, General Manager at İş Digital Asset Technologies. That’s an important development for Türkiye and is likely to bolster growth among services.“Offering equity and crypto asset services within the same financial group, with due regard to the relevant authorizations and separation of activities, is increasingly on the agenda,” said Salim Karaman, CEO of BtcTurk, Türkiye’s largest crypto exchange. “The key change over the past 12 months has been a shift from assessing interest and potential toward developing services and taking steps to enter the market within the regulatory framework.”Türkiye’s $3.56 billion peer-to-peer economy has nowhere to goEven with its maturing institutional landscape, Türkiye retains a flourishing grassroots crypto economy. Its peer-to-peer economy grew fivefold to hit $3.56 billion in the 2026 period, the largest in the region by far. Türkiye’s peer-to-peer crypto economy is nearly three times larger than the rest of MENA’s combined. Nearly all of that growth was in stablecoins.While Türkiye has a sizable peer-to-peer market, that activity is not allowed to touch the real-world economy in ways we see elsewhere in the world.“In Türkiye, the use of crypto assets for payments for goods and services is prohibited by regulation,” said Günaydın. “However, stablecoins feature in individuals’ savings, primarily due to the advantages of low spreads and ease of transfer. On the commercial and SME front, they are used to a limited extent in international trade, within the limits permitted by the laws of both countries.”“Today, most activity is still about trading and protecting savings,” Küçükünal said. The appeal is straightforward: the U.S. dollar offers a stable store of value in a country where lira inflation has eroded household wealth for years, and dollar-pegged stablecoins put that stability in reach of anyone with a wallet. The same pattern shows up in other high-inflation markets around the world.But the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye prohibits using crypto assets to pay for goods and services, so none of that $3.56 billion in domestic wallet-to-wallet volume is moving between buyers and sellers in the real economy. It is moving between Turkish wallets primarily as a dollar-denominated savings and transfer mechanism.Küçükünal is explicit about the gap: “The strongest use cases for stablecoins in Türkiye are payments and money transfers, both domestic and cross-border, and these are not yet possible. A clear legal framework for stablecoin-based payments could grow demand well beyond trading.”Changing regulations prompted surge in Türkiye’s tokenized gold marketsDespite their surging popularity, stablecoins are not the default savings instrument in Türkiye. That would be physical gold, the “traditional store of value” for Turkish households, as Küçükünal put it. Turkish society’s centuries-old attachment to gold sees residents literally stash the precious metal under their mattresses; the government estimates the population hoards 5,000 tons of gold.In the 2026 period we began to see that trend move on-chain: Türkiye has become a world leader in the adoption of tokenized gold. Activity climbed from virtually zero in earlier reporting periods to nearly $1 billion in 2026. Küçükünal noticed a tokenized gold trading surge on Stablex: “Demand for tokenized gold shows that Turkish investors want familiar assets on new rails.”One place Türkiye’s desire for gold appears is in exchange order book data. We looked at the popularity of buying tokenized gold with Turkish lira; we found that it was the second most popular currency for buying tokenized gold globally, behind only the U.S. dollar. In fact, a greater share of Turkish lira trading volume flowed into tokenized gold than any other currency with an order book above $100 million.The rush came right as Türkiye’s Treasury and Finance Ministry changed its approach to gold. In January 2026, it announced a ban on purchasing physical gold (for example, jewelry and bars) using cash. The stated goal of the framework (called the Precious Metal Tracking System or KMTS) was curbing the informal economy and combating counterfeit gold.The cash ban did not reduce demand for gold. It redirected it and put a new floor under tokenized gold volumes: Trading in tokenized gold began to boom immediately after KMTS was announced. In February, for example, trading hit $183.9 million, representing 2.51% of the entire lira book. Traders appeared to be moving ahead of the pending restrictions.Then, when the restrictions actually came online a few months later, the trading rush subsided, but notably at a higher baseline than before, creating a new volume floor for tokenized gold.The government is already moving to formalize the trend. In July 2026, it issued new directives for trading digital precious metals in a regulated manner. This formalization will likely further boost the existing trend.“With the implementation of clear regulations, the market is rapidly evolving from a structure based solely on transaction volume into a mature ecosystem focused on institutional products,” said Günaydın.The UAE’s embrace of crypto businesses pays offThe United Arab Emirates has for years courted crypto business as part of a wider bid to diversify its historically oil-dependent economy. By leading on crypto regulation in particular, both the UAE could influence an emerging piece of global financial markets.That successful diversification campaign helped the Emirates’ crypto economy grow in a time of uncertainty. Even as the Iran war brought regional conflict and slowed the Emirates’ broader economic growth, its crypto economy grew by 32% to reach $104.8 billion. In fact, excluding the UAE, the rest of MENA contracted 8.6% instead of 1.4%. “Whilst the war impacted other areas of the UAE like tourism and hospitality, the impact on the crypto industry has been limited,” said Henri Arslanian, co-founder of Nine Blocks Capital Management, the first crypto hedge fund to be licensed by Dubai’s crypto regulator VARA.“Outside of the U.S., MENA and in particular the UAE has become the main hub for crypto firms’ global operations,” Arslanian added. He credits UAE financial regulators’ readiness to issue licenses as a catalyst for adoption; it “reduced in large part the career risk for any corporate executive in dealing with digital assets.”“A year ago, the growth conversation here was about retail access,” said Laurent Girouille, Senior Executive Officer at Rain Trading Limited. “Today the questions we get are operational: who is the regulated counterparty, where are the assets held, how does settlement reconcile. Those come from treasuries, family offices and licensed intermediaries rather than from first-time buyers.”The data reflect this. The UAE’s $102.3 billion services sector provided the vast majority of its cryptoeconomic growth in the 2026 period. Overall this category grew 29% period over period, with centralized exchange inflows growing 22%, to $55 billion, and institutional platforms (custodians and market-makers among them) growing 75% to reach $11.7 billion. Decentralized finance exchanges also saw over $31 billion in total inflows, up 31% over the prior period.While the services sector was the UAE’s crypto juggernaut in raw economic terms, its far-smaller peer-to-peer economies grew even faster. Domestic P2P payments were up 786% period-over-period, and cross-border peer-to-peer inflows jumped 18-fold. Cross-border business payments also spiked nearly 400%, buoyed by a surge of major stablecoin transfers of $1 million or more.“Many globally underestimate how much stablecoins are being used in B2B transactions” in the UAE, said Arslanian. “The UAE has become a global hub for such transactions.” He credited this to the UAE’s many regulated OTC brokers; they have “solid fiat offramps” that make moving out of crypto very easy for businesses.“Stablecoins are increasingly being viewed as financial infrastructure rather than simply an asset used within crypto markets,” said a spokesperson for Fuze Finance. “We are seeing more interest in using them for cross-border settlement, corporate treasury, merchant payments and remittances.”Together, the UAE’s fast-growing crypto economy is vaulting it toward the top of the region. It ended the 2026 period nearly three-quarters as large as Türkiye, MENA’s longtime leader. On current trajectories, the UAE’s crypto economy is on pace to surpass Türkiye in 2027.“The UAE’s rise as a global crypto hub will be analyzed for years by other jurisdictions as an example of how to grab an opportunity,” said Arslanian.How the Iran war affected crypto adoption in the UAEWhile the Iran war did not stunt growth of the UAE’s crypto services sector, it did coincide with a change in investing behavior in the Emirates: a rise in holders in tokenized gold, and comparative fall among holders of bitcoin. As in Türkiye, where the KMTS cash ban redirected gold demand on-chain, the catalyst in the UAE was different but the pattern was the same: uncertainty pushed investors toward a familiar asset on new rails.To be clear, bitcoin remains far more popular than tokenized gold in the UAE—and the world. They can both represent a form of “safe haven” asset in many cultures, as we saw in Türkiye most especially, that flourishes amid uncertainty. Gold “is a savings habit with centuries behind it,” said Girouille, the Rain executive. Indeed in March 2026, when the UAE first began getting targeted in Iranian attacks, the ranks of bitcoin holders and tokenized gold holders in the UAE both climbed.But the twin trends diverged in the comparative quiet that followed. After a ceasefire declaration was broken, the relative share of tokenized gold holders kept climbing in the UAE. More people were buying tokenized gold than before. Comparatively, the number of bitcoin holders began to shrink. Investors who had bought bitcoin during the uncertainty of war were dumping it during the calm.This stickiness may partly be due to the cultural perspective of gold in the region. It is less an asset to be traded than a savings instrument to be accumulated and held. Bitcoin may serve the same function elsewhere, but in the UAE the data suggests it did not during this period: investors bought it at the onset of conflict and sold it once the pressure eased. Gold holders held on.A cash-for-gold ban accelerated Türkiye’s adoption of tokenized gold adoption; war influenced the UAE’s. The catalysts were different, but the outcome was the same: when regulated infrastructure exists for a familiar asset, demand finds a way.In Iran, blackouts, bombs, and protests shape domestic adoptionIran is both home to one of the world’s most robust crypto economies, and one that has been compromised by illicit use. For one, regular Iranians use assets like bitcoin and stablecoins to hedge persistent inflation and conduct their everyday lives. Against this, the Iranian regime uses crypto to evade sanctions and fund the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and it relies on the country’s crypto sector to do it. For that reason, our analysis of grassroots crypto adoption in Iran focuses exclusively on the subset of in-country activity that we understand to be everyday use, not illicit behavior.To begin, we looked at how Iran’s rolling internet blackouts impacted crypto usage in 2026. The government twice shut down regular Iranians’ digital link to the world: First, for 20 days in January following the eruption and suppression of economic protests; and second, for 88 days immediately following the start of the war. In both cases the blackouts severely inhibited Iranians’ ability to use crypto.The chart below demonstrates the impact that turning off the internet had on internet-based money. Iranian bitcoin wallets made nearly 90% fewer bitcoin transactions in the first week of the first blackout than in our baseline period. Activity sprang back, eclipsing the baseline, as soon as the blackout lifted. Then one month later, when the war and the second blackout began, Iranian bitcoin transactions once again fell, this time by around 80%.Critically, in neither instance did bitcoin activity within Iran fall to 0% of baseline. In fact, during the second, extended blackout, activity gradually climbed back. This is one indication of the domestic population’s resilience and ability to bypass even the most severe digital restrictions. Over the course of weeks more and more Iranians figured out ways to get around the blackout, perhaps through Starlink connections or other means. As they did so, they made more and more bitcoin transactions. By the end of the second blackout activity had returned to over 75% of baseline.Then, when the restrictions began to be lifted in late May, and everyone had access once again, activity sprang upward to nearly double the baseline. Rather than crush bitcoin activity, the blackouts had bottled it up.Internet blackouts only stop one from spending cryptocurrency within an unplugged country, not receiving it. Outsiders could still send crypto into Iran throughout the impacted periods. Even so, our analysis of transaction activity found that cross-border stablecoin flows into Iran shifted during both blackout periods.Stablecoin transfers jumped to nearly 150% of baseline level. Then when the blackout took hold the cross-border flows dropped by around 80%. They rebounded immediately after the restrictions were lifted. As soon as the foreign wallets knew their Iranian counterparts could spend what they sent, they resumed the steady flow of stablecoins.The acute conflict between the U.S. and Iran initially prompted similar behavior: cross-border stablecoin activity fell by nearly 50%. But unlike the longer run suppressive effect of the second domestic internet blackout, cross border inflows to Iran resumed, and surpassed their baseline, even during the course of the blackout. The ceasefire on April 7 was the pivot point. After that, activity quickly surpassed the baseline rate.The activity patterns highlight how crypto-using populations adapt to real-world crises. Turning off the internet does stop people from using their internet money — but only to a point. They can still receive their crypto. And the longer a restriction stays in place, the more they will learn to bypass the blockade.Israel’s crypto economyIsrael’s crypto economy held steady amid 12 months of turbulence in MENA, growing only 0.7% period-over-period. In fact, it was one of the few markets globally that neither contracted nor grew amid bear market’s drag.Traders are driving this $37.9 billion story; the vast majority of activity we tracked were inflows into services, like exchanges. This is in line with what we heard from experts in Israel’s crypto scene. The country saw very limited peer-to-peer activity (making it an outlier in our region) and similarly negligible cross-border flows, both of which are still developing.“While trading and investment remain the primary use cases, crypto is increasingly being explored for cross-border payments, decentralized finance, and blockchain-based financial services,” said Noam Kaplan, a partner at KPMG Israel.Governing those future use-cases is an expanding rule book. In the months following our study period Israeli financial watchdogs issued regulations impacting stablecoins, token offerings, and, critically, capital requirements for virtual asset service providers. All of the new rules could help make the entire industry more resilient.“These changes could help bridge the gap between Israel’s crypto industry and its traditional financial system, supporting broader adoption,” said Kaplan.Israel remains a retail-driven crypto market“The Israeli crypto market is still predominantly retail-driven,” said Ilan Sterk, CEO of Israeli investments firm Altshuler Shaham’s crypto wing, Horizon. “Israel has not yet reached the level of institutional adoption seen in some larger international markets.”The transfer-size data corroborate this. In the 2026 period, 98.4% of Israeli transfers into services were under $10,000 but carried just 11% of the value. Transfers of $1 million or more carried 57% of the value, $21.3 billion. Institutional platforms took 10.8% of service inflows, down from a 2025 peak of 13.6% but still well above the 5.6% they held in 2024.Israel and stablecoinsStablecoins’ share of Israeli service inflows has risen in each of the past three reporting periods: from 48.1% in 2024 to 51.6% in 2025 to 57.0% in 2026. Their rising share reflects a tendency among Israel’s retail crypto base to buy locally and send internationally in pursuit of “trading opportunities that may not be available” in the country, said Sterk.“In Israel, stablecoins are currently used primarily as a bridge between the local crypto market and the broader global digital asset ecosystem,” he said.That international market captures the vast majority of Israeli activity. The one Israel-domiciled exchange we track took 0.06% of Israeli stablecoin service inflows, with the rest going abroad. Most Israeli stablecoin inflows go to offshore exchanges.Israelis buy stablecoins, hold them, and send them to offshore exchanges, but they rarely transact with each other. Israel’s domestic stablecoin velocity, which measures how many times a year the stablecoins held in Israeli personal wallets turn over through peer-to-peer transfers, was 1.46 in the 2026 period against 9.31 for the world.“A smaller but meaningful segment of Israeli users is using digital assets for practical financial purposes, particularly payments and cross-border transfers,” Sterk said. “These non-trading use cases still represent a relatively small share of the Israeli market compared with investment activity.”How the Iran war shaped Israel’s crypto industryWhat makes Israel different from the other MENA markets we studied is that the 2026 war produced no visible shift in its crypto activity. The early 2026 Iran war saw Israeli service inflows fall 18.9% against the three months before, slightly less than the world’s 23.6% drop. The 12-day war in June 2025 saw Israeli inflows fall 29.2% against the world’s 9.3%. Neither event came close to producing the kind of spike that followed October 7, 2023, when Israeli service inflows rose 96.9% in the two months after the attack while the world rose 16.3%, lifting Israel’s share of world service inflows by 68.9%. That share has averaged 0.42% in the three years since, against 0.30% in the three months before October 7.In the UAE, where Iranian drone and missile strikes directly hit Emirati territory and disrupted economic activity, users responded by piling into tokenized gold during the acute phase of the conflict and continuing to accumulate it through the ceasefire. In Türkiye, a country far from the fighting but inside the regional pressure zone, the war coincided with the KMTS cash ban to incentivize users onto tokenized gold rails they had not been using before. Both markets adjusted their behavior in direct response to 2026’s events.Israel did not, because the adjustment had already happened. By the time of the 2025 and 2026 conflicts, Israeli users were operating in a crypto market that had already absorbed the post-October 7 adjustment. The behavior that defines it now (holding stablecoins, bridging to offshore venues, waiting for regulated infrastructure to mature) does not swing with each new round of conflict in the way earlier adoption patterns would have.Four responses to one yearWhat makes MENA worth watching in 2027 is which of this year’s shifts become permanent. The UAE’s institutional buildout now runs well ahead of the rest of the region, and its lead widened in 2026 across every category we measure. Türkiye’s retail users have moved durably onto peer-to-peer rails, and the licensing framework that reshaped the service side will keep pulling banks and licensed platforms deeper into the market. Israel’s adjustment, which happened after October 7, 2023, rather than in 2026, has settled into a steady state where the market no longer swings sharply with each new round of conflict. The regional map we published this year will almost certainly look different a year from now, and the direction of that change will say as much about MENA’s broader stability as it does about crypto adoption.

The 2026 Geography of Crypto Report

Reserve your copy
FAQsWhich country has the largest cryptocurrency economy in the Middle East and North Africa in 2026?Türkiye leads MENA with $144.5 billion in all-in crypto value received between July 2025 and June 2026, roughly a third of the entire region. The UAE ranks second at $104.8 billion, followed by Saudi Arabia at $50.5 billion, Israel at $37.9 billion, and Egypt at $18.8 billion. The UAE grew 32% while Türkiye contracted modestly, closing the UAE to 73% of Türkiye’s size and positioning it to potentially overtake Türkiye in the 2027 period.Why is the UAE emerging as a global crypto hub?The UAE’s regulatory framework, which includes licensing authorities such as VARA, FSRA, and DFSA, has attracted a concentrated base of institutional crypto firms. Dubai’s VARA alone has licensed over 50 firms, including nearly all of the top 20 global crypto companies. Inflows to institutional platforms in the UAE rose 75% to $11.7 billion in the 2026 period, four times the global growth rate for the same category.What drove the surge in tokenized gold trading in Türkiye?Türkiye’s Precious Metal Tracking System (KMTS), announced in January 2026 and brought into force in April 2026, banned cash purchases of physical gold at jewelers and required all transactions to flow through banks. Users responded by moving into tokenized gold as an alternative that sits outside KMTS. Turkish lira-denominated gold trading went from effectively zero in the 2024 period to $974 million in 2026, giving Türkiye the highest tokenized gold share of any currency with an order book above $100 million.How did the 2026 Iran war affect cryptocurrency activity across MENA?The war shaped different markets in different ways. UAE users responded to direct Iranian strikes by piling into tokenized gold and continuing to accumulate it through the ceasefire. Turkish traders moved on-chain in parallel with the KMTS cash ban. Iranian crypto activity was suppressed by two internet blackouts (one in January during protests, one during the war) but recovered as users found ways to bypass restrictions. Israel showed no visible reaction to the 2026 war because its crypto market had already adjusted after October 7, 2023.Why is Türkiye’s peer-to-peer crypto economy so large?Türkiye’s domestic peer-to-peer stablecoin volume grew fivefold to $3.56 billion in the 2026 period, nearly 3x the combined P2P activity of the other 25 MENA markets. The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye prohibits using crypto assets as a means of payment for goods and services, so Turkish users treat stablecoins primarily as a dollar-denominated savings and transfer mechanism in a country where persistent lira depreciation has eroded household wealth.What role do stablecoins play in Israel’s crypto market?Stablecoins’ share of Israeli service inflows rose from 48.1% in the 2024 reporting period to 57% in 2026, as Israeli users increasingly bought stablecoins locally and sent them to offshore exchanges to access trading opportunities not available on domestic platforms. The one Israel-domiciled exchange in the data took just 0.06% of flows, meaning Israel’s crypto economy is functionally hosted outside its own borders. articles.title: Learning about earnings: Can we rely on labour market slack to mitigate the latest supply shock? − speech by Megan Greene
articles.text:
Learning about earnings: Can we rely on labour market slack to mitigate the latest supply shock? − speech by Megan Greene

Given at London School of Economics

Published on
20 October 2026

The extent to which the latest energy price shock feeds into more persistent inflation through second-round effects remains a key consideration for policymakers. The presence of slack in the labour market could suggest that wage pressures will remain contained, limiting the scope for second-round effects. But is this likely to be the case?
In this speech, Megan challenges this argument, drawing on a wide range of wage indicators to assess recent developments in pay growth and the likely path ahead for wages and domestically-generated inflation. She then turns to broader measures of labour market slack to examine whether current conditions are likely to restrain second-round effects via the wage-setting channel.

Speech
Introduction
Thank you for inviting me to the LSE to speak. It’s nice to be back here—I often studied in your library when I was an undergraduate in the US working in London for the summer. Come to think of it, I may have snuck in so please don’t alert the authorities.
Over the past few months, a lot has happened in the world of geopolitics…and yet very little has fundamentally changed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains beset by attacks and potential new chokepoints in shipping have emerged such as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Although Middle Eastern oil flows have at times returned to near pre-war levels, expensive and inefficient workarounds have kept energy prices high (Figure 1). Wholesale gas prices are close to triple their level at the start of the year, with oil spot prices just under double their early-January level.footnote [1] And the prices for refined products have remained elevated despite volatile spot prices. Even if the conflict in Iran ends tomorrow, we have already been hit by a protracted energy shock.

Figure 1: Evolution of energy prices since start of 2026
Index, 100 = price at 1 Jan 2026

Footnotes

Source: ONS, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.

(a) Dashed vertical lines denote selected key events. Dates may not be exact due to frequency of data. Latest datapoints are for 19 October 2026.

I have previously laid out the various avenues via which such a negative supply shock can propagate through the UK economy, highlighting the important role of second-round effects in embedding inflation in the economy. As I set out in my last speech Opens in a new window in June, they can take hold through the price- or wage-setting channel, or both. For today’s purposes, I will focus specifically on the wage-setting channel.
Wages represent a material cost for firms, particularly in the services sector where labour accounts for a large share of total costs. Wages are also a significant determinant of incomes, thus underpinning consumption. As a result, measures of wage growth offer useful insight into domestically-generated inflation. Of course, not all wage growth is inflationary. If wages rise because productivity improves, the implications for inflation may well be limited. But wages can also act as the mechanism through which temporary negative supply shocks become embedded in domestic inflation, particularly when workers seek to protect real incomes and firms then raise prices to protect their margins.
The MPC has judged that there is slack in the labour market, as evidenced by the ratio of vacancies to unemployment relative to equilibrium (Figure 2). Some of my colleagues and I have argued that the wage-setting channel poses a smaller risk of generating second-round effects than the price-setting channel. If firms are facing higher costs and have experienced years of margin compression, they are likely to pass on some of their higher costs by raising prices. This is consistent with intelligence that we’re hearing from our Agents. But if there is slack in the labour market, worker power is relatively weak. Even if workers demand higher pay as their costs go up, employers may deny that request given the large pool of talent from which to choose.

Figure 2: Vacancy-unemployment (V-U) ratio and V-U equilibrium
Ratio(a)

Footnotes

Source: Advertising association/ World Advertising Research Centre Expenditure Report, ONS and Bank calculations. Latest data point is for 2026Q2.

(a) The equilibrium V/U ratio is estimated using an error-correction model over the period 1982–2024. The real cost of vacancy posting and hourly labour productivity are included as long-run determinants for the level of vacancies. The model also includes controls for short-term movements in these variables (Stelmach, Kensett , & Schnattinger, 2025 Opens in a new window)

Given our monetary policy strategy has relied partly on slack mitigating the impact of second-round effects, it’s worth exploring how much labour market slack there really is. The wider economy has proved surprisingly resilient, implying there is less slack than some labour market indicators suggest. If so, there is a greater risk of second-round effects emerging through the wage-setting channel than we initially thought.
We may not have a clear steer on whether the shock from the Iran conflict gives rise to material second-round effects through wage- or price-setting until early next year when our Agents’ pay survey is out in February and the brunt of 2027 pay settlements are agreed in January and April. But if we wait for this evidence to lean against second-round effects with a tighter monetary policy stance, we will already be too late given the lags with which monetary policy affects the economy and inflation.
As outlined in our Forecast Evaluation Report and the Macro-technical paper Opens in a new window alongside it, predicting wage growth has been a challenge for the Bank, particularly since the Global Financial Crisis. As shown in Figure 3, Bank forecasts tended to systematically predict higher wage growth than what we experienced until the Covid period, after which our forecasts systematically underestimated the strength of wage growth.footnote [2]

Figure 3: MPR forecasts and outturns of wage growth(a)
Annual growth (%)(a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) The grey lines show forecasts from different vintages. The aqua line shows the outturns k=12 quarters after the first data release.

Our suite of wage models, like many macro forecasting models, are largely driven by historical relationships. The recent persistent undershooting of wage growth forecasts may suggest something structurally shifted in the labour market during the pandemic. As I argued in my 2024 speech (Greene, 2024), this could reflect reduced matching efficiency, lower search intensity, labour hoarding, persistent recruitment difficulties and weaker participation. It could also reflect stronger real wage resistance following the 2022 energy shock than historical relationships have implied (Pill, 2025). Wage growth has generally decelerated since 2023, suggesting these upward pressures have been unwinding, but they may not have unwound entirely.
Models inevitably simplify reality, and their performance depends critically on the quality of the signals they are trying to capture. One important development over the past decade has been an expansion in the range of wage indicators we look at, reflecting efforts to measure underlying wage pressures from multiple perspectives.
But this richer information set has brought its own challenges. At the moment, wage data are like a Rorschach Test; they can be used to confirm anyone’s preconceived view of slack in the labour market because they are giving mixed signals (Figure 4). Different indicators often tell different stories, reflecting differences in coverage, frequency, composition and methodology (Villar, Moyon, & Ahn, 2025 Opens in a new window). The task for policymakers is therefore not simply to monitor wages, but to understand the dynamics underpinning different metrics.

Figure 4: Measures of private sector wage growth
Annual growth (%)(a)

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England settlements database, DMP survey, HMRC, Indeed, ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) The private sector regular pay growth line shows the ONS measure of private sector regular AWE growth, measured as the three-month average on the same period a year earlier. The DMP lines show average realised pay growth and average expected pay growth (shifted 12 months forward) from the DMP survey on the same basis. The HMRC RTI line shows a proxy of growth in median pay in the private sector, also measured as the three-month average on the same period a year earlier. Bank staff construct the HMRC RTI measure by taking median pay for each industry – excluding public administration and defence, education, health and social work – and weighting them by industry shares in payrolled employment. Annual growth is then calculated using the Laspeyres formula, holding industry weights fixed at their levels a year earlier to reduce the effect of changes in workforce composition. The Indeed Wage Tracker line shows annual average job title matched pay growth for UK job vacancies. The latest data points are for the three months to August 2026 for private sector regular pay and the Indeed Wage Tracker and September 2026 for the HMRC RTI private sector median, BoE settlements and the DMP survey.

This brings me to my main focus today. Given the importance of understanding wage-setting behaviour and what it might mean for slack and second-round effects, I want to dig into some of our key wage indicators to parse signal from noise. I will start by examining how these indicators differ and where in the wage-setting process they are likely to be most informative. I will then consider what they can tell us about the recent developments and what signal we might glean about wage dynamics going forward. Finally, I will examine how confident we can be that a material degree of slack will restrain second-round effects and inflation via the wage-setting channel.
Getting into the weeds isn't always glamorous, but in policymaking as in gardening, sometimes you just have to get your hands dirty.
Measures of wage growth
When confronted with a range of indicators, it is often useful to take a step back and consider exactly what information each one conveys. After all, wage indicators measure different things and are collected in different ways. This is a feature, not a bug - the differences between measures allow us to build a richer picture of wage developments within the domestic economy to assess the degree of current and emerging wage pressures.
In light of this, Table 1 brings together some of the key metrics used by the Bank of England to monitor UK wage growth. While not exhaustive, the selection illustrates the breadth of information available to policymakers and the different insights a variety of measures can provide, as demonstrated by the range of questions presented in the second column: each of these metrics has something different to offer when it comes to understanding wage pressures.

Table 1: Wage growth measures(a)

Footnotes

Sources: ONS, Bank of England settlements database, DMP, Indeed Hiring Lab

(a) Table 1 gives an overview of wage measures. Coverage estimates are approximate and reflect monthly figures. PAYE stands for Pay As You Earn. Estimates relating to the Bank’s pay settlements database refer to private sector firms. Number of Indeed job vacancies is not publicly available. However, previous research suggests that there were 16 million job postings with wage data over 2018-2022 for the UK (Adrjan & Lydon, 2023 Opens in a new window).

Naturally, some measures receive more attention than others. Chief among these is the average weekly earnings (AWE) series, which helps us answer the question “what is the growth of the average wage?”. AWE is an accredited official statistic published with a two-month lag by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), derived from the Monthly Wages and Salaries Survey (MWSS).footnote [3] The MWSS is issued to around 9,000 businesses and covers approximately 15 million employees across Great Britain. While adjustments are made to account for smaller firms, the survey includes only businesses with 20 or more employees. Nevertheless, AWE provides a broad measure of the change in pay levels across the economy and is thus useful for gauging domestic inflationary pressures stemming from changes in wages.
At the Bank, we tend to focus on private sector regular AWE growth as opposed to the whole economy (including the public sector) for a few reasons. Private sector pay feeds more directly into the CPI measure of inflation, particularly when it comes to services, where labour costs make up a large chunk of total costs. In addition, UK public sector pay is often determined by government policy decisions. As such, wage-setting in the private sector is generally more closely tied to labour market conditions, whereas institutional pay setting arrangements and fiscal constraints can often influence public sector pay outcomes. Monetary policy therefore has more influence over private sector pay. Furthermore, private sector regular pay excludes volatile bonuses while they’re included in total pay. For these reasons, I’m going to focus on private sector regular AWE pay growth for the rest of this speech.
Pay As You Earn (PAYE) Real Time Information (RTI) data provides an alternative read on wage growth. This is published by the ONS on a monthly basis, in conjunction with HMRC, and can be used to help answer the same question as the AWE: “what is the growth of the average wage?”. Median estimates of the data are available with less of a lag than the official AWE measure, though they are often heavily revised. In addition, its production does not rely on survey responses. Instead, the information comes directly from HMRC’s PAYE RTI system, which covers the whole population of employees payrolled by employers, allowing for more detailed breakdowns of the data. The data is presented as gross pay, which includes bonus pay and other one-off payments (but not pension contributions) unlike private sector regular AWE. Arguably, this can make it harder to gain a clear view on wage growth and makes it more difficult to compare RTI and AWE.
We can also draw on wage growth measures derived from responses to the Decision Maker Panel (DMP) survey to answer the question “what assessment do firms make of their own wage growth?”. The DMP is a large, monthly panel survey of Chief Financial Officers from small-, medium- and large-sized UK businesses. Since 2022, the survey has included a number of questions focused on firms’ wages. This means that the back data available for wage analysis is limited. In 2026, the survey included wage growth data from approximately 700 firms, covering around 300,000 employees each month. Responses are used to construct measures of both realised and expected wage growth. The former tells us what has actually happened to firms’ own wage growth over the last year, while the latter gives us an idea of what firms anticipate will happen to their wage growth over the next year. Forward-looking indicators are hard to come by – an unfortunate truth for those of us in the forecasting business – but they are particularly useful given that both shocks and monetary policy take their time to work their way through the economy. As such, I am monitoring this measure closely as the current shock unfolds.
Pay settlements data can also provide us with a glimpse into the future path for wage growth. Such data allows us to shed some light on the pay decisions firms are making with regard to their current employees, helping us answer the question “what pay increases are firms agreeing for their existing employees?”. However, settlements data captures changes in basic pay and does not capture all sources of earnings growth, such as progression, merit and performance-related pay, or bonuses. We can access pay settlements data through the Bank of England’s settlements database. This database brings together information collected from businesses across the UK economy by the Bank’s Agents and external data providers, collected at various frequencies. Given that these figures can be updated retrospectively as more settlements are finalised, they are subject to some revision. We also get a sense of how pay settlements are likely to evolve over the next year in the Agents’ pay survey, released in February but with intelligence coming in from our Agents in the lead up to that.
Settlements data can only tell us so much. By its nature, its focus is on those workers already employed. But what are firms willing to pay new hires? The Indeed Wage Tracker provides insight into this, measuring the median annual change in advertised wages and salaries found on the Indeed platform across job title, region and salary-types. The sample size of each is reliant on a number of different factors, including the amount of total job vacancies, the proportion that is posted online and the share of these postings that contains wage or salary information (Adrjan & Lydon, 2023 Opens in a new window). This data is collected in the UK and a range of developed countries, allowing for cross-country comparison.
This is a whistle-stop tour of wage growth metrics. Each tells us something slightly different about wage growth pressures in the economy. I’ll now put them to use to explore present and future developments in wage growth.
Recent and current wage growth: two measures, different stories
Having gone through the various wage metrics, let’s use them to try to work out how much slack there is the labour market now and whether the wage-setting process has changed. For this, I’ll look at private sector regular AWE and its median RTI equivalent (proxied for the private sector), which both answer the question “what is the growth of the average wage?”. The good news is that both metrics show wage growth broadly continuing to moderate since recent peaks in 2023 (Figure 5). But these two indicators tell very different stories about the extent of that progress.

Figure 5: Private sector pay growth according to AWE and RTI
AWE private sector regular pay, RTI private sector proxy median(a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) See note (a) under Figure 4 for an explanation of how HMRC RTI private sector proxy is constructed.

After almost 3 years of gradual easing, recent AWE data broadly suggest a further and more rapid leg down in wage growth, coming in at 3.0% in August (the aqua line in Figure 5). In contrast, our primary RTI metric of private sector wage pressure – growth in median pay – remains at a considerably higher rate of 4.4% in September (the orange line in Figure 5). Historically, these measures have tracked each other reasonably closely, albeit over a relatively short sample given RTI data are only available from 2014. Since early 2026, the divergence between them has become unusually large by historical standards.
RTI and AWE measures are answering the same question and both are constructed using sectoral wage growth and weighted according to the level of employment.footnote [4] So what's behind their divergence now? To decompose the wedge between these different measures, I’ll use a measure of mean pay growth derived from the RTI data (showing annual wage growth of 5% in August), which is more comparable to mean private sector regular pay growth from AWE (showing annual wage growth of 3% in August).
The wedge between these measures is explained primarily by three factors:

Differences in wage growth within industries: for a given industry wage growth in AWE is different to that in RTI. This is possible due to the different data underlying the two (a survey in the case of AWE, administrative data for RTI).
Between-industry compositional effects: This arises because the industry shares underlying the two differ and can change over time as employment shifts between industries.
Differences in flexible pay such as bonuses: AWE regular pay doesn’t include bonuses and arrears, whereas RTI does.

Differences in wage growth between industries and within industries can both help us understand underlying wage dynamics. Wage growth driven by changes in industry shares has implications for aggregate wage pressure and can give us a sense of overall slack. Wage growth within sectors reflects firms’ pay-setting decisions and can reveal whether they have changed in the face of a shock.
Figure 6 isolates the contributions to the wedge from the three sources. In August the wedge was 2 percentage points and has grown since late 2025 due to steadily rising compositional differences (pink area), fluctuating contributions from within industry differences in pay growth (purple area) and bonuses (blue area).

Figure 6: The wedge between RTI and AWE has been growing
Decomposition of the wedge between RTI mean private sector proxy and private sector regular AWE (a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) ‘Wedge’ is the difference between mean RTI pay, private sector proxy and private sector regular AWE. In August the RTI metric was 5% and AWE was 3%, giving a wedge of 2%

Of the three main components explaining the wedge between AWE and RTI, let’s first address the easiest to interpret: flexible pay. AWE private regular pay data exclude bonuses and arrears, while private sector RTI data include them. We want to compare apples-to-apples when we are gleaning signals from the two series. To do this, we assume that the bonuses (and arrears) captured in the AWE measure of total pay are also present in the RTI data and subtract their contribution from the RTI measure. This is necessarily a simplifying approximation and so the results should be interpreted with some caution. Bonuses and cost of living payments played a significant role in explaining the wedge between the two series in 2022-23 and earlier this year before waning more recently. During 2022-23 bonuses and one-off payments were common across sectors, whereas more recently these have been concentrated primarily in finance and professional services.
Now let’s turn to the role of compositional effects in creating a wedge between AWE and RTI. We can do this by comparing the changes in sectoral employment weights in private sector AWE and private sector RTI over the past year (Figure 7). This chart shows the year-on-year changes in the latest data, but it reflects trends that have persisted throughout 2026. AWE shows employment shifting towards lower-paid sectors, with rising weights for industries such as accommodation and food services and falling weights for higher-paying sectors such as financial and professional services. RTI, however, paints the opposite picture, with employment shifting slightly away from lower-paying sectors towards higher-paying ones.

Figure 7: According to AWE employment has been shifting to lower-paid sectors, but RTI suggests the opposite
Change in sectoral shares across RTI and AWE over past year ranked from lowest to highest average monthly earnings(a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) The change in each sectors’ share of total employment is calculated from August 2025 in the case of AWE and September 2025 in the case of RTI. Ranking is based on the level of non-seasonally adjusted regular AWE averaged between August 2025 and August 2026, rather than RTI.

What signal can we draw from this? There is really no silver bullet here, and this is exactly why we look at multiple indicators to get a complete picture of the labour market. But on balance, I’d put slightly more weight on the compositional story from the RTI. The RTI series is drawn from administrative data rather than a survey. RTI doesn’t require imputing employees who work in small firms (under 20 employees) as the AWE series does. Finally, the narrative from the RTI data chimes with the Labour Force Survey (LFS), which also indicates that employment has shifted to higher paid industries over the past year. There are reasons to treat the LFS with caution; it suffers from low response rates and the industry classifications are self-reported and may not always be accurate. On balance, I place slightly more weight on the RTI’s narrative that workers are shifting towards higher paying industries. This means that the AWE may be giving us an artificially low reading of wage growth because of the specific compositional effects it incorporates.
Let’s now take a look at differences in pay growth within industries in the AWE and RTI series. Figure 8 shows wage growth within various sectors in the latest AWE and RTI releases. This chart shows year-on-year changes in the latest data, but this is consistent with the trends we have seen over the past year. The AWE data suggests that, on balance, wage growth in lower paying sectors was running hotter than for higher paid sectors. The RTI data, however, suggest wage growth was faster in higher paying sectors.footnote [5] For the reasons I’ve just explained, I have a bit more faith in the RTI data. But again, these discrepancies point to the importance of making use of a range of metrics.

Figure 8: Wage growth has been stronger across most sectors according to RTI
Annual pay growth by industry in AWE and RTI, ranked from the lowest to highest in average monthly earnings (a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) Ranking is based on the level of non-seasonally adjusted regular AWE averaged between August 2025 and August 2026, rather than RTI.

To isolate wage growth within industries, we can adjust AWE and RTI for compositional effects and strip out bonuses from RTI (Figure 9). These adjusted measures are shown in the solid lines, whereas the original series are represented in the dotted lines. Comparing the solid and dotted aqua lines shows that compositional effects are currently pushing down on the AWE by 0.4pp. Doing the same for the purple lines shows that compositional effects and bonuses are pushing up on RTI by 0.6pp (0.2pp due to compositional effects and 0.4pp due to bonuses). These adjusted measures indicate wage growth of 3.4% according to the AWE and 4.5% for the RTI measure.footnote [6] In my view, both remain above levels consistent with an inflation target of 2% and suggest there may be less labour market slack than we thought.footnote [7]

Figure 9: Our adjusted measures suggest pay growth is higher than implied by AWE but lower than implied by RTI
Private sector AWE and RTI mean private sector proxy with constant weights and removing bonuses(a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) Dotted lines show headline measures; solid lines show private sector regular AWE adjusted for compositional effects and a private sector proxy measure of mean RTI adjusted for compositional effects and bonuses and arrears.

Where does this leave us? Our adjusted measures of wage growth remain above levels consistent with our inflation target of 2%. The most frequently cited indicator that we use, private sector regular AWE, seems to have been consistently undercooking actual private sector wage growth since late-2025.
Looking ahead: what can guide us?
Over the past year, different metrics of wage growth have told different stories. However, there is strong evidence to suggest that underlying wage growth is higher than that reported by private sector regular AWE. What we ultimately want to know, however, is how wage setting will evolve going forward, particularly in light of yet another negative supply shock. For this, I’ll look at some forward-looking indicators—specifically the DMP, pay settlements and the Indeed Wage Tracker.
The DMP has been an invaluable source of information on wages since wage questions were introduced in 2022. The survey directly asks firms about wage changes for their employees, and so arguably provides the clearest window into firms’ wage-setting processes. Realised wage growth has broadly tracked the trends in AWE and RTI, though there have been some periods of divergence. The DMP recorded a lower peak in 2023 and indicated more gradual moderation in wage growth thereafter. We can see this in Figure 10, which plots DMP realised wage growth and one-year ahead expected wage growth, at the time of the survey, alongside the RTI and AWE measures.

Figure 10: Realised wage growth according to DMP has tended to track RTI and AWE
Private sector regular AWE, private sector proxy median RTI, expected and realised DMP annual wage growth

Footnotes

Source: ONS, DMP and Bank calculations.

Expected wage growth and realised wage growth have also diverged, most notably when the wage questions were introduced in 2022. When asked in the middle of 2022, DMP respondents reported year-ahead expected wage growth of around 5%. A year later, realised wage growth was close to 7% according to the DMP and 8% according to AWE.
The DMP wasn’t alone in underestimating the strength in wage growth during this episode—we also undercooked the rise in wage growth in 2022/23. Figure 11 shows the DMP own-wage growth forecast errors and our MPRs’ private sector regular AWE forecast errors. Positive values indicate that realised wage growth exceeded expectations or forecasts. The DMP errors appear smaller than the MPR forecast’s; firms have seemingly been better at anticipating wage growth than we have. In the three months to September, the DMP's one-year-ahead wage growth expectations point to a levelling-off in wage growth at 3.4% rather than a material further easing.

Figure 11: DMP firms have tended to have lower forecast errors for wage growth than the MPR
Forecast errors in wage growth (a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS, DMP and Bank calculations.(a) The chart starts in 2023 because that’s the first year in which we were able to see how accurate answers to the DMP expected wage growth question was.

Pay settlements, both expected and realised, provide a narrower view of wage-setting than the DMP. They capture the pay increases employers agree, or expect to agree, with existing employees over the coming year and only cover basic pay.footnote [8] Settlement expectations collected by the Bank's Agents—including in the Agents’ pay survey—have tended to provide a decent guide to subsequent realised settlements, including during the recent period of elevated wage growth in 2022/23.
Figure 12 shows that median pay settlements across sectors (the purple line) also tracked AWE growth (the aqua line) closely from the early 2000s until 2020, though this relationship has weakened post-Covid. The range of median settlements across sectors (shaded purple area) has also varied over time, falling back more recently from Covid-era highs.

Figure 12: Pay settlements have tended to track private sector regular AWE growth
Private sector regular AWE pay growth and pay settlements(a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS, Bank of England settlements database and Bank calculations.(a) The private sector regular pay growth line shows the ONS measure of private sector regular AWE growth, measured as the three-month average on the same period a year earlier. The range and median of sector settlements are estimated from the Bank of England’s settlements database. Classification of sectors into SIC codes involves some judgement. Sector settlements are measured as the three-month weighted average on the same period a year earlier, the median refers to the median sectoral settlement, the range is the range of sectoral settlements. Latest datapoint is for August 2026.

The noticeable gap between private regular AWE and pay settlements over the past five years can be explained by the state of the labour market. Faced with recruitment difficulties and elevated staff turnover, firms had stronger incentives to raise pay to attract and retain workers. As a result, there was ‘pay drift’; actual wage growth often exceeded that implied by pay settlements, reflecting pay for new workers, retention-related pay increases and other adjustments outside formal settlement rounds. This is consistent with academic literature that finds that workers achieve faster pay growth when outside job opportunities improve, and that the threat of higher turnover can prompt firms to raise pay more broadly across their workforce (Jäger, Roth, Roussille, & Schoefer, 2024 Opens in a new window) (Sokolova & Sorensen, 2021 Opens in a new window).

Figure 13: Post-pandemic wage growth for existing employees diverged from settlements
Wage growth of stayers and baseline pay settlements (a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS, New Earnings Survey (NES) and Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (ASHE) and Bank of England settlements database.

(a) ‘Existing employees’ are people who remain in the same employment in successive waves of the survey.

As shown in Figure 13, this meant that basic pay settlements became a less reliable guide for the wage growth of existing employees. In 2023, pay settlements were 5.2% whereas wage growth for existing employees was 8%.
Figure 14 shows the contributions of job switchers and existing employees to wage growth. Relative to historical experience, retention pressures meant wage growth has been driven disproportionately by pay increases for existing employees rather than job-switchers since 2022.

Figure 14: Existing employees have made an even larger contribution to wage growth in the past 5 years
Contribution of existing employees and those switching jobs to wage growth (a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS, New Earnings Survey (NES) and Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (ASHE).

(a) ‘Existing employees’ are people who remain in the same employment in successive waves of the survey. Those switching jobs are those who are in a different employment in the subsequent wave of the survey.

As I outlined in a recent speech (Greene, 2026), the labour market is considerably weaker now than it was in 2022. As aggregate demand has softened, demand for labour has also eased, reducing recruitment difficulties and, in turn, the pressure on firms to grant large pay increases. Expected pay settlements may therefore provide a more reliable guide to future wage growth than they did during the post-pandemic period.
At present, our Agents report that expected settlements for 2027 will be similar or only slightly lower than in 2026, suggesting the wage disinflation process may be stalling. For the past two years, actual settlements have come in above what was projected in the Agents’ pay survey (4% in 2025 vs 3.7% in the pay survey; current estimate of 3.6% in 2026 vs 3.4% in the pay survey), so I expect the risk to the latest guidance is to the upside. Moreover, the vast majority of pay settlements will be agreed between January and April (Figure 15), when we expect inflation to be above 4%. This is well above the threshold in which households are more sensitive to inflation outturns in forming their expectations.

Figure 15: Settlements over the year
Millions of employees

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England settlements database and Bank calculations. The latest datapoints are for August 2026.

Finally, the Indeed Wage Tracker offers a highly forward-looking and high frequency insight into wage pressures. The Indeed Wage Tracker captures the pay firms are willing to offer new recruits and therefore captures those workers that the pay settlements data omits. Their main limitation is that they – typically – represent a small proportion of the work force who have in recent years made a relatively small contribution to overall wage growth. However, as retention pressures have eased and firms are less reliant on large pay increases to retain staff, wages offered to new recruits may play a somewhat larger role in explaining overall wage developments as they did in the years before the pandemic.
Since late 2023, the Indeed Wage Tracker has tended to imply slightly higher wage growth than private sector regular AWE (on average about 0.8pp) (Figure 4). In August, the UK Indeed UK Wage Tracker stood at 4% (Figure 15) and while UK wage growth remains high relative to many of its peers, it has become less of an outlier in recent months. However disinflationary wage momentum here also seems to be levelling off, with the wage tracker remaining stuck at around 4% since the turn of the year.

Figure 16: Growth in advertised wages in the UK has been at the top of the range of comparator countries
Annual growth in advertised wages across countries

Footnotes

Source: Indeed Hiring Lab, 2026 Opens in a new window. The latest datapoints are for August 2026.

Taken together, I place considerable weight on the DMP and pay settlements, while monitoring the Indeed Wage Tracker as a higher frequency indicator of broader labour demand conditions. Collectively, these measures suggest that the wage disinflation process is stalling out with pay growth likely to stabilise over the coming year closer to 3.5% than 3%. I believe this remains above levels consistent with our inflation target and suggests there is less labour market slack than we thought.
What will I be monitoring for the emergence of second-round effects?
There is a plethora of wage growth indicators that can help inform our view of slack in the labour market. Our investigation of these different measures leads me to believe that underlying wage growth is running above rates consistent with our 2% inflation target and this looks set to continue. This suggests there is not as much slack as we had expected, and so there is a greater risk of second-round effects emerging from the wage-setting channel.
But we need not only focus explicitly on wage measures in making our assessment of slack. Other labour market and activity measures can provide insights on the degree of slack in the economy, and as I have demonstrated previously Opens in a new window, wider economic conditions play a role in determining the extent to which second-round effects are likely to take hold. Taking stock of these conditions suggests that it may be unwise to assume that labour market slack and weak demand will mitigate the risks. Other labour market indicators also suggest there is less labour market slack than we thought and that it may have peaked. As with wages, there is no one perfect metric of employment growth – particularly in recent years given issues with the Labour Force Survey. Bank staff produce an estimate of underlying employment growth drawing on a range of surveys and hard data. Figure 17 shows that employment growth was essentially flat in 2025 and below the rate of population growth—consistent with a degree of slack opening up. However, underlying employment growth has been steadily rising this year. This has recently been corroborated by the KPMG/REC jobs report, according to which measures of employment and labour demand have risen above pre-conflict levels.

Figure 17: Underlying employment growth has started to pick up in the past few months
Indicators of employment growth (a)

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England Agents, DMP survey, HMRC, KPMG/REC UK Report on Jobs, Lloyds Business Barometer, ONS, S&P Global and Bank calculations.(a) Bank staff’s indicator-based measure of underlying employment growth is constructed using a dynamic factor model, following the approach of (Doz, Giannone, & Reichli, 2011 Opens in a new window). The model extracts a common component from monthly survey indicators, capturing comovements across series. The common component is scaled to align with LFS employment growth between 2000–19.

Meanwhile, there are other signs that labour market slack may have peaked: the unemployment rate has fallen from 5.2% in the three months to January 2026 to 4.7% in August; redundancies have come down from their peak of 150,000 in the three months to October 2025 and are currently running at just above 100,000, in line with the average observed since 2012; and vacancies show signs of stabilising.
A stable or slightly improving labour market is consistent with more resilience in activity than we and other forecasters had been expecting. In April, HM Treasury’s summary of independent forecasts for the UK economy showed a median GDP forecast of 0.7% in 2026, roughly in line with our middle projection (Scenario B) in April of 0.8% growth this year. By September, HM Treasury’s summary of forecasts showed median growth of 1.3% this year and our central projection in July predicted 1.1% growth in 2026 . There has been a trend towards revising UK GDP forecasts for this year up, particularly as stronger-than-expected data has come in.
Surveys of firms and consumers tell a similar story. September's flash PMI ticked down modestly but remained in positive territory, reflecting an expansion of output. Purchasing managers are reasonably positive about the future as well, with the future output index at 67.4, just a little below the long-run average of 68.2.
The economy has proven surprisingly resilient even in the face of tighter financial conditions. Since the outbreak of the Iran conflict, financial conditions have tightened largely as short-term interest rates and mortgage rates have increased. But while the price of credit has risen, the impact on credit volumes has been muted. Although mortgages for home purchases have fallen since the conflict began, overall gross mortgage lending was £23.6bn in August—slightly below pre-conflict levels (an average of £24bn in the second half of 2025), but above the average level since 2024 (£21.9bn). Monthly consumer credit (credit cards, car finance and other non-mortgage credit) hit a high of £2.5bn in August, and over the past 6 months monthly net finance raised by corporates has remained above the average level since 2024. It is not obvious to me from this data that our monetary policy stance is meaningfully restrictive.
Meanwhile, household and firm inflation expectations remain elevated. As I have previously argued Opens in a new window, attentiveness to inflation has risen after over five years of inflation remaining above target. Inflation is also currently already within the threshold at which outturns impact expectations. Greater inflation attentiveness is reflected in an increase in the frequency of UK Google searches for a variety of inflation-related terms in recent years (Figure 18).

Figure 18: UK google searches for inflation-related terms
Frequency(a)

Footnotes

Sources: Google and Bank calculations.(a) The series are three-month rolling averages. The frequency is a relative measure for each individual search term, over 2005 – September 2026, where 100 indicates the highest frequency over that time period. Latest data points are for September 2026 and data are not seasonally adjusted.

According to the DMP, firms’ expected year-ahead own-price growth remains elevated at 3.7%, compared with 3.4% in February before the outbreak of the Iran conflict. Similarly, households’ inflation expectations jumped following the Iran conflict, abated but remained elevated subsequently and picked up sharply in September to 4.5% for short-term expectations and 4.3% for longer-term expectations (Figure 19). The risk of elevated inflation expectations translating into second-round effects is greater if there is less slack in the economy.

Figure 19: Inflation expectations have risen since the conflict began
Household inflation expectations(a)

Footnotes

Source: Citigroup, YouGov and Bank calculations.(a) The data are from the Citi/YouGov survey and are based on responses to the questions: ‘How do you expect consumer prices of goods and services will develop in the next 12 months?’, and ‘And what do you think will happen to the prices of goods and services, on average, over the longer term – say five to ten years?’. The dashed lines represent the series averages over 2010–19. The latest data points are for September 2026.

Conclusion
Our monetary policy strategy since the outbreak of the Iran conflict has relied to some degree on labour market slack mitigating the risks of second-round effects taking hold. But not all of our wage metrics support this argument. A closer look at the two main metrics we use to understand the recent evolution of wage growth—private sector regular AWE and private sector RTI—suggests wage disinflation has stalled at levels above those consistent with inflation at 2%.
If getting a better handle on the evolution of wage growth to date is tricky, devising a clear view of the future is trickier. The forward-looking indicators we consider—the DMP, pay settlements and the Indeed Wage Tracker–all point to wage growth that is likely to plateau closer to 3.5% than 3% over the coming year. The risks to this are skewed to the upside, in my view. Not only have we tended to underpredict wage growth since the pandemic, but realised pay settlements have been above those predicted in the Agents’ pay survey the past two years. Furthermore, the majority of 2027 pay settlements will be agreed at a time when inflation is above 4%.
Our broad range of wage indicators suggests there is less slack in the labour market than we thought and it may have peaked. This is reflected in broader indicators for the labour market and activity. All together, this suggests the risk of second-round effects taking hold is higher. This is even more so the case as energy prices have remained high and volatile for longer. In my view, this makes a risk management approach to our monetary policy strategy even more appropriate.
When it comes to managing risks around second-round effects, we face two main scenarios. In the first one, we proactively lean against second-round effects by hiking interest rates and later discover this was unnecessary and adjust our policy stance. In the second one, we are too sanguine about second-round effects and set policy accordingly before course correcting. I believe the evidence laid out in this speech shows the risk of second-round effects is greater than we thought. Furthermore, staff simulations suggest setting policy as if you were in a stronger second-round effects scenario and then adjusting policy upon learning you are in a minimal second-round effects scenario leads to better outcomes than doing the opposite. I therefore continue to believe we should proactively lean against the risk of second-round effects.

In practice, and as discussed later in this speech, the MPC often focuses on private regular pay but results are broadly invariant to that distinction.

The AWE measure is also used to calculate earnings growth under the current Triple Lock framework.

The RTI data provides mean and median figures, AWE provides only the mean.

Another reason weekly (as measured by AWE) or monthly pay (as measured by RTI) could be changing is due to changes in hours worked. If pay is rising because people are working more hours that has different implications for wage pressure than if their hourly pay is rising. The LFS is the only timely source of data on hours worked but comes with an additional health warning. The ONS recently explained Opens in a new window that declining response rates on the LFS, coupled with the non-response imputation method and reliance on respondent recall, had led the LFS to overstate hours worked on average. Nevertheless, across the whole economy, the LFS suggests average hours worked for employees increased from 31.8 to 32 per week in the year to the second quarter of 2026. In some sectors where pay growth has been weak according to the AWE data – such as accommodation and food services – average hours worked have fallen. Similarly, in some sectors where the RTI data suggests monthly pay growth has been strong – such as finance and insurance – there has been a rise in average hours worked. Overall, we can tentatively conclude that shifts in hours may account for a marginal part of changes in wage dynamics over the past year.

The ONS provides its own decomposition of private sector regular average weekly earnings. In August it estimated that the wages contribution was 3.4%.

The wage growth consistent with an inflation target of 2% depends on labour productivity growth, the share of imports in consumption and import price inflation, and margins. I think that labour productivity growth is likely to be lower and import price growth higher than 1% and so my estimate of target-consistent wage growth is closer to 3%.
