articles.title: From survival to scale: How Senegal is building a pipeline of growth firms
articles.text:
Published on
Private Sector Development Blog

From survival to scale: How Senegal is building a pipeline of growth firms

Jana Malinska

Seydina Alioune Djigo

Douglas Pearce

Mazen Bouri

October 28, 2026

This page in:

English

Français

English

Français

Photo by MandriaPix, Adobe Stock #457695401

Logidoo, formerly 2W Logistics, is a Senegalese logistics company. It had been operating for years before growth constraints began to weigh. Foundations were already in place, but scale remained elusive. The company faced familiar hurdles: limited visibility, organizational challenges, and difficulties expanding internationally. Like many small businesses, it was looking less for a shortcut than for clearer pathways to move forward.
That opportunity took shape when Logidoo engaged with the Agence de Développement et d’Encadrement des Petites et Moyennes Entreprises (ADEPME), as part of a broader national effort to provide small businesses with more structured, practical support to scale up operations.
Through the support of the Senegal Jobs, Economic Transformation and Recovery Program for Results (JET Program), or ETER in French, Logidoo received strategic support covering promotion, distribution, certifications, e-commerce, and expansion abroad. It completed an organizational, financial, and commercial upgrade, developed subregional franchises in Guinea, and made a major technology upgrade, with 75 percent of the technology development costs financed by the program. Its establishment in Côte d’Ivoire was also supported through legal and tax assistance and coverage of 75 percent of its annual rental costs.
One year later, the business had increased its revenue by 21.2 percent, while export revenue rose by 85.97 percent after expansion to Guinea and Cote d’Ivoire markets. Its permanent workforce grew from 21 to 57 employees, including 19 women. Logidoo’s transformation shows what the JET Program is designed to achieve: helping promising Senegalese firms scale, enter new markets, and create more and better jobs.
What Holds Senegal's Businesses Back?
Logidoo’s journey from a constrained local business to a growing regional firm is the story the JET Program was designed to make possible.
To understand what the program set out to achieve, it's important to first understand the context. Senegal’s formal private sector is among the smallest in sub-Saharan Africa: only 1.3 percent of firms are formal and have five or more employees. More than 94 percent of businesses operate informally, with low productivity and limited capacity to grow, hire, or export.
The constraints are well documented: a burdensome regulatory environment, limited access to finance, low technology adoption, and market failures along key value chains. The latest Enterprise Survey data (2025) show 23.7 percent of Senegalese companies identify business licensing as a major constraint, that’s nearly double the global average.
The World Bank’s Firm-level Adoption of Technology survey (2020) also found that Senegalese firms still rely on pre-digital technologies to perform basic business functions. Among 1,800 surveyed firms, only 36 percent use a computer, 30 percent use a smartphone, and just 34 percent use the internet for business purposes. These are the challenges the JET Program was designed to address.
How Is the JET Program Helping Businesses Grow?
Businesses like Logidoo did not benefit from a single intervention. Launched in 2021 with a $125 million International Development Association (IDA) investment, the JET Program was designed to work on several fronts: strengthening institutions that support businesses while directly supporting firms. It operates through the government's Program for the Acceleration of Competitiveness and Employment (PACE), coordinated by the Ministry of Economy, Finance and Plan with eight implementing agencies working across sector competitiveness, SME technology adoption and support, access to finance, and reforms to mobilize private investments.
What makes this program distinctive is the institutional architecture it helped create with institutions intended to outlast any individual project cycle and to sustain support at scale:

Four new SME service windows at ADEPME, provide structured support to firms at different stages from formalization to technology adoption to export readiness.

The Competitiveness Task Force develops targeted action plans for priority value chains to identify local firm champions that are supported by structured public-private dialogues to diagnose constraints.

The Oyass Fund, launched by Senegal’s Sovereign Fund for Strategic Investments (FONSIS) in January 2024, Senegal’s first SME-dedicated investment equity fund. By end 2025, it had a pipeline of 49 projects across 13 sectors (about €38 million in financing needs), with 27 percent of businesses led by women.

The PPP Project Preparation Fund and a strengthened UNAPPP unit, to improve the identification, preparation, and structuring of PPP projects.

These are not administrative boxes checked. They represent a step in the government’s capacity to support the private sector at scale. Implementing JET reinforced a core lesson: supporting individual firms without building the ecosystem around them produces limited and short-lived results. Firms need sustained access to information, services, finance, and markets, and properly equipped institutions can provide that support.
How Is the Program Driving Growth and Jobs?
As of early 2026, the program has already:

Supported over 8,000 SMEs through ADEPME’s matching grants (exceeding the original target of 2,500 by over 300 percent) with over 40 percent of beneficiaries in agribusiness and 52 percent of beneficiaries women-owned or women-managed.

Allocated more than $17.8 million in performance matching grants for technology adoption, helping firms digitize operations, adopt sector-specific technologies, and improve management.

Mobilized over $26 million in partial credit guarantees through the Priority Investment Guarantee Fund (FONGIP), including $3.4 million for women-owned SMEs.

Supported the formalization of more than 5,000 companies.

Businesses supported by the program collectively created or maintained more than 71,000 jobs based on government reports by ADEPME (54%) and FONGIP (46%)

Beyond the indicators, the program has built a pipeline of high-potential firms that adopted new technologies, accessed new markets, and in some cases began exporting.
This is where the One World Bank Group approach comes in to support capability-building and de-risking through ADEPME services and matching grants, and FONGIP guarantees, while IFC helps mobilize longer-term capital and advisory support for firms ready to invest and grow, through initiatives such as AgriConnect, which supports Agri finance and agricultural value chains.
What's Next for the JET Program?
The restructuring and additional financing of $65 million, approved at end-2025, brings the total budget to $195 million and extends the program to December 2027. Aligned with Agenda Senegal 2050, the additional financing sharpens the program’s focus in three ways: it concentrates support on the firms in sectors and regional “poles” with the strongest job and export potential; it accelerates priority reforms to reduce the cost and complexity of starting and running a business (business registration, investment promotion, and digitization and transparency of procedures); and it deepen catalytic support to high-potential firms to preserve jobs and promote economic transformation by connecting capability-building and de-risking to scalable private solutions in partnership with the upcoming IFC Local Champions Initiative in Senegal, currently under preparation.
Senegal’s JET Program experience is showing that results at scale are possible when firm support is paired with durable institutions and finance. The next step is to consolidate delivery and document what works, so this One World Bank Group, institution-building-and-capital-mobilization model can be adapted and replicated in other countries facing the same challenge: turning a thin formal sector into a pipeline of competitive, job-creating growth firms.

Key takeaways

We expect a hold in October. The Fed is likely to pause while maintaining a tightening bias and signaling that further hikes are possible.
Financial conditions will likely inform the Fed’s next move. Higher long-term Treasury yields are partly offsetting the growth boost from strong equity markets.
AI complicates the policy calculations. It is supporting demand and wealth while potentially reshaping investment, employment, productivity, and saving.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the policy-setting group within the U.S. Federal Reserve, meets on 27–28 October to discuss the economic outlook and appropriate monetary policy. We expect the FOMC to hold the policy rate at 3.75%–4.0% while keeping a clear tightening bias. The most likely next move is a 25-basis-point (bp) rate hike in December.
Since the September hike, the Fed’s leadership has steered markets away from expecting back-to-back moves; even the hotter-than-expected September inflation data did not change that. As of this writing, the week before the October meeting, markets are pricing roughly an 80% chance of a hold.

Three questions about the October Fed meeting

With no new economic projections at this meeting, the decision itself likely matters less than three other questions: How does Chair Kevin Warsh frame the hold? Does the majority of the FOMC still characterize the September move as a risk management adjustment? How many officials dissent in favor of a hike?
We see both the September hike and the overall rate path outlook as a recalibration, with one or two more hikes still to come that would effectively reverse last year’s cuts. We also think Warsh and the FOMC will want to frame it that way, while avoiding sending overly dovish signals to markets that could ease financial conditions.
Warsh seems well aware of the power of financial conditions. We interpreted his description of the September hike, “removing a dose of accommodation,” as a reference to the growth impulse from easier conditions. According to the Federal Reserve Board staff measure, the Financial Conditions Index, strong equity performance has been an important support to growth (and to easier financial conditions) over the last several years through the “wealth effect,” where households enjoying the boost from their equity holdings feel more empowered to consume and spend across the economy. (Learn more in our 30 September 2026 Macro Signposts.)
Since Warsh took the helm in June, however, longer-dated interest rates have risen. By our calculations using the financial conditions impulse from the Fed’s model, that rise in longer-dated rates has offset some of the wealth effect. For example, as of this writing, the 5-year, 5-year-forward real interest rate is now roughly 3%, a level last seen in the early 2000s; it’s up about 50 bps just since June. Higher rates should be an increasing headwind to growth over the next several quarters and beyond, and should reduce the risk that inflation stays persistent.
In the September Summary of Economic Projections, nearly all FOMC participants expected one or two more hikes after the September adjustment. That baseline is consistent with a modest recalibration. We think the Fed will want to see how higher rates are affecting the economy before revising that outlook, and economic data since the September meeting have been mixed.
It’s possible a few FOMC participants dissent from the majority “hold steady” vote. At the September meeting, Beth Hammack, Lorie Logan, and Neel Kashkari were likely the participants who submitted rate-path projections implying hikes at every remaining meeting this year. They dissented at the July meeting, favoring a rate hike instead of the hold that was delivered. However, despite their possible disagreement with other participants on rate hike timing, the projections signal that they too are looking for only a modest adjustment – not a rate hike cycle.

Taking a step back: why AI makes this so complicated

The combination of supply and demand shocks from energy, tariffs, and AI creates a complicated environment for the central bank. The textbook policy response to supply shocks is to look through them. These shocks, however, are coinciding with – and potentially accelerating – investment in and implementation of AI, which has also supported demand.
AI is raising domestic demand both through a faster pace of investment and through the wealth effect (see last week’s Macro Signposts). That has contributed to the Fed’s pivot toward rate hikes, as policymakers look to lean against the domestic demand impulse through higher rates and tighter financial conditions.
Markets may have adjusted up their neutral rate expectation this year in response to the evolving macro fundamentals, and similarly we expect rates to remain elevated for longer (learn more in our latest Cyclical Outlook). Nevertheless, several factors still argue for a measured Fed trajectory, despite an ongoing AI-related investment boom.

High import content curtails the domestic demand impulse. A large share of AI investment, particularly chips and computer equipment, is imported into the U.S., which limits its impact on domestic production. The more the buildout relies on foreign chips and equipment, the smaller the required rise in U.S. rates to balance demand and domestic supply. That said, prices of imported chips and some other imported tech components have risen sharply this year and are showing up in U.S. inflation.
The U.S. labor market is looser than the unemployment rate suggests – rising labor costs aren’t a source of inflationary pressures. AI implementation is colliding with demographic factors, specifically an aging population; this is structurally shifting the composition of the labor market in ways that are depressing firms’ unit labor cost growth. Specifically, an elevated pace of retirements and falling participation have kept the unemployment rate low even as the employment-to-population ratio has declined. Because of these retirements, and the way the AI-related labor adjustment disproportionately affects higher-skilled white-collar workers, the composition of employment is shifting toward lower-paid jobs, which is weighing on measures of average wage growth. (Learn more in the 13 August 2026 Macro Signposts.)
The cost of Fed tightening falls on the parts of the economy that aren’t driving inflation – AI-related investment is less interest rate sensitive, but other parts of the economy are more sensitive. If the Fed pushes harder to tame inflation, it risks overtightening the sectors that aren’t the source of inflation pressure. Higher interest rates work to restrain the economy in large part by raising what economists call the user cost of capital for businesses and households. User cost depends on the required real return on capital (i.e., the return on investment one could make from the next best investment option), depreciation, and taxes. AI capital, which is dominated by computer equipment, depreciates much faster than longer-lived investment, so depreciation costs dominate AI firms’ user cost of capital. A given rise in interest rates therefore raises AI firms’ cost of capital proportionately much less than it does for firms investing in other forms of capital. One could argue this means rates must rise further to slow investment spending. Outside of AI, however, investment in the U.S. is already contracting, evidence that the rest of the economy remains rate-sensitive.
AI could change saving behavior as well as investment. The wealth effect is likely lowering saving rates for some households. Higher energy prices have squeezed real incomes, and households have smoothed consumption by drawing down savings, which further clouds the picture of whether and how saving habits are shifting. Over time, however, uncertainty about job prospects amid economic reallocation could push households toward more precautionary saving, which in turn would weaken demand.
The payoff from AI is uncertain, and the risks are asymmetric. It is unclear how quickly AI investment will generate productivity gains and returns. History suggests transformative technologies can deliver disappointing short-run returns on capital, even if their innovations transform the economy over the medium to long term. A disappointment (or even just a meaningful deceleration) in AI returns could quickly reverse the wealth effect and tighten financial conditions, which is yet another reason not to front-load hikes.

Bottom line

The Fed has been clear that it’s aware AI is boosting U.S. demand. With inflation still above target across a range of measures, leaning against that impulse through modest rate adjustments and tighter financial conditions is sensible policy, in our view.
However, the economic adjustments now underway could evolve in several ways, and inflation is elevated but not accelerating. This likely gives the Fed room to take a measured approach, pausing to see how the tightening already priced into the yield curve is affecting the economy before deciding how much further to go. This was their preferred strategy at the September meeting, and we believe the incremental data revealed since that meeting will likely reinforce that strategy.

PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | ARTICLE – 4 min read
Multi-Asset Investment Views: “Will of the people”

By
LAURENT CLAVEL 27.10.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
Growth remains resilient, but momentum may moderateAsset allocation summaryEquities: Broaden the sources of returnFixed income: Favour higher income over long durationDiversification and dispersion

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

Moderate overweight global equities: Despite geopolitical uncertainties, resilient earnings and economic activity continue to support the asset class. Elevated bond yields and unease associated with AI hype justify a balanced exposure to growth and value stocks. We favour the US, Japan and emerging markets, and selective opportunities in financials and healthcare sectors

Moderate overweight commodities: Energy remains an important hedge against supply disruption and geopolitical risks. Precious metals benefit from central-bank demand and investment flows; selected industrial metals such as copper retain structural support

Fixed Income: Moderate underweight sovereign bonds and investment-grade credit; moderate overweight high yield and emerging-market debt: persistent inflation, heavy issuance and term-premium pressures still argue for caution on duration, while shorter-duration high-yield credit offers attractive carry amid low default rates and strong profit growth

By Chief Investment Officer (CIO) and Global Head of Multi-Asset, Laurent Clavel

Politics has returned to the forefront of market attention. Social unrest and fiscal uncertainty in France have together pushed sovereign borrowing costs higher and weighed on domestic equities, particularly banks, with some spillover into European credit and neighbouring bond markets.

The CAC 40 has underperformed but represents less than 2% of global equity market capitalisation. Brazil’s presidential election has prompted some moves in local assets, but the main drivers are elsewhere, while the approaching US midterm elections raise questions about policy direction, but are unlikely to change the course of action, notably in the Middle East.

Yet political events do not have a uniform or predictable market effect; historical midterm patterns alone offer little reason to reposition portfolios. The S&P 500 returned an average of 6.6% in the fourth quarter of US midterm election years, and since 1950, has been up 84% of the time.1

The more relevant question is whether political developments alter fiscal credibility, financing conditions or corporate fundamentals. For now, we see reasons for vigilance rather than a broad reduction in risk.

Growth remains resilient, but momentum may moderate

The global economy has remained more resilient than many expected. Manufacturing activity has recovered over recent months and services remain supportive, although the purchasing managers’ index cycle appears to be maturing.

Our economists are somewhat more cautious than consensus, anticipating a gradual slowdown rather than a recession. China’s growth outlook remains challenged, and we will closely monitor the outcomes of this week’s plenum – the policy meeting of Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

Inflation is proving sticky, notably because of energy, but there is still limited evidence of sustained second-round wage effects. Against this backdrop, market pricing of roughly two-and-a-half policy-rate increases over the next year for both the Federal Reserve, and the European Central Bank looks more hawkish than our economists’ expectation of approximately one increase each.

This combination continues to favour selective exposure to equities and credit. However, the margin for disappointment has narrowed: higher oil prices, tighter financing conditions or weaker earnings could challenge market confidence. Following the increase in equity exposure at the end of September, we are comfortable maintaining the current risk budget rather than adding to it.

Asset allocation summary

UW: underweight; MUW: moderate underweight; N: neutral; MOW: moderate overweight; OW: overweight, signs = unchanged compared to last month, Source: BNP Paribas Asset Management

Equities: Broaden the sources of return

We retain a moderate overweight in global equities. In the US, earnings growth and artificial intelligence-related investment remain powerful supports but we increasingly favour diversification beyond the largest technology names.

Financials offer attractive valuations, resilient credit fundamentals and solid fee income, notwithstanding recent weakness linked to yield-curve and sovereign-risk concerns. Healthcare also offers comparatively attractive valuations and improving earnings prospects, supported by innovation and technology.

We remain neutral on Europe. Corporate earnings have been relatively resilient, but valuations are less compelling, revisions are losing momentum and persistent inflation could trigger a derating. We continue to favour selected banks, while defence has become more interesting after the sector’s valuation derated and amid improving order prospects.

In France, depressed valuations have prompted a move to neutral at the country level, although political and sovereign-spread risks warrant caution.

We are neutral on Japan. Although it is supported by corporate-governance reforms and fiscal stimulus, we prefer to gain equity exposure through the US and emerging market stocks. In Japan, we favour banks, which benefit from higher rates and strong earnings momentum, alongside selected AI-related companies. Unhedged yen exposure may provide additional diversification.

We also maintain a moderate overweight in emerging markets, supported by exports, earnings and potentially lower US real yields. Recent weakness in Korea appears greater than warranted by semiconductor fundamentals, but index concentration argues against a larger tactical allocation; a broader advance would benefit from improving performance in China and India.

Fixed income: Favour higher income over long duration

We retain moderate underweights in sovereign bonds and investment-grade credit. Government issuance, inflation uncertainty and rising term premia remain challenging, although the repricing of interest-rate expectations has made valuations more interesting.

Deeply negative sentiment could support a short-term recovery, and we are reassessing the size of duration underweights closer to neutral in portfolios with greater flexibility.

We continue to favour shorter-duration, higher-quality high-yield bonds: resilient earnings, stabilising defaults and higher income levels provide a cushion despite recent spread widening. Emerging-market debt also remains attractive, with a growing preference for local-currency exposure where yields are compelling.

Diversification and dispersion

Commodities remain a key portfolio diversifier. Oil markets continue to face supply constraints, shipping disruptions and elevated transport costs; a further spike in prices would pose a material threat to inflation and risk assets.

Precious metals benefit from central-bank buying and renewed exchange-traded fund demand, while copper retains supportive longer-term supply fundamentals, albeit with a need for tactical discipline.

We retain a broadly neutral fundamental view on the euro versus the US dollar and see value in maintaining unhedged dollar exposure as a diversifier, while reviewing contrary quantitative hedging signals.

Equity volatility remains relatively subdued even as cross-asset spillovers become more normal. We therefore continue to favour selective, short-dated equity protection, including three- to six-month put options, rather than materially reducing core risk exposures.

Wide differences in stock and sector performance reinforce the value of diversification and active management.

[1] Source: BNP Paribas Asset Management, October 2026.

Investing in emerging markets, or specialised or restricted sectors is likely to be subject to a higher-than-average volatility due to a high degree of concentration, greater uncertainty because less information is available, there is less liquidity or due to greater sensitivity to changes in market conditions (social, political and economic conditions). Some emerging markets offer less security than the majority of international developed markets. Security and Fraud Awareness
KKR prioritizes the security of our clients’ information and assets and is committed to ensuring that clients and employees are made aware of fraudulent schemes and activities when communicating with KKR. Fraud is an issue that companies may face regardless of size, industry, or country.
While we maintain robust cybersecurity measures, cyber criminals may seek to impersonate or claim affiliation with KKR and create fraudulent websites, email domains, applications, and social media accounts. Fraudsters may pose as legitimate organizations and send emails or make phone calls to extract personal data that can be manipulated for the use of financial crimes. These scams are complex as the perpetrators may use real employee names and replicate proprietary documentation.
KKR encourages clients to be aware of the different types of fraud and to exercise caution when disclosing personal information. To help improve awareness and knowledge, we offer the following information about cyber threats and guidance to help protect from falling victim to a cyber-attack or scam.
When communicating with KKR please note:
KKR does not engage in cold calling or in sending unsolicited messages or emails to clients. KKR only contacts people from official kkr.com e-mail addresses. Confirm you are visiting a KKR authorized website.Do not share your password and login ID with anyone, including anyone from KKR.Do not communicate or deal with personnel who are not affiliated with an authorized KKR office. All authorized office locations are listed on our locations page.KKR does not conduct business over chat platforms. Imposters can use the KKR name in furtherance of a variety of criminal activities. In particular, beware of scams purportedly affiliated with KKR that promise extraordinary returns on your investment at little to no risk.

International Micro Cap Quant Equity

ABOUT

Investment Objective*
Seek long-term capital appreciation by outperforming the MSCI World ex. USA Micro Cap Index over a full market cycle, while maintaining a diversified portfolio of equities across developed micro-cap markets outside of the US.

Investment Approach
A disciplined, systematic investment process that combines fundamental and behavioural insights to identify attractively valued companies with high-quality fundamentals and improving growth prospects. Risk-aware portfolio construction seeks to translate these insights efficiently into a diversified portfolio while maintaining controlled active risk.

Key Features

A diversified portfolio of micro-cap equities across developed countries outside of the US.
An active, benchmark-aware approach designed to serve as a consistent core international micro-cap equity allocation.
Systematic stock selection incorporating Growth, Quality, and Value insights.
Pragmatic portfolio construction designed to maximise exposure to intended alpha sources while limiting uncompensated risks.
An experienced investment team supported by three decades of live quantitative equity track records and an ongoing commitment to rigorous research.

articles.title: The institutional form of independent central banks: from history to contemporary challenges - speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
The institutional form of independent central banks: from history to contemporary challenges - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at LSE TRIUM Anniversary Conference

Published on
04 September 2026

In his speech Governor Andrew Bailey argues that the foundation of independent central banks rests on more than technocratic expertise alone and elaborates on the long intellectual and historical tradition of their accountability. He contends that central banks exist to protect public goods, namely stable money and a resilient financial system, by insulating key decisions from short term political pressures while remaining accountable within a democratic framework.

Speech
I would like to reflect on independent central banks as institutions, and how their authority is grounded and is challenged.
On 3rd September 1780 (246 years ago yesterday) a 23 year old aide to George Washington wrote that: “the Bank of England unites public authority and faith with private credit and hence we see what a vast fabric of paper credit is raised on a visionary basis.” That 23 year old was Alexander Hamilton.footnote [1]
The meaning of central bank independence is not just a technical point about monetary policy or financial stability, or just a point about the design of public institutions. It is about the relationship between societies and the institutions they create to serve them. This brings to mind Douglass North's definition of institutions as the rules of the game in a society or, more formally, the humanly devised constraints that shape human interaction.footnote [2]
Institutions are not just organisations. They are durable arrangements through which societies solve collective problems. To do this, they must embody understandings about how authority should be exercised, how conflicts should be managed, and how common interests should be protected.
Independent central banks are among the most distinctive institutions modern societies have created. They exercise important powers. Their decisions influence borrowing costs, saving decisions, employment prospects, investment plans and the broad stability of the financial system. Their powers, and how they are used, are always the subject of debate, and that's fair enough given the importance.
Now, there are critics of these arrangements. Some critics argue that central banks disproportionately reflect the interests of financial markets and financial institutions. In a similar, but distinct, spirit others argue that central banks are too detached from the preferences of citizens. These criticisms often differ in their origins and motivation, but they converge on a common question. Why should an unelected institution possess such significant authority?
My purpose today is not just to defend central bank independence, though you can be assured I am happy to do that robustly. Rather, it is to reflect on the deeper intellectual traditions from which it has emerged and to consider what those traditions can tell us about the challenges we face.
When economists explain central bank independence, they often begin with questions about the credibility of policy regimes and their time consistency. These arguments are important. They explain why in many countries independence emerged because governments at crucial times had demonstrated incentives to pursue short-term monetary policies that ultimately undermined economic stability, and to undercook financial stability outside more immediate proximity to a financial crisis.
But they do not fully answer a more fundamental question: why should society trust an institution that operates with a degree of independence from day-to-day political control? To answer that question, it is useful to look further back.
One important tradition begins with the French philosopher Montesquieu.footnote [3] Writing in the eighteenth century, Montesquieu was preoccupied with the problem of concentrated power. His great concern was how societies could prevent authority (in that case royal authority) from becoming arbitrary. His answer was that power should be moderated through institutions that stood between rulers and citizens.
Parliaments, courts of law and other intermediary bodies performed this role. They constrained power, not simply through legal rules but because they possessed recognised standing within society. They had identities, traditions and sources of legitimacy independent of those they were intended to restrain. For Montesquieu, these roots mattered. Institutions could not simply be invented and expected to command authority. They required legitimacy that grew over time.
At first sight, modern central banks appear rather different. A central bank derives its authority primarily from legislation. Its independence is granted through statute. It does not rest upon inherited privilege, social rank, or customary authority. Modern central banks are deliberately designed to be technocratic institutions. And yet, the questions Montesquieu asked remain relevant. His central concern was how societies create institutions capable of constraining the exercise of power for the common good. In that sense, the challenge he identified remains with us.
A second intellectual tradition is also relevant. This tradition emerged from English political thought in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and from debates about sovereignty, money and commerce. As David Hume put it, in the seventeenth century commerce, for the first time, became a “reason of state”.footnote [4]
Thomas Hobbes provided one starting point in this development.footnote [5] In the world of Hobbes, the authority to determine the value of money belonged to the sovereign. Just as the sovereign commanded armies and administered justice, so too the sovereign controlled the monetary system of the day, such as it was. Given this overriding concern with political order and stability, for Hobbes dividing authority over money risked dividing authority itself.
But this view was challenged. John Locke argued against the idea that governments should be able to alter the value of money according to political convenience.footnote [6] During the monetary controversies of the 1690s, Locke insisted that arbitrary changes in the value of money damaged trust, disrupted commerce and undermined the public faith upon which economic exchange depended.
This marked a significant intellectual shift. Money was no longer seen just as an instrument of sovereign authority. It became something that served a broader public purpose. Its stability mattered not merely because government or the Sovereign desired it, but because society required it.
David Hume developed this argument further.footnote [7] Hume observed that commerce had become central to the prosperity and strength of nations. Economic life was no longer peripheral to statecraft. It had become one of its defining concerns. Stable money and reliable credit systems became essential foundations for expanding commerce. They enabled people to transact, invest, save and plan with confidence.
In this tradition, monetary stability became a public good. It is from this intellectual lineage that modern central banking most directly emerged. The founding of the Bank of England in 1694 illustrated this evolution, reflecting two powerful forces.footnote [8]
The first was the rapid expansion of trade and commerce. As markets became more sophisticated and more interconnected, the need for a stable and reliable monetary and financial framework grew.
The second was the necessity of financing war. In 1694, England's conflict with France created urgent demands for finance. The arrangement that established the Bank of England enabled private capital to be mobilised in support of public objectives.
One of the interesting points in The Spirit of the Laws is that Montesquieu linked England's financial credibility to its constitutional arrangements (comparing it to France). In England, public credit was not merely a matter of financial technique; it depended on institutions capable of generating public trust. This interpretation is entirely consistent with the quote from Alexander Hamilton.
But the opposite view is also powerful, as set out by John Pocock and summarised by Istvan Hont:-
“The understanding of commerce and commercial society in late seventeenth century England was most advanced by just those thinkers who saw the political health of the English nation as jeopardised by the pervasive corruption that resulted from the intrusion of the demands of the war economy into the sphere of domestic politics.” There was a growing awareness of the distractions which the new of kind of war finance, the running of a huge public debt, might cause to the balance of the English constitution. A political and military regime financed by the public debt implied a danger of the rising in influence of a financier class, which could exercise power without enjoying a proper and legitimate place in the politics of the country.footnote [9]
One way to describe the importance of the growth of commercial societies is to show how they led to the emergence of some of the most profound issues of political economy, namely:

The rise of nation states as economic and commercial agents in their own right;
The need for a properly constituted system of sovereign power to settle internal and external disputes;
The demand for state finance;
The role of justice in economic distribution;
The growth of elaborate divisions among economic interests;
Greater complexity and opacity in the workings of economies; and
The development of tools for authorities to modify the workings of markets, and the risk of a variety of motives for doing so.footnote [10]

These issues remain at the heart of economic policymaking today. The early Bank of England was an important part of the development of commerce. It is however important to recognise that the original Bank of England looked very different from the institution we know today. It was not conceived as an independent guardian of monetary stability. It emerged from a partnership between government and a relatively small and concentrated group of financially sophisticated investors. And, unlike the modern institution, the early Bank was not removed from politics.footnote [11]
The origins of the Bank align as much with Mancur Olson's later analysis of organised interest groups as with any modern idea of an independent public institution.footnote [12] My point is not to criticise those origins. They reflected the realities of the time. But they do remind us that central banking did not emerge fully formed. It evolved gradually as understandings of money, credit, commerce and public authority evolved. Nonetheless, the big themes we wrestle with today were beginning to emerge at that time.
The modern central bank is therefore the product of a long historical process. On one hand lies the Montesquieu tradition, concerned with limiting arbitrary power through institutional checks. On the other lies the tradition of Locke and Hume, concerned with establishing money and credit as public goods upon which society depends.
Modern central banks bring these traditions together. Their essential purpose is to safeguard the stability of money including the resilience of the financial system. These are not interests that belong exclusively to any group. They are public goods from which society as a whole benefits.
The important distinction between the public interest and the public good, as set out by Brian Barry, is important in this respect.footnote [13] Individual citizens naturally have different preferences, priorities, and interests. Democracies exist in part to sort out those competing claims. But some goods are valuable to the public as a whole precisely because they are universally shared.
Monetary and financial stability is one such good. Whatever our views on taxation, spending, regulation or public services, we all operate within a common monetary and financial framework. The value of money is something upon which every household and every business rely. To be effective in the sense of trust and legitimacy in society, support for such a public good should come from the plurality of society rather than any single member group.
This does not mean that monetary policy and financial stability are devoid of distributional effects. Interest rates affect borrowers and savers differently. Financial stability policies can affect sectors and institutions in different ways. Public policy inevitably has consequences that are not distributed uniformly.
But recognising those consequences should not obscure the broader purpose that these policies serve. The objective is not to favour one group over another. It is to preserve the monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible.
In that sense, central bank independence represents a modern adaptation of Montesquieu's thinking. The institution exists not to accumulate or counter arbitrary power but to protect the value of money from short-term pressures that could damage the public interest. But this arrangement also creates an enduring challenge.
Unlike the institutions that Montesquieu had in mind, central banks do not possess deep social roots of their own. Indeed, they must be careful not to become identified with any single interest group. A central bank that became closely aligned with particular sectors or political movements would undermine the very rationale for its independence, and therefore its legitimacy
As John Dunn has argued, this gets us to the issue of the constitutional theory of how power can be institutionalised and thus be implemented effectively in practice. This is the critical relationship between “the constitutional order of power and the pragmatic determination of economic policy”. It’s the modern version of the problem Montesquieu identified and sought to solve. As Dunn notes, constitutional order can appear very settled and continuous, whereas economic policy can appear anything but at times. Writing in the mid 1980s, Dunn argued that a constitutional order which rendered the benign conduct of economic policy more likely than not had not yet been constructed. Solving this challenge has been critical for the legitimacy of modern central banks.footnote [14]
So where does legitimacy come from? The answer, I believe, is now straightforward. Modern independent central banks are not independent of democratic government in the important sense that their authority originates in legislation or the like enacted by elected representatives. In the Bank of England’s case, Parliament defines the objectives, establishes the powers, and retains the authority to amend the framework within which we operate. This role is critical.
This brings me to the contemporary challenge. Across many countries we have witnessed growing scepticism towards public institutions generally. In the case of central banks, as I mentioned earlier, some critics argue they are too close to financial interests and that they stand in the way of popular preferences.
This challenge is not new, but some aspects of it are sharply set out at present, particularly in the area of financial regulation. The argument goes that central bank policies affect the distribution of returns, wealth and welfare directly, which pulls economic interests back into the picture. This concern applies more to financial stability policy than to monetary policy, though monetary policy is not immune from it. One version of the criticism is that the central bank remains too close to financial interests. A central bank's usual response is that the public good of stable money substantially outweighs any distributional effects. But this response can return the argument to Olson's thinking, since the financial world does contain well organised and concentrated interests.
The irony is that central banks can, and today do, face an opposite accusation from the financial interests themselves, who argue that regulation has gone too far. So, criticism arrives simultaneously from two directions that contradict each other.
The fact that criticism can come simultaneously from opposing directions does not prove that central banks are correct. On their own, two perceived wrongs don’t make a right. But it does underline that independence often requires making decisions that do not align with the private interests of any constituency or group, and that at times resisting pressure from the concentrated interests that Mancur Olson identified is part of the task of protecting a public good like the value of money.
A second challenge comes from populist political movements. As Jan-Werner Müller has argued, populism often rests on the claim that a particular political movement alone represents the authentic will of the people.footnote [15] Put thus, the public interest is something that a single ideology can capture and deliver directly. This effectively collapses Barry's distinction between the public interest and the public good.
Any institution seen to get in the way becomes an unrepresentative elite standing between the people and their will, and thus an obstacle to popular sovereignty. This is a serious challenge. We have developed systems of government (in the broadest sense of this term) in which legitimacy rests in the plurality of society, not in the preferences of any single group within it. Courts of law, universities, regulatory bodies and central banks all derive authority through forms of democratic delegation set within a framework of that plural society.footnote [16] Maintaining the trust that goes with that delegation matters deeply.
Central banks cannot take legitimacy for granted. They must explain their decisions clearly. They must engage openly with the public. They must remain accountable to elected representatives for their statutory objectives. In our case that means the Treasury Select Committee of the House of Commons. Through this engagement and accountability, we must demonstrate how our actions serve the public good, in its traditional meaning.
Let me conclude. Institutions that exercise significant authority should expect scrutiny. Such scrutiny is a sign of democratic health. But we should also recognise what is at stake.
Sustained economic prosperity depends upon confidence in the future. Households must be able to spend and save. Businesses must be able to produce and invest. Financial markets must be able to allocate capital efficiently. All of these activities rely upon confidence that the value of money will remain stable including that the financial system will remain resilient.
Those conditions cannot be created overnight. They depend upon institutions that are trusted, durable and credible. Central bank independence does not mean detachment from democracy. It means insulation from short-term political pressures within a democratic framework. Its legitimacy derives from a parliamentary delegation and accountability goes with that independence. It is the basis on which independence legitimately rests.
In our own time, as in previous generations, the challenge is therefore not to weaken that foundation but to strengthen it: through accountability, through transparency, through public engagement and through an unwavering commitment to the public good of sound money that independent central banks exist to serve.

articles.title: Why Now Is the Time to Add and Hold BTC
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Why Now Is the Time to Add and Hold BTC

Research • October 26, 2026 • 20 mins
Why Now Is the Time to Add and Hold BTC
We believe the bottom is in. Selling pressure has diminished, the debasement case has strengthened, and the crowd has left.

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

Bitcoin

Markets & Macro

This research alert was originally sent directly to clients of Galaxy Trading and Galaxy Asset Management on Oct. 22, 2026. Trade or invest with Galaxy to receive the most timely research directly in your inbox.
SummaryBitcoin traded at $81,391 yesterday (Thursday, Oct. 22), 3% below Wednesday’s close of $84,176. At Thursday’s price, bitcoin is off 35% from its October 2025 high and 39% above the June 30, 2026, low. We think the bear market ended in June and that bitcoin is in the accumulation phase that has preceded every prior advance. On a technical basis, the 200-week moving average held, the 50-week moving average has been regained for five straight weeks, and at day 916 of the halving cycle, bitcoin is past the window in which every prior cycle bottomed. Positioning says the sellers are mostly gone: the basis traders and macro tourists who were long into October 2025 have cut their ETF and futures exposure by more than half, while everyone else has mostly held. Equities sit near records, while BTC needs a 53% rise just to retake its own all-time high. The fundamental case has only strengthened: the likelihood of medium-term debasement by a sovereign running $2 trillion deficits at 5% yields. A bet against stocks and hard assets is a bet on fiat, the one position that makes no sense today. And sentiment has swung to “blockchain, not bitcoin” for the third time (the first two times marked lows). Our conclusion is simple: we believe now is an attractive time tobuy and hold bitcoin. Late last month I attended Korea Blockchain, a fantastic conference that showcased South Korea’s large and growing interest in digital assets. Despite the broad-based enthusiasm, the nexus of the event was squarely on one thesis: the great convergence of digital assets and traditional capital markets. The conference featured dozens of panel discussions on tokenization, real-world assets, stablecoins, and upgrading payments infrastructure. I spoke on one of the few panels that focused on bitcoin and crypto asset markets. It reminded me of Consensus 2018 in New York, which was littered with men in suits from the Big Three consultancies talking about “enterprise blockchains” like R3’s Corda and IBM’s Hyperledger. After the 2017 blow-off top and resulting decline in bitcoin’s price, the pendulum then had swung dramatically away from bitcoin and crypto toward the less threatening and more “mature” concept of “blockchain technology.” In 2015 and 2016 (another deep bear market trough), from my vantage point at Fidelity Investments, a similar sentiment was visible: no one wanted to talk about bitcoin, but the bankers were all gassed up about “blockchain.” The backlash from the Silk Road (“bitcoin is for criminals”) and the ICO boom (“crypto is a scam”) combined with the underlying technology’s clear benefit to push institutions away from bearer assets, censorship resistance, and permissionless finance, and into more “respectable” endeavors. Bitcoin and crypto were definitively not dead, but like today, attention had swung dramatically away from the ethos of decentralization and coalesced around a less revolutionary concept: let’s upgrade the financial system’s technology.While efforts in 2016 and 2018-2019 to embrace blockchains on Wall Street didn’t amount to much, this time will likely be different. The institutional embrace of digital assets and blockchain technology is undeniable now, and likely to result in a more efficient financial system. Even so, the case for non-sovereign, censorship-resistant, hard money should not be forgotten because it will not go away.Bitcoin traded at $81,391 yesterday (Thursday, Oct. 22), 3% below Wednesday’s close of $84,176. The institutional embrace of digital assets and blockchain technology is undeniable now, and likely to result in a more efficient financial system. Even so, the case for non-sovereign, censorship-resistant, hard money should not be forgotten because it will not go away.
1. Technical: we believe the bottom is in and accumulation is under wayBitcoin's bear markets have one reliable map: the 200-week moving average is the floor and the 50-week average the ceiling. The price lost the 50-week average in the week ended Nov. 16, 2025, and spent 44 weeks below it. The June low tested the floor and held: the worst weekly close came in 4.7% below the 200-week average (against 1.4% in 2015, 2.8% in 2018 and 32% in 2022). In the week ended Sept. 20, 2026, the price closed back above the 50-week average, and the week ended Oct. 18 was the fifth straight close above it. In every completed bear market since 2011, the first sustained run back above the ceiling came after the low (Chart 1). Thursday’s spot price of $81,391 sat 6% above the average: the decline since Wednesday’s close did not threaten the reclaim.

Chart 1. Weekly closes against the 50- and 200-week moving averages since 2016. Bitcoin lost the 50-week average in the week ended Nov. 16, 2025, tested the 200-week floor in June (-4.7% on the worst weekly close), and regained the 50-week average in the week ended Sept. 20; the week ended Oct. 18 was the fifth consecutive weekly close above it. The open marker is the spot price at 19:51 UTC on Oct. 22, +6.3% from the 50-week average.How often has a reclaim been followed by a new leg down? Of the 13 completed reclaims since 2011, the split is how long the price had been below the average. The four that ended spells of 20 weeks or more 1) never closed more than 8.4% below the reclaim level in the following year; 2) were +1497%, +128%, +55%, +142% higher a year later; and 3) regained the prior all-time high within 33–83 weeks. Of the nine that ended spells of 14 weeks or less, seven fell more than 25% within a year. September's reclaim ended a 44-week spell (Chart 2). This is a pattern.

Chart 2. Every reclaim of the 50-week average since 2011, indexed to the reclaim close and followed for a year. The four reclaims that ended spells of 20 weeks or more never closed more than 8.4% below the reclaim level; of the nine that ended shorter spells, seven fell more than 25% within a year. September's reclaim ended a 44-week spell.The four-year cycle agrees. The three completed cycles printed their lows on days 777, 889 and 912 after their halvings; this cycle's low so far came on day 802, and yesterday was day 916. From this day count, the prior cycles rose 87x, 19x and 7.6x to their next peaks (multiples that shrink every cycle and that we do not forecast). The direction has not failed (Chart 3).

Chart 3. Each halving cycle indexed to its halving-day close. The three completed cycles bottomed on days 777, 889 and 912; yesterday was day 916, and this cycle's lowest close so far came on day 802. The open marker is yesterday’s spot price.This was the shallowest bear on record (-53% against -93%, -85%, -84%, -77% before it) and the first in which price never traded below the network’s cost basis: the ratio of market value to realized value bottomed at 1.10, against 0.56, 0.69 and 0.75 at the three prior lows. The coins that carried the recovery from $58,525 have an average cost of $74,811; price first closed back above that cost basis on Aug. 19 (Chart 4), when it stood at $69,268, and at yesterday’s price their owners sit +9%, with the spent-output profit ratio at 1.009: no profit-taking wave, which is what accumulation looks like.

Chart 4. Daily closes since 2023 against the realized price and the short-term holders' cost basis. The bear market's closest approach to the realized price was +10%; the price regained the short-term holders' cost basis on Aug. 19, and Thursday’s spot price sits +9% against it.And the sellers who capped the 2025 top are fading. Coins unmoved for five years or more moved at 67k BTC a month in 2024 and 47k in 2025… totaling 1.11 million BTC since October 2024, the largest old-coin distribution of any cycle, most of it absorbed by the spot ETFs and BTC digital asset treasury (DAT) companies. In 2026, the pace is 34k a month, 50% of 2024's (Chart 5).

Chart 5. Bitcoin spent each month after five or more years unmoved, by age at spend. The monthly average has fallen from 67k BTC in 2024 and 47k in 2025 to 34k so far in 2026.
2. Positioning: the fast money has left, the base stayed, and everything else is priced for perfectionThe futures market shows how little macro money owns bitcoin today. In the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)'s Traders in Financial Futures data, asset managers' net long in CME bitcoin futures was 43.3k BTC in the week of the all-time high and is 18.4k now (-57%); leveraged funds' net short, the futures leg of the cash-and-carry trade against spot ETFs, shrank from 71.4k to 30.6k BTC; open interest is down 51% in dollars (Chart 6). The carry that paid for those shorts has all but gone: the front-month basis averaged 7.9% annualized in the 30 days to the high, 3.9 points over the 3-month bill, and 4.8% in the 30 days to Oct. 21, +0.6 points over (Chart 7). Further out the curve still pays something — the November and December contracts priced 6.3%–6.5% at the Oct. 21 close, about 2 points over bills before costs — but a basis desk never keeps the gross. The ETF's fee, the monthly roll and the margin that must sit at the clearinghouse take most of a point, leaving about 1.5 points over cash, where the same arithmetic left about 3 points in the month of the high and more still on the 9.8% the front month alone offered at the top. Leverage adds little once the long leg is financed at SOFR plus a spread, and what remains does not pay for the trade's tail: the basis inverted to -31% annualized in December 2022 (Chart 7). That arithmetic is why the multi-strategy desks left.

Chart 6. Net positions in CME bitcoin futures by trader group, in BTC. Asset managers' net long is 57% smaller than in the week of the all-time high and leveraged funds' net short is 57% smaller; open interest is down 28% in BTC and 51% in dollars.

Chart 7. The CME front-month basis (30-day average, annualized) against the 3-month Treasury bill since 2020; the shaded area is the carry trade's edge over bills. In the 30 days to the high the basis ran 3.9 points over bills; in the 30 days to Oct. 21 it ran +0.6 points over.Money managers’ 13F filings tell us about many of the institutional sellers, and they are the basis traders and the macro tourists. Reporting institutions held 355k BTC-equivalent of the spot ETFs at the Sept. 30, 2025, quarter-end, the last before the high, and 307k by June 2026 (-14%), and the decline sits almost entirely with the multi-strategy and macro funds, basis desks, and bank trading books that used the ETFs for carry and momentum. Millennium Management, Brevan Howard, Goldman Sachs Group, Capula Management, Farallon Capital, D. E. Shaw, Schonfeld Strategic Advisors, Symmetry Investments and Tudor Investment Corp cut by between 29% and 100%, 68k BTC between the nine of them. That is more than the 48k BTC decline across all 2,200 filers, so every other filer, in aggregate, added (Table 8). Wealth platforms and sovereign funds bought what the tourists sold (Morgan Stanley's wealth arm, Mubadala and the Abu Dhabi Investment Council added; Horizon Kinetics held), and the non-filer base of advisors, family offices and individuals fell only 6.6% while the price fell 49% (Chart 9). The ETFs' holdings dropped 11% from peak to trough against a 53% fall in the price, and they have added 87k BTC since the June low while leveraged funds' shorts fell: directional buying, not carry (Chart 10).

Table 8. The named 13F filers by what they did between the Sept. 2025 quarter-end and June 2026. The nine funds in the first group cut 68k BTC between them, more than the 48k BTC decline across all filers, so every other reporting institution added 20k BTC in aggregate.

Chart 9. Bitcoin held by the U.S. spot ETFs at each complete quarter end, split between 13F-reporting institutions and everyone else. From Sept. 2025 quarter-end to June 2026, 13F filers' holdings fell 14% and the 10 largest filers' stacks shrunk 17%; the non-filer base fell 6.6% while the price fell 49%.

Chart 10. Bitcoin held by the U.S. spot ETFs since launch, against the price. Holdings fell 11% from the Oct. 9, 2025, peak to the July 13 trough while the price fell 53%; they have added 87k BTC since the June low.That likely is why this year's scares passed through bitcoin without a sell-off, and it frames the relative-value case. The S&P 500 is 0.8% below a record set on Oct. 6 and the Nasdaq 100 4.5% below its own; gold is 22% below January's high. Bitcoin, at Thursday’s price, is 35% below its high, so a 53% rise only returns it to a price it traded at a year ago (Chart 11). The alternative to all of them is cash. A bet against stocks and hard assets is a bet in favor of fiat, the one asset its issuer has promised, through $2 trillion deficits and a 5% 10-year Treasury, to keep diluting, and that is the one position that makes no sense in the current environment.

Chart 11. Last close against each market's highest close since 2020, with bitcoin at the spot price of $81,391 (19:51 UTC, Oct. 22). The S&P 500 is 0.8% below a high set on Oct. 6; bitcoin is 35% below its own, a 53% rise away.
3. Fundamental: the debasement case is stronger than it was at the highFederal debt stood at $40.44 trillion on Oct. 20, 2026, up from $23.2 trillion at the start of 2020; fiscal 2026 closed with a $1.99 trillion deficit, 6.2% of GDP, and the government’s interest payments run at $1.28 trillion a year (Chart 12). The bond market has begun to charge for it: the 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.31% on Oct. 5, 2026, its highest since 2007, and the Federal Reserve raised rates to 3.75%–4.00% on Sept. 16, 2026, into CPI inflation of 3.7% and M2 growth of 5.7%. A sovereign refinancing $40 trillion at 5% while running 6% deficits faces mounting pressure to inflate, and history points in that direction. Every stress brings the central bank back as a buyer of last resort, as in 2020 and March 2023.

Chart 12. Total U.S. federal debt and the annual run-rate of federal interest payments since 2000. Interest costs have risen 2.4x since early 2020.The AI build-out, usually cast as bitcoin's competitor for capital, is itself a debasement machine: Morgan Stanley expects AI-related debt issuance to reach $570 billion in 2026 and about $1.5 trillion of the build-out through 2028 must be financed externally. If it pays off it will have been financed by credit expansion; if it does not, the losses will be socialized. Either way, the supply of claims on the future grows, and so does the value of a hard money asset with a fixed issuance.The second fundamental is older than any rate cycle: the need for money that no one can freeze, surveil or reprogram grows with the capacity to do those things, and AI has made that capacity cheap. Tokenized deposits and stablecoins are freezable by design; bitcoin is the only bearer asset of scale with no issuer, and demand for an exit valve rises with every step toward programmable money.
4. Sentiment: the pendulum has swung to “blockchain, not bitcoin” for the third time since I’ve been in the marketTwice before, mainstream finance embraced the technology and dismissed the asset. In 2015–16 the banks' R3 consortium and The Economist's “Trust Machine” cover made “blockchain, not bitcoin” the respectable position; the episode's lowest weekly BTC close was $231 and the next cycle high was 83x higher. In 2018–19 the refrain became “blockchain, not crypto.” JPM Coin and Libra were unveiled while bitcoin was left for dead at $3,195; the next cycle high was 20x higher. The 2026 version is “stablecoins and tokenization, not bitcoin”: banks are piloting tokenized deposits, the CLARITY Act failed cloture vote on Sept. 15, and AI has taken the growth narrative wholesale. Each time the pendulum swung this far, bitcoin was within a year of a cycle low (Chart 13).

Chart 13. The three episodes in which mainstream finance embraced the technology and dismissed the asset, on the weekly price. From the lows of the first two, bitcoin rose 83x and 20x to the following cycle highs.The 2026 version shows up in the data. The dollars have come onchain: stablecoins in circulation have grown 129% since the start of 2024, to $304 billion. Meanwhile bitcoin, the asset those rails were built to settle, sits a third below its high (Chart 14). That is dry powder parked inside the system, not capital that has left it.

Chart 14. USD stablecoins in circulation (per DefiLlama) against the bitcoin weekly close. Stablecoin supply has grown 129% since the start of 2024, to $304 billion, while bitcoin sits 35% below its high.The attention data confirm the neglect: Google searches for “bitcoin” fell to their lowest level in several years on Oct. 13, 2026; the crowd Fear & Greed index that read 71 at the October high printed 5 in February 2026 and 15 at the June low (per alternative.me); ETF flows are flat this month. Bitcoin is 39% off its low with nobody watching. This is a market that is dismissed, under-owned, and rising.
Risks & MitigantsDrawdown risk. Bitcoin can always go lower. The mitigants are the two records above: in the four prior reclaims after a long spell below the 50-week average, the worst subsequent close was -8.4% from the reclaim level (Chart 2), and every bear has been shallower than the last (Chart 15). Our tripwire: a weekly close back below the 50-week average ($76,540, 6% below yesterday’s spot price) not regained within a month would suggest the reclaim failed.

Chart 15. Each cycle's decline from its all-time high, over 400 days. The current cycle's maximum drawdown of 53% is the shallowest on record; on day 381 the spot price stands at -35%.AI risk. I see three channels of risk from AI: 1) capital competition (the Nasdaq 100 is +18% year to date against bitcoin's -7%); 2) AI-enabled hacking and social engineering ($3.4 billion was stolen across crypto in 2025, and roughly $1.1 billion–$1.3 billion was stolen in the third quarter of 2026 alone: the $387.5 million Bitget exploit, the implanted-Ledger reseller scheme that drained about $91 million by our count, the Coldcard seed-entropy theft of 1,837 BTC from 9,218 addresses); and 3) an AI bust that takes risk assets down with it. The mitigants: none of those losses touched the Bitcoin protocol, only an exchange, a vendor, a device, or a user; the build-out is debt-financed and tax-subsidized (about $570 billion of AI-related debt this year, and since July 2025 a tax code that lets servers and chips be expensed in the year they are bought, a provision scored at $363 billion over ten years) so it widens the deficits that make a fixed supply valuable; and nothing in AI weakens SHA-256 or the signature scheme. An AI bust that forces the Fed's hand is an example of the fundamental case, not a refutation of it.Quantum computing. 7.1 million BTC, 35% of supply, sit in outputs whose public key is already visible onchain (Chart 16). No cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) exists: the largest elliptic-curve key broken on quantum hardware is 15 bits against bitcoin's 256, and Google's best chip has 105 physical qubits against the fewer than 500,000 its own March 2026 paper says are needed. Galaxy Research's March 2026 report, Bitcoin Is Rising to the Challenge of Quantum Readiness, concluded that “the risk is real but recognized, and the people best positioned to address it are working on it,” and the work is funded: BIP-360, a quantum-resistant output type, was merged in February 2026; Galaxy's Bitcoin Quantum Readiness Initiative committed up to $5 million; and the Bitcoin Security Consortium (nine firms, Galaxy among them) pledged $15 million over three years. The same clock runs on every bank's cryptography; Bitcoin's migration is arguably the most advanced and the best funded.

Chart 16. Unspent bitcoin whose public key is already visible onchain, by cause: 7.1 million BTC, 35.4% of supply, 1.7 million of it in Satoshi-era pay-to-public-key outputs.
What would change our viewSome things that would change our view: a weekly close below the 50-week average ($76,540) not regained within a month; ETF holdings falling through the July 13 trough of 1.22 million BTC; a credible, dated path to a cryptographically relevant quantum machine; or a U.S. fiscal consolidation. None are evidenced today. We believe the bottom is in, selling pressure has diminished, the debasement case has strengthened, and the crowd has left: these are all reasons we remain bullish on bitcoin. Bitcoin has proven its ability to run to at least $125k, and we see no reason why it can’t retake that level, and indeed the setup looks favorable.

articles.title: Daily: Higher oil and AI concerns drive risk-off move
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, and interest rates (4 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Why bank stocks are falling amid rising rates (6 mins)Video: The AI Show |The AI trade's two-sided test (4 mins)Podcast: Across the Pond: Europe’s bond stress test, on Apple , Spotify (22 mins)Thought of the dayTechnology shares fell on Thursday as investors focused on the financing and potential returns from the next phase of the AI buildout. The Nasdaq fell 2.6%, its steepest one-day decline since 5 June, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 6.7% to its lowest level since July. Meta's shares declined 7% following its results, reversing an initially positive after-market reaction as concerns grew over the company’s rising capital expenditure plan. But two-thirds of S&P 500 constituents advanced on the day, and the equal-weighted index gained 0.8%, suggesting the equity weakness remained concentrated in technology. Brent crude also rose 4% to a five-month high of USD 113/bbl amid renewed concerns over energy supplies. The resulting risk-off move pushed the 10-year US Treasury yield down nearly 17 basis points to 4.95%, its largest daily decline since August 2024.But the latest moves do not alter our view that robust earnings should continue to support equities. AI demand remains strong, current bond yields provide attractive income, and geopolitical developments alone do not justify a broadly defensive investment stance.Strong earnings growth extends beyond technology, although greater selectivity is needed within the AI ecosystem. We expect third-quarter S&P 500 earnings per share to grow 28% from a year earlier, driven by AI demand, an improving industrial cycle, and resilient higher-income consumers. Semiconductor profits are expected to contribute around half of that growth, while average cloud revenue growth is forecast to accelerate from 48% in the June quarter to 58% year over year in the September quarter. That said, risks are rising among specialized AI computing providers known as neoclouds, whose single-product business model focuses on renting compute capacity. In these more capital-intensive parts of the AI buildout, funding pressures and execution risks could reinforce each other. We therefore continue to limit exposure to neoclouds and favor well-funded hyperscalers for their better risk-reward. Beyond technology, nine consecutive months of expansion in the new-orders component of the ISM Manufacturing Index and 6% year-over-year growth in September US retail sales support our view that cyclical parts of the market should also see robust earnings growth.The bond market repricing in recent months has restored meaningful return potential to high-quality fixed income. The 10-year US Treasury yield reached 5.36% in early October, its highest level since 2002, before falling to 4.95% during Thursday’s flight to safety. We continue to rate fixed income as Attractive, with current yields offering an appealing income cushion. For capital losses to offset one year of income, two-, five-, and 10-year Treasury yields would need to rise by around 246, 109, and 63 basis points, respectively, from current levels. We consider increases of this scale unlikely and expect a moderate decline in yields over the next 12 months. We continue to favor selective exposure to medium- and longer-duration high-quality bonds. By contrast, we are cautious on the longest maturities given fiscal concerns and elevated issuance.While higher energy prices pose risks to growth and inflation, the global energy system is continuing to adapt to disruption. Middle East crude and refined-product exports recovered to around 80% of pre-conflict levels in September, supported by a partial restoration of flows through the Strait of Hormuz and rerouting through pipelines. However, in October geopolitical risks have intensified, with increased Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the failure of Russia and Ukraine to agree to a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, pushing energy prices higher again.The impact on global GDP growth from higher oil prices has so far been limited. Oil prices have risen by around USD 40/bbl on average compared with last year. In isolation, we estimate such a price increase could reduce global GDP growth by 0.3-0.5 percentage points, with the amount varying for each economy depending on how much energy they import. But the AI investment cycle and the strength of household balance sheets have enabled consumption to remain resilient. Moreover, following the 2022 oil shock, economies have become more adaptable to rising energy prices. Looking ahead, energy prices will likely continue to present a headwind for the global economy, but barring a significant and sustained rise from here, this should fade over the next 12 months.So, we remain positioned for market gains through diversified exposure to cyclical and structural growth opportunities while reducing concentrated single-stock positions. Within AI, we favor well-funded hyperscalers, high-quality semiconductor and hardware beneficiaries, and defensive technology companies over more capital-intensive neoclouds. We also favor medium- and longer-duration high-quality bonds, while broad commodity exposure can improve portfolio diversification and provide protection against a prolonged energy-supply disruption.
