23 October 2026
Weekly Market View

Download Report

Policy, politicsand earnings
We retain our defensive and diversified stance across assets, sectors and regions amid near-term uncertainty around monetary policy, politics and earnings.
The next two weeks will be busy for major central banks, US political watchers and technology leaders powering the AI supercycle. We expect the Fed, ECB and BoJ to hold rates next week, but markets will focus on whether central banks are turning more hawkish due to the latest surge in fuel prices.
The US mid-term elections are expected to give Democrats control of the House and Senate, with implications for taxes and the AI-led investment boom. Meanwhile, the consensus is expecting the US tech sector to report over 60% y/y earnings growth for Q3.
Each of these three drivers has the potential to surprise markets. We close and lock in gains on our European CoCo1 bond and US 10-year government bond opportunistic ideas amid French and US political risks.

What are the takeaways from US tech sector earnings reported so far?

Are you still bullish on US 10-year government bonds?

Does Euro area fiscal and political uncertainty affect your EUR/USD view?

Charts of the week: Watching earnings and a potential ‘Blue wave’

US Big Tech earnings, mid-term elections and major central bank policy meetings are the near-term market drivers

Consensus S&P500 index Q3 earnings estimates by sector

Chance of Democrats winning control of US House and Senate*

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered; *Polymarket probability
Editorial

Policy, politics and earnings

Strategy summary: We retain our near-term defensive and diversified stance across assets, sectors and regions amid near-term uncertainty around monetary policy, politics and earnings. The next two weeks will be busy for major central banks, US political watchers and technology leaders powering the AI supercycle. We expect the Fed, ECB and BoJ to hold rates next week, but markets will focus on whether central banks are turning more hawkish due to the latest surge in fuel prices. The US mid-term elections are expected to give Democrats control of the House and Senate, with implications for taxes and the AI-led investment boom.
Meanwhile, the consensus is expecting the US tech sector to report over 60% y/y earnings growth for Q3, the biggest jump in over two decades outside the post-COVID rebound. Each of these three drivers have the potential to surprise markets.
Big Three to hold monetary policy: We expect the Fed, ECB and BoJ to hold policy rates next week, after September’s hikes, as they assess whether higher bond yields have tightened financial conditions enough to offset fuel-price-driven inflation. We expect the Big Three to hike next in December as fuel prices are likely to stay elevated into early next year due to refining capacity constraints. Nevertheless, the Fed and ECB are likely to deliver less than around 60bps of rate hikes priced in by money markets over the next 12 months on the back of an eventual easing of oil and fuel prices leading to disinflation by H2 2027. This outlook means 3-7-year Developed Market investment grade bonds currently offer attractive risk-reward.
Opportunity in Australian bonds. Other major central banks, such as the Bank of England, Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of New Zealand are likely to hike rates by 25bps in the next two weeks given their focus on taming near-term inflation. However, we believe the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is close to the end of its hiking cycle, even if it hikes one last time in the coming months (money markets give a 60% chance of a hike on 3 November). Australia’s domestic labour and housing markets and business confidence are softening after the RBA hiked its policy rate four times this year to a 15-year high.

Meanwhile, Australia’s cash rate is 60bps higher than the US policy rate, supporting the AUD. We continue to see attractive income and FX gain opportunities from AUD corporate bonds.
A ‘Blue Wave’ in the US? Prediction markets strongly favour Democrats taking the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate in the 3 November US mid-term elections. While an opposition sweep in the mid-terms has historically delivered the best 12-month returns for equities among all scenarios, partly due to the resulting policy gridlock, a decisive Democratic “blue wave” could increase longer-term risks of higher taxes and uncertainty over policy towards AI investment and data centres. With the Senate race still close and prediction markets fallible, we remain cautious on risk assets in the near term.
Closing EU bank contingent convertible bonds (CoCos1) and US 10-year government bond ideas: We lock in 2% gains in EU CoCos and 1.7% gain in US 10-year government bond ideas amid French and US political risks (page 5-6). We continue to hedge any inflation risks through inflation-protected bonds and geopolitical risk through an Overweight in gold.
Watching Big Tech earnings: Upcoming Big Tech earnings raises uncertainty as market leadership remains concentrated and share-price reactions more mixed. With valuations less likely to drive returns, earnings delivery and sustainability of AI investment, funding and monetisation and broadening out of earnings beyond tech will be critical, raising the risk of volatility and sector divergence. We remain invested but defensively positioned, favouring diversification across sectors and regions.
Staying defensive and diversified. We recently upgraded the defensive US Healthcare sector to Overweight, while retaining our Overweights to US tech and materials as well as financials in the US, Euro area and Japan. We also downgraded the more volatile Communications Services sector to Neutral and took profits on the semiconductor segment earlier this month before the latest correction. Our defensive and diversified stance should preserve participation in further equity upside, while reducing exposure to earnings disappointments and supporting resilience through the reporting season.
— Rajat Bhattacharya

The weekly macro balance sheet

Our weekly net assessment: On balance, we see the past week’s data and policy as negative for risk assets in the near-term
(+) factors: Resilient China growth; potential China fiscal policies(-)factors: Softer Euro area sentiment; geopolitical and trade tensions

US housing starts slumped in September as high mortgage rates hurt, while housing permits offered limited support to future construction
US housing starts, building permits and the NAHB Housing Market Index

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Euro area ZEW expectations fell to a four-month low in October, with Germany’s expectations missing estimates
Euro area and Germany ZEW survey expectations

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

China’s recovery remains uneven, with resilient industrial production contrasting with subdued retail sales and contracting fixed asset investment
China retail sales, industrial production and fixed asset investment growth

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions

What are the key takeaways from the technology sector earnings reported so far this week?

Our view: Recent technology sector earnings results point to strong compute demand and continued capex expansion, supporting our positive long-term view on the AI investment theme. However, rising funding and execution risks warrant near-term caution. We prefer to avoid increasing exposure to higher-risk areas within the technology sector for now.
Rationale: Earningsresults reported this week suggest major tech companies remain committed to expanding their AI infrastructure. While this bodes well for AI infrastructure providers, ambitious expansion plans imply that an increasing share of AI capex is likely to depend on debt financing. We expect debt-financed AI capex to rise from c.25% of AI capex in 2026 to c.40% in 2027.
Greater reliance on borrowing increases sensitivity to interest rates, while deployment delays could postpone revenue recognition amid ongoing financing costs. However, evidence of improving AI monetisation and adoption should strengthen operating cash flows and support internal capex funding. Against this backdrop, we will assess Big Tech earnings next week for greater clarity on capex guidance and funding and AI monetisation trends.
— Ryan Goh, Investment Strategist

AI capital expenditure (capex) is expected to become more reliant on debt financing
Estimated share of AI capex financed through debt

Source: Company reports, Standard Chartered

Are you still positive on Euro area bank equities amid heightened political and fiscal uncertainty in the region?

Our view: We remain positive on Euro area bank equities, supported by resilient earnings and shareholder-friendly capital return policies. While France’s fiscal uncertainty and a softer growth outlook warrant caution, the recent pullback in Euro area bank equities offers selective opportunities. We favour well-capitalised banks with strong deposit franchises and diversified earnings.
Rationale: We expect Euro area banks’ Q3 2026 net interest income to grow 1.5-3.0% q/q, led by Spanish banks, driven by higher rates and continued asset repricing. Resilient fee income from wealth management and investment banking activity, as well as dividends and buybacks, should provide further support. Price-to-book (P/B) valuations have eased, despite expectations for healthy return on equity (ROE), thus improving risk-reward.
Fiscal uncertainty in France has widened sovereign spreads, pressuring banks’ bond holdings and funding costs. Although French banks represent 13% of the Euro area Bank Index, volatility could spread to regional financial markets. However, stress in the broader banking system appears limited, supported by strong capital buffers and ECB tools to contain disorderly market moves and sovereign market contagion. We will continue to monitor credit trends, sovereign spreads and banks’ 2027 earnings guidance.
— Robin Xie, Senior Investment Strategist

Euro area banks’ valuations have eased despite resilient profitability expectations
Forward P/B ratio vs. expected ROE

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What has driven the recent weakness in China equities, and what is your outlook from here?

Our view: We maintain China equities as a Core holding, as valuations remain inexpensive. Rapid technological innovation and investment in AI localisation provide tailwinds, but the potential for a re-rating appears delayed. Investors should seek to diversify their portfolios and reduce concentration risk.
Rationale: China equities have weakened, driven by mounting scepticism over AI capex returns, structural margin compression and concerns about the country’s significant financing requirements. Another notable feature in China has been significant share issuance, which has diluted earnings per share and weighed on the MSCI China Index’s performance. These pressures have been compounded by geopolitical headwinds, restrictions on advanced chips, an enduring property sector contraction and weak domestic demand. September’s stimulus measures also disappointed markets in terms of their scale and pace of delivery.
Notwithstanding these headwinds, valuations remain inexpensive, supported by rapid domestic innovation and structural tailwinds in AI localisation, leading us to retain China equities as a Core holding. Elevated volatility reinforces the need to be defensively positioned, favouring diversification rather than relying on technology sector concentration. We also remain Overweight China’s healthcare, financial and materials sectors.
— Cindy Lam, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

Significant share issuance has kept the market capitalisation fairly stable, while the MSCI China Index has declined c.20% over the past one year
MSCI China Index price and market capitalisation

Source: FactSet, Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Are you still bullish on US 10-year government bonds?

Our view: We are closing our opportunistic bullish idea on US 10-year government bonds at a gain of 1.7%. The risk-reward has become less compelling after the yield broke below 5%, the lower bound of our three-month forecast range of 5.00-5.25%.
Rationale: The US 10-year yield fell over 17bps to 4.97% on 22 October – its first move below 5% since 23 September and biggest one-day drop since March 2023. A sell-off in AI-related equities and renewed Middle East tensions drove investors towards safe havens. Earlier this month, the yield hit its highest level in over two decades. The forces behind the rally are fragile, though. Oil prices remain elevated amid escalating Middle East tensions, and September US consumer inflation rose to 3.7% y/y. Fed officials have signalled there is no urgency to raise rates at the 27-28 October meeting, but persistent price pressures keep further tightening on the table. We prefer to lock in gains and close our opportunistic bullish idea on 10-year government bonds at a gain of 1.7%.
— Jonathan Liang, CFA, CIO, Fixed Income & FX

Risk-reward of US 10-year government bond yields is less compelling after the yield broke below 5%
US 10-year government bond yields

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

What is your outlook for French bank bonds, especially ahead of France’s upcoming sovereign credit rating reviews?

Our view: The recent sell-off in French bank bonds is a repricing of tail risks, not a credit story. We expect further price volatility until the April 2027 French presidential election, particularly at the junior end of the capital structure, so we are closing our opportunistic EU bank contingent convertibles (CoCos1) idea at a gain of 2.0%.
Rationale: We believe the recent sell-off in French bank bonds reflects domestic political and fiscal risks rather than weaker credit fundamentals. The sustained widening of the OAT-Bund spread has raised concerns about the profit and loss (P&L) impact on banks’ sovereign debt holdings. Banks provide limited disclosure on these exposures. However, banks’ investment portfolios are generally diversified, and holdings booked at amortised cost should soften the P&L impact. Near-term catalysts include the upcoming sovereign credit rating reviews. A sovereign downgrade could trigger bank rating downgrades, with domestically focused lenders potentially more exposed than regionally diversified peers. A sovereign credit event is not our base case, but we expect headline risks to persist until the French presidential election. Against this backdrop, we are closing our opportunistic EU bank CoCos idea.
— Cedric Lam, Senior Investment Strategist

A widening France-Germany 10-year government bond yield spread and a stable investment-grade (IG) bond option-adjusted spread (OAS) suggest a repricing of political and fiscal risk rather than credit risk
France-Germany IG bond OAS and 10-year government bond yield differentials

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Will the November US mid-term elections and European bond volatility support a sustained Swiss franc (CHF) rebound?

Our view: We expect a near-term CHF rebound, supported mainly by safe-haven demand amid European bond volatility. We believe the US mid-term elections will be a secondary driver.
Rationale: European sovereign bond volatility provides the stronger catalyst for CHF strength. The France-Germany government bond yield spread remains elevated near 160bps, reflecting heightened French fiscal concerns and reinforcing the CHF’s safe-haven appeal. The US mid-terms could provide additional support for the CHF. A Democratic victory in either chamber is expected to constrain further fiscal expansion, potentially weighing on the USD. However, this would not necessarily lead to faster fiscal consolidation.
The SNB’s 0% policy rate leaves the CHF at a sizeable interest-rate disadvantage vs. the USD, constraining sustained CHF gains. With EUR/CHF below 0.90, excessive CHF strength could also increase the risk of SNB intervention. A decisive USD/CHF break below 0.8130 would strengthen the technical case for a more sustained CHF rebound.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

USD/CHF failed to break above 0.8400 and is likely to test support at 0.8130
USD/CHF and technical indicators

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Top client questions (cont’d)

Would worsening budget deficits and political uncertainty across parts of Europe affect your view on EUR/USD and Euro area government bond yields?

Our view: Fiscal and political concerns constrain near-term EUR/USD gains, with France being the primary vulnerability. We expect EUR/USD to recover towards the 1.17-1.18 range over the next 12 months, supported by continued Euro area economic growth and an expected fading of USD support. We expect wider differentials in Euro area government bond yields, with political risk premium elevated in French government bonds (OATs) and German government bonds (Bunds) supported by safe-haven demand.
Rationale: France’s high public debt, large budget deficit and political obstacles to fiscal adjustments are weighing on market confidence, with the country’s 10-year government bond yield rising above 5%. The risk of stress spreading to Italy and Spain adds to regional concerns, although current evidence does not establish a broad European fiscal crisis. German government bonds should benefit from safe-haven demand, while fiscal concerns keep risk premia on vulnerable countries’ bonds elevated. EUR/USD remains more sensitive to US-Germany interest-rate differentials and broader market confidence than to French bond yields alone.
France’s fiscal risks, elevated energy costs and high US interest rates weigh on the EUR in the near term. Over the next 12 months, Germany’s multi-year public investment programme, resilient exports and sound banking-sector fundamentals are expected to support Euro area growth. We expect the Fed’s rate-hiking cycle to peak by mid-2027, reducing USD support and driving the EUR towards 1.17-1.18 .
The principal tail risk is fiscal stress widening government bond yield spreads and spilling over into bank funding conditions and lending activity, weakening growth and delaying the EUR’s recovery.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist— Cedric Lam, Senior Investment Strategist

articles.title: A detailed, affordable plan for transition insurance in the AI era | Brookings
articles.text:
Research

A detailed, affordable plan for transition insurance in the AI era

Robert E. Litan

Robert E. Litan

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

October 30, 2026

Shutterstock / Na_Studio

39 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Artificial intelligence (AI) holds enormous promise. Properly deployed, with suitable guardrails against its risks, AI is likely to raise living standards by enhancing productivity growth and to lead to new scientific discoveries, the development of new cures for all kinds of disease, and the creation of new products and services. Yet even as China accelerates efforts to develop and diffuse AI throughout its economy, public attitudes in the United States are markedly more wary. In 2025, nearly equal shares of Republicans (50%) and Democrats (51%) said that the growing use of AI in daily life made them more concerned than excited.1 This apprehension is reflected in broad opposition to local AI data center construction, which 71% of Americans opposed in a 2026 Gallup poll, including majorities of Republicans, independents, and Democrats, and in concern that AI can enable misinformation, fraud, and other misuse and may disrupt jobs and careers.2 Since that poll, concerns about AI’s potential existential risks have intensified, following public warnings from current and former employees of leading AI companies that current AI systems have insufficient oversight.3
I focus here, however, on just the job-displacement fears, which are likely to persist because AI use nonetheless will continue to grow even if data center construction and AI model development in the U.S. are slowed or halted. Even recent warnings that AI could take over the internet seem unlikely, by themselves, to halt AI adoption. AI is also being deployed to strengthen cyber defenses, and surveys document its growing use by businesses and individuals.4 So the job threat will remain. In July 2026, over 1,000 economists signed an online petition organized by Stanford’s Erik Brynjolfsson urging action to deal with the threat of future labor market disruption posed by AI.5 Even if those worries eventually prove unfounded as they so far appear to be—and even if over the longer run our economy and workers will adapt to AI just as they have adapted to previous technological advances—it makes sense for the government to have policies in place to ease the pain of transitioning to a post-AI economy.
In the following sections I lay out three such transition proposals—wage insurance, retraining assistance, and entry-level tax credits—as well as their annual costs under different scenarios, and suggest ways to pay for them. Under a reasonable set of assumptions, labor market disruption equivalent to a sustained 6% unemployment rate would require about $60 billion a year to finance these policies. Each policy addresses a different dimension, and so I view these as complementary proposals that, together, could serve as insurance that protects our economy and its workers from the potential downside of AI-driven job and income losses.

The role of social insurance for job market disruption
At minimum, to the extent the AI revolution has been causing a temporary jobs boom in the creation and usage of AI, including the industries constructing the infrastructure, those new jobs are not suitable for many, perhaps most, workers whose jobs AI may replace.6 Having the government take on an insurance role to ease the AI job transition for these displaced workers is no different from other government insurance programs in place for other low-probability, high-consequence events: for farmers against risks to their crops, for individuals and businesses against the risk of floods, let alone the many forms of insurance provided by the private insurance companies against risks to property and health.
In the case of AI-induced job and income risk, however, the private insurance market is likely to fall short for two reasons. First, there is no actuarial basis for private insurers to set premiums because future AI-induced job and income displacement could be so different from past technological change. Second, private insurance only works if the events insured against are independent from each other; private insurers will not take on highly correlated risks. That is the situation with AI-induced job and income losses: if they materialize, they are likely to be too highly correlated across people and areas of the country for private insurers to offer insurance.
To some, a universal basic income (UBI) is the answer. However, UBI would be far too expensive at the scale it might be needed. Unlike trade or automation, whose job and income displacement effects tend to be concentrated on middle-income manufacturing workers, AI threatens not only those workers (through AI-assisted robots), but potentially a broad swath of white-collar workers with substantially higher incomes. Accordingly, even a UBI program promising a poverty-level floor income, which has been estimated to have a net annual cost of approximately $784 billion after accounting for taxes clawed back (as of 2025),7 would do nothing to quell the anxieties of many, perhaps most, higher-income AI-displaced workers.
Fortunately, there are other more effective and politically viable approaches. One such program is wage or income insurance, which would reimburse displaced workers for some portion of their income loss for some period of time after taking a new, but lower-paying job. Another set of ideas would assist workers to retrain for new jobs and careers, either through government lifetime retraining accounts for individuals themselves and/or tax credits for employees and/or employers who provide such training. A third idea is to subsidize the hiring of entry-level workers, who would not be eligible for either wage insurance or retraining assistance.
So far, however, these programs have been advocated only in general terms, with minimal details and no cost estimates. The purpose of this report is to fill in those blanks, as well as to provide more detailed thoughts about how the three programs would be paid for. In doing so, I will draw on my own prior published work, spanning over three decades, with multiple authors, in advocating for both wage insurance and, separately, from my own earlier proposal for lifetime retraining accounts.

Wage loss insurance
The most recent comprehensive survey of wage insurance and its effects by Benjamin G. Hyman, Brian K. Kovak and Adam Leive (“HKL”)8 identifies the origins of the concept of wage insurance for displaced workers in a chapter of a Brookings publication, “Economic Choices,” in 1984, co-authored by Robert Lawrence.9 Two years later I teamed up with Lawrence to offer a few details of such a program targeted only for workers displaced by trade in a book titled “Saving Free Trade.”10 We proposed that trade-displaced workers receive payments up to 50% of their income loss once they obtained a new job, subject to an unspecified ceiling, and for an unspecified limited time. We suggested that the reinsurance percentage might be phased down over the eligibility time limit. We offered the proposal not as a replacement for unemployment insurance, but as a supplement, the idea being to encourage displaced workers to find jobs more quickly in order to receive the insurance payments. To finance the program, we suggested converting existing import quotas on textiles, sugar, and steel into tariffs.
Fifteen years later I teamed with a different co-author, Lori Kletzer, not only to flesh out more details about a wage insurance program, but to estimate its annual cost.11 In particular, we proposed a universal program, not tied to any specific reason for job loss, for all displaced workers (those involuntarily unemployed for reasons other than cause) with tenure of at least two years, with insurance making up 50% of the income loss upon the worker’s obtaining a new full-time job, up to a $10,000 annual maximum. Insurance payments would be triggered on the date of reemployment, providing incentives for quick reemployment, even as the newly employed workers could continue to look for better jobs. The proposal was largely designed for displaced manufacturing workers, victims more of technological advances than trade. Available evidence back then indicated that displaced service-sector workers tended to suffer little or no wage losses, or minimal wage losses, when they found their new jobs. On reasonable assumptions, we estimated then that such a universal program, serving approximately 800,000 eligible displaced workers who suffered an average 22% cut in wages upon taking new jobs would cost approximately $3 billion, at a national unemployment rate of 4.9%. Five years later, I teamed with Lael Brainard and Nicholas Warren to update the annual cost estimate for an eligible population of approximately 500,000, which we pegged at $3.5 billion given a 4.7% national unemployment rate.12 The costs were higher than those estimated in my study with Kletzer, even with a smaller eligible population, because the estimated annual earnings loss in absolute dollars was roughly double the amount in that study (approximately $17,000 versus the earlier $8,800 wage cut).13 We also suggested that the program could easily be financed by a small increase in the federal unemployment tax (FUTA).
Remarkably, wage insurance, albeit limited to trade-displaced workers and not universally extended, quickly found its way into public policy in the U.S., following Canada’s experimentation with it in 1995. In 2002, the administration of George W. Bush worked with Congress to introduce a version of wage insurance as an alternative Trade Adjustment Assistance for workers over the age of 50 determined to be trade-displaced, who found new work in less than 26 weeks from the date of unemployment, and were compensated for 50% of their wage loss up to a lifetime (not annual) maximum of $10,000. President Obama, with congressional approval, later extended that program, before proposing in his last State of the Union address in 2016 that the program be extended to all displaced workers regardless of cause.14
For illustrative purposes, I now model the gross costs of a generous wage insurance program available to all long-tenured displaced workers earning below $250,000 in their last job. The Displaced Worker Survey in recent years only reports on workers with at least three years’ tenure at their prior jobs, and that is the eligibility criterion used here. The insurance covers such workers who obtain either a new full-time or part-time job. The compensation for both is capped at a level that produces an average income loss for estimation purposes here of $30,000 per year. The $30,000 average loss roughly scales for inflation the $17,000 wage loss figure that Brainard, Litan, and Warren estimated for the year 2001. A more precise average wage loss figure cannot be determined from the current Displaced Worker Survey, which only breaks down the number of workers who suffer income loss of less than or more than $20,000. A more granular analysis of the average wage losses would be required to set actual compensation caps. The estimates here apply the same wage losses to displaced workers who may prefer part-time work initially, while they are looking for new full-time employment, in order to encourage such searches. Based on the 2023–25 Displaced Worker Survey, 66% of long-term displaced workers found new full-time work, 51% of whom took a cut in wages on reemployment.15
The proposed program also has some additional features. Workers must be involuntarily displaced for reasons other than cause, the definition used for unemployment insurance (UI) programs. Benefits are provided for three years (not two, as in the earlier proposed program), from the date of reemployment, with 80% of earnings loss compensated in the first year, 60% in the second year, and 40% in the third year, with no annual or lifetime cap.
I have estimated the gross and net costs of wage insurance under the foregoing assumptions, under three different national unemployment rates: 4% (approximately the rate at this writing), 6% (mild recession and/or relatively mild AI impact), and 8% (severe recession and/or severe AI impact). The costs for the higher unemployment scenarios are scaled linearly from the 4% base case, so the 6% scenario implies 50% higher cost than the 4% unemployment scenario and the 8% scenario implies a doubling of the cost under the 4% scenario. The net costs offset the gross amount for (1) an illustrative two months’ quicker reemployment rate with wage insurance in place, and (2) additional tax revenues collected on such reemployment, at an illustrative tax rate of 15%, reflecting a conservative estimate of the average tax rate likely paid by displaced workers. The costs are “steady-state” costs, or those that take full account of all three years of compensation.
Table 1 provides net cost estimates using the assumptions described above, under three different scenarios. Table 1 shows that in the “base case” estimates the net costs range from $25 billion under 4% unemployment to $50 billion under 8% unemployment. The annual cost estimates are conservative, since they assume that the accompanying level of unemployment is sustained indefinitely, which would not be true as workers and labor markets adjust over time. The annual cost estimates are expressed in 2025 dollars; if the wage loss compensation amounts are scaled with inflation, as they should be, the 2025 cost estimates should be viewed as real costs going forward. In the midpoint 6% unemployment scenario, the annual net costs of wage insurance are $38 billion, or a little more than 0.1% of GDP at year-end 2025.

Table 1

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

These steady-state cost estimates may be understated, however, to the extent that policymakers extend coverage to workers with less than three years’ tenure at their prior job. On the other hand, it is possible that the presence of wage insurance could raise reemployment incomes relative to what occurred in the past. The HKL study of the limited wage insurance program found that it “increased employment probabilities by 8 to 17 percentage points during the two years following displacement before fading to zero after four years.” The study also found that earnings replacement rates increased by 10 percentage points under the program and cumulative earnings increased by over $18,000 during the four years following displacement, a 26.6% increase relative to the average four-year cumulative earnings of ineligible workers.16 Most striking is their finding that the program more than paid for itself: the net cost to the government was negative because of reduced UI payments and tax receipts on the higher earnings. Although the authors caution that this favorable result could be the consequence of the limited nature of the program,17 the prior experiment with more limited wage insurance suggests that there could be an additional tax receipts offset due to enhanced earnings that is not reflected in the net cost estimates for the universal program suggested here.

Retraining assistance
Not all displaced workers will look immediately for a new job. Some may opt to retrain for a different career path by going back to school or entering a retraining program.
In principle, the federal government can support retraining either through much expanded tax credits for all or a portion of an individual’s expenditures on retraining, or through a version of “lifetime retraining accounts.” The reason for expanding the existing tax credits for retraining is that they are very limited. Federal law now offers a Lifetime Learning Credit (LLC) of up to $2,000 annually for qualifying postsecondary job-skills coursework, but its nonrefundability (it doesn’t help workers who pay no federal income tax), limited eligible expenses, and income phaseout materially limit its usefulness as a displacement-retraining benefit.18 The American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) is a federal, partially refundable income-tax credit for the early years of postsecondary education, but because it is designed chiefly to help students, and often their parents, pay the costs of beginning an undergraduate degree or recognized credential, it does not function as a general, lifetime retraining benefit.19 Given these limitations, Davidson and Slaughter propose an unspecified, presumably additional, tax credit to either or both displaced employees and employers for retraining.20 Anthropic proposes unspecified “incentives for firms who retain and redeploy their workers.”21
Although tax credits are relatively easy to administer, since they build on the existing tax code, they have drawbacks. When extended to employers, there is no easy way to ensure that the credit is not rewarding training that employers would otherwise undertake. When extended to employees, even if they are refundable in the full amount of any retraining, tax credits can’t help those who don’t have the cash or borrowing capacity to pay for the costs upfront, though the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 (OBBBA) extended Pell Grants to short-term training programs that alleviate some of this concern.
Given the liquidity issues associated with paying for lengthier careers, I and others have advocated instead a lifetime training account (LTA) available to every working person that could be drawn down for retraining, at multiple stages of a worker’s life. About 10 years ago, Ed Alden and I suggested a flat $100,000 loan account only, with federal regulation aimed at ensuring that the training programs meet minimum standards.22 Shortly thereafter, the Aspen Institute proposed a retraining savings account that would be matched with federal dollars.23 Earlier, Robert LaLonde (University of Chicago) and Daniel Sullivan (Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago) proposed increasing Pell Grants for training-ready displaced workers rather than creating accounts per se.24
I propose here instead for illustrative purposes a much more targeted version of my original proposal with Alden, focusing on the 1.1 million displaced workers each year with at least three years’ tenure on their prior job. This feature aligns with the eligibility criteria for the wage insurance proposal. The annual flow is scaled linearly to each unemployment scenario off a 4.0% baseline, roughly the 2024 average. As with the wage insurance estimates, the cost figures are scaled linearly with the unemployment rate. I model worker take-up rates of 20% (low), 30% (medium), and 40% (high), respectively. The LTA program I envision would provide grants to cover training. One way to estimate that cost is to use the average in-district cost of $4,150 for attending community college, and assume a two-year retraining period, to arrive at annual training costs of $8,300.25 Displaced workers may or may not require a living cost subsidy, depending on whether they have a working spouse or partner. Living costs under the proposal would be paid for through an income-contingent loan—one that is paid back at a certain percentage of future income. I assume here a gross annual borrowing of $30,000, and a subsidy rate of 50%, meaning that on average only half the loans would be repaid. This scores the loan portion of the LTA, for those who take it, at $15,000 per year.

Entry-level job tax credit
Early evidence is mixed as to the impact of AI on entry-level jobs so far. Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen find a relative post-ChatGPT employment decline among U.S. workers ages 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations.26 In contrast, Hernæs and Kostøl find no statistically precise corresponding decline across the complete distribution of AI-exposed occupations among young Norwegian private-sector workers,27 and Danish matched employer–worker evidence finds no difference in entry-level hiring between AI-adopting and nonadopting firms.28 A subsequent study by Fairlie and Wu, using data for 2026, comes to a similar conclusion.29
Nonetheless, there are widespread fears that in the future AI will negatively affect entry-level jobs. The federal government can address this problem in a cost-effective way without limiting any hiring incentives to AI-specific sectors, which can be difficult to define. I do so here by modeling a variation of the tax deduction for hiring young workers advocated by Leicht and Ball.30
More specifically, I propose a first-year 50% tax credit for hiring recent graduates of two- or four-year colleges within 12 months of their earning their degree who have been hired into a job paying more than $40,000 annually, but not more than $100,000. The wage floor is designed to address real entry-level jobs. The wage ceiling is designed to exclude jobs that are not truly entry-level. Both the floor and ceiling obviously can be adjusted in the legislative process, and both numbers should be indexed to inflation.
Table 3 depicts the annual cost of the proposed entry-level job tax credit, across a reasonable range for the annual take-up rate. The cost estimates are built off an annual cohort of graduates from two- and four-year colleges of 3 million,31 an employed rate of 72%,32 and my estimate that of those employed, 65% of those have annual earnings between $40,000 and $100,000. Under these assumptions, approximately 45% of each young cohort, or about 1 million young people each year, would be eligible for an employer tax credit. The take-up rates are likely to be inversely proportional to the level of the unemployment rate, with more take-up expected when unemployment rates are low and employers more willing to hire young people for entry-level jobs, and less take-up when unemployment is high. This pattern is opposite to that of the cost estimates for wage insurance and LTA, which rise as the national unemployment rate rises (or the displacement effect of AI is greater).

Paying for transition insurance
So how will the government pay for the different policies suggested here? It would be nice if the HKL result, that at least wage insurance can actually pay for itself through reduced UI payments and higher tax collections, could be generalized to a program serving all displaced workers. Such an outcome is possible, or at the very least, the Congressional Budget Office, the official federal scorekeeper, might offset some of the gross costs of the wage insurance component with these credits. Still, some portion of the wage insurance, plus the estimated costs of the LTAs and entry-level job tax credit will need to be financed.
In theory, the amount of financing could vary with projected outlays for a given year, which in turn depends on the degree of AI job displacement and/or macroeconomic projections (here proxied by the unemployment rate). That way, again at least in principle, there would be no net fiscal impact on the budget each year. But as a political matter, the notion that Congress must appropriate sufficient funds every year to pay for wage insurance/LTAs/entry-level job tax credit is a nonstarter, especially in years of recession, when Congress would be loath to pass anything that looks like a tax increase. For this reason, I suggest that when launching the package of “AI transition insurance,” Congress raise sufficient funds through any of the mechanisms suggested below to pay at least for the 6% unemployment scenario, the version of wage insurance outlined here, and the medium take up rates for LTA withdrawals and the entry-level job tax credit—assumptions that would produce a total annual net cost, and hence need for annual financing, in the $60 billion range. This is a bit smaller than annual earned income tax credit expenditures,33 and totals about 0.8% of total federal outlays.34 Net annual surpluses (receipts minus the outlays for the program) in any individual year would go toward reducing the deficit, which at the current 6% of GDP range clearly needs reducing. In worse years, for example if AI displacement is higher, the program would not be fully paid for, which is the right outcome because then the absence of full financing acts, on net, as a countercyclical stabilizer.
Now, to the “how” question. It is tempting to say that only AI companies should pay for the transition insurance program. But who counts as an AI company and why limit it to them? Just the companies that make large language models (LLMs)? Companies that make robots, increasingly powered by AI? Companies or individuals who use AI to become more productive? There are no clear answers to these questions, but the cloudiness suggests we look to broader-based sources of revenue. For related reasons, I reject calls for taxes on AI “tokens” or on “robots,” not just because they directly impair innovation, but because they would be highly complex to design and administer.
Here are some possible alternative ideas. Davidson and Slaughter suggest a new 25% payroll tax on all equity compensation, to get at the fact that most executive compensation is paid in the form of stock or stock options, rather than in cash.35 Although such a tax reaches beyond those working for “AI companies,” however defined, it would cover those who stand to benefit from the AI boom. The authors estimate such a tax would generate at least $100 billion in annual revenue.
Alternatively, a second idea suggested by Greg Ip of the Wall Street Journal,36 Nobel Prize winners Paul Krugman37 and Daron Acemoglu (with co-authors Andrea Manera and Pascual Restrepo) is to rectify the current imbalance of taxation on labor and capital, by increasing the taxes on physical investment.38 As Ip points out, since the 2017 tax bill, while the marginal tax on labor has dropped a bit, from 29% to 27%, the marginal tax rate on new equipment is now just 4%, down from 14% before that legislation.39 This glaring disparity calls out for rectification especially because of the very limited effect that tax rates are having on physical investment and in turn GDP.40 Moreover, all three authors point to the secular decline in labor’s share of national income and the corresponding rise of the capital share (represented by profits), trends which AI is likely to accentuate. Hence at least a modest tax increase on capital seems in order. It is not clear what form such an increase should take—a reversal of the 100% expensing of capital investment “made permanent” in the OBBBA and/or an increase in the corporate tax rate generally—but it ought to total roughly $60 billion annually to fund the full transition insurance program.
The $60 billion increase is less substantial than it may appear. Given that corporate income tax receipts for 2025 were approximately $450 billion,41 the amount required to fully fund the AI transition program would represent a 13% increase in average corporate taxes, or an increase of about 2.5 percentage points of corporate income, from the current 21% to 23.5%. The higher average rate would still be well below the top marginal rate of 35%, which was replaced by the 21% flat rate in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 during the first Trump term.42 If assessed on corporate income, generally, the tax increase would fall on a combination of shareholders, customers, and workers. That is a reason to favor the Davidson and Slaughter tax on equity compensation, whose incidence would be split among those executives and the corporations paying them, resulting in less pass-on to corporate customers and labor compared to a tax on corporations directly.

Closing caveat: Status loss of potentially many displaced workers
I close with one important caveat and commentary on it. The transition insurance program outlined here would not eliminate the loss of status many displaced workers suffer when forced to pursue new careers and jobs. A career is not only an income stream; it’s a source of identity, mastery, and social standing, and asking a 50-year-old professional to move into hands-on work they were raised to see as a step down is asking them to absorb a real status loss.
The only honest answer to this legitimate concern is that over time AI will change the culture, which will assign more value to hands-on work and careers it entails, such as electricians, plumbers, and nurses. Some portion of those white-collar workers who will learn these skills also will be entrepreneurial and will build businesses that employ others in the skilled trades that AI or artificial general intelligence (AGI) will not hollow out. Indeed, insufficient attention is given to the several million entrepreneurs, many if not most without fancy college degrees, who have done precisely that over the last few decades.43 In the AI age, those opportunities for building business empires in “hands-on” activities, especially in the service sector, will continue to exist. Others may find comfort in the fact that the work AI leaves for humans is disproportionately the work that requires care, judgment, and trust, which is to say the work that is most recognizably human. But the hard reality is that the AI genie is out of the bottle, and there is no sugarcoating that fact. The transition insurance program here at least might help many people adjust to the new reality.
Admittedly, some may balk at the $60 billion a year price tag, which should be viewed as the equivalent of an insurance premium paid to avert a self-defeating populist backlash against AI, or even the capitalist system that has produced it. The stakes are that high, and the fears about future AI job and income displacement are sufficiently legitimate, in my view, to justify the payment of that premium.

articles.text:
Webinar

The Horn on Edge: Ethiopia’s Tigray crisis and rising tensions with Eritrea

Register Now

5 November 2026 – 1.00pm SAST

online

The return of fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region has raised fears that the country could once again descend into a protracted internal conflict, with potentially far-reaching consequences for the wider Horn of Africa.

The breakdown of the fragile post-war settlement has coincided with a sharp deterioration in relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara, raising the prospect of a direct confrontation between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Beyond Tigray, competing strategic interests, shifting alliances and unresolved disputes over Red Sea access and Nile waters are deepening regional fault lines, drawing in neighbours including Somalia, Sudan and Egypt. With Ethiopia’s internal security challenges increasingly intertwined with regional rivalries, the risk of escalation extends well beyond its borders.

This webinar will examine the drivers behind the renewed conflict, the calculations shaping Ethiopia and Eritrea’s increasingly hostile relationship, and the interests of other regional actors. It will also assess potential pathways for escalation or de-escalation, the prospects for a durable political settlement in Tigray, and the implications for regional stability, trade and investment.

This webinar is being held on our new platform, ON24. If you do not receive your confirmation email, please check your junk and spam folders.

Speakers

Jervin Naidoo

Jervin is a political analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, specialising in the political coverage of the DRC, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, and several East African countries. Before joining OEA, Jervin honed his expertise in academia and research at the University of Pretoria’s Department of Political Science, the Institute for Security Studies, and the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime. He holds an MA in International Political Economy from the University of Warwick. His areas of expertise include security and intelligence, foreign policy, and the illicit economy.

articles.title: One Health through the lens of today’s investment megatrends - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Alex Bernhardt, Global Head of Sustainability Research; Rachel Crossley, Head of Stewardship, Europe; and Robert-Alexandre Poujade, Head of Nature

The One Health concept recognises that human health is inextricably linked to the health of animals and the environment, moving beyond a narrow medical perspective to a systemic view of health-related value and risk

Assessing One Health through the lens of four megatrends – geopolitics, innovation, demographics, and the environment – helps to identify impacts on worker productivity, supply chain reliability, and market growth

For long-term investors, health determinants are viewed as material factors that can influence corporate earnings, sovereign credit, and labour markets, helping to identify risks that may currently be underappreciated by the market

The forces shaping human health outcomes are far broader than hospitals, pharmaceuticals and medical devices. Human health is dependent upon animal health and the health of the environment. Together the health of these three systems are inextricably intertwined, creating the One Health concept (Exhibit 1).

For long-term investors, these health determinants are not peripheral; they shape and are shaped by productivity, labour participation, the resilience of communities and economies and other social systems.

While the pathways for One Health impacts are not always linear or clear, they can nevertheless be material to economic and financial outcomes for investors. Indeed, understanding how corporate investment can drive negative or create positive health outcomes for its stakeholders – employees, customers, communities, plants and animals – will be increasingly important in an increasingly interconnected world.

The One Health theme, grounded in preceding work by the World Health Organization and other supranationals, therefore gives us a useful frame for moving from a narrow sector view of health to a more systemic view of health-related value creation and risk.

It recognises that a workforce’s health can affect operating performance; that the health of consumers can influence the growth of markets; and that the health of ecosystems can determine the reliability of supply chains; the quality of natural inputs and the exposure of communities to disease.

Companies do not operate outside these systems. They depend on them and affect them.

This does not mean treating every social or environmental issue as a health issue. A disciplined One Health approach should improve, not dilute, investment analysis. The challenge is to identify where health determinants are financially material for a sector, issuer, or asset and through which transmission channels. To support related analysis BNPP AM’s megatrends provide a useful framework:

Geopolitics: Global health outcomes depend on food security, access to medicines, resilient supply chains and international cooperation on health and environmental risks. Geopolitical fragmentation can increase vulnerabilities while cooperation can improve system resilience

Environment: Human, animal and ecosystem health are deeply interconnected. Environmental pressures such as pollution, climate change, biodiversity loss and water stress affect public health, productivity and economic stability

Demographics: Ageing populations, urbanisation and changing disease patterns are reshaping demand for healthcare, nutrition, housing and care services. Understanding demographic trends is essential to improving long-term health and economic resilience.

Innovation: Breakthroughs in biotechnology, diagnostics, precision agriculture, data analytics and preventative care can improve health outcomes across interconnected human, animal and environmental systems. Innovation expands the range of investable health solutions

Geopolitics: Health security, resilience and strategic dependence

Access to healthcare and other social determinants of health – notably housing, food and water – is increasingly shaped by geopolitics. At the multinational level, restrictive trade policy, increased conflict, and decreased cooperation all serve to heighten the risk of future pandemics, worsening climate-related health impacts, and medicine or food shortages.

At the national level, shifts in the political landscape can result in declining quality of public services which can have cross-border effects. For instance, softening vaccine requirements could result in greater incidence of preventable disease.

Moreover, loss of public benefits like food or housing assistance can increase the public burden of disease which can have many knock-on effects for communities beyond the added frictional costs of increased emergency health treatments.

A One Health perspective shows that company resilience is dependent to a significant degree upon public institutions. This creates risks for companies dependent on vulnerable global supply chains, low-cost labour, or weakened public systems, but it also creates opportunities in healthcare security, diagnostics, and other solutions that support preparedness without simply shifting costs to consumers or governments.

Innovation: new solutions, new dependencies and new questions of access

Innovation is central to One Health because it changes what can be prevented, detected, treated and measured. Advances in medicines, environmental monitoring and AI-enabled discovery can improve health outcomes and strengthen resilience.

They can also help investors identify companies whose products and services reduce preventable harm while addressing structural demand. Healthcare innovation remains important, but the investable universe is broader than healthcare alone. It includes technologies and business models that improve the health of people, animals and ecosystems together.

At the same time, innovation can create new dependencies and unintended consequences. Digital health tools may improve access but raise questions about privacy, exclusion and quality of care.

Artificial intelligence can accelerate drug discovery, diagnostics and environmental monitoring, but it can also increase energy and water demand and concentrate benefits among firms with data, compute and distribution advantages.

Agricultural technology can reduce chemical and antibiotic use, but it can also deepen dependence on proprietary inputs. The investment question is therefore not whether innovation is positive in general, but whether the business model, governance, affordability, lifecycle impacts and measurable outcomes support durable value creation.

A One Health lens helps distinguish innovation that genuinely improves resilience from innovation that merely increases efficiency while shifting health or environmental costs elsewhere.

Demographics: Demand, vulnerability and health’s social determinants

Demographics are reshaping One Health considerations with different trends driving different outcomes. Ageing populations, particularly in developed markets, create significant risks if the transition is unmanaged.

But well managed, it can create huge opportunities for investments in the care economy including long-term care, mobility solutions and age-friendly housing.1

Urbanisation, particularly pronounced in emerging markets, increases the importance of sanitation, air quality, housing quality, green space, transport design and heat resilience.

Migration and regional demographic divergence influence labour availability, fiscal capacity and the vulnerability of communities to public health and climate shocks. Labour market participation and socioeconomic inequality can create political risk and shift aggregate demand patterns.

Environment: Ecosystems as health infrastructure

Environment is perhaps the most intuitive One Health lens because air quality and ecosystem health are a foundation for human and animal health. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and water availability all influence exposure to disease, heat stress and unsafe living conditions.

An estimated nine million premature deaths each year are caused by pollution and 90% of the global population is exposed to ambient concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) above the WHO annual air quality guideline.2 Additionally, over 60% of emerging infectious diseases originate in animals.3

Perhaps one of the most trenchant examples of the human health and animal health connection is antimicrobial resistance. It arises when bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites evolve to resist the medications that once effectively treated infections.

And its rise in humans can largely be traced to the overuse of antibiotics in livestock. Understanding the societal ramifications of consumer preferences for meat and business preferences for efficient solutions to problems (in this case, animals often living in close-quarters getting sick) is supported by a One Health perspective.

Why investors should care

Within BNPP AM’s Global Sustainability Strategy, One Health therefore sits alongside Transition and Sustainable AI as part of our forward-looking research agenda. One Health matters for investors because it connects health outcomes to the systems that sustain long-term economic value.

It broadens the investment lens from healthcare spending to the determinants of health that for example shape worker productivity/availability and supply-chain reliability. It also helps identify risks that markets may underprice because they sit between sectors, time horizons or asset classes.

Antimicrobial resistance, unsafe food systems, pollution exposure, heat stress, biodiversity loss, weak health access and social isolation may each appear narrow at first, but together they can affect corporate earnings, sovereign credit, labour markets and long-term market performance.

The investor implications are practical. First, One Health supports better risk identification by linking health determinants to financially material transmission channels such as input costs, workforce productivity and tail risks.

Second, it supports opportunity identification by clarifying where durable demand may emerge for prevention-oriented healthcare, affordable housing, climate adaptation and nature-based solutions.

And third, it supports stewardship by helping investors ask whether companies are reducing preventable harm, strengthening resilience and measuring outcomes, rather than relying on broad claims.

Measurement will be central. One Health is powerful because it captures interdependence, but that also makes it vulnerable to over-claiming. Investors need fit-for-purpose indicators that distinguish inputs, outputs and outcomes; recognise time horizons; and avoid overstating causality. We will continue our work on this over the years to come.

[1] https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_The_Future_of_the_Care_Economy_2024.pdf

[2] Global Environment Outlook 7 | UNEP – UN Environment Programme

[3] Editorial: Zoonotic diseases originating from wildlife: Emergence/re-emergence, evolution, prevalence, pathogenesis, prevention, and treatment – PMC
