The evolution of hedge fund performance: From enhancer to diversifier
[Music]
John Schlegel: Welcome to J.P. Morgan's Making Sense. I'm John Schlegel, head of the Global Data Assets and Alpha Group within Prime Financial Services. Today, I'm joined by Kumar Panja, who is the Head of the Capital Advisory Group for the EMEA region. Kumar, it's great to be sitting down with you as I'm in London this week.
Kumar Panja: I'm glad that you're here. Glad we can make this work, John.
John Schlegel: It's great being with you because there's a lot I think we can really discuss between the two of us around what we're seeing in the hedge fund space. But first, I'd just like to note that we're recording this in early October. And while much of our focus will be less on the immediate past or future, if there are some big surprises this month, some of this conversation could be a little bit different. Before we get to the focus of this episode, Kumar, do you mind giving us a brief overview of your role?
Kumar Panja: Sure. So the Capital Advisory Group is a value-added hedge fund client-focused function that sits in the sales and marketing division of the investment bank. We work very closely with our prime financial services business. One of our lines of business is capital introduction, which as the name suggests, introduces our hedge fund clients to institutional investors who allocate to hedge funds as part of a wider portfolio. That would include investors ranging from sovereign wealth funds to pension funds, endowments and foundations, private banks, family offices, among others. I run the group for the EMEA region and is run globally by my colleague, Mike Monforth.
John Schlegel: Thanks, Kumar. For those who aren't familiar with my role as head of this Data Assets and Alpha Group, I generally focus on things covering tactical market takes as well as focus on data that we can deliver to our clients. But really for the purposes of this podcast, I'll be focusing mostly on what we call positioning intelligence, which centers around what we see in the hedge fund community amongst other allocators and how that affects the markets. So it's really interesting to have this discussion as the year has been quite the whirlwind of events, whether it was the Iran conflict that started off in March or the AI momentum rally that really affected a lot of funds in the second quarter, as well as the unwind we saw post that in the third quarter. So a ton to potentially discuss, but maybe starting off with what we're seeing on the performance side, given the volatility, what do you see in the high level data?
Kumar Panja: Sure. If we look at performance year to date, it's very clear that equity remains the clear winner. Equity long short and long only are for us, at least from our data, the standout strategies, while relative value macro and credit have lagged the broader hedge fund universe. And I stress by saying these are averages, there's a dispersion in individual manager performance. And the biggest story is for us is dispersion, not just returns, because within equity long short, managers at the 75th percentile have generated over 12%, while those at the 25th percentile are barely positive at 0.5%. So even in the best performing strategy outcomes do vary dramatically, highlighting the importance of manager selection. Long only has been more consistently successful. Despite a similar average return to equity long short, the median long only manager is up 12%, significantly higher than the 5.65% median number we have for equity long short.
John Schlegel: That's really interesting. And I think it does jive a lot with what we've seen and heard. One thing that we track based on the positions clients hold with us is what we see for their equity performance of the book. So we can't necessarily see everything, but the overall story has been one of very strong performance in equities, particularly in the second quarter, which drove a ton of the gains. When you think about what drove that, a lot of that was related to AI in some way, shape, or form. But what's also been interesting is a strategy that has been very much in focus over the last few years, namely the quants, typically had a bit of a rougher time in the second quarter with some of the volatility that was going on. And they, from our data, seem to be the ones really holding up very well in the last few months. So the third quarter, I would say, very strong for a lot of the quantitative managers and a lot more mixed for more of the fundamental funds. But I think another element of what we're seeing recently is the focus regionally. So by this, I mean, when we look at alpha year to date, and arguably even the last couple of years, it seems like a lot of this is coming from Asia. Is that something that you're also seeing and feeling?
Kumar Panja: Well, we've definitely seen an increase in global investor interest in Asia Pacific, as well as greater China. And that is partly performance chasing, but it's also a reflection of the fact that Asia has been perhaps an underweight in those portfolios. So those two factors have come together quite happily, which has definitely generated a lot more interest. And my colleague, Stephen Kelly, and his and James Tan in Asia, who cover the capital team there, have been very, very busy in terms of global investors that want to learn more about APAC specialist managers.
John Schlegel: Can you give us a sense as to how the returns compare regionally, maybe in the equity space?
Kumar Panja: Sure. And as we said before, I think the overarching theme is that geography mattered as much as strategy selection. And in several cases, the gap between the same strategy in different regions was larger than the gap between entirely different strategies. And so if we pick on equity long short, that saw, again, according to our data, the most dramatic regional divergence in the data set. APAC managers delivered an exceptional average return of 22% compared with just 4% in EMEA and 9% in the Americas.
John Schlegel: When you compare it to market indices year to date, that gap in performance is actually wider than what you see for the broader market. So if you know, if you look at different ways of measuring alpha, the alpha generation in Asia has been far superior to what we've seen in other regions year to date. So I guess moving on from what the facts of the returns are and have been, when you talk to allocators, are they generally happy with the returns? Are they starting to chase it a bit more? It does seem like hedge funds have become popular again. What's your take on this?
Kumar Panja: The team is full employment in terms of incoming from investors. And so I think hedge funds have definitely been going through a resurgence, probably fit to be fair for the last sort of 24 months. But as you say, the $64 million dollar question is, you know, what do those investors feel about the go forward? And interestingly, I was with three very large institutional investors just yesterday, and we discussed the same question. And their answer is their hedge fund books overall, and that's across all strategies, have done very well this year, despite some of the drawdowns that we've talked about during this year. Now, one needs to keep in mind that institutional investors typically look at investments, even in public market hedge funds, over a multi-year period. They don't like admitting that to their hedge fund managers they invest in, but they do tend to look at these investments over a multi-year period. So the fact there's been one or two months of dislocation doesn't necessarily change their allocation strategy. What it might do is, as you would expect, it delays the deployment of capital to take advantage for them of a lower watermark or a lower net asset value NAV entry point into that manager. But feedback overall from our wider investor base would suggest that we'll see continued inflows into the hedge fund space.
John Schlegel: So investors being thoughtful about, not trying to necessarily, perhaps, chase the returns. I think it's interesting that they're looking for better entry points, which historically, I would have argued maybe 15 years ago or so, it was more about chasing whoever's doing really well. Related to that, as clients or investors are looking at hedge funds in their portfolio, is it more about diversifying returns or enhancing returns?
Kumar Panja: And it's a really good question, John. And I think you've hit the nail on the head in terms of what institutional investors now expect from that hedge fund portfolio. So traditionally, a hedge fund portfolio was very much built to be, in some cases, a return enhancer. And that was many, many years ago. Nowadays, they're built to be a diversifier. But some of the issues that investors raise today is, the level of leverage that some managers are running. And then when they take that together with crowding or concentration, there is a sentiment, and it is a sentiment, it's not backed up with flows yet, a sentiment that hedge funds may well provide less diversification than originally planned in that portfolio. Going back to hedge funds as a protector, if you mean specifically tail hedging strategies, there are some hedge fund strategies managers that specialize in this space. And whilst portfolio theory tells us that it's a useful tool to have, tail hedging strategies have been very expensive in terms of capital bleed and capital erosion over the last few years. And as I caveat that by saying, there have been and continue to be some notable exceptions. So fewer investors use hedge funds as a protector, but they do use diversification as the main benefit.
John Schlegel: That makes a lot of sense. I think one of the interesting things that you just brought up in terms of, will they be as much of a protector? There is kind of an open question of, if they're growing so much, do they become the market? Often this is one of the arguments against some of the large companies and the concentration risks in the U.S. equity market is, at what point do the companies be so large that they can't really grow and outperform the wider market because they are the market, right? I don't think we're there yet on the hedge fund side. When you look at something like a measure of leverage in the hedge fund universe, this has certainly been a focus by many different folks within the industry, outside of the industry, regulators, et cetera. And there is potential cause for concern that sometimes comes up. Leverage levels and the amount of borrowing is objectively higher and has been trending higher over time. But I think what that oftentimes misses is the wider context. And by this, I mean, if you think about how much the market has grown, it's grown significantly in the last 5, 10 years, whether it's the performance of a lot of markets or the overall market cap or the turnover. I mean, one of the things in the equity market that's happened is you have this influx of retail investors. And so the thing is, when you have higher asset levels and more turnover, well, if you are a hedge fund that likes to make long and short bets and trade around things, there's more to do, right? And so we're only seeing the total assets on a levered basis kind of keep up in line with those market metrics rather than exceed them. I think it's one of these things where as long as the markets hold up, really, there's not necessarily this big disconnect where we've overshot in terms of the hedge fund leverage. So that'll be something to watch, though, over the next few years and could depend on do we continue to see this AI-led growth in wider market performance and economic growth continue, or is it something that really causes that to slow down or reverse? So maybe to shift gears again a little bit, Kumar, I know that you had recently done a very large investor survey. What are the areas in particular that you see allocators looking to deploy more capital into?
Kumar Panja: Thanks, John. so just to back up, so the investor sentiment, which we talked about earlier, continues to be positive. And just to give you a stat from that survey, 98% of investors expect to maintain or increase their hedge fund exposure. Now, interestingly, 53% of incremental hedge fund exposure is coming from new capital deployed. So some of it's compound growth, of course, but there is new money flowing in, which is obviously the big barometer of whether-
John Schlegel: That's good to hear.
Kumar Panja: Yeah, whether those investors are voting that hedge funds continue to grow in their portfolios. Now, your question earlier was around strategies of interest, what's interesting. It is actually quite diverse, but it's skewed towards larger managers. So another statistic from that survey, that's quite interesting is 86% of the $90 billion of flows in the first half of 2026 this year have gone to managers with greater than $5 billion of AUM. So clearly, there's a preference towards the larger managers. In terms of particular strategies, it's macro specialist equity long, short. And as you mentioned, quant, quant's done very well, statistical arbitrage, high-frequency quant have been most in demand. If we then put a regional lens on it, then as we discussed earlier, APAC regionally has been most in demand.
John Schlegel: That's really interesting. I mean, on the strategy side, would you say a lot of this is kind of a reflection of this desire for diversification?
Kumar Panja: It is. What is healthy to see is that specialist equity long, short has come back in because there's a long period where specialist equity long, short was not performing, So while quant has always been popular, it's grown in the understanding of how systematic strategy and quant can fit into a wider portfolio. So there's a growing number of investors who will include quant in that portfolio. And as we said before, multi-strats have proven that they can provide that high single, low double digit, uncorrelated return through the cycle. And that's been very attractive to investors, particularly going into a period where there are worries perhaps around levels of leverage and they need managers to kind of perform. There's also a question of scale as well. These large multi-strats can take the type of capital that these investors want to deploy.
John Schlegel: Yes. Now supply and demand, they're very much at work. And when there's certainly a decent amount of demand to write large checks, you need the supply to provide that in a thoughtful way.
Kumar Panja: The other interesting thing I'll mention, is investor innovation. And by that, I mean enhancing returns through leverage and customization. And that's steadily growing. So of course, hedge funds have been doing it for a while, but we've seen institutional investors utilizing tools. So again, another stat here to say 18% of investors surveyed leveraged their hedge fund portfolio. And 14% of investors surveyed use things like custom baskets to manage their exposure. So they are now mature enough to say, well, we'll let managers run their strategies. There may well be correlations. We'll dampen that at the overall portfolio level, something they didn't used to do. And I think there's been an increase in sophistication at the institutional investor level together with a flourish of products that banks like ourselves provide to those investors.
John Schlegel: More transparency on their front and ability to monitor things so they can actually take action and be more front footed.
Kumar Panja: Exactly. So John, what are your views on where you think that the markets go from here? And particularly, the question I know that you've been asked by our investors have been, what's the impact then on particular hedge fund strategies?
John Schlegel: Yeah, so I think the house view from J.P. Morgan is still, I would say, fairly constructive. So equities generally we think will go higher into year end. Bond yields may come off a little bit from the recent highs that we're seeing, but still could remain a bit more elevated. And I think what that means is for a lot of the strategies, what we're seeing is there is still exposure to the AI theme. People still are bullish on it, and that is expected to be the continued driver for the time being of the market. And so I think in general, as long as that theme continues, that should be helpful and additive to clients' portfolios. That being said, we don't think clients are overly exposed on a directional basis to the wider market. I think there is the obvious risk then, if for whatever reason, the AI theme were to reverse very significantly, that would be pretty challenging for a lot of funds. But once again, it's not because funds are taking outsized, market bets overall, but more so that they still have a preference for this theme. I think on the broader macro side, it's a little bit less clear. We think funds have been leaning more short bonds in the hedge fund space. So some, especially on the systematic side, have been making a decent amount of money, as the trends have been what they are with yields trending higher. You know I guess the thing could be, if you get the surprise of yields much lower, bonds rally really hard, especially if that were because of a more negative scenario. Usually yields can fall if there's fears of recession or downturn, right? That would generally be a very negative thing. But just to give you a stat, when we look at U.S. equity markets since 1950, whenever the S&P has been up over 10% through the end of September, only in five out of the last 30 years that that's happened has the market been down. And only one year it's been down more than 1% in the fourth quarter. So statistically, the likelihood that the market sells off very sharply in the fourth quarter is very low. I think one of the interesting things is we actually see, in the equity space at least, clients delivering more alpha when the markets are down than when they're up. And so if that pattern, persists, then even if we do get a bit of a downturn, a lot of hedge funds have been historically able to take advantage of that. Maybe on a net basis, if they're running that long, they don't actually make positive money, but they tend to protect capital decently well.
Kumar Panja: Good. Thanks, John. And I think that also aligns with our view from investors that hedge funds, for them in their portfolios, have done what they were supposed to do so far this year. And you've outlined that the market could pivot a number of different ways, but as long as it carries on in the way they're performing today, hedge funds should continue to perform positively for our investors. So overall, pleased to say, what a good story.
John Schlegel: Yes. I think it's been a very good story, not without some bumps here or there, we'll have to see where we go from here. But overall, I think there's some risk, but perhaps manageable for now. So thanks again, Kumar, for doing this with me and on a lovely London day. And yeah, it's great to see you as always.
Kumar Panja: Thanks, John. It was a lot of fun.
[Music]

How is the role of hedge funds evolving? In this episode of Making Sense, John Schlegel, head of the Global Data Assets and Alpha Group for Prime Financial Services, sits down with Kumar Panja, head of the Capital Advisory Group for EMEA, to unpack what they’re seeing across hedge funds in 2026. From regional outperformance to the strategies attracting fresh capital, they explore how institutional allocators increasingly frame hedge funds as portfolio diversifiers, not simply return enhancers. They look at the debate around leverage and crowding, as well as the growing trend toward “investor innovation” using portfolio leverage and custom baskets to manage exposures. They also touch on how current macro dynamics relate to hedge fund positioning.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesArtificial IntelligenceHow Small Business Owners Are Using AI to Help Propel Growth Oct 22, 2026ShareMarie Hunter, president of KRG Oil Company and 2016 graduate of 10,000 Small Businesses Small business owners are increasingly using AI to propel growth and develop new products, according to the Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses program’s report, The AI Economy is a Small Business Economy. 42% of the program’s graduates who responded to a survey say they use AI for financial analysis and business planning, which is more than double the rate in 2024. More than 85% of 10,000 Small Businesses graduates who responded to a survey say they use AI in some form. When Marie Hunter and her colleagues hit on a new idea earlier this year for her fuel distribution firm, she used an artificial intelligence (AI) agent to crunch the numbers.
She wanted to add solar panels to the tanks to help power their pumps and make other modifications. Rather than analyzing the cost of customizing a few fuel storage tanks for select customers, the agent delivered an ambitious blueprint for a new business.
“It came back with a plan to upsell a new product line of tanks with additional services,” says Hunter, the owner and president of KRG Oil Company, a small family firm outside Atlanta. The agent “is my force multiplier,” says Hunter.
She jokingly named the agent Billi Jean, her take on the name of one of her favorite songs. Hunter developed the agent with a colleague and originally used it to help manage emails. It also analyzes finances and prepares strategic growth plans in line with Hunter’s vision for the company.
In the last two years, small business owners such as Hunter are increasingly using AI to help shape the fortunes of their enterprises, according to a report released this month by Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses, an education and support program that has helped thousands of enterprises grow and create jobs. Hunter and the other 10,000 Small Businesses alumni interviewed in this article have been independently exploring and integrating AI into their companies.
In a survey of graduates of the program, 42% of respondents say they use AI for financial analysis and business planning, which is more than double the rate in 2024. And more than half of respondents say they use the innovation to develop or research new projects and products, according to the report, The AI Economy is a Small Business Economy.
How are small businesses using AI?
Small business owners are rapidly putting AI to work. More than 85% of survey respondents say they use AI in some form. Accounting for 43.5% of US economic output, small businesses are responsible for 61% of net new job creation, according to the US Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy. Small businesses are poised to play a significant role in the dissemination of AI.
Asahi Pompey, global head of the Office of Corporate Engagement and chair of the Urban Investment Group, says the new Goldman Sachs Small Business AI Institute is designed to support small business owners as they navigate changes brought about by AI. The Institute will help guide entrepreneurs through AI adoption and integration, positioning them to push their businesses into this new frontier.
“It is clear that AI is already changing how small business owners are making decisions, serving customers, and planning for growth,” she says. “The challenge is no longer whether small businesses will adopt AI. It is how they harness it fully and turn experimentation into lasting results.”
Interviews with graduates of Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses show just how dynamic their AI applications are, and how strategically they have designed and deployed their own AI agents.
The business owners are using AI to manage customer service at campgrounds, assist control rooms in petrochemical plants, and help design Spanish language lessons for online education. These businesses all share a common goal: using AI to get the most out of their businesses.
Using AI on the shop floor
Automation is nothing new for Bob McClure, the co-owner of McClure’s Pickles in Detroit. As the producer of more than 3 million jars of pickled cucumbers, onions, and peppers annually, the firm has long used industrial robots to label, pack, and stack its inventory. What is new is applying AI to the company’s critical functions, says McClure.
Bob McClure, co-owner of McClure’s Pickles and 2014 graduate of 10,000 Small Businesses Take food safety. Nothing is more important in his business, McClure says. The company constantly runs tests of its reporting system in the event of a food recall. In the past, employees manually entered information on the origins of the raw ingredients used to make pickles in a database, and it took 30 to 45 minutes to run a trace.
After McClure integrated professional versions of large language models (LLMs) into the firm’s enterprise resource management program, the system could show the journey the ingredients took from their source to the jar in less than two minutes. It provides an online dashboard to show where the pickles were shipped, how much of the batch is left in the warehouse, and even its pH or acidity levels.
McClure also used AI to create a maintenance application to automatically monitor production equipment, an accounting app to draft accounts payable for suppliers, and another app to review jar labels for accuracy.
Integrating LLMs into business systems has its challenges
There are challenges. Writing instructions for the LLMs takes finesse and sometimes a few “iterations” are needed to get it right. And sometimes there are bugs to work out. Because McClure, a former actor with no code training, can use natural language to engage the models, he says he does not need to license software or pay a technician. He can do it himself.
Even better, he says he can apply the AI models to multiple tasks without paying more for their services. “I think AI is uniquely suited to small business entrepreneurship because you are so strapped for resources in terms of time, people, and money,” McClure says. “I now need to hire humans to manage my AI.”
Naomi Stone, the owner and CEO of an environmental engineering consulting firm in Hermosa Beach, California, has gone a step further. She has made an AI application the cornerstone of a new venture, a company called Enso.
Can AI connect producers and consumers?
Companies already pay to dispose of their surplus materials, and Stone says Enso is designed to turn that expense into a new revenue stream. The firm uses AI to match companies holding surplus materials and industrial byproducts with buyers who can put them to work. Some byproducts, like coal ash, have long been used to strengthen building materials. Other byproducts, from packaging to equipment to manufacturing scrap, simply need the right buyer, she says.
For Stone, putting waste materials back to work advances the circular economy, a key tenet in sustainable finance. AI can facilitate matches between coal ash producers and buyers at a speed and scale Enso would have a hard time doing on its own.
“It makes matches we haven’t even thought of,” says Stone. “And the best part is it can help our clients convert waste from a cost into a new revenue stream.”
AI’s potential to illuminate unforeseen opportunities is a theme that comes up regularly among small business owners. Back in Roswell, Georgia, Marie Hunter says she has considered focusing more on her coaching business for entrepreneurs. So she gave her AI agent new instructions: to compile M&A data and prepare KRG Oil for an exit. “What does that look like, and what do I need to think about?” Hunter says. She adds that she’s ready to aspire to get her company to “the multiple it deserves.”

Survey data is based on responses from 2,473 Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses alumni who participated in the 2026 Alumni Survey, conducted by Babson College from August 10–24, 2026. The survey was sent to 14,967 program alumni.

articles.title: KPMG firms recognized as a global leader in Sustainability Consulting
articles.text:
KPMG firms have once again been recognized as a global leader in Sustainability Consulting in the Verdantix Green Quadrant: Sustainability Consulting 2026. In our view, this recognition reflects KPMG’s strength in helping organizations move beyond aspiration — integrating sustainability and ESG considerations into strategy, operations, and governance in ways that are practical, scalable, and value‑focused. As sustainability expectations continue to evolve, organizations are seeking advisory partners that can connect environmental and social priorities to financial performance, risk management, and long‑term resilience. KPMG brings together global scale, deep sector insight, and operational execution to help organizations navigate complexity, respond to stakeholder and regulatory expectations, and embed sustainability into enterprise decision‑making.

KPMG’s strengths recognized by Verdantix

“Strong emphasis on a value-driven approach to sustainability transformation. KPMG’s sustainability offering is increasingly differentiated by its focus on value-led transformation, positioning sustainability as an enabler of enterprise-wide change, rather than a standalone advisory capability. This repositioning is underpinned by investment in embedding sustainability in proprietary platforms, notably Velocity, its AI-enabled transformation framework, and KPMG Elevate, its data-driven methodology to identify, quantify and execute value opportunities across more than 400 sub-sector analytical building blocks; together, these strengthen clients’ ability to quantify value creation and preservation, and support sustainability-aligned transformational outcomes.”

“At a market level, KPMG’s work on initiatives around the financial business case for sustainability reinforces this orientation, by seeking to address structural misalignment between sustainability risks and traditional accounting and valuation models through cross-stakeholder collaboration. The emphasis on value also informs KPMG’s persistent focus on social sustainability, illustrated by its work with island nations such as Barbados to support inclusive climate resilience strategies.”

“Balanced scale and granularity in sustainability delivery. KPMG is best-suited to organizations seeking to evaluate sustainability initiatives through a clear return on investment (ROI) lens, particularly where the commercial rationale is still emerging or contested. The firm combines the scale required to support large, complex organizations with the operational granularity needed to translate ambition into implementable change. As such, KPMG is a strong fit for both large and smaller businesses at varyiith broader operational and financial objectives.”

We are proud of the commitment KPMG firms have demonstrated in building a leading ESG team focused on helping clients harness the power of ESG to transform their business. KPMG firms’ ESG solutions are both holistic and practical, and designed to help organizations turn their ESG aspirations into action. Through industry-leading knowledge, data-driven technology and global alliances, KPMG’s experience across critical ESG issues means our professionals can assist clients in creating the right roadmap for their ESG journey and execute on that plan.According to the report, "Large firms at various levels of ESG maturity, looking for integrated sustainability solutions, should approach KPMG, to profit from its synergistic approach to sustainability. KPMG is also well-suited to firms that require a strategy lens for climate, carbon, circular economy, and water- and nature-related reporting and disclosures. In addition, businesses should contemplate using KPMG’s services for projects involving the testing of governance models for ESG-relevant inadequacies, and to benefit from the provider’s capabilities in anticipating and managing ESG-related reputational risks, and threats from potential litigation and shareholder activism.”

In my conversations with clients, leaders are asking how sustainability translates into real business value. Verdantix’s recognition reflects that KPMG professionals know how – and we deliver. By combining data, technology, and our multidisciplinary strengths, we’re helping deliver outcomes that build trust and drive performance.

Rob Fisher

Global Head of Advisory, KPMG International and Advisory, Vice Chair,

KPMG in the US

This recognition validates our focus on value led transformation, leading to the strategic reporting that stakeholders seek. We’re helping clients embed sustainability directly into how they define value and make critical business decisions.

Simon Weaver

Global ESG Advisory Lead,

KPMG International

KPMG firms work with organizations across industries to help embed sustainability and ESG into enterprise strategy, transformation programs, and performance management. KPMG’s approach connects sustainability initiatives to measurable outcomes — supporting improved decision‑making, enhanced resilience, and long‑term value creation.From strategy and transformation through execution, measurement, and reporting, KPMG professionals help organizations advance sustainability priorities while maintaining focus on commercial objectives and operational realities.

articles.title: Equities update - Week 43 - October 23 2026
articles.text: Equities update - October 23rd 20268 min readFinanceDataWeek 43 brought further volatility to the AI infrastructure trade as financing constraints and concerns over eventual overbuilding weighed on sentiment despite strong revenue growth and constructive demand forecasts. SpaceX reported robust growth, Western Digital cited demand visibility through 2030–31 across its largest customers, and Meta continued advancing its Muse AI rollout alongside substantial infrastructure investment. However, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang highlighted that capital availability is constraining neocloud expansion even as demand remains strong. This captures the central tension: accelerating demand can support infrastructure investment, but shareholder returns still depend on financing costs, delivery schedules and the price paid to build capacity. Elsewhere, demand for Treasuries pulled the US 10-year yield below 5% on the week, however, sharp upside moves in the VIX and MOVE indices reflected uncertainty across both equity and bond markets. Bitcoin and select crypto-native equities proved more resilient, with Bitcoin unchanged over the week. Corporate progress also remained constructive, Mastercard’s expanding stablecoin and agent-payment capabilities, alongside Coinbase’s partnership with Thunes, demonstrated continued investment in the distribution and services needed to turn digital-asset activity into practical financial applications.Week 43 Key Developments in Blockchain Equities:Index Performance: Index Performance: The Index declined 1.6% over the week, while Bitcoin was unchanged, against a backdrop of elevated energy prices, uncertainty over monetary tightening and renewed scrutiny of AI investment returns. The US economic calendar was relatively light this week, although weekly labour-market data remained resilient, with initial unemployment claims falling by 6,000 to 194,000, providing little evidence of an acceleration in layoffs. Expectations increasingly centred on an October Fed pause followed by a December hike; a Reuters poll found that 94 of 100 economists expected unchanged rates at the 27–28 October meeting, while all anticipated an increase in December. Nevertheless, Treasuries rallied as weakness in technology shares encouraged demand for safer assets, pulling the 10-year yield below 5% on Thursday. Gold’s weaker performance over the week highlighted the uneven response across traditional safe-haven assets, underscoring the complexity of the current market environment.Block Index Key Movers: 7-day top performers: Sony Group (+5.9%), CME Group (+5.7%), Nextera Energy (+3.7%) 7-day worst performers: Cipher Digital (-17.1%), Riot Platforms (-16.8%), Galaxy Digital (-16.2%) Mastercard’s developments this month highlight how established payment networks can capture value from stablecoin adoption while providing resilience within BLOCK amid equity market volatility - Mastercard has been a standout performer, gaining approximately 15% month-to-date and reaching new all-time highs. The company has made meaningful progress in developing its stablecoin capabilities this year, particularly through its acquisition of BVNK. This week, it launched Stablecoin Security, initially with Borderless.xyz and Keyrails, extending fraud and sanctions screening across traditional and blockchain payment flows. It also opened early access to Agent Pay for Machines, following pilots involving Coinbase, Base, Cloudflare and BVNK, allowing AI agents to purchase digital services within approved budgets and permissions.In our view, the significance lies in Mastercard broadening the services it provides around the movement of money. Banks and businesses adopting stablecoins still require conversion, merchant acceptance, local payouts and risk controls. Bringing these capabilities together could strengthen customer relationships and create opportunities to generate revenue across several stages of a payment. This builds on an established services franchise: value-added services and solutions revenue grew 18% on a currency-neutral basis in Q2, compared with 8% for the payment network. Services growth will therefore be a key metric to watch when Mastercard reports its Q3 results next week. The agent-payments initiative offers another potential avenue for growth, extending Mastercard’s spending controls and payment authorisation capabilities to software that increasingly transacts independently.For BLOCK, Mastercard combines an established earnings base with further growth opportunities in digital payments. Its strong performance also highlights the diversification available within blockchain equities as investors place greater scrutiny on the financing requirements of AI infrastructure.Earnings Recap – Key Holdings:CME Group – PositiveMeta Platforms, Nextera Energy - MixedOther news - Index constituents:Coinbase and Thunes announced a partnership on 19 October combining Coinbase’s stablecoin infrastructure with Thunes’ connections to local payment systems, bank accounts and mobile wallets. The opportunity lies in completing the payment journey: a faster blockchain transfer has limited practical value if the recipient cannot readily receive and use the money locally. Thunes could help Coinbase address this constraint across supplier payments, gig-worker payouts and remittances, extending its infrastructure business beyond exchange trading.Circle and Proof announced a collaboration on 19 October demonstrating how AI agents can present verified identity credentials and make USDC payments from a Circle Agent Wallet. The demonstration addresses a practical obstacle to agent-led commerce: establishing who authorised a purchase and retaining evidence if it is disputed.SBI VC Trade and SBI XDC Network APAC announced an agreement with South Korea’s Shinhan Card on 21 October to explore blockchain-based payments. Planned work includes testing how yen-denominated stablecoins could connect with physical merchant payments, alongside potential cross-border trade settlement. The significance is the combination of SBI’s digital-asset capabilities with established merchant-payment infrastructure, potentially addressing acceptance and conversion barriers simultaneously.Strategy’s 19 October disclosure showed purchases of 267 BTC for US$22.1m,. Taking holdings to 848,517 BTC, alongside US$93.1m of STRC repurchases. It increased its preferred-securities repurchase authorisation to US$3bn, with 1.16bn remaining. As of 18 October, its USD Reserve was US$4.83bn, with a separate US$447.3m of USD Cash.Other news – Non - Index constituents:OKXICE, the joint venture between OKX and NYSE owner ICE, filed with the SEC for a platform offering 24/7 tokenised US-stock trading. Its proposed structure uses permissioned Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on XLayer, with securities traded against supported payment stablecoins. This brings exchange infrastructure into closer competition with crypto-native trading platforms and creates another potential source of stablecoin settlement demand.Securitize launched tokenised exposure to 12 US stocks, initially on Solana, with USDC settlement. Each token is backed by a share and represents a security entitlement, with applicable economic and voting rights; holders become registered shareholders only if they convert where available. Initial trading uses its broker-dealer platform during extended hours.OCBC and Ant International launched a ‘tokenised-deposit’ solution on 7 October enabling 24/7 movement of SGD- and USD-denominated deposits between Ant’s entities in Singapore and Malaysia through WhaleRTP. The practical benefit is greater flexibility in deploying working capital outside banking cut-off times, alongside improved reconciliation. This is also relevant to the competitive landscape: banks are developing blockchain payment capabilities while retaining customer funds as commercial-bank deposits, giving corporate treasurers an alternative to transferring liquidity into stablecoins. Separately, HSBC and Ant International expanded tokenised treasury activity into the Middle East, following pilot transactions involving UAE-dirham transfers and cross-border dollar payments.Published onOct 23rd, 2026WritersSatish PatelInvestment AnalystCo-manages the Invesco CoinShares Global Blockchain ETF with expertise in payments and technology.Alex SchmidtIndex Fund ManagerManages the first and largest fund offering exposure to listed blockchain companies.

articles.title: More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales
articles.text:
More than a change of address: Reflections from previous part VIII transfers − speech by Manuel Sales

Given at Association of Financial Mutuals Annual Conference 2026

Published on
05 October 2026

Speech
Opening remarks
Thank you for inviting me to speak today.
Having been in my role for a few months, I have been reflecting on the insights it has given me into how firms operate. One thing that has stood out about mutuals is not just that they are owned by their members, but how that ownership shapes the decisions they make. We can see this in the important role they play in serving parts of the market that may otherwise be underserved.
Against this background, you can understand why the Mutuals Landscape Report sets out our ambition to support the sector’s sustainable long-term growth. What that means will differ from one mutual to another. Many mutuals will continue to operate sustainably. Some will grow organically, while others may pursue acquisitions.
For some mutuals, the strategic challenge is different. They have told us that their current business models may not be sustainable over the longer term. The reasons for this include high levels of competition, keeping pace with technological change, and responding to rapidly-changing economic pressures. Some of these firms are responding by adapting their strategies and exploring new opportunities. Others are considering whether a solvent exit, including through transferring some or all of their business to another firm, may provide the best outcome for their members.
Where the firm being acquired is a friendly society, the transaction will take place through the Part VIII transfer process under the Friendly Societies Act 1992, with the PRA being ultimately responsible for deciding whether a transfer should proceed. While that process is grounded in legislation, we heard feedback that firms would benefit from having a clearer understanding of both the process itself and the factors that inform our decisions. In the Mutuals Landscape Report, we committed to providing more clarity, and CP12/26 (the CP) fulfils that promise. It sets out proposals intended to make our approach clearer and gives firms a more structured sequence of steps to follow. And alongside that, we are also improving the way we manage these transactions internally.
With these initiatives, we aim to promote a dynamic market and support sustainable growth of the mutuals sector.
But the PRA is not the only one working to make this process more efficient. We have also observedfootnote [1] practical approaches developed by firms to improve how these transactions are managed. Today, I want to provide an overview of the Part VIII process. As I do so, I will weave practical insights on how we have seen firms successfully navigate that process, so that others can benefit from the experience of previous transactions.
Reflections from a recent mover
Before turning to those insights, let me take a step back and explain why the process matters.
A Part VIII transfer can offer significant strategic benefits, such as realising economies of scale, improving service standards, and becoming more resilient. All of these improve outcomes for members. But it also requires firms to commit considerable time and resources, with the costs ultimately borne by members. At the PRA, we are very conscious that if a transfer cannot be confirmed, those costs may still have been incurred without the expected benefits being realised. That’s why we work with firms to try to help them build the evidence needed to demonstrate that the legislative requirements have been met.
Meeting those requirements is not just about ticking a legal box. Members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, to protect their interests.
So, how should firms approach the Part VIII process?
While no analogy can fully capture the significance of a Part VIII transfer, particularly for mutuals with long histories and strong member communities, it may be helpful in illustrating the process itself, especially for those who are less familiar with Part VIII transfers. The decisions surrounding a transfer are often complex and significant. But when it comes to the process, it has some parallels with moving house. Driving the moving van into your new driveway may feel like the culmination of the journey, but a successful move depends on everything that happened beforehand. You need to understand why you are moving, weigh up the options, complete the necessary checks, and prepare carefully for what follows.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer.
As the slide shows, we have split that journey into five parts. Let me take each in turn.

Chart 1: Part VIII Transfer Process

Part A: Planning and preparation
Let me start with planning and preparation.
Every house move begins with a reason for moving. When my wife and I bought our home, we spent as much time discussing why we wanted to move as we spent choosing the house. Did we need more space? Or a shorter commute? Once we were clear about our objectives, many of the decisions that followed became easier.
A1: Intention to transfer, A4: Details of transfer plans
When similar questions are considered in the context of a Part VIII transfer, firms may have many avenues to explore. To help firms navigate these factors, the CP highlights the matters the PRA is likely to focus on early in the process, including members' interests.
Of course, firms will generally pursue a transfer because they believe it will deliver better outcomes for members. However, those benefits may not be shared equally between all members, and they may emerge at different times. It is possible that in some circumstances, particular groups of members could be worse off. The key question then is whether the transfer is in the interests of the members of each friendly society participating in the transfer.
Part of answering that question comes from how the benefits are expected to arise. Where a proposal relies on cost savings, operational changes, or integration programmes, those assumptions help explain how the combined business is expected to operate after the transfer. They can provide an important indication of whether there is a credible strategy and a realistic plan to deliver the expected benefits to members.
We have also found it helpful to consider the proposal from another perspective: in what circumstances might some members be worse off? Firms often undertake careful analysis of that question to understand whether potentially adverse impacts have been appropriately considered.
We can work with you as you develop your thinking in this area, which will help with later stages of the transfer. For example, some benefits may depend on integrating the two firms and could take several years to emerge. Whilst there are different ways to ensure that members will be protected in the meantime, the PRA can work with firms to establish what evidence could help show that the legal test has been met. These discussions could inform the transfer documentation, actuarial analysis, and communications with members.
A2: Preparations, updating rules, and applying for permission
Moving on to the preparations step, we have seen firms take a careful and considered approach to the practical aspects of the process. That includes considering whether the acquirer has the necessary regulatory permissions. This matters because permissions do not transfer with the business.
As an extra check, some firms have used the FCA’s register to compare the transferring society’s permission with the acquirer’s permission. This has allowed the acquirer to confirm whether it has identified and addressed any gaps in its permission.
This has also helped firms explain why a permission will no longer be required to cover specific regulated activities and, in doing so, show that the relevant statutory test has been met. These checks may appear relatively small. But when carried out early, they help the wider process run more efficiently.
A3: Considerations of overseas members and regulators
Turning to overseas members, this relates to one of the statutory tests, where the PRA must assess whether there is a substantial risk that the acquirer will be unable legally to carry on the business being transferred. This is usually relatively straightforward for members in the UK, but firms have found it more challenging for members based overseas.
Much of that work begins with a simple question: where are your members based? Maintaining up-to-date member records has helped firms with this work. There are other useful ways of checking those records. Some firms may find it helpful to consider payments to and from non-UK bank accounts to identify any other overseas members.
With that information in hand, firms can consider their overseas members in the context of the legal test and develop a reasoned explanation of why the legal test is met. There is a range of different forms of evidence to consider, from local legal advice to the relevant EIOPA recommendationfootnote [2]. The CP highlights engagement with overseas regulators, which firms may find to be a practical and cost-effective way of exploring the position.
While these steps should help, we recognise that firms continue to face challenges in this area. Indeed, we engaged with the Law Commission on the issue ahead of its recently published proposals. At our recent roundtablefootnote [3], firms also suggested ways in which the PRA could help firms with the overseas member part of the process. We are considering if we can further clarify what information we might need from firms in order for the PRA to assess the legal test under the existing legislation. We will, of course, consider this feedback alongside any responses we receive to the CP.
A5: PRA’s approach to special resolution: consent for Part VIII transfers
Let me turn to the final part of planning and preparation: what many firms call the dispensation process. This is where the acquiring society can seek the PRA's consent for the transfer to be approved by its board, rather than through a special resolution voted on by its members.
Giving the acquirer’s members the opportunity to vote is an important safeguard, so it is not a requirement the PRA will dispense with lightly. But we also recognise that holding a vote comes at a cost, which is ultimately borne by members.
In the past, firms have told us that this is one of the less predictable parts of the process, so we have added more clarity on our approach in the CP. It provides some reference points for how the PRA is likely to consider whether to consent to a dispensation. One of these is that firms will also need to show that the transfer is in the interests of the acquirer’s members and that there are no factors likely to lead a material number of them to vote against it. Firms are likely to benefit from discussing this with their transfer partner and considering this point together.
For example, that collaboration may bring to light a history of tension between the societies that could influence how members would vote if they were given the opportunity. Factors like this don’t necessarily mean that consent couldn’t be granted. But open discussions on such matters can help the PRA understand the position more quickly and reduce the need for further questions.
Part B: Recording and analysing the transfer
Let me move on to recording and analysing the transfer.
Once my family had decided which house to buy, our attention turned to the practicalities. The paperwork began, surveys were commissioned and the important decisions had to be documented.
The same is true of a Part VIII transfer. Once firms have developed their proposal, the focus shifts to documenting the terms of the transfer and analysing its effects.
B1: Instrument of Transfer
Once firms are clear about the purpose and structure of the transaction, that understanding must be captured in the Instrument of Transfer. Producing the Instrument is a statutory requirement, but it can also provide important protections for the members of both firms.
The Instrument can cover a wide range of matters, from service standards to membership rights. We have seen firms benefit from bringing together legal, risk, and actuarial specialists to develop it. It has also helped firms consider not only what is needed to give effect to the transfer, but what additional protections could be provided to members, both now and over the long-term.
Those protections will depend on the circumstances of each transfer. We have seen firms consider important safeguards for the management of transferred funds, appropriate governance arrangements, and commitments about the future treatment of policyholders.
Where with-profits policies are involved, firms have found it helpful to specify the fund to which those policies will be allocated and how expenses will be apportioned. They have also considered what support may be available from other funds, particularly where this could affect the receiving fund’s investment strategy. Setting out these details in the draft Instrument can then provide a clear basis for the actuarial analysis supporting the transfer.
B2: Internal actuarial reports, B3: Independent actuary report and supplementary report(s)
The actuarial analysis is an important part of the process. Internal actuarial reports help boards and regulators understand how a proposed transfer is expected to affect members. Clear and balanced reports can also provide a strong foundation for communications with members, particularly where outcomes are uncertain or depend on judgement. The more useful reports explain the assumptions, evidence, and reasoning behind the conclusions they reach.
In our experience, the more complete internal actuarial reports consider how members are expected to be affected before the transfer, immediately after the transfer, as well as after any integration of the two businesses. This helps all of us – including members – understand both the destination and the journey to get there.
The firms’ own analysis is important. However, in some cases, the process also requires an independent perspective. Much as an independent surveyor provides an objective assessment when someone is purchasing a property, the Independent Actuary provides independent scrutiny of the firms’ analysis. The CP provides greater clarity on when we are likely to require a report from an Independent Actuary. We hope this will help firms better understand the likely costs of a transfer.
Where an Independent Actuary provides a report, the legislation requires it to address the likely effects of the transfer on members who are long-term policyholders. We have found that reports are most useful when they explain both the positive and adverse effects, how those effects may differ between groups of policyholders, and the basis for any conclusions about materiality. Of course, this balanced analysis helps members understand the proposal. But it also supports the PRA’s assessment of whether the transfer is in members’ interests, alongside the FCA’s consideration of fairness.
As an aside, we have found that it is often a good idea for firms to also consider any FCA requirements that apply to the transaction (for example, if the FCA's reattribution rules for with-profits business apply).
There is also an important relationship between the internal actuarial reports and the Independent Actuary’s report. If an internal report contains material information that is not reflected in the summary of the Independent Actuary’s report included in communications sent to members, firms will need to consider whether members have received all the information they need to understand the proposal and make an informed decision. This is one of the statutory tests the PRA must assess. In previous transfers, we have worked with firms to understand how they have met it.
Even where an Independent Actuary is not appointed, another form of independent review may still be valuable. We have seen firms benefit from independent peer review of their internal actuarial analysis and key judgements. This can strengthen the overall assessment and give members greater confidence in the analysis, particularly where they are considering whether to make representations about the proposed transfer.
Part C: Member engagement and member vote(s)
Having considered the key documents supporting a transfer, the next stage is to translate them into communications that members can understand and engage with.
When my family moved house, it wasn’t enough for me to know the plan. Everyone needed to understand what was happening, why it was happening and what it means for them (or, in our case, who was getting the biggest bedroom). Member engagement is similar. The technical analysis may be robust, but it only serves its purpose if members can understand what the transfer means for them.
C1: Member engagement: general approach, C2: Member engagement: Schedule 15 statement, C3: Resolutions
Member communications play an important role in informing how members vote. So, as you would expect, the FCA considers them through the lens of the Consumer Duty, with a focus on ensuring that they are clear and easy to understand. What makes the Part VIII transfer process slightly different is that the PRA also has a statutory role in reviewing one of the key communications sent to members: the Schedule 15 statement.
The CP provides more details on what the PRA considers as part of that review. I want to reflect on some practical approaches that we have seen work well in previous transfers.
The more developed Schedule 15 statements are those that clearly explain what the transfer means for members. They present the key considerations fairly and help members reach their own view. One approach that could work well is testing communications before they are finalised. We have read documents that include all the relevant technical details, but it is not always clear whether these messages are framed in the best way for members to fully understand them. To ensure that the proposed messages can be understood, it may be helpful to run the proposed communications past a colleague who has not been involved in the transfer or seek feedback from a small group of members.
We have also seen the value of careful and balanced drafting. The stronger summaries of the Independent Actuary’s conclusions tend to be those that faithfully reflect the full report while focusing on the matters most relevant to members’ decisions.
Of course, even the clearest communication is only effective if it reaches the people for whom it is intended. The legislation requires the Schedule 15 statement to be sent to all eligible voting members. Where firms have faced challenges contacting members, we have seen a range of practical approaches, including tracing exercises, updating records, using alternative contact methods, and contacting members directly to confirm their details. Firms have also used press notices and other engagement channels to raise awareness of the transfer and the voting process. In some cases, firms have supplemented this with dedicated webpages containing information about the transfer.
Although I have focused on the Schedule 15 statement, we have seen firms engage with their members in different ways. This includes with letters, frequently asked questions, presentations, webinars, and online material. The aim is to help members understand the proposed transfer and give them a genuine opportunity to engage with the proposal before casting their vote. Where members are effectively engaged, it helps firms address issues and reduce the likelihood of unexpected representations arising later in the transfer process.
Part D: Formal application, public notices, and representations
When buying a house, arguably the most important stage is the period leading up to the exchange of contracts. During that stage, surveyors, solicitors, mortgage brokers, and banks can all raise questions, identify risks or challenge assumptions underlying the proposed purchase.
D1: Formal notice of the application
The formal notice of the application plays an important role in the period leading up to the transaction, bringing it to the attention of interested parties and ensuring that those affected have an opportunity to engage with the process.
Firms will submit the formal notice after the member vote. So, whilst the progression of these tasks remains subject to member approval, there is preparatory work we can do ahead of that. In previous transfers, firms have provided draft notices for our review.
The PRA will also direct firms to publish the notice in the London, Edinburgh, or Belfast Gazettes as well as other newspapers where appropriate. However, firms can suggest which Gazette(s) and newspapers they feel would be the most appropriate.
D2: Approach to representations, D3: Representations Hearing
Once the formal notice has been published, the representations period begins. It gives members and other stakeholders an opportunity to raise concerns about the transfer.
But the representations process is about more than formal representations submitted directly to the PRA. Firms also consider whether concerns, complaints, or queries received through their own channels raise issues that are similar in nature to a formal representation. These interactions can provide valuable insight into the matters that are most important to members.
Part E: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s) and related processes
The final stage of buying a house is exchanging contracts and moving into the property. By that point, much of the hard work has already been done. The legal issues have been addressed and the financing agreed. What remains is to finalise the purchase arrangements. The same principle applies to the final stage of a Part VIII transfer.
E1: Preparations for the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s), E2: Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
The Preclusion Grounds Analysis sits at the heart of this stage. It explains why none of the statutory grounds that would prevent the PRA from confirming the transfer have been met. The stronger submissions tend to be balanced and leverage the evidence already generated throughout the transfer process and present it in a thorough and structured way.
Let me give you an example. When looking at the solvency ground, some firms carefully consider whether the acquiring society will maintain an adequate margin of solvency after the transfer. They bring together the evidence supporting that conclusion, such as post-transfer financial projections, actuarial analysis, audited financial information, and any material changes since the latest valuation date.
We have seen a similar approach taken when considering whether the members’ vote was representative. Firms’ analysis usually explains why the requirements of the legislation and the relevant society rules have been met. The more developed analyses also consider factors such as how voting turnout compares with previous member votes and whether the outcome would have changed under different assumptions. For example, where some members could not be traced despite reasonable efforts being made to contact them, firms could consider whether the outcome of the member vote would have been different if those members had voted against the transfer.
Perhaps the area where we have seen the greatest variation is the assessment of whether the proposed transfer is in the interests of the members of both societies. The more developed analyses bring together actuarial, risk, and legal evidence to consider factors such as benefit security, benefit expectations, service standards, and membership rights. They also identify situations in which some members may be disadvantaged and explain how those risks have been assessed and mitigated.
In considering firms’ post-transfer target operating models, we have taken a proportionate approach, with discussions often centred on three related questions.

How will the enlarged business operate immediately after the transfer?
What is the target operating model?
How does the firm intend to move from one to the other?

E3: The PRA’s decision, E4: Processes after the Confirmation Assessment Meeting(s)
After the PRA has reached its decision, it is not the end of the journey. There are a few procedural steps left including issuing the decision notice and registering the Instrument of Transfer.
Firms will also continue implementing aspects of their target operating model after the transfer has completed. Boards should continue to satisfy themselves that members are seeing the expected benefits from the transfer.
Closing remarks
I appreciate that this statutory process may feel a long and complex journey. But members rely on the safeguards built into the Part VIII process, including scrutiny by the PRA and FCA, so it’s right that we approach the statutory requirements with care.
At the same time, we recognise that members ultimately benefit from an efficient process. CP12/26 sets out our proposals to make our approach clearer, more transparent, and easier to navigate. Your engagement has already informed those proposals, and I would encourage you to respond to the consultation so that we can continue refining our approach together.
I don’t want to close without recognising the important work being undertaken by the Law Commission to modernise the legislative framework for friendly societies. We have engaged with the Law Commission as it has developed its final report and draft bill Opens in a new window. Should any legislative changes be made, the PRA stands ready to update its approach and guidance as necessary.
I hope that what I’ve shared today will highlight that a successful transfer is not simply about completing a transaction or changing an address. It’s about finding the right long-term home for a friendly society’s members.
I am grateful to Hannah-Kousar Rashid for preparing these remarks. I am also grateful to Abi Batchelor, Alex Tapp, Giles Woodruff, Nozipho Gazi, Robert Kipling, Robyn Dwyer, Sanjeev Chandran, and Wayne Snow for their support and comments.

The observations shared in this speech are based on a range of firms and transfers at different times. They are illustrative of the general approach taken. Some details may have been changed or combined from different transfers to ensure confidentiality. As such, the information included should not be considered attributable to any one firm or transfer.
