articles.title: Harnessing the wind: A strategy for HBCU campus and community development | Brookings
articles.text:
Research

Harnessing the wind: A strategy for HBCU campus and community development

Andre M. Perry and

Andre M. Perry

Senior Fellow
- Brookings Metro,

Director
- Center for Community Uplift

Yonina Gray

Yonina Gray

Vice President
- Commercial Real Estate Banking

October 28, 2026

Photo credit: Sharkshock / Shutterstock.com

36 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Introduction
In September 2022, Brookings published “A call to action for HBCU investment,” which examined approaches for increasing access to investment capital for campus and community development for historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs). Drawing from structured conversations with HBCU executives, bankers, and development and philanthropy professionals, the report identified three needs: 1) greater access to capital markets; 2) a clearly articulated value proposition that conveys the returns HBCUs generate for students, communities, and society; and 3) institutional capacity-building.
That report ended with a call to action for lenders, funders, and HBCU leaders to build the trust and familiarity that segregation and discrimination had foreclosed; to develop a shared, HBCU-driven theory of change that maximizes their collective strength; to translate the social and knowledge capital HBCUs hold into forms that capital markets recognize; to collaborate across sectors in pursuit of thought leadership exchange and public-private partnerships; to expand revenue support for students through the economic and community development surrounding their campuses; and to explore collective approaches to financing that draw on the shared strength of the nation’s 100-plus HBCUs rather than the balance sheet of any one campus.
As a follow-up to that report, over the course of the past year, Brookings’ Center for Community Uplift convened HBCU presidents, senior administrators, capital providers, developers, and policymakers in a structured listening process to identify how HBCUs are operationalizing aspects of the 2022 call to action to craft a broader blueprint for policy action.
Five central themes emerged from these listening sessions and analysis:

The primary constraint is capital design—the structures, timelines, and underwriting rules that determine how capital reaches institutions—not institutional vision or leadership.
Land is an asset only in combination with site control and trusted partners, particularly developers.
Institutional capacity is systematically misread and underwritten accordingly.
Campus and community futures are inseparable, and institutions are underwritten as though they were not.
HBCU leaders are ready to move beyond pilot projects and create structures built to last.

This work unfolds at a moment of heightened constraint surrounding HBCUs. Place-based and equity-oriented investment frameworks face renewed legal and political challenges. Recent executive actions reshaping federal posture on diversity programs—alongside legal pressure on race-conscious philanthropy and grantmaking—have introduced hesitation across philanthropic and private capital markets at precisely the moment when HBCUs are advancing the kind of anchor-driven projects this report documents. These conditions make existing gaps in development finance more consequential, stalling otherwise viable HBCU-led projects.
This report attempts to move beyond diagnosis to outline institutional responses that can be used to build a roadmap for reform. It identifies near-term interventions—de-risking mechanisms, coordinated capital strategies, and targeted policy adjustments—that can unlock campus and community development projects and accelerate investable pipelines. It also advances longer-term structural reforms aimed at normalizing HBCUs’ participation in development finance, public investment programs, and regional growth strategies.

Background on HBCUs
Though they represent just 3% of the nation’s four-year nonprofit colleges and universities, HBCUs enroll 10% of all Black college students, and award 15% of all bachelor’s degrees as well as 19% of all STEM bachelor’s degrees earned by Black graduates.
But HBCUs’ economic footprint extends well beyond the campus gate. According to the United Negro College Fund’s (UNCF) 2024 economic impact report, HBCUs generate $16.5 billion in direct economic impact annually and support more than 136,000 jobs; measured by job creation, the nation’s HBCUs would rank among the top 50 companies on the Fortune 500. The HBCU graduating class of 2021 alone can expect $146 billion in work-life earnings—57% more than they could expect without their degrees. Moreover, HBCUs have produced some of the most impactful individuals in our nation’s history, including Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall, civil rights leader Martin Luther King, Jr., and Vice President Kamala Harris.
Despite these impacts, HBCUs have been underfunded for decades. Between 1987 and 2020, 16 of 19 historically Black land-grant universities were underfunded by their states by an estimated $12.6 billion, according to a 2023 joint letter from the secretaries of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and Department of Education.
For decades, public policy and capital markets have treated HBCUs the same as highly endowed, predominantly white institutions (PWIs). For instance, historic discrimination is not generally accounted for in underwriting. As a result, HBCUs pay roughly 14% higher underwriting fees on tax-exempt bonds than comparable PWIs—a gap that persists even when comparing AAA-rated HBCUs to AAA-rated PWIs (and this gap grows three times larger in Deep South states). Because credit ratings reward accumulated wealth and financial performance, past and present discrimination create a ratings gap.
The wealth gap between these institutions mimics the racial wealth gap between families, in which the average white family possesses six times the wealth of the average Black family. Based on data from the National Association of College and University Business Officers (NACUBO), the 10 largest HBCU endowments hold a combined $2.4 billion, while the 10 largest PWI endowments hold a combined $340 billion—a difference of more than 140 to 1.
Across the country, Black wealth is increasing, but so is the racial wealth gap. HBCU endowments have followed a similar course: According to HBCU Money, HBCU endowments have grown meaningfully in recent years. Yet while 169 PWIs maintain endowments above $1 billion, Howard University only just became the first HBCU to surpass that mark, and four more HBCUs crossed the $100 million threshold. Spelman College’s endowment is over $500 million, reflecting sustained fundraising momentum and disciplined institutional management.
Public HBCUs hold roughly one-third the endowment per student of comparable public institutions. HBCUs comprised 1.4% of the 678 institutions reporting to NACUBO in Fiscal Year 2025, but held just 0.3% of the $953.7 billion in reported endowment assets. Meanwhile, the 32 PWIs with endowments above $5 billion control 57.4% of all reported endowment wealth. This pattern mirrors the broader national racial wealth gap: growth at the top for a few, concentrated wealth elsewhere, and a structural chasm that individual institutional success cannot alone close.
HBCU wealth levels are lower than PWI wealth levels, but the demands that families, communities, and society place on them are the same as other postsecondary institutions. Like other postsecondary institutions, HBCUs can leverage specialized degree programs and students to support local economies, and are often the largest employers in their region. Students, faculty, and visitors desire attractive retail, housing, and hospitality markets; their spending, along with institutional contracting, help sustain surrounding communities. HBCUs provide entertainment through athletics and arts programing, and educate their communities beyond tuition-paying students with their libraries, museums, and lectures. Colleges shape the built environment and local economies with their campus footprints, housing developments, and commercial investment.
Yet about half of the nation’s 100-plus HBCUs are in majority-Black cities where housing and commercial real estate are devalued. Many sit in communities that have suffered from decades of public disinvestment. When HBCUs are undervalued—including their land, infrastructure, workforce pipelines, and deep community ties—communities go underserved. They remain structurally undercapitalized and largely excluded from the policymaking and investment frameworks that shape campus, community, and regional development at scale. But despite these challenges, HBCUs continue to deliver returns in social mobility, economic resilience, and civic leadership.
This is the paradox at the heart of this report. HBCUs are proven engines of mobility, employment, and community wealth, yet the systems that price risk, allocate capital, and set development priorities treat them as marginal—restricting access to much-needed resources for campus and community development. This problem cannot be reduced simply to institutional performance; these institutions operate within a system of investment frameworks that were never designed to recognize the unique value HBCUs create. Closing that gap requires more than celebrating individual campus successes or expanding one-time philanthropic gifts. It requires rethinking how public policy and capital markets see these institutions in the first place: not as charitable causes, but as undervalued assets generating returns to students, communities, and regional economies despite systemic inequities.
That reframing raises a broader question this report sets out to address: What would it mean to treat HBCU campus and community development as a policy and investment priority?

Listening to the field
This report examines how HBCU leaders and their partners are operationalizing aspects of the 2022 call to action in service of policy and capital reforms needed to scale HBCUs’ community development efforts. It draws on a yearlong engagement process between May 2025 and April 2026 structured around four convenings, a two-day site visit to Wiley University, standardized case study intakes from four institutions selected for institutional variation (Wiley University, Morgan State University, Tuskegee University/East Chop Capital, and the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff), and supplementary individual consultations.
Across these engagements, the Center for Community Uplift engaged senior leaders from 12 HBCUs spanning the public, private, land-grant, urban, and rural categories of the field, alongside developers, capital providers, philanthropic partners, and policy thinkers from five additional organizations. (A complete list of participating institutions appears in Appendix B.) A panel session at the UNCF Unite summit in July 2025 used a live audience-response survey to capture anonymous reflections from seven additional HBCU leaders on the same themes explored in our convenings. Findings were developed through cross-case synthesis of these inputs.
Named quotations reflect on-the-record remarks recorded with participant consent. The full methodology, including case selection criteria, facilitation protocols, and limitations, appears in Appendix A.

Findings: What we heard
Our analysis yielded five themes that held across institutional types, geographies, and stakeholder categories. First, the primary constraint on HBCU campus and community development is not institutional vision or leadership, but capital design—the architecture of how money is structured and delivered. Capital design includes the terms, timelines, risk allocations, eligibility rules, and underwriting standards that determine who can access capital and on what conditions. Second, land functions as an asset only in combination with site control and partners the surrounding community trusts. Third, institutional capacity is systematically misread by funders and lenders, and underwritten accordingly. Fourth, campus and community futures are inseparable, though institutions are financed as if they were not. Fifth, the field is ready to move beyond pilots and toward durable platforms and permanent capital.
These themes are mutually reinforcing rather than independent: capital design determines whether land assets can be activated; underwriting practices that misread capacity restrict the capital available for community-integrated strategies; and the episodic character of the resulting investment prevents institutions from accumulating the track record that would correct the misreading. The following sections explore each theme, illustrated with representative quotations from convening participants and supported by evidence drawn from the case study institutions. Full case study profiles appear in Appendix B.
Theme #1: The constraint is capital design, not vision or leadership
Across every convening and case study, institutional leaders articulated specific plans for housing, mixed-use development, innovation districts, and community-serving infrastructure. What varied was not the presence of vision, but the availability of capital structured to match institutional time horizons, balance sheets, and public missions.
The case evidence illustrates the pattern at every scale. Morgan State University has secured redesignation as Maryland’s preeminent public urban research university and stood up eight specialized research centers backed by recurring state appropriations. Notably, the strategy of redesignation preceded the capital. Recalling his approach to the state legislature, President David K. Wilson explained, “I didn’t ask anyone for any money. I just wanted the designation at that time.”
The designation established the institutional argument; the appropriations, now $22 million annually supporting 70 new tenure-track faculty, followed it. This sequence matters because it inverts the assumption embedded in most underwriting: When HBCU leadership executes sophisticated, multi-year strategy, capital follows. The constraint was never the quality of the strategy.
Yet even Morgan State University’s scale does not exempt it from the structural gap. Describing the financing of the redevelopment of the long-vacant Northwood shopping center adjacent to campus, Wilson recounted the developers telling him they could not make it work financially absent federal New Markets Tax Credits (a competitive federal funding source designed to inject equity into high-impact real estate developments). This admission is analytically important: Even a community-trusted developer working with a committed anchor institution on a viable project could not close the deal on private capital alone. Public credit instruments are not subsidies for weak projects—they are structural requirements for viable ones.
At the other end of the scale, the capital margin is thinner still. Reflecting on the Reinvestment Fund’s $1 million commitment to Paine College, President Lester A. McCorn observed, “That’s a bit of a game changer for us to access that kind of capital.” A sum that would be a rounding error at a flagship institution is transformative at a small private HBCU, which demonstrates both how constrained the current capital environment is as well as how much leverage modest, well-structured capital can achieve. (Note: Co-author Yonina Gray was previously employed by the Reinvestment Fund as director of external relations.)
Prairie View A&M University, a public land-grant institution holding roughly 14,000 acres in the fastest-growing county in Texas, is planning enrollment growth from 10,000 to 13,500 students (nearly 60% of whom are Pell Grant-eligible), and is actively seeking development partners with capital and capacity to match its scale. Wiley University’s Economic Improvement Zone—a $5 million to $10 million multi-phase initiative—remains in early planning not for lack of design, but for lack of the layered federal, foundation, corporate, and CDFI capital its structure requires. In each case, the project pipeline exists—the capital architecture does not.
Theme #2: Land is an asset, but only with site control and trusted partners
Many HBCUs hold valuable land, frequently in growth markets, yet participants consistently reported that land value is realized only when two conditions are met: 1) control of the relevant parcels; and 2) the presence of development partners the surrounding community trusts. Participants across multiple convenings described a shortage of culturally competent developers, and the case evidence documents what acquiring such partnerships costs in time and capital.
Carrington Carter—general partner at East Chop Capital, a multi-asset private equity firm with a focus on real estate development and angel investing—named the specific mechanism through which conventional deal structures push risk onto institutions: a “letter of interest,” which is an informal document that signifies an institution’s project intentions to help them court development partners. “Often, developers, especially if [they’re] not culturally competent and don’t understand the asset, want letters of interest from the university,” said Carter. “We want fully leased-up apartments and dorms and homes before we even break ground. And I think a lot of HBCUs have been unwilling to do that. And I understand why.”
The demand for guarantees before ground is broken asks the institution to absorb risk before the developer assumes any. East Chop Capital inverts that structure, and has spent more than three years acquiring parcels around Tuskegee University at its own risk, deliberately keeping early-stage land assembly off the institution’s balance sheet before any construction begins. The inversion supplies this theme’s operational definition of trust: Trust is measured by who carries early-stage risk.
Trust also carries historical weight that conventional underwriting neither prices nor funds. At Morgan State University, President Wilson described a 10-year process of community relationship-building before $100 million in New Markets Tax Credits could be deployed to redevelop the Northwood shopping center—a process that required identifying what he called “a community-trust developer.” That decade was not inefficiency—it was the actual cost of repairing a trust deficit accumulated over generations of exclusion and dispossession. The same trust infrastructure subsequently produced a 470-bed student housing complex that opened in fall 2025 as well as the city of Baltimore’s gift of a 59-acre former high school site after three years of engagement.
Site control extends beyond parcels to planning power. As President McCorn of Paine College observed, “Municipalities and county governments need to include our institutions in their master plans,” noting that “so many of our institutions are late to the party because the plan has been set for the next 10, 20 years and we don’t even know about it. They’re deciding about us, and when we try to make a move, we’re restricted.”
Even where an HBCU owns land, prior municipal decisions, zoning, and covenants can foreclose its use. McCorn’s prior institution’s experience points to the remedy: When the city of Rock Hill, S.C., co-developed a district plan with Clinton College and named it the Clinton Connection Action Plan, the institution’s profile and planning position changed together. The cross-case pattern is consistent: Where site control and trusted partnerships are present, land converts to development; where either is absent, land remains a dormant asset. Ownership without access does not translate into wealth.
Theme #3: Capacity is often misread, and underwritten accordingly
Participants rejected the prevailing narrative that HBCUs inherently lack capacity, pointing instead to a shortage of partners willing to underwrite early-stage work, fund predevelopment, or invest in the internal infrastructure that builds expertise. The distinction matters analytically: A capacity deficit is an institutional attribute, while an underwriting deficit is a system attribute, and the two imply different remedies.
President McCorn recounted this gap, and its remedy, in the same breath: “A lot of our institutions, number one, we don’t even think this way. But number two, we don’t have the infrastructure to do a lot of these projects. There’s not the institutional knowledge. People have never done these kinds of deals. They don’t know what capital stacks are…There has to be an investment in the education and development of people to build the capacity.”
The framing is an investment deficit, not a competence deficit. Henry Golatt—founding member of the HBCU Coalition, a national effort to help HBCUs and minority-serving institutions grow, and leader of Growth AdvantEDGE, a private sector consulting firm that offers strategic planning and growth strategies to mission-driven institutions such as HBCUs—underscored the same point: “The work of community development is a discipline, it is long term, it is not something that happens overnight,” adding that asking an academician to lead development work is “a sea change for that individual.”
Community development is a field with its own expertise; institutions cannot simply reassign it to advancement offices, and underwriters should assess it as a staffing and investment question rather than a proxy for institutional quality.
Participants also reversed the standard risk narrative. Golatt noted that institutional caution is frequently justifiable: “Some of them have been burned—let’s be honest about that. Investors, developers coming to the table, some able to deliver, some not able to deliver. And so there’s this caution there.” What underwriters read as institutional caution is often the imprint of prior partners who failed to follow through. In those cases, the burden of demonstrating reliability sits with capital providers, not with the institutions they are evaluating.
The case evidence supports the system-attribute reading in both directions. Where investment has been made, results followed: The Economic Research and Development Center at the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff, established in the late 1980s, generated roughly $75 million in economic activity at its peak. Its subsequent stagnation following the withdrawal of sustained leadership and financial investment—rather than any change in institutional mission—demonstrates the same mechanism in reverse. The Reinvestment Fund’s current pilot, which pairs 11 HBCUs with $1 million in capital each plus technical assistance, represents the category of capacity investment that participants identified as missing. Across cases, observed capacity tracked prior investment, not institutional quality.
Theme #4: Campus and community futures are inseparable
Participants consistently framed institutional success as inseparable from the well-being of surrounding neighborhoods, and the case evidence shows this framing operating as strategy rather than sentiment. Henry Golatt of Growth AdvantEDGE linked the supposed tension between educational mission and development work directly: “At the end of the day, you’re creating education to create economic mobility for people…they’re not two different things. They’re really one and the same.” The observation rebuts, from a practitioner’s experience, the persistent claim that HBCUs should educate students rather than develop neighborhoods; in underinvested regions, the two are a single undertaking.
Yvonne Harris, vice president for research and innovation at Bowie State University, drawing on prior anchor work at Sacramento State, described the operational method that follows from that recognition: “The cry from the community is, ‘Not us without us.’ And we took that seriously. So we swung away from what the university needs to what [the community needs].” Harris’ team convened community organizations and leaders, organized task forces around community-identified needs, and deployed university expertise, including a digital equity initiative in the region’s most underserved community.
The community’s refrain in that work—“not us without us”—recurred across convenings as a test of whether engagement was genuine or performative. The method is replicable: The shift from asking “What does the university need?” to “What does the community need?” changed institutional posture and produced more durable outcomes.
The inverse posture—or simply being “in the community” rather than “of the community”—was a theme that participants recognized all too well. President Wilson of Morgan State, describing an institution where he served earlier in his career, recalled that it “was in Camden but had absolutely zero desire to be of Camden.” The distinction echoed the observation of one Wiley University participant who said that institutions sometimes assume they are “in the community” when community members would say otherwise; closing that gap is itself a discipline. Notably, President Wilson’s example was not an HBCU, which underscores that the anchor failure mode is not unique to any institutional type. What is distinct to HBCUs is being denied the capital to do the work while being expected, by history and by their communities, to do it anyway.
Wiley University’s describes its Economic Improvement Zone as “a strategy built with” the New Town neighborhood rather than a program imposed on it, targeting business incubation, workforce credentialing, and employer pipelines to the residents who live close to the institution. Participants also identified a measurable cost of treating campus and community as separate: retail leakage (the spending that students, faculty, and staff conduct outside the surrounding community because local infrastructure cannot meet their needs) and its labor market counterpart (staff who live 25 miles or more from campus because nearby housing stock cannot serve them).
Theme #5: The field Is ready to move beyond pilots
Participants expressed little appetite for one-off demonstration projects, describing instead a need for replicable platforms, pooled capital, and approaches that scale across institutions. Several HBCU presidents observed that pilots, however well intended, often introduce new volatility once funding sunsets, leaving institutions positioned worse than before.
The problem, participants emphasized, is alignment rather than scarcity. Surveying the landscape of development programs and capital, Henry Golatt of Growth AdvantEDGE said, “There is ample supply. I don’t think it’s targeted and directed as much toward the needs of HBCUs. That’s where the opportunity lies.”
This claim reframes the theme as a systems-design finding: The field does not need new experimental programs so much as the redirection of existing capacity toward HBCU-specific structures. Golatt’s proposed intervention makes the point structurally: HBCUs “should be the residency of an institute that is training future developers,” so that, in his words, “we are not waiting on the next person to knock on the door. We are training them as we go.” Such a proposal converts the developer shortage from an external dependency into an institutional production function, with HBCUs manufacturing the capacity the market has failed to supply.
Carrington Carter of East Chop Capital identified two further post-pilot mechanisms. The first is the sector’s own constituency: alumni who hesitate to donate might readily invest. Engaging alumni as investors with a financial return, as East Chop Capital has done with Hampton University and Tuskegee University alumni, converts the sector’s most loyal supporters into a capital source rather than a donor base. The second is institutional wealth itself: “It’s worth having a discussion around how HBCU endowments can help participate in the revitalization of their communities,” Carter said. Both mechanisms presuppose durable investment platforms rather than time-limited demonstrations, which is precisely what distinguishes them from the pilot model.
The case evidence gives this theme its sharpest expression through contrast. The University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff built one of the first HBCU-anchored economic development centers in the country; its infrastructure remains operational, but without institutionalized funding for the people and stewardship the model requires, momentum was lost across leadership transitions and budget cycles. The through-line across cases is that permanence—not novelty—is the unmet need. Participants requested continuity of capital and capacity, but the field has largely received only episodic investment.

Policy recommendations
The institutions profiled in Appendix B are not failing institutions. They operate inside policy and capital frameworks that were not designed to recognize the value they create or repair the inequities they were built to endure. For years, the dominant response has been to help HBCUs compete more effectively within existing rules: expand grant funding, increase philanthropic support, strengthen leadership pipelines, and deepen partnerships. These efforts matter, but they leave the underlying architecture intact.
The recommendations below follow directly from the five themes detailed in the previous section. Each recommendation was derived through the same triangulation that produced the themes: 1) field convenings with HBCU leaders and cross-sector stakeholders; 2) policy and market analysis spanning state funding formulas, federal program design, land-grant compliance history, and capital market practices; and 3) practitioner experience in community development finance. Only interventions supported across all three inputs are presented here. The list is not exhaustive; it identifies the structural changes where reform would unlock the most progress most quickly.
Recommendation #1: Restore public baseline funding and redesign capital instruments to share early-stage risk
The first theme established that the binding constraint on HBCU campus and community development is capital design, and the origin of that constraint is public. State legislatures withheld an estimated $12.6 billion from historically Black land-grant universities between 1987 and 2020, and public policy at every level excluded HBCUs from the wealth-building systems that capitalized their peers. The consequences now surface in capital markets, where credit ratings, bond markets, and federal financing tools treat weak balance sheets as evidence of poor management rather than the predictable outcome of that exclusion. Research quantifies the cost: HBCUs pay roughly 14% higher underwriting fees on tax-exempt bonds than comparable non-HBCUs, a disparity that persists even at AAA credit ratings and grows three times larger in Deep South states. A constraint that public policy created requires a public remedy.
Philanthropy has a role, as Recommendation #5 later describes, but voluntary giving is discretionary, uneven across institutions, and subject to donor priorities and political climate. HBCUs should not have to rely on philanthropy to recover from public underfunding; restitution for a public debt is a public obligation.
Congress and the states should therefore establish baseline equity funding that gives HBCUs a durable foundation to build upon rather than a deficit to climb out of. The most direct federal vehicle would be new land-grant legislation in the tradition of the Second Morrill Act of 1890, which created many of these institutions by conditioning federal funds on the provision of higher education to Black students. A modern successor could take several forms: a federally funded endowment match that brings HBCU endowments closer to parity with PWIs over a defined period; dedicated capital funding for facilities and infrastructure comparable to what flagship institutions received during their growth decades; or stronger federal enforcement of the 1:1 state matching requirements attached to land-grant funds, which states have repeatedly failed to meet, as documented in the 2023 joint letter from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and Department of Education.
This report supports the kind of policy recommendation that scholars and HBCU advocacy organizations have advanced: a third Morrill Act that provides baseline equity funding, lessening the need for debt financing. At the state level, the 2023 joint letter calculated the shortfall institution by institution, and repayment schedules would convert a documented debt into a funded commitment. States should also correct the funding formulas that produce weak balance sheets going forward, adjusting base formulas to account for cumulative underinvestment and separating capital appropriations from prestige-based metrics or metrics that reward institutions that benefited from discrimination.
Alongside restored public funding, federal policymakers and philanthropic capital providers should shift early-stage development risk away from individual campuses through pooled first-loss capital, federal and philanthropic guarantees, and credit enhancements that allow lenders to engage earlier in the development cycle. Baseline funding repairs the balance sheet; risk-sharing instruments correct how the balance sheet is read. Both are necessary, because absent public correction, federal guarantees and philanthropic dollars will continue to backfill state disinvestment rather than finance growth.
Neither intervention requires invention. The land-grant system itself is the founding precedent: The Morrill Acts of 1862 and 1890 demonstrate that Congress can build enduring institutional wealth by statute, and the endowments and campuses of today’s flagship universities began as federal land grants sustained by public appropriations. What is proposed here is the completion of that commitment, extending to HBCUs the same patient public capitalization that built the institutions they are now measured against.
Maryland’s 2021 settlement with its four public HBCUs, structured as a 15-year commitment of $577 million in supplemental appropriations, offers states a repayment template that does not require litigation. And on the risk-sharing side, the U.S. Treasury’s CDFI Bond Guarantee Program, established by the Small Business Jobs Act of 2010, has guaranteed nearly $3 billion in long-term, fixed-rate capital for community development; extending or adapting that mechanism for HBCU campus and community development through CDFI intermediaries already engaged with HBCUs or through a parallel HBCU-specific authorization would directly address the documented mispricing of risk.
Recommendation #2: Finance site control and build a pipeline of trusted developers
The second theme showed that land converts to development only when institutions or aligned partners control the relevant parcels and when the surrounding community trusts the developer. Both conditions are currently financed by exception rather than by design: Land assembly is typically carried at private risk, and the supply of developers with demonstrated cultural competence and HBCU project experience is far smaller than the project pipeline requires. If land is to function as the asset it represents on paper, both conditions need dedicated financing.
Capital providers and philanthropy should establish predevelopment and land-assembly financing that allows institutions or mission-aligned intermediaries to secure site control without carrying speculative risk on institutional balance sheets. Public and philanthropic funders should also invest in the developer pipeline directly by supporting training, mentorship, and balance-sheet growth for emerging developers with community ties. Finally, municipal and county governments should include HBCUs in master planning as a default practice; institutions cannot activate land that prior planning decisions, zoning, and covenants have already foreclosed.
Working models exist for each element of this recommendation. The East Chop Capital approach at Tuskegee University, in which a mission-aligned private equity firm assembled parcels at its own risk over three years before construction, demonstrates the site-control function that dedicated financing could scale. Structured as risk-sharing rather than risk transfer, public and philanthropic first-loss capital would catalyze early-stage deals while preserving the incentives for developers and lenders to conduct full due diligence. The emerging-developer programs operated by the Urban Land Institute, Local Initiatives Support Corporation (LISC), and others show what pipeline investment looks like in practice, and could be adapted to HBCU markets. The city of Rock Hill, S.C.’s joint district planning with Clinton College illustrates the municipal-inclusion practice, and the West North Avenue Development Authority in Maryland, a state-created corridor authority chaired by an HBCU president, shows what formalized planning authority can look like.
Recommendation #3: Underwrite capacity as an investment, not a screening criterion
The third theme found that institutional capacity is systematically misread. Funders and lenders treat the absence of in-house development expertise as a fixed institutional attribute, yet the evidence shows it is a function of prior investment. Federal research funding exhibits the same path dependence: Institutions with early wins build the infrastructure required to win again.
HBCUs collectively account for less than 1% of federal research and development expenditures despite producing roughly 25% of Black STEM bachelor’s degree recipients. If capacity follows capital rather than the reverse, then the order of operations in funding decisions is itself the problem.
Funders at every level should therefore sequence capacity investment before competition. In development finance, this means funding predevelopment work, technical assistance, and dedicated staff positions as core project costs rather than overhead. In research policy, it means dedicated, long-term investment in laboratories, faculty support, and administrative infrastructure preceding competitive grantmaking. Underwriting standards should also incorporate institutional context: Risk assessments that ignore documented historical underfunding will systematically misjudge the institutions that survived it.
The sequencing principle has a long federal track record. For decades, the National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR) has directed capacity-building investments to states underrepresented in federal research funding before requiring head-to-head competition; the bipartisan HBCU Research Capacity Act introduced in March 2026 would create an analogous mechanism for HBCUs. At the project level, the Reinvestment Fund’s pilot pairing 11 HBCUs with $1 million commitments plus technical assistance represents the category of capacity investment the field identified as missing.
Recommendation #4: Embed HBCUs in development policy as delivery infrastructure
The fourth theme demonstrated that campus and community futures are inseparable, yet policy treats them separately. At the federal level, HBCUs are addressed primarily through carve-outs, pilots, and special initiatives rather than embedded in the core design of workforce, infrastructure, research, climate, and economic development policy. These dedicated programs matter, but they sit alongside federal architecture that defaults to flagship research universities when distributing the largest pools of strategic funding. Institutions that already function as community infrastructure should be treated that way in program design.
Congress and federal agencies should position HBCUs as preferred program delivery partners for federal resources—embedding them in authorizing statutes, agency guidance, and procurement frameworks from the start rather than appending them afterward. Statutes related to community development can have eligibility requirements that are inclusive of institutional types. HBCU leaders can be consultants, while colleges and universities located in low-income areas can receive preferences in competitive funding. In practice, this means both statutory eligibility (naming HBCUs in authorizing language for workforce, infrastructure, and research programs) and competitive preference (scoring bonuses or set-aside allocations in relevant federal grant programs), with formal consultation roles for HBCU leadership in program design. Because roughly half of HBCUs anchor majority-Black communities that other federal delivery channels often overlook, this is an efficiency argument as much as an equity argument: HBCUs are existing infrastructure in precisely the places federal programs struggle to reach. State and local governments should apply the same logic to economic development strategy, workforce systems, and regional planning.
Congress has already demonstrated what this looks like. The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 authorized roughly $200 million to $250 million per year through Fiscal Year 2027 to build HBCU and minority-serving institution capacity to compete for and administer NSF grants, and directly enabled the launch of the HBCU CHIPS Network in February 2024. Writing HBCUs into the authorizing statute itself—rather than appending them to appropriations afterward—is a model replicable across other federal priority areas.
Recommendation #5: Replace pilots with permanent platforms
The fifth theme established that the field is ready to move beyond pilots, but the funding architecture is not. HBCUs receive less than 2% of philanthropic giving to higher education instructions (much of it short-term and program-restricted), and endowment per student at private HBCUs averages roughly one-eighth that of non-HBCU private institutions. Short-term restricted grants do not stabilize institutions; in some cases, they introduce new volatility when funding sunsets. Institutions simultaneously navigate a fragmented landscape of agencies, intermediaries, funders, and compliance regimes that consumes leadership bandwidth at the institutions least equipped to absorb the cost. A field ready to scale needs architecture built for permanence.
Philanthropy should shift toward permanent capital: endowment matching, recoverable grants, guarantees, and unrestricted operating support tied to long-term institutional health. Federal agencies, philanthropy, and the HBCU community should jointly resource coordinated, HBCU-governed platforms that aggregate capital, technical assistance, guarantees, and policy advocacy—reducing the fluency burden that fragmentation currently imposes on institutional leadership. Institutions themselves hold levers as well, such as engaging alumni as investors rather than solely as donors, and exploring how HBCU endowments of all sizes can prudently participate in the development of their own communities. In practice, this participation is most likely to take the form of pooled investment vehicles that allow institutions to contribute at levels appropriate to their individual risk capacity, rather than requiring individual endowments to concentrate scarce assets in illiquid local investments. Keon Holmes of the investment firm Cambridge Associates is currently exploring exactly this structure with HBCUs.
Both halves of this recommendation have working demonstrations. Lilly Endowment’s $100 million unrestricted grant to UNCF in 2024 anchors a $370 million pooled endowment shared across 37 member institutions; the endowment is large, unrestricted, structured to compound, and pooled for professional management. On coordination, EPSCoR operates across multiple agencies, the Cooperative Extension System has provided coordinated land-grant infrastructure for more than a century, and intermediaries including the 1890 Universities Foundation, the Thurgood Marshall College Fund, and UNCF are positioned to anchor an analogous HBCU platform if resourced to do so.

2. Site control and trusted partners

3. Capacity

4. Campus-community integration

5. Beyond pilots

Who belongs at the table next
The convenings that informed this report drew the right voices into the room to surface what HBCU leaders are building and where they are stalled. Acting on the recommendations above will require partners with the capital, scale, and authority to move them.
Five categories of partner are positioned to do so. Large institutional investors with an appetite for place-based, long-duration assets can supply the patient capital that Recommendations #1 and #2 require. State economic development agencies and governors’ offices hold the funding formulas and planning authorities addressed in Recommendations #1 and #4. Developers with balance sheet capacity and a track record of culturally competent execution are the pipeline that Recommendation #2 seeks to finance and expand. Philanthropy positioned to provide general operating, balance sheet, or guarantee support—rather than programmatic grants alone—is the actor Recommendations #3 and #5 call on directly. And Black-owned banks and mission-aligned financial institutions—several of which are already engaged in HBCU development financing—are natural anchors for the risk-sharing structures and coordinated platforms described in Recommendations #1 and #5.

Conclusion
Taken together, this report’s recommendations reflect a single structural observation: Capital without policy reform eventually hits a wall, and policy without meaningful capital allocation lives on a shelf. Progress requires the alignment of both with the operational realities of HBCUs.
The timing is consequential. Place-based and equity-oriented investment frameworks face renewed legal and political challenges, and recent shifts in the federal posture toward diversity programs have introduced hesitation across philanthropic and private capital markets at the very moment HBCU-led development is gaining momentum.
This report frames HBCUs as undervalued economic infrastructure because that is what the evidence shows, and because the case for investment must now rest on returns rather than rhetoric. The returns are documented: $16.5 billion in annual economic impact, more than 136,000 jobs, and mobility outcomes that few institutional categories match at any funding level. What the current environment changes is not the strength of that case, but the urgency of grounding it in economic rather than solely equity terms.
What HBCU leaders told us across a year of convenings is that the institutions are ready. The voices from the field that run through this report describe institutions that have carried an anchor role for generations without the systems other sectors take for granted. Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer Tashia Bradley of Wiley University gave this report its title when she described her institution’s posture: “We are not chasing the wind. We are harnessing it.” HBCUs have been harnessing the wind for more than a century. The recommendations above describe what becomes possible when they no longer have to do it alone.
Three conclusions carry the weight of the evidence. First, the undervaluation of HBCUs is structural and measurable, not anecdotal, and correcting it requires policy change at the governmental and corporate levels. Second, effective responses are systemic rather than institutional: changing the rules that govern underwriting, funding formulas, and program design, rather than only helping individual campuses navigate broken systems. Third, the case for HBCU investment rests on returns, not rhetoric, and that economic framing has proven most durable in a political environment where equity- and place-based frameworks face renewed challenges.
This report therefore closes the way its predecessor did, with an invitation. Each of the partners named in the policy recommendations section—from institutional investors to state governments to Black-owned banks—will find in this report both the evidence for engagement and a working model to follow: an investable pipeline documented in the case studies, state-level templates in Maryland’s settlement and the West North Avenue Development Authority, a federal model in the CHIPS and Science Act, a demonstration of permanent capital in the Lilly-UNCF pooled endowment, and proof that early risk-sharing produces execution in the East Chop Capital and Reinvestment Fund models. HBCU leaders, who have never waited for permission, will find in one another’s strategies the outlines of the coordinated platform the field is ready to govern.
The question is no longer whether HBCUs can deliver. It is whether the systems around them will be redesigned to match what they already do, and who will move first.

But falling unemployment payments in September indicate a relatively healthy overall picture. Lower-income households' wage growth remains strongest, despite a narrowing gap. After-tax wage growth eased to 4.5% YoY for lower-income households in September, while rising to 3.8% and 3.7% for middle- and higher-income households, respectively. Lower tax withholdings and a relative strengthening in the younger/lower-income end of the labor market are driving this story. articles.title: Market update - October 23rd 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Market update - October 23rd, 20263 min readDataHousing weakness buys the Fed time, inflation takes it backBitcoin has remained relatively resilient this week despite another bout of volatility across risk assets. The strongest explanation is renewed spot demand, supported by improving equity sentiment and some short covering. More broadly, markets appear to be moving away from rewarding AI narratives alone and are now demanding a much higher bar for earnings delivery. Disappointing earnings results in the US have therefore produced some sharp moves in equities, and Bitcoin has been caught up in that volatility at times, but on the whole has held up comparatively well.The US macro picture remains mixed. Housing has weakened sharply, with homebuilder confidence falling three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012,¹ housing starts down 5.2% in September to an annualised 1.221M² and pending home sales falling 7.3% month-on-month to 66.0, a record low since the index began in 2001.³ That is increasingly clear evidence that higher borrowing costs are biting into activity.For rates, a hold at the 28 October Fed meeting remains overwhelmingly the more likely outcome. As of 20 October, Polymarket put the probability of a 25bp hike at around 12%, while CME-based pricing has been closer to 17%, down from above 40% a week earlier.⁴ December is a different story, with markets assigning a probability near 83% to another increase later in the year.⁴ The Fed therefore still has scope to sound firm on inflation even if it pauses in its meeting next week. Housing weakness argues for patience, but last week’s hot CPI and PPI prints mean another hike remains credible.⁵Bitcoin remains highly sensitive to that distinction. A surprise October hike would likely be more disruptive than a well-signalled December move because it would represent an abrupt tightening of financial conditions relative to current expectations. By contrast, a pause combined with firm guidance would probably be easier for markets to absorb. The recent resilience suggests investors are already becoming more selective about which macro signals genuinely alter the broader liquidity outlook.Overall, the market remains finely balanced. Spot demand is improving, Bitcoin has absorbed equity volatility reasonably well, and housing weakness gives the Fed some room to wait. But inflation remains the binding constraint, and the next move in crypto is still likely to be dictated more by rate expectations than by any single sector-specific catalyst.More about a new Bitcoin forkElsewhere, eCash (ECX), Paul Sztorc’s proposed Bitcoin hard fork, continues to make tangible technical progress, although adoption remains too early to call a success. It should not be confused with eCash (XEC), an unrelated and older project. The ECX beta opened on 19 September, with mainnet still targeted for around 31 October depending on Bitcoin block timing. The project dashboard currently shows 10 activated sidechains, including seven core projects and three community additions, which is encouraging in terms of participation.⁶ However, activation does not yet equate to meaningful usage. Operational readiness also remains mixed: the same dashboard shows several core sidechain nodes unreachable by its monitoring hub, and developer activity is concentrated among a relatively small number of contributors.⁶SourcesNational Association of Home Builders / Wells Fargo, Housing Market Index, 19 Oct 2026US Census Bureau and Department of Housing and Urban Development, New Residential Construction, September 2026, released 20 Oct 2026National Association of Realtors, Pending Home Sales Index, September 2026, released 20 Oct 2026CME Group FedWatch and Polymarket, as of 20 Oct 2026US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index, September 2026 (+0.6% m/m, 3.7% y/y), released 14 Oct 2026, and Producer Price Index, September 2026 (+1.3% m/m, 6.3% y/y), released 15 Oct 2026eCash (ECX) project dashboard, accessed 22 Oct 2026Published onOct 23rd, 2026WriterJames ButterfillHead of ResearchFormer Head of Research at ETF Securities, James leads CoinShares' Research department with deep expertise in equity and fund management.

articles.title: Great ideas should see the light
articles.text:
Great ideas should see the light

Our focus is clear: supporting major carbon reduction projects and nurturing new sustainable businesses.
We are fully committed to supporting major carbon reduction projects and helping sustainable businesses grow. By collaborating with our clients, we contribute to building a future where bold ideas become meaningful realities.A financial commitment aligned with climate challenges: Societe Generale has set an ambitious target of €500 billion in sustainable financing for the 2024-2030 period. This includes €400 billion dedicated to financing and advisory services, as well as €100 billion allocated to sustainable bonds.Comprehensive support for the energy transition: We are involved throughout the entire value chain of the energy transition:- Responsible sourcing of rare resources essential to this transformation, - Financing infrastructure for the storage and distribution of renewable energy, - Supporting CO2-intensive sectors in their reinvention process to reduce emissions.Empowering pioneers of sustainability: We are also committed to supporting emerging leaders in the sustainable transition by providing tailored advisory and financing solutions to bring their innovative projects to life.Together with our clients, we are contributing to a new industrial revolution, paving the way for a more sustainable and resilient world.Concrete projects for meaningful impact: The best way to illustrate our commitment is by sharing concrete examples of innovative projects carried out with our clients. These inspiring initiatives embody our vision of a more sustainable future.Embracing the energy transition and driving sustainable innovation>> OPEN THE DOCUMENT

articles.title: Types of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks
articles.text:
Financial Stability

What Is Financial StabilityTypes of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks Monitoring Risk Across the Financial System Proactive Monitoring of Markets and InstitutionsFinancial Stability and Stress Testing

Types of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks

Related Content

Financial Stability Report

Monetary Policy Report

Financial Stability Monitoring (PDF)

Mapping heat in the U.S. financial system

Federal Reserve staff regularly and systematically assess a standard set of vulnerabilities as part of their periodic review of financial stability. These assessments generally are provided to the Board and Federal Open Market Committee four times per year. Using a range of data sources as well as insights gained from discussions and engagement with domestic and foreign counterparts, staff regularly monitor vulnerabilities in four areas:

1. Elevated valuation pressures are signaled by asset prices that are high relative to economic fundamentals or historical norms and are often driven by an increased willingness of investors to take on risk. As such, elevated valuation pressures imply a greater possibility of outsized drops in asset prices.

2. Excessive borrowing by businesses and households leaves them vulnerable to distress if their incomes decline or the assets they own fall in value. In the event of such shocks, businesses and households with high debt burdens may need to cut back spending sharply, affecting the overall level of economic activity. Moreover, when businesses and households cannot make payments on their loans, financial institutions and investors incur losses.

3. Excessive leverage within the financial sector increases the risk that financial institutions will not have the sufficient capacity to absorb losses when hit by adverse shocks. In those situations, institutions will be forced to cut back lending, sell their assets, or, in extreme cases, shut down. Such responses can substantially impair credit access for households and businesses.

4. Elevated funding risks can occur when financial institutions raise funds from the public with a commitment to return investor money on short notice, but those institutions then invest much of the funds in illiquid assets that are hard to sell quickly or in assets that have a long maturity. This liquidity and maturity transformation can create an incentive for investors to withdraw funds quickly in adverse situations, commonly referred to as a “run.” Facing a run, financial institutions may need to sell assets quickly at “fire sale” prices, thereby incurring substantial losses and potentially even becoming insolvent.

These vulnerability assessments inform internal Federal Reserve discussions concerning both supervision and regulatory policies and monetary policy. Two times a year, the Federal Reserve publishes its Financial Stability Report summarizing its current assessment of these vulnerabilities, the salient risks to the financial system originating in the United States and abroad, and how they might interact. A shorter summary of current vulnerabilities is included in the twice-yearly Monetary Policy Report to Congress. They also inform Federal Reserve interactions with broader monitoring efforts, such as those by the Financial Stability Oversight Council and the Financial Stability Board.

Asset Valuations and Risk Appetite

Asset valuations are the prices of assets after accounting for economic fundamentals, such as future expected cash flows and interest rates. Valuations that are high relative to history or to economic fundamentals constitute a vulnerability because the unwinding of high prices can be destabilizing in the financial system and economy. Moreover, stretched asset valuations may be an indicator of a broader buildup in risk appetite leading to investors taking on higher levels of risk, or new risks that are not fully understood.

This dynamic can be more concerning when (1) the assets are widely held and the values are supported by excessive borrowing, (2) the maturity of the asset is significantly longer than the maturity of the liability financing that asset, or (3) there is a lack of publicly available information about the asset.

However, it is very difficult to judge whether an asset price is overvalued relative to fundamentals. As a result, analysis typically considers a range of possible valuation metrics, as well as developments in areas where asset prices are rising especially rapidly, the size and pace of inflows to an asset class, or the implications of unusually low or high levels of volatility in certain markets.

Borrowing by Businesses and Households

Excessive borrowing by businesses and households leaves them vulnerable if their incomes decline or the assets they own fall in value. In the event of such shocks, businesses and households with high debt burdens may need to cut back spending sharply, affecting the overall level of economic activity. A default can significantly limit their ability to obtain credit in the future. Moreover, when businesses and households cannot make payments on their loans, financial institutions and investors incur losses.

Leverage in the Financial System

Highly leveraged financial system intermediaries—those with significantly more debt than equity—can amplify the effect of negative shocks in the financial system and broad economy. For example, if highly leveraged institutions collectively respond to a negative shock in the economy (e.g., a sharp decline in house prices) by tightening lending standards and shrinking their balance sheets more than called for by the shock itself, perhaps because outsized credit losses threaten their solvency, the resulting contraction in credit will aggravate the decline in economic activity resulting from the shock.

Sufficiently large losses for highly leveraged institutions, especially if those institutions have a significant share of short-term funding, can lead to “fire sales,” where assets are unloaded quickly at extremely low prices. These fire sales then reduce the value of similar assets held by other financial institutions, potentially leading to a negative feedback loop.

The Federal Reserve monitors leverage in the banking sector with the help of an extensive data collection program. This includes the data collected in support of the Dodd-Frank Act stress tests for large banking institutions, the quarterly Reports of Condition and Income for all banks, and the Consumer Credit report. Additionally, periodic surveys of nonbank providers of leverage, such as the Senior Credit Officer Opinion Survey, as well as collaboration and data sharing among all the financial regulatory agencies offer valuable insights on nonbank financial leverage.

Funding Risks and Maturity Transformation by the Financial System

One key benefit provided by the financial system is to aggregate short-maturity liabilities so that they can be used to fund long-maturity assets. This function has historically occurred primarily in the traditional banking system or other depository institutions, which use deposits from consumers as part of the financing to provide multiyear auto or mortgage loans. In recent decades, nonbank financial institutions have grown substantially. For example, mutual funds offer their investors the convenience of daily withdrawals even though they invest in longer-term debt instruments.

However, as seen during the 2007–09 financial crisis and the outbreak of COVID-19 in March 2020, the mismatch between long-term assets and short-term funding creates systemic vulnerabilities that can threaten the functioning of financial markets and the broader economy. This manifests when a large fraction of those investors withdraw their funding suddenly in response to an increase in risk aversion after a negative shock.

Deposit insurance provides some protection against this vulnerability within the traditional banking system. However, firms that use short-term liabilities such as repurchase agreements (or “repos”) or commercial paper, and the financial institutions that invest in them, like money market mutual funds, are also prone to run risk. Indeed, money market mutual funds came under considerable pressure during both the 2007–09 financial crisis and the pandemic in 2020. For this reason, the Federal Reserve actively monitors—as best it can, given available data and measurement—both liquidity risk and the degree of maturity transformation in the financial system.
