There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesTalks at GSDimensional’s David Booth on How to Interpret Risk and 'Stay Calm' Amid UncertaintyOct 28, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptDavid Booth, the founder and chairman of Dimensional Fund Advisors, uses academic research and market evidence to manage more than $1 trillion in assets. Booth, the author of Stay Calm, joins Raj Mahajan, a senior partner in Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets, to discuss how to interpret risk and uncertainty, how outsiders can participate in the market as effectively as insiders, and the long-term magic of compounding.
Transcript:
David Booth: Where you end up in life, you know, it is the result of the compounding of many decisions you made over time. You won some of the time, you lost some of the time. There are no shortcuts, and maybe that's where wisdom comes from.

[MUSIC INTRO]

Raj Mahajan: I am thrilled to be joined by my friend David Booth, co-founder and chairman of Dimensional Fund Advisors. Welcome David.

David Booth: Well, thanks for having me.

Raj Mahajan: From selling shoes in Kansas to studying under Nobel Laureates at the University of Chicago, ultimately founding Dimensional, not too far from here in Brooklyn. And then it has now, over the last five decades, become this extraordinary institution that is educating investors on markets, risk, and evidence-based investing. And then you wrote a book, Stay Calm. And that's what I'd love to jump into today and talk about some of those insights.

Let's go back to the University of Chicago. Something galactic happened where you became galvanized by these big ideas that ultimately inspired you to start Dimensional. What were some of these big ideas?

David Booth: Well, first off, these ideas were really new. Before 1960, there really wasn't research-quality data where you could test out much of anything in investing. And that all changed in the 1960s with the CRSP data. Then all of a sudden, you have the development of investing as a science. You can't have a science without testable hypotheses. So, now they have data, and they could test a lot of things.

And one of the things, of course, they've been testing for the last 60 years is professional money management.

Raj Mahajan: Yeah, active management.

David Booth: Worth the cost? Yeah. And those were really exciting ideas. Because the conclusion was, we can't seem to find the value in professional management. I mean, there are undoubtedly people out there that can beat the market. There are just too few of them. When you have fewer than you would expect by chance, you can't separate out skill from luck.

And so, depending on your point of view, that was either exciting and innovating, or it was, you know, something that was threatening to you. And it was basically threatening at first to Wall Street before they realized how cool it was to trade with index funds.

Raj Mahajan: You tell this lovely story about finding $15,000 in your late father's lockbox that had not been invested. And it lost 80% of its purchasing power by the time you found it. And one of the reasons you cite is that your parents felt like outsiders, and as a result, didn't trust investing. So, tell us a little bit more about this ethos of being an outsider and how it's influenced you in your approach.

David Booth: My parents, they didn't trust markets because they thought as an outsider, if they invested, the insiders would take advantage of them and just take all their money. So, they never invested.

Now in 1985, when I opened the lockbox, it was 40 years later. If you'd gotten the market return over the last 40 years, what would it have grown to? It would have grown to over a million dollars. That's just an example of the magic of compounding. And one of the lessons that I wish I'd been able to convince my parents of, the magic of compounding.

The second part of the story, of course, is back when they were around, you know, market portfolios weren't readily and easily available. So, forget about this idea about being an outsider. You know? You can do apparently about as well as the insiders just by buying the market.

Raj Mahajan: I like this connection you drew in the book between being an outsider and uncertainty. And that actually uncertainty creates more optionality and opportunity for you. Can you talk more about uncertainty and why it's something to be embraced, in particular, if you're an outsider?

David Booth: Investing is uncertain and complex. So is life. If there is no uncertainty, I mean, if everything had been predetermined, you know, you wouldn't have been able to progress the way you have in life. And in investing, if there were no uncertainty, in other words, then everything would be riskless and all investments would have a riskless rate of return. So, it's the uncertainty creates the opportunity. And so, it's not about eliminating uncertainty. It's about managing uncertainty in life and investing.

And there are some kind of general themes that are in the book. How do people go about doing that? Well, you know, first thing is don't bet all your money on your ability to predict. You know? The market is inherently unpredictable. And so much of life is unpredictable. Very few people here could have said 20 years ago that they'd be sitting in this auditorium. You know?

So, what you want to do is plan rather than predict. You know? Observe outcomes, be flexible, adaptive. And over the long haul, you know, there's a good chance you'll be okay.

Raj Mahajan: Speaking of be okay, for those who have been investing in equity markets, over the last hundred years, the return has been 10.2%.

David Booth: Yeah.

Raj Mahajan: So, how do you interpret that risk premium and why it's persistent? And then if you extrapolate forward, we're also in another moment in time with artificial intelligence and the transformational effects it might have. Are the gains in the stock market going to accrue to 10 firms and not the balance? Do you think it'll persist? And if so, tell us why.

David Booth: I mean, there are two parts to the story. The first is 10% by itself is amazing. When you figure all the economic scenarios we've had over the last hundred years, somehow, and it's kind of one of my passions, you know, the market, the stock and bond markets in the US, they're really miracles. Anyway, as you pointed out, there's about a 6% risk premium. In other words, stock returns over riskless assets, it's been about 6% a year. And that's really the story that I like to talk about because academics have studied this like crazy.

And I think they're kind of missing one crucial factor here, which is human ingenuity. And by that, I mean, you know, we've had all kinds of economic scenarios. And when you get into a bad economic scenario, you know, people don't just give up and go, "Oh, gosh, that's boo-hoo." They figure out how to get back on track and figure out how to do things new and different. I mean, I think most of you remember in the pandemic, all of a sudden, you've got Peloton and DoorDash, and all the kinds of things spring up. I said, you know--

Raj Mahajan: Zoom.

David Booth: Zoom. In 2020 they're saying, "What's going to happen?" I go, "I don't know what's going to happen. But here's what I believe. I believe that you'll see this human spirit take shape and be entrepreneurial. And there'll be winners and losers. Yeah, I don't know who the winners and losers will be, but there'll be a lot of both. And what I do believe is this will cause us to get back on track faster than you might think."

And as you recall, that recession was one quarter long. I mean, that's a miracle given the magnitude of the problem.

Raj Mahajan: Utter mistake if you would have sold stock at the lows during, you know, the most fearful parts of COVID.

David Booth: So, people are pulling their hair out. Then they look at it, the market's down 20%. They go, "Oh, gosh, you know, holy cow, I've got to get out." And then, of course, the market ended up 20% for the year. So, if it's down 20% to begin with, you have to come back 40% to get up to that total of 20%.

Raj Mahajan: Exactly.

David Booth: And as we've talked about, you know, there are no mulligans in this business. I mean, if you missed out on that rise, there's no do-over. To get that 10.2% that you've talked about, you've got to be there to be assured of getting it. You know, our goal is if we can help more people better understand how markets work, the stock and bond markets, public markets, then they'll be able to make more sensible choices. And if they can make more sensible choices, they're going to feel calmer.

Raj Mahajan: And one of my favorite quotes in the book is, quote, "By owning a share of the market, we get to participate in the upside of human ingenuity."

David Booth: That's it. I mean, that's really what we're talking about here. We don't know individual stocks or which companies are going to really have a great time and when bad times hit. But the overall market, that's really what we're talking about.

And, you know, sometimes people say I'm an optimist, because that all sounds pretty. I don't think I'm an optimist, I think I'm a realist. I mean, it can't be any other way. People aren't going to invest unless they think they can have a positive expected outcome. It's where buyers and sellers come together. You know, they don't trade unless each side thinks they got a good deal.

Raj Mahajan: By the way, there's no shame of being an optimist. Maybe there's a strong connection between true wealth and optimism.

David Booth: Yeah, I don't know which one comes first. But I would say if you're lucky enough to be an optimist, you're really wealthy already. If you really know what your values are, and one of the keys to investing is figuring out, you know, what do I really care about? Where am I headed in life?

And that's why I said my parents, even though they didn't have much money, were wealthy. For them, it was all about family.

Raj Mahajan: Let's pivot to David Booth, the business builder at Dimensional. In 2003, you had $50 billion of assets under management. You tell a story in the book of, in 2004, you really challenged your leadership team to 10X and be a $500 billion asset manager.

You got there, spoiler alert. But tell us about what you learned about leadership on that journey and how some of that may be applicable to anyone in the room today.

David Booth: Well, I believe strongly in giving people a lot of autonomy and so forth. Nevertheless, you have to have some kind of collective vision.

Raj Mahajan: Aspiration.

David Booth: Aspiration or where are we headed? I didn't say, "Look, in 15 years, we're going to go 50 to 500 billion." I said, "Plan on being 500 billion."

Raj Mahajan: Basically, setting the aspirational goal accelerated those conversations internally.

David Booth: Yeah.

Raj Mahajan: Another aspect to Dimensional's extraordinary success is tapping into RIAs and investors via the RIA channel. Can you tell us about the story of how that came to be? Because it sounded like in the book, you may have been a little reluctant at first to embrace that.

David Booth: When we started, all of our clients were large institutional clients. In 1981, pension funds were huge and those were our clients. So, we had an advisor in Sacramento come up to us and say he'd like to have access to our funds. Now, what was unusual was that right from the get-go, even though our clients were institutional clients, we wanted to commingle for administrative ease and mutual funds.

So, the price of these funds are institutionally priced. You know, they're very low, which made them very attractive to RIAs. So, we're not so sure. You know, commingled funds are great as long as everybody behaves themselves. What you don't want to have are people getting in and out all the time and generating costs, you know, for the other shareholders.

So, he said, "No, no, I'm not that kind of person." So, we said, "Okay, we'll give you access, but we'll monitor what you're doing." And about a year later, he comes back and goes, "You know, I think there's a business in this."

At that time, the RIA market was teeny tiny. I go, "Okay, well, here's what we're going to do. First off, advisors, if they want access to our funds, they've got to go through a platform like a Schwab or Pershing or Fidelity. And secondly, before we give them access to the funds, they have to come meet with us at one of our seminars." I mean, to a casual observer, that doesn't sound like that's the best marketing strategy, forcing people to come to your offices and spend a couple of days learning about what you do.

Raj Mahajan: Dimensional boot camp?

David Booth: Dimensional boot camp. But funny, in a way, that turned out to be kind of clever marketing, because people, once they got accepted, they felt kind of pride in, hey, look, I've got access to these funds. And that took off. Now more than two thirds of our assets come from the RIA market. It's been amazing.

Raj Mahajan: Now, at a trillion. I'm sure there's a lot of lessons in leadership. And you've built this culture that prizes evidence over ego. And how do you hire and develop people who can allow you to scale from $500 billion to a trillion and where you're going next?

David Booth: One of the things we don't have difficulty doing, same with Goldman, is we don't have trouble finding really bright people that want to work hard. That's kind of a given. But what we're looking for, first off, is this person a team player. And the other thing is, you know, they kind of have to believe our story. I mean, we have a different point of view about markets and how they work. If you want to do a lot of trading, you probably won't last in our firm.

Raj Mahajan: We've seen a massive rise in retail. And their participation seems to be in equal parts active trading, you know, prediction markets. You know, you can't watch a sports game without sports betting. How do you help educate people on the distinction between whatever you want to call that and investing? Because they're coming into the market, which is a good thing. But how do you characterize the distinction?

David Booth: Well, let's talk about risk and return. In the prediction markets, you're taking a risk. You wonder, is there going to be a return there? Gambling is gambling. You know? As you start with the market, I call buying the market investing. And it's perfectly reasonable for people to take some of their money and say, "Look, I'd like to do something else with it. You know, private equity or pick a few stocks." It's irresistible. I wouldn't do it. It's okay for some people, but it's not right for me anyway. Anyway.

Raj Mahajan: There are a couple of stories in the book that I know had a profound impact on you. Do you mind sharing a little bit about your high school math teacher and what that lesson learned was? Because I'm seeing it as a through line in a lot of what you're talking about.

David Booth: Yeah, I think that-- actually her name was Mrs. McReynolds. What I've learned is almost everybody has a Mrs. McReynolds story. Well, mine was that my senior year in high school I was taking a calculus class. And this is where the University of Kansas is. And they had arranged with the university that at the end of the first semester if you took a test, you did well enough, they would give you college credit for it. And so, I took the test and I didn't do well enough to get college credit. And I was totally humiliated because I'd always taken great pride in my math. And so, I transferred out of calculus.

And in my new class, you know, the first day of class, I'm sitting there and Mrs. McReynolds walks into this new class. I'm trying to look inconspicuous and she's out there pointing, "see me in the hall." And so, I go out there and she just tells me how badly she feels. And she wants me back in the class.

She'd realized when I wasn't there in the class that, you know, she wondered where I was. She went down to the office, found out where my new class was, came out and found me. And that changed everything for me.

Raj Mahajan: She believed in you.

David Booth: Believed in me. And so, as you know, I mean, kind of my career from that point on, basically, was a heavy dose of math, econometrics, and stuff. But I wouldn't have done it without her.

Raj Mahajan: It's amazing how even someone as successful in this field needed somebody to say, "You can do this and, you know, don't quit at this, you know, I believe in you."

David Booth: Sometimes it's the little, seeming little things that you do can have a huge impact long-term for people that you work with. That's one of the points we try to stress with people. And sometimes I ask people, tell me a story about how you dealt with uncertainty. You had a big decision to make, what did you do? And often it comes down to, well, first off, I played for the long haul. I wasn't that concerned about, you know, next month, which gets into compounding. And where you end up in life, you know, it is the result of the compounding of many decisions you made over time.

Raj Mahajan: There's no shortcuts.

David Booth: There's no shortcuts. And maybe that's where wisdom comes from.

Raj Mahajan: David, you're an inspiration and a legend in our industry. Thank you for being here today. And everyone should read this book. Thank you very much.

David Booth: Thank you.

articles.title: Business Checkpoint: Bigger and better
articles.text: Taylor Bowley September 2026 Bank of America Institute's Business Checkpoint is a new evolution of our Small Business Checkpoint, broadening the data set from firms with <$5M in annual revenue to those with <$50M. Not only does this increase the number of businesses in our dataset, but mid-sized firms generate more than double the share of revenue of smaller firms, according to Census Bureau data. Since May, small business profitability growth has exceeded that of mid-sized firms, with hiring-related payments also improving, while mid-sized firms have shown more modest gains across both measures in August, according to Bank of America business account data. Meanwhile, payroll growth in August has strengthened among mid-sized firms despite weaker employment gains, while both small and mid-sized businesses have exhibited accelerated AI-related spending growth, suggesting firms are adapting to the current environment in different ways depending on their size. Read our full analysis for a more in-depth look at these trends. Business Checkpoint is a new, regular publication from Bank of America Institute. It provides a real-time view of the financial health, opportunities and challenges facing small and mid-sized businesses across the US economy, leveraging the depth and breadth of Bank of America's proprietary data. By analyzing activity among both small and mid-sized firms, Business Checkpoint offers timely insights into business profitability, hiring, investment and spending trends. Such data is not intended to be reflective or indicative of, and should not be relied upon as, the results of operations, financial condition or performance of Bank of America. Published on
23 October 2026

James Talbot, Executive Director for International at the Bank of England and the Bank’s Executive Sponsor for climate, explains how physical climate shocks can affect inflation and output, and how central banks can assess and respond to them. He considers two connected horizons: their near-term effects on monetary policy, and the longer-term role of economic resilience, adaptation and insurance in helping economies absorb future shocks and support price and financial stability.

Speech
Physical shocks increasingly matter for central banks
Governor, distinguished guests, I am sorry that I cannot be there with you in person at such a prestigious event. It is very much an honour and a pleasure, and my thanks to Dr. Fabrizio López-Gallo Dey for inviting me to speak today.
The physical impacts of climate change are becoming larger and more proximate, and their short-term economic impacts are also increasing. Annual global damages from weather-related events have more than doubled since the early 2000s, reaching over $200bn in 2025footnote [1].
In light of that, the economic effects of climate change are increasingly on the radar of central bankers. When extreme weather events affect production, output and inflation, that matters for our primary goal of maintaining price stability.
Let me take two examples that are close to home:
Increasingly high summer temperatures reduce water levels on key transport arteries for industrial trade, like the River Rhine in Germany. When water levels fall, ships reduce the amount of cargo they carry, disrupting the movement of goods and increasing transport costs.
Such exceptionally low water levels have become a recurring feature in recent years. The economic effects have also been material: recent research estimates that 30 days of low water on the Rhine reduces German industrial production by around 1%footnote [2].
In October 2024, extreme rainfall caused devastating flash floods in Valencia. Aside from the tragic loss of human life, economic losses amounted to over 20% of regional GDP. Spanish Q4 GDP growth was reduced by between 0.1 and 0.2 percentage pointsfootnote [3].
The economic impact would have been larger were it not for the high level of insurance protection for affected households and businesses. Around 250,000 insurance claims were filed following the floods and Spain's Insurance Compensation Consortium had paid more than €4bn in compensation by late 2025, making this the largest event the scheme has ever managedfootnote [4].
Even countries like the UK, which may be less susceptible to large physical shocks, can be affected by the impact of events abroad.
Over the past four years, as chair of the NGFS Workstream on Monetary Policy, I have worked together with more than sixty central banks to set out a framework to assess the impact of climate change on the economy, to measure its effects and to determine what monetary policymakers should do about it.
I’ll talk today about how the physical impacts of climate change can affect the economy in the near term; how we diagnose their magnitude, persistence and propagation; whether their effects belong in the central forecast or in the risks around it; and how that diagnosis informs monetary policy judgements. We set out each of these steps in an NGFS guide for monetary policymakers that we published earlier this yearfootnote [5].
I also want to look beyond the near-term policy horizon. In particular, how repeated losses, adaptation, fiscal space and insurance protection gaps shape the capacity of economies and financial systems to absorb future shocks.
I will argue that these two horizons are connected: The resilience an economy has built determines the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic impact of a shock over the monetary-policy horizon. And, in turn, repeated shocks can erode that resilience over the longer term, eventually exacerbating the effects of climate shocks when they occur.
How physical shocks transmit through the economy
Let me start with how physical shocks can affect the economy.
Physical hazards can operate through several channels at once: They can damage capital. They can reduce labour supply and lower productivity. They can disrupt transport and supply chains. They can weaken demand and confidence among economic agents, tighten credit conditions and raise uncertainty.
Importantly for monetary policymakers, those channels can interact and may also move output and inflation in different directions, making the policy response more challenging.
But different physical hazards can transmit through the economy in different ways. To give some examplesfootnote [6]:

Heatwaves transmit as a shock to productive capacity and labour supply. They push down on GDP while increasing inflation volatility, making them relevant for monetary policy even though direct physical damage is not as visible as for a flood or storm.
Droughts reduce productive capacity in agriculture pushing down on production and up on prices. They can raise inflation both through the effect on domestic production and through more expensive imports.
Floods and cyclones damage the capital stock, reducing demand and investment, which can in turn push down on output and inflation. But floods can also be inflationary where they hit food supply, logistics or essential infrastructure.

So while there is no one-size-fits-all pattern for the effects of a physical shock, there are some common themes:

Shocks are often transmitted through a disruption to production;
That usually means that output and inflation often move in opposite directions; and
Even when shocks occur overseas, these can be transmitted through changes to exports and commodity prices, particularly for open economies. Indeed, a 2022 study for the euro area showed that for every 1% unanticipated increase in globally traded food prices, overall inflation rose by 0.1%footnote [7].

This latter channel is also particularly important for the UK since we import around 40% of our food. In recent work at the Bank of England, we have looked at the impacts of extreme weather events on commodity prices and UK inflationfootnote [8]. The estimates from the model suggest that global weather-related disruption has played a non-trivial role in UK food and headline inflation over the past two decades
This makes climate-related shocks relevant to our regular inflation forecasting. Indeed, many central banks are now assessing the impact of food, energy, supply-chain, and weather-related shocks. That is because these shocks are affecting inflation and output forecasts, or the risks around them, in an increasingly meaningful way.
The NGFS note on the economic and financial impacts of extreme weather events, produced for the 2026 French G7 Presidency, uses 31 case studies to show that these effects repeatedly appear in output, employment and prices across a geographically diverse range of countriesfootnote [9]. Supply-chain and trade linkages can also propagate these shocks beyond the country or region directly affected.
With that in mind, let me turn next to consider how central banks should diagnose the shock, assess its impact on their forecasts and the risks around them and therefore their monetary policy judgements.
A framework for assessing the impacts of climate shocks
Here I will draw on the recent NGFS guide on monetary policy strategy that I mentioned earlierfootnote [10]. The report provides a five-step approach to assess these impacts: identify, assess the propagation, assess whether a trade-off arises, set policy, communicate and monitor.
Step one is to identify the nature of the shock itself: How large is it? How long is it likely to last? Which regions and sectors are affected? Is it localised or widespread? And is it a one-off event or one in a sequence of shocks?
Those distinctions matter.
A short-lived disruption affecting a relatively narrow part of the economy during the low season of economic activity poses a very different challenge from a shock affecting food, energy, or critical infrastructure, or services such as tourism during peak season. And a sequence of individually temporary shocks may have quite different macroeconomic consequences from an isolated event.
Having identified the shock, step two is to assess how it propagates through the economy.
Here, the familiar distinction between direct, indirect and second-round effects is particularly useful.
Direct – or first round – effects are the immediate relative-price effects from the shock: for example, a drought raising food prices, a heatwave reducing labour productivity, or a flood disrupting production and logistics.
Monetary policy cannot repair infrastructure, restore a harvest, or offset the initial physical damage. If the shock is short-lived and expectations remain anchored, the standard monetary policy response is usually to look through the first-round effects, because policy operates with a lag and tightening in response to a temporary supply shock can impose unnecessary output costs.
But the initial shock can spread more widely, having indirect effects, as firms pass higher input costs across supply chains. And there can be second-round effects through wages and inflation expectations. Workers may seek compensation for higher living costs; businesses may adjust their price-setting behaviour; and households and firms may revise their inflation expectations.
Food and energy prices can be particularly important here. Households observe them frequently and a well-established literature shows that they have an outsized effect on expectations about future inflation. Research conducted at the Bank of England reinforces that result for the UK, finding that more than 60% of households report that food prices heavily influence inflation perceptions. Food prices also matter significantly more for household inflation-expectations dynamics than other components, with effects at short, medium and long horizons.
Frequency of shocks matters too. An isolated rise in prices will feel different to a series of repeated upward moves. Indeed, a sequence of individually temporary shocks which arrive before the effects of previous disturbances have dissipated can look and feel like more persistent inflationary pressure. Repeated disruption can also erode fiscal buffers and weaken private-sector resilience.
Central banks should therefore focus closely on frequency, persistence and pass-through to overall inflation and inflation expectations.
From diagnosis to the monetary-policy response
Step three is next: does the identified shock create a trade-off between inflation and output?
As I noted earlier, hot and dry events provide relatively clear examples. By reducing agricultural production, a drought can weaken output while putting upward pressure on food prices. A heatwave pushing down on productivity can increase inflation volatility at the same time as hitting output. But if shocks primarily damage capital and reduce output, such as floods and storms in some circumstances, they can push down on inflation where demand effects dominate.
If you permit me a brief digression at this point, the situation becomes no easier when considering the economic impact of the policies enacted by governments to ensure that the necessary climate transition happens. These policies can also drive large and persistent relative price movements, shifts in investment and reallocation of production across sectors of the economy. Modelling the impact of these shocks is therefore no less important. Here, the NGFS and IMF published joint work earlier this year on how countries’ Nationally Determined Contributions to reducing emissions under the Paris Agreement will affect inflation and output across a range of economiesfootnote [11].
Step four is to set policy and communicate the decision.
Here, the assessment depends importantly on the wider economic environment at the point the shock arrives. If inflation is already elevated and expectations are less firmly anchored, the risk that an initial price increase develops into broader inflationary pressure may be greater, and the case for responding becomes stronger. If the economy has spare capacity and demand is weak, the case for looking through is stronger.
This is also where a central bank faces an important judgement: if the effects of a physical shock are material and sufficiently well understood, they may belong in the central forecast.
But where there is substantial uncertainty around the scale of a shock or the way it will propagate, scenarios can allow policymakers to explore and communicate risks. Scenarios can complement the central forecast by helping us explore precisely the kinds of uncertainty I have described today: whether a shock proves temporary or persistent; whether supply or demand effects dominate; and whether initial price increases generate material second-round effects.
The fifth and final step is to monitor and assess whether the economy is evolving in line with expectations and adjust policy in response to new data developments. Since there is also evidence that climate shocks can affect credit supply, collateral values or financial intermediation, central banks should also monitor the operation of the monetary transmission mechanism.
You will notice, of course, that the process I describe here is not that different to how central banks assess and respond to other economic shocks. That is because the impact of climate change is now one of the set of economic shocks that monetary policymakers consider.
From immediate shocks to the resilience threshold
Since climate shocks are likely to increase in both magnitude and frequency, another important question is whether economies and financial systems can continue to absorb rising losses from these shocks over the longer term.
The capacity of households, businesses, governments and financial systems to absorb losses is a key determinant of the recovery profile from a climate shock. Fiscal space, insurance penetration, climate adaptation, infrastructure quality, financial-market depth and institutional capacity all help to determine a country’s resilience threshold. Where those buffers are stronger, shocks are more likely to be absorbed. Where they are weaker, the effects can become more persistent and can spill into credit, financial stability and public-finance channels.
Less developed economies typically have lower resilience thresholds, meaning similar physical hazards can generate larger and more persistent macroeconomic damage. A previous study by Raddatz (2009) estimated that a climate-related disaster resulted in a cumulative per capita output loss of 0.25%, 0.5% and 1% for high, middle and low-income countries respectivelyfootnote [12].
But resilience is also not fixed. Repeated shocks can gradually erode the very buffers that help economies absorb losses in the first place, including fiscal space, private-sector balance sheets and insurance capacity. Without effective mitigation and adaptation, economies may therefore become less resilient over time, with the same physical hazard generating increasingly persistent effects on output, inflation, credit and public finances.
There is also evidence that these interactions can be non-linear. The NGFS’s 2023 work on compound risks examines precisely what can happen when shocks combine, either across time or across locations. It shows that the overall macroeconomic impact of compounding shocks can be materially greater than the sum of the partsfootnote [13].
This in turn feeds back to the short-term policy response. Resilience directly affects the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic consequences of a shock, and therefore how difficult it is for monetary policy to look through it. But if losses are absorbed quickly through insurance mechanisms or other buffers, the inflation-output trade-off may be shorter-lived.
There is therefore an important interaction between resilience and monetary policy. The more resilient an economy is, the easier it is to absorb physical shocks. As resilience erodes, the same shock can become progressively harder to look through.
Insurance protection gaps and why they matter for central banks
The provision of insurance helps economies to cushion the effect of physical shocks by pooling and transferring losses. High insurance penetration and rapid payouts can reduce household distress, firm insolvency and credit losses as well as supporting a faster recovery in output.
But as physical risks increase, rising and repeated losses could place pressure on the availability and affordability of insurance in areas exposed to these shocks. If insurance coverage falls, losses will instead fall on households, businesses, banks and governments.
Two recent events provide a sobering comparison. In Spain, public-private insurance arrangements helped absorb a significant share of losses from the 2024 floods whereas in Pakistan, following the 2022 floods, only around 1% of total damages were insured, leaving households and small firms far more exposed to income and wealth losses, generating larger macroeconomic impacts.
From a microprudential perspective, withdrawal of insurance provision may enhance the safety and soundness of insurance firms, because rising insured damages can significantly dent profitability and potentially threaten firm resilience.
As the insurance supervisor, our role is not to direct underwriting decisions by individual firms. But as a macroprudential authority, we will need to take a broader view of the implications for the financial system as a whole. Indeed, the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee highlighted this issue at its September 2026 meetingfootnote [14].
Where insurance coverage falls, uninsured risks will need to be redistributed:

For households, this means higher repair costs when physical risks strike, lower property values and potential difficulties obtaining a mortgage.
For businesses, it can mean bearing losses from the destruction of physical goods, capital and infrastructure.
For banks, it can mean weaker collateral values and higher credit losses.
For governments, it can mean more frequent pressure to act as insurer of last resort.

For the UK, Bank of England staff have modelled how a widening flood-insurance protection gap could spill over to the UK mortgage marketfootnote [15].
This analysis suggests that the share of UK mortgagors without insurance could rise from around 5% today to around 7-10% in 2050, or up to 16% following a severe flood event. The aggregate effects on house prices and mortgage impairments in that modelling are relatively small compared with the severe macroeconomic stresses against which the UK banking system is tested. But that does not mean the issue is trivial: the consequences for affected households, exposed lenders and local economies could still be significant.
There is an important lesson here: the answer cannot simply be more of the same insurance. Insurance capacity cannot sustainably compensate for underlying physical risks that continue to rise. Insurers will likely increasingly need to include risk prevention in product design, underwriting, and pricing practices.
Indeed, while a successful transition to net zero can limit the future increase in physical hazards, we will also need to consider the role of adaptation in a world where climate shocks are more frequent.
Investment in ensuring resilience to climate shocks can support insurability. This may require collaboration between businesses, households and governments. Updates to planning rules and building regulations could further mitigate the impact of increased physical hazards.
Actions to improve climate-related risk identification, measurement and modelling capabilities across the insurance sector, as envisaged under the recent update to the Bank of England’s supervisory expectations, should strengthen firms' ability to assess and price climate-related risksfootnote [16].
But the financial sector also has a long tradition of coming up with innovative solutions to difficult problems. In this regard, there may be scope for greater collaboration between insurers, reinsurers and banks to share data, develop products and risk-transfer mechanisms that support resilience and help narrow protection gaps.
International cooperation
Let me finish with a word on international cooperation. Climate change is an issue which transcends borders and cannot be fixed by one country acting alone. In recent years, great strides have been made in multilateral fora like the NGFS to assess and model the impacts of climate change on the financial system. The NGFS’ flagship climate scenarios are an important tool in underpinning climate risk assessment in the financial sector. The work of the International Sustainability Standards Board to ensure consistent and better climate disclosures is helping financial firms to better manage climate-related risks and to make better decisions on where to allocate capital.
The 2025 South African G20 Presidency focused on the issue of natural catastrophe protection gaps, drawing on joint work from the World Bank and the International Association of Insurance Supervisorsfootnote [17]. That work helped to raise our collective understanding of these issues as well as suggesting a range of approaches to tackle them, tailored to country circumstances.
In 2026, the French G7 Presidency took this work forward by strengthening the evidence on the macro-financial consequences of extreme weather, while examining how to tackle protection gapsfootnote [18]. This issue is also on our radar as the UK develops priorities for its own G20 Presidency in 2027. In my view, there is value in better understanding how insurance protection gaps affect the economic impact of extreme-weather events and in exploring what can help sustain insurability and resilience as physical risks increase.
That could include looking at what constrains insurability, which approaches appear capable of operating at scale, and the conditions needed for them to work sustainably.
Insurance cannot close protection gaps on its own. But better data, investment in adaptation and more resilient infrastructure can help sustain affordable cover. Timely mitigation also remains essential to limit the future increase in physical risk.
That brings me back to the two connected horizons. In the near term, central banks will need to understand how physical and transition-related shocks affect inflation, output and expectations in order to deliver on their price stability mandate.
Further ahead, the availability of insurance will determine both the economic impact of climate shocks and the capacity of economies to absorb the resulting losses. It will also shape the prevailing environment in which central banks will pursue their price and financial stability goals.
As macroprudential policymakers, we understand that the availability of insurance matters to the resilience of the financial system as a whole. So as protection gaps widen, addressing them will require concerted action across governments, regulators, international institutions and the private sector. Multilateral fora can play an important role in supporting that dialogue and sharing lessons on what works.
As climate change increasingly affects our economies and financial systems, central banks will need to understand these effects, just like any other shock. This will enable us to make sure that the financial system remains stable and that price stability is maintained. And in turn that can provide a sustainable platform for governments to deliver the climate transition.
I would like to thank Danae Kyriakopoulou for assistance in writing this speech. I would also like to thank Lukasz Krebel and Fergus Booker for their input and helpful comments, as well as India Rimmer, Hannah Copeland, Boromeus Wanengkirtyo, Dario Bonciani, Riccardo Masolo, Silvia Sarpietro, Nikoleta Anesti, Vania Esady, Matthew Naylor, Will Banks, Kemal Erçevik, Alex Curtis and Jemima Hall for their underlying research.

articles.title: European strategic autonomy: a €1.8 trillion investment opportunity - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
Europe is embarking on a far-reaching drive to strengthen its strategic autonomy, reducing dependence on external partners across critical areas including defence, energy, technology, healthcare, food security and industry.

For investors, the scale of this transformation could be significant. As Lazare Hounhouayenou, Portfolio Manager, tells Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, around €1.8 trillion of investment is expected to be deployed by 2035 under major European and national initiatives.

The spending could create powerful long-term opportunities for European companies exposed to these strategic sectors, potentially supporting growth and corporate profitability. Defence is already seeing increased investment, while measures to protect strategic industries and accelerate investment in space and technology point to a broader industrial policy shift.

Progress, however, is unlikely to be linear. Differing national priorities, regulatory hurdles and Europe’s complex decision-making processes could generate short-term volatility. “Yet the direction of travel is becoming clearer: Europe is recognising its vulnerabilities and taking concrete steps to address them.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast to discover how European strategic autonomy is opening new horizons for investors.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Lazare Hounhouayenou

Daniel Morris: Hello and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode will be discussing European strategic autonomy. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Lazare Hounhouayenou, Portfolio Manager. Welcome, Lazare, and thanks for joining me.

LH: Happy to be here.

DM: We’re all aware of the capex that’s being devoted to the development of artificial intelligence technologies – trillions in the US but significant amounts of money elsewhere, certainly in Europe. But we may not be quite so aware of what is going on in Europe around strategic autonomy initiatives. I hear that there’s supposed to be about €1.8 trillion devoted to this theme in the years ahead. Let’s get back to basics. To begin with, could you give us a simple and concise definition of strategic autonomy?

LH: Strategic autonomy refers to the ability of a state – or a group of states such as the EU – to act independently on the international stage and defend its interests against the world’s major power[s] in areas considered essential.

The means used to achieve these objectives, as well as the assessments criteria for sovereignty, evolve over time. In the ’60s, a state’s sovereignty was measured by its industrial and military power. Today, with the rise of AI, it is also determined by data centres, AI models.

This evolution raises new questions such as ‘has the control of [micro]chips and data centres replace[d] the control of physical borders?’ Or ‘does the state still maintain its cultural and political sovereignty when its citizens access information, communicate and form opinion[s] through AI algorithm[s] developed under a different jurisdiction?

In this polarised world, what is Europe’s position and where the region can create value according to its strengths in the long term? We think that regaining sovereignty is an absolute necessity for Europe, which must reposition itself within this new geopolitical landscape.

This requires reducing its dependence on partners and former partners across a number of sectors. Defence is one of them, but energy resources, industry, technology, healthcare and food security must also be mentioned.

DM: That sounds quite comprehensive. Can you make the connection, though, between these initiatives, and why Europe undergoing this shift to greater strategic autonomy is important for investors?

LH: Since 2022, the European Union and several European countries have launched a number of major initiatives involving significant level of investments aimed at strengthening Europe’s autonomy in sectors consider strategic and essential. Looking at the main programmes alone, we estimate that nearly 1.8 trillion of investment will be deployed by 2035.

Naturally, European industrial companies with exposure to these sectors are expected to benefit from this powerful long-term investment trend. In this context, investors have an opportunity to position themselves for the long term by investing in sectors with strong growth prospects while at the same time supporting Europe’s strategic autonomy agenda.

DM: When you look at these initiatives, are you seeing practical consequences from Europe’s decisions? That is, are you seeing progress or, conversely, obstacles, delays, rivalries that justif[y] some people’s scepticism and arguably could generate volatility in the short term?

LH: Europe is moving in the right direction, even if progress is never fast enough. Given the urgency of the situation, Europe is reconsidering its governance framework and recognises that its decision-making process[es] are not sufficiently agile.

Recently, Germany and France proposed to create a new cooperation format bringing together the European Union’s six largest economies. This is intended to overcome the slow pace of decision-making within the EU and allow the core group of countries to make faster progress on economic and strategic priorities.

At the same time, Europe has taken concrete measures in defence. For instance, we are seeing EU member states accelerating spending to meet NATO targets of three and a half [per cent] of GDP for core defence expenditure by 2035. The NATO summit held in Turkey last June just confirmed this trajectory.

Europe protected its steel industry through a protectionist steel action plan, reflected in a 50% increase in tariffs and a 47% reduction in import quotas.

And in the crucial space sector, the European Space agency has approved €22 billion for [20]26 to 20. This is an increase of nearly 30%. The objective is to strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy in space technology and mission[s].

This non-exhaustive list of proposals and decisions clearly show that Europe is advancing its thinking and governance and taking concrete action. However, Europe has still many challenges to overcome as interest[s] and priority[ies] differ from one country to the other, which is only natural when 27 countries are involved. These disagreements will create volatility around strategic autonomy themes.

But we believe it is important to take a step back and focus on the medium and long-term trajectory, which appear[s] to be moving in the right direction.

DM: Lazare, if I can summarise some of the key points that you shared with us? You explained that simply, European strategic autonomy is a group of policies/initiatives that enable Europe to act more independently on the international stage, with a focus on many sectors – industrial policy, defence, AI, to cite just a few. You highlighted that we’re talking about €1.8 trillion planned to be invested in the years ahead.

The significance of this for investors is simply that a lot of that money will flow to companies and ultimately should drive corporate profits. You acknowledge that it’s not as smooth or quick as we might like, but the important thing to keep in mind is that Europe is moving in the right direction. It does recognise the problems it’s facing and is working to tackle those problems. Well, Lazare, thank you very much for joining me.

LH: Thank you, Daniel. It was a pleasure to have the discussion with you.

The race for electricity, and the companies positioned to profit.
Energy is the only universal currency.
— Vaclav Smil
In 1900, the historian Henry Adams wandered into the Gallery of Machines at the Paris Exposition and found himself standing before a forty-foot dynamo. He later recalled that he “began to feel the forty-foot dynamos as a moral force, much as the early Christians felt the Cross.” Adams grasped something his contemporaries were only beginning to see: humanity had discovered a new object of reverence, a seemingly limitless source of power around which it would reorganize society and direct its collective ambitions.
Over the next half-century, the United States acted on that insight. It strung wire across the continent, built Hoover Dam in about five years, sent the Tennessee Valley Authority into places that had never seen a light bulb, and split the atom to boil water for the grid. The conviction behind all of it was that abundant energy would pay for itself many times over, in ways no one could yet imagine.
Then the ambition faded. American electricity demand, which roughly doubled every decade after the war, slowed through the 1970s and 1980s, and from the mid-2000s to the early 2020s it barely moved at all. Efficiency gains and offshored industry kept demand flat, which hid the decay, and a nation that once measured its ambition in gigawatts learned to treat flat consumption as a virtue. Institutions that had raised dams in five years began taking ten to approve a transmission line. Permitting became a sport of attrition. By the early 2020s, more generating capacity was waiting in interconnection queues for permission to plug in than existed on the entire grid.

That complacency is now colliding with the largest new source of demand in generations. AI offers the chance to bring skilled physicians, patient tutors, capable lawyers and first-rate scientists to everyone who needs them, rather than rationing that expertise by geography and fortune. If the dynamo was the moral force of Adams’ century, diffused intelligence is the moral force of ours.
But intelligence runs on electricity. Wherever power is scarce, intelligence will be too.
The Size of the Problem
The amount of AI compute that can be deployed is limited by two physical inputs: the chips available, and powered, cooled, grid-connected space in which to put them. Whichever is scarcer sets the limit:
Deployed Compute = min(chips available, powered capacity)
Both are constrained today, but power is harder to fix, for two reasons. The first is speed: chip production can expand in a matter of quarters, while new generation and transmission take years. The second is how each is allocated. Chips are sold in a market, so a buyer can pay more for earlier access, and higher prices draw more supply. Grid access is allocated through planning processes, interconnection queues and, ultimately, politics. Paying more does not move a project to the front of the line, though agreeing to be cut off when the grid is tight increasingly can. When price can’t clear a market, the rents go to whoever controls the allocation (queue positions, permitted sites) and whoever sells a substitute that is priced in a market (on-site generation). That is where this report looks for returns: turbine slots, castings, engines, fuel cells, transformers, crews, and guaranteed, uninterrupted electricity supply, or “firm power”. Inputs in global oversupply, such as battery cells, are not where the money is.
The strain is already visible. PJM’s capacity auctions have cleared at the price cap three times in a row, and the last two still fell 6.6 to 6.8 GW short of the reliability target, the first such shortfalls in its history. The market offered the highest price allowed, and the supply still did not appear. In Texas, ERCOT’s queue of large loads grew from 63 GW at the end of 2024 to 474 GW by June, about 90% of it data centers. In August the governor ordered an audit of every data center in the queue, and ERCOT has since paused energization approvals for data centers and crypto miners of 75 MW or more, including 17 projects that had already passed stability studies.
Because chips scale faster than the grid, the gap between what is asking to connect and what can connect is more likely to widen than to close. We can measure both sides in gigawatts. On the chip side, AEI’s Voltcraft paper estimates that NVIDIA, Google and Amazon will produce about 15 GW of accelerators this year, measured at the chip, rising to about 25 GW in 2028. Once you add the servers, networking and cooling around them, that comes to roughly 26 GW at the meter in 2026 and 46 GW in 2028. On the power side, SemiAnalysis expects about 25 GW of new server capacity to come online outside China this year, or roughly 30 GW at the meter. Two independent methods land in the same range. We use 26 GW this year and 46 GW in 2028 as the yardstick throughout.
Forecasting the Future of Energy Needs
No one knows how much electricity AI will need, and we won’t pretend to. The answer rests on three variables nobody can forecast with confidence: how much power each unit of compute will need, how many tokens a task will take as models improve, and whether usage spreads until most people use AI like today’s heaviest 1% of users, or fleets of always-on agents run around the clock.
So the official estimates agree on the direction of data center demand but differ widely on its magnitude, and each forecast keeps being revised up:

In share terms, data centers used about 4.7% of U.S. electricity in 2024. LBNL now projects 9.5% to 15.3% by 2030, and EPRI up to 17% by 2030.
Supply looks worse. NERC expects summer peak demand to rise 224 GW over the next decade and warns that 13 of 23 regions could face shortfalls by 2030, starting with the Midwest as early as 2028. DOE found that only 22 GW of the roughly 209 GW of generation planned by 2030 can run on demand, and that scheduled retirements could raise outage risk a hundredfold.
If the grid can’t connect the forecast demand, timelines will slip, and grid construction will set the pace of AI this decade. Anyone who can deliver power sooner than the grid can will be able to charge for it.
Generation
Every source of new power can be judged on three things: how soon it can deliver, what it costs, and whether it runs on demand. For most of the grid’s history, cost mattered most, because a utility that waited a few extra years for the cheapest plant lost little. For an AI campus, every month without power is a month of idle chips losing value. In a 1 GW facility, that is $2.8 to $3.3 billion of chip depreciation a year, whether or not the chips are running, or roughly $8 million for every day the power isn’t there.

The cheapest firm power, a large combined-cycle gas plant, is among the slowest to arrive. The fastest options, fuel cells and smaller on-site engines, cost more for every megawatt-hour. Solar and wind are cheap, but they are not firm. Nuclear restarts come closest to all three, but only three retired U.S. reactors are being brought back, and all of them are already spoken for.
Faced with that trade-off, the largest buyers have declined to choose. Instead they are placing bets across nearly every technology at once:

The sections that follow take each source in turn, starting with the one carrying the most weight today.
Gas Turbines
The grid can’t connect load fast enough, so the industry is increasingly building its own power. SemiAnalysis expects more than 40 GW of U.S. data center capacity to run behind the meter by 2028, meaning power plants built on site, outside the grid’s interconnection queue. That would supply more than half of the new data centers coming online that year. In 2026, if you’re building your own power plant, it almost certainly runs on gas.
That puts the AI industry in line for gas turbines. Wood Mackenzie counted about 110 GW of turbine orders at the end of 2025, against 60 to 70 GW of worldwide manufacturing capacity a year (a snapshot that excludes slot reservations and predates 2026’s surge).
Running one year of 2026 accelerator output entirely on new gas would take about 40% of everything the major turbine makers can build in a year. For 2028’s output it would take about 70%. And data centers are competing for those slots with everyone else: at GE Vernova ($GEV), about 80% of the roughly 100 GW it had under contract in Q1 2026 was with utilities, power producers and industrial customers, and only about 20% was tied explicitly to data center load.
As a result, a large turbine now takes about five years to deliver.
The Oligopoly
The large-frame gas turbine business is essentially an oligopoly of three: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy ($SMERY), and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries ($MHVIY). Together they hold about two-thirds of global manufacturing capacity, and all three are sitting on enormous backlogs:

The textbook response to the backlog would be to build capacity as fast as possible. Still marked by the gas turbine bust of the early 2000s, and in GE’s case by a $22 billion write-down of its power business in 2018, all three are instead expanding cautiously and letting customers carry the risk:

Slot reservations. Customers pay deposits to hold a production slot and forfeit them if they don’t convert to a firm order, so the manufacturer gets paid either way.
Incremental expansion. GE Vernova’s plan works out to about 11% a year and Mitsubishi’s to about 12%, against backlogs several years deep.
Higher prices. GE Vernova’s first-half 2026 orders were priced 10 to 20% higher per kilowatt than its Q4 2025 orders, and Wood Mackenzie expects turbine prices to reach $600/kW by the end of 2027, nearly triple 2019 levels.

For shareholders, the turbine makers’ discipline extends pricing power, and the deposits cushion the downside if the cycle turns.

The North American power landscape is evolving
Utilities, hyperscalers, and other offtakers are seeking a broader mix of resources to balance affordability, reliability, and emissions goals – from collocated solar and storage to SMRs and gas. Solar and energy storage are gaining share, bolstered by their cost profile and development timeline. These advantages help meet the surge in demand from data centers and reshored manufacturing. At the same time, geopolitical volatility and supply-chain pressures are reshaping market conditions.

Why attend the North American Power & Renewables Forum 2027?

The solar & energy storage journey
For 20 years, the Solar & Energy Storage Summit has grown alongside the solar and storage sectors to become a key industry gathering for developers, IPPs, and investors. The new North American Power & Renewables Forum will continue to cover solar and storage markets in depth, while placing them in the broader context of North America and global power markets. As the audience expands, the solar and energy storage community will gain greater access to their utility and C&I customers, along with crucial interconnected intelligence across technologies and markets.
What’s new at the North American Power & Renewables Forum?
The expanded Forum will bring together leaders from across the power sector, including renewables, conventional generation, utilities, data centers, other commercial and industrial offtakers, and government, to examine the forces reshaping North America’s power market.
What will remain the same at the North American Power & Renewables Forum?
The Forum will continue to showcase the deeply researched data and insight from Wood Mackenzie’s interconnected intelligence. It will dive deep into technology and market issues that drive North America’s power mix to allow attendees to understand the root of the problem and different viewpoints on solutions.

articles.title: View from the markets: The earnings season has been good, but is it good enough? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

At first blush, there is little to complain about regarding the third-quarter earnings results so far (about half of the companies in the S&P 500 and MSCI Europe have reported). Compared to the third quarter in 2025, profits have risen by 26% for the S&P 500 and by 40%(!) for Europe, with double-digit figures for other major indices, based on data from FactSet (see Exhibit 1). This is well above historical norms.

The worry is that those values are not far off what was expected by analysts, and in one case it was below. Earnings have come in only 2% better than expected for the S&P 500. Typically, earnings surprises (how much better or worse results are versus consensus) run in the 3-4% range. Over the previous few quarters, they were even higher. This quarter few indices have matched that.

The chart shows clearly what the source of the disappointment has been: technology. The surprise for the Nasdaq 100 index is -3% and for emerging market (EM) tech stocks it is -8%. The disappointments in emerging markets were almost entirely driven by tech stocks; results for the other sectors were 1% better.

There are two questions: Are these disappointments surprising and how much do they matter?

Given not only how high expectations have been for technology stocks, and how rapidly the artificial intelligence theme is developing, it is not surprising that companies have reported results that are further off the mark than is typically the case.

Though there has been some disappointment in the short term (which will drive the short-term performance of the stock), the more important consideration for investors is the medium-term outlook (which will determine the stock’s medium-term path).

It is worth recalling that consensus estimates for Nasdaq 100 earnings growth in 2027 is 35% and for emerging market technology stocks it is 39%. Even if actual results are a few percentage points lower, and if valuations do not change significantly, indices would typically appreciate in line with earnings.

Sector drivers

It is not only the tech sector that has boosted EPS (earnings-per-share) growth rates. Higher energy prices have contributed to strong results for indices like MSCI Europe and Russell Value. Excluding the energy sector, earnings growth for MSCI Europe is a (still good) 17%. But even setting aside the gains from tech and higher oil prices, results across other sectors are robust. The automobile industry continues to be a drag on the consumer discretionary sector, but most of the others are seeing high single or double-digit earnings growth (see Exhibit 2).

Whether this broadening in earnings continues, or even accelerates, will partly depend on the rate of adoption of AI technologies. There is already significant anecdotal evidence of companies finding meaningful productivity improvements through AI. One example is insurance companies reducing their claims review times and credit losses by using micro-expression recognition technology.

Stories of CFOs becoming alarmed by high AI bills also suggests adoption is accelerating. This will be critical not only for the future rate of non-tech company earnings growth, but also for the hyperscalers, as they look for the return on their massive capital expenditure.

Performance data/data sources: FactSet, BNP Paribas AM, as of 30 October 2026, unless otherwise stated. Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

New UBS Investor Watch research reveals

that business owners remain remarkably optimistic,

but many are also navigating significant decisions

around AI adoption, exit planning and political uncertainty.

We'll explore the findings and what they could mean for business

owners and investors alike right here on UBS.

Trending.

Welcome back to UBS Studios I'm Dan

Cassidy, as we look ahead to the 2026 election.

UBS recently released the latest Investor Watch survey

gathering perspectives from business owners across the country.

The findings offer some fascinating insights into how owners

are thinking about growth, the economy, artificial intelligence

and the future of businesses they've spent years building.

Joining me here at the table today, glad to welcome James Jack,

Head of the Business Owners Client Segment at UBS,

and Paul Hsiao from the UBS Chief Investment Office.

James, Paul, it's great to be at the table with you both.

Thank you for dropping by.

Thanks for having us. Thanks for having us.

So, James, let's dive right into it.

The survey was quite fascinating.

The findings, it seems,

despite a lot of uncertainty surrounding the economy,

the upcoming election,

business owners remain remarkably optimistic.

Why do you believe that is?

Yeah, I think,

what really stood out to me is just how much at stake,

personally, these business owners have.

When in the survey, we saw that 87% of business owners

were highly optimistic, like you said,

about their business outlook.

But we also uncovered that more than half of the owners

we surveyed

said that at least half of their wealth

is tied up in their business.

And, I think that helps really explain

why the election matters differently for a business owner.

When they're thinking about taxes, interest rates, tariffs

or potential policy changes,

they're not just thinking about what

those things mean for the economy,

but they're tying

it back to their own business and their own personal wealth.

You really see that come together when you look at exit timing.

About a third expect to exit within five years.

But 63% worry

that the midterm elections could affect their exit strategy,

and 57% have either accelerated

or are considering accelerating their timetable

because of the uncertainty around the political environment

or potential policy changes.

So I think that's an interesting tension between optimism and,

practicality,

especially on something so meaningful to their wealth.

Now, Paul, it's interesting, if you look at the markets,

they seem to be looking past traditional recession markers.

I think about slow job growth, low consumer confidence,

higher interest rates.

Why do you believe that is?

Right, so I'd say it's soft

data like sentiment indicators

indicate some challenges ahead for the economy.

But really when you look at the fundamentals

from both a corporate side

and the household side, things look really, really strong.

For example, on the corporate side,

our EPS estimates for this year

keep getting revised up whenever we have earnings season.

And that's really driven

by these large hyperscalers, which are really

what the markets are paying attention on.

In fact, they've been so good that the CapEx expectations that

they announced in the first half of this year

have been revised up by a couple hundred billion dollars,

showing how much of this demand has materialized,

and that they keep saying

that the amount of supply that's coming online has less than what

can operate right now.

Then you look at the consumer side of the economy,

which is still the bulwark of the US

economy, and consumer confidence is near recession territory.

And that's quite important going into these midterm elections.

However, when you look at spending tensions and actual spending,

that's held up either

at historic standards

or actually quite a little bit stronger than historic standards.

So consumers are gloomy, but they keep spending.

And when we look into that with even with a slower job growth,

looking at median net worth has gone up

1.5 to 2 times

depending on what income quartile you are since 2019.

So a lot of it is driven by the high stock market,

which is also feeding back into the corporate side.

And that's

because the stock market is driven

by these healthy amount of earnings.

Now, James,

given the interplay around

monetizing their businesses, especially over the next few years,

what should business owners be doing right now

to prepare

both the business and themselves for

what could be the most significant financial

event of their lives?

The biggest thing

is to, start early and be intentional.

There's a lot that can be done to create a great outcome,

but that planning often needs

to happen months or even years in advance.

I think about it in three parts.

First.

Work with your advisors to think through your financial plan.

Tax considerations, trusts, philanthropy,

and ultimately how much you keep after a transaction.

At the same time, get the business itself ready.

Understand the drivers of value

and what you can do today

to put the company in the strongest possible position.

And the survey really reinforces why starting early matters.

Owners may feel prepared going into a sale, but,

those who have actually been through it tell a different story.

84% said they wish they had spent much more time preparing,

and 80%, actually, of former owners felt

a real sense of loss after selling their business.

So finally, prepare yourself emotionally and personally.

Selling a business.

I say often it changes so much more than your balance sheet.

For many owners, the business provides their time,

their social life, and their sense of purpose.

So thinking about that

next chapter should really be a part of your planning as well.

James, I have to ask you about artificial intelligence AI.

How are business owners right now thinking about AI adoption

as we look forward?

We, we really see both optimism and concern.

So 82% expect

AI to impact their business over the next 12 months.

To me, that tells us

AI has moved well beyond technology companies and is becoming,

a real strategic issue

for businesses across all different industries.

At the same time, though, owners are,

I think, very clear eyed about the risks.

66% are concerned about data privacy.

64% about misinformation, and 63% about loss of human control.

So owners recognize the opportunity, but they're also thinking

carefully about how to capture those benefits,

while certainly managing all of the risks.

Now, Paul, from a top down perspective, AI application,

how do you see business owners putting this technology to work?

Yeah, I think

it's worthwhile

talking about AI both in a macro and micro perspective.

So on the macro front,

the way CIO likes to think about

AI usage is really as a flywheel.

You have these frontier companies coming out with models

that can do more and more productive things.

That's driving demand.

And we're tracking demand through token usage and broad adoption,

which also powers CapEx investment,

because more CapEx investment,

you have more compute power to then

do those really productive things that we were talking about.

So it's sort of a virtuous cycle there.

And from a demand front,

we're seeing so far this year, we've seen frontier models,

launch very new capabilities like broad based agentic AI.

We've seen token usage

really explode in the last couple of months,

despite prices coming down.

And then we've seen CapEx expectations for more compute power

built out.

So it's clear to us that more and more

AI demand is coming online.

And that's reflected

both in private and public surveys of AI adoption.

Depending where you look at,

anywhere between a quarter to half of US firms are adopting AI.

But more importantly, looking at the trajectory

they're going upwards.

And we expect that

to even accelerate coming into 2027. From a micro point of view.

and I think this is worthwhile

for a lot of our business owner clients, is that it really

has yet to materialize in both productivity and,

margin expansion.

And I think

that's where a lot of the benefits

when it comes to asset allocation can happen in 2027.

We're not looking at those

who just build the picks and shovels, but also which firms,

which sectors are adopting AI to really expand their margins.

And I think an underreported statistic right now is that business

formation in the US

has risen and is now at the highest levels since,

the survey was recorded back in 2005.

So 20 year high.

A lot of that is a lot of entrepreneurs are taking these AI tools

to help them launch a business for the first time.

So what we're seeing is AI is being used in business and jobs.

But it's going to take a while for it

to really be implemented in workflows to see that productivity

and margin expansion.

Well, Paul James, it's really fascinating to hear about

what's top of mind for our business owner clients.

Just one takeaway

before we close out. I want to highlight to our viewers

one of the key themes from today's discussion

is that business owners aren't standing still.

They're investing, planning, preparing for the future,

and evaluating everything from elections

to artificial intelligence

through the lens of long-term business value and personal wealth.

With that, the latest Investor
