articles.title: The Foundations of a Russian Dictatorship: The Kremlin’s New Ideology
articles.text: Source: GettyPaperCarnegie Russia Eurasia CenterThe Foundations of a Russian Dictatorship: The Kremlin’s New IdeologyThe concept authored by Sergei Kiriyenko and his team can be considered not only an apologia for the Putin regime, but also a blueprint for Russia’s future configuration.Link CopiedBy Andrey PertsevPublished on Oct 29, 2026In the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine and more than a quarter-century since Vladimir Putin entered the Kremlin, his regime finally has something approaching an ideological foundation: a set of ideas formulated by First Deputy Chief of Staff Sergei Kiriyenko and his domestic policy team. There is no single compilation of these ideas, but their essence can be gleaned from detailed ideological writings by Kremlin officials and from Putin’s own statements. This quasi-ideology justifies the existence of an imperial-style state in which society is relegated to the status of a passive object, with the ruling authorities setting the agenda and guarding control over the tools for implementation.One of the key elements of Kiriyenko’s approach is the articulation of a set of norms—described in Kremlin parlance as “Russia’s civilizational code”—by which the population is supposed to live. The key tenets of this code include the sacralization of power, collectivism, a preference for faith over rationality or logic, and readiness to sacrifice one’s interests and even life for the sake of the state. They are laid out in articles written by Kremlin officials1 and in the new compulsory course for university students, “Foundations of Russian Statehood.”2The other pole of Kiryenko’s conceptual framework is a “theory of civilizations” that borrows heavily from the work of Lev Gumilev, a Soviet-era historian and cult figure who was the son of the famed poet Anna Akhmatova. According to Gumilev, Russia is a young civilization with everything still ahead of it, unlike the supposedly decaying West.3 In this multipolar world of civilizations, there are no universal rules. This concept is in line with President Putin’s public views, enabling him to justify virtually any action, including the ongoing war against Ukraine.Kiriyenko’s team is striving to graft this doctrinal construct onto another of its inventions: the technocratic dictatorship. This is a model of governing the country in which the bureaucracy works efficiently and in harmony with the objectives for the Russian state that are determined by the leadership. According to this construct, society at large is excluded from both the processes of power formation and strategic decisionmaking. The technocratic dictatorship can be clothed in the doctrine of a civilization and sacrifice, or it can be left in its de-ideologized form.Perhaps equally important is that in the event of Putin’s departure from the Kremlin, Russia’s current political model could be embraced by virtually any autocratic leader or dictator who replaces him. Put another way, technocratic dictatorship is distilled Putinism—without the disadvantages of real Putinism, including personal obsessions like the reassertion of Moscow’s dominion over Ukraine.The Kremlin’s political bloc has already succeeded in creating mechanisms for disseminating this doctrine. Those mechanisms reach all first-year university students in Russia and are also gradually being introduced to the corporate sector.4This paper assesses in detail the elements that make up the jigsaw puzzle of the Kremlin’s ideological foundations and shows how they are interlinked. It argues that the concept authored by Kiriyenko and his team can be considered not only an apologia for the Putin regime, but also a blueprint for Russia’s future configuration. Finally, it analyzes the specific mechanisms that are being used to indoctrinate the population.White Russian Émigré RootsFor most of its existence, the Putin regime managed to govern the country without an official ideology. When Vladislav Surkov was in charge of the Kremlin’s domestic political team (until the end of 2011), he and his team prioritized ideas over ideology, placing their emphasis on the importance of “stability under Putin” and “sovereign democracy.”5 The former notion sought to shape the attitudes of the general public, highlighting a rapid rise in living standards under Putin and an implicit assurance that the county’s economic situation would not worsen on his watch. The latter was aimed at the more politically active part of society and solicited their buy-in for “Russian-style democracy.” (How the Russian version actually differed from the universally accepted definition of democracy was never made clear.) Under Surkov’s successor Vyacheslav Volodin (who served until October 2016), “sovereign democracy” was replaced by the “Crimea consensus.”6 Ideas or ideology meant far less to the Kremlin than leveraging a spike in public support for the regime following the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014.Yet none of these concepts offered a clear vision of the future or explained why the relationship between the Russian authorities and society was constructed the way it was. When Kiriyenko, who had always emphasized that he was first and foremost a technocrat, entered the Kremlin in 2016, he replaced any hints of ideology with corporate practices such as key performance indicators (KPIs).7 This was a deliberate tactic: Kiriyenko appreciated that foisting a distinct ideology on Russia would inevitably alienate citizens who did not share the key tenets, which ran against Putin’s belief in always seeking the approval of the majority.At the same time, Putin himself steadily became more ideological over the years of his lengthy reign. Starting in 2012 when he had to campaign to be re-elected as president after a term as prime minister to circumvent constitutional term limits, his public speeches increasingly featured musings on “spiritual bonds,”8 “traditional values,”9 and Russia’s “special civilizational path.”10 Putin’s ideas were (and remain) more historical, philosophical, and geopolitical than ideological per se. Putin also repeatedly expressed regret over the collapse of both the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union,11 which he described as vast, powerful, and populous states.12Putin’s early political career was within the circle of the liberal Anatoly Sobchak, the first mayor of St. Petersburg. Sobchak had a keen interest in Russia’s pre-revolutionary history, and, long before many other regional and municipal leaders, he initiated a referendum on changing his native city’s name back from Leningrad to its historical name of St. Petersburg. Interest in the pre-Soviet era and the search for positive sides to it were not all that unusual, especially among representatives of the late-Soviet intelligentsia and dissidents who typically viewed the period as a time of sustained development that was interrupted by revolutionary upheaval.In the late 1980s and early 1990s, historians and writers who had once been banned from the political mainstream were finally given a platform. Gumilev, the aforementioned historian who had developed a theory of passionarity to describe the unique qualities of the Russian people, became a constant on TV. According to Gumilev, passionarity is the desire of an individual or a group of people to change the world around them and move forward, as well as to sacrifice their comfort or even their lives for certain goals, which are often abstract and illusory.13In 1994, Gumilev’s fellow Gulag survivor, the Nobel Prize-winning dissident author Alexander Solzhenitsyn, returned to Russia after decades in exile. Works by émigré philosophers including Nikolai Berdyayev and Ivan Ilyin started being published inside Russia. Their presence in Russian intellectual currents in the early 1990s—a time of great hardship for ordinary Russians—helped foster a prevailing feeling of nostalgia for the pre-Soviet era, even though few people had any lived experience of that time.By all indications, Putin shared some of these sentiments. His speeches have included favorable references to Gumilev,14 Ilyin, and Berdyayev, and over time became more pointed in their hostility toward the 1917 October Revolution and Vladimir Lenin’s role in taking Russia off-course. The longer Putin remains in office, the more such ideas seem to have taken hold. This interest is also shared by others in his inner circle, including longtime crony Yury Kovalchuk; the head of the Foreign Intelligence Service, Sergei Naryshkin; and former culture minister Vladimir Medinsky.After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it was no longer possible to manage without a vision of the future and explanations for Russia’s economic problems and rows of freshly dug graves at cemeteries.For the Kremlin’s political bloc under both Volodin and then Kiriyenko, the widespread embrace of what were effectively White Russian émigré ideas was, if anything, counterproductive. (As noted above, during the Surkov era, Putin showed no inclination toward ideology.) The musings of Putin’s favorite philosophers and historians did not contain a clear vision of the future, which made them less useful for forming the foundations of an ideology. Worse still, they actually threatened to reduce public support for the regime and deepen a rift within the so-called Putin majority. The president’s core electorate included groups with varying and often opposing views, such as those who were nostalgic for the Soviet Union and fervent anti-Communists. The same phenomenon applied to proponents of a market economy versus those who preferred a planned economy. All of them could fill the vacuum with an ideology of their choosing and ascribe it to the regime, while adopting a White Russian émigré set of values would inevitably have raised concerns among both staunch Putinists and apolitical Russians alike.Ahead of the 2018 presidential election, the Kremlin’s political team was actively searching for a vision of the future. The old argument about stability under Putin no longer looked so convincing following the annexation of Crimea, a wave of U.S.-EU sanctions, and a decline in living standards. But the search proved fruitless.15 It largely boiled down to attempting to find technical solutions (such as studying populist election strategies and tactics) and to the abstract triad of “fairness, respect, and trust.”16 In the end, Putin’s campaign was just the same as those of previous years, with a focus on maintaining stability.After that election, the search for a vision of Russia’s future became irrelevant. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic reduced the planning horizon even further. The 2021 State Duma elections were held at the tail end of the pandemic, and key factors in United Russia’s victory included corporate mobilization tactics (galvanizing public sector and state-owned company employees to vote) and attempts to use electronic voting in Moscow.17After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it was no longer possible to manage without a vision of the future and explanations for Russia’s sudden economic problems, partial mobilization of the population to fill out the army’s badly depleted units, and the rows of freshly dug graves at cemeteries. The authorities had no explanation beyond Putin’s rhetoric about the “de-Nazification” and “demilitarization” of Ukraine.18 Following the failure of Russia’s planned blitzkrieg in spring 2022, the Kremlin’s political bloc began trying to formulate a more coherent ideological framework.19 But those attempts proved futile.In the end, it proved easier for Kremlin officials to fall back on the illusion of stability. Essentially, the message was that the war was taking place far away, and that the people fighting it on Russia’s behalf were professionals. Sanctions would have no impact on the economy (most importantly, on the assortment of goods available). This very simple psychological reassurance, when combined with the efforts of the government’s financial and economic bloc, proved highly effective. The partial mobilization in fall 2022 tested the public’s nerve (Putin’s approval rating fell by 5 percent, according to the Public Opinion Foundation), but was hardly critical, since the mobilization mainly affected those living in small towns and rural areas.20 Luckily for the Kremlin, the resulting unwelcome wave of political uncertainty was over relatively quickly.The Kremlin’s political team returned to the issue of ideology at the end of 2022, first and foremost at the instigation of Putin, who was becoming increasingly ideological. He moved from occasional references to Ivan Ilyin to presenting Russia as a distinct civilization, in the spirit of Gumilev, in 2020.21 The target audience for the Kremlin’s renewed efforts was Putin himself, and those around him who shared his views. At the same time, the general public continued to be fed the idea of stability with an added sprinkling of patriotic ideas (such as “Sanctions aren’t working” and “We’re doing just fine, despite the enemy’s best efforts.”)The focus of the quest for an ideology was obvious from the start. Kiriyenko’s team had to take into account Putin’s conservative-imperial views and develop congruent ideas. Accordingly, the same political team that had in 2016–2017 started by consulting with very progressive philosophers, sociologists, and political scientists now turned to figures who had previously been considered marginal. The corridors of power were now frequented by the fringe nationalist philosopher Alexander Dugin,22 who was erroneously described in Western media reports as “Putin’s brain,” and the historian Vardan Bagdasaryan.23 Bagdasaryan had made his reputation as the proponent of the theory that Western countries have lost their sovereignty and are controlled by global corporations.The Ideal CitizenFollowing the outbreak of the full-scale war, Alexander Kharichev, the head of the presidential administration’s directorate for social analysis and a Kiriyenko associate since the late 1990s, was given responsibility for ideology within the Kremlin. At the end of 2022, Karichev and a group of authors from the Expert Institute for Social Research published an article titled “The Perception of Key Values, Factors, and Structures of Russia’s Socio-Historical Development.”24 The authors tried to describe a so-called nationwide civilizational code: Russians’ ideas about the role of the state and the individual in society, as well as the sum-total of their “pan-national values.”Their research can hardly be described as thorough or serious: It is based on the results of brainstorming sessions held among university students loyal to the regime. But Karichev still tried to adhere to academic standards in this first ideological text. He cited the sociologists Serge Moscovici and Jonathan H. Turner. The authors concluded that the “basic factors and structures of socio-historical development” were what they called a “pentabasis”: a five-pronged structure consisting of the individual person, family, society, the state, and the country. Each of those factors, according to Kharichev, has its own “dominant.” As luck would have it, these “dominants” are all concepts that Putin loves to talk about. For the individual, it is “creation;” for the family, “tradition;” for society, “consensus;” for the state, “trust in public institutions;” and for the country, “patriotism.”According to Kharichev’s “code,” the sacralization of power is supposedly ingrained in Russians.The article also contained some early tentative reflections on the supposedly unique nature of the Russian people—a subject explored in more detail in another article by Kharichev published in spring 2025 titled “Civilization Russia.”25 According to Kharichev, the country had long been a bridge between the civilizations of the East and the West. Russia constituted a civilization in its own right as a result of its “special statehood” that supposedly plays a “leading role in shaping society” and is “not just a political institution, but a spiritual center.” Hence, wrote Kharichev, “the unique attitude of the Russian people: paternalism, an inclination toward centralized authority, and the personification and sacralization of power.”Kharichev claimed that spiritual values—“service, love for mankind, and self-sacrifice”—are more important to the Russian people than material riches. They prefer faith to rationality and logic, he argued, and “fairness” to “the letter of the law.” He also attributed the characteristic of “team spirit,” one of Kiriyenko’s favorite corporate buzzwords, to Russians. Russians are, Kharichev concluded, “patriots by conviction, capable of collective work, and of building and improving the world.”In May 2025, Kharichev’s article “Who Are We?” rehashed some of his previous work while also introducing new ideas.26 The authorities’ main aim, wrote Kharichev, was to cultivate a “person of the future” who would be responsible for “preserving and developing our civilizational system.” In this article, the neutral, corporate concept of “teamwork” was replaced by that of ideologically charged “collectivism,” and the idea of “self-sacrifice” was taken to absurd levels. “As it turns out,” wrote Kharichev, “life is worth far less to us than it is to a Westerner.”It’s hard not to notice that Kharichev’s works describe the perfect characteristics for the subjects of any dictatorship, autocracy, or tyranny. At the same time, his writings are more akin to state doctrine than to ideology per se. Ideology presupposes a vision of the future, and goals, whereas for a doctrine—as a system of beliefs—they are not necessary. Kharichev’s articles describe a present in which the state dominates the general public and can do what it wants with people. After all, according to his “code,” the sacralization of power is supposedly ingrained in Russians. People are prepared to sacrifice their comfort and even their lives if the state asks it of them.The “Foundations of Russian Statehood”Kharichev’s first two articles also had input from another longtime Kiriyenko associate, political scientist Andrei Polosin. In 2022, Polosin was put in charge of developing a compulsory propaganda course for university students titled “Foundations of Russian Statehood.”27 Starting in fall 2023, first-year students at all Russian universities have been required to take and pass this course.At the initial stage of the course’s development, Polosin—who has a doctorate in political science—tried to conform to at least basic academic standards. Back then, the recommended reading list included works by prominent Russian and Western political thinkers and historians such as Vladimir Gelman, Daniel Bell, and Alvin Toffler. Students were encouraged to study various approaches to understanding history. The “civilization” approach—a concept espoused by Russian Slavophiles such as Gumilev, and Western thinkers like Oswald Spengler and Arnold Toynbee—was presented as just one of several legitimate approaches. But ultimately, only the “civilization” approach made it through to the final curriculum, all because of Putin’s love for Gumilev’s theory that civilizations emerge and flourish (thanks to “passionaries” who are prepared to sacrifice themselves) before declining and dying out.The course features by now familiar concepts such as “self-sacrifice for the sake of lofty goals” inherent to passionaries. The educational film “Russia’s DNA: State-Civilization” echoes Kharichev’s idea, arguing that “rationalism never caught on” in Russia.28 “The changeable climate could contain surprises, and an impromptu decision that was often not the most obvious one saved the day more than the pragmatic approach,” the film teaches students. It also informs them that Russian avos—faith in chance or hoping everything will turn out OK in the end—has become “a mainstream decision-making technique.”Another element of the course is the justification of Moscow’s imperial ambitions. The authors consider empire to be Russia’s natural state of existence. Students are taught that “empire was not tantamount to imperialism,” and that the attempt made during the presidency of Boris Yeltsin to “borrow a way of ruling from another country was not just a failure—it was almost lethal.”29The conclusions drawn by Kharichev and Polosin complement each other and comprise a state theory that perfectly suits Putin and his inner circle. The ideas of a “special composition” of the Russian people—a youthful civilization loyal to the authorities—are very convenient for the aging autocrat in the Kremlin. If the civilization is young, that means it is destined to flourish in the near future, while its opponents—the countries of the West—are doomed to die out. Meanwhile, the notion of the “special character” of each civilization offers a get out clause from rules that are generally seen as universal. Putin says that outright in his musings on the “multipolar world” and the diversity of rules.30 Within this paradigm, any deviation from generally accepted norms can be explained by a “special path” and national traditions.The Technocratic DictatorshipAlso telling in this context is the article “Digital Legitimacy,” written by another ideologist from Kiriyenko’s team, the political strategist Gleb Kuznetsov.31 The article compares the efficiency (a term lifted straight from the corporate lexicon) of “liberal” and “non-liberal” regimes that use modern digital services. It’s likely that Kuznetsov actually means democratic and non-democratic, since his article focuses on concepts such as free elections and media freedoms.Kuznetsov defines efficiency by the number of infrastructure projects completed and the speed with which they start operating. In this respect, democratic regimes are losing, according to the author, because they are dependent on electoral cycles. “Every four to five years, there is a change in priorities, long-term projects are abandoned . . . Liberal politics is degenerating into performance . . . What matters is not solving the problem, but demonstrating that you care about it.” In this respect, Kuznetsov also considers the principle of the separation of powers to be a hindrance: It only “slows the actions” of the state.The apologia for dictatorship crafted by Kiriyenko’s team appeared first as a program for cultivating the ideal citizen, before being developed as an ideological construct.In the meantime, the author continues, non-liberal technocracies “are focused on results,” and derive their legitimacy not from competitive elections, public oversight, and the separation of powers, but thanks to technical efficiency and providing people with digital services. In such a system, state management remains a closed loop: It sets priorities, the criteria for “efficiency,” and the internal selection mechanisms itself. Ideology takes a back seat, or might be lacking entirely. Comfort in their everyday lives and “efficient” services, Kuznetsov explains, might be enough for people.This approach of technocratic autocracy appeals to Kiriyenko: a man who has long expressed disdain for public politics and political battles.32 He has introduced key performance indicators (KPIs) into all the sectors he is involved in,33 adheres to “meritocratic” selection processes, and works to tighten the government’s control over society. As a result, society itself is again becoming an object that is acted upon by the authorities, rather than a body with its own goals and the ability to define its own relationship with the powers that be. This view of the composition of the state can also be considered as quasi-ideological or a doctrine. The framework of a “technocratic dictatorship” might remain bare, or it might be clothed in another quasi-ideological layer, or even an ideological one. The “public well-being,” for example, that the technocratic dictator is supposedly working toward, might be presented as universal material equality, or, on the contrary, as a meritocratic utopia, in which everyone who proves themselves worthy of a managerial post is guaranteed to get one.The Machinery of IndoctrinationThe Kremlin needs channels to transmit these elements of an ideological doctrine to the broader masses, and propaganda is simply not sufficient in this instance. What’s needed is a full-fledged teaching mechanism complete with tests to check that the “knowledge” has been absorbed by the target audience. The Kremlin’s political team also needs to show the leadership that they have introduced such mechanisms.The path chosen was the most straightforward and predictable one. Putin and his entourage are, of course, well acquainted with Soviet-era indoctrination. In its day, the formal ideology of the Soviet state—Marxism-Leninism—was taught to all students: Every university had courses of “scientific communism” and compulsory examinations for students. Today, the process has happened the other way around: The apologia for dictatorship crafted by Kiriyenko’s team appeared first as an academic subject—a program for cultivating the ideal citizen—and only then began to be developed as a broader ideological construct.This further underscores the utilitarian nature of the initiative. The primary task is to ensure the general population’s loyalty and obedience, and the corresponding “ideology” is predicated upon that specific premise. The scale of the indoctrination machinery that has been created is impressive. The Kremlin has already trained approximately 8,500 teachers, and in the three years the course has been taught, some 4 million first-year university students have taken it.34The Kremlin has also set its sights on older generations of Russians. In February 2026, employees of Gazprom, Rostec, and other state corporations attended a week-long “Foundations of Russian Statehood” course.35 That experiment could easily be expanded to public-sector workers, with lectures held at the regional and municipal levels. People dependent on the state, the so-called budzhetniki, would effectively have no choice in the matter if the state ultimately decides to force them all to attend such a course.How effective the Kremlin’s propaganda course will be in practice remains to be seen. The theses expounded during lectures will inevitably differ from any individual’s own reality in today’s Russia. It’s all reminiscent of the teaching of “scientific communism” at the twilight of the Soviet era, when teachers of the subject were simply going through the motions. When the Soviet Union collapsed, people did not take to the streets en masse in support of the Communist Party. They simply shrugged their shoulders and adapted to the new reality. Absent various types of coercion by the state, it is easy to anticipate that this latter-day form of indoctrination is not likely to be very effective.The Soviet system, of course, forced people to adopt its language, taught them to understand the demands of the state, explained the rules of the game, and imposed a code of desired behavior. Sadly, the historical antecedents of Putin’s presidential administration’s political team are all too easy to spot.An Apologia for DictatorshipThe Kremlin doctrine that has emerged during the full-scale war against Ukraine thanks to Kiriyenko’s team is a jigsaw puzzle. The outside pieces are the “technocratic dictatorship” described by Gleb Kuznetsov: the justification for turning away from democratic procedures and for excluding the general public from decisionmaking processes. The inside pieces are Kharichev’s articles on Russians’ “civilizational code” and the “Foundations of Russian Statehood” course that teaches students that Russian civilization is young and therefore has a bright future ahead of it.All the pseudo-research done by Kremlin officials and political strategists boils down to one thing: an apologia for dictatorship and the legitimization of any actions taken by Russia’s current leadership. It describes a nation-state in which the collective takes precedence over the individual, power is sacred, and ordinary people should be prepared to give up everything, even their lives. This is an extremely convenient construction for an autocratic leader and a dictator. It’s particularly convenient for Putin, who shows no sign of wanting to end the war in Ukraine and who has been completely indifferent to the staggering loss of life on the Russian side. Even as war fatigue among the Russian public and economic problems mount, it is hard to envision circumstances that would force Putin’s hand.In its current form, the doctrine is primarily aimed at mobilization. It demands sacrifice and concessions from people and explains this need through a civilizational code. People are not even told what goals the state and regime are pursuing. Indeed, the doctrine eliminates any need for the regime to expound upon its vision for the future. In any case, the Kremlin has conveniently avoided articulating one.The technocratic-autocratic part of these ideas looks a little more positive, since it at least envisages efficient work by the state to benefit the general public. It effectively amounts to an improved version of the concept of “Putin stability” that accompanied the early years of his tenure. Such notions would have been perfectly viable at a time of economic growth, limited political repression, relative freedom of expression, and, of course, no unprovoked full-scale war against Ukraine. But to restore those conditions, the regime would need to reverse course and try to reestablish the prevailing conditions as of February 2022. Neither Putin nor the Kremlin have shown the least desire to do any such thing.A nation-state in which power is sacred and ordinary people should be prepared to give up their lives is an extremely convenient construction for an autocratic leader and a dictator.The country’s public and elites, meanwhile, are already beginning to show signs of growing discontent.36 The authorities’ approval ratings have fallen so much that the VTsIOM pollster that works with the Kremlin is having to change the methodology of its polls to produce figures that are more palatable to the powers that be.37 The comforting illusions of eternal rule enshrined in the doctrine of Kiriyenko and his team could ultimately collide with reality for Putin and his system. At the same time, the doctrine—if stripped of its civilizational-patriotic elements—could prove more than viable in post-Putin Russia, too. The framework of a technocratic dictatorship onto which any desired façade can be mounted would suit virtually any of the people currently being discussed as potential successors to Putin, from Kiriyenko himself to Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin. The machinery for corporate indoctrination is already up and running: It would just need some adjustments to its operating software.About the AuthorAndrey PertsevAndrey Pertsev is a journalist with Meduza website.Recent WorkCommentaryHow the Latest Election Changed the Role of Russia’s ParliamentAndrey PertsevCommentaryHow the Kremlin Achieved Its Latest Implausible Election ResultsAndrey PertsevNotes1See, for example, Alexander Kharichev, “Восприятие базовых ценностей, факторов и структурсоциально-исторического развития России (по материалам исследований и апробации)” [“Perception of basic values, factors and structures socio-historical development of Russia (based on research and testing materials)”], Nauka, October 21, 2022, https://naukaru.ru/ru/storage/viewWindow/105963; Kharichev, “Кто мы?” [“Who Are We?”], Gosudarstvo journal, issue 2, November 2025, https://www.scribd.com/document/950709851/Кто-мы-Харичев-А-Д; and Andrey Pertsev, “Сотрудник АП Александр Харичев написал статью, которая выглядит как инструкция для «строителя путинизма» [“Presidential administration official Alexander Kharichev has written an article that reads like a manual for ‘builders of Putinism’”], Meduza, April 18, 2025, https://meduza.io/feature/2025/04/18/sotrudnik-ap-aleksandr-harichev-napisal-statyu-kotoraya-vyglyadit-kak-instruktsiya-dlya-stroitelya-putinizma.2Alla Konstantinova, “‘Reflections that verge on Nazism.’ A new course devoted to ‘foundation of statehood’ is introduced in Russian universities,” Meduza, September 13, 2023, https://en.zona.media/article/2023/09/13/org-trl/.3Andrey Pertsev, “Кажется, Путин и правда думает, что может победить Запад. articles.title: Weekly Research Brief: Binance Hacked; Hyperliquid on Wall Street; Prediction Markets’ Brazil ‘Miss’
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Weekly Research Brief: Binance Hacked in Record Theft; Hyperliquid on Wall Street; Prediction Markets’ Brazil ‘Miss’

Research • October 30, 2026 • 16 mins
Weekly Research Brief: Binance Hacked in Record Theft; Hyperliquid on Wall Street; Prediction Markets’ Brazil ‘Miss’
This week, Thad Pinakiewicz and Alex Thorn reflect on the massive Binance hack; Will Owens breaks down the landmark partnership between TradeXYZ and NYSE parent ICE to build Hyperliquid perps; and Zack Pokorny considers an apparent prediction market miss.

Alex Thorn
Head of Firmwide Research

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz

Will Owens

Weekly Research Brief

Welcome to Galaxy Research's Weekly Research Brief. Subscribe to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. This week, Alex Thorn and Thad Pinakiewicz reflects on the massive Binance hack; Will Owens breaks down the landmark partnership between TradeXYZ and NYSE parent ICE to build perps on Hyperliquid; and Zack Pokorny considers an apparent rare miss by prediction markets.Find all our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. We’d love to hear from you.
Here We Go Again: Binance Loses $6.3b in Largest Robbery in History Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, was drained of roughly $6.3b across 10 blockchains on Thursday night. TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s Lazarus-linked unit. As of writing, the exchange has not yet re-enabled withdrawals. Start with scale. The benchmark for the largest robbery ever has long been the roughly $1b Saddam Hussein’s regime took from the Central Bank of Iraq on the eve of the 2003 invasion, about $1.8b in today’s dollars. Bybit beat that in nominal terms but not after inflation. Binance beats it on any measure. Even after roughly $2.5–3bn in freezes, this is the biggest heist of all time. Binance’s BTC outflows yesterday were 11 standard deviations higher than their 30-day average.

Then the method. On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702 to turn a Binance hot wallet into a sweeper contract that took orders only from the attacker. It was backed by 50 pre-signed authorizations, one for each upcoming transaction number (nonce), so whichever one came up next would work. The code was rehearsed on three test wallets hours beforehand. Within minutes of each other, nine more chains were emptied, each with different key types and signing schemes. That is someone with intimate knowledge of how Binance’s withdrawal systems work. This is Binance’s preliminary finding: a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop gave access to a service container, with “no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”

Our take We believe our previous thesis from Bitget is consistent here. Nobody attacks the private-key math. They attack whoever, or whatever, tells the math what to do. The biggest mitigating factor of this exploit was stablecoin issuers. Tether froze about $1.77b in USDT, Circle about $825m in USDC, Ripple about $40m in RLUSD, and World Liberty about $28m in USD1. That’s a big part of why this appears to be a painful week rather than an existential one, and we believe Tether deserves credit for moving fast and at scale. We also believe Circle deserves credit for the freeze. Circle has long said it freezes only when directed by law enforcement or a court, not in real time during an active hack. After April's $285m Drift exploit, CEO Jeremy Allaire went further, saying a private company deciding "what is the right path or not" would be a "moral quandary." During the Drift exploit, about $232m in stolen USDC moved through Circle's own cross-chain transfer protocol over roughly six hours without being frozen. But, on Thursday, Circle froze $823m about 40 minutes after the Ethereum sweep, "in coordination with law enforcement." Does Binance have enough to cover the hole? The SAFU fund, about $1b in BTC, does not come close to covering it, so Binance says it will cover all losses from its own corporate funds. Last year’s 10/10 liquidation event cost Binance about $283m in depeg compensation plus its $400m “Together Initiative” ($300m in user vouchers and $100m in low-interest loans to institutions). That’s under $700m; this hack is roughly nine times that. A better yardstick is the BNB burn. 2026’s three quarterly burns so far have retired about $3.2bn of BNB. Net of freezes, the hole is roughly one year of burns, or about 4% of the ~$144bn in assets Binance held before the attack. It is a staggering amount of money, but Binance does appear to have it, or at least the ability to earn its way out of a hole based on our own calculations of their revenue-funded BNB burns. While we can’t independently verify Binance’s whole financial condition, and we don’t know exactly what Binance plans to do, Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said plainly: “Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and company funds.”What’s left: when will withdrawals reopen, where will the roughly $2.4b in ETH and BTC still in the attacker’s hands go next (THORChain, Tornado Cash, etc.), and how did an outsider come to know Binance’s systems this well? These are among the key specific questions we will be following in the coming days and weeks. But how the market reacts to the event broadly is also top of mind.Bitcoin and other crypto assets are trading lower on the news. Alex Thorn’s piece from Monday (Why Now Is the Time to Add and Hold BTC) relies heavily on the 50-week moving average as a key level to maintain a bullish trend, with a break below that is not retaken within 1 month cited as invalidating the paper’s thesis. That 50w MA currently sits at $76,103, and at the time of writing BTCUSD is trading at $77,000. So far, the 50w MA has held, with BTC trading as low as $76,301 overnight on Coinbase. Whether the 50w can hold this weekend is a key test that could be consequential for the next several months of Bitcoin’s technical market structure. – Alex Thorn & Thad Pinakiewicz
NYSE Parent Signs Deal to Bring Compliant Hyperliquid Perps to U.S.WHAT HAPPENEDIntercontinental Exchange (ICE), parent of the New York Stock Exchange, announced a definitive agreement with Trade[XYZ] to bring the latter’s Hyperliquid perpetual futures to the U.S., pending regulatory approval. As part of this deal, ICE will be the exclusive operator of Trade[XYZ]’s regulated markets and is also making a strategic investment. Notably, Wall Street legend Stan Druckenmiller is investing as well, making his first-ever tweet. HYPE, the native token of Hyperliquid, pumped ~20% on the news, from $78 to $94 at time of writing. Hyperliquid will supply the rails via HIP-3* (note the asterisk), which is not exactly the same thing as HIP-3, the year-old protocol upgrade that allows third-party builders to deploy perps. HIP-3* is the newer, gated version designed for regulated entities. Trade[XYZ] will design and deploy the markets, and ICE will run the exchange and clearing. This partnership will allow for the creation of a KYC-gated venue with its own clearinghouse. It will list perps on equities, crypto, indices, commodities, and foreign exchange, with access through futures commission merchants (remember ICE’s venture with OKX).Trade[XYZ]’s HIP-3 markets have done more than $650b in volume and will stay as they are. What makes this new partnership possible is HIP-3*. Hyperliquid unveiled it recently, and it’s live on testnet. It lets deployers run permissioned perpetual markets through an onchain allowlist. On Oct. 26, Hyperliquid announced that Payward, Kraken’s parent, plans to be the first CFTC-regulated deployer. This is a huge announcement, but it’s not entirely surprising. President Donald Trump mentioned Hyperliquid on Aug. 19, stating that CFTC Chair Michael Selig was working to bring the platform to the United States. Also, ICE CEO Jeffrey Sprecher said he’d met the Hyperliquid team multiple times at investment bank Bernstein’s conference in May. TradFi participants love to cite the oil use case. When ICE’s energy markets close, Hyperliquid keeps trading, which has proven useful in times of geopolitical duress. OUR TAKE U.S. traders will get a separate, permissioned venue with its own clearing. The existing open HIP-3 markets will keep trading 24/7 for everyone else. The liquidity will not be shared, meaning the U.S. venue will start from zero. It will be interesting to see how different books react to a Sunday night geopolitical shock, and how tightly arbitrage keeps the two prices together. The backstop for HyperCore (the trading engine of Hyperliquid) is onchain liquidation and, in the tail, auto-deleveraging, as evidenced by last year’s devastating Oct. 10. Nothing announced so far says whether ICE’s clearinghouse will sit on top of HyperCore’s risk engine or replace part of it. It’s also an open question whether ICE already owns any HYPE. Last month, Hyperliquid Labs, the software development company behind the blockchain, sold 3.75m HYPE OTC to an undisclosed institution. Prominent Hyperliquid onchain analyst MLM found 3.125M of it staked with the Hyperliquid Strategies x Unit validator. He traced the other 625k (through a few hops) to a wallet linked to Trade[XYZ], where it was staked this week. This isn’t fully confirmed, though. It’s also uncertain whether trades on the planned U.S. venue would go through HIP-3 and pay the same protocol fees. It’s a little ironic that ICE spent the spring lobbying against this sort of thing. Shortly before Sprecher’s Bernstein remarks, ICE and fellow trading colossus CME pressed U.S. officials to scrutinize Hyperliquid’s role in offshore, oil-linked trading. This announcement is probably the largest positive catalyst in Hyperliquid’s short history, and it will be exciting to see how competitors in the perps space such as Lighter and Kalshi respond. What once seemed like a Hyperliquid bull’s wildest dream is now reality. – Will Owens
What’s the Difference Between a 20% Chance and a 0% Chance?WHAT HAPPENEDPrediction market skeptics are crowing (again) after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva upset Flávio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s runoff election on Oct. 25. Heading into the election, prediction markets had Bolsonaro holding a 75% to 80% chance of winning the election to Lula’s 11% to 20% probability after Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil’s presidential election on Oct. 4. Lula ended up winning the runoff and remains Brazil’s president, and Bolsonaro fled to the United States.Traditional polls had shown a statistical dead heat. The polling firm Datafolha had the two candidates tied at 50% each, while AtlasIntel/Bloomberg had Bolsonaro ahead 51.1% to 48.9% and an average compiled by The Rio Times put Bolsonaro at 50.9% to Lula’s 49.1%. Lula ultimately won with 51.8% of valid votes to Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, so most polls leaned slightly toward Bolsonaro and understated Lula’s share by one to four points. Even so, the polls never suggested Bolsonaro was a heavy favorite. Prediction markets offered a far more opinionated stance on the outcome of the election compared to polls that, when compensating for margin of error, offered no tangible takeaway. This setup was similar to that of the 2024 U.S. presidential election, where polls showed an ultra-close race with Kamala Harris barely in the lead while Polymarket gave Trump roughly a 60% chance of winning, a figure that stood at 62% on Election Day.The difference was the ultimate outcome. In 2024, the markets’ bet that polls were understating the Republican candidate’s chances paid off, while in Brazil the equivalent bet failed. This gap is where critics point to an inaccuracy and apparent lack of efficacy in prediction markets’ implied odds. OUR TAKEThe picture is not as black and white as the skeptics make it out to be. The take that prediction markets failed in this setting breaks down when taking into consideration what these markets actually tell you: predictions on probabilities. What the detractors miss here is that implied odds are not an implied prophecy. A prediction market price is a statement about frequency, not a guarantee that something will or won’t happen (e.g. a probability >50% does not imply the event must always happen just because the market suggests it is more likely than not). A contract trading at 80% is saying that if you could replay this event many times, the outcome would occur about four times in five, and fail the fifth. A 20% chance is expected to happen one time in five, not never. Lula winning at roughly 11% to 20% was a longshot, not an impossibility, and one longshot landing tells you very little about whether the price was wrong.Human brains struggle to cope with this idea when looking at probabilities. Psychologists have documented for decades that people judge probability with mental shortcuts, and that these shortcuts lead to systematic and predictable errors (see Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in Science, 1974). The problem shows up in elections specifically. In a Journal of Politics study, Sean J. Westwood, Solomon Messing, and Yphtach Lelkes found through experiments that probabilistic forecasts increase certainty about an outcome and confuse many readers. When one candidate is ahead, win probabilities convey substantially more confidence than vote share estimates do. The authors tied this observation to 2016, when forecasts gave Hillary Clinton a 70% to 99% chance of winning and left voters thinking the race was far less competitive than it was. A 60/40 or 80/20 market reads to many people as a verdict, when it is still a description of uncertainty. This misconception turns Bolsonaro’s 75% to 80% probability into “the markets said Bolsonaro would win,” and a Lula victory into a breakdown in market efficacy, when an 80/20 market is still just a description of some uncertainty.Historically, over many markets, prediction platforms’ prices hold up. Kalshi Research tested more than 2.2 million resolved markets, and found prices generally behave like genuine probabilities, with a contract at 70 cents resolving “Yes” about 70% of the time. The calibration plots below show this. Each dot groups markets by their price (horizontal axis) and shows how often those markets actually resolved “Yes” (vertical axis). The dashed diagonal is perfect calibration, where a 70% price means a 70% hit rate. The dots hug that line, and they sit closest to it in the panels measured one week and one day before resolution, which is the window most relevant to the Brazil runoff. Prices are also more accurate as resolution nears, with Brier scores (a standard error measure where lower is better) falling from roughly 0.08 to 0.09 at three months out to about 0.02 at close. This shows that even in the markets that were well calibrated, the favorite didn’t always win. For elections, the favored outcome came in about 90% of the time across most horizons, which means roughly one favorite in 10 lost. The authors also note that in a race with more than two viable candidates, a favorite priced at 60 cents should win only about 60% of the time, and that near-perfect hit rates would point to underpriced favorites rather than better forecasting.

Source: Kalshi Research (https://kalshi.com/research/kalshi-research-calibration.pdf)Brazil’s stock market made a similar bet to that of prediction market odds. After Bolsonaro won the first round, the Ibovespa index jumped almost 8% on Oct. 5, from 192,138 to 206,912, and peaked at a close of 209,067 on Oct. 9. It chopped around this level until after the runoff, when it fell 13.9% in a single session, from 205,083 to 176,608, and kept sliding. As of Oct. 29, it was trading below 170,000 which is about 17% below its pre-runoff close and below where it stood before the first round of the election. The Brazilian Real also lost more than 8% after an election result the market seemingly did not expect. Equity investors didn’t have a secret read on Lula that the prediction markets missed. Everyone seemed to price Bolsonaro as the favorite.Taking this into consideration, prediction markets worked as a viable hedge. A trader long Brazilian stocks could have bought Lula “Yes” contracts as insurance. A contract priced near 20 cents paid five times the stake, so the Lula position would have paid out many multiples as the Brazilian stock market entered a free fall. A 20% price was never a claim that Lula couldn’t win. It was the market rate for protection against this outcome.The data suggests prediction markets were not wrong in the way their doubters are claiming. A price of 75% to 80% means the favorite loses one time in four or five, and Kalshi illustrated this is roughly the case in aggregate. Then again, if the election was stolen, as Bolsonaro has claimed, maybe the markets were wrong, at least about the ultimate outcome (even if they were right about his popularity) - Zack Pokorny

articles.title: Long-term projections of the world economy
articles.text:
Publication Type
Working Papers

Long-term projections of the world economy

Weifeng Larry Liu (Reserve Bank of Australia) and

Warwick J. McKibbin (PIIE; Australian National University)

Working Paper 26-16

October 2026

Photo Credit: SOPA via Reuters/David Canales

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
This paper surveys long-term projections of global GDP per capita and presents the authors' own projections through 2050 using a multicountry-multisector general equilibrium model (G-Cubed). Studies generally agree that global GDP per capita growth will continue to slow in the coming decades, driven by several global challenges such as rapid population aging, slower technological progress (in pre-AI projections), weaker capital investment, and stagnating educational attainment. Projections tend to be consistent for advanced economies but vary considerably for developing regions, highlighting the importance of alternative methodologies and assumptions, as well as inherent long-term uncertainty. While existing studies rely on neoclassical models with an aggregate production sector, the G-Cubed model takes a disaggregated approach to projecting productivity and output that accounts for dynamic interactions between sectors and across economies. The authors' projections incorporate the impacts of three fundamental factors: productivity growth, population aging, and climate change. Productivity growth in advanced economies is expected to slow, but AI could counteract the decline and serve as an engine for sustained growth. Population aging in most advanced economies will continue to constrain labor supply, potentially reducing GDP per capita through changes in age structure. Climate change poses challenges to economic growth through multiple channels, with moderate quantitative impacts by midcentury. The extent to which developing regions can boost productivity, leverage demographic advantages, and navigate climate change will depend on policy choices as well as governance and institutional improvements. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of geopolitical fragmentation, government debt, and public infrastructure on economic growth.

articles.title: Multi-Asset Investment Views: “Will of the people” - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
Moderate overweight global equities: Despite geopolitical uncertainties, resilient earnings and economic activity continue to support the asset class. Elevated bond yields and unease associated with AI hype justify a balanced exposure to growth and value stocks. We favour the US, Japan and emerging markets, and selective opportunities in financials and healthcare sectors

Moderate overweight commodities: Energy remains an important hedge against supply disruption and geopolitical risks. Precious metals benefit from central-bank demand and investment flows; selected industrial metals such as copper retain structural support

Fixed Income: Moderate underweight sovereign bonds and investment-grade credit; moderate overweight high yield and emerging-market debt: persistent inflation, heavy issuance and term-premium pressures still argue for caution on duration, while shorter-duration high-yield credit offers attractive carry amid low default rates and strong profit growth

By Chief Investment Officer (CIO) and Global Head of Multi-Asset, Laurent Clavel

Politics has returned to the forefront of market attention. Social unrest and fiscal uncertainty in France have together pushed sovereign borrowing costs higher and weighed on domestic equities, particularly banks, with some spillover into European credit and neighbouring bond markets.

The CAC 40 has underperformed but represents less than 2% of global equity market capitalisation. Brazil’s presidential election has prompted some moves in local assets, but the main drivers are elsewhere, while the approaching US midterm elections raise questions about policy direction, but are unlikely to change the course of action, notably in the Middle East.

Yet political events do not have a uniform or predictable market effect; historical midterm patterns alone offer little reason to reposition portfolios. The S&P 500 returned an average of 6.6% in the fourth quarter of US midterm election years, and since 1950, has been up 84% of the time.1

The more relevant question is whether political developments alter fiscal credibility, financing conditions or corporate fundamentals. For now, we see reasons for vigilance rather than a broad reduction in risk.

Growth remains resilient, but momentum may moderate

The global economy has remained more resilient than many expected. Manufacturing activity has recovered over recent months and services remain supportive, although the purchasing managers’ index cycle appears to be maturing.

Our economists are somewhat more cautious than consensus, anticipating a gradual slowdown rather than a recession. China’s growth outlook remains challenged, and we will closely monitor the outcomes of this week’s plenum – the policy meeting of Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

Inflation is proving sticky, notably because of energy, but there is still limited evidence of sustained second-round wage effects. Against this backdrop, market pricing of roughly two-and-a-half policy-rate increases over the next year for both the Federal Reserve, and the European Central Bank looks more hawkish than our economists’ expectation of approximately one increase each.

This combination continues to favour selective exposure to equities and credit. However, the margin for disappointment has narrowed: higher oil prices, tighter financing conditions or weaker earnings could challenge market confidence. Following the increase in equity exposure at the end of September, we are comfortable maintaining the current risk budget rather than adding to it.

Asset allocation summary

UW: underweight; MUW: moderate underweight; N: neutral; MOW: moderate overweight; OW: overweight, signs = unchanged compared to last month, Source: BNP Paribas Asset Management

Equities: Broaden the sources of return

We retain a moderate overweight in global equities. In the US, earnings growth and artificial intelligence-related investment remain powerful supports but we increasingly favour diversification beyond the largest technology names.

Financials offer attractive valuations, resilient credit fundamentals and solid fee income, notwithstanding recent weakness linked to yield-curve and sovereign-risk concerns. Healthcare also offers comparatively attractive valuations and improving earnings prospects, supported by innovation and technology.

We remain neutral on Europe. Corporate earnings have been relatively resilient, but valuations are less compelling, revisions are losing momentum and persistent inflation could trigger a derating. We continue to favour selected banks, while defence has become more interesting after the sector’s valuation derated and amid improving order prospects.

In France, depressed valuations have prompted a move to neutral at the country level, although political and sovereign-spread risks warrant caution.

We are neutral on Japan. Although it is supported by corporate-governance reforms and fiscal stimulus, we prefer to gain equity exposure through the US and emerging market stocks. In Japan, we favour banks, which benefit from higher rates and strong earnings momentum, alongside selected AI-related companies. Unhedged yen exposure may provide additional diversification.

We also maintain a moderate overweight in emerging markets, supported by exports, earnings and potentially lower US real yields. Recent weakness in Korea appears greater than warranted by semiconductor fundamentals, but index concentration argues against a larger tactical allocation; a broader advance would benefit from improving performance in China and India.

Fixed income: Favour higher income over long duration

We retain moderate underweights in sovereign bonds and investment-grade credit. Government issuance, inflation uncertainty and rising term premia remain challenging, although the repricing of interest-rate expectations has made valuations more interesting.

Deeply negative sentiment could support a short-term recovery, and we are reassessing the size of duration underweights closer to neutral in portfolios with greater flexibility.

We continue to favour shorter-duration, higher-quality high-yield bonds: resilient earnings, stabilising defaults and higher income levels provide a cushion despite recent spread widening. Emerging-market debt also remains attractive, with a growing preference for local-currency exposure where yields are compelling.

Diversification and dispersion

Commodities remain a key portfolio diversifier. Oil markets continue to face supply constraints, shipping disruptions and elevated transport costs; a further spike in prices would pose a material threat to inflation and risk assets.

Precious metals benefit from central-bank buying and renewed exchange-traded fund demand, while copper retains supportive longer-term supply fundamentals, albeit with a need for tactical discipline.

We retain a broadly neutral fundamental view on the euro versus the US dollar and see value in maintaining unhedged dollar exposure as a diversifier, while reviewing contrary quantitative hedging signals.

Equity volatility remains relatively subdued even as cross-asset spillovers become more normal. We therefore continue to favour selective, short-dated equity protection, including three- to six-month put options, rather than materially reducing core risk exposures.

Wide differences in stock and sector performance reinforce the value of diversification and active management.

[1] Source: BNP Paribas Asset Management, October 2026.

articles.title: The outlook for inflation − speech by Clare Lombardelli
articles.text:
The outlook for inflation − speech by Clare Lombardelli

Given at the Sixth Biennial Conference on Macroeconomic Policy, Warsaw

Published on
24 September 2026

In this speech Clare sets out the outlook for inflation. She describes the framework the Monetary Policy Committee is using to monitor and learn how recent energy price increases will affect inflationary pressures. She considers the size and volatility of the energy shock, the response of the UK economy, and the underlying inflationary dynamics. Monetary policy is already leaning against the risk of persistent inflationary pressures and will be tightened further if needed.

Speech
It is an honour and a pleasure to be invited to speak to you today at the Sixth Biennial Conference on Macroeconomic Policy.
Policymakers often say we are dealing with an unusually uncertain time. And I will not disappoint you. The economy faces large and complex uncertainties: geopolitical tensions, global structural shifts and the rapid march of technology. The world is changing, and those changes are interacting, with significant implications for inflation.
Today I will discuss the global energy shock and its implications for inflation and monetary policy. I will first review the framework that the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is using to assess how the global energy shock is affecting UK inflation.footnote [1] I will then assess the near- and medium-term outlook before discussing what it means for policy, both through the lens of the Committee’s recent decisions and my own perspective. I have three main messages.
First, the main driver of near-term inflation is developments in global energy prices. The energy shock due to the conflict in the Middle East has already pushed up UK inflation, and we expect it to continue to do so in the coming months. There is significant uncertainty about how the conflict will develop, and so about the evolution of energy prices.
Second, the medium-term outlook depends on how the energy shock propagates through the economy through indirect, demand and second-round effects. The key judgement for monetary policy is whether emerging evidence suggests inflation may become persistent. This risk is cumulative. The longer energy prices remain high and volatile, the greater the risk for pass-through more widely into domestic wages and prices.
Third, given the uncertainty, policy decisions are necessarily made with incomplete information. As evidence emerges we will learn about the shock, its transmission, and the risks around these. We cannot offer firm guidance on the path of policy, but we can be transparent about the reaction function: this depends on how the shock evolves, how it propagates through the UK economy and what that implies for medium-term inflation.
The effects of a global energy price shock on UK inflation
A global energy price shock affects UK inflation through four channels: direct effects on household energy costs; indirect effects through firms’ production costs and supply chains; demand effects through real incomes and spending; and second-round effects through expectations, wages and domestically set prices. Table A summarises the mechanism, timing and potential policy response for each channel.
Table A: Global energy shocks can affect UK inflation through several channels

Channel

Mechanism

Typical speed

Effect on inflation

Policy response

Direct effects

Increase in fuel and utility prices

0–1 year

0–2 years

0–3 years

Energy is an important part of households’ consumption, and pass-through from global oil and gas prices to the petrol and utility prices that households pay is relatively fast.footnote [2] Large changes in energy prices can have quick and significant direct effects on aggregate inflation. Monetary policy cannot prevent the initial rise in inflation caused by higher energy prices. Rather, its role is to ensure that temporary increases in inflation do not become persistent inflationary pressure, as I will return to in more detail later.
Energy price increases also have indirect effects on inflation, as energy is an important input to the production of many goods and services, for example, the production and delivery of food. Firms may try to pass on the increases in energy costs they pay to consumer prices. Indirect effects tend to feed through more slowly than direct effects. And they can increase disproportionately with the size and persistence of an energy shock as firms become less able to absorb cost increases in their margins.
The most pernicious effects are second-round effects. These arise if the increase in energy prices generates inflationary pressures across domestically set wages and prices beyond the direct and indirect costs of higher energy. Second-round effects are likely to be stronger the larger and more long-lasting the energy price shock is. For example, higher inflation arising from larger direct and indirect effects could feed through via higher inflation expectations into the prices companies set. Higher inflation could also make it more likely that wages rise to maintain purchasing power – which in turn would push up firms’ costs and could lead them to raise prices by more.
Finally, the decline in real incomes due to higher energy prices could lead households to reduce consumption or firms to reduce investment, reducing economic activity.footnote [3] Such demand effects are likely to be stronger the more persistent households and firms expect the energy shock to be, and the more financially constrained they are. Weaker demand can reduce the inflationary impulse of an energy price increase. It also worsens the policy trade-off, as monetary policy cannot at the same time lean against upside risks to inflation and protect against downside risks to demand and the labour market.
The near-term outlook for inflation
So, what have we seen? The direct effects from higher energy prices have raised inflation broadly as expected, while indirect pass-through has so far been weaker and firms’ and households’ demand more resilient than anticipated. I will examine each part of that evidence, before turning to the medium-term risks.
The conflict in the Middle East has caused the near-term outlook for inflation to be unusually volatile. In the pre-conflict February 2026 Monetary Policy Report, we expected CPI inflation to fall back to the 2% target by the summer. As Chart 1 shows, the projections rose materially with the onset of the conflict and have been volatile since. Without clear resolution in the Middle East, volatility in estimates for near-term inflation will likely continue.
Brent crude oil prices have fluctuated between lows of around $70 to well over $110 per barrel since the start of the conflict. In the weeks since our most recent July Report, they have increased by 26% to around $98 as of Tuesday. Natural gas prices have similarly been volatile and have increased by around 50% in recent weeks. In addition, pressures on refineries in several countries mean that crack spreads – the difference between the prices of refined petroleum products and Brent crude oil – have risen well above their pre-conflict levels. This has amplified the increases of petrol, diesel and jet fuel prices.

Chart 1: The near-term outlook for CPI inflation has shifted materially in recent months
CPI inflation and near-term projections (a)

Footnotes

Sources: ONS and Bank calculations.
(a) The solid grey line shows CPI data to August 2026. The dashed purple, orange, and aqua lines show near-term projections at the time of the February, April and July 2026 Reports, respectively. The dashed gold line shows a mechanical update of near-term projections following the release of the August CPI data on 16 September.

Higher global energy prices have pushed up motor fuel prices for UK consumers. For example, petrol prices have increased from around 132 pence per litre to around 172 pence per litre between February and September. And the Ofgem energy price cap will increase by almost 4% in October, taking an average annual household utility bill to £1,723. That is currently projected to rise further to over £2,000 in the first quarter of next year. The Bank’s latest near-term inflation forecast now points to CPI inflation rising from its current level of 3.1% to around 3.7% in 2026 Q4 and to around 4.2% in 2027 Q1, materially higher than our projection in July. Measures announced in last year’s Budget and the temporary cut to VAT on electricity until March 2027 are mitigating the direct effects of higher energy prices on inflation. Without these measures, the inflation projection for the first quarter of next year would likely be closer to 4.5%.
While direct effects have evolved broadly as expected, indirect effects have been smaller. In April we projected indirect effects would add about 0.3 percentage points to CPI inflation in August.footnote [4] But so far there is little evidence that firms are passing higher energy costs through to the prices of other goods and services. Inflation for energy-intensive parts of consumption such as food have come in below projections. A key question is whether these indirect effects will ultimately prove to be lower or slower.
So far, businesses have proved more resilient to higher energy costs than we expected. Firms may have had greater hedges than we thought. They may be temporarily absorbing higher energy costs in their margins given subdued demand conditions and limited pricing power. But there will be a limit to businesses’ ability to absorb higher costs, and any hedges that may be in place will eventually run out. If energy prices revert to a lower level soon, we may never see these indirect effects.
But the larger the energy shock becomes and the longer it persists, the more likely it is that we will eventually see significant pass-through of higher energy costs to other prices. And the level and persistence of energy prices are not the only things that matter. Greater volatility can affect pricing dynamics by increasing attention to inflation and making expectations more responsive to shocks (Mann (2025a)). If wages and prices are sticky downwards, volatility can bring an upward inflation bias. And greater uncertainty about the outlook can also encourage households to build precautionary savings buffers, affecting demand as well as inflation dynamics (Mann (2025b), Fischer et al (2025)).
Energy prices are not the only risk or uncertainty we face. Other global costs could add to inflation. Strong demand for AI components is already pushing up global export prices and weather-related shocks add upside risks. On the other hand, trade diversion is reducing inflation. Recent empirical work by Bank staff suggests that trade diversion in response to tariffs has lowered UK CPI inflation by 0.1–0.2 percentage points in 2026.
Food price inflation has surprised to the downside in recent months, but is expected to rise from here. At 1.3%, it is at a 2-year low. This reflects a reversal in sharp rises for some specific items (such as beef and cocoa), receding pressures from labour costs and packaging regulations and the slower-than-expected pass-through of higher energy costs. Despite this welcome respite, the outlook for food prices is far from benign. Bank staff expect external pressures including high energy prices to push food price inflation up over coming quarters, to a little under 3% by the end of the year and towards 4% in 2027 Q1. Recent droughts across parts of Europe are likely to increase food prices, and extreme weather events such as a particularly strong El Niño pose material upside risks. Continued conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine could disrupt agricultural exports and raise fertiliser prices. Some industry associations such as the Food and Drink Federation already forecast food price inflation to peak at over 6% in the summer of 2027.
Food prices are particularly important. Food accounts for about 11% of the overall consumption basket in the UK, so changes in food price inflation have a direct and sometimes material impact on CPI inflation. They account for a higher proportion of spending for those on low incomes. In addition, because many food items are essential goods that households regularly purchase, people tend to be particularly attentive to changes in food price inflation. Food prices have an outsized effect on households’ inflation perceptions and expectations (e.g. D’Acunto et al (2021) Opens in a new window, Bonciani et al (2024) and Anesti et al (2025)). This means that high food price inflation could contribute to second-round effects in domestic wage and price setting.
Higher energy prices do not yet appear to be weighing significantly on demand. GDP growth has been stronger than expected, and within that private consumption has held up well. While consumer confidence dipped immediately after the conflict, it has since recovered. Households appear to be smoothing through the real income shock, so we see a falling household saving ratio, though households’ ability to do this will be limited. Demand may weaken if energy prices remain high or rise further. But to date, both households and firms have proven more resilient to higher energy prices than expected.
Looking beneath the fast-paced changes driven by global energy prices, the underlying disinflation process has continued over the course of the year. Wages are a key driver of moves in underlying inflation because they are the largest cost component for many domestic firms, in particular in the services sector.

Chart 2: Private sector wage growth has continued to slow
Measures of private sector wage growth (a)

Footnotes

Sources: DMP survey, HMRC, Indeed, ONS and Bank calculations.
(a) See the footnote to Chart 1.4 in the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report for further details on these data.

The Bank monitors a broad set of indicators for wage growth (Chart 2). The Bank’s Agents report average pay settlements of 3.6% for 2026, below the average settlement of 4% in 2025. Contacts cite a lower National Living Wage (NLW) increase this year, lower inflation at the time of settling and a looser labour market as driving that fall. Overall, we have seen downward momentum across different indicators of pay growth this year, consistent with a relatively weaker labour market continuing to weigh on wages.
The rate of wage growth consistent with the inflation target depends on productivity growth and import price inflation (Lombardelli (2025)). Wage growth around 3¼% could be consistent with the inflation target in the long run, assuming productivity growth of around 1% and import price inflation in line with historical averages.footnote [5] But for as long as higher energy prices continue to generate import price inflation, the rate of wage growth consistent with returning inflation to the 2% target will be lower.
The medium-term outlook for inflation
The near-term evidence leaves two medium-term questions unresolved: where energy prices go from here, and how strongly the shock will propagate through the UK economy—especially through second-round effects. The first determines the size and duration of the initial inflation impulse; the second determines whether it becomes persistent. Scenarios help us assess those risks without suggesting that either can be forecast precisely.
Recent reforms to our monetary policy processes in response to the Bernanke Review (Bernanke (2024)) have put risks and uncertainties more explicitly at the heart of our policy framework. This helps us make and communicate monetary policy decisions in the face of uncertainty. We use alternative scenarios to explore how the economy may evolve in ways that are key to the decisions we are taking. These scenarios capture plausible alternative outcomes rather than tail risks. And they provide a common framework for internal and external discussions about monetary policy.footnote [6] Using the scenarios as a starting point, MPC members can express their personal views in a consistent and comparable way (Pill (2026)).
In July we published two scenarios alongside the central projection. In the central projection, energy prices followed their futures curves, second-round effects were assumed to be moderate, and were calibrated using the Bernanke-Blanchard model.footnote [7] In a milder scenario, energy prices follow a slightly lower path, demand weakens and there are no second-round effects. In an adverse scenario, energy prices follow a persistently higher path consistent with repeated re-escalations of the conflict, and with additional second-round effects. These additional second-round effects stem from the scaling of the Bernanke-Blanchard model to higher energy prices and an additional mechanism in which inflation expectations drift higher, generating stronger and faster second-round effects through greater amplification in wage and price-setting.
Across the scenarios we consider the two key forms of uncertainty policy makers are facing: the size of the energy shock and the strength of propagation through second-round effects, as summarised in Table B. Our scenarios are based on the diagonals, because of the expected positive relationship between energy prices and second-round effects, but off-diagonal combinations are also possible.

Table B: Energy prices and second-round effects

Second-round effects
