These scenarios lead to different medium-term outlooks for inflation. In the near-term, differences largely reflect different energy price assumptions (Chart 3, left panel). But in the medium term, differences in second-round effects are important (Chart 3, middle panel). Conditioned on market interest rates at the time, inflation fell slightly below the 2% target in the medium term in the central projection and in the milder scenario but remained above 2% in the adverse scenario (Chart 3, right panel).
The geopolitical situation in the Middle East remains unresolved. And energy spot and futures prices have increased again. To date energy prices have evolved more in line with our adverse scenario. In contrast, news on how energy prices are feeding through the economy via indirect, demand, and second-round effects have been more mixed. As noted, indirect effects have so far been smaller than expected. But the longer energy prices stay high, the more likely indirect effects are to eventually come through. We have similarly seen little evidence of demand effects to date. But demand could still weaken if the energy shock persists or worsens further.

Chart 3: Relative to the central projection, inflation is higher in the adverse scenario and lower in the milder scenario, in part due to second-round effects
Brent crude oil prices, the additional impact on inflation from potential second-round effects, and annual CPI inflation in the central projection and scenarios (a)

Footnotes

Sources: Bloomberg Finance L.P., LSEG Workspace, ONS and Bank calculations.
(a) The scenarios shown here are conditioned on the same market curve for Bank Rate. Further details on conditioning assumptions can be found in Table 3.A of the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report and the Projections Databank accompanying that Report. The final projections are for 2029 Q3.

The likely scale of second-round effects remains a key as well a difficult judgement to make. Second-round effects can’t be observed directly and would occur with a lag. Our July scenarios suggested that in our adverse scenario second-round effects would start to emerge by Q4 this year, including indications from our 2027 pay survey. In the meantime, we continue to monitor a wide range of indicators (Boxes A and B in the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report). The data flow since the end of July has not materially changed the picture. Year-ahead wage growth expectations in our Decision Maker Panel survey have remained close to 3.5% through 2026 and continue to point to wage growth slowing by around 0.5pp compared with recent outturns. And the Bank’s Agents report that estimated average pay settlements for 2026 ticked up only very slightly to 3.6%. Firms expect to make very few one-off cost-of-living payments. Most contacts do not yet want to give a figure for expected 2027 pay deals, but some suggest it would be similar or slightly lower than in 2026. Meanwhile, firms’ own-price expectations in the DMP survey remain elevated but likely reflect expected pass-through of indirect effects rather than strong second-round effects.
The absence of evidence of second-round effects tells us something, but not much. It is likely still too early to see evidence in the data, especially given that indirect effects are coming through more slowly than expected.
Where the economy was pre-conflict is relevant. Inflation has been above target for much of the past five years, leading to households and firms being more attentive to inflation than in the past. This means that inflation expectations could respond more strongly to any near-term increase in inflation. There is mixed evidence for this in the recent data, but this could change as headline inflation continues to rise in the months ahead. On the other hand, weak domestic pricing power and limited underlying wage pressure could limit the extent of second-round effects. Different views on the size and importance of these factors account for some of the differences in policy views across MPC members.
The size and persistence of the energy shock matter for second-round effects because they shape the direct and indirect inflation impulse and the time available for expectations and wage-price setting to respond. But, as Megan Greene (Greene (2026)), Alan Taylor (Taylor (2026)) and Huw Pill (Pill (2026)) have each illustrated, the relationship is not mechanical: persistently high energy prices need not generate strong second-round effects, and strong second-round effects need not require exceptionally high or persistent energy prices.
My own take is that circumstances have changed since July. The conflict has continued with consequences for the level and volatility of energy prices. Energy prices have evolved more in line with the adverse scenario whereas their second-round effects look more like the treatment in the central case. So I now put higher weight on us being closer to the adverse scenario for energy prices than I did in July. The stronger treatment of second-round effects in the adverse scenario still seems less likely than those captured in the central case. With the weaker indirect effects observed so far supporting that view. This means even if energy prices continue to sit closer to the adverse scenario, the policy consequences of that are not a forgone conclusion. That said, I continue to think it most likely that second-round effects and energy prices are positively related so the risk of material second-round effects has risen the longer higher energy prices are visible in prices people observe.
The monetary policy response
Monetary policy cannot change global energy prices; our task is to prevent the shock from generating persistent inflation without imposing undue costs on activity. That means looking through direct effects. These cannot be tackled with monetary policy as energy price volatility affects inflation more quickly than monetary policy can respond, given it impacts the economy with a lag. This principle is symmetric. If energy prices were to fall back and their contribution to inflation were eventually to turn negative, monetary policy should equally look through that temporary weakness and focus on returning inflation sustainably to the 2% target in the medium term.
The response to indirect effects depends on the shock: they can often be looked through when modest or temporary but may require tighter policy when large and persistent because prolonged pass-through raises the risk of second-round effects. Finally, monetary policy should lean strongly against second-round effects, which risk de-anchoring inflation and preventing it from returning sustainably to target.
Judging the likely extent of second-round effects in real time is difficult. We should learn more in Q4 as information on price and wage expectations arrives, although the evidence may still not be conclusive. There is little in the data so far to suggest that second-round effects are large, but it is too soon to tell.
The change in the policy outlook since before the conflict has been significant. Prior to the conflict, the Committee was gradually reducing monetary restriction as domestic inflationary pressures eased. That process was gradual because domestic disinflation itself was gradual and remained vulnerable to further inflationary shocks. We had reduced rates by 150 basis points since their peak, pausing at 3.75% when the conflict broke out. Since then, Bank Rate has remained unchanged and financial conditions have tightened materially. For example, quoted rates on two-year fixed-rate mortgages are now more than one percentage point higher than prior to the conflict. Current monetary and financial conditions are restrictive and are already leaning against inflationary pressures.
Different MPC members will naturally place different weight on different pieces of evidence, as reflected in their individual paragraphs and speeches. But the MPC shares an analytical framework for thinking through the implications of the energy shock for inflation and monetary policy. That framework provides a disciplined way of learning and updating our judgements as new information arrives.
To date, a majority of the MPC have not judged that an increase in Bank Rate is needed but, as outlined in the September minutes, have noted that the inflation risks are currently to the upside and waiting for evidence had limits. Financial market participants have looked at the same information and reached a broadly similar conclusion about the balance of risks, assigning a greater probability to states of the world that require higher policy rates in the near term.
There is uncertainty not just about the next move, but the path beyond. We are in a very different place from the tightening cycle of 2021/22. Then policy rates started at the historically low level of 0.1% and policy was highly accommodative. Today Bank Rate is 3.75% and overall financial conditions are leaning against inflationary pressures in the economy. Decisions beyond the next meeting will depend on how energy prices evolve and how the shock propagates through the economy. On both questions we will learn more over the coming months. This is reflected in market pricing: the option-implied probability distribution for future interest rates has widened since our July Report.
I will conclude with my views on the policy outlook. There remains material uncertainty about the size and duration of the shock and how it will pass through the economy. We are learning about the impacts. What we have seen so far shows the direct pass-through to inflation has been broadly as anticipated. Activity has been stronger – both the underlying economy and the response to the shock. Yet to date indirect effects have been more limited than expected.
This gives pause for thought. Firms have shown a surprising ability to absorb higher energy prices to date, but this ability will be limited. If elevated energy prices persist for long enough, direct cost pressures are increasingly likely to eventually turn into indirect and second-round inflationary pressures. The relevant question is therefore not whether we can already observe indirect and second-round effects in the data, it is whether the conditions for those indirect and second-round effects are becoming more entrenched. The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response.
On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity. But this is by no means suggesting that monetary policy should respond mechanically to movements in energy prices. The key issue is not the spot price of energy itself but the interaction of the underlying economy, higher energy prices, and the nature of their transmission. That, ultimately, is what will determine whether Bank Rate needs to rise.
I would like to thank Lukas von dem Berge and Brad Speigner for their help with preparing this speech. I also thank Carleton Webb, Michal Stelmach, Alex Kontoghiorghes, Amarjot Sidhu, Giulia Gardin, Tim Willems, Tim Munday, Neha Jain and Marcus Buckmann for their help with data and analysis. And Jamie Bell, Fergal Shortall, Becky Maule, Rohan Churm, Geoff Coppins, Sean Maloney, Chris Duffy, Catherine Mann, Huw Pill and Sarah Breeden for their helpful comments on earlier drafts.

More details can be found in our Monetary Policy Reports. This framework provides a structured approach for navigating uncertainty while enabling MPC members to hold and express different views of the outlook and the appropriate policy response.

Pass-through to utility prices is somewhat slower than to petrol prices due to fixed-term contracts and the Ofgem price cap mechanism.

An energy shock can affect the balance of demand and supply in the economy in various ways. Higher energy prices could lead to a reduction in potential supply, though this effect is likely to be modest (Box B in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report). Demand effects tend to outweigh supply effects, which is why we typically focus on the former and on the net impact on slack.

Chart 1.4 in the April MPR.

Like most countries, the UK has seen a material step down in estimated UK productivity growth since the Global Financial Crisis, and a likely further deterioration since Covid. Developments in artificial intelligence are expected to increase productivity.

Scenarios do not represent alternative central cases for different members, but enable members to locate their views within that common framework (Greene (2026) and Taylor (2026)).

Second-round effects are calibrated using the Bernanke-Blanchard model applied to UK data (see Haskel et al (2025) Opens in a new window). In that model, higher energy prices affect short-term inflation expectations, which feed into wage-setting and subsequently prices.

Quantitative Equity

Emerging Markets All Cap Quant Equity

Table of Contents

Investment Objective*
Investment Approach
Key Features
INVESTMENTS
INSIGHTS
ABOUT

Investment Objective*
Seek long-term capital appreciation by outperforming the MSCI Emerging Markets IMI Index over a full market cycle, while maintaining a diversified portfolio of equities across emerging markets.

Investment Approach
A disciplined, systematic investment process that combines fundamental and behavioural insights to identify attractively valued companies with high-quality fundamentals and improving growth prospects. Our innovative stock-selection model evaluates each company in context, placing greater emphasis on the factors most relevant to its stage of development. Risk-aware portfolio construction seeks to translate these insights efficiently into a diversified portfolio while maintaining controlled active risk.

Key Features

A diversified portfolio of large, mid and small cap equities across emerging markets.
An active, benchmark-aware approach designed to serve as a consistent core emerging market equity allocation.
Systematic stock selection incorporating Growth, Linkages, Quality and Value insights.
Contextual modelling that dynamically adjusts the emphasis on Growth and Value at the company level.
Pragmatic portfolio construction designed to maximise exposure to intended alpha sources while limiting uncompensated risks.
An experienced investment team supported by three decades of live quantitative equity track records and an ongoing commitment to rigorous research.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesMarketsWhy Luxury Goods Companies’ Revenues Are Forecast to ClimbOct 22, 2026Share Makers of luxury goods are poised for faster revenue growth after several years of sluggish sales. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts 7% revenue growth for luxury-goods companies in 2027, up from 6% in 2026, based on a basket of key luxury-brand stocks. This represents a solid recovery and a rebuttal of the argument by some bears “that the sector may have gone ex-growth for an extended period,” according to Goldman Sachs Research. The US has become a surprising bright spot for luxury goods, with behavior shifting in a market where buying habits have not fully reflected the significant number of wealthy consumers. The outlook for luxury brands is improving after several years of lackluster performance, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
A basket of large, publicly traded luxury-goods makers is forecast to increase revenue by 7% in 2027, Erwan Rambourg, head of Europe Luxury and Lifestyle in Goldman Sachs Research, writes in a report. This is an improvement from an expected 6% growth rate in 2026, when the sector came out of several years of weaker performance.
“We view this as a solid recovery for an industry that has faced a prolonged period of sluggish performance,” Rambourg writes.
The market capitalization for luxury-goods stocks increased in 2022, after the stock market swoon caused by the Covid pandemic. Luxury stocks benefited from “exuberant spending,” Rambourg notes, but this was followed by a period of aggressive price increases and a slower pace of innovation from the sector.
What is the outlook for luxury goods companies?

Luxury-goods makers’ share prices have fallen over the past three or four years, but so have earnings estimates, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The result is that valuations do not look particularly attractive, and they also don’t appear stretched. “But we think valuation alone is rarely a catalyst for investors to buy or sell shares in the sector,” Rambourg writes. “Instead, it is more a function of sales momentum, which we see picking up soon.”
Why luxury goods sales have been sluggish

The industry has faced multiple challenges. China’s ongoing property slump, US tariffs in 2025, jittery equity markets, upcoming midterm elections and higher rates, as well as the ongoing Middle East conflict and other geopolitical tensions have weighed on spending decisions.

“There have been many reasons for consumers to cancel or delay purchases of discretionary products,” Rambourg writes. Still, these broader factors probably haven’t been the main constraint, he says, attributing the weak performance in recent years mostly to “a degree of strategic inertia” among luxury brands.
Price hikes after the Covid pandemic, which were perceived as excessive by some observers, likely played a larger role in the slowdown in growth for luxury goods. More affordable luxury brands benefited as traditional high-end names hiked prices—estimated at around 60% between mid-2019 and mid-2026—opening space in the market that they could fill, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
“As a direct impact of elevated price points and a value proposition that became less compelling across many brands, it appears that many target consumers decided to pass on purchasing luxury goods,” Rambourg writes.
Alongside the aggressive price increases, limited innovation by the industry in the post-Covid period led to diminished consumer interest, and store traffic tailed off. That said, a number of luxury companies have new CEOs and creative directors who started presenting their collections last year. “We believe that it likely takes three to four collections for consumers to recognize—and possibly buy into—the change,” Rambourg writes.
Why the US may still be an emerging market for luxury

For many years there has been “a surprising disconnect between wealth in the US (high) and luxury demand among American consumers (low),” Rambourg points out. The market was likely restrained by a “guilt factor” or by “outlet culture,” he says. However, behaviors have begun to change since the Covid pandemic.
“The appetite of American consumers for luxury goods has picked up strongly,” he writes. Luxury brands have taken notice, and store openings are multiplying.
“While it may sound counterintuitive, we still think the US is an emerging market for luxury goods,” he adds.
Elsewhere in the world, South Korean demand growth may be somewhat fragile because it is linked to wealth in the country’s tech-heavy and volatile equity market. The importance of Hong Kong for luxury brands has diminished over time, but the market is showing signs of recovery, with both local consumers and visitors from mainland China supporting sales growth, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
The luxury goods companies Goldman Sachs Research covers have recorded average top-line growth of 6% annually over the past 25 years.
“While growth has been pedestrian of late,” sales levels exceed what a 6% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) would have implied since just before the Covid pandemic in 2019, Rambourg points out. “In other words, the bear argument that the sector may have gone ex-growth for an extended period is not one we agree with,” he writes.
What is the longer-term outlook for the luxury goods sector?

To help understand where the sector and individual luxury goods makers may be headed, the report includes a benchmarking framework. This provides a way to think about long-term growth drivers, broken down as seven Cs.
One of the Cs is clout, and Rambourg posits that “big is beautiful” in the luxury sector. He notes that bigger brands not only tend to secure better locations, but they also benefit from lower rent as a percentage of sales. Another is categories, with some consumer verticals, such as jewelry, having better growth potential than others, such as beauty products.
Other considerations in the framework include: consumer caliber, referencing the relative resilience of high-net-worth consumers, which can likewise make high-end brands more resilient; and creativity, which may be difficult for equity analysts to quantify but does come into play in assessing prospects for luxury companies.
Rounding out the list are consistency, which gets to the clarity of brand positioning; codes and icons, which are not necessarily loud logos but can be a discreet symbol, pattern, or logo only identifiable by people who know the products well; and finally, corporate considerations, as many luxury-goods companies are partly owned and run by family members.

articles.title: One Health through the lens of today’s investment megatrends
articles.text:
FORWARD THINKING | ARTICLE – 6 min read
One Health through the lens of today’s investment megatrends

By
ALEXANDER BERNHARDT, RACHEL CROSSLEY, ROBERT-ALEXANDRE POUJADE 22.10.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
Geopolitics: Health security, resilience and strategic dependenceInnovation: new solutions, new dependencies and new questions of accessDemographics: Demand, vulnerability and health’s social determinantsEnvironment: Ecosystems as health infrastructureWhy investors should care

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

By Alex Bernhardt, Global Head of Sustainability Research; Rachel Crossley, Head of Stewardship, Europe; and Robert-Alexandre Poujade, Head of Nature

The One Health concept recognises that human health is inextricably linked to the health of animals and the environment, moving beyond a narrow medical perspective to a systemic view of health-related value and risk

Assessing One Health through the lens of four megatrends – geopolitics, innovation, demographics, and the environment – helps to identify impacts on worker productivity, supply chain reliability, and market growth

For long-term investors, health determinants are viewed as material factors that can influence corporate earnings, sovereign credit, and labour markets, helping to identify risks that may currently be underappreciated by the market

The forces shaping human health outcomes are far broader than hospitals, pharmaceuticals and medical devices. Human health is dependent upon animal health and the health of the environment. Together the health of these three systems are inextricably intertwined, creating the One Health concept (Exhibit 1).

For long-term investors, these health determinants are not peripheral; they shape and are shaped by productivity, labour participation, the resilience of communities and economies and other social systems.

While the pathways for One Health impacts are not always linear or clear, they can nevertheless be material to economic and financial outcomes for investors. Indeed, understanding how corporate investment can drive negative or create positive health outcomes for its stakeholders – employees, customers, communities, plants and animals – will be increasingly important in an increasingly interconnected world.

The One Health theme, grounded in preceding work by the World Health Organization and other supranationals, therefore gives us a useful frame for moving from a narrow sector view of health to a more systemic view of health-related value creation and risk.

It recognises that a workforce’s health can affect operating performance; that the health of consumers can influence the growth of markets; and that the health of ecosystems can determine the reliability of supply chains; the quality of natural inputs and the exposure of communities to disease.

Companies do not operate outside these systems. They depend on them and affect them.

This does not mean treating every social or environmental issue as a health issue. A disciplined One Health approach should improve, not dilute, investment analysis. The challenge is to identify where health determinants are financially material for a sector, issuer, or asset and through which transmission channels. To support related analysis BNPP AM’s megatrends provide a useful framework:

Geopolitics: Global health outcomes depend on food security, access to medicines, resilient supply chains and international cooperation on health and environmental risks. Geopolitical fragmentation can increase vulnerabilities while cooperation can improve system resilience

Environment: Human, animal and ecosystem health are deeply interconnected. Environmental pressures such as pollution, climate change, biodiversity loss and water stress affect public health, productivity and economic stability

Demographics: Ageing populations, urbanisation and changing disease patterns are reshaping demand for healthcare, nutrition, housing and care services. Understanding demographic trends is essential to improving long-term health and economic resilience.

Innovation: Breakthroughs in biotechnology, diagnostics, precision agriculture, data analytics and preventative care can improve health outcomes across interconnected human, animal and environmental systems. Innovation expands the range of investable health solutions

Geopolitics: Health security, resilience and strategic dependence

Access to healthcare and other social determinants of health – notably housing, food and water – is increasingly shaped by geopolitics. At the multinational level, restrictive trade policy, increased conflict, and decreased cooperation all serve to heighten the risk of future pandemics, worsening climate-related health impacts, and medicine or food shortages.

At the national level, shifts in the political landscape can result in declining quality of public services which can have cross-border effects. For instance, softening vaccine requirements could result in greater incidence of preventable disease.

Moreover, loss of public benefits like food or housing assistance can increase the public burden of disease which can have many knock-on effects for communities beyond the added frictional costs of increased emergency health treatments.

A One Health perspective shows that company resilience is dependent to a significant degree upon public institutions. This creates risks for companies dependent on vulnerable global supply chains, low-cost labour, or weakened public systems, but it also creates opportunities in healthcare security, diagnostics, and other solutions that support preparedness without simply shifting costs to consumers or governments.

Innovation: new solutions, new dependencies and new questions of access

Innovation is central to One Health because it changes what can be prevented, detected, treated and measured. Advances in medicines, environmental monitoring and AI-enabled discovery can improve health outcomes and strengthen resilience.

They can also help investors identify companies whose products and services reduce preventable harm while addressing structural demand. Healthcare innovation remains important, but the investable universe is broader than healthcare alone. It includes technologies and business models that improve the health of people, animals and ecosystems together.

At the same time, innovation can create new dependencies and unintended consequences. Digital health tools may improve access but raise questions about privacy, exclusion and quality of care.

Artificial intelligence can accelerate drug discovery, diagnostics and environmental monitoring, but it can also increase energy and water demand and concentrate benefits among firms with data, compute and distribution advantages.

Agricultural technology can reduce chemical and antibiotic use, but it can also deepen dependence on proprietary inputs. The investment question is therefore not whether innovation is positive in general, but whether the business model, governance, affordability, lifecycle impacts and measurable outcomes support durable value creation.

A One Health lens helps distinguish innovation that genuinely improves resilience from innovation that merely increases efficiency while shifting health or environmental costs elsewhere.

Demographics: Demand, vulnerability and health’s social determinants

Demographics are reshaping One Health considerations with different trends driving different outcomes. Ageing populations, particularly in developed markets, create significant risks if the transition is unmanaged.

But well managed, it can create huge opportunities for investments in the care economy including long-term care, mobility solutions and age-friendly housing.1

Urbanisation, particularly pronounced in emerging markets, increases the importance of sanitation, air quality, housing quality, green space, transport design and heat resilience.

Migration and regional demographic divergence influence labour availability, fiscal capacity and the vulnerability of communities to public health and climate shocks. Labour market participation and socioeconomic inequality can create political risk and shift aggregate demand patterns.

Environment: Ecosystems as health infrastructure

Environment is perhaps the most intuitive One Health lens because air quality and ecosystem health are a foundation for human and animal health. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and water availability all influence exposure to disease, heat stress and unsafe living conditions.

An estimated nine million premature deaths each year are caused by pollution and 90% of the global population is exposed to ambient concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) above the WHO annual air quality guideline.2 Additionally, over 60% of emerging infectious diseases originate in animals.3

Perhaps one of the most trenchant examples of the human health and animal health connection is antimicrobial resistance. It arises when bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites evolve to resist the medications that once effectively treated infections.

And its rise in humans can largely be traced to the overuse of antibiotics in livestock. Understanding the societal ramifications of consumer preferences for meat and business preferences for efficient solutions to problems (in this case, animals often living in close-quarters getting sick) is supported by a One Health perspective.

Why investors should care

Within BNPP AM’s Global Sustainability Strategy, One Health therefore sits alongside Transition and Sustainable AI as part of our forward-looking research agenda. One Health matters for investors because it connects health outcomes to the systems that sustain long-term economic value.

It broadens the investment lens from healthcare spending to the determinants of health that for example shape worker productivity/availability and supply-chain reliability. It also helps identify risks that markets may underprice because they sit between sectors, time horizons or asset classes.

Antimicrobial resistance, unsafe food systems, pollution exposure, heat stress, biodiversity loss, weak health access and social isolation may each appear narrow at first, but together they can affect corporate earnings, sovereign credit, labour markets and long-term market performance.

The investor implications are practical. First, One Health supports better risk identification by linking health determinants to financially material transmission channels such as input costs, workforce productivity and tail risks.

Second, it supports opportunity identification by clarifying where durable demand may emerge for prevention-oriented healthcare, affordable housing, climate adaptation and nature-based solutions.

And third, it supports stewardship by helping investors ask whether companies are reducing preventable harm, strengthening resilience and measuring outcomes, rather than relying on broad claims.

Measurement will be central. One Health is powerful because it captures interdependence, but that also makes it vulnerable to over-claiming. Investors need fit-for-purpose indicators that distinguish inputs, outputs and outcomes; recognise time horizons; and avoid overstating causality. We will continue our work on this over the years to come.

[2] Global Environment Outlook 7 | UNEP – UN Environment Programme

[3] Editorial: Zoonotic diseases originating from wildlife: Emergence/re-emergence, evolution, prevalence, pathogenesis, prevention, and treatment – PMC

articles.text:
PERSPECTIVES Quarterly update

PERSPECTIVES: Economic and asset class update – March 2026

Ready to talk?

×

Robust economic growth is expected due to solid consumption and sizeable investment, although geopolitical tensions could act as a drag. We see stable sequential quarterly growth in the US in 2026, while in the Eurozone extensive German fiscal stimulus should keep growth near potential. In Japan, the government’s pro-growth policy will help sustain robust economic activity. Policy support for strategic industries and households will continue in China.

On investment, we argue that discipline will continue to beat drama. Equities started the year on a strong footing and, despite recent reverses, are still on track for future gains. A strong earnings outlook is supportive and sectoral strength is broadening. On fixed income, deficits are keeping the US long end elevated but investment grade is steady despite AI disruption risks. Recent events in the Middle East and investors’ reactions have underlined the case for gold; oil remains fundamentally well-supplied but more short-term price spikes are possible. In FX, previous USD weakness has not been sustained but future possible headwinds from asset diversification are still relevant.

articles.title: Power Lessons From China
articles.text:
Power Lessons From China

AJ Cortese

Gavekal Technologies: New Energy | 26 Oct 2026

The US data center boom is facing a power crunch. So far, delays and cancellations due to electricity shortages have been sporadic. By some point in 2028, they could become systemic, and might force a significant slowdown in data center construction. The main response by hyperscalers has been to build their own captive power plants. But this is an expensive stopgap that will be slowed by shortages of turbines and transformers. Building more on-grid power capacity will inevitably take time, so it will be important for the US to figure out how to better use batteries and distributed renewables generation to make power demand and supply more flexible. And third, it supports stewardship by helping investors ask whether companies are reducing preventable harm, strengthening resilience and measuring outcomes, rather than relying on broad claims.

Measurement will be central. One Health is powerful because it captures interdependence, but that also makes it vulnerable to over-claiming. Investors need fit-for-purpose indicators that distinguish inputs, outputs and outcomes; recognise time horizons; and avoid overstating causality. We will continue our work on this over the years to come.

[2] Global Environment Outlook 7 | UNEP – UN Environment Programme

articles.title: Why generals need economists to win long wars
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Why generals need economists to win long wars

Elina Ribakova (PIIE)

Date
October 30, 2026 1:15 PM

Photo Credit: Hans Lucas via Reuters

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
The US National Defense Strategy(link is external) published by the Trump administration in January 2026 reassures allies that the European component of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) "dwarfs Russia in economic scale, population, and, thus, latent military power." Non-US NATO GDP is $26 trillion compared to Russia's $2 trillion. Their economic clout is not even close. But this comparison is misleading. At purchasing power parity, which reflects the purchasing ability of different currencies, Russia's military spending is almost the same as that of the European Union and the United Kingdom(link is external).
On the other hand, Russia's economy(link is external) itself is more than 10 times the size of Ukraine's. Yet four and a half years into an invasion Moscow expected to finish in three days, Ukraine is still fighting back.
In a different part of the world, Iran's economy(link is external) is barely 1 percent the size of the United States' economy. Yet over the eight months of war, Tehran has tied down US forces, burned through half to two-thirds of US missile defense interceptors that will take at least five years to rebuild(link is external), and is still holding global energy markets hostage, while driving up US inflation. Composite measures such as the Composite Index of National Capability(link is external) narrow the gaps, but they measure potential, not mobilization.
What explains this imbalance between the size of an economy and its ability to wage war?
If countries seek to convert economic power into military success(link is external), economists and the military need to cooperate more closely. Indeed, economists' contributions grow in importance as wars settle into long wars, wars of attrition, or asymmetric conflicts. In such cases, economic management must be part of military strategy, not just a backdrop.
Of course, economists cannot replace the military's ability to deploy armed forces(link is external). Nor can economists replace bargaining: Wars still end at the negotiating table(link is external). But converting economic power into military power determines how long each side can hold out and how much each side can afford to lose, thus setting the stage for negotiations.
A proposed new research agenda on the economics of war
This blog post presents a brief overview of the current literature on the economics of war(link is external)—much of it outdated and siloed in the different disciplines of economics, international relations, and political science—and maps out a research agenda, highlighting what work has been done and what still needs to be done rather than attempting to resolve central questions. Four building blocks—generating resources, converting resources into military capabilities, denying resources to an adversary, and staying in power—can help us understand how economic size becomes sustained fighting power, where that conversion breaks down, and what economists and military specialists need to understand together.
For example, nationwide mobilization requires paying for production, finding cost-effective ways to wage war, mobilizing the right number and type of people, adopting new technologies faster than the adversary, and denying the other party resources through economic warfare. These imperatives raise economic issues as much as military ones.
The post Cold-War record indicates that economists and generals rarely work together, except in rare cases like Finland, Singapore, and increasingly Russia and Ukraine.The absence of a large-scale war between industrial states in recent history has erased wartime economic expertise from institutions on both sides. Defense studies have recently begun to take an interest in the economics of mobilization(link is external), and the economics profession should refresh its own frameworks for the economics of war.
Historians of past wars—including Paul Kennedy(link is external), Mark Harrison, and Stephen Broadberry in their comparative volumes on the First(link is external) and Second(link is external) World Wars, and Alan Milward(link is external) in the postwar period—have shown that productive capacity shapes outcomes over the long run. Recent work has advanced individual topics. Economists Jonathan Federle, Dominic Rohner, and Moritz Schularick find that windfall revenue gains raise a country's odds of winning(link is external), enabling them to increase military spending. Political scientist Rosella Cappella Zielinski explains how states choose to pay for wars(link is external). Economists Jeffrey J. Schott of PIIE; Edward Fishman(link is external), author of Chokepoints; and the historian Nicholas Mulder(link is external) trace the rise of sanctions as a tool of modern war. Mark Harrison now distills lessons for defense industrial policy(link is external), among them that costs matter in long wars and autarky is a costly delusion, and Phillips Payson O'Brien, strategic historian, argues, controversially, that wars are won by full-spectrum powers(link is external) able to sustain them. The field even has its own journal Defence and Peace Economics(link is external). The recent wars suggest that it is time to bring it back to the mainstream.
The four building blocks that can help us understand the importance of economics as it relates to war are as follows:
1. Generating resources: Mobilizing funding and labor, and related trade-offs
War finance depends on the speed and credibility of mobilizing capital and the trade-offs between taxation, debt, money creation, and, increasingly, reliance on external financing. The core choices are how much to finance through taxes versus debt, with which instruments, particularly which taxes, and which nominal or inflation-indexed bonds.
The economist John Maynard Keynes's volume How to Pay for the War(link is external), written nearly a century ago for an economy constrained by supply rather than demand, remains an important part of the debate on rearmament. Central banks make up the financial rear: keeping payment systems running, banks liquid and solvent, and monetary policy predictable. Central banks not only help avoid a financial crisis but also help preserve confidence that the state still governs and will survive the war.
External support has increasingly become an important but still understudied input. We can also think of the absorptive capacity of countries receiving such support as the multiplier: Ukraine converts allied aid(link is external) into fighting power, while the $145 billion(link is external) the United States spent rebuilding Afghanistan over 20 years did not prevent its government's collapse. Labor mobilization also requires trade-offs—between the war front and the home front. Ukraine lost roughly a quarter of its effective labor force during Russia's 2022 invasion. Yet wage flexibility, remote work, and hiring women and older workers kept the decline in job-matching efficiency to about 15 percent(link is external). In Israel, prolonged call-up of reservists and exclusion of Palestinian workers are weighing on the economy(link is external).
2. Converting resources: Technological adaptation and innovation
Choosing where to focus military production is a critical economic choice. Over the past few decades, the United States and Germany have tended to invest more in highly sophisticated and expensive materiel that takes years, if not decades, to produce. Ukraine and Iran are at the opposite side of the spectrum. Ukraine has been forced to mobilize production rapidly because of shortages of manpower and financial resources, and Iran by decades of isolation.
But these scarcities can serve as an advantage: Existing large corporates in the United States and Germany have a history of government contracts for specific types of capital-intensive, bespoke, highly sophisticated military equipment. These companies want to protect their status, so when cheap drones are suddenly needed, it is hard for new companies to enter the market. By contrast, in Ukraine and Iran, there are few incumbents to resist shifting away from capital-intensive military industry.
Russia lags Ukraine in innovation, though it is closing that gap and is also more successful at scaling production, mostly of older, proven technology. Ukraine's ability to expand its industrial base across more than 180 European partnerships should help it achieve scale as well. Finally, recent wars have reversed the traditional defense research and development model: After decades of lower post–Cold War spending, civilian technology is now pulled into military use rather than the other way around.
3. Denying resources: Economic warfare
Denying the adversary its capacity to convert economic power into military advantage is the flip side of building your own. Economic warfare cannot win wars by itself but can make an important contribution. Sanctions are one instrument of economic warfare(link is external) alongside blockades, strategic bombing, and long-range strikes on oil refineries(link is external) and shipping lanes. Coalition size, costs borne by the sanctioning country, adaptation, and enforcement are the main constraints. US Senate hearings with experts(link is external) and companies(link is external) revealed a pressure point: More than 40 percent of 2,500 components in Russian weapons used in Ukraine came from four American suppliers(link is external). Meanwhile, Iran's disruption of the Strait of Hormuz shows how a much smaller economy can wage asymmetric warfare, imposing steep, far-reaching costs on a much richer adversary.
4. Constraints: Staying in power
Narratives directed at the domestic or international community can reduce the cost of every other input. Credibility with bond markets, the public, and allied militaries—whose supply chains can assist a smaller state—keeps finance and materiel flowing and people at work. Government can also use its ability to shape narrative to suppress statistics or shape how people understand wars being waged. Leaders' choices are constrained(link is external) by the need to keep the support of those who can keep them in power, even when doing so comes at the expense of the wider public. As political scientist Stephen Biddle and defense analyst and researcher Robert Zirkle explain, what secures the cooperation of elites is not always what is best for the economy, and coup-proofing(link is external)—organizing the military to keep a country's ruler safe from overthrow, rather than for maximum efficiency—and patronage impose deadweight loss on converting economic power into military power. Political scientists Abramo Fimo Kenneth Organski(link is external) and Jacek Kugler demonstrate how relative political capacity(link is external) measures how much a government can use its potential. Political scientist Randall L. Schweller(link is external) shows why fragmented states fail to do enough to counter an external threat because internal disagreements prevent them from building defenses or forming effective alliances.
After the Iran-Iraq war, Iran's Revolutionary Guards understood the need to control resources to continue to militarize; Iranian economists are often left to manage the consequences, and the best are often pushed out of government. Venezuela shows how a regime can survive while an important economic resource, in this case the oil industry, decays. It offered no resistance to an intervention by a foreign power, namely the United States. Regime survival and national capability are different things(link is external).
As the United States and Europe commit trillions of dollars to increasing their military capabilities, they cannot rely on aggregate GDP, or even defense spending as a share of GDP, to deter or win protracted conflicts. They must measure what that spending actually delivers: using purchasing power parity to compare resources, and tracing how funding, including allied support, becomes production, deployable capabilities, and battlefield effects. That work requires economists and military specialists to build a common framework.

Data Disclosure

This publication does not include a replication package.
