articles.title: Approving the US-Saudi nuclear deal while reducing proliferation risks | Brookings
articles.text:
Research
Approving the US-Saudi nuclear deal while reducing proliferation risks

Robert Einhorn

Robert Einhorn

Senior Fellow
- Foreign Policy, Strobe Talbott Center for Security, Strategy, and Technology, Arms Control and Non-Proliferation Initiative

October 26, 2026

There are inherent nuclear proliferation risks in supporting uranium enrichment in Saudi Arabia, which has vowed to acquire nuclear weapons if Iran does and refused to accept the most effective form of verification, the IAEA Additional Protocol.
The U.S.-Saudi 123 agreement—especially its provisions intended to ensure that Saudi Arabia will engage in nuclear cooperation almost exclusively with the United States—reduces but does not eliminate those risks.
Congress should adopt a joint resolution of approval that contains understandings and conditions designed to clarify the agreement, strengthen its non-proliferation guardrails, and preserve Congress’ role in the agreement’s implementation.

The Trump administration’s civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia—commonly called a 123 agreement, referring to the section of the Atomic Energy Act governing U.S. civil nuclear cooperation with other countries—departs from long-standing U.S. non-proliferation policy in two important ways. Although Washington has long opposed the spread of fuel-cycle (i.e., uranium enrichment and plutonium reprocessing) capabilities to additional countries, the agreement established a potential pathway to enrichment in Saudi Arabia. And although the United States has led international efforts to make the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Additional Protocol (AP) the universal standard for effective non-proliferation verification, the administration was willing to conclude the agreement without requiring Riyadh to adhere to the AP.
These departures have been heavily criticized by some members of Congress, influential media, and non-governmental experts. Citing the Saudi leadership’s publicly declared determination to match any Iranian nuclear weapons capability, the critics argue that supporting enrichment in the kingdom and failing to require the AP could eventually result in Saudi Arabia producing nuclear weapons. With the 123 agreement now before Congress for the legislatively mandated 90-day review period, congressional opponents have introduced a joint resolution of disapproval in an effort to block it.
The Trump administration believes that the non-proliferation constraints built into the agreement—together with its economic and geopolitical benefits—more than offset the proliferation risks. Supporters of the agreement, including some former senior Democratic officials who previously negotiated with the Saudis, contend that, if Washington rejects the agreement, the Saudis will turn to other nuclear suppliers, including perhaps the Russians or Chinese, who would be less insistent than the United States on rigorous non-proliferation controls.1
Key features of the 123 agreement—particularly its provisions giving the United States a near-exclusive role in the development of the Saudi nuclear energy program—reduce but do not eliminate the proliferation risks. And critical details about the agreement’s operation will only be worked out after it takes effect. Still, given the Atomic Energy Act’s very high bar for voting down a civil nuclear deal, the U.S.-Saudi 123 agreement will almost surely enter into force, probably as early as December 2026.
It will be up to Congress to authorize the agreement’s entry into force in a way that further reduces proliferation risks while allowing its substantial benefits to be realized. The stakes are large. Whether, how, and under what conditions the agreement goes forward has important implications for the future of the global non-proliferation regime, prospects for revitalizing the U.S. industry and enabling it to make a major contribution to the anticipated worldwide expansion of nuclear energy, and the role the United States will play in an uncertain and rapidly evolving Middle East geostrategic environment.
A possible pathway to uranium enrichment
Critics of the U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear deal focus heavily on its handling of uranium enrichment, a dual-use technology that can produce low-enriched fuel for nuclear reactors as well as highly enriched uranium for nuclear weapons. By establishing a possible pathway toward enrichment in Saudi Arabia, the agreement is a major departure from the long-standing, bipartisan U.S. policy of opposing the spread of enrichment and reprocessing capabilities.
The agreement does not permit enrichment in the kingdom from the outset. The two parties will conduct an enrichment and conversion study within two years that will consider such factors as the economic viability of enrichment in the kingdom and the implications of Saudi enrichment for nuclear proliferation. While some critics suspect that the study will be designed to recommend enrichment in Saudi Arabia, administration officials maintain that the conclusion is not preordained, given the many uncertainties that exist about the feasibility and commercial viability of domestic enrichment in the kingdom.2
Domestic enrichment would be prohibited while the study is underway. Indeed, according to reports that have not been confirmed in the documents released to date, if Washington persists in withholding its consent, domestic enrichment—whether carried out by Saudi Arabia on its own or with third-party assistance—would be banned for as long as 10 years after the study is completed.
However, the United States could also consent to enrichment in the kingdom once the study is completed. With the agreement widely expected to enter into force toward the end of 2026, the study would be completed by the end of 2028, with Donald Trump still in the White House and able—and many observers believe likely—to give his consent. Then, once further legal requirements are met, exports of enrichment-related equipment and technology to Saudi Arabia could begin. Enrichment in Saudi Arabia would initially be limited to 5% uranium-235, but after another study, the level could increase to nearly 20%, much closer to weapons-grade.
Critics argue that greenlighting enrichment in the kingdom would significantly increase the risks of an eventual Saudi nuclear weapons program and damage the global non-proliferation regime. For decades, the United States has refused to transfer fuel-cycle equipment and technology to countries that do not already possess them and has led the very successful international effort to discourage other nuclear suppliers from doing so.
Opponents of the 123 agreement caution that making an exception for Saudi Arabia could lead to a growing number of countries with the ability to enrich uranium for nuclear weapons. It could increase the difficulty of denying similar requests from treaty allies like South Korea and Turkey, dissuading Russia, China, and others from offering their non-nuclear weapon state (NNWS) customers an enrichment plant as an incentive to buy their nuclear reactors, persuading Iran to accept a multiyear suspension of enrichment, and discouraging the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from reconsidering its renunciation of enrichment, as it has a right to do under the U.S.-UAE 123 agreement.
No requirement to adhere to the Additional Protocol
Another focus of criticism of the U.S.-Saudi 123 agreement is its failure to require Saudi Arabia to accept the IAEA AP. The AP is a voluntary measure that supplements the basic comprehensive safeguards agreements (CSAs) mandated by the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Accepted by the vast majority of countries, the AP gives the IAEA stronger verification tools than CSAs alone, including more extensive and timely inspector access and greater information about an adherent’s nuclear program. It is particularly important for investigating suspicious activities at undeclared locations and enabling the IAEA to determine whether undeclared facilities or activities exist in a country.
The Obama administration, the first Trump administration, and the Biden administration all pressed Saudi Arabia to accept the AP as part of a 123 agreement. But the Saudis adamantly refused, arguing that inspections at culturally sensitive locations, such as holy sites and palaces, would be unnecessarily intrusive. Concluding that continuing to insist on the AP would be a deal-breaker, the second Trump administration decided to drop it as a requirement.
Instead, the Trump administration negotiated a bilateral safeguards agreement (BSA) with the Saudis that would supplement the kingdom’s CSA and be implemented by the IAEA. The BSA would apply to “all uranium conversion, uranium enrichment, fuel fabrication, reprocessing, or any associated research and development activity undertaken pursuant to the Nuclear Cooperation Agreement.”3 It would thus apply to the most proliferation-sensitive areas of U.S.-Saudi cooperation. Moreover, the BSA’s enhanced information and access provisions were based very closely on the AP’s rigorous information and access provisions. The BSA could thus help build international confidence that sensitive, declared U.S.-Saudi nuclear cooperation was not being diverted to a nuclear weapons program.
There is a significant difference between the BSA and AP, however. The BSA applies only to a list of “covered sites” agreed upon by Washington and Riyadh. It does not authorize the use of expanded verification tools at undeclared locations anywhere in the kingdom, as would be the case under the AP. Critics maintain that this gap significantly increases the risk that the Saudis could pursue an illicit nuclear program at undeclared locations. They also argue that not requiring Saudi adherence to the AP could increase the difficulty of persuading current AP holdout states to join, and it might encourage some current AP adherents to renounce their existing AP commitments in favor of less effective substitutes. The overall effect could be to undermine the decades-long effort to establish a strong and universally accepted standard for non-proliferation verification.
The agreement seeks to minimize proliferation risks
The Trump administration recognizes that potentially supporting enrichment in Saudi Arabia and not requiring adherence to the AP are hardly ideal from a non-proliferation perspective. But it also believes that the agreement it negotiated significantly reduces the proliferation risks, due largely to its provisions on “exclusivity.” The agreement only allows Saudi Arabia to engage in nuclear cooperation with U.S. companies, entities approved by both governments, or entities meeting technical criteria indicating a current relationship with the United States (e.g., one that has a U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission license).4
Although apparently not explicitly provided for in the agreement, the Saudis are also expected, in the initial phase of their ambitious nuclear power program, to buy two large Westinghouse nuclear power reactors rather than competing models from China, France, Russia, and South Korea.
The administration maintains that the central role the United States will play in Saudi Arabia’s nuclear program will allow it to exert major influence over Saudi choices on a wide range of nuclear energy, non-proliferation, safety, and security issues. If Washington eventually agrees to enrichment in the kingdom, the expectation is that U.S. companies and their trusted partners would construct the enrichment facility as well as associated fuel-cycle facilities. They would design, build, and operate the enrichment plant as a “black box,” designed to be capable of preventing the transfer of highly sensitive centrifuge enrichment technology to the Saudis and of denying them the ability to replicate the facility covertly.
The administration also says that U.S. exclusivity greatly facilitates verification of Saudi compliance with both the 123 agreement and other Saudi non-proliferation obligations. The broad, multi-decade, public-private U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear partnership would involve close, continuous, on-site interactions between American and Saudi government officials, company representatives, engineers, technicians, trainers, and regulators. This heavily integrated relationship will give the United States a firsthand window into Saudi nuclear energy thinking and planning and greatly reduce opportunities for the kingdom to engage in illicit activities without U.S. knowledge.
While the BSA does not provide for IAEA access to undeclared locations outside of the listed covered sites, exclusivity helps to limit that deficiency. Any evidence of foreign nuclear activity on Saudi territory would indicate a violation of the 123 agreement’s exclusivity provisions, giving Washington legitimate grounds for pressing the Saudis for any information and access required to resolve the situation. In the absence of U.S. exclusivity, foreign nuclear entities could operate legally on Saudi territory, conceivably at sites not subject to traditional IAEA safeguards (e.g., sites without nuclear material present). The foreign entity’s legal presence could provide cover for hard-to-detect illicit activities carried out at the site.
Moreover, supporters of the 123 agreement point out that the absence of an AP does not leave the IAEA without tools to address suspicious activities at undeclared locations in Saudi Arabia. If a country does not cooperate with an IAEA request for more information or access to resolve discrepancies or uncertainties about activities at undeclared locations anywhere in the country, the CSA allows the IAEA to declare that the situation is “essential and urgent” and ask the IAEA Board of Governors to authorize a “special inspection.” Special inspections, however, hardly make up for the absence of an AP. The AP’s timely access rules do not apply to special inspections. And as special inspections have come to be seen as a highly confrontational and controversial verification tool, their use has become exceedingly rare.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, whose Board of Governors will need to authorize the IAEA to implement the BSA, seems to be taking a positive attitude toward the bilateral verification arrangement. On August 26, he told an audience at the Stimson Center, “The IAEA will never allow or endorse an agreement that does not provide us with the ability to inspect what needs to be inspected. And I believe this is going to be the case with this agreement.” As the head of the organization that traditionally favors the most rigorous verification tools, Grossi’s assessment of the BSA is likely to carry considerable weight with the IAEA Board.
In responding to criticism that administration negotiators should have held out for an enrichment ban and acceptance of the AP, supporters of the deal assert that the United States no longer has the clout it once had in international nuclear markets and is unable to dictate terms to its customers. They make the case that, if the United States had not been willing to compromise on enrichment and the AP, the Saudis would have turned to other suppliers, including the Russians and Chinese, who would have been willing to accommodate Saudi demands on enrichment and verification without pressing for non-proliferation controls as rigorous as those in the U.S.-Saudi agreement.
Supporters contend that the realistic choice for the United States was not between the ideal outcome and the current U.S.-Saudi agreement. It was between the current agreement and the deal the Saudis could have concluded with other suppliers, which may have been content with less stringent non-proliferation safeguards.
Other experts counter that there’s little basis to believe that alternative suppliers would accept weaker non-proliferation controls than the United States. They point out that Russia and China have never transferred sensitive fuel cycle technology to NNWSs and that there is no evidence that either one has offered such technology to Saudi Arabia as part of its bid to sell the kingdom nuclear reactors.
The administration and outside supporters maintain that, in addition to reducing proliferation risks, the agreement will bring significant commercial and geopolitical benefits to the United States. In their view, the Westinghouse reactor sale and a wide range of other potential commercial projects, including possible Saudi investment in U.S.-based enrichment operations, could give a much-needed boost to the U.S. nuclear industry and help it play a more prominent role in the anticipated expansion of nuclear energy worldwide.
Supporters further argue that codifying a high-profile, multi-decade U.S.-Saudi partnership would help Washington resolidify its strategic relationship with Saudi Arabia at a time when traditional U.S. partners in the region have begun to question their reliance on the United States and look to other outside powers to diversify their foreign ties. They also emphasize that the 123 agreement’s exclusivity will deny Russia and China the opportunity to gain a politically and strategically important foothold in a critical sector of the Saudi economy.
The deal should go forward but could still be strengthened
As its supporters claim, the 123 agreement now before Congress can significantly reduce the inherent proliferation risks of engaging in enrichment cooperation with Saudi Arabia in the absence of the most effective verification mechanism available. While advocates for the deal may overstate the extent to which alternative nuclear suppliers like Russia or China would accept lax controls on proliferation-sensitive Saudi activities, they have a valid point that giving the United States a central role in designing and operating the kingdom’s nuclear program will likely provide a stronger barrier to a Saudi military nuclear program than if other suppliers became the Saudis’ nuclear energy partners.
Rejecting the deal could well be a loss for non-proliferation. It could also be a loss for efforts to revitalize the U.S. nuclear industry and to maintain a significant U.S. presence in a strategically important partner in the Middle East at a time of great uncertainty and shifting alignments.
But the U.S.-Saudi civil nuclear agreement officially submitted to Congress on August 24 is hardly ideal. It reduces the proliferation risks of fuel-cycle cooperation with Saudi Arabia but doesn’t eliminate them. And the extent to which those risks will be reduced will depend on how the agreement operates in practice. In particular, much will hinge on whether the agreement’s exclusivity provisions will give the United States the central role that has been advertised. Also critical will be whether black-boxing measures can be devised and agreed that would effectively preclude transfers of sensitive enrichment technology; whether the combination of bilateral safeguards, existing CSA measures, national intelligence collection, and credible penalties for violations can deter illicit Saudi activities; and whether U.S. companies can contribute significantly and in a timely way to the Saudi nuclear energy program and provide continuing incentives for Saudi Arabia to remain bound and compliant.
We don’t yet know all the answers to these questions. The agreement leaves some important details to be worked out after entry into force, such as how a black-box arrangement would operate and what would be the respective roles of the IAEA, Saudi Arabia, and the United States in implementing the BSA. The framework agreed by Washington and Riyadh is promising, but the value of the agreement—both in reducing proliferation concerns and in delivering economic and geopolitical benefits—will become clearer only as it is further developed and implemented.
How Congress can strengthen the agreement
Congress has the opportunity to influence how the 123 agreement is approved and implemented, particularly as it relates to the decision to permit enrichment in Saudi Arabia. But it doesn’t have much time, and its leverage is limited.
The Atomic Energy Act prescribes an entry into force procedure that makes it difficult for Congress to block a 123 agreement. According to this procedure, after the executive submits an agreement for congressional “review,” it enters into force after 90 days of “continuous session,” unless Congress adopts a joint resolution of disapproval. Such a resolution would require a two-thirds supermajority in both houses to override an anticipated presidential veto.
Entry into force, therefore, does not require an affirmative vote. The agreement does not need to be approved by Congress; it simply has to avoid disapproval. If Congress does nothing, it enters into force.
The 123 agreement now before Congress has been strongly criticized by non-proliferation experts outside government and in the editorials of major media outlets, including The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post, and Bloomberg. Representatives Brad Sherman and Gregory Meeks and several fellow House Democrats have introduced a joint resolution of disapproval. Democratic Senators Ed Markey, Jeff Merkley, and others have introduced a bill in the Senate expressing the “sense of Congress” that the United States should oppose a 123 agreement with Saudi Arabia until it renounces enrichment and reprocessing and agrees to an AP. The bill also requires that a 123 agreement with Saudi Arabia can only enter into force with the affirmative approval of Congress.
But opponents have no chance of blocking entry into force. With Republican majorities in both houses, a veto-proof joint resolution of disapproval is clearly out of reach. Despite small, vocal pockets of resistance, the agreement has not attracted widespread public attention. With both houses in recess for the midterms, members focused on their electoral campaigns, and no committee hearings scheduled, building sufficient momentum in Congress for a disapproval resolution by mid-December—when the congressional review period ends—is an insurmountable challenge.
This process suits the Trump administration well. It would be happy to keep the issue below the radar and let the 90-day clock run out without Congress getting engaged, allowing the agreement to take effect without even a perfunctory review.
Rather than focusing on a futile effort to adopt a joint resolution of disapproval, members of Congress who see the agreement’s benefits but have concerns about proliferation should pursue a joint resolution of approval. A resolution of approval could clarify its key provisions, reinforce its non-proliferation guardrails, and preserve a continuing role for Congress in its implementation. It would require simple majorities in both houses. Although most existing U.S. civil nuclear agreements with other countries have followed the normal entry into force procedure—taking effect in the absence of a joint resolution of disapproval—there are precedents for affirmative votes of approval, in particular with China and India.
A joint resolution of approval could contain a wide range of elements. Some could clarify key provisions of the agreement and promote greater transparency and congressional oversight:

The resolution could state Congress’ understanding of key features of the agreement (e.g., “qualified suppliers” eligible to participate in Saudi nuclear energy projects, “covered sites” that would be subject to enhanced verification under the BSA, “restricted data” that could not be transferred to Saudi Arabia in the absence of a new 123 agreement).
It could require the executive to provide regular reports and briefings to Congress on the agreement’s implementation (including nuclear cooperation carried out under it) as well as unclassified and classified reports and briefings on Saudi compliance with the agreement.
It could require the executive, in reporting to Congress any decision to grant consent to enrichment in Saudi Arabia, to provide a detailed justification for its decision (with information unclassified or classified, as appropriate). The justification could be required to cover such issues as the commercial viability and proliferation implications of domestic enrichment; the prospects and timing for U.S. companies to participate in the construction of an enrichment facility; plans for constructing a “black-boxed” facility, together with a technical assessment of its ability to deny Saudi access to sensitive enrichment technology; an assessment of the capability of the IAEA, using the tools available under the CSA and BSA, and national intelligence means to detect illicit nuclear activities at declared and undeclared sites; and an evaluation of penalties and other means available to deter Saudi illicit nuclear activities or nationalization of the facility.

Some elements could address the executive’s decision to consent to enrichment:

Congress could require that any decision to grant consent to enrichment in Saudi Arabia be sent to Congress for a 90-day review period (rather than the current requirement of 15 days).5
It could require that the executive’s decision to consent to enrichment could only take effect if Congress passes a joint resolution of approval.6
It could require that, instead of allowing the executive to grant consent for enrichment once the enrichment and conversion study is concluded, the executive could only grant consent after an additional period (e.g., five years).
It could call on the executive to encourage Saudi Arabia to invest in a U.S.-based enrichment operation.

Some elements could deal with verification and penalties for violations:

Congress could require that, before U.S. consent to enrichment could be granted, Saudi Arabia must adhere to the AP.
It could direct the executive to review and, in collaboration with Congress, strengthen the penalties for violations of the 123 agreement and other non-proliferation obligations.

Prospects for such a joint resolution of approval
Some of these illustrative elements of a joint resolution of approval are relatively modest and may be uncontroversial, including congressional statements for the record to clarify terms, calls for periodic reports, and a requirement for the executive to provide detailed justification for any decision to grant consent to enrichment. Others are more consequential—such as requiring that Congress approve the decision to grant consent to enrichment, conditioning such consent on Saudi adherence to the AP, and increasing the number of years before the United States could grant consent. These would likely require more time to gain agreement.
None of these elements would condition the 123 agreement’s entry into force on Saudi acceptance of an enrichment ban or the AP, as many opponents would prefer. Indeed, the resolution would ensure entry into force, probably as planned in December 2026, and mutually beneficial nuclear cooperation (other than fuel cycle cooperation) could soon begin.
None of the elements would require changes in the text of the123 agreement or explicit Saudi agreement. The elements pertaining to consent to enrichment would only affect internal U.S. government decisions on how, when, and under what conditions consent would be granted.
A joint resolution of approval along these lines would give Congress a critical voice in the enrichment decision, ensure that the question of enrichment would receive careful scrutiny, increase incentives for Saudi Arabia to accept the AP, and strengthen deterrence against cheating.
As to the element of deferring a consent decision for several years, a delay would be defensible. U.S. enrichers are years away from having the capability to build an enrichment facility in the kingdom, and it will be even longer before the Saudis have nuclear reactors whose fuel requirements could provide a plausible justification for an indigenous enrichment capability. Deferring any enrichment decision would provide more time for U.S. enrichment companies to build their capacity and to develop and agree with Saudi Arabia on the design of a facility capable of denying the transfer of sensitive enrichment technology. It would also provide more time to assess international nuclear market conditions that would have a bearing on the purpose and scale of any enrichment facility in the kingdom.
The Trump administration might see some advantage in such a resolution of approval, which would be a much stronger expression of political support for its achievement than simply having the agreement take effect in the absence of congressional action. Moreover, the administration may not have strong substantive objections to a resolution along these lines. It is not eager to move ahead with enrichment in Saudi Arabia—which has always been a Saudi goal, not a U.S. one. U.S. policymakers have preferred to see the rebuilding of enrichment capacity in the United States, where currently the sole commercial enriched uranium producer is foreign-owned Urenco. Support for enrichment in the kingdom was the price Washington (under both Presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump) was prepared to pay to achieve other goals, including commercial and strategic opportunities (and especially for Biden, Saudi normalization with Israel). Giving careful scrutiny to and even delaying the consent decision may not be a problem for the Trump administration.
The administration may worry, however, that Saudi Arabia could take issue with some elements of the resolution and decide not to proceed with the agreement. But that might not be the case. With the 123 agreement’s entry into force, the Saudis will achieve some of their key priorities, including getting their ambitious nuclear energy program underway and reinforcing their strategic ties to the United States for the long term. While they will remain adamantly opposed to renouncing enrichment altogether, they may be prepared to subject a potential enrichment program to more detailed congressional review and to defer the U.S. consent decision for a few more years.
The Saudis are more likely to raise concerns about conditioning a future U.S. decision to allow enrichment on their adherence to the AP. But the Saudi leadership may be willing to go along with the linkage, calculating that a few years of productive nuclear cooperation with the United States—during which U.S. and IAEA officials will be making the case that AP adherence would not compromise Saudi interests—could weaken domestic resistance to the AP.
If the Trump administration and key members of Congress could agree on a joint resolution of approval, building affirmative majorities in both houses should not be politically difficult. Most Republicans could be expected to follow the administration’s lead. And while some Democrats would balk because of the agreement’s failure to ban enrichment or require adherence to the AP from the outset, enough Democrats would support the resolution because the agreement offers economic and geopolitical benefits and the resolution could help reduce proliferation risks. The fact that the Biden administration, in its unfinished 123 negotiations with Saudi Arabia, had been prepared to build a black-boxed enrichment facility in the kingdom and not to insist on the AP could make it easier for some Democrats to go along with a resolution of approval.7
Reducing proliferation risks globally
The U.S.-Saudi 123 agreement does not eliminate the inherent proliferation risks of engaging in sensitive fuel-cycle cooperation with Saudi Arabia. However, key features of the agreement, if further developed and implemented effectively and if supplemented by a strong congressional resolution of approval, have the potential to reduce the likelihood that Saudi Arabia will acquire nuclear weapons, especially when compared to the situation that would exist if the United States were not the Saudi partner of choice.
The U.S.-Saudi 123 agreement’s implications for the global non-proliferation regime may be harder to predict. On the one hand, in the wake of Saudi Arabia potentially acquiring an enrichment facility from the United States, some NNWSs may make greater efforts to acquire their own enrichment capabilities. Some nuclear suppliers may also become more willing to engage in fuel-cycle cooperation with NNWSs. But on the other hand, familiar impediments to acquiring enrichment and reprocessing capabilities will still exist for NNWSs, including financial costs, competing national priorities, and the risk of inviting economic pressures and sanctions or even preemptive military attacks. And nuclear suppliers such as Russia may prefer to have lucrative fuel-supply contracts with their reactor customers rather than give them the capability to make their own fuel.
Similarly, the U.S.-Saudi 123 agreement’s reliance on the BSA rather than the AP could reinforce some key countries’ current resistance to the AP. Conceivably, some current AP adherents might even consider withdrawing from the AP in favor of a weaker bilateral arrangement. But existing AP holdouts are already well entrenched in their resistance, and the prospects for getting them to adhere were already low before the U.S.-Saudi agreement. Therefore, continued Saudi unwillingness to adhere to the AP is unlikely to make a major difference in the currently uncertain prospects for achieving a universally accepted verification norm. Moreover, existing AP adherents may be reluctant to abrogate their commitment to the AP for fear of signaling nuclear weapons intent and inviting economic or military coercion.
Thus, while the U.S. departure from established non-proliferation norms in its 123 agreement with Saudi Arabia creates risks for the global non-proliferation regime, the extent to which damage to the regime will actually materialize is far from clear. But whatever the risks, the United States should do what it can to reduce them. That will mostly involve policies applicable to the regime at large rather than to the specific Saudi case, although preventing a Saudi nuclear weapons program would naturally have a positive effect on the wider regime.
Few developments would undermine the non-proliferation regime more than Iran acquiring nuclear weapons. Not only would it be a key driver of Saudi nuclear ambitions—and could well result in Saudi Arabia either withdrawing from or clandestinely violating the U.S.-Saudi 123 agreement—but it would also increase proliferation pressures worldwide. Thus, preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon must remain a top U.S. priority.
The Trump administration’s deviations from previous U.S. policy in the Saudi case should not mean the abandonment of the traditional U.S. objective of preventing the spread of fuel-cycle technologies and capabilities. In consultations with other fuel-cycle possessors, Washington should seek to discourage them from drawing the conclusion from theSaudi 123 agreement that the United States has become relaxed about the spread of enrichment capabilities. Washington should make clear that, unless and until the United States gives its consent, domestic enrichment will be banned in the kingdom. It should also make clear that any future U.S. construction of an enrichment plant on Saudi soil would be carefully restricted to preclude the transfer of sensitive enrichment technology and prevent Saudi Arabia from acquiring a truly indigenous enrichment capability.
The message would be: don’t engage in any fuel cycle cooperation with NNWSs—not even building black-boxed facilities. At a minimum, do not pursue fuel-cycle transfer policies less restrictive than in the U.S.-Saudi agreement. And the message to NNWSs would continue to be: don’t pursue indigenous fuel cycle capabilities; you don’t need them to have a successful nuclear energy program; and doing so will only raise concerns about your intentions. Does this present a double standard? Yes, but it would not be the first double standard in U.S. non-proliferation policy.
Regardless of whether the 123 agreement with Saudi Arabia ultimately succeeds in persuading Saudi Arabia to adhere to the AP, the United States should act to strengthen deterrence against violations of 123 agreements and other non-proliferation obligations, especially by NNWSs that have not accepted the AP. Richard Nephew has recommended that the IAEA Board of Governors establish expedited procedures for the “special inspections” provided for in the IAEA’s comprehensive safeguards agreements, providing the agency with a more timely and reliable tool for investigating suspicious activities at undeclared locations, even in the absence of an AP. Congress could also deter both AP adherents and non-adherents from violating their commitments by reaffirming and strengthening penalties, such as the cutoff of military exports, for violations of nuclear-related agreements with the United States.
In general, as Eric Brewer proposes, any negative fallout for the global non-proliferation regime from the U.S.-Saudi 123 agreement needs to be countered by prioritizing non-proliferation, not just in the Saudi case but in U.S. policy more broadly. The agreement’s departures from long-standing U.S. non-proliferation policies have been widely interpreted as a weakening of U.S. support for the goal of non-proliferation. This perception has been reinforced by Trump administration actions and statements that have raised doubts among U.S. allies about the reliability of U.S. commitments to their defense, prompting some of those allies to consider whether they would be more secure with their own nuclear deterrent.
In word and deed, the U.S. government in the coming years will need to demonstrate that it firmly supports nuclear non-proliferation and opposes the acquisition of nuclear weapons, even by “friendly” countries. How it proceeds on the Saudi 123 agreement—how strongly it implements and enforces the agreement’s non-proliferation guardrails—will be an important indication of its commitment to non-proliferation.
Conclusion
The U.S.-Saudi agreement on civil nuclear cooperation will almost surely enter into force, probably in the next couple of months, but its consequences for non-proliferation will depend on how the agreement is further developed and implemented. It is still a work in progress.
The Trump administration hopes the agreement will achieve significant commercial and geopolitical benefits for the United States and reduce the inherent proliferation risks of engaging in fuel-cycle cooperation with a country that clearly wants to keep its future nuclear weapons options open. That remains to be seen.
For now, Congress can play an important role in promoting a positive outcome by participating actively in the legislatively mandated review process. Rather than pursuing the futile course of seeking a joint resolution of disapproval, members of Congress who see the potential benefits of the agreement but have concerns about its potential negative implications for nuclear proliferation should adopt the much more constructive approach of seeking a joint resolution of approval with understandings and conditions that can strengthen the agreement. By choosing that course, Congress can get mutually beneficial U.S.-Saudi nuclear cooperation underway while reinforcing non-proliferation guardrails and preserving Congress’ future oversight role.

Why networks are moving to the heart of utility investment, and how opportunities differ between markets.

articles.title: Why bond yields and term premia are likely to remain high
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

28 Oct 2026

Why bond yields and term premia are likely to remain high

To understand the recent surge in government bond yields and whether high yields are here to stay, it’s useful to look at the main yield components over a longer horizon. A 10-year government bond yield can be decomposed into the expected path of safe short-term rates and a broadly defined term premium that compensates investors for risks in holding the bond. Since 2020, more than half of the increase in advanced-economy government bond yields came from the term premium.

What you will learn:

Term premia are now back to their mid-2000s levels – high compared to the last 10 years, but still low in a broader historical context.

We find that an important driver is the strength of bond-stock co-movements. Across major advanced economies, bond-stock correlations were negative for most of this century but turned positive again in Q3 2023 and have risen steeply since.

This means bonds are a worse hedge against stock returns – similar to the 1980s and 1990s – so that investors require a higher term premium as compensation, but now also for inflation-indexed bonds.

We think the bond-stock correlation and bond term premia will remain high because we’ve entered an era of more frequent supply shocks and more hawkish central banks.

articles.title: Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann
articles.text:
Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann

Given at the Nomura London Macro Forum

Published on
01 October 2026

Catherine L. Mann discusses how UK financial markets have priced in greater risk premia since the Middle East conflict intensified. She uses several models to uncover their sources and considers how monetary policy and communication can help reduce premia to ensure inflation returns to target.

Speech
Introduction
The conflict in the Middle East has generated significant volatility and financial market repricing in the UK, relating to uncertainty around the evolution of the conflict, the outlook for UK inflation, and our monetary policy response. Financial conditions are an essential mechanism through which monetary policy transmits and therefore form an important input into my monetary policy decisions. In this speech, I will evaluate the information that financial conditions provide about the current monetary policy stance and transmission, and carefully examine what they reveal about the types of risks driving recent moves.
Financial conditions
Let me start with a headline indicator of financial conditions, which summarizes how a broad range of asset price movements contribute to changes in nominal and real financial conditions. The effect of policy tightening since 2022 on nominal financial conditions in the UK is clearly visible, as the pink line in Chart 1 shows. Despite a modest loosening over 2025, this measure of nominal financial conditions resumed a slight tightening since the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East on account of higher short and long-term nominal interest rates.

Chart 1: Changes in UK financial conditions since 2020
Index points

Footnotes

Source: Burr (2023) Opens in a new window using Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and LSEG.
Notes: The real financial conditions index uses real interest rate variables, exchange rate and equity prices – that is, net of inflation compensation. Latest observation: August 2026.

Nominal financial conditions incorporate inflation expectations and inflation risk premia, which may distort the signal about real tightness, particularly following an inflationary shock. The real financial conditions index in Chart 1 (white line) strips out the effects of rising inflation compensation following the start of the conflict in the Middle East at the end of February. This index suggests that real financial conditions loosened around the beginning of the conflict (consistent with inflation compensation measures rising significantly in March), some of which have since retraced, albeit with a notable compression in spreads.
Given that inflation has been well-above target for five years already and the conflict in the Middle East has contributed to further upside risks to inflation, real and nominal financial conditions need to remain tight. There are two mechanisms through which I can tighten real financial conditions: reducing measures of inflation compensation, and/or, raising nominal yields (and expectations), both of which can be achieved through an increase in Bank Rate. In my view, our current monetary policy stance is not sufficiently tight, which is why I voted in the last two meetings for a 25 basis point increase in Bank Rate.
As financial conditions indices summarize a range of underlying market dynamics, I will unpack some of their key drivers and explore what they reveal about what is priced in. This assessment concludes that the MPC cannot simply rely on policy restrictiveness coming from an upward shift in the nominal yield curve. At some point, we need to follow-through with Bank Rate rises – to maintain credibility, and to avoid policy expectations repricing downwards and inflation expectations repricing further upwards.
What does the gap between markets and participants imply?
Overall nominal financial conditions have remained relatively tight, but what are financial market expectations for the future path of monetary policy? We can gauge market expectations of the policy rate path from a variety of sources. For the UK, these are the yield curve, such as the overnight index swap (OIS) curve, and the Bank of England Market Participants Survey (MaPS).footnote [1]
Chart 2 plots the OIS curve across the UK, US and euro area (EA), and survey-based policy rate expectations from the respective central banks’ latest surveys of market participants. The survey-based measures should offer a cleaner read on policy rate expectations than the OIS curve, because they do not include risk premia or other market-based technical factors. As the differences between the light and dark solid lines in Chart 2 show, there are gaps between the two measures for all three jurisdictions, but the difference is largest for the UK.
If the OIS curve only reflected expectations for policy rate changes, it would imply almost 75 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the next 12 months, in contrast to a prolonged hold (and subsequent cuts) implied by the MaPS. I have plotted the OIS curve at the respective dates of survey closure. Since then, the gap has widened further, implying over 100 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the coming 12 months. The swathes indicate the interquartile ranges of the survey-based distributions; however, taking that into account does only a little to explain the gap in the UK.

Chart 2: OIS curves and survey-implied expectations for policy rates
Percent

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, European Central Bank, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Notes: UK survey data shows the median response (solid light aqua line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses (shaded aqua area) to the September 2026 Market Participants Survey. US survey data shows the median response (solid light purple line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses (shaded purple area) to the July 2026 Survey of Market Expectations Opens in a new window. Euro area survey data shows the median response (solid light orange line) and the 25th-75th percentile of responses to the September 2026 ECB Survey of Monetary Analysts Opens in a new window. OIS curves (dark solid lines) on the respective dates of survey closure (4th September, 20th July and 26th August). Survey measures typically ask for policy rate expectations (Bank Rate, Federal Funds Rate/Range and Deposit Rate Facility) for UK, US and EA respectively. These do not exactly match the interest rate underlying the OIS (SONIA, SOFR and €STR).

The UK seems to be an outlier internationally, but is the current gap also large by historical standards? Chart 3 shows how the average difference between the OIS curve and market participants’ median expectations for Bank Rate has evolved over a 3-year horizon (left panel). There has been a material increase in the gap since the beginning of the conflict in the Middle East, to levels last seen following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Because the survey-based measure only captures market participants’ expectations for Bank Rate, movements in the gap can be a crude measure of risk premia. The widening observed this year therefore suggests that investors are demanding greater compensation for UK risk.

Chart 3: Average gap between market-based and survey-implied expectations for policy rates over a 3-year horizon
Basis points

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, European Central Bank, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Notes: The height of the bar reflects the average gap between the respective survey’s median ‘most likely’ (modal) profile for the policy rate and the average OIS curve observed across the survey window over a 3-year horizon.

What risks are investors demanding greater compensation for? There is no single model that allows us to decompose this risk premium into its various sources and drivers. In the remainder of this speech, I will go through various hypotheses, using a variety of different models and data, to pinpoint the types of risks relevant to driving this gap.
The role of the term premium
Movements in nominal government bond yields can be decomposed into contributions from changes in expected interest rates and a term premium. The term premium is the additional compensation required by investors (above and beyond their interest rate expectations) to hold interest rate risk. Before discussing what the charts show, it is worth noting that the term premium, and risk premia in general, are unobservable. We rely on a suite of models to estimate them.
Chart 4 shows a model-implied structural decomposition of a 3-year nominal yield into these two categories across the UK, US and Germany. The model decomposition is an average of three term structure models: Malik and Meldrum (2016) Opens in a new window, Vlieghe (2016) and Andreasen and Meldrum (2015). For the UK, this structural model-based decomposition complements the survey-based evidence from MaPS on policy expectations.footnote [2] In both the UK and Germany, 3-year government bond yields have risen by around 100 basis points over the past year, but the drivers appear to be different.
According to this term structure model, higher term premia account for around 24 basis points of the increase in the UK, compared with just 4 basis points in Germany. This contribution has been increasingly positive in the UK throughout the year. In the US, a positive contribution from the term premium is only visible more recently, accounting for around 25 basis points of the 140 basis points rise in yields.

Chart 4: Decomposition of UK, US and German 3-year nominal yields
Cumulative differences since January 2026

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Bank calculations.
Note: The expected rates and term premium contributions may not sum exactly to the observed nominal yield because they are averages of model-implied decompositions and contain residuals that reflect model fitting error. Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

To compare results across different models I show, in Chart 5, a decomposition from a different model (Lengyel and Walker, 2026) that adapts a standard affine term structure framework to identify near-term risk premia more cleanly. Relative to classic models, which are typically calibrated to fit the yield curve as a whole, this approach uses OIS instead of government bond yields, allows for a richer factor structure, and directly incorporates survey-based expectations for Bank Rate. While term premia make a larger contribution to yields overall across the UK, US and EA, the result that its contribution is largest for the UK is robust.

Chart 5: Decomposition of UK, US and German 3-year OIS yields
Cumulative differences since January 2026

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.
Note: The expected rates and term premium contributions may not sum exactly to the observed nominal yield because they are averages of model-implied decompositions and contain residuals that reflect model fitting error. Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

In a historical and international context, it is somewhat unusual that the term premium has contributed significantly to the rise in short-term yields. The term premium is often defined as the additional compensation investors demand to hold a longer-term bond relative to a series of shorter-term bonds (Kaminska, Meldrum and Young, 2015 Opens in a new window). It is therefore common for the term premium to show up at the longer end of the yield curve. That is, the further into the future you go, the more uncertain the future path of interest rates is. So why is the UK term premium such an outlier, and such a significant driver of short-term yields?
Chart 6 plots the model-implied 1-year and 3-year term premium between 2009 and today. Over this period, the 1-year and 3-year term premium have been negative throughout the 2010s and after the Russia-Ukraine shock. A negative term premium is not unusual. Joyce, Kaminska and Lildholdt (2008) discuss various drivers for the UK, including regulatory changes, excess liquidity, and “flight to quality” dynamics away from risky assets in times of uncertainty. This could also be explained by a negative inflation risk premium (Cieslak and Pflueger, 2023 Opens in a new window).

Chart 6: UK model-implied 1-year and 3-year term premium
Percent

Footnotes

Source: Lengyel and Walker (2026) using Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and Bank calculations.
Note: Latest observation: 25th September 2026.

However, term premia rose at the start of the conflict in the Middle East and have recently turned positive. That is also true for the 3-year term premium, which stands out as particularly high in recent history, and was only exceeded during the post-GFC period and when Russia invaded Ukraine. The Middle East energy shock is notable, but not as large as the Russia-Ukraine energy shock.
Staff work finds that the UK term premium, especially at the short end, has become more volatile and responsive to news about economic and financial market developments. In part, this reflects higher sensitivity of (international) investors (Mann, 2026) and a different composition of demand for government debt, including a reduced role of preferred habitat investors such as insurance companies and pension funds, as Beltran and Li (2026) Opens in a new window also find for the US.
Lengyel and Walker (2026) argue that risk premia at the short end of the curve reflect the compensation investors require for uncertainty around the policy rate path. It is therefore important for monetary policymakers to understand whether changes in nominal yields reflect changing policy expectations or uncertainty around them – distinguishing between the two has important consequences on how to interpret the moves in financial conditions.footnote [3]
I explore the role of near-term policy uncertainty in the next section.
What is the role of uncertainty?
Chart 7 shows the option-implied distributions of SONIA (the risk-free overnight interest rate for sterling markets, and the rate underlying the overnight index swap) 12 months ahead, and its equivalents for the US (SOFR) and the euro area (€STR) based on the methodology of Clews et al. (2000).footnote [4] While the OIS rate shown in the earlier Chart 2 reflects a summary statistic of the underlying distribution, the full distribution in Chart 7 contains additional information. Prior to the conflict (orange), the distributions for all three jurisdictions are tight – implying little uncertainty, and high conviction, about the future path of policy rates. Since the conflict began, the distributions for all three have shifted to the right and widened. The UK distribution, however, has widened slightly more, implying that perceived risks and uncertainty about the future policy rate have increasingly been priced in by markets, and particularly more so for the UK.

Chart 7: Option-implied distribution of interest rates, 12 months ahead
For SONIA, SOFR and €STR

Footnotes

Source: ICE, CME and Bank calculations
Note: The underlying rate for the UK distribution is the 3-month SONIA rate 12 months ahead. Latest observation: 25th September 2026

Furthermore, the skewness of SONIA has turned sharply positive following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, which implies that upside risks to interest rates are perceived to be materially larger than downside risks. This degree of positive skewness was last observed following the post-Covid supply chain disruptions in 2021 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The increase in uncertainty and the positive skewness could simply reflect a repricing of the outlook for the economy – reflecting uncertainty about how the conflict in the Middle East could play out, how the resulting supply shock will affect the UK economy going forward, and how it is passed through to broader pricing dynamics. However, such trade-off inducing shocks (shocks that are inflationary but have contractionary effects on activity) also make it more challenging for monetary policymakers to set policy, and uncertainty about the policy rate path could also be higher.
Financial markets are trying to price in both: uncertainty about the economic outlook and uncertainty about the monetary policy response. There is no “textbook” monetary policy response to supply shocks, and therefore, the market’s understanding of how members of the MPC might respond (that is, our reaction function) could be incomplete or unclear. Given that inflation has remained above target for five years and is expected to increase further as the energy shock propagates, the market might be pricing in a reaction function that is not consistent with bringing inflation back to the 2% target sustainably in the medium-term.
Is there a monetary policy uncertainty premium?
Could uncertainty about the monetary policy response to the conflict in the Middle East have also contributed to the gap between the OIS curve and market participants’ expectations for Bank Rate? Research about the effects of monetary policy has generally focused on the effect of changes in the level of Bank Rate on the UK economy (see for instance Brandt et al., 2026 Opens in a new window; Braun et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Di Pace et al., 2025 Opens in a new window). Uncertainty about future interest rates and its effects on financial markets and the real economy has received less attention.
Based on a methodology developed by Bauer et al. (2022) Opens in a new window, Raviraj (forthcoming) constructs a financial market-based measure of UK monetary policy uncertaintyfootnote [5] surprises that uses changes in the standard deviation of the option-implied distribution of SONIA around MPC announcement dates. Using the surprise series as an instrument for a monetary policy uncertainty shock in a structural VAR allows the author to causally identify the effects of monetary policy uncertainty on a set of outcome variables.
Let me start by showing what this monetary policy uncertainty variable looks like and how it relates to MPC announcements. On average across the sample period (1997 to 2026), a monetary policy announcement leads to a resolution of uncertainty about short-term interest rates, as the decrease in the aqua line following the day of an MPC announcement in the left panel of Chart 8 shows. Monetary policy and communications around MPC decisions have acted as a stabilizing force in the economy, resolving uncertainty around the future path of interest rates.

Chart 8: Changes in monetary policy uncertainty around MPC announcementdates
Percent (LHS) and factor score (RHS)

Footnotes

Source: Raviraj (forthcoming).
Note: The solid aqua line in the left chart shows the average change in short-rate uncertainty on trading days around MPC announcements from June 1997 until July 2026. The pink line shows the change in short-rate uncertainty around the March 2026 MPC announcement. The shaded area represents the 95% confidence interval. In the right chart, monetary policy uncertainty factors are constructed by applying Varimax rotation to principal components of changes in short-rate uncertainty and first moment interest rates around MPC announcements.

However, there is one notable meeting where our decision and communications do not seem to have played that role. In the left panel of Chart 8, I also plot (in pink) changes in uncertainty around the March 2026 decision – the first monetary policy meeting after the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East. One may argue that this simply reflects elevated levels of uncertainty following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East. However, the identification strategy for the monetary policy uncertainty shock isolates changes in uncertainty on MPC announcement days – these changes should therefore largely reflect news associated with the monetary policy decision and associated communications. It strips out any first moment, level effects of monetary policy and captures shocks associated with MPC announcements beyond what markets had already priced in. I plot the estimated monetary policy uncertainty factor in the right panel of Chart 8, which shows that monetary policy uncertainty increased significantly following the March decision, which cannot simply be attributed to uncertainty around the economic outlook resulting from the conflict.footnote [6]
What are the implications of an increase in monetary policy uncertainty? Using the monetary policy uncertainty shock series, we can evaluate the impact of such a shock on financial market variables. The left panel of Chart 9 shows the impulse response function of short rate uncertaintyfootnote [7] to a one standard deviation increase in monetary policy uncertainty. An increase in monetary policy uncertainty also leads to a rise in the 1-year OIS rate, driven by both a higher term premium and higher interest rate expectations. An increase in monetary policy uncertainty tightens financial conditions.

Chart 9: Impulse response functions of short rate uncertainty, term premium and expected interest rates to a monetary policy uncertainty shock
Percentage points

Footnotes

Source: Raviraj (forthcoming).
Note: Impulse response functions to a one standard deviation structural monetary policy uncertainty shock, proxied by the monetary policy uncertainty factor presented in the right panel of Chart 8. Shaded areas represent 68% and 90% confidence intervals.

Yet, why did such a clear signal, a unanimous decision to hold Bank Rate, result in higher uncertainty? It could be because our communication about the outlook for the economy, beyond what was already priced in by markets, was too focused on the uncertainty resulting from the conflict in the Middle East, rather than the underlying dynamics of the economy. Or our reaction function to the shock – the balance between looking through the shock and responding to signs of propagation – was not clearly articulated.
What does this mean for the role of monetary policy uncertainty in driving current risk premia? The committee’s vote splits in the past have revealed differences in views about both the economic outlook and the appropriate monetary policy response. The unanimous vote at the March meeting deviated from these previously communicated reaction functions in light of the conflict in the Middle East. Central bank communication – including our Monetary Policy Report, Monetary Policy Summary and minutes, press conferences, and speeches – is an important tool to explain past monetary policy decisions and to manage expectations about the economy and potential Bank Rate paths. Communication should provide clarity about our reaction function and reduce uncertainty around the future interest rate path (Blinder et al., 2008 Opens in a new window; Gebauer et al., 2024 Opens in a new window), even without having to provide explicit forward guidance.
Our communications in March highlighted larger uncertainties. Perhaps they were not clear on how the MPC’s reaction function would evolve with new information – it appeared we were in “wait mode”, which discounted our assurance to the markets that we would “act as necessary” to reach the inflation target. And, as discussed by my colleague Alan Taylor (Taylor, 2026), not publishing a baseline forecast in April most likely did not help either.
The March announcement and the uncertainty it reflected did trigger a strong upward shift in the OIS curve, contributing to the gap between OIS and MaPS. My concern is that this gap has continued to increase, and that one spike in monetary policy uncertainty may have had lasting effects, particularly in an environment with a higher sensitivity of term premia to shocks.
What about risk premia in other assets?
Risk premia and term premia are not synonymous. Term premia specifically refer to the additional compensation required for interest rate risk on risk-free bonds. Risk premia is a general term referring to the additional compensation required by investors for holding risky over risk-free assets.
One would expect uncertainty about the economic outlook arising from geopolitical and energy shocks to be reflected in risk premia for a range of assets. For example, the equity risk premium is the additional compensation for risk associated with holding stocks. Chart 10 plots model estimates of this risk premium (Kontoghiorghes et al., 2025). While there is a temporary spike following the conflict in the Middle East, equity risk premia do not appear elevated in historical context (other than in the US since 2020), likely driven by a robust demand for equities as an asset class in general, or reflecting lower perceived (relative) risk across asset classes.

Chart 10: Equity risk premium
Percent

Footnotes

Source: Kontoghiorghes et al. (2025).
Note: The measure used follows the lower-bound ERP estimate of Chabi-Yo and Loudis (2020) Opens in a new window over a one-year time horizon, and uses options on the FTSE 100, S&P 500, and EUROSTOXX 50 for the UK, US, and euro area, respectively. Latest observation: 16th September 2026.

But there is another source of risk premia that is of particular concern for an inflation-targeting central bank – the inflation risk premium. Chart 11 (left-hand panel) shows cumulative changes in the 3-year inflation swap since February, decomposed into contributions from changes in inflation expectations and inflation risk premia. It shows that the inflation risk premium has contributed significantly to the rise in the 3-year inflation swap this year. Rising CPI inflation expectations have also played a considerable role. This reduced slightly in June and July, when the Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran was in place, but subsequently rose again following re-escalation of the conflict.

Chart 11: Decomposition of UK 3-year inflation swap rate (LHS) and 3-yearnominal yield (RHS)
Cumulative differences

Footnotes

Source: Kaminska et al. (2018) Opens in a new window for LHS, and Bloomberg Finance L.P., Tradeweb and Bank calculations for RHS.
Note: The left panel is estimated using a model proposed in Kaminska et al. (2018) Opens in a new window. Latest observation: September 2026 (LHS) and 25th September 2026 (RHS).

The right-hand side panel shows that the contribution to the rise in 3-year nominal yields has been almost entirely accounted for by a rise in inflation compensation, which is a combination of inflation expectations and the inflation risk premium. This brings me back to my very first chart where I showed that while nominal financial conditions have tightened following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, real financial conditions remained looser.
Monetary policy strategy
What does all this mean for my monetary policy strategy?
The supply shock resulting from the conflict hit at a time when the disinflationary process from previous supply shocks was still incomplete, with nominal rigidities limiting the speed of normalization. Inflation has been above target for the last five years and the Bank’s updated short-term inflation forecast from September projects inflation to increase to over 4% in Q1 2027. This raises inflation above the attentiveness threshold of households and firms ahead of wage negotiations next spring.
Given rising upside risks to inflation, a risk management strategy to monetary policy is appropriate. When there is uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects, raising Bank Rate to commit to the inflation target can help ensure a sustainable return of inflation to the 2% target, with smaller losses to economic activity.
With the ‘sporadic continuance’ of the conflict in the Middle East, uncertainty around the outlook for the economy and inflation risks have remained elevated. Uncertainty about the MPC reaction function should not compound the problem. Ensuring that this communication is clear and that the reaction function is well understood is the purpose of collective communications. When a policy decision deviates from the collective, speeches such as this can provide additional clarity on the outlook, risks, and decisions.
Against this backdrop, as a monetary policymaker, I cannot take comfort from tighter nominal financial conditions when much of that tightening reflects a higher inflation risk premium and, possibly, a monetary policy uncertainty premium that our own decisions and communications may have contributed to. These premia raise nominal yields without necessarily tightening the real financial conditions that matter for demand and inflation. In my view, real financial conditions are insufficiently tight. The appropriate response therefore is not to rely on risk premia to do the work of policy, but to reduce inflation risk and policy uncertainty through a clearly communicated reaction function and a sufficiently restrictive path for Bank Rate.
The views expressed in this speech are not necessarily those of the Bank of England or the Monetary Policy Committee.

About the Deloitte Center for Integrated Research

The Deloitte Center for Integrated Research offers rigorously researched and data-driven perspectives on critical topics affecting businesses today including workforce trends, enterprise growth and innovation, technology and transformation, and environmental and societal issues. We sit at the center of Deloitte's industry and functional expertise, combining the leading insights from across our firms to help leaders confidently compete in today's ever-changing marketplace.

Visit the Deloitte Center for Integrated Research to explore our research and insights
