articles.title: What stablecoins mean for banks, rates and equities
articles.text: The four ways stablecoins reach an equity portfolio9 min readFinanceAltcoinsDataStablecoins have grown beyond a crypto-market story. They can move the earnings and valuations of listed banks, exchanges and payment networks without an investor ever buying one. When people move cash from current accounts into tokens backed by Treasury bills, banks lose cheap funding and may have to replace it at a higher cost.Do stablecoins take deposits away from banks, and which banks are most exposed?Treasury advisers flagged $6.6T of US transactional deposits as exposed in April 2025 and total stablecoin supply equals 4.6% of that figure. An IMF study with data to June 2025 found no significant share price reaction in large or community banks to stablecoin demand shocks. So far, stablecoin adoption looks more like a margin risk than a funding shock. A stablecoin works like a very simple bank. Someone hands over a dollar and the issuer keeps safe assets against it, known as stablecoin reserves. A current account is cheap, steady funding, because customers rarely move it and earn little for leaving it there. When that dollar moves into a stablecoin, the bank has to replace it with funding that costs more.The scale so far is small next to the pool at stake. Total supply stood at $305.83B on 27 September 2026, 0.8% below the $308.16B of 31 March. Two issuers, Tether and Circle, hold 84.7% of it. A static market is itself the finding: the deposit threat is a question of years and policy, not of this quarter's growth rate.Exposure is uneven. Investors can screen on net interest income as a share of total revenue: lending-heavy banks, such as US regional lenders, score higher than diversified banks or investment banks, so they have more to lose if funding costs rise. The same screen works on European financials.The policy fight sets the speed. The GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025, requires one dollar of reserves for every token and bars issuers from paying interest to holders. It does not clearly stop exchanges paying rewards on tokens held on their platforms, and many do. According to the Congressional Research Service (6 March 2026) and the Council of Economic Advisers (April 2026), banks want exchanges to stop paying rewards on stablecoins, because those rewards make the tokens compete more directly with bank deposit accounts. Exchanges want to keep offering them. It is a fight over whether a token is allowed to look like a current account, with bank equities on one side and exchange equities on the other.How do stablecoins affect Treasury bill yields and short-term rates?Stablecoin reserves sit mostly in short-dated US government instruments, so supply growth adds demand at the front end. BIS research using data through March 2026 finds that a $3.5B inflow lowers three-month bill yields by 0.7 basis points on impact and about four basis points within ten days, with a larger effect when Treasury-market liquidity is strained.A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so the effect is real but small. An earlier version found that equal-sized outflows had a larger effect. The current BIS research does not restate that comparison, so treat the asymmetry as unsettled.In its Q2 2026 attestation release of 31 July 2026, Tether reported $187.8B of total assets at 30 June, with most reserves held in US government-backed instruments and short-term liquidity facilities.For an equity investor, growth is a mild tailwind for bill prices. A shrinking market could be a sharper shock, because the stress that triggers redemptions is when the bill market can least absorb the selling. The BIS paper measures the yield response to stablecoin flows; it does not show that redemptions occur when bill-market liquidity is weakest. Treat this as a risk scenario, not an observed outcome. Redemptions on that scale have not been tested. The largest seven-day fall in supply in the past year was $3.83B, in the week to 1 February 2026.What an equity investor takes from this is not a level but a variance. Stablecoins add a little to rate swings and do not set the level, but short rates feed bank funding costs, money market fund yields and the discount rate on every other asset.How are stablecoins changing settlement and market infrastructure?Stablecoins are becoming the cash leg of on-chain settlement, so distribution and settlement revenue is now contested. Circle’s five-year agreement with Binance, announced on 22 September 2026 with a $100M Binance equity investment, shows how much issuers lean on large distributors for reach.The settlement leg is the cash side of a trade, where money changes hands as the asset is delivered. On blockchains, that leg increasingly uses stablecoins. This is the most structural channel: its importance depends less on today’s supply growth than on where tokenised assets eventually settle. Where an asset settles, in which currency and on whose rails are revenue questions for exchanges, clearing houses, custodians and card networks, all of which are listed.Two features of the plumbing matter. A dollar that settles in seconds, at any hour, can be posted, moved and recalled in ways a bank wire cannot, which lets intermediaries hold smaller buffers and changes what their service is worth. And because stablecoin settlement never closes while shares trade on exchange hours, a timing gap opens between the two markets.Ethereum’s share of stablecoin supply fell from 53.0% to 48.0% between 31 March and 27 September 2026, while Tron rose from 28.0% to 30.9%, Solana from 4.8% to 5.4% and Hyperliquid from 1.7% to 2.5%. The shift indicates which networks are gaining a larger share of stablecoin liquidity and, with it, greater economic relevance.Distribution is where the rent settles. Circle’s release describes a $100M share purchase by Binance at a 5.0% discount, and a commercial agreement under which Binance promotes USDC and Circle provides infrastructure. It gives no fee terms. With total supply broadly flat and USDC share little changed (24.7% against 25.1% on 31 March), the deal suggests distribution has become a cost of defending reach. Whether it reduces issuer margins depends on terms Circle has not yet disclosed. The question for investors is not whether stablecoins win but which listed layer keeps the margin.Why are stablecoins starting to be backed by tokenised equities?Ethena said on 25 September 2026 that Binance will be its first venue for extending USDe’s basis trade into equity perpetual futures, and The Block reported that part of the backing will be tokenised US equities. Equities are becoming collateral for instruments priced like cash, which makes the quality of that collateral a diligence question.USDe is a synthetic dollar backed by a trade rather than bank deposits. Ethena holds tokenised equities, blockchain tokens that track listed shares, and shorts matching perpetual futures, derivatives without an expiry date, so price movements are designed to offset. The remaining return is the funding rate, a payment between traders for leverage. Cash-and-carry, in other words, with equities in place of commodities.This creates a new source of demand for tokenised shares and equity perpetuals, driven by collateral needs rather than a view on the company. The key question is whether the hedge holds under stress, given that equity-perpetual markets are far thinner than their crypto equivalents. Synthetic dollars can blur the line between cash-like instruments and equity-backed collateral.Ethena deserves a fair counterweight. USDe supply fell 74.7%, from $14.83B on 4 October 2025 to $3.75B on 28 April 2026, a redemption of that size settled without the instrument breaking, which is the test the design exists to pass. It stood at $4.94B on 27 September 2026. The practical step is not to form a view on any stablecoin. It is to know where in a portfolio the exposure already sits: regional bank margins, front-end rate swings, exchange and payment network revenue, and now the collateral behind instruments treated as cash.FAQsDo stablecoins take deposits away from banks, and which banks are most exposed? Some deposits move, but supply is flat and equals 4.6% of the $6.6T of US transactional deposits flagged as at risk. Deposit-funded lenders, such as US regional banks, carry the most exposure.How do stablecoins affect Treasury bill yields and short-term rates? Slightly: BIS research finds a $3.5B inflow lowers three-month bill yields by about 4 basis points within ten days.How are stablecoins changing settlement and market infrastructure? Settlement and distribution revenue is now contested between exchanges, custodians, clearing firms, card networks and issuers.Why are stablecoins starting to be backed by tokenised equities? Equity hedges widen the pool of assets that can back a synthetic dollar beyond crypto, at the cost of tying its stability to thinner equity derivatives markets.Published onOct 23rd, 2026WriterCoinShares

articles.title: The US Small-Cap Bull Market: A Correction, Not a Conclusion | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
For some time now, we have marveled at the strength and resilience of the small-cap market following the tariff-induced lows of April 2025. What began as a sharp recovery from deeply depressed levels has increasingly looked to us like something potentially more meaningful. From the April 8, 2025 market lows through September 30, the Russell 2000 Index advanced 61.9%, outpacing the 55.5% gain for the large-cap Russell 1000 Index.

We think this is important context for understanding the market’s recent volatility. As recently as early October, for example, large-cap indexes were reaching new all-time highs even as the Russell 2000 Index subsequently corrected by more than 11% from its mid-August high, reaching its most recent low on October 19.

Rather than viewing this pullback as necessarily signaling the end of small-cap’s advance, we believe it may be better understood as a correction within an emerging bull-market cycle for small-caps. History provides useful context as well as helping flesh out our view. From 2002 through 2025, the Russell 2000 Index experienced an average intra-calendar-year decline of 19.6%, despite generating an average calendar-year return of 10.2%.

Significant corrections have frequently been part of otherwise rewarding years for small-cap investors. In fact, some of the strongest years for small-caps have included substantial drawdowns along the way, reminding us that bull markets rarely advance in a straight line. We believe this historical perspective is particularly relevant today, as the recent pullback may be better understood as a correction within the small-cap cycle that we believe began in April 2025, rather than evidence that the cycle has run its course.

What has been especially intriguing to us is the relative price action amid the recent volatility. In one extraordinary trading session during the week of October 19, the Nasdaq Composite Index declined more than 2.5% while the Russell 2000 finished in positive territory. Since January 1979, this combination has reportedly occurred on only five trading days—approximately 0.04% of all sessions. The four previous instances were concentrated between April 1999 and March 2001, a period that saw the beginning of the last extended cycle of small-cap leadership.

We are not suggesting that one trading day can confirm the direction of the market or determine its leadership. However, we believe the historical parallel is particularly interesting because it is consistent with the broader shift in market leadership that we have been observing since April 2025. More importantly, our conviction in the potential durability of this small-cap cycle rests on fundamentals rather than price action alone.

Today, we see a potentially powerful combination for small-cap investors: Accelerating earnings, attractive relative valuations, and low expectations. These are conditions that we believe can support a sustained period of improved relative performance, particularly among higher-quality small-cap companies with strong balance sheets, consistent profitability, and disciplined capital allocation.

We also think it is important to keep in mind that the distinction between a correction and the end of a market cycle is often easier to recognize in hindsight. We certainly recognize that economic uncertainty, changing interest-rate expectations, and market volatility could interrupt or even reverse the progress small-caps have made.

Nevertheless, we believe the evidence increasingly supports the possibility that the small-cap leadership cycle began in April 2025. If that assessment proves correct, the recent correction may ultimately be remembered not as the end of the advance, but as one of the inevitable periods of volatility along the way.

For long-term small-cap investors, we think that distinction matters.

Stay tuned... Follow Francis D. Gannon Co-Chief Investment Officer

Investment Insights

In Brief: The Case for Asia Private Equity

October 2026

5 minute read

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

Asia is an increasingly important driver of the global economy, yet many investment portfolios have not kept pace. The region accounts for more than 60% of global growth, while structural shifts in consumption, technology, trade and corporate governance are changing where and how value is created.
For private equity investors, the opportunity isn't simply about gaining exposure to Asia's economic growth. It's also about creating value through active ownership. And because the region's markets have distinct economic characteristics and structural drivers, understanding those differences is key to identifying where and how private equity can help businesses grow and transform.

Sign up to subscribe to the latest insights from KKR

Email Address

Please enter your business email.

Please enter a valid email address.
Please enter a professional email address.

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

There is no single Asia story
One of Asia's defining strengths is its diversity. To understand the breadth of the private equity opportunity, it's worth looking more closely at the dynamics shaping individual markets.
Japan is undergoing a significant corporate transformation. Corporate governance reforms and an increased focus on capital efficiency and shareholder value are encouraging companies to reassess their portfolios and non-core businesses. The unwinding of cross-shareholdings is further changing long-standing corporate ownership structures. Private equity has become an increasingly important part of this transformation, with average annual deal value rising from ¥0.56 trillion in 2011–2015 to ¥4.12 trillion in 2021–2025.[1] For investors, these shifts are expanding the scope for corporate carve-outs, take-privates and other transactions where active ownership can help drive transformation.
India combines strong economic growth with rising consumption and deepening capital markets. Its economy has surpassed $4 trillion, while a large and increasingly affluent population is supporting growth across sectors. India's young and expanding workorce provides another long-term tailwind, while the continued formalization of the economy is shifting activity toward larger, more organized businesses. The private equity market has matured alongside these changes, with investment rising from approximately US$48 billion in 2010–2014 to US$218 billion in 2020–2024, while buyout activity grew nearly eightfold.[2] Together, these shifts are creating more opportunities to partner with businesses seeking capital and operational expertise as they scale.
Southeast Asia is benefiting from rising consumption, expanding digital adoption and shifts in global supply chains. As companies diversify manufacturing and sourcing across a wider range of markets, countries across Southeast Asia are attracting new investment and becoming more integrated into regional and global production networks. Combined with a population of approximately 700 million and growing intra-Asia trade, these shifts are creating opportunities for businesses serving both domestic and regional markets.
South Korea is a large, sophisticated economy with a private equity market that continues to mature. Corporate governance reforms are encouraging greater focus on shareholder value and capital efficiency, while generational change at family-owned businesses is creating succession and ownership-transition needs. At the same time, large corporate groups are reassessing portfolios and non-core assets. Together, these shifts are expanding the opportunity for buyouts, carve-outs and strategic partnerships, creating more ways for private equity owners to help businesses professionalize, sharpen their strategic focus and pursue their next stage of growth.
Greater China is entering a new phase of growth, with the opportunity increasingly shaped by consumption, innovation and advanced manufacturing. The region remains a major manufacturing and technology center, but the composition of growth is changing as businesses develop new products, capabilities and sources of competitive advantage. For private equity investors, that evolution is creating opportunities to back companies positioned to benefit from changing consumption patterns, technological innovation and the continued development of higher-value manufacturing. Navigating those opportunities requires selectivity, particularly against a backdrop of geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty.
Australia and New Zealand combine developed-market characteristics with sophisticated capital markets and deep pools of institutional capital. Australia's superannuation system, with approximately A$4.5 trillion in assets[3], is an important source of long-term capital and has helped support the development of a mature private markets ecosystem. Against that backdrop, corporate carve-outs, founder partnerships and opportunities to improve and expand businesses provide another distinct source of private equity opportunities within the region.
A changing private equity landscape
Across Asia, these structural shifts are creating opportunities that extend beyond providing growth capital. As businesses scale, ownership structures evolve and industries consolidate, private equity investors can play an active role in helping companies navigate change and realize their potential.
Private markets remain relatively underpenetrated in parts of the region. Many industries are fragmented, businesses are transitioning from founder ownership and large corporations are reassessing non-core assets. At the same time, governance reforms are changing how companies think about capital allocation, ownership and shareholder value.
Private equity owners can bring operational expertise, support geographic and product expansion, pursue strategic acquisitions and help businesses navigate periods of transformation. In markets where companies are scaling rapidly or ownership structures are evolving, these capabilities can be particularly valuable.

Looking beyond the regional narrative
Investors considering greater exposure to Asia also have legitimate questions. Geopolitical tensions, currency movements, regulatory differences and uncertainty around exits can all affect outcomes. Liquidity and the timing of realizations are particularly important considerations for private market investors.
These risks should not be minimized, but neither should they be applied uniformly across a region as diverse as Asia. Economic drivers, regulatory environments, capital markets and geopolitical exposures differ substantially from one market to another. That makes selectivity important and increases the value of local knowledge, relationships and operating capabilities.
For investors, Asia's diversity can be a source of opportunity, offering exposure to different markets, growth drivers and stages of development. The case for Asia private equity is therefore not dependent on a single macroeconomic outcome.
Asia's economic growth is an important part of the investment story. But for private equity investors, we believe the opportunity goes further, with structural change creating new avenues for active ownership and value creation across the region.

This set of issues is entering a more pragmatic phase. The long-term direction remains intact, but the path forward requires navigating greater complexity—across policy, markets, and operations.
Our approach remains grounded in a simple principle: focusing on the issues that are most material to value creation and protection. This informs how and where we invest, how we support our companies, and how we assess performance over time.

articles.title: Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks -  speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at the Central Bank of Turkey, İstanbul Economic Forum

Published on
08 October 2026

Andrew Bailey says that although the financial system has remained resilient through repeated geopolitical and economic shocks, weaker growth, persistent supply disruptions, rising sovereign debt, leveraged markets and expanding AI-related exposures create risks. Policymakers should therefore pursue sustainable growth, maintain credible monetary and fiscal frameworks, and strengthen core financial markets so they can absorb future shocks without amplifying them.

Speech
The financial system has so far weathered the latest period of uncertainty. But lower growth, repeated supply shocks and changing market structures mean that resilience cannot be taken for granted.
The conflict in the Middle East has created major uncertainty about growth, inflation and interest rates. Existing vulnerabilities in sovereign debt markets, credit markets and asset valuations could crystallise together. The rapid expansion of financing connected with artificial intelligence has created new exposures, while incidents involving frontier AI have underlined the associated operational, cyber and financial risks.
However, an important part of the story so far is economic resilience in the sense that recent supply shocks have hit the world economy at the same time as the potential growth dividends from AI have become clearer.
Moreover, the story of the financial system so far has been one of resilience. Banking systems generally remain well capitalised and we are not seeing funding stress. Despite a succession of economic shocks and heightened volatility, most financial markets have continued to function without a major breakdown in liquidity or trading conditions.
Financial markets have so far withstood significant increases in sovereign bond yields, and most market adjustments have remained orderly. This resilience owes much to the reforms introduced after the global financial crisis. Those reforms are sometimes criticised as burdensome. Today, their value is clear.
But we cannot be relaxed. Experience teaches us that specific problems can emerge even when the wider system appears stable. The lesson of the global financial crisis is that such problems are much easier to manage when the wider system is resilient and the authorities are committed to keeping it that way.
The deeper economic challenge
Behind the immediate risks lie two longer-term developments.
The first is weaker potential growth, driven in many economies by slowing productivity, which determines how rapidly national income and living standards can rise.
The second is the frequency of large negative supply shocks. Covid, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East have each disrupted the supply capacity of economies. Covid was also both a supply and demand shock, with the balance changing over time. But all these episodes were exceptionally large, and they followed one another with unusual speed.
Are repeated shocks the new normal? Central bankers should be wary of becoming political soothsayers. But a more multipolar world, in which economic policy is increasingly an arena for geopolitical competition, may produce more frequent disruptions. We should therefore prepare for a world in which larger shocks are not rare exceptions.
This creates a particular difficulty for monetary policy. A negative supply shock pushes inflation and output in opposite directions, producing weaker output but higher inflation.
The textbook response is to look through a one-off increase in the price level. Interest rates cannot produce more oil or gas, and monetary policy affects the economy with long lags. But looking through a shock is possible only if inflation expectations remain well anchored.
If households and businesses begin to incorporate higher inflation into wage demands and pricing decisions, a temporary shock can become persistent. These second-round effects are slower to emerge. Central banks must make forward-looking judgements and update them as the evidence changes.
The difficulty becomes greater when shocks arrive in quick succession. A recent history of higher inflation can cause people to expect further inflation. The sequencing of Covid and the invasion of Ukraine have made this risk particularly acute.
The interaction with financial stability
Supply shocks can also create tension between monetary and financial stability. Interest rates may need to rise even as economic activity weakens. Debt-servicing costs increase just as household incomes and corporate earnings come under pressure. Asset prices can fall, reducing the value of collateral and restricting the supply of credit.
This is why resilience before a shock is so important. Strong banks and sound household and corporate balance sheets give policymakers room to respond without turning an economic adjustment into a financial crisis.
Fiscal policy faces a related challenge. Lower growth and repeated supply shocks weaken the public finances while increasing pressure on governments to provide support. Higher borrowing costs and weaker growth raise debt-to-GDP ratios. If markets begin to doubt the fiscal trajectory, bond yields can rise further, tightening monetary and financial conditions.
Governments can ordinarily use their balance sheets to cushion a severe downturn and rebuild fiscal space when conditions improve. That is the principle of countercyclical policy. But when shocks become more frequent, underlying growth is weaker, and the succession of shocks leads to a higher level of government debt, this becomes much harder to sustain.
A changing market structure
Global government bond markets have also changed profoundly. They were once dominated by long-term investors, often described as “real money” and “price insensitive”. Today, leveraged investors play a much larger role, while traditional demand for long-duration debt has declined, partly because of changes in pension provision and ageing populations.
This new structure has so far increased the capacity of markets to absorb the additional supply of government debt. But greater absorption has come with greater fragility. Leveraged positions can be unwound rapidly. Losses can trigger margin calls, model-driven repricing and stop-outs, producing further forced selling that can amplify market moves. The buyers are typically more price sensitive.
The same funds may hold large leveraged positions across several countries and asset classes. Deleveraging that begins in one market can therefore spread quickly to others.
The policy response must have several parts.
First, we must pursue sustainable growth. There is no single solution, but major technological advances have historically lifted productivity. Artificial intelligence and robotics can drive scientific discovery, improve efficiency and raise prosperity. Financing that investment is essential. But greater financial exposure to AI also creates risk. If earnings expectations or confidence in the pace of AI adoption were sharply revised, the consequences could spread through equity, credit and sovereign markets. AI safety and financial stability are therefore becoming increasingly connected. Safely deployed, we should see AI as a growth opportunity.
Second, monetary and fiscal frameworks must remain credible. For monetary policy, that means an unwavering commitment to returning inflation to target. I remain sceptical of unconditional promises about future interest rates. The world is too uncertain. But central banks should explain clearly how policy would respond under different economic conditions.
Fiscal policy must likewise be directed towards stability and be seen by markets as credible. Clear frameworks, including fiscal rules, can help contain risk premia when shocks occur.
Third, we must strengthen the resilience of core markets. Greater central clearing, appropriate minimum haircuts and stronger risk management all merit consideration.
There is no quick fix. But the direction is clear: raise sustainable growth, maintain credible policy frameworks, and ensure that financial markets can absorb shocks without amplifying them.
The system has been resilient. Our task is to make sure it remains so.
I would like to thank Nat Benjamin, Sarah Breeden, Karen Jude, Andrea Rosen, Vicky Saporta and James Talbot for their assistance in preparing these remarks.

Andrew Bailey
Governor, Bank of England

The authors gratefully acknowledge the Asfari Foundation’s generous support for this project.IntroductionThe Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region has been a major producer and exporter of hydrocarbons since the 1930s. In 2025, around 30 percent of global hydrocarbon exports originated in the MENA region, with collective regional revenues amounting to over $1 trillion.1 Since 2000, when the second oil boom began (the first being in October 1973), MENA has sold $25 trillion worth of oil and gas (adjusted for 2025 prices). As demonstrated by the conflict between the United States and Iran, events in the region remain consequential for international energy markets. But equally, hydrocarbons have shaped the region’s economies, governance structures, and societies in ways that now define the nature of the challenge ahead.The challenge in question is one of fundamental economic transformation. The global hydrocarbons order is facing profound change, as environmental and geopolitical pressures undermine the foundations on which many MENA economies have rested. In this context, economic diversification is no longer optional; it has become both strategic and urgent. Yet diversification is not merely a technical exercise. It brings with it at least three types of fundamental and interconnected challenges. The first is economic, and involves countries determining how to increase their labor productivity and build sustainable productive capacity outside hydrocarbons in economies long structured around resource rents. The second challenge is social and political, affecting how to renegotiate social contracts that support more inclusive societies. The third is regional, where the success or failure of transformation will depend not only on domestic reform, but on whether a more stable regional order can emerge, one in which economic cooperation prevails over conflict, fragmentation, and escalating tensions. Escaping the current vicious cycle and turning it into a virtuous one is essential for the region’s future.This paper does not offer a single prescription and acknowledges that the MENA region encompasses countries at very different stages of development, with very different resource endowments, institutional capacities, and political settlements. The analysis focuses on three groups of countries: high-income hydrocarbon exporters (Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries), middle-income hydrocarbon exporters (Algeria, Iraq, Libya, and Iran), and middle-income hydrocarbon importers (Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, and Tunisia). We offer an integrated approach to the economic, political, and regional dimensions of the diversification imperative and the need to strengthen productivity, as well as policy recommendations organized around the five key questions that structured the commission’s deliberations.The first question is the most fundamental one: Why must MENA countries diversify, and why now? For all the countries examined here, the answer is that, for various reasons, the demand for hydrocarbons is falling in a world shaped by a volatile energy transition and a pressing imperative of energy security. This will inexorably reduce oil and gas exports and revenues over the medium to long term, sharply constraining these countries’ access to foreign exchange and deepening their fiscal pressures. Many of the hydrocarbon exporting countries understand therefore that, because they will not be able to finance employment of their growing labor force in the public sector, they must immediately begin investing in productive jobs if they are to meet future challenges. Energy importers face a different challenge: They realize that it will be impossible in the coming years to export carbon-intensive manufactured goods to Europe as carbon border adjustment mechanisms and other environmental regulations take effect. The war with Iran has exacerbated such tensions. For one thing, oil revenues will fall more rapidly, implying a need to diversify more rapidly. Additionally, the war is likely to force changes in the way in which diversification takes place. The oil importing countries, especially Egypt, Jordan, and Lebanon, will sustain indirect losses, which is one more reason why they need to try harder to improve their labor productivity through growth-enhancing reforms.The second question concerns the current state of play: What is the situation when it comes to diversification efforts in the MENA region? The picture is highly uneven:GCC countries are heavily engaged in investing in productivity and diversification, but the results remain mixed. The most dynamic sectors have been oil products, entrepôt trade, tourism, hospitality, entertainment, and more recently renewables and artificial intelligence (AI) centers.2 However, generating productive jobs has been challenging, and the globally oriented model that underpins Gulf diversification strategies is threated by regional instability. The ability of the GCC countries to navigate a turbulent global energy transition is also in jeopardy.Among the middle-income hydrocarbon exporters (Iraq, Algeria, Libya, Iran), the pattern is one of rent consumption rather than investment. Productivity growth is absent, rent per capita is falling, and there is as yet no credible exit path from this trajectory.Middle-income hydrocarbon importers present an equally troubling picture, as they have been stuck in a severe form of the middle-income trap: They are operating below potential, with fragile social and financial situations, and are failing to pursue growth-enhancing reforms. Savings are low, as is investment, underemployment is rampant, and these countries each face a brewing debt crisis, while state services have been severely rolled back. The main problem is an unbalanced form of capitalism dominated by a closed economic elite that is unwilling to allow space for competition from firms not under its control. Political connections are based on loyalty, not productivity, which represents a key obstacle to transformation.The third question is political. What are the social and political implications of the current trajectory? Across the MENA region, the social contracts that offered material provision in exchange for political acquiescence are under mounting strain. The generation now entering the labor market is better educated than its predecessors, holds higher aspirations, and has grown up with direct exposure to different global living standards. However, it also faces higher unemployment than preceding generations, deteriorating public services, and more precarious labor markets. The nature of this strain diverges across country groups, reflecting fundamentally different distributional bargains. In the GCC, the rentier bargain is being restructured through nationalization of the labor force and subsidy reform, generating grievances with few formal outlets to express them.3 In middle-income hydrocarbon exporting countries, revenues sustain narrow patronage networks, but cannot finance mass consumption or broad legitimacy. In hydrocarbon importing states, such as Egypt and Jordan, external geopolitical rents that once underpinned the social contract are being eroded, leaving governments with shrinking fiscal space and facing rising social instability.What unites all three country groups is the dilemma of how to deal with the fact that the reforms needed to build productive diversified economies are politically costly in the short run, even as inaction is economically unsustainable in the long run. Faced with this dilemma, governments have responded across the board by centralizing power and intensifying control, either to manage reform (in the case of the GCC countries) or avoid it (in the case of other states, such as Algeria, Egypt, Jordan, and Tunisia). However, this approach is straining the very foundations on which a durable economic transformation must rest—rule of law, investor confidence, legitimate channels for objection. The difficulties reformist politicians are facing are complex. They must propose attractive reforms that generate support from a coalition of reformist parties or pressure groups, create mechanisms that compensate losers and bring them into the fold, put in place checks and balances to avoid costly mistakes and learn from experience, and finally permit the voicing of grievances to avoid the type of explosion that was common during the decade of Arab uprisings.The fourth question concerns the external environment. How do regional and global dynamics shape, and potentially undermine, diversification efforts? Falling hydrocarbon revenues will intensify regional competition in the oil and gas market if it is not matched by improved regional cooperation, as countries seek to defend their share of a shrinking market. This reality has become more acute since the beginning of the war with Iran, which dampened global appetite for Gulf oil and gas due to elevated perceived risks. Moreover, increased insecurity has also disrupted Gulf diversification strategies in areas that are highly sensitive to security conditions—foreign direct investment, tourism, or trade.In this more volatile environment, countries need to imagine growth paths that are more resilient to shocks and less likely to generate them. This requires building regional economic interdependencies, which today remain underdeveloped. It would mean expanding intraregional trade and investment, advancing a regional security architecture that reduces business risk and lessens reliance on any single external guarantor, and diversifying external economic relationships in a world increasingly organized around geopolitical blocs. To be able to sustain diversified relations, stronger regional bargaining power helps. This could come in the form of more robust soft power derived from better management of regional public goods such as defending the environment, improving security, caring for refugees, and preventing states from failing. There are other arguments for improved regional cooperation in the form of the growth of a regional market: the need to bring some accumulated savings in the form of globally placed Sovereign Wealth Funds’ assets closer to home, given rising expropriation risks; the fact that environmental challenges are regional; and the advisability of preserving and diversifying regional trade routes.The fifth and final question is a holistic one: How do these elements interact, and under what conditions can the region move from a vicious to a virtuous cycle? The elements discussed above can interact positively or negatively. The status quo increases regional tensions, political risk, and doom loops—or self-reinforcing cycles that exacerbate problems—of economic decline and violence. The overlapping aspects of the transition—economic, social, political, and environmental—create structural tensions, but progress on one front can create momentum for broader reforms and a virtuous cycle that facilitates progress:A regional security deal would be much enhanced by regional economic cooperation. Moreover, the financial rates of return to the region of sovereign wealth fund investment would be greater if invested in large rather than small markets. Cooperation is also needed to fight climate change.The ability to implement industrial policy to develop new value chains in a secure regional environment would enable the region to bargain for a fairer role in a fragmented world order.Reduced regional instability and the development of a regional market would create positive incentives for recalcitrant regimes to invest in growth, especially in middle-income countries.Insufficient Progress in Productivity and DiversificationWhile some hydrocarbon exporters have made progress on diversification, they mostly remain insufficiently diversified. Oil importers, for their part, have achieved only low levels of labor productivity. As a result, diversification should be an important aim for oil and gas exporters, and oil importers should target efficiency gains with more determination. At the same time, there are many ways in which the world is changing, which offer additional reasons for accelerating diversification and efficiency efforts.In absolute terms, countries with larger oil and gas revenues per capita have managed to diversify their economy more than those with lower levels of revenue.The Appeal and Challenge of Economic DiversificationFor the past fifty years, oil and gas revenues have enriched Middle Eastern countries. Hydrocarbons have financed the building of modern states, infrastructures, and social services. In some but not all oil and gas producing countries, these revenues have also supported the development of productive private sectors beyond fossil fuels. Paradoxically, in absolute terms, countries with larger oil and gas revenues per capita have managed to diversify their economy more than those with lower levels of revenue (see figure 1). The United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar have the highest levels of hydrocarbon revenues per capita, though these revenues have come to constitute a small share of their countries’ total GDP. This reflects their wide-ranging diversification into non-oil and gas sectors as well as financial earnings from their sovereign wealth fund. In contrast, in Iraq and Algeria, hydrocarbons revenues are relatively modest on a per capita basis, but they constitute a large share of GDP, as national production outside hydrocarbons remains modest.
Most economies in the region remain highly dependent on hydrocarbons in two additional dimensions of their economic structure—fiscal revenues and exports (see figure 2). In Oman, Qatar, Kuwait, and Iraq, the share of hydrocarbon revenues as a proportion both of state revenues and exports is close to or above 80 percent. Other countries are making progress in diversifying either revenue sources or exports, or both. For example, Bahrain has diversified its exports more than any other GCC country, with 50 percent of its exports being non-hydrocarbon. Saudi Arabia and Algeria now receive around 40 percent of their state revenues from non-hydrocarbons. The UAE has made progress on both fronts: 30 percent of its exports and 60 percent of its state revenues are from non-hydrocarbon sources.Hydrocarbon producers have long aspired to diversify their economies, and there are good reasons for accelerating this process. The end of the global thirst for hydrocarbon consumption can now be seen on the horizon. This will not happen because of oil and gas running out, but rather because of an inexorable fall in demand, which will reduce the MENA region’s hydrocarbon revenues over the medium to long term. Global demand for oil and gas from the region is predicted to recede over time for three reasons: technological change will impose a reduction; the climate transition will push countries to cut back on carbon-dioxide emissions; and risks specific to the Middle East might deter oil and gas companies and producers from investing in new reserves in the region. It is also difficult to predict the speed of this decline in revenue, since it will depend not just on global demand, but also on oil and gas prices and the share the region will retain of global demand. Technological change: Hydrocarbons, which are mainly being used to fuel vehicles, are being overtaken by alternative types of energy. In the past ten years, the expanded use of electrical automobiles, which run on electricity produced from various sources—nuclear, hydro, solar and wind, as well as biofuels, gas, and coal—has been rapid. The development of battery technologies has allowed the prices of electrical vehicles to reach parity with vehicles that have internal combustion engines, something that will affect future hydrocarbon demand. These developments have been in large part driven by China, which is keen to capture a new global market in renewables, but also to secure its own energy autonomy. Beijing has made a determined and increasingly successful effort to wean itself off imported fuel. Between 2022 and 2025, China emerged as the main producer and exporter of advanced and competitive renewable energy technology.4 As of 2025, the country dominated solar, wind, and battery technology, and was exporting cost-competitive alternatives to oil and gas on a global scale. Climate transition: The 2015 Paris agreement, signed by 196 countries, committed the signatories to ensuring that global temperatures would not rise more than 1.5°C by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.5 While the exact path and speed of the global temperature increase remain uncertain, because hydrocarbons are major carbon-dioxide producers, their consumption will have to be curtailed. Admittedly, the collective commitment to a rapid reduction in the carbon-dioxide footprint has been weakened in Europe, and especially in the United States, because of budgetary pressures and mounting opposition from constituencies that stand to lose out. Nevertheless, technological progress and geopolitical divergences are creating new incentives to avoid depending on oil and gas and to develop renewable energies.Wars and insecurity: The consequences of the Iran war have lessened the desirability of purchasing Middle Eastern oil. If the risks do not decrease significantly, global demand for oil from the region may fall more precipitously. This would be ironic, given that hydrocarbon production in the Gulf is the cheapest in the world. The Gulf states had counted on benefitting from this advantage to remain the last global producers of oil and gas, but geographical risks are increasing transport and insurance costs in ways that neutralize geological advantage.Recent estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA) illustrate the possible magnitude of the fall in hydrocarbon revenues.6 The IEA presents three scenarios: Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE), as per the Paris agreements; an Announced Pledges Scenario (APS), which assumes that all climate commitments as of August 2023 are fully met on time; and a Stated Transition Energy Policy Scenario (STEPS), which reflects the energy policies that were in place as of August 2023 (see figure 3 and box 1). In the NZE and APS reform scenarios, global oil demand is projected to fall by 50 to 75 percent by 2050—enormous shifts compared to the status quo STEPS scenario. Change is already in motion, as reflected by the steep fall in investment in new oil and gas capacity, and an equally steep rise in investment in renewable capacity worldwide. This is especially true of the United States, the European Union, and China, which together dominate renewable energy production. Total revenues accruing to oil and gas producers are projected to decline rapidly under the NZE and APS scenarios. Currently, production in the MENA region represents around 38 percent of global production. In the reform scenarios, GCC revenues are expected to fall precipitously, even if they may manage to increase their share of smaller global demand, due to lower extraction costs (the dashed line scenarios in figure 3). Even in the status quo scenario, the revenues of the states in the MENA region are also projected to fall, albeit by much less, due to reduced demand and lower prices.A second reason for countries to diversify relates to population growth and the rise in education. These two factors require economies in the MENA region to generate more and better jobs for their populations. But oil and gas rents per capita have declined since 2010. This is in part due to a drop in prices, which stabilized at around $60 per barrel before the Iran war (a figure that is expected to fall further following a permanent end to hostilities). But the decline in per capita rents is also very much due to demographic pressures that will continue to progressively increase the fiscal cost of redistribution (see figure 4).
Most importantly, population growth and progress in education mean it is no longer possible to hire all educated citizens for government jobs, as in the early days of oil and gas. In many hydrocarbon-producing countries, secondary education is near universal and nearly half of all graduates acquire a university degree.7 Integrating them all into the public sector is not just onerous for the state, it represents a highly inefficient use of their potential. This new challenge requires creating jobs outside the bureaucracy, in productive activities.
This is particularly true for countries already running high fiscal deficits, such as Algeria, Bahrain, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia, all of which have had a hard time maintaining around 40 percent of labor in the public sector and trying to balance their books with oil below $100 per barrel (see figure 5). Kuwait’s challenge is even more daunting, as the country still employs over 80 percent of its national workforce in the public sector, which requires large fiscal expenditures, producing fiscal deficits unless oil and gas prices remain at an elevated level. Only Qatar, the UAE, and Oman can afford to pay for large public sectors, even at low oil and gas prices. As hydrocarbon revenues must be invested to prepare for the hoped-for, productive non-hydrocarbon economy of tomorrow, a growing share of state budgets must come from other sources, such as taxation. More ambitiously, the decline in oil and gas revenues requires developing new sources of exports to continue generating foreign exchange as revenues shrink.The third rationale for diversification into productive activities is to create opportunities to invest the region’s savings closer to home, given the rising risks posed by an increasingly volatile world. In such a context, investing in diversification reduces the dangers to a country’s financial assets. Currently, 42 percent of the sovereign wealth funds of GCC states are invested in the United States and 32 percent in Europe (see figure 6). Yet both regions have extremely elevated ratios of public debt to GDP, something that presages high risks of macroeconomic and foreign exchange instability. In contrast, only 19 percent of the sovereign wealth fund resources are invested in Asia. And only a very small share is invested in the MENA region: No more than 3 percent of sovereign wealth fund resources are invested in the GCC and 4 percent in the rest of the Middle East. From a diversification perspective, it would make sense to invest a larger share in Asia and the Middle East. Investing in the MENA region today may seem risky, but in a longer-term perspective it can contribute to fueling higher growth and enhancing regional security though interdependencies, thereby improving the long-term security of savings for future generations.

Box 1. The Future of Demand for Middle Eastern Oil.
Karen E. Young
The IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2025 finds that oil will remain the dominant fuel until 2050 if current policies remain in place. Growth would be largely a Global South phenomenon—India, Asia, the Middle East, and Africa account for the bulk of long-term demand growth, with India alone adding 8.2 mb/d, while OECD demand is expected to fall by 8.5 mb/d. Gas is the fastest-growing hydrocarbon, driven substantially by AI data center electricity demand.
The Iran war may incentivize countries to reduce oil demand across their transportation sectors more rapidly. This short-term disruption could have much longer term impacts, as global perceptions of the Strait as a dependable conduit for oil begin to change. The challenge for Gulf and Middle Eastern producers will be that there may be more capital expenditure on other regions, especially in the Americas and also in Africa, as the global concern for energy security and diversity of suppliers justifies new exploration and production.
Gulf producers are not passive in this transition. Their strategy is sophisticated and multi-track. First, they are moving aggressively down the value chain: SABIC is pivoting into advanced polymers and specialty chemicals; ADNOC’s Ruwais hub integrates petrochemicals, hydrogen, and carbon capture; and QatarEnergy is framing LNG exports increasingly around low-carbon and hydrogen derivatives. Second, they are locking in Asian demand as their primary market, deepening refinery and petrochemical investments (and in the post-war context, more oil storage) across the Indo-Pacific, where consumption growth is concentrated. Third, their ultra-low extraction costs—Aramco produces at roughly $3–5/barrel—will give them a structural advantage over higher-cost producers, which will find themselves obliged to drastically cut or even cease production. Under the IEA’s current policies scenario, OPEC+ production in 2050 is projected to be 15 percent higher than at any point in history. How OPEC+ maintains cohesion, however, is more uncertain. The UAE’s exit from OPEC in May 2026 set a precedent for regional producers eager to invest now to increase production and reach the market while demand and prices are firm. They are bolstering domestic renewables not for climate reasons, but to displace crude used domestically for power and to free up more barrels for export.
The current geopolitical situation may also have a longer-term impact on oil demand by accelerating renewable energy use, especially in the form of electric vehicles. Current geopolitical developments are sending mixed signals for the pace of the energy transition. Trade barriers and rising protectionism increase the risk of global economic slowdown, which in turn reduces hydrocarbon consumption and makes capital investment in both clean and fossil fuel energy sources more difficult and expensive. Conflict and growing nationalist politics heighten energy security risk, incentivizing countries toward domestically produced fossil fuels and renewables over imported energy. Meanwhile, China’s export orientation means that the country will continue directing surplus clean tech products—solar panels, batteries, and EVs—toward developing economies in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. China’s share of clean-tech exports to emerging economies has risen from 23 percent to 31 percent since 2022, according to a study by Bloomberg NEF.1
The net result is likely a bifurcated transition: slower in the United States and trade-war-affected economies, but faster across much of Asia and Europe. Middle East producers, with unmatched cost structures and a deliberate pivot toward petrochemicals and Asian markets, are positioning themselves to be the last hydrocarbons producers—the survivors of a decades-long shakeout among global producers. The real risk they face is not near-term demand collapse, but a 2040s world where EVs dominate transport, while petrochemicals become the final major-use case for crude. Global demand for oil is strongest now in road transport; as that demand declines, there is likely to be resilient demand in the realm of petrochemicals, manufacturing and construction, and aviation and shipping.
