Such tensions are unfolding against the backdrop of a precarious dual wager made by most GCC governments.57 The first wager is economic, and holds that diversification can generate enough well-paying private-sector jobs to replace the economic security the state once provided directly. Yet building globally competitive industries, persuading a population accustomed to wealth distribution to compete in a market economy, and replacing oil revenues with export-driven growth represent major challenges, especially in countries with lower hydrocarbon rents per capita such as Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain. The second wager, this one sociopolitical in nature, is that diversification can happen quickly and broadly enough to keep the social contract from unraveling under the pressures it faces. These two wagers are mutually dependent in that a faltering economy negatively affects a country’s political situation, while a dissatisfied or restive population undermines the conditions necessary for economic success.58Yet there is a deeper political dilemma at the heart of the diversification project. A productive economy requires a genuinely competitive private sector insulated from political interference. But if the private sector becomes autonomous enough, it could become a source of independent power that threatens the stability and security of GCC regimes accustomed to controlling their business elites by keeping them dependent on state patronage. Indeed, the very dynamism that diversification demands is also what rulers have historically had reason to fear and avoid. It is precisely to address such fears that most regimes in the GCC have concentrated power and constructed new narratives legitimizing their authority. Each of these steps has its own logic as a tool of social engineering and population management. Yet taken together, they may actually compound rather than resolve the underlying dilemma. And, in doing so, they could gradually undermine the very conditions on which the economic wager depends.Over the past decade, most GCC states have seen a significant concentration of decisionmaking authority in the hands of a single leader. The old model of dynastic rule, in which power was distributed across different branches of ruling families, has given way to more centralized personal rule, most visibly under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Saudi Arabia and Mohammed bin Zayed in the UAE. This has extended into the economic sphere, with the appointment of senior royals to lead major state-owned enterprises, sovereign wealth funds, and economic ministries, reflecting the degree to which centralized political control has infiltrated economic governance. Such consolidation has gone hand-in-hand with the marginalization of established business elites in most GCC states. Such elites, which once had some degree of access and influence, now largely operate at the state’s discretion, with little institutional voice in economic decisionmaking and effectively none in political life.59When decisionmaking is reduced to a small circle of people shielded from scrutiny, bad decisions are harder to catch and reverse.While centralization enables quick decisions and provides the unified political will that reform programs require, the risks of power concentration are considerable, especially since they strike directly at the foundations of the diversification project itself. When decisionmaking is reduced to a small circle of people shielded from scrutiny, bad decisions are harder to catch and reverse. No institutional channel exists allowing outside voices to identify problems or challenge assumptions before costs become irreversible. The recurrent revisions made to flagship initiatives, such as Saudi Arabia’s NEOM, illustrate the cost of such a shortcoming. In systems where major projects are overseen by a single leader, the reasons behind major reversals or modifications in projects are never fully transparent, and there is little accountability for wasted public funds or the fate of communities that may have been displaced by the projects.60A further risk is that when political and economic powers are fused, the conditions for genuine market competition can become compromised, with investment decisions reflecting political considerations rather than efficiency or long-term productivity. This is fertile ground for the approval of expensive projects that ultimately become liabilities. Lack of competition also stifles innovation and prevents efficient small and medium enterprises from growing and taking market shares from the established corporate sector. If returns in the private sector lag behind expectations and political freedoms are constrained, the most mobile and skilled nationals—precisely those upon whom successful diversification plans depend—will have strong incentives to leave. To be successful, diversification cannot afford to lose the people it most needs.Fundamentally, a vibrant private sector requires rule of law, secure property rights, and investor confidence. The tension between power concentration and private-sector dynamism was most clearly demonstrated in the detention of prominent Saudi businessmen at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Riyadh in 2017. Framed as an anti-corruption campaign, in which those arrested had to pay large sums of money or hand over property to be released, the move was widely interpreted as an attempt by Mohammed bin Salman to concentrate power.61 Whatever the intent, the episode signaled that property rights were not guaranteed by law and were subject to political discretion—at precisely the moment investor confidence was most urgently needed.62Alongside power consolidation, GCC governments have worked to build new bases of legitimacy that do not rely on the redistributive logic of the old social contract, and do not require expanding political participation. Two instruments have been central to this shift, namely new nationalisms and selective social liberalization. Within Gulf countries, nationalism anchored in the leadership of ruling figures and tied directly to their reform programs has gradually displaced other forms of identity, including pan-Islamist or pan-Gulf identities. In Saudi Arabia, this has taken a populist twist. For example, the Ritz-Carlton crackdown was welcomed by many young Saudis as a long-overdue reckoning with the privileges afforded the country’s elites, an attitude those behind the campaign encouraged.63 In parallel, social liberalization has expanded personal freedoms meaningfully, so that women can now drive and work with fewer restrictions, mixed-gender entertainment venues exist, and religious policing has been curtailed. While these changes are real, it remains unclear whether they can compensate for the material losses resulting from replacing the old rentier system, or the restrictions placed on political expression.Middle-Income Countries, the Pressure on Social Contracts, and the Reform TrapMiddle-income hydrocarbon exporters and importers occupy different positions in the regional political economy than the GCC countries, but also a more precarious one. They lack the fiscal depth to sustain the old social bargain, or the state capacity to implement a new one. Unlike the GCC states, which are attempting, however imperfectly, to move to a new pact with its society, governments in middle-income countries face a starker situation. The reforms required for long-term stability could threaten the patronage networks and power structures on which regime survival depends. Therefore, in response, these regimes engage in centralization and repression, yet not as instruments of transformation, but as substitutes for it.Three factors are straining social contracts in middle-income hydrocarbon exporting countries. The first is demographic growth, which is steadily eroding rent per capita. The second is high youth unemployment and underemployment, which is generating persistent unrest. And the third is a widening gap between connected elites and the broader population, which is having a deleterious impact on the legitimacy of political and economic orders. At the heart of these countries’ difficulties is the interplay between fragile governance and moderate hydrocarbon wealth. Revenues are large enough to fund patronage networks and security apparatuses, but not the investment and inclusive distribution that brings wider legitimacy.64 From this emerges narrow, exclusionary political settlements in which access to public resources comes through loyalty to the regime.In Algeria, for example, different regions, social groups, and economic sectors relate to the state through highly unequal access to patronage, producing a deeply uneven distributional bargain.65 Demographic dynamics may also become a stronger constraint than declining external rents. Even if hydrocarbon revenues remain significant in the medium term, demographic pressures will progressively increase the fiscal and political costs of redistribution, rendering social contracts increasingly difficult to sustain. In Iraq, to provide another example, public-sector employment has been an important factor in the social contract, with 4.5 million people employed by the state.66 Yet individual access to public jobs flows through party and sectarian patronage networks and is itself an indicator of political alignment. Even reformist movements that emerged from the October 2019 protests have been unable to challenge this logic. Their own constituents also demand public-sector employment, and electoral incentives push even independent candidates toward patronage rather than reform.67The hydrocarbon windfall that followed the start of the Ukraine war offered these states a temporary reprieve. It allowed their governments to reinforce fragile political settlements through renewed rent distribution, although underlying vulnerabilities remained in place. These included fiscal exposure to oil and gas price volatility, weak diversification, high youth unemployment, and a deepening sense among populations that their system was rigged on behalf of insiders, which threatened social cohesion and political stability.The social contracts of middle-income hydrocarbon-importing countries, in turn, face four simultaneous pressures. The first is a fiscal squeeze that is hollowing out state capacity; the second, a rollback of subsidies that once underpinned popular legitimacy; the third, stagnant job creation at a time of rapid demographic growth; and the fourth, the erosion of external financial flows that once allowed governments to defer difficult choices. Specifically, the distributional bargain that sustained oil-importing countries, such as Egypt and Jordan, rested on what can be called geopolitical rents, or transfers provided to these countries due to their strategic and geopolitical importance by Gulf states, Western governments, and international financial institutions. These financial allocations, aimed at maintaining political stability, have long funded public spending, subsidies, and payrolls. For instance, energy and food subsidies have served to keep prices far below market rates, while the public sector remained a key driver of formal employment. For example, in Egypt, 45 percent of new formal jobs were created in the public sector between 1998 and 2006.68 While these kinds of arrangements held together for as long as external financing remained available, they are under mounting stress today. As governments turned to debt-financed spending after the Arab uprisings to ensure social stability, economic growth declined. In Egypt, for example, public debt now exceeds 90 percent of GDP, with interest payments absorbing roughly a third of government expenditures and two-thirds of tax revenues.69 This leaves almost no fiscal space for social investment.70 Healthcare spending declined sharply from 4.6 percent of GDP in 2016 to 1.1 percent in 2024, while nearly 60 percent of the Egyptian population is now poor or vulnerable.71 Jordan’s public debt, in turn, reached 116 percent of GDP in 2023, with debt-servicing crowding out both public investment and private-sector credit.72 Subsidy rollbacks have not been adequately replaced—targeted cash transfers in Egypt, for example, reach only a fraction of the population—and youth unemployment and inequality are on the rise.Foreign support bolstering old social contracts has also declined. Backing from the Gulf states has shifted from providing unconditional financial patronage to conditional engagement tied to performance on reforms. This has compelled countries such as Egypt and Jordan to enter into IMF programs that impose measures their social pacts are not equipped to implement. The war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February 2026 has also shown how oil-importing countries can be pulled into crises not of their making, as longstanding financial assistance provided by GCC countries creates expectations of political and military support. For instance, Egypt’s latest deployment of military personnel and advanced air defense systems to the UAE came in the context of rising Gulf pressure on Egypt to show support for its financial backers.73 At the same time, remittances, once nearly 25 percent of Jordan’s GDP, fell below 10 percent by 2022 as GCC labor nationalization efforts reduced migrant employment.74 Therefore, the multiple pillars of the old bargain—Gulf transfers, remittances, subsidized consumption, mass public employment—are being weakened simultaneously, increasing social instability.The predicament for leaders in middle-income countries is that building productive, diversified economies requires establishing regulatory institutions capable of taking action against firms that enjoy political access. The predicament for leaders in middle-income countries is that building productive, diversified economies requires establishing regulatory institutions capable of taking action against firms that enjoy political access. It also necessitates ending the connections that concentrate economic activity among politically loyal elites. Public investment has to be redirected from paying wages toward productive infrastructure and human capital, even as the authorities create conditions for firms without connections to enter and compete in the market.Yet such reforms directly threaten the economic foundations of those in power, including the connected elites, military-linked enterprises, and patronage networks whose rents depend on obstructing the entry of new competitors. The political costs also extend beyond the elites. Genuine reform entails restructuring the subsidy system and public employment—measures directly affecting ordinary households that depend on public-sector jobs and subsidized goods for their economic security. Any credible reform program, therefore, imposes immediate losses for these constituencies, before generating gains. While the “losers” of such reforms are well-known, the “winners” are only hypothetical and dispersed. This reality systematically creates conditions for opposing reform,75 while coalitions that might support structural transformation, when such coalitions begin to form, tend to invite repression rather than accommodation.The response of governments among middle-income hydrocarbon exporters and importers to the dilemmas of reform has been primarily based on centralizing power and engaging in repression to forestall reform altogether and protecting patronage networks and elite rents that serious diversification efforts would threaten. The result is a strategy of deferral, in which short-term political survival consistently trumps long-term stability, and in which each cycle of delay deepens fiscal vulnerability, narrowing the margin of maneuver when the reckoning comes. Across middle-income oil exporters and importers, this approach has translated into similar institutional patterns: the concentration of executive authority, the expansion of military or security actors into economic life, and the use of limited distributive concessions to pacify constituencies that might otherwise demand more fundamental change.For example, in Egypt, under President Abdel-Fattah al-Sisi, power has become increasingly concentrated in a military-presidential nexus. The expansion of the military’s economic role, which has been characterized by opacity and privileged access to state resources, has concentrated decisionmaking in a narrow circle of institutions linked to the executive, sidelining civilian channels.76 Similarly, in Algeria, following the Hirak movement, the country’s leadership under President Abdelmadjid Tebboune moved to reassert executive authority, strengthening presidential control over political institutions and constraining opposition.77 This reflected a broader strategy of recentralizing power in response to sustained pressure from society.78 This went hand in hand with reinforcing patronage instruments through expanded subsidies, wage increases, and unemployment benefits to pacify the population and manage social unrest. There are several examples in which repression has been used as a substitute for undertaking reform.There are several examples in which repression has been used as a substitute for undertaking reform. In Egypt, a crackdown that was initially focused on the Muslim Brotherhood extended to journalists, labor unions, human rights defenders, and other corners of civil society.79 This effectively cut off channels through which complaints might be addressed. The Sisi regime recast the social contract from one that provided to one that protected, with the security narrative replacing that of redistributing goods and services, which had provided legitimacy but was no longer sustainable.80 In Algeria, following the Hirak movement, the authorities arrested activists, journalists, and protesters in a sustained crackdown on dissent that stifled civil society.81 In Iraq, since the October 2019 protests, security forces have been implicated in the killing, abduction, and intimidation of activists.82 In Jordan, the authorities have increasingly restricted civic space in recent years through arrests and the introduction of broad cybercrime laws targeting online speech, further restricting political expression.83Ultimately, these responses are economically self-defeating and produce predicaments with no good exits. Such systems are too fragile to reform, too indebted to maintain the status quo, and too repressive to build the coalitions required for transformation. Across all three groups of countries, the political responses used to manage the short-term costs of reform are undermining the conditions that would make reform viable in the long run. What is therefore needed is a process of renegotiating social contracts, one in which citizens are active participants, not passive recipients. The process also has to be one in which reform is portrayed as a sacrifice shared by all, credible mechanisms are in place to compensate those bearing the costs of reform, and durable coalitions are built to advance reforms and are entitled to a genuine political voice. The legitimacy of reform can only come from foundations allowing for the participation of different social groups. However, the constraints visible in reform are not purely domestic. The political economy of transformation in the MENA region is also shaped by regional interdependencies and geopolitical dynamics beyond the control of any individual government in the region.The Effect of Regional and Global Dynamics on Diversification EffortsThe economic transformation of the Middle East and North Africa will be influenced not only by decisions made within countries, but also by the regional and global context in which those decisions are made. Several countries have launched ambitious reform programs, from the long-term development visions of the Gulf states aiming to diversify their economies beyond hydrocarbons to efforts by energy-importing countries to restore macroeconomic stability, address deep fiscal imbalances, and build more productive economies.84However, the success of these approaches will depend on factors that no country can control alone. First, a minimum level of regional security is a precondition for sustained economic development. Recent conflicts have shown that investment and trade cannot thrive in a context of war, instability, and displacement.85 Second, the region needs to prepare for an uncertain energy future. As the world moves away from fossil fuels, oil- and gas-producing countries should prepare for a time when hydrocarbon revenues are no longer the only basis for prosperity.86 The challenge is not just to respond to falling demand, but to anticipate change and accelerate diversification before external pressures make painful adjustments inevitable.87 And third, more regional integration is required for economic transformation. Greater market integration, deeper economic ties, and effective collective action mechanisms can help countries overcome the limitations of fragmented national approaches and make interdependence a source of resilience and growth.88 What happens in the region will therefore hinge not only on domestic reforms, but also on the emergence of a more stable and cooperative regional order.Rebuilding a Stable Regional OrderConflict across the Middle East reminds us that economic transformation requires a stable region.89 Yet, such stability is lacking. For decades, Gulf countries counted on U.S. security assurances for protection. But even with this security architecture, the region has become increasingly unstable and the gradual erosion of Pax Americana has created greater uncertainty, compelling states to rethink their security strategies.90 The challenge for the Gulf states is not to supplant the United States, although they recognize the limitations of Washington’s security guarantees, but to reduce their dependence on a single security guarantor.91 Therefore, the Gulf states are increasingly tempted to hedge, diversifying their partnerships and expanding diplomatic and security ties beyond the United States.92The Gulf states are increasingly tempted to hedge, diversifying their partnerships and expanding diplomatic and security ties beyond the United States.Security concerns manifest differently for middle-income hydrocarbon-exporting countries. To give three examples, Algeria seeks to curb the spread of instability from the Sahel, Libya, and a fragile Tunisia, while vying with Morocco for influence in North Africa.93 Iraq has sought to insulate itself from rivalries involving Iran, Israel, and the Gulf states. And Libya remains a battleground for competing regional powers, whose interventions have entrenched fragmentation and weakened state institutions.94 To stabilize the MENA, therefore, these rivalries have to be curbed. Much the same can be said of middle-income hydrocarbon importers, such as Egypt and Jordan. A less conflictual environment would improve their chances of engaging in economic reform and development. For conflict-affected countries—Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen—the priorities are reconstruction, economic recovery, and the prevention of further fragmentation. This will require some form of regional settlement, which will depend on the geopolitical environment.Two issues will inevitably impact regional security. The first is the hedging strategy adopted by the Gulf states amid the shortcomings of the U.S. security order. The second is the future relationship of states in the region with Iran and Israel, which will be shaped by different perceptions of threat. Hedging does not mean that the United States will no longer be a security provider. Despite growing attempts to diversify their partnerships, the Gulf states remain deeply tied to the United States. Washington remains a source of advanced military capabilities, defense infrastructure, and access to the broader financial and monetary system underpinning regional stability for the Gulf states. Most oil is still priced in U.S. dollars, Gulf surpluses are invested in American markets, and security cooperation is extensive.95Moreover, attempts to identify other security partners have revealed significant constraints. Russia has become a close collaborator of Iran and has little interest in being a regional mediator.96 China, in turn, has extended its economic influence and helped facilitate a Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023.97 However, Beijing has not made any formal security commitments in the region, even as it has been providing Iran with technology and military components in order to weaken the United States.98 Regional countries, such as Egypt, Pakistan, and Türkiye can provide political and military support, but they cannot substitute for American security guarantees. Such limitations highlight the constraints in Gulf hedging strategies.99Meanwhile, the economic gravity of the Gulf states is increasingly being pulled in Asia’s direction. The bulk of Gulf energy exports goes to Asian markets and the Gulf countries’ trade and investment ties with China are deepening.100 This has created an ever-widening gap between the geography of Gulf wealth and the geography of Gulf security. But this should not be confused with a strategic pivot toward Beijing. Gulf governments are using their links with China mainly as a lever in their relations with the United States, not as a substitute for them.However, this has not resulted in convergence toward a single Gulf strategy, but experimentation with multiple, even competing, approaches. The UAE has used the Abraham Accords to establish new economic and geopolitical partnerships with Israel. Saudi Arabia has engaged with Iran diplomatically, while remaining dependent on the United States and strengthening ties with China. Qatar and Oman have continued to perform mediating roles, developing relations with a range of actors. Taken collectively, these approaches indicate varying security arrangements driven by differing calculations, as opposed to a unified Gulf vision.Much of the future regional order will also be shaped by how states in the region interact with Iran and Israel. Both countries have become major sources of instability, albeit in different ways. Iran’s future trajectory is unclear.101 The country has experienced simultaneous crises of political legitimacy, economic hardship, environmental stress, and the disastrous impact of decades of sanctions. Its choice between reform and appeasement with its neighbors or authoritarian entrenchment led by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which will only add to its international isolation, will have major implications for regional stability. Equally important is its economic trajectory. Reengagement with the global economy could reshape regional dynamics, while continued isolation could further erode Iranian state capacity and foster destabilizing behavior. For regional players, the challenge is to balance deterrence with engagement. Deterrence without engagement invites cycles of escalation, but engagement without credible deterrence creates vulnerability.102 A sustainable regional order will require a balance between these two approaches.Deterrence without engagement invites cycles of escalation, but engagement without credible deterrence creates vulnerability.While conflicts with Iran remain a major source of regional instability, the ongoing and illegal Israeli occupation of Palestinian and Arab land has long constituted a fundamental obstacle for a regional settlement.103 This situation has worsened since October 2023 because of Israel’s growing regional assertiveness. Israeli military interventions, territorial incursions, and efforts to reshape the regional balance of power have heightened tensions and eroded the sovereignty of neighboring states. For Syria and Lebanon, stability rests in the reconstruction of effective state institutions, the restoration of territorial integrity, and the return of displaced populations. But Israel’s actions have often led to the opposite outcome by undermining state authority, violating sovereignty, and entrenching territorial fragmentation.104The effect of Israel’s hegemonic ambitions is likely to provoke counterbalancing dynamics among states in the region. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Egypt are increasingly aligned in wanting to prevent a regional order based on Israeli domination, facilitated by state collapse.105 Even normalization initiatives such as the Abraham Accords have not translated into broad-based legitimacy for Israel in the Middle East, with geopolitical pushback remaining strong, particularly in the absence of progress on the Palestinian issue.Therefore, it is unlikely that a regional order grounded in coercion, fragmentation, and recurring conflict can generate the stability necessary for economic transformation (see figure 14). Durable stability will require a more cooperative security framework that combines deterrence with diplomacy, reduces regional rivalries, and builds state institutions rather than undermining them.The Oil Transition TrapThe evolution of global hydrocarbon demand, shaped by market dynamics and geopolitical disruptions, will be decisive in determining the MENA region’s ability to sustain economic transformation. As the global energy landscape shifts, the central challenge for exporters will be to navigate a narrowing window of opportunity in maintaining oil and gas revenues while accelerating the transition toward diversified, productive, and resilient economic models.106 As the energy transition advances and global oil demand growth slows, plateaus, and eventually declines, oil exporters will face mounting pressure to adapt to an increasingly competitive and volatile market environment. One possible response is for low-cost producers, especially in the GCC, to accelerate production in order to monetize reserves more rapidly and capture market share. The UAE’s withdrawal from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and OPEC+ in April 2026 illustrates the growing strains within producer alliances and the temptation to compete more aggressively over a shrinking market.107 It also reflects the fact that the UAE, similar to Qatar’s earlier withdrawal from OPEC in 2021, does not feel bound by institutions that no longer align with its strategic and economic interests. Increasingly, GCC countries are prioritizing their own economic objectives, including using their reserves to secure revenues more quickly to support diversification strategies. Yet if several producers were to adopt such an approach simultaneously, it would mean moving toward a competitive global energy market that could accelerate a decline in hydrocarbon prices, with revenues converging in the longer term toward marginal production costs. This would result in a lose-lose outcome for producers, undermining fiscal stability and weakening diversification efforts.108The strategic calculations of energy producers regarding the future of energy markets underscore a central tension: Even as competition intensifies, coordination among producers remains essential. Managing output collectively will be critical if these countries are to stabilize revenues and preserve the financial resources needed to fund economic transformations. At the same time, geopolitical instability in the Middle East, particularly disruptions to energy infrastructure and maritime routes, will likely accelerate the global energy transition, putting pressure on producers to speed up the diversification of their economies.109 Recurrent supply shocks and heightened risk perceptions are pushing major Asian importers, the main drivers of future hydrocarbon demand with around 40 percent of their oil imports transiting through the Strait of Hormuz, to diversify energy sources, accelerate investments in renewable energy, and reduce dependency on Middle Eastern hydrocarbons (see figure 14).110 This, in turn, could hasten a structural decline in oil and gas demand, exacerbating competition among exporters.The relationship between the global energy transition and economic diversification is therefore bidirectional. Countries that succeed in diversifying their economies will be better positioned to adopt flexible, forward-looking hydrocarbon strategies and manage the impact of this transition smoothly. By contrast, those that remain dependent on hydrocarbon revenues may be driven toward short-term revenue maximization that would reinforce market volatility and potentially accelerate the global shift away from fossil fuels. The implications are profound. If oil and gas prices weaken steadily due to declining demand or oversupply, per capita income in hydrocarbon producing economies could fall significantly in the coming decades. This would intensify political and social strains, making economic diversification away from hydrocarbons both urgent and more difficult. For hydrocarbon exporting countries, it’s better to anticipate change than be forced to react to it.Regional Integration and the MENA Region’s Place in the Global EconomyFor several reasons, regional integration is essential for advancing structural economic reforms and improving the Middle East and North Africa’s insertion into the global economy. First, the region remains among the world’s least economically integrated despite decades of economic liberalization.111 A larger, more integrated regional market would help the countries diversify their economies by combining the Gulf’s financial resources with the labor force, industrial capacities, and entrepreneurial potential of middle-income economies. Greater integration can generate new complementarities in investment, production, and supply chains, and countries would therefore be able to take advantage of each other’s comparative advantages rather than work in fragmented national markets. It would also boost the region’s collective economic power, giving it greater leverage to negotiate trade and investment agreements with major partners such as the United States, the European Union, and Asian economies.Second, building on regional integration could help channel more of the region’s financial wealth back into regional economies. For decades, much Gulf capital has been invested in Europe and North America. But the rise in geopolitical tensions and the increasing uncertainty about the treatment of sovereign assets abroad have highlighted the benefits of investing closer to home. If more of the Gulf’s assets were invested in the MENA region, it could have a transformational effect on recipient countries, giving them an incentive to pursue reform agendas. There has been a shift in Gulf financial engagement in the region over the past several years, a trend that will undoubtedly persist as the GCC’s diversification plans move forward. The era of relatively unconditional assistance to highly indebted countries such as Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, and Lebanon in the form of budget deposits, aid, and other forms of assistance is over and has been replaced by a more selective approach.112 Gulf governments have been moving away from direct budgetary support to asset acquisition and investments in key sectors such as infrastructure, energy, agriculture, and renewable energy.113 This shift changes the dynamics between investors and recipient countries. Gulf investments are being directed at bankable projects and participation in strategic sectors. This is compelling recipient countries to improve the business environment, reform state-owned enterprises, and improve economic governance.114 The challenge down the road will be to turn Gulf investment into a driver of regional integration. Greater transparency, clearer norms, and regional institutional mechanisms could help align investments with development strategies, thereby harnessing financial flows in order to expand regional economic integration.Third, many of the region’s most urgent challenges are shared problems that transcend national boundaries. Water scarcity, climate change, environmental degradation, food security, and the return of refugees and displaced populations are problems of common concern and cannot be addressed effectively through isolated national policies. They need to be coordinated, planned jointly, and addressed collectively. In the near term, among the region’s most urgent priorities will be rebuilding countries shattered by conflict and enabling displaced people to return home. The way in which Gaza, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen are rebuilt will affect the lives of millions of people, but also the economic and political future of the region.Israel’s participation in such a regional economic framework will depend on progress toward a resolution of the Palestinian question, which is crucial to broader regional acceptance and cooperation. Addressing these common regional challenges requires building adequate institutions. A MENA bank for reconstruction and development can serve as a platform to anchor regional integration in concrete projects.115 An institution of this kind could steer investment toward long-term priorities such as infrastructure, climate resilience, and post-conflict reconstruction. Without institutions to support such longer-term objectives, it will be difficult to lay the groundwork for lasting economic transformation and regional stability.A MENA bank for reconstruction and development can serve as a platform to anchor regional integration in concrete projects.Lastly, securing trade routes and improving regional connectivity are inherently collective enterprises. Recent tensions with Iran have highlighted the vulnerability of key maritime chokepoints, particularly the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab, and have accelerated efforts to develop alternative transport and energy corridors (see figure 15). Governments in the Gulf are seeking to bolster economic resilience by investing in projects that connect their countries to the Levant and Türkiye through railways, pipelines, ports, and logistics networks.116 In this context, deeper regional integration is an important driver of growth and increasingly an important element of economic security.
However, regional integration should not be confined to the Arab world. It must also involve Türkiye and Iran in order to have a transformative and pacifying impact. Economic integration can help ease regional tensions by creating common interests and mutual dependencies based on prosperity.117 A stable regional order will require an inclusive framework that incorporates all major regional players into cooperative arrangements. Türkiye and Iran have large domestic markets and industrial capacities and enjoy strategic geographical locations, while the Gulf countries have major financial resources and investment capacity. These assets together could unlock new trade, investment, and industrial development opportunities across the region. But realizing this potential will demand political deescalation and sustained efforts to build trust between Iran and its Arab neighbors. Without such progress, the economic gains from regional integration are unlikely to be fully realized.The MENA region has undergone decades of economic liberalization, but these efforts have not translated into deeper regional integration or a stronger position in the global economy. Despite international trade agreements, such as the Euro-Mediterranean agreements linking several MENA countries to the European Union, the region plays a minor role in the global economy, limiting its ability to develop regional value chains, attract investment, and shape the terms of its engagement with global economic actors.118 Regional integration is a key and urgent step to rethinking the region’s global insertion in a world distinguished by growing geopolitical competition and the emergence of competing economic blocs. In this new environment characterized by protectionism, a return of tariffs, and global competition, building a regional bloc is essential to increasing the bargaining power of the states involved.Conclusion: Vicious or Virtuous Cycle?The MENA region is at a critical stage in its trajectory. The interaction between domestic reform pathways, regional developments, and wider geopolitical shifts will shape the region in the coming years. This will determine not only the success or failure of economic transformations within individual states, but also the prospective regional order. The central question is whether the region will move toward greater stability, economic reform, and integration, or toward further fragmentation, insecurity, and cycles of economic decline.Structural tensions are building up across the region as a result of stagnant growth models, demographic pressures, climate vulnerabilities, fiscal constraints, and geopolitical tensions that can no longer be addressed through short-term crisis responses. In many countries, existing political and economic arrangements will deepen vicious cycles that shaped outcomes for much of the past decade. Economic stagnation has created social frustration, which undermines legitimacy, leading to political instability, which discourages investment and reform. This has led to rising unemployment, disenchantment, and conflict, and consequently to regional instability caused by a fear of uprisings. However, an alternative trajectory remains possible.If managed carefully, reformist momentum can create a virtuous cycle that might transform not only domestic political economies but also the regional order. Economic transformation must not be narrowly conceived as a technical process of economic diversification. Fundamentally, it is a political project that requires building new sources of legitimacy, new social contracts, and new regional arrangements facilitating cooperation. The challenge is common to all countries and requires moving from fragile, often rent-dependent economic systems to more productive and resilient economies. Yet each country needs to determine its path on its own, depending on its resources, institutional capacities, and political constraints.Economic transformation, whether toward more diversified economies in the case of energy-exporting countries or more productive ones for energy-importing countries, imposes difficult political choices. Governments will have to build reform coalitions, manage resistance from vested interests, and redefine the role of the state. To secure long-term stability, they need to abandon short-termism and act strategically. Stability cannot be built indefinitely on the narrow logic of regime-survival or on fiscally unsustainable distributive mechanisms. Legitimacy must be rooted more in productivity, inclusion, open access to economic opportunities, and credible visions of development that can rally societies around a common national project. Four interlinked conditions will determine whether countries in the region choose to enter a virtuous cycle or perpetuate a vicious cycle: an ability to make reforms politically and socially acceptable; creating conditions for a new regional security architecture; advancing regional integration; and acting collectively as a constructive global actor.The first condition is ensuring the political and social acceptability of reforms. No matter how technically sound economic reforms are, they cannot succeed if they are perceived as being externally imposed and serving the narrow interests of elites. Reform agendas, therefore, need to be embedded in larger national narratives of economic sovereignty, national security, and collective prosperity. Societies must see reforms as part of a long-term project of transformation, rather than as sacrifices imposed to preserve existing political systems. Therefore, strengthening state capacity to design, coordinate, and implement lasting development policies is essential, as states are the primary actors responsible for driving and sustaining reforms. Transformations are possible only with planning capacity, credible institutions, and the ability to design coherent sequencing of policies and compensation mechanisms. Knowledge ecosystems can play an important role in this area: think tanks, research institutes, universities, and policy networks can contribute to the development of strategic visions, policy expertise, and elite consensus on enduring priorities.It is also important to build broad reform coalitions. Economic elites, the middle class, labor groups, and the younger generations need to see that they have a stake in the transformation process. Reforms perceived as being socially unjust or politically exclusionary are likely to generate contestation, deepen distrust, and encourage defensive responses from societies and regimes. Regimes will be more concerned with survival than with structural transformation. This ultimately degrades economic situations and makes political systems fragile over time.The second condition that helps determine whether regional countries can enter a virtuous cycle is the creation of a new regional security architecture. However, there are major hurdles in doing so. Perceptions of threat vary widely among the Gulf states, including in relation to Iran and Israel. Some countries view Israel as a possible security partner in dealing with Iran, while others fear that Israeli regional dominance could itself be destabilizing. At the same time, competing security approaches have been increasingly defining the region. The UAE is deepening its ties with India and Israel, while Saudi Arabia seems to be increasingly interested in working with Türkiye and Pakistan. Meanwhile, Iranian influence in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen continues to fuel regional tensions. Egypt, in turn, is walking a tightrope between Emirati and Saudi strategic orientations, juggling its financial dependence on both countries and its security priorities. These competing security alignments might escalate and produce a fractured, unstable regional security landscape. Intra-Gulf rivalries, unresolved tensions with Iran, and competing external alliances could prove especially destabilizing, diverting resources away from development and generating cycles of insecurity. However, if a stable regional security order can arise, it could significantly encourage cooperation, investment, and long-term economic transformation.The third condition is enhanced regional integration. Economic integration is not only desirable but also structurally necessary if diversification and economic transformation strategies are to succeed. Trade integration must be complemented by broader reforms to improve the business environment, reduce bureaucratic red tape, strengthen competition, modernize customs systems, and improve infrastructural connectivity. Lowering transportation and logistical costs and improving the efficiency of border procedures will increase trade integration and participation in global value chains.119In contrast, the absence of regional integration will anchor the region in its current vicious cycle. Continued political rivalries, weak trade connectivity, and limited economic cooperation will constrain efforts to build diversified and productive economies by denying countries access to larger markets. They will also discourage investment in a region suffering from chronically low investment levels. Fragmented markets and persistent insecurity, in turn, will exacerbate domestic political fragilities, reinforcing economic stagnation and geopolitical competition.The fourth condition that will determine whether countries can enter into a virtuous cycle involves the region’s relations with the global order. The MENA region needs to become, collectively, a constructive global actor rather than a geopolitical battleground. This means creating regional institutions and mechanisms that can address transnational challenges such as migration, refugees, climate change, state fragility, and reconstruction of conflict areas. The absence of such mechanisms has contributed to a perception of the region as being chronically unstable and unable to manage collective problems.The MENA region needs to become, collectively, a constructive global actor rather than a geopolitical battleground.The comparison with Southeast Asia is instructive. Despite their political differences and a history of conflict, leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations understood that cooperation would increase stability, shared prosperity, and collective bargaining power. This is not the case in the MENA region, which is perceived globally as made up of rich yet fragile states that fail to cooperate and have been unable to articulate a shared vision for the future. The region’s exposure to external influence, coupled with the enduring legacy of colonialism, which is still present given Israel’s settler colonialism and occupation of Arab lands, has undermined prospects for meaningful regional cooperation and playing a beneficial global role. Changing this perception is not simply a matter of regional branding, even though many Gulf countries have invested heavily in entertainment, sports, tourism, and other forms of soft power to burnish their international profile. Rather, there should be an effort to make the region a “good” global actor—in other words able to manage internal conflict, build mechanisms for cooperation despite divergent interests, and work collectively to address common challenges. This means taking responsibility for the region’s future rather than waiting for external powers to intervene, and preventing internal crises from breeding instability that affects the rest of the world.All this will be essential for the MENA region’s ability to negotiate internationally and position itself within future global transformations, such as the energy transition, the AI revolution, the end of American unilateralism, and the emergence of a multipolar world.About the Commission MembersMuna Abbas, Chief Executive Officer, Asfari FoundationMohammed Abdel Raouf, Director of the Environmental Security and Sustainability Research Program, Gulf Research Center.Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, Expert at the Emirates Center for Strategic Studies and Research (ECSSR) and Visiting Professor at Harvard University.Youssef Al-Ebraheem, former Minister of Finance of KuwaitZiad BahaEddin, Egyptian economist and lawyer, former Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Development and Minister of International Cooperation.Ferid Belhaj, former World Bank Vice President for the Middle East and North Africa.Noha El Mikawy, former Dean of the School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, American University in Cairo.Rima Khalaf, former UN Under-Secretary-General and Executive Secretary of ESCWAAli Kooli, banker, former Minister of Economy, Finance and Investment Support of TunisiaSlim Othmani, Algerian businessman and former Chairman of NCA-Rouiba and President of the Algerian think tank CARETarik Youssef, Senior Fellow, Middle East Council on Global AffairsMaha Yahya, Director, Malcolm H. articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

28 Oct 2026

Higher US gas prices boost odds of a Democratic sweep

Since our last midterms update in early September, Democrats have become favored to win back the House of Representatives and the Senate, rather than just the House.

The odds of a Democratic sweep in the midterms on November 3 continue to rise. Our baseline forecast has long called for a divided government after the midterms, but Democrats flipping both chambers of Congress would raise the probability of downside risks from trade and geopolitical policy and increase the chance of a deficit-financed expansion of federal spending.

Democratic candidates lead in all eight competitive Senate races. In recent days, Republicans have slightly reversed some of the Democrats’ earlier polling momentum, which slowed this month. With Kansas emerging as an unexpected tossup, Democrats have more paths to a Senate majority, even if the party falls short in Michigan or Minnesota.

Democrats are still cruising to a House takeover. High inflation, weak consumer confidence, and a lack of voter enthusiasm are creating a challenging backdrop for House Republicans. Historically, the party that suffers an enthusiasm deficit loses the House popular vote.

articles.title: Quantitative tightening: the next chapter − speech by Dave Ramsden
articles.text:
Quantitative tightening: the next chapter − speech by Dave Ramsden

Given at the Bank of England, co-hosted by the Money, Macro and Finance Society

Published on
28 September 2026

Dave Ramsden describes the MPC’s September 2026 decision on Quantitative Tightening, alongside the set of announcements by the Bank and HM Treasury which, together, mark the beginning of the next chapter in the approach to unwinding the assets built up through Quantitative Easing.

Speech
Thank you to the Money, Macro and Finance Society (MMF) for co-hosting this event today. It’s a little over three years ago that I delivered my last speech on Quantitative Tightening (QT)footnote [1], where again the MMF kindly co-hosted the event.
In my 2023 speech, I set out what the MPC and Bank had so far learnt after nearly a year of delivering the MPC’s first annual QT decision. After another three years of QT progress and learnings, we are now ready to move to the next chapter.
The MPC’s September decision, alongside the set of announcements from the Bank Executive and HM Treasury (HMT), marked a significant step in the approach to unwinding the assets built up through Quantitative Easing (QE) – a process dubbed QT. Alongside the MPC's decision that it would shift to a multi-year path for QT, the Bank Executive and HMT also released a set of announcements relating to how QT would be implemented in future and the Bank Executive set out its long-term strategy for backing current and future banknote issuance.
I will spend some time today walking through the details of those announcements, both from my perspective as an MPC member, and as the Deputy Governor at the Bank with executive responsibility for the Bank’s balance sheet. I will not focus on the continuing transition to a demand driven, repo led balance sheet though – those aspects of the Bank’s balance sheet have been well explained and detailed by my Bank Executive colleagues in recent speeches and publications.footnote [2]
Much of what I’m covering today is the collective view of the MPC and set out in the September decision minutes, though I will share some personal views too on the monetary policy approach, and highlight when I do. I do also want to note that the MPC considered important institutional questions regarding the potential interaction between monetary and fiscal actions and the independence of MPC decision making over monetary policy, which led to a robust discussion.
As I am marking this as a closing of one chapter of QT, let me also take a step back and provide a longer term, historical perspective. Over my career I’ve been involved, in one way or another, with every QE and QT decision in the UK taken since 2009.
I’ll start with a brief recounting of why we’re undertaking QT, following the rounds of QE that saw a total of £895bn of asset purchases accumulated onto the Bank’s balance sheet. I’ll then look back on the last four years of QT and how the MPC and Bank Executive continued to build on the learnings of the first year of QT that I described in 2023, before then explaining the September announcements, and how QT will operate going forward. I will conclude with some comments on our active monetary policy tool – Bank Rate – and my views on the outlook.
Why is the MPC undertaking QT?
Before getting into the specifics, it’s always helpful to remember why the MPC is undertaking QT in the first place. There are a few good reasons – to create headroom for future QE purchases, and to reduce interest rate risk on the Bank’s balance sheet. But perhaps the most important is that QE was always intended to be a temporary monetary policy stimulus.
Back in 2009 I was Chief Economic Adviser to the Treasury. Amongst other things, that meant I was the HMT representative at MPC meetings and attended the March 2009 meeting when the MPC decided to undertake its first round of QE. The minutesfootnote [3] of that meeting are clear on why the Committee concluded that asset purchases were necessary to meet its 2% inflation target sustainably in the medium term.
There had been several letter exchanges between the Chancellor and the Governor in the early months of 2009, establishing the Asset Purchase Facility (APF) and authorising monetary policy asset purchases through the APF.footnote [4] These lettersfootnote [5] established the framework for QE, including: a clear division of responsibilities between the MPC and HMT; that the Bank would ensure regular reporting of its asset purchase programme to ensure transparency; and that the implementation of the MPC’s decisions on asset purchases would be delegated to the Bank Executive.
A key tenet of QE, communicated consistently through the rounds of QEfootnote [6], is that the MPC would decide on the most appropriate way to unwind its asset purchases. QE is a monetary policy tool to provide temporary stimulus to the economy and deal with specific shocks, to achieve the MPC’s inflation target. It is not intended to be a permanent change to the monetary framework or the Bank’s balance sheet.
By unwinding earlier QE purchases, the MPC reinforces the credibility of QE as a monetary policy tool for the future. As I reiterated recently to the Treasury Committeefootnote [7], QE can support the economy through the most severe stresses, when Bank Rate has reached the lower bound. If the MPC cannot commit to and evidence a credible exit strategy, the viability of the tool in future is put at risk.
In terms of how the MPC has undertaken that unwind, I think it’s helpful to distinguish between the principles that underpin the MPC’s approach to QT, and then the strategy the MPC and the Bank Executive take to execute that unwind. The principles do not change, but the strategy can evolve as the MPC and Bank Executive learn from doing QT over time and respond to market developments.
As a reminder, the MPC’s three key principles for undertaking QT arefootnote [8]:

First, Bank Rate is the MPC’s active policy tool when adjusting the stance of monetary policy.
Second, sales should be conducted so as not to disrupt the functioning of financial markets, and only in appropriate conditions.
Third, to help achieve that, sales should be conducted in a gradual and predictable manner over a period of time.

In terms of the QT strategy, I’d identify three phases, or chapters. Initially a short period from February 2022, where the MPC decided to stop reinvesting maturing gilts and corporate bonds, allowing the stock of assets held in the APF to begin declining naturally. In doing so, the Bank became one of the first major central banks to begin unwinding the extraordinary monetary stimulus put in place following the global financial crisis, the euro area crisis, the Brexit decision, and the pandemic.
By September 2022, the Committee was ready to shift to an annual approach to unwinding asset purchases, through a combination of maturities and sales, supported by the Bank Executive’s work on the operational details of asset sales.footnote [9]
We are now entering a new chapter, the multi-year strategy. We have been working on this for some time and in my view it is a coherent next step. Given my responsibilities at the Bank I’m very focused on the situation in bond markets. But within that context the QT package appears to have been generally well received by markets and market commentators. The different elements seem to have been individually and collectively understood.
Indeed, one of the more common questions I’ve received since the announcement is why didn’t we move to this new approach sooner? In a way, that’s great to hear – clearly the multi-year strategy has been received well. But we shouldn’t forget that the MPC and Bank Executive have learnt a lot over the first few years of QT. And the annual strategy was itself an effective strategy for delivering QT.
To evidence that, and help to answer the question of why we’re moving to the next chapter of QT now, let me provide an overview of the last four years of QT.
Looking back – the annual strategy
Since February 2022, the size of the APF has fallen by over £400bn from a peak of £895bn to around £488bn today, through the MPC’s unwinding of both holdings of gilts and corporate bonds.

Where the Bank’s approach has sometimes been described as different to its peers has been the use of sales to the secondary market, alongside maturities, to deliver the annual reduction in the stock of assets or QT pace. So far, approximately £259 billion of gilts have rolled off through maturities, alongside £129 billion of gilt sales and approximately £20bn of corporate bond sales and maturities. The Riksbank has also used sales to the market in its QT implementation, but other peer central banks, like the Federal Reserve and the ECB, have relied on maturities.
There were good reasons for undertaking sales. It is a prominent feature of UK government debt that the average maturity is much longer than international peers. In implementing QE, the Bank sought to purchase gilts in a way that reflected the structure of the gilt market, consistent with a principle of market neutrality. This meant that QE purchases were conducted across the maturity spectrum of the gilt market, rather than targeting a particular segment of the curve. Given the long maturity profile of UK government debt, this meant that the Bank’s gilt purchases included much longer maturities than many peer central banks.
Relying solely on maturities would have meant the unwind taking over 50 years, as shown in Chart 4. This would have left a significant amount of interest rate risk on the Bank’s balance sheet, limiting the headroom available for future policy interventions and failing in the objective that QE should represent a temporary intervention. Sales to the market have allowed the MPC to reduce the portfolio in a timely manner, retaining future flexibility and credibility of our policy tools.

Monetary policy assessment of QT to date
Starting first with the monetary policy impact of QT, as I set out in my 2023 speech, our strategy for QT has turned off some channels that were important during QE.footnote [10] That should have reduced QT’s potential impact on gilt yields, certainly when compared with the impacts of QE. The main way through which QT does impact financial conditions is through the so-called portfolio rebalancing channel, which can in theory lead to modest increases in gilt yields through term premia.footnote [11]
Term premia can be influenced by a wide range of factors, and isolating the specific effect of QT is not simple, though our estimates suggest the impact of QT has been relatively modest. Other factors influencing term premia over the last four years have been a structural reduction in domestic demand for long-term government debt, global economic policy uncertainty and high issuance of government bonds across countries.
Between the start of QT in February 2022 and late September 2026, 10-year gilt yields rose by around 450 basis points. Term structure model estimates indicate that around 200 basis points of this increase was driven by term premia, with the remaining rise accounted for by higher expected rates, as shown in Chart 5.

To estimate the specific effect of QT, one approach is to look at movements in term premia in short periods directly around announcementsfootnote [12] of QT policies or around the time of QT auctions; this is the approach taken by Bank staff. This helps to identify the impact of QT because gilt market pricing tends to adjust quickly in response to market news, and the short window helps to limit the influence of other factors on the estimates. But, given that there have been a limited number of QT announcements and auctions and that QT has been operated in a predictable manner, there remains considerable uncertainty around these estimates.
There is also uncertainty around the persistence of QT’s effects on term premia. One drawback of event study estimates of QT (or QE) is that they cannot identify effects that fall outside of the short window used for the estimation. Bank staff’s estimates cumulate effects across QT announcements and auctions going back to 2022 and therefore assume that the effects of QT are highly persistent. While there is, so far, limited evidence on the persistence of QT’s effects, Bank staff analysis of QE has assumed, based on available studies, that impacts may start to fade after one to four years.footnote [13] If the same is true for QT, then these central estimates could overstate its impact on the current level of yields.
In the July Monetary Policy Report, analysis by Bank stafffootnote [14] pointed to an estimated total increase in 10-year gilt yields from cumulative QT to date of 20–30 basis points.footnote [15] Given the overall increase in the term premium for 10-year gilt yields since February 2022, this suggested QT has driven between a tenth and a sixth of that total.
The reaction to the MPC’s September 2026 QT announcement of a multi-year strategy saw yields fall across the curve. The effect was larger at the longer end, for example 30-year gilt yields fell by around 10bps which persisted over subsequent days. The 10-year gilt yields fell by a similar amount with term premia falling around 7 basis points. At the shorter end the effect was smaller and has subsequently reversed. This suggests the market was expecting more QT, either in total or at a higher pace. And some positioning for increases in long-dated yields were subsequently unwound, which may have exacerbated the moves after the announcement. It is also possible that the removal of uncertainty about the path of future QT reduced risk premia.
Other estimates of the impact of QT over the last four years have been published, some of which suggest QT has had a larger impact than the Bank staff’s estimates. But importantly, to the extent any QT impacts – while relatively modest – are coming through, the MPC will have observed the associated effects on asset prices, conditioned its forecasts accordingly and has full flexibility to adjust its active tool – Bank Rate – to the extent that any offsetting action is deemed necessary.
The Bank Executive’s implementation of QT to date
Turning to the implementation of QT, throughout the period from 2022 to 2026, the Bank Executive designed its sales to market approach, such that it delivered the MPC’s QT decision, in line with the MPC’s principles – particularly that sales are conducted so as not to disrupt the functioning of financial markets, and that they should be conducted in a gradual and predictable manner. Subject to that, the Bank Executive should maximise value for money by minimising cost and risk over the lifetime of the APF.
To achieve that, the Bank Executive worked closely with the DMO to design an auction schedule that fitted around gilt issuance and other market events. Auction schedules have been published in advance and sales have been conducted through a consistent auction framework, providing the market a clear view of the QT programme. Together, these features ensured that QT remained predictable, allowing the programme to remain in the background while supporting orderly market functioning.
Gilt sales have been conducted via multi-stock auctions to the secondary market. The auction design itself plays an important role in achieving the value for money objective. By offering multiple bonds in each operation and using a discriminatory price format, the Bank aims to maximise participation and competition, helping deliver value for money across the programme. Offers were ranked and allocated according to the attractiveness of the yield for the Bank.
Over this period, the Bank has sold £129 billion (in purchase proceeds) of the MPC’s APF holdings across 120 auctions, selling gilts across three maturity buckets; short, medium and long.footnote [16] The programme's success can be seen in auction outcomes. We monitor both the level of demand for auctions and the prices achieved relative to prevailing market rates. One measure of demand is the cover ratio – the ratio of offers to accepted bids (Chart 6), while a key pricing metric is the weighted average (WA) spread of accepted prices relative to market mid-yields (Chart 7). To date, QT auctions have received an average cover of 2.3x, meaning there have been 2.3 times more bids than those accepted. And, the average WA spread has been -0.5, meaning that accepted pricing has on average been 0.5bp lower than market mid prices (in favour of the Bank).
These measures suggest that Bank auctions have on the whole consistently attracted strong demand and delivered favourable pricing outcomes. This sentiment is reiterated by market contacts in our MI gathering, who generally describe QT operations as running smoothly and being readily absorbed by the market. These metrics, alongside our market monitoring, indicate that we have achieved our desired aim of reducing the size of the APF in a timely manner while achieving value for money and supporting orderly market functioning.
A key feature of the Bank’s implementation to QT so far has been responsiveness to the needs of the market. Ahead of each annual MPC decision, staff have assessed the capacity of the gilt market to absorb additional supply, and the potential impact to financial markets of different sales paces. That information helps to inform the MPC on potential pace options for subsequent years of QT, in line with the MPC’s principle that sales should be conducted so as to not disrupt the functioning of financial markets. As such, the QT programme has adapted when necessary, including the decision to skew away from longs in September 2025, showing that the Bank is sensitive to changing market conditions.

The next chapter of QT – the MPC’s multi-year strategy
The annual strategy since September 2022 has delivered on the MPC’s principles and provided a solid foundation for the MPC’s decision to shift to a new, multi-year strategy for delivering QT.
There was a lot of information in the set of announcements released just over a week ago and, as I’ve said, these seem to have been well understood and well received. The Governor’s letter to the Chancellorfootnote [17] set out the key elements of the package, taking the current APF stock of £488bn as the baseline, they are:

The MPC’s decision to set a multi-year path for unwind, fully unwinding the stock of gilts held for monetary policy purposes by the end of 2034.
As a result, the Bank would not sell the £222bn of gilts with redemption dates earlier than 2035.
The Bank Executive’s announcement that £120bn of the longest-dated gilts will remain in the APF to back current and future banknote issuance.
The Bank Executive is considering adjusting the way it conducts gilt sales of the remaining £146bn, and intends to implement the MPC’s multi-year plan via sales to the Government rather than to the market.

For me the package was a coherent next step which continue to respect the division of responsibilities between the authorities. Importantly the MPC’s three key principles for delivering QT continue to frame the approach.
The first element of the package is the MPC’s decision to set out a multi-year path for unwinding the APF. Before deciding on the pace of that unwind, there was one critical decision for the MPC to take – the stock of gilts that should be held for monetary policy purposes. This is a key element of the UK’s monetary policy framework, going back to those letters from 2009 that I highlighted.
I have previously set out the case for the MPC to fully unwind its stock of assets built up through QEfootnote [18], but the MPC had yet to take a formal decision on the issue. Consistent with the earlier sets of documentation, the MPC agreed that the stock of assets built up through QE should be fully unwound. Supporting this, the MPC judged that there were no monetary policy reasons to hold a structural gilt portfolio in the APF, particularly given the ongoing and successful transition to a demand-driven, repo led framework for supplying reserves, where money market rates have continued to trade in a narrow spread to Bank Rate.
Having confirmed its desired end point, the MPC discussed the merits of setting out a more forward-looking plan for the remainder of QT. Relative to the annual strategy, shifting to multi-year ensures the pace of QT is as predictable as possible. By removing uncertainty over the pace and end point of QT, the MPC can ensure QT is put even more firmly into the background. As the full intended path for QT can be embedded into financial conditions, this better enables the MPC to take it into account when setting Bank Rate, its primary tool for adjusting the stance of monetary policy.
The MPC’s confirmation that it planned to fully unwind the APF’s holdings of gilts for monetary policy purposes meant the Bank Executive had clarity to confirm the long-term strategy for backing banknotes. The Bank Insights article published alongside the QT announcementfootnote [19] details how banknotes have been indirectly backed by gilts in the APF since 2009. The Bank Executive determined that a portfolio of long-dated gilts would be well suited to backing banknotes as its maturity profile provides a good match for the long-term nature of banknote liability. To ensure notes continued to have appropriate backing, the Bank Executive determined that £120bn of gilts should remain in the APF, no longer held for monetary policy and solely to back notes. Using existing APF gilts to back banknotes avoids the transaction costs associated with purchasing gilts from the market directly onto Issue Department.footnote [20]
That means, of the £488bn of gilts in the APF at the time of the MPC’s September decision, the MPC could determine what the multi-year path should be in the knowledge that £120bn of those gilts would remain in the APF to back notes. In other words, the MPC’s decision on pace would be in relation to the remaining £368bn of gilts.
The MPC discussed the appropriate pace for the multi-year path as part of its September decision. Consistent with previous annual QT decisions, Bank staff assessed the appropriate pace options over the multi-year path, in line with the MPC’s principles that sales should be conducted so as not to disrupt the functioning of financial markets. Given the change in strategy to a multi-year unwind with a fixed pace of sales throughout, the MPC considered the relative benefits of unwinding more quickly or slowly. The MPC recognised the chance that future economic and market shocks could occur over the period of QT unwind and the strategy, including the pace of unwind, has been designed with that context in mind.
After discussion, the MPC unanimously agreed that the remaining £368bn of gilts should be unwound at an annual average pace of £46bn by the end of 2034, through annual sales of £20bn alongside maturing gilts. That means of the £488bn of gilts remaining in the APF, £222bn would be held to maturity (shown by the blue bars in Chart 7), £146bn would be sold (orange bars), and £120bn would remain in the APF to back banknotes (purple bars). The final maturity will be the £28.2bn September 2034 gilt, and the MPC expects that will mark the completion of the QT unwind.
