One point of particular discussion amongst MPC members was the extent to which the committee should retain flexibility within that multi-year plan. There’s an obvious trade-off here, the more flexibility the MPC has, the greater its ability to respond to evolving market conditions over time, and potentially increase or decrease its pace of unwind in subsequent years. But on the other hand, a fixed intended pace of unwind would provide more certainty and clarity over the future QT path. On balance, most MPC members felt that the benefits from the predictability of a fixed pace outweighed the loss of flexibility.
The MPC judged that unwinding the APF at a constant and fixed pace would further put QT in the background. Given the variation in the maturity profile in coming years, to make this as simple and transparent as possible, it specified its multi-year strategy as a constant annual sales pace of £20bn each year over the remainder of the path of unwind.
To ensure the MPC’s QT strategy remained consistent with its principles – both that Bank Rate remains the active tool, and that sales do not disrupt the functioning of financial markets – the MPC reiterated that there would only be two specific circumstances where the pace of unwind in the multi-year plan would be reconsidered.footnote [21] These two ‘knockouts’ are designed such that high bars would have to be met in order for them to be triggered, First, if the MPC judged that potential movements in Bank Rate alone were insufficient to meet the inflation target. And second, if markets were judged by the Bank to be very distressed. The Financial Policy Committee would have a role in this second circumstance through its assessment of financial stability.
From my perspective, the obvious example of the first knockout is if repeated shocks mean that Bank Rate is approaching the effective lower bound and there is a risk of running out of headroom to achieve the MPC’s price stability objective. Of course, it would be for the MPC at the time to judge whether the knockout had been triggered, dependent on the circumstances at the time.
The final element of the package set out in the Governor’s letter to the Chancellor is the Bank Executive’s intended approach to implementing the MPC’s multi-year plan. The intended approach – to sell gilts to the Government rather than to the market – has been developed through engagement with HMT and the DMO over the last year, and is subject to final agreement with HMT.
The Bank Executive’s intention to change its approach to gilt sales – subject to HMT agreement – is driven by its responsibility to continue to maximise value for money by minimising cost and risk over the lifetime of the APF, subject to achieving the MPC’s chosen unwind target and in line with the MPC’s key principles. As I’ve described, the Bank Executive’s approach to sales to date has been successful and delivered on its value for money responsibility through careful design of its auctions to market. But given the MPC’s multi-year plan for QT, the Bank Executive is mindful that a portion of the gilts remaining in the APF will likely become less aligned with market demand as unwind continues.
As an alternative, the Bank has engaged with HMT and the DMO to consider a model whereby the MPC’s decision could instead be implemented through APF sales to the Government. At a high level, the model would see HMT instruct the DMO to purchase, over time, the £146bn of 2035-2049 APF gilts that the Bank is selling, which the DMO would on-sell to the National Loans Fund for cancellation and subsequent refinancing, with the DMO better able to align its issuance with market demand. It would also see a return to a single public sector supplier of gilts to the market.
The operational details of this model need to be worked through between the Bank, HMT and DMO. To ensure monetary independence, and to prevent any blurring of fiscal and monetary responsibilities, sales would be set in advance by the Bank Executive and conducted at market prices. This means that sales parameters, including the pace and frequency, would be pre-defined and non-discretionary. The lifetime costs of the APF unwind are neutral whether starting with the longest or shortest maturities. Of course, starting sales from the longest maturity and working backwards reduces interest rate risk on the Bank’s balance sheet the most quickly. Under this sales model, the Bank Executive would therefore expect to sell the £146bn of APF gilts designated for sales to the DMO in reverse order, starting with the longest maturity gilts. The indemnity from HMT to the Bank will remain in place.
The Bank will announce its approach to implementing the MPC’s QT strategy by April 2027. Regardless of the method of sales, the Bank Executive will ensure that the MPC’s agreed sales pace is implemented and full unwind is completed by the end of 2034. The £20bn sales pace refers to the 12-month period following the start of sales; for the avoidance of doubt, if sales were to begin in April 2027, the £20bn of sales would be completed by April 2028. As long as sales begin by end-Q2 2027, the exact start date of the sales programme does not influence the expected end date of the QT unwind, given the MPC expects the final APF gilt held for monetary policy purposes will be the one that matures in September 2034. In the meantime, APF gilt maturities continue, with the next maturity occurring on 22 October 2026.
Once the Bank announces its approach to implementing the MPC’s QT strategy, from my perspective, we will have brought to a close the chapter of QT I first described in 2023. And we will have embarked on the next chapter, which should see the current stock of APF gilts fully unwound for monetary policy purposes over the next eight years.
The MPC’s active monetary policy tool
Before closing, I wanted to share my latest view on the MPC’s active monetary policy tool – Bank Rate. At its September meeting, the MPC voted by a majority of 6-3 to leave Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75%. I voted in the majority, as I have since the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%.
For my part, Bank Rate being the ‘active’ tool doesn’t always mean it has to change. Indeed, a decision to hold can be an active response to the risks to the inflation outlook. In February of this year, prior to the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, I voted in the minority for a cut to Bank Rate to 3.5%. Indeed, with evidence that the disinflation process was on track at the time (and subsequently confirmed from my perspective with the data outturns we have seen this year) I would have expected at least two cuts by now, such that Bank Rate would be at least 0.5% below where it is today, and slightly below the UK OIS curve at the time (shown in Chart 8). Therefore, my holds to Bank Rate since March have effectively delivered a tightening relative to where I thought we might otherwise have been.
I think the tightening we have seen in financial conditions since the outbreak of the conflict, shown by the increase in the OIS curve since February, has helped to limit the potential for some of the direct effects from the energy shock to propagate through to second round effects. But, as I set out in my individual paragraph in the September meeting minutes, I think the risks to the inflation outlook, whether external or domestically generated, have tilted more to the upside. Whilst the policy stance continues to provide restrictiveness, were upside pressures on the inflation outlook to continue to build, there could be a case for increasing Bank Rate.

Looking ahead to upcoming meetings, the inflation pressures I will continue to focus on are external pressures from energy prices, including from crude oil and gas prices as well as those of refined products, but also from extreme weather events and the AI supply chain. Domestically, I will be focused on the outlook for indirect effects, particularly in food prices, and any early signs of second round effects apparent from firms’ responses to the DMP survey and the Bank’s Agents’ intelligence on upcoming wage negotiations, looking ahead to 2027 settlements.
Conclusion
To conclude, based on mine and the market’s current assessment of the economy, I don’t foresee that we will be considering further QE any time soon. However, we have to recognise that the external environment can change very rapidly, as it did with the shocks of the Global Financial Crisis in 2008 and again with the Covid pandemic in 2020.
For today’s purposes let’s assume it doesn’t. In which case, the MPC’s decision at its September 2026 meeting should see the stock of assets held for monetary policy purposes fully unwound by 2034. That will be 25 years after QE was first undertaken. The MPC’s multi-year QT strategy provides a credible and coherent strategy for unwinding QE purchases, which should mean we’ve built a stronger foundation should QE be undertaken again in future.
Back in 2009 I certainly did not envisage that QE would take place in multiple phases over a 12 year period, and would take a similar period to unwind. The last 25 years has raised a lot of questions and points of discussion – in relation to both QE and QT – that need to be worked through. There are further lessons to be drawn from that experience, and more chapters to be written.

For instance, while QE affected gilt rates through a ‘signalling channel’ by changing market expectations for the future path of Bank Rate, the QT strategy is likely to have switched this channel off. During QT, the MPC has used Bank Rate as the active tool of monetary policy, which means that news about QT is not intended to contain any information about the future stance of monetary policy. QE also operated via effects on gilt market liquidity, but as QT sales have been gradual, predictable and only conducted in appropriate market conditions, it has had no marked effect on market liquidity.

This can occur via two main effects. First, increasing the supply of certain bonds can increase the yield on these bonds and on other assets that investors might consider close substitutes (the ‘local supply’ channel). articles.title: How dirty tricks harm, and institutional safeguards protect, the integrity of US elections | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

How dirty tricks harm, and institutional safeguards protect, the integrity of US elections

Elaine Kamarck and

Elaine Kamarck

Founding Director
- Center for Effective Public Management (CEPM),

Senior Fellow
- Governance Studies

Darrell M. West

Darrell M. West

Senior Fellow
- Governance Studies, Center for Technology Innovation (CTI), Center for Effective Public Management (CEPM),

Douglas Dillon Chair in Governmental Studies

October 28, 2026

Election dirty tricks, from fake date-change notices to decoy candidates with the same name, are old tactics that digital tools have made easier to carry out.
Safeguards such as chain-of-custody rules, air-gapped voting machines, and post-election audits make large-scale tampering difficult, and multiple audits found no evidence of widespread fraud in the 2020 election.
No safeguard is foolproof, but because both major parties deploy volunteers and lawyers to watch the polls and the count, attempts to rig an election would likely be exposed and litigated.

RENTON, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 23: An election worker opens midterm elections ballots at the King County Elections headquarters on Oct. 23, 2026, in Renton, Washington. Workers have already begun processing ballots in Washington, which uses mail-in voting. (Photo by David Ryder/Getty Images)

11 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Elections have always been beset by dirty tricks—a topic to which we devoted an entire book in 2019. The term was made infamous during the Watergate scandal, and in the digital age, efforts to confuse voters are easier to carry out than ever. Some election tricks are used time and time again, and informed voters should be on the lookout for them in the coming weeks. In this piece, we will present common strategies deployed to confuse voters, as well as illustrate important procedural safeguards designed to ensure that every eligible vote is counted fairly and accurately.

Back to top

Misleading voters on dates and times

AI makes it easy for bad actors to send out convincing but fake notices announcing election date changes, for example by attributing them to a weather event. However, election dates are rarely changed. In all of American history, a presidential election has never been delayed—including during wars. The 9/11 attack took place during a primary election day for New York City mayor and other city officers; a special act of the legislature moved quickly to conduct it on a later day.
In 2018, Rep. Lee Zeldin (R-N.Y.) was running for reelection in New York’s First Congressional District amid what turned out to be a “blue wave.” His campaign sent out flyers telling voters of the First Congressional District to postmark their absentee ballots by Nov. 6. However, there was a problem: The actual deadline was Nov. 5, and under state law, ballots postmarked after that date would not be counted. Perry Gershon, Zeldin’s Democratic opponent, jumped on the error, alleging that it targeted college-age and minority voters, and called for a federal investigation. The Zeldin campaign provided a statement from its printer alleging the misinformation was not intentional but rather a simple printing error. Some observers were skeptical: The Zeldin campaign had made the same “mistake” in 2016, fueling suspicion that this was a deliberate effort to mislead voters. Zeldin won his 2018 race with about 51.5% of the vote—a much narrower result than his 16-point victory in 2016.

Back to top

Claiming another action replaces voting

Republican Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker was elected in November 2010 on a conservative platform that included repealing collective bargaining rights for state employees. By 2012, state employees, their unions, and other labor unions were so incensed by the move that they mounted a successful recall petition, triggering a new election. The vote was set for June 5, 2012, between Walker and Democrat Tom Barrett. As Election Day approached, voters reported receiving robocalls telling them that if they had signed the recall petition, they were not required to cast their ballots in the recall election. Walker won the race with 53% of the vote.

Back to top

Recruiting spoiler candidates

Third-party candidates rarely win American elections and are often feared as potential “spoilers.” Most races are run without a third-party candidate on the ballot.
But in 2010, when a Republican operative in Arizona recruited a slate of third-party candidates to run for three offices, a lawyer representing Democrats described the effort as “a cynical manipulation of the process,” intended to siphon off votes from their nominees. Steve May signed up people he had met on Mill Avenue in Tempe, several of them homeless or marginally housed and none of them with any political background. One, a tarot card reader with less than a dollar to his name, was signed up to run for state treasurer. Another, a pedicab driver who went by “Grandpa,” was recruited to run for the state Senate. And finally, a young street musician was recruited to run for a seat on the Arizona Corporation Commission (the candidate eventually left the race). Democrats were furious, as were Green Party officials, who disavowed the candidates. Democrats filed a formal complaint but failed to get the candidates off the ballot.

Back to top

Fielding candidates with the same name

Dirty tricks don’t belong to the digital age, nor do they belong to one political party. John F. Kennedy made his first run for office in the 1946 Democratic primary for 11th Congressional District of Massachusetts. The two dominant ethnic groups in his district were people of Irish and Italian origin. Ethnic voting, the tendency to support candidates from one’s own ethnic community, has always been part of American politics and was especially strong in that era.
One of Kennedy’s opponents was an Italian-American Boston city councilor named Joe Russo. Kennedy’s father, Joe, set about to confuse voters by allegedly paying another Joe Russo, a janitor with no political experience, to run on the primary ballot as well—in hopes of splitting the Italian vote. As it turned out, it wasn’t necessary to get the other Joe Russo into the race—Kennedy won the primary by a large margin.
In this year’s Alaska Senate race, two Dan Sullivans are running against former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska). One of them, Dan S. Sullivan, is the incumbent senator. The other, Dan J. Sullivan, is a retired high school teacher with little background in government or public service. The Republican Party accused Dan J. of being put up by the Peltola campaign to siphon votes off of the incumbent senator, calling his campaign a “sham” and suing him. Peltola denied any involvement in getting Dan J. to run. On Oct. 23, 11 days before this year’s midterm elections, the Justice Department moved to block certification of the race if the incumbent loses, in order to “not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion.”

Back to top

'Swatting' on Election Day

“Swatting” refers to calling in a fake emergency (for instance, a bomb threat or an active shooter situation) to law enforcement, causing them to rush to the scene. During the 2025 New Jersey gubernatorial election, seven places received bomb threats. Although they were all hoaxes, they did cause brief shutdowns.
Needless to say, when called in, law enforcement will often immediately clear the area to ascertain the presence of a threat. This might frighten people away and prevent many from returning even once the area is deemed safe. An emergency call about an incident at a polling place has the potential to spread like wildfire on social media and might lead some voters to decide to simply stay away from polling places altogether.
Similarly, the presence of uniformed men dressed in riot gear and holding weapons might create a sense of danger even in the absence of any threats. This is why the Trump administration’s threats to deploy ICE at polling places are causing such an uproar, and why groups led by the NAACP are suing preemptively to keep ICE away.
Once votes have been cast, how can the public be sure that the count will be accurate? In our election system, many procedural safeguards exist to protect the security and safety of ballot counting. Here are some of the most relevant.

Back to top

Ballots have a chain of custody

The term “chain of custody” is usually heard in the context of evidence in a criminal trial. It is the process dictated by law to make sure that evidence is protected from tampering at every stage of the legal process.
In election law, states define a “chain of custody” that details what must happen to ballots at every stage: from printing and distribution to polling places, to transport to a tabulating center, to retention for any recount, and finally archiving. While the details vary from state to state, every state has its own chain of custody. This explains why it is so difficult to inject fake ballots, premarked for one candidate or another, into the election process. In 2021, conspiracy theories circulated alleging that tens of thousands of counterfeit ballots had been shipped from Asia to Maricopa County, Arizona, to benefit Joe Biden. A Republican-led review of the 2020 election even examined ballot paper for bamboo fibers in an attempt to investigate the allegation. Multiple audits and investigations ultimately found no evidence of widespread election fraud.

Back to top

Most voting systems aren’t connected to the internet

Most election machines in the United States today are “air-gapped,” meaning that they are isolated from the internet and thus hard to penetrate. In addition, most election machines now issue paper ballots, making it possible to check the machine results against a sample of paper results—known as a post-election audit or a risk-limiting audit. So even if a machine were compromised, the errors would likely show up in one of these audits.
Most states restrict access to the rooms where the machines are stored. However, bad actors could still manage to get in and tamper with the machines themselves, so safeguarding machines and having post-election audits remains critical.

Back to top

Vote totals shift as different areas report

A great deal of paranoia has resulted from the “red mirage” or the “blue shift.” They refer to the fact that small rural counties, which have recently tended to vote Republican, are usually able to report results relatively quickly. In contrast, large urban areas frequently have long lines—delaying the closing of the polls—and many more ballots to count. These places have recently tended to vote Democratic.
Early returns sometimes look like a Republican win, but this discrepancy in how fast votes are counted across rural and urban areas is key. The fact that one candidate led early in the evening and went on to lose an election is not an indicator of any malfeasance.
Another complicating factor is when a state decides to count mail-in ballots. Recently, due to President Trump’s campaign against mail-in ballots, they have tended to be more Democratic than Republican. Some states count them early and release them early; others release them only after the in-person ballots have been counted. And some states count mail-in ballots that arrive a certain number of days after Election Day.

Back to top

Party representatives can watch the count

Most states have statutes governing the participation of partisan poll watchers at each point in the election cycle—including the tabulation room. However, these are not usually required; instead, it is up to the political parties or the candidates to designate their representatives to election officials prior to the election. Most state statutes outline rules that the partisan observers must abide by, such as what distance they need to keep from the people doing the work.
None of these measures are foolproof. A campaign of fear and confusion directed at minority voters can keep legitimate citizens from voting; and election deniers who have, since 2020, gotten jobs in election administration can operate from the inside to undermine the final count. But often forgotten is the fact that both major parties mobilize volunteers and sophisticated attorneys to watch the polls and the count. Unless these observers are asleep at the switch, attempts to rig an election will likely be exposed and litigated.

Sponsors, spreads and stress testing: Navigating 2026’s rate reset
[Music]
Ben Berkey: If markets have felt harder to read lately, you're not imagining it. Over the past six months, the rate backdrop has shifted toward a world for higher for longer and more volatility. Longer term yields have climbed sharply with the US 10-year treasury reaching levels not seen since the early 2000s. Market participants are rethinking not only where policy rates may go, but also how much compensation they need to take on risk and hold longer duration assets. Rate volatility has picked up too, with the move index rising nearly 30% in September alone. But simply, financing and hedging decisions now have to account for a much wider range of outcomes. Welcome to JP Morgan's Making Sense. Today, we'll unpack what all of this means on the ground, how client behavior is changing, where sponsors and portfolio companies are finding opportunity, and what it takes to stay prepared when markets move quickly. I'm Ben Berkey, a senior vice president in our corporate derivatives franchise. Joining me today are Brian Tramontozzi, Head of North American Leverage Finance Capital Markets, and Kim Hernas, Global Head of Sponsor Private Side Sales. Brian, Kim, great to have you both here.
Brian Tramontozzi: Great to be here.
Kim Hernas: Nice to be here.
Ben Berkey: So Brian, let's start with you. What has changed most in how companies are thinking about financing?
Brian Tramontozzi: Yeah, I think the big thing that's changed year to date, uh, and really accelerating the last month and a half is base interest rates. We've seen yields in high yield increase by 100 basis points. The index has increased by 100 basis points since the beginning of September. That's a, that's a significant movement. We, we're not used to seeing moves like that in non-recessionary times. The majority of that is base treasury rates and, and there has been some spread widening. But I, I'd say the biggest change that we've experienced is just increase in yields. Similar in the term loan market, we are just experiencing now the start of a, a Fed tightening cycle. And so while absolute yields have maybe not risen as much in the loan market, I think we all expect that to catch up with the high yield market in short order.
Ben Berkey: Thank you, Brian. And Kim, on the Sponsor side, what has changed in your most recent conversations about the market with your Sponsor clients?
Kim Hernas: Yeah, so I, I think on the backdrop of the movement in rates and just overall sort of market volatility, a lot of our conversations are focused on how does that change your investment opportunities or capital allocations if you're a sponsor, but also increasingly, how does that change holding periods on investments? So we've seen, uh, a rise of evergreen vehicles, retail funds. That means that where an exit timeline might have been for an investment historically three to five years away, now it could be much, much longer. So that could change how people think about how they want to finance, uh, their fund, how they want to finance the asset, and also how they think about, uh, risk management both on the entry and the exit of investments.
Ben Berkey: Thanks for that, Kim. And then as it relates to liquidity with the Sponsor investment horizon kind of growing in, in nature, how are sponsors thinking and finding liquidity? How are they using back leverage and other tools to find liquidity in their portfolios where it otherwise may not be?
Kim Hernas: So I think part of the conversations that we've had this year and, and a change that we're seeing is that for sponsors, they're thinking about financing across the GP, the fund, and the asset, and sometimes interchangeably. So where those were three discreet conversations, we're now having more conversations on how do I unlock value with some combination of the value that I have, uh, uh, in all three of those areas across my GP balance sheet, across my fund investments, and then on an individual asset level. So you're seeing kind of more coordination, more partnership within sponsors to try to figure out how to unlock value and navigate liquidity.
Ben Berkey: And Brian, as it relates to the, the asset space, which you primarily focus in, how do you see issuers positioning across the broadly syndicated loan space, the high yield bonds and private credit?
Brian Tramontozzi: So the good news about the leverage market is we don't have a maturity wall facing us. And that's a function of 2024 through today. We've enjoyed strong liquidity. Investor cash balances have been robust. CLO creation has been strong. Mutual fund inflows have been positive. And so our issuers have taken advantage of strong market conditions to extend their runway, to reprice their debt, and really, unless a company is in financial distress today, it's likely that their maturity wall is at least three or four years out.
Ben Berkey: And as it relates to that, do you think the, the cost of capital is, is posing any resistance? You know, you mentioned treasury yields rising in the beginning of the conversation. Do you, do you find that causing any, I guess, disturbance in the markets?
Brian Tramontozzi: I think it's interesting when you look at spreads, single-B and BB spreads have held relatively constant year to date, whereas CCC spreads have increased by over 300 basis points. And what that tells me is companies with tight cash flow coverage, namely CCC-rated credits, the market is penalizing them in their trading levels for fear of economic distress either because of a slowing economy or because of tight interest coverage and cash flow coverage. So I think that's something we should watch very carefully because similar to what we saw in 2022, we're now seeing the lowest end quality names increase in yield the most, and that could be a sign of things to come.
Ben Berkey: Kim, on the sponsor side, the cost of capital conversation, which everyone navigates as it relates to new financings and refinancings, what, what have you seen in your space?
Kim Hernas: I think there's two things. One, I think there's a general desire to make sure that across the complex that risks are identified and that there's a decision around risk management. So oftentimes what you'll see, you know, maybe perhaps at the portfolio company level, there's been a lot of engagement around risk management there, but maybe less so if you look up at the fund or at the GP. So where are all of the risks or is it FX versus rates versus commodities? So where are all of the different risks that exist in the, let's call it kind of capital stack, for lack of better word, and have I really made a decision a- about those risks? Second, I would say, we've certainly seen an increase in, uh, what we'll call kind of deal contingent hedging or hedging that exists, which is very specific to either an acquisition or an exit of an asset. And so this kind of how do I protect the value that I've assumed in my models around an investment has become certainly more prevalent in the market and more top of mind.
Ben Berkey: Let's pivot to a question about teamwork. In these high pressure situations which we currently find markets confronting us with, Brian, where do teams get tripped up and what's the best way to navigate that when time is a constraint, getting a deal into market?
Brian Tramontozzi: Well, so JP Morgan, we've got almost 30% lead left market share in leverage loans and high yield bonds. And we've been the dominating force in those markets for, you know, the better part of 40 years in loans and almost 20 years in the high yield market. What allows us to stand apart is our capability and our ability to execute transactions in good times and bad times. We're so constantly in market, we just know how to get deals done, how to be smooth, how to be efficient, and how to, how to navigate through the bumps and twists and turns that naturally will happen in any situation. So I think with, with a JP Morgan, you just have experience that nobody else can bring to the table.
Ben Berkey: That makes a lot of sense. Thanks, Brian. For you, Kim, cross-asset collaboration, you span so many different products and spaces in the global sponsor community. What does the best sequencing look like when cross-asset collaboration works the best across the bank?
Kim Hernas: So Ben, to answer that question and also to pull on some of what Brian had noted, you know, one of the things that you s- clearly see as a strength of JP Morgan is the ability to assemble a team cross asset and across regions to deliver solutions. So increasingly, we're trying to move to a solution-oriented business versus an asset-class-aligned or product-aligned-business. And in doing so, you know, I think we hopefully create more value, think through different questions to ask, and also, you know, show different alternatives, right, for people to evaluate when they're coming to market. And that doesn't necessarily mean taking a lot more time.
Brian Tramontozzi: Understood. Actually, I'd like to build on something Kim just said. In leverage finance, we talk about a vineyard mindset, but we also talk about providing our customers with the financing that they need. A lot of times, companies will come to us and believe they need a financing alternative in high yield. We will show them converts. We will show them private credit. We will show them straight equity raise. Like, we are product-agnostic. The way we've set up our capital markets desk is literally to be as flat as possible. We sit on the same floor in leverage finance as converts, as common equity, as Kim and her rates team. We wanna provide our clients with exactly what they want as opposed to what we think they want based off of the capabilities that we have in whichever team is making the pitch.
Ben Berkey: So you hit on a great point there, Brian. You're talking about flexibility across the spectrum. How are clients truly balancing certainty in the financing markets versus flexibility while markets are ever-changing right now? Let's talk about certainty versus flexibility. Do you find a lot of borrowers and issuers right now are going to market so they know the devil that they do versus the devil that they don't? Or are they holding off to try to grasp at some better financing conditions that may exist in the future?
Brian Tramontozzi: So September was a record month in high-yield new issuance activity. We also saw very elevated levels in the loan market. Most of that was M&A driven. The majority of what was a $54 billion high-yield financing month was M&A-related. That's a record. And that really did take a lot of liquidity in the market, and that's part of the reason why spreads widened as much as they did in September. I believe that our issuers appreciate when market windows are open, they take advantage of those windows. And we certainly had an open window in September for those issuers to come to market. Conditions are very uncertain. We are always facing volatility. In particular, we're s- facing elevated volatility today in rates, spreads, the VIX. And I think companies that have a need to raise capital today are certainly very seriously going to market on an accelerated basis to take that risk off the table.
Ben Berkey: Thank you for that, Brian. And Kim, I'm gonna pivot over to you next. What should your clients be preparing for next and what are the best prepared sponsors actioning or thinking or asking today?
Kim Hernas: So I think ultimately, what makes for good preparation and what are some of the things that we do in our business to think about sort of good preparation? One is truly, again, assessing what we have, right? So what exists, uh, within the platform or portfolio that could create different forms of risk? How do you think about stress cases against that risk? Having a good understanding of the products that are available to address some of that risk and uncertainty, and whether you decide to use them or not, right? It's really just understanding the market and, and products have continued to evolve and are constantly evolving. And so understanding kind of the tools in your toolkit and then having intentional decision making. So I feel like the combination of those things generally make for the best preparation, you know, whether that's, uh, for the way we try to operate here, but also the way that we see some of our clients trying to tackle uncertainty in the market.
Ben Berkey: Thanks for that. And for our last question, we're gonna shift to the market outlook and what you folks think would change your market outlook as we head into the final months of 2026. So, uh, for Kim, what market move or shift in client behavior would signal a meaningful change in portfolio strategy or, or risk appetite across the sponsor universe?
Kim Hernas: I'm gonna let Brian take the sort of market outlook of view, on view on rates question, and we can look back at this, you know, in six months and see, see how he did. The things that I'm looking for in kind of cues in the market is, is deal activity, fundraising activity, the pace of exits, and the composition of those things, right? So, uh, th- those are the things that I watch kinda most closely, 'cause I think those then lead to hopefully kinda clues for us in where we can be most supportive, regardless of the market environment, right? We are trying to be responsive and thoughtful, and again, wh- whether that's across FX and if people are starting to reach more and fundraise more internationally, right? If pe - If exits are starting to look more like private versus public exits versus other types of exits. And so, again, regardless of market environment, people need to get on with their business and with their deals, and so we're trying to make sure that we're sort of at the front end of thinking through what comes next.
Ben Berkey: rian, I'll turn it over to you.
Brian Tramontozzi: Deficits are inflationary just by their nature, and so I think we're preparing to face an elevated interest rate environment for at least the near term or foreseeable future. But also, one of the things that's been allowing our market to be as strong as it is has been no recession. And a lot of that is a function of capital spend, infrastructure spend, in particular around AI and, and energy infrastructure. Any meaningful negative change to that, I think we could see spreads widen as well. So I don't think this is gonna happen, but we're certainly more cautious today than we've been in a long time about spread widening as well as higher base interest rates around, um, deficit spending as well as, um, you know, infrastructure CapEx.
Ben Berkey: Brian, Kim, I think that's a great place to wrap up. Thank you for sharing such an insightful conversation today. Markets are clearly keeping everyone on their toes. There's clearly a lot to watch a month ahead. And to everyone listening, thanks for spending time with us. We'll see you next time on Making Sense.

In volatile markets, trade-offs sharpen: pay for certainty now, or preserve flexibility for later. In this episode of Making Sense, Ben Berkey from the corporate derivatives franchise talks with Brian Tramontozzi, head of North American Leveraged Finance Capital Markets, and Kim Hernas, global head of Sponsor Private Side Sales, to discuss how leveraged finance and private markets are weighing these trade-offs in a higher-for-longer rate environment. They discuss how higher base yields are affecting leveraged loan and high-yield markets, and what spread behavior across rating tiers may be signaling.
