articles.title: Mixed signals, research findings, and policy judgements − speech by Catherine L. Mann
articles.text:
Mixed signals, research findings, and policy judgements − speech by Catherine L. Mann

Given at the Natixis CIB Private Debt Forum

Published on
02 July 2026

Catherine L. Mann highlights how disaggregated data can improve our understanding of trends in headline economic variables. She also examines how volatility in inflation and financial markets has influenced financial conditions. Catherine then explains how research about de-anchoring of inflation expectations and the speed of monetary policy transmission has underpinned her activist policy strategy.

Speech
Introduction
As I think about my recent policy decisions, my assessment has evolved with incoming data and ongoing research. At the start of this year, moderation in price and wage growth, alongside slowing activity, had brought me closer to considering a reduction in Bank Rate. However, since the onset of the conflict in the Middle East, the reemergence of the trade‑off between inflation and activity has led me to place more weight on inflation persistence, shifting my view towards a longer hold, and potentially a need to lean against that risk.
This remains my view, as notwithstanding a sporadic reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, infrastructure rebuilding, future-proofing, and restocking supplies imply that higher energy prices will likely persist. Associated firm pricing reactions are also likely to keep inflation from moderating to the two percent target within the monetary policy horizon. That said, the discussion for today addresses the timing of a hike versus hold decision. The first topic is how an assessment of disaggregated data provides important nuances to the economic picture relative to the headline numbers. The second topic is how key research findings for both inflation persistence and monetary policy transmission inform my policy strategy.
The disaggregated assessment of the data shows mixed signals across key indicators. Realized inflation and expectations differ across households, firms, and financial markets, and have been influenced in the aggregate by fiscal measures. Wage developments differ across the public and private sectors, with further variation across industries. Public sector activity growth continues to outpace that of the market sector, alongside continued government budget overruns, including on account of interest costs. Volatility in both inflation and financial conditions has increased, affecting the degree of restrictiveness as well as the signal-to-noise assessment.
Interpreting mixed and noisy signals is nothing new for central bankers, but it is more challenging in the current environment where more frequent shocks are building on already persistent inflation with embedded second-round effects, amid higher volatility with elevated uncertainty (see Mann 2024b). In this speech, I will evaluate some of these mixed signals, explain how I interpret them and how – in light of research – they have shaped my recent decisions, especially the last one in June, and what they could mean for my monetary policy strategy going forward.
Uncertain underlying trend inflation
Prior to the conflict in the Middle East, inflation – as indicated in the February 2026 Monetary Policy Report – was expected to come down to our two percent target by the second half of 2026. However, that sanguine projection masked the underlying economic patterns, as increases in administered prices and national insurance contributions (NICs), which contributed 0.7 percentage points to the inflation hump in 2025, were assumed to dissipate in Q2 2026. The projected fall in inflation also reflected the energy bills package introduced in the Autumn Budget. The latter accounted for a reduction of nearly 0.25 percentage points to CPI inflation, as Chart 1 shows. Finally, slack in the economy was projected to weigh on inflation through the projected tightening of the fiscal position. The latter two factors underscore the importance of fiscal measures in getting us back to the inflation target.

Chart 1: Contribution of budget measures to deviation from inflation target
Percentage point deviation from the 2% inflation target

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: ‘Administered prices, NICs, and electric vehicle (EV) mileage charge’ includes the estimated direct effects of changes to Vehicle Excise Duty, bus fares, VAT on school fees, and water charges. The NICs component represents Bank staff’s allowance for the effects of the recent increase in employers NICs on CPI inflation. The EV mileage charge component relates to the mileage-based charge on electric vehicles announced in Budget 2025.The ‘Energy budget measures’ bars represent the estimated direct effects of the energy bills package. The ‘Import prices’ bars includes an MPC judgement on the price of tradables (see May 2024 Monetary Policy Report) which has little effect on the profile beyond 2026. The ‘Other’ bars represent other deviations of inflation not attributable to the listed influences including the estimated effects of changes to tobacco and vaping products duties.

Of course, that projection was prior to the US-Israel-Iran war. The economy and our projections have evolved since then. For starters, the conflict resulted in a higher forecast for CPI inflation across all three scenarios presented in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report. While outturns for price growth – so far lower than expected – continue to reflect lagged pass-through from pre-war moderation in commodity and domestic cost pressures, household inflation expectations have picked up materially since the conflict.
Because inflation shocks are amplified and attention to inflation rises when inflation is elevated – both with thresholds of around 3 to 3.5 percent CPI inflation – inflation expectations could pick up even more (Weber et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Gaffney and Potjagailo, 2026).footnote [1] Staff research also shows that the latest rise in households’ short-term inflation expectations move back into the non-linear region, even if not quite as far as in 2022 (Buckmann et al., 2025). While the most recent observation of the Citi/YouGov measure of household inflation expectations has decreased from its April peak, it remains within the region of these non-linear dynamics, and both short- and long-term expectations remain elevated relative to historical averages and their pre-Iran war levels.
On the firm side, research surveys reveal that the recent inflationary episode spurred an increase in the share of firms setting prices in response to changes in economic conditions – so-called state-dependent pricing – instead of adjusting their prices at fixed intervals (Bunn et al., 2026a). State-dependent firms increased their prices more quickly when inflation rose but also raised their prices by less relative to time-dependent firms as inflation decreased (Chart 2) as the time-dependent firms’ adjustment caught-up. A higher frequency of price adjustments yields an upside inflation bias as well as more volatile inflation, as prices respond more quickly, more often, and more strongly to positive inflation shocks.

Chart 2: Firm output price growth by price-setting behavior
Own-price growth and expected year-ahead own-price growth, percent

Footnotes

Source: Bunn et al. (2026a).

Notes: Chart depicts trends in own-price growth (solid lines) and expected year-ahead own-price growth (diamonds), split by firms’ price-setting behavior. Firms are split into state-dependent and time-dependent pricing based on each firm’s most recent response to this question (as of April 2026). The series are three-month moving averages, with the latest data up to May 2026. Percentages in brackets denote share of firms using state- and time-dependent pricing.

To get a better understanding about the current conjuncture and prospects for nominal conditions, I look at firms’ responses to the Decision Maker Panel (DMP) survey, particularly the distributions of responses to questions about expected CPI inflation and expected one-year-ahead price- and wage-setting. Following the outbreak of the Iran war, the survey data show that firms’ CPI inflation expectations quickly responded, (left panel in Chart 3). Although the distribution has shifted to the right in the latest quarter (purple) relative to the three months preceding the Iran war (orange), it remains below 2022 (aqua) and is also much less dispersed. This implies that the pattern of firms’ responses does not yet exhibit the same degree of uncertainty about future inflation as it did during the
Russia-initiated inflation surge.
The distribution of firms’ expectations for their own-price growth in the year ahead has shifted modestly to the right, too. This is most apparent for consumer-facing firms and goods producers, while services firms and business-facing companies have adjusted their expectations by less. These changes in firms’ expectations and price-setting behavior are a key ingredient for the evolution of CPI inflation itself.
The DMP survey data also show that some firms have modestly altered their realized prices in recent months, with the distribution for goods-producing firms exhibiting a bit more mass in the right-hand side of the distribution, suggesting that there could be more inflation in the pipeline. Input and output PMIs have also been elevated.

Chart 3: Distributions of firms’ inflation and wage growth expectations
Expected one-year-ahead CPI inflation (left panel) and expected year-ahead wage growth (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: Decision Maker Panel.

Notes: Charts show kernel density plots for expected one-year-ahead CPI inflation (left panel) and year-ahead wage growth expectations for 2022, December 2025 to February 2026 (three months prior to the Iran war), and March 2026 to May 2026. Distributions are weighted by industry and employment shares.

Widening the aperture on potential wage dynamics from the firm-level survey data, current official wage statistics show mixed signals. Despite a continued easing in private sector regular pay growth (left panel in Chart 4), which is now within the Bank staff’s estimates of target-consistent wage growth, whole-economy total pay has not decelerated to the same degree. We therefore continue to see a wedge between the two pay measures, as illustrated by the right panel in Chart 4.
Over the past year, that wedge has largely been driven by stronger public sector wage growth and the impact of bonuses. In recent months, the contribution from the public sector has eased somewhat. Drawing on the evidence from February 2026 Monetary Policy Report on heterogeneity in wage setting, this pattern is consistent with stronger pay growth in sectors characterized by more structured or collective bargaining where inflation and inflation expectations play key roles. This includes the public sector and similar “union-type” segments within the private sector, as well as cost-minimizing firms, which together account for around 80% of private-sector workforce.
Pay settlements have largely been finalized for the year, and there is limited evidence (as shown in Chart 3 above) from firms in the DMP of a pick‑up in what they expect to offer their employees next year. Looking ahead, the risk is that wage pressures are deferred rather than dissipated, particularly if future pay settlements – including in these more collectively bargained segments – are set against the backdrop of higher realized inflation and elevated expectations in the second half of this year.
Furthermore, even if energy prices moderate, the temptation will be to maintain the own- price and wage strategies to partially rebuild margins, which, according to the survey data, have been absorbing the current shock (Bunn et al, 2026b Opens in a new window). All told, distributions are important indicators to evaluate whether inflationary pressures, the wage setting process, and resulting price setting feed into overall inflation.

Chart 4: Regular pay growth and contributions to the wedge between whole-economy and private sector pay growth
Three-months-on-year growth (left panel) (a) and percentage point contributions to the difference (right panel)(b)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Left panel (a) depicts three-months-on-year public and private sector regular pay growth in percent and the range of target-consistent estimates for regular pay growth. Right panel (b) depicts percentage point contributions by bonuses and public sector regular pay growth to the wedge between three-months-on-year whole economy total and private sector wage growth. Latest data: April 2026.

The trade-off re-emerges
Alongside the higher projected paths for inflation in the April Monetary Policy Report is a slower projected pace of GDP growth across all scenarios relative to February (Chart 5). The trade-off between inflation and activity has re-emerged, as I have noted in previous speeches (see Mann 2025a, 2025b).

Chart 5: Real GDP in the February and April 2026 Monetary Policy Reports
Index (2025 = 100)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Aqua line shows the forecast for real GDP from the February 2026 Monetary Policy Report. Orange, purple, and gold lines show the respective forecasts for scenarios A, B, and C from the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

While headline GDP growth remains subdued, looking beneath the aggregate number reveals a divergence between the role of public and private sector activity. While GDP growth has recently been primarily driven by market sector output (MSO, right panel in Chart 6), public sector output has grown by around 4.5 percent since Q4 2023, outpacing the cumulative growth of market sector output by around one percentage point (left panel in Chart 6).

Chart 6: Growth in market sector and public sector GDP and their contributions to GDP growth
Cumulative change since 2023 Q4 (left panel) and contributions to change since 2023 Q4 (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Notes: The government sector comprises public administration, education, and health, while the market sector comprises all other industries, including agriculture, wholesale and retail trade, accommodation and food services, and other market-based activities. Latest data: April 2026.

Why do I highlight the different growth rates of government and market sector GDP? The MPC’s forecast is conditioned on announced fiscal policy, as reflected in the Office for Budget Responsibility’s (OBR’s) projections. In simple terms, fiscal policy is funded by a mix of public sector borrowing and taxes. As noted in the Bank’s recent Forecast Evaluation Report, “looser-than-expected fiscal policy has […] contributed to there being less spare capacity” (Bank of England, 2026b). As shown in Chart 7, this reflects higher outturns for public sector borrowing than embodied in the OBR’s forecasts, consistent with the OBR’s own forecast evaluation Opens in a new window (Office for Budget Responsibility, 2026 Opens in a new window). Using a structural VAR model, Brignone and Piffer (2026) demonstrate that upward revisions in inflation forecasts following the post-pandemic inflation surge can be attributed to a combination of expansionary shocks on the demand side, revisions to past shocks, and contractionary supply-side shocks. Going forward, the question is whether there will be upside surprises in fiscal policy,footnote [2] which could provide additional support to public sector activity and can have broader implications for productivity, aggregate demand, inflation, and financial conditions.

Chart 7: Successive forecasts and outturns of public sector net borrowing
Public sector net borrowing as a percent of GDP

Footnotes

Source: Office for Budget Responsibility.

Notes: Data shows successive forecasts (grey) and outturns (orange) of public sector net borrowing as a percent of GDP. Latest forecast: March 2026.

Labor market data also show a mixed picture, with implications for the strength of demand. Beneath the rise in headline unemployment in recent years and its projected increase, the dispersion in unemployment rates across industries has also increased. Chart 8 illustrates how unemployment rates across different industries have changed since 2022. The shaded area (aqua) shows that the dispersion of unemployment rates across different sectors has increased since mid-2025, suggesting that unemployment is more unevenly distributed across industries. For instance, the unemployment rate remains higher in accommodation and food services and has risen faster in that industry compared to overall unemployment since mid-2025. By contrast, the professional and technical sectors are closer to the lower end of the distribution of unemployment rates across sectors.
Some of these differences may reflect varying exposure to recent changes in fiscal policy, such as changes to national insurance contributions and the national living wage, as well as sector-specific demand conditions, including exposure to the energy shock. The result is a labor market that is far from uniform, indicating that some industries are more resilient than others, and that headline unemployment may overstate weakness in the labor market. Therefore, demand may be more resilient than projected by the aggregate numbers.

Chart 8: Dispersion in unemployment rates across industries
Unemployment rates by previous industry (percent)

Footnotes

Source: April 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

Notes: Data show ONS estimates of unemployment by previous industry. This measure will not fully capture new entrants to the labor market who do not find a job as they have no previous industry, nor will it reflect the capacity for workers to transition across industries. The shaded area shows the range of industry-level unemployment rates by previous industry over time. Given data limitations and relatively small sample sizes, it can be difficult to draw firm conclusions from changes in these data. These data are not seasonally adjusted. The latest data shown are for the three months to April 2026.

Financial conditions are volatile
I also considered financial conditions in forming my June decision, as has always been the case. Global spillovers, as discussed in one of my speeches last year, have importantly contributed to the volatility of financial market variables, particularly in a small open economy like the UK. That remains the case today (Chart 9).
Looking at the time-varying volatility of asset price factors extracted from a daily structural VAR based on Brandt et al. (2021) Opens in a new window, we see that the Iran conflict has been associated with a material increase in the volatility of international monetary policy factors but also in the volatility in the UK-specific risk factor. In fact, the UK-specific risk factor is now furthest away from its historical normal. By contrast, volatility in the model's macro factors and global risk (which is a flight-to-safety factor) is little changed. This divergence suggests that markets are interpreting the conflict less as a shock to the growth outlook and more as a source of uncertainty about inflation and the associated monetary policy response, as well as perhaps the consequence of the behavior of an evolving investor base in the gilt market, a topic I discussed in my speech on the UK's external exposures (Mann, 2026).

Chart 9: Volatility of asset price factors
Rolling standard deviation of shocks

Footnotes

Source: Mann (2025c), Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.

Notes: The calculations are based on a structural VAR identified using sign and magnitude restrictions following Brandt et al. (2021) Opens in a new window. The model is extended to analyze monetary policy spillovers between the UK and its two most important trading partners and dominant currency blocks, the US and the euro area (as described in Mann (2024a)).

We can also directly observe the increase in financial market volatility in how UK overnight index swap (OIS) curves have evolved since the onset of the Middle East conflict. Following the outbreak of the Iran war, OIS curves have become increasingly volatile, as the widened range in their movements post-conflict (aqua) relative to pre-conflict (purple) in Chart 10 (left panel) shows. During this period, these large increases in OIS rates have been passed-through rapidly into mortgage rates faced by households: interest rates on two- and five-year fixed rate mortgages with a 75% loan-to-value ratio have risen by 87 and 73 basis points, respectively (right panel in Chart 10). The asymmetry in price and wage developments I highlighted earlier – more robust adjustments to upside shocks and relatively slow adjustment to downside shocks – can also be observed in financial markets, as increases in OIS rates pass through to mortgage rates more quickly than do decreases.
As I noted in my 200-word paragraph in the latest MPC minutes, higher financial market volatility acts as a headwind to both consumption and investment. For firms, increased uncertainty around financing conditions raises the hurdle for investment. For households, more volatile inflation can result in uncertainty about future inflation, which tends to encourage precautionary behavior and the maintenance of higher savings buffers (Fischer et al., 2025). At the same time, my preferred measure of financial conditions (see Burr, 2023 Opens in a new window), has not tightened that much. Taken together, just like other parts of the economy, financial conditions are sending mixed signals, too.

Chart 10: Volatility in OIS curves and pass-through to mortgage rates
UK instantaneous forward OIS curves (left panel) and daily quoted mortgage rates and OIS rates (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P., Bank of England and Bank calculations.

Notes: Swathes of UK instantaneous forward OIS curves in the left panel cover an equivalent period of time. Range of moves in OIS curves pre-Iran war (purple swathe) observed from 28 October 2025 until 27 February 2026. Range of moves in OIS curves since the Iran war (aqua swathe) observed from 27 February to 26 June 2026. Right panel shows 2-year and 5-year OIS rates and 2-year and 5-year fixed rate mortgages with 75% loan to value ratios. Latest observation for daily quoted mortgage and OIS rates: 26 June 2026.

Research informs my monetary policy strategy
Against the backdrop of the data and prospects discussed above, two research strands inform my strategy. The first strand emphasizes the importance of leaning against upside risks to inflation to reduce risks of de-anchoring and to ensure that monetary policy remains credible. I’ve discussed research on persistent upside risks to inflation and the consequences in numerous previous speeches.footnote [3] The second research strand emphasizes the speed with which firms adjust their expected pricing strategies and the capacity for Bank Rate decisions to feed through relatively quickly into expectations, firms’ price-setting behavior, and overall inflation, a topic that I addressed last in 2023 (see Mann, 2023a).
Let’s look at what’s new in the first research strand. This research on de-anchoring examines how responsive medium- to long-term inflation expectations are to changes in short-term inflation expectations by regressing the former on the latter alongside a set of control variables.footnote [4] A regression coefficient close to zero indicates firmly anchored expectations – in that case, expectations about inflation in the medium- and long-term are insensitive to short-term fluctuations. By contrast, a coefficient close to one suggests that expectations are de-anchored. Chart 11 shows the analysis for households, firms, and financial markets.
Data from household and firm surveys show an increased responsiveness of their inflation expectations to near-term inflation developments since the Covid pandemic and the energy shock following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, suggesting that these two groups are not firmly anchored (left and center panel in Chart 11). Financial market participants’ expectations are more anchored relative to households and firms, despite the responsiveness of their long-term expectations to short-run expectations being more volatile (right panel in Chart 11). Taken together, these findings point to some erosion in credibility and potential risks of de-anchoring among households and firms.

Chart 11: Responsiveness of medium/long-term inflation expectations to short-term inflation expectations
Regression coefficients (percentage points)

Footnotes

Source: Bank of England/Ipsos Inflation Attitudes Survey, Decision Maker Panel, Market Participants Survey and Bank calculations.

Notes: Household measure shows the slope of 5-year-ahead inflation expectations on 1-year-ahead inflation expectations from the Bank of England/Ipsos Inflation Attitudes Survey. Firm measure shows the slope of CPI 3-year-ahead expectations on CPI 1-year-ahead expectations from the Decision Maker Panel. Financial Markets measure shows the slope of 5-year-ahead inflation expectations on 1-year-ahead inflation expectations from the Market Participants Survey. Shaded areas denote 95% confidence bands.

Staff research has also used the Boosted Inflation Model – a machine learning model based on boosted decision trees that is designed to capture non-linear relationships between a range of indicators and CPI inflation (Buckmann et al., 2025). It can decompose inflation into its underlying drivers, reflecting the price Phillips curve as well as potential drift of that curve. Chart 12 shows the model’s decomposition of predicted inflation relative to the two percent target. The contribution of the trend inflation component (aqua), which comes from elevated household inflation expectations has started to increase since the Iran war, but remains below the levels last seen in 2023 and 2024. Since household expectations can feed into both wage and price developments, this can be a harbinger of second-round effects.
These developments increase upside risks to the inflation process and raise the risk of
de-anchoring, particularly given the extended period of above-target inflation and the increase in inflation volatility. As discussed in Mann (2022), once expectations drift from the two percent target, monetary policy needs to tighten more, to both control expectations and to moderate inflation itself. So, considering this research strand alone would typically point towards a tighter policy stance.

Chart 12: Decomposition of CPI inflation from Boosted Inflation Model
Annualized and smoothed (left) and annualized month-on-month (right)

Footnotes

Source: Buckmann et al. (2025).

Notes: Colored bars show the block-wise predictive contributions to 1-month-ahead annualized month-on-month CPI inflation (white line), around 2% target. Blockwise boosted inflation model estimated via cross-validation over 1989m1-2026m5 sample. Dashed line: CPI inflation, annualized.

What’s new in the second strand of research – the speed of transmission of monetary policy. Evidence points to a relatively more rapid transmission of monetary policy to borrowing costs, but also directly to inflation expectations as compared to what is embodied in most traditional slack-driven models of inflation process. Although even the more familiar approach finds that monetary transmission to GDP has been quicker.footnote [5]
With regard to the first stage of transmission of monetary policy,footnote [6] the relatively quick increase in mortgage rates in response to the rise in inflation and market expectations of tighter monetary policy that I showed in Chart 10 illustrates a key channel through which the financial environment will affect households considering a new mortgage or seeking to remortgage by making their monthly repayments more expensive. Note as well that the moderation from the peak has been slower than the advance, pointing to asymmetry in the institutional response to the policy environment.
Besides the fast pass-through to financial variables, Brandt et al. (2026) Opens in a new window use
high-frequency credit and debit card spending data to show that monetary policy shocks can affect real economic activity very quickly, too. They show that consumer spending declines within a few days in response to a contractionary monetary policy shock, while web searches for terms related to unemployment rise. This result suggests that a fast adjustment in households’ expectations about their economic prospects can drive a change in consumption behavior.
Firm-level research by Yotzov et al. (2026) Opens in a new window also shows that firms update both their CPI inflation perceptions and expectations as well as their own-price growth expectations upon CPI releases. Specifically, the authors find that between 2022 and 2024, a one percentage point increase in headline CPI inflation raises firms’ expected year-ahead own-price growth by 0.3 percentage points. On CPI perceptions, they respond quickly within a few hours of data releases. Firms’ expected own-price growth also increases a few hours after a positive change in CPI inflation, although to a smaller extent.
Research by Di Pace et al. (2025) Opens in a new window analyses how firms update their price expectations in response to monetary policy announcements by the Bank of England. They find that within days following the Bank Rate decision, firms revise down their year-ahead price growth expectations if the increase in Bank Rate is sufficiently large. As Chart 13 shows, Bank Rate increases of 50 basis points or more result in a statistically significant and economically sizeable downward revision in firms’ expected price growth for the year ahead. While this pattern is evident across the distribution of firms’ expected own-price changes, it is more pronounced in the left tail. This means that firms revise the lower-price outcomes in their pricing plans more than the higher-price outcomes, suggesting an asymmetric updating of expectations. Chart 13 also shows that firms do not seem to significantly alter their price growth expectations in response to announcements of Bank Rate changes smaller than 50 basis points.

Chart 13: Responsiveness of firm price expectations to Bank Rate changes
Regression coefficients

Footnotes

Source: Di Pace et al. (2025) Opens in a new window.

Notes: The chart plots regression results for different moments of the distribution of firms’ price expectations on monetary policy shocks within a 5-day window around policy announcements. Monetary policy shocks are measured using actual Bank Rate changes. The series is normalized so that coefficients correspond to the response to a 25 basis point shock. BR change < 50 bps indicates a Bank Rate change below 50 basis points in absolute value. BR change >= 50 bps indicates a Bank Rate change equal or above 50 basis points in absolute value. Analysis uses data from November 2016 until December 2023. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Implications for monetary policy strategy
How do I use the underlying data and these two strands of research to inform my policy strategy? Consider the following three dimensions generally, but with specific reference to my June decision.
First, the importance of a disaggregated assessment. Disaggregated data is always key to how I evaluate the economic conjuncture. In June, these data exhibited mixed signals, which provided a more nuanced view of the inflation-activity trade-off than the macro data. Wage growth has differed between private and public sectors. Pricing behavior of firms has varied in speed of responsiveness. The administered one-off changes in prices masked underlying trend inflation. Disaggregated labor signals in some sectors were less weak than the overall unemployment rate. Tracking fiscal outturns has been important, especially given the gap between GDP and market-sector output, and the evidence from the Forecast Evaluation Report.
Second, on the topic of volatility and noise versus signals. Whereas both higher inflation and financial market volatility do make it harder to distinguish signals from transitory movements, because inflation volatility goes hand-in-hand with inflation rates, and financial volatility is reflected in risk premia, the noise contributes to the signal. It puts upside pressure on inflation and tightens financial conditions, at least in nominal terms. The source of inflation pressures – from costs versus from demand matters. The source of financial risk premia – from domestic drivers versus foreign spillovers – matters. In June, the cost-oriented inflation pressures were being offset by domestic-oriented financial restrictiveness. Bearing these factors in mind has been key to many of my policy decisions.
Third, on the topic of timing. Energy price developments, profit margin behavior, and the underpinnings of the 2027 wage negotiations will be critical in determining whether current cost pressures become more embedded. All these conditions are still unfolding. Given the seasonality of wage negotiations and their dependence on previous inflation and inflation expectations, data outturns (including the expectations for one-year-ahead) in the second half of this year are particularly important for my future decisions.
Considering my June decision, by the disaggregated data assessment, there was more upside risks to inflation compared to downside risks for activity. On that basis and considering the research about risks of de-anchoring alone, tightening Bank Rate could have made sense. But, at the time of the June meeting, financial markets had tightened considerably at least in nominal terms.
Research on the responsiveness of pricing and consumer behaviors to CPI announcements and to monetary policy shocks is clear evidence that monetary policy can have quick effects on the key variables of inflation expectations and CPI inflation, which is the Bank of England’s remit. In June, observing these forward-looking and high-frequency data in the context of both strands of the research meant that an activist hold was the appropriate decision.
Going forward, as I evaluate the disaggregated data, the sources of signal-to-noise in financial conditions, and the inputs to firms’ pricing strategies, I am confident that if outturns – especially in expectations – are unfavorable to the underlying inflation process, an activist move can bring inflation expectations and outcomes toward the two percent target.

articles.title: The Commodity Markets Outlook in eight charts
articles.text:
Published on
Let's Talk Development

The Commodity Markets Outlook in eight charts

John Baffes

Kaltrina Temaj

October 30, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Commodity prices are set to remain elevated, with the global index projected to rise 23 percent in 2026 before declining 7 percent in 2027. Global commodity prices are projected to increase 23 percent in 2025 before retreating 7 percent in 2027. The outlook hinges on continued supply disruptions, particularly in energy and fertilizer markets, whose price indexes are expected to rise 32 and 14 percent, respectively, in 2026 before easing in 2027. Food prices are projected to increase 10 percent in 2026 amid an intensified El Niño, disruptions to Black Sea grain supplies, higher input costs, and increased diversion to biofuels, especially biodiesel. Metals and minerals prices are expected to rise 28 percent in 2026, reflecting strong demand and limited supply growth, while precious metals prices are projected to increase nearly 40 percent. Risks are tilted to the upside and include prolonged hostilities in the Middle East, stronger-than-expected effects from El Niño, and extended disruptions to Black Sea supplies.

Commodity markets were highly volatile for much of 2026 amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and, more recently, disruptions to Black Sea grain supplies. Energy prices were hit particularly hard: Brent crude exceeded $110/bbl in mid-October as hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz constrained supply flows, while refinery damage pushed up prices for petroleum products, particularly for diesel. Reduced Middle East exports also intensified competition for LNG, lifting natural gas prices in Asia and Europe. Meanwhile, a very strong El Niño and elevated input costs added pressure to food markets, with the World Bank Group’s food price index reaching a three-year high in September. Metals and minerals prices remained elevated as well reflecting strong industrial demand, tight supplies, and limited near-term supply growth.

Oil prices have been exceptionally volatile in 2026Q3, amid renewed hostilities in the Gulf and Red Sea, an attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, and intensifying attacks on Russian oil facilities. In mid-October, front-month Brent futures exceeded $110/bbl, even as markets weighed rising crude supply and accelerated releases from IEA emergency stockpiles. Brent is expected to average $91/bbl in 2026 before declining to $79/bbl in 2027 and $70/bbl in 2028 as the market moves into surplus. Near-term risks remain tilted to the upside, particularly from conflict-related supply losses and tighter OPEC+ production policy amid depleted inventories. Further out, downside risks dominate, including a faster restoration of Gulf supply, stronger-than-expected non-OPEC+ output, weaker global growth, and a more rapid shift to electric vehicles.

Natural gas prices surged in 2026Q3, with the World Bank Groups natural gas index reaching a four-year high in September. European and Asian LNG prices more than doubled from pre-conflict levels by September, amid prolonged Gulf supply disruptions, stronger Asian power-sector demand, and low European inventories. By contrast, U.S. natural gas prices generally remained below their February levels. Global gas markets are expected to remain tight, despite a partial recovery in Gulf LNG exports in 2027Q1 as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz rebound and damaged Emirati capacity is restored. With Qatar’s damaged LNG trains assumed to remain offline, however, regional exports are expected to stay below pre-conflict levels. European prices are projected to rise about 60 percent in 2026 before declining 8 percent in 2027 and almost 30 percent in 2028 as markets normalize. U.S. prices, meanwhile, are expected to remain broadly unchanged in 2026 before rising about 6 percent in 2027 and 5 percent in 2028, largely reflecting growing external demand for LNG.

The World Bank Group’s agricultural price index rose 5 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q), driven by a surge in food prices. The index is projected to rise slightly in 2026 and 5 percent in 2027. Food prices, however, are expected to increase 10 percent in 2026 and a further 7 percent in 2027, following a 21 percent decline between 2022 and 2025. The increases reflect elevated input costs, disruptions to Black Sea grain and oilseed shipments, and harvest losses associated with a very strong El Niño. Rice production is expected to fall for the first time in a decade, while palm oil production in Southeast Asia is also expected to be constrained. Trade disruptions and hot, dry conditions in the European Union and elsewhere are expected to push wheat prices sharply higher. In contrast, beverage prices are projected to fall 24 percent in 2026 as coffee and cocoa production recovers, before rising 3 percent in 2027. The outlook assumes that Black Sea shipping disruptions ease and agricultural input costs decline in 2027. Risks are tilted to the upside: intensified conflict and larger-than-expected weather losses could push food and grain prices 12 percent and 20 percent above the 2027 baseline, respectively, while additional export restrictions or policies favoring biofuels could add further pressure.

The World Bank Group’s fertilizer price index fell 22 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q) and declined further in October, fully reversing the 2026Q2 surge following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Urea prices drove both swings, while other fertilizer prices rose less sharply but remained elevated. Despite the recent retreat, the index is projected to rise about 14 percent in 2026 (y/y), reflecting Middle East shipping disruptions, higher input costs, and trade restrictions. Following a projected 14 percent increase in 2026, prices are expected to fall 12 percent in 2027 and 8 percent in 2028 as input costs ease and supplies recover, aided by increased exports from outside the Gulf region. Risks remain tilted to the upside, particularly from renewed shipping disruptions and higher input costs.

The World Bank Group’s metals and minerals price index is on track to rise 25 percent in 2026, reaching a record annual average amid resilient demand and supply constraints for several base metals. Prices are expected to edge lower in 2027 but remain historically high, with the index still 16 percent above its 2021 peak. Demand is expected to remain firm, supported by investment in electrification, renewable energy, and data centers, while weak construction in many economies and softness in China’s steel sector weigh on iron ore. The precious metals price index fell 7 percent in 2026Q3 after reaching record highs earlier in the year but is still expected to rise 40 percent in 2026, before declining 8 percent in 2027 as investor demand moderates. Risks are two-sided: supply disruptions, stockpiling, and stronger global investment could push metal prices higher, while weaker global growth could weigh sharply on prices. For precious metals, geopolitical tensions and financial volatility pose upside risks, while higher-for-longer interest rates or a stronger U.S. dollar could push prices lower.

Precious metal prices eased in 2026Q3, partially reversing a historic surge that had pushed gold, silver, and platinum to record highs. The retreat partly reflected rising bond yields, tighter monetary policy, and a stronger U.S. dollar. Safe-haven demand and central bank gold purchases are expected to moderate but remain supportive of elevated gold prices, while silver and platinum prices are likely to ease as demand growth slows and supply improves. Overall, the World Bank Group’s precious metals price index is projected to rise 40 percent in 2026 before falling 8 percent in 2027 and 6 percent in 2028.

What does this mean for developing countries?
Elevated food and energy prices, amid overlapping risks, have important implications for food price inflation and food insecurity. In response, policymakers often turn to trade restrictions, particularly export bans. While such measures may appear attractive domestically, they can fragment markets and push global prices higher, as seen in 2007-08 and 2010-11. A more effective approach combines targeted social safety nets to protect the most vulnerable with longer-term investments in resilience, including efforts to turn natural endowments into lasting prosperity.

Commodity Markets Outlook

articles.title: Sustainability as a driver of long-term investment outcomes - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
How can investors navigate a world reshaped by environmental pressures, technological disruption and geopolitical uncertainty? For BNP Paribas Asset Management, sustainability is central to answering that question.

Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer, discusses BNPP AM’s updated Global Sustainability Strategy, which sets out its priorities through to 2030. Building on the recent merger with AXA Investment Managers, the strategy embeds sustainability expertise across asset classes, using ESG research, due diligence and stewardship to achieve better-informed investment decisions.

Jane explains how integrating sustainability considerations with financial analysis can help investors identify material risks and opportunities, while recognising that clients have different objectives and preferences. From net zero alignment and carbon footprint reduction to positive contributions towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the approach aims to deliver tailored solutions and better client outcomes. “Our underlying ambition is to connect sustainable investment practices with long-term returns to help clients navigate a rapidly changing world.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into solutions across many asset classes can help investors achieve their sustainability ambitions.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Andrew Craig: Hello and welcome to this week’s BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis through the lens of sustainability on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing our new revised edition of the Global Sustainability Strategy. This provides the framework for action on the environmental, social and governance considerations that are embedded in our investment processes and are grounded in the conviction that traditional financial analysis alone is insufficient to capture all the risks and opportunities in today’s global economy.

I’m Andy Craig, Co-Head of the Investment Insights Centre, and I’m joined today by Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management. Welcome, Jane. Thank you for joining me today.

Jane Ambachtsheer: Thanks, Andy. It’s a pleasure to be here.

AC: Can you explain why we need [a] Global Sustainability Strategy?

JA: Well, sustainability, is a core part of how we invest and how we operate as an entity, so it’s important to have a strategy which really articulates how we go about doing that and what our objectives are.

Our previous sustainability strategy took us to 2026, so it was time for us to launch our new one, which we’ve recently done, which takes us out to 2030. The other important component of our new strategy is that it reflects our new entity having evolved and completed the integration of AXA Investment Managers, which now results in BNP Paribas Asset Management being one of the world’s 10 largest investors, with over €1.7 trillion in AUM (assets under management) across liquid and alternative asset classes and a local presence in 35 countries.

So given our new size and scale, it was also certainly time for an evolved approach to our global sustainability strategy.

AC: How does the sustainability strategy fit with the new corporate strategy for the combined entity? What are the key components and how has it evolved?

JA: When we launched at the beginning of 2026 ‘AMplify 2030’, the overall strategy for the new entity, we identified sustainability as one of the core enablers of how we’ll achieve that strategy. That then opened the door for us to publish this new specialised strategy really focused on sustainability.

As a long-term investor, we believe our client outcomes and real economy outcomes are closely connected. Resilient companies, well-functioning markets and sustainable economic growth are really fundamental to the long-term returns our clients seek.

Our strategy sets out our forward-looking priorities and milestones through [to] 2030 and is organised around the pillars of how we achieve that. So, a focus on the future and identifying system level risks around how we do ESG research and due diligence stewardship. Our approach around articulating responsible business conduct expectations which can lead to different exclusions. Our approach to sustainable products and solutions and also around leading by example – our approach to our own culture, sustainability education and the corporate responsibility practices that we’re adopting for our own entity.

AC: How does this new strategy enable us to deliver the best outcomes for our clients?

JA: That’s at the core of everything we do. Our strategy is built for clients, informed by our clients’ expectations and what we believe best practice to be in the global market.

The first [thing] is around making sure we’re helping our clients navigate a changing world. We know that the world is being reshaped by a number of powerful forces:

Environmental pressures: reshaping industries, supply chains, capital allocation, presenting both risks and opportunities

Technology and innovation: creating new technologies, disrupting business models, creating different opportunities

Demographic shifts: transforming labour markets, changes to inequality around the world, consumption patterns and ageing

Geopolitical developments: influencing trade, energy security, energy systems, our approach to climate in nature and access to resources around the world in this changing geopolitical framework.

These megatrends are inter-connected and we try and take a forward-looking lens to help our clients navigate them through understanding the risks and the opportunities that they present. So that’s the broader macro perspective.

We also believe that by integrating ESG considerations alongside financial analysis from a bottom-up asset class perspective, we can have better insights and make better decisions on behalf of our clients.

So sustainability is not a separate investment decision. It’s an important component of informed decision-making from an asset class basis. One of the new evolutions in terms of our overall framework is that we now embed sustainability expertise across the different asset classes.

We have a central team which I lead, which is really responsible for driving the overall strategy and ambition, with our global leadership team overseeing stewardship, supporting our clients, supporting our overall external commitments and reporting stewardship and CSR (corporate social responsibility).

Then we have a number of sustainability experts embedded across the organisation within the different asset classes, reporting up to the different CIOs to make sure we have best quality ESG data, tools, research capabilities embedded into our investment decisions.

That takes me to this final point – the fact that the strategy is built for clients. We have clients from all around the world. They have different objectives, regulatory environments and sustainability preferences. To be able to cater to those different clients, we offer a range of investment approaches and have the opportunity to build structured, custom[ised] sustainability portfolios for our clients.

We have clients optimising around their own preferences or the preferences of their beneficiaries, whether that’s measuring a positive contribution to some of the specific sustainable development goals, achieving certain net zero alignment outcomes, measuring and achieving a certain carbon footprint reduction target.

Different clients have different preferences. A big part of our strategy and our new size and scale is that we have the ability to bring the firm in terms of helping our clients to achieve the best outcomes for them, tapping into the resources across BNP Paribas Asset Management, but also often working in partnership with our colleagues and the broader resources across BNP Paribas Group.

AC: Of course, there are implications for us, BNP Paribas Asset Management as a firm and our own practices. Can you talk us through those?

JA: At the end of the day, we’re a people business. Our people, the intellectual capital that they bring, their relationships with clients, are the greatest opportunity for embedding sustainability into who we are, how we deliver investment outcomes and how we’re operating as an entity.

So we have a strong focus on integrating sustainability into our culture and our own corporate practices. This is one of the unique differentiators for the way we’re approaching sustainability as an organisation.

In terms of our own corporate reporting, we seek to meet and exceed the standards and expectations we’re setting for the companies we’re investing in. That’s really important to our credibility as an asset manager – to live up to those expectations where we’re asking others to do the same.

We have a strong focus on sustainability education and we’ve developed different training pathways for different portions of our population, depending on their existing levels of expertise and focus areas – whether it’s investment teams or legal teams or client-facing teams – to make sure they have the right opportunities around internal training, but also the opportunity to pursue external certifications or training programmes.

We also have a strong focus on being active in the communities where we’re operating –volunteering, philanthropy and developing partnerships with organisations in different communities. Also our annual Community Impact Week, where we have a volunteering fair that we set up around our offices around the world, which is really a chance to engage in some of those organisations, but also to further enhance our internal community, give employees an opportunity to spend time together and spend time giving back.

So there’s a rich ecosystem of things we’re doing internally around creating awareness, providing educational opportunities and volunteering engagement opportunities for colleagues across the different offices around the world in BNP Paribas Asset Management.

AC: Can you talk [to] us about the key upcoming milestones and how you’ll be measuring success as we go forward?

JA: The first and most important measure of success is that we’re able to deliver the outcomes that our clients are engaging us to deliver. That’s front and centre for what we’re doing around our overall sustainability strategy.

But we will also continue to provide our annual sustainability report, which includes progress across all of the different six pillars of our sustainability strategy, including stewardship, which is an area of significant interest for many of our clients. We’re happy to be able to continue to evolve the level of detail around our different approaches for stewardship, be it statistics across the whole platform, a rich range of different examples of company engagement, as well as public policy advocacy.

Later this year, we’ll also be updating our new Net Zero commitment as a combined entity. That’s something we’ve committed to publish and we’ll be sharing in the coming months. We’ll also be introducing our new progress monitor in our next annual report, where we share a number of key indicators that [we] will be measuring and reporting on every year.

We view communication on sustainability as an ongoing opportunity, both at a portfolio and at a firm level, and it’s something that we’ll continue to share updates on with clients as we go.

AC: Jane, thank you. We’ll be looking forward to joining you to talk about those updates as the months go by. Thank you very much for joining me today.

JA: Thanks so much for having me. It was a pleasure to be here.

AC: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you’d like to learn more about our Global Sustainability Strategy, please reach out to your BNP Paribas Asset Management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings you commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Andy Craig and Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

Please do join us again next time. Until then, take care.

articles.title: Supporting equity market transparency and considering market structure developments | Norges Bank Investment Management
articles.text:
We appreciate the opportunity to respond to the Financial Conduct Authority's consultation paper CP26/30 on supporting equity market transparency and considering market structure developments. Our response is based on our experience as an active participant in UK markets.
NBIM is the investment management division of the Norwegian Central Bank ("Norges Bank") and is responsible for investing the Norwegian Government Pension Fund Global in a globally diversified manner. NBIM held assets valued at NOK 21 268 billion as of 31 December 2025, of which GBP 86 billion was in UK equities and bonds of UK issuers.
As a long-term investor NBIM has an interest in well-functioning financial markets that facilitate the efficient allocation of capital and promote long-term economic growth. This means that we engage in market structure developments that affect market liquidity, transparency and execution quality.On market transparency and market structure
We agree with the FCA's assessment that UK equity markets remain liquid, resilient and efficient and the conclusion that the evidence presented does not justify steering trading towards specific execution mechanisms at this point. We agree that there is no evidence that would justify limiting investors' choices about where and how to trade, and that any such intervention should require a high evidential bar and a clear risk to market integrity.For us it is important that competition between execution mechanisms is fair, and that mechanisms performing the same economic function are treated alike. Transparency should show where liquidity resides and at what price, and we believe the introduction of a consolidated tape will serve as a coordinating mechanism in a fragmented market. Innovation should be accommodated and judged on its merits, because new mechanisms emerge to meet genuine investor needs. Our advice to regulators in other jurisdictions has been on the same basis. We support correcting asymmetries through functional equivalence and not by restricting the mechanisms concerned. The reformulated reference price waiver, which lets venues integrate midpoint orders within transparent order books, is an example of innovation accommodated on its merits.Spreads on UK central limit order books have widened on average, but spreads are one indicator among several and not a direct measure of trading cost, because execution draws on the full set of liquidity sources available.
As a large buy-side investor we judge market quality by the trading outcomes we achieve over time. Investors' implementation experience, and how it varies across participants and over time, is a quality indicator, but not one a regulator can observe in market data. We therefore support monitoring through a range of indicators combined with regular engagement with market participants, and would welcome the opportunity to contribute a buy-side perspective through the FCA's market intelligence channels.We support the FCA's recalibration of systematic internaliser (SI) quoting. Requiring SIs to quote the size they are generally prepared to trade, rather than a fixed minimum, ties published quotes to actual trading interest, and pre-trade transparency at those sizes supports price formation. Standard market size (SMS) is a reasonable ceiling for the obligation. It is not a hard line in the market, but trades well above it are of a different nature, negotiated and risk-managed case by case rather than quoted. Price improvement should remain available, as proposed.Our detailed response is set out in the appendix and covers the questions on which we have a distinct view. We thank you for considering our perspective and remain at your disposal should you wish to discuss these matters further.
Yours sincerely
Emil FramnesGlobal Head of Equity Trading and Transition
Vegard VikSpecial Advisor

Samuel Kofi Tetteh Baah

Samuel Kofi Tetteh Baah is an Economist with the Global Poverty and Inequality Data (GPID) team in the Development Data Group of the World Bank. He has been conducting research to improve the quality of global poverty estimates by incorporating new data and methodologies for poverty measurement. In particular, he has been actively involved in the technical work underpinning the new international poverty line. He collaborates with members of the GPID team to update the World Bank’s global and regional poverty numbers twice a year. He contributes to the publication of the Poverty and Shared Prosperity Report (PSPR), which is a biennial flagship report of the World Bank.

Samuel holds a Ph.D. in development economics from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) in Zürich, Switzerland. He holds a master’s degree in development economics from the University of Göttingen in Germany and a bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of Ghana.

articles.title: What can the sky tell us about economic recovery? The case of the West Bank & Gaza
articles.text:
Published on
Perspectives: MENA, Afghanistan, and Pakistan

What can the sky tell us about economic recovery? The case of the West Bank & Gaza

Gianluca Mele

Nur Nasser Eddin

Sahiti Sarva

Farhan Reynaldo Hutabarat

October 29, 2026

This page in:

English

العربية

English

العربية

Economic crises are usually measured through national accounts, employment surveys, business records, household data, and other traditional indicators. But what happens when conflict increases uncertainty while making conventional data harder to collect, precisely when quantitative evidence is most needed?
Satellite observations can help fill part of that information gap. A growing body of research has shown that indicators visible from space, particularly nighttime lights and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), can complement conventional measures of economic activity. Nighttime lights provide information on changes in radiance and electrified activity, while NO₂ offers a different signal linked more closely to fuel combustion, transport, power generation, and industry. Neither can replace official statistics, but together they can provide a more timely and geographically detailed view of economic change, including disruptions that unfold unevenly across locations or remain obscured within aggregate figures.[1]
One potentially useful nontraditional indicator is nitrogen dioxide, or NO₂. This short-lived air pollutant is produced largely through fuel combustion, including from vehicles, power generation, and industrial activity. Because these sources are closely connected to mobility, electricity use, and production, changes in NO₂ can provide an independent signal of combustion-intensive economic activity. Research has shown that satellite observations of NO₂ can help as a validation signal for economic activity, especially in the short term, particularly where conflict or other data limitations affect conventional statistics[2],[3]
The results for the West Bank and Gaza are revealing, although they must be interpreted carefully. Using weekly observations of NO₂ from the European Union’s Copernicus Satellite Sentinel-5P[4], we separated the underlying trend from seasonal patterns and short-term fluctuations. We then compared the average fitted trend during the 52 weeks before and after October 2023. Compared with the preceding year, NO₂ levels in the year following October 2023 were nearly 10 percent lower in Gaza and around 2 percent lower in the West Bank. In the West Bank, this decline is consistent with the sharp tightening of movement restrictions and reduced access to the Israeli labor market after October 2023, both of which constrained mobility and economic activity.

The decline in NO₂ did not reverse following the October 2025 ceasefire. Instead, the satellite record suggests that the disruption to economic activity, as approximated through NO₂ levels, persisted well beyond the initial shock and continued even as headline macroeconomic indicators in Gaza began to show modest improvement in early 2026. In fact, Gaza’s 3.1 percent year-on-year real GDP growth in Q1 2026 came from an exceptionally depressed base and indicated continued economic paralysis rather than meaningful recovery.
These findings do not tell us how much production or GDP was lost, but can help reveal the scale, breadth, and persistence of disruption. More specifically in this case, they indicate that the NO₂ levels associated with movement and fuel-burning activity remained unusually weak across much of the Palestinian territory during the conflict and after the ceasefire. Satellite observations therefore add texture to the picture provided by conventional economic data. They suggest that the disruption was not only deep, but also geographically widespread and persistent.
Nighttime lights provide a useful second lens through which to interpret these results. In Gaza, monthly radiance dropped immediately after the conflict began and did not return to pre-conflict levels, including after the ceasefire. In the West Bank, by contrast, nighttime lights remained broadly stable even as NO₂ declined.
The divergence between these two satellite indicators may offer interesting clues about the changing features of economic activity. Nighttime lights are typically sensitive to electricity availability and illumination after dark. NO₂ instead captures a different, though partly overlapping, range of activity associated with daytime road traffic, generators, machinery, power generation, and some forms of industrial production. In the West Bank, stable nighttime radiance alongside lower NO₂ could therefore be consistent with reduced daytime mobility and other fuel-combustion activity while electricity use remains broadly sustained. This interpretation is not conclusive, yet it points to an economy that may remain illuminated at night while moving, producing, and circulating less during the day. This pattern is consistent with the intensified movement restrictions and limited access to the Israeli labor market after October 2023, and with the broader economic deterioration described in our forthcoming Fall 2026 Economic Update.

These findings are informative, but the methodology has important limitations. NO₂ is not generated exclusively by economic activity, and the relationship between emissions and output can vary across sectors and locations. Weather conditions, cloud cover, atmospheric chemistry, fires, and changes in the composition of energy use can all affect observed concentrations.
Satellite indicators should therefore be treated as corroborating evidence, not as an alternative set of national accounts. Their value lies in data triangulation: official statistics quantify changes in measured output, while satellite observations can reveal their geographic reach, identify which physical activities may have weakened, and help assess whether improvements in headline figures correspond to a broader restoration of economic life. In contexts where conventional data are limited or slow to capture rapidly changing conditions, these tools could become a more systematic part of economic monitoring, helping policymakers identify disruptions, target responses more effectively, and distinguish early signs of recovery from statistical rebounds.
_________________________________________________________________________________
[1] The literature is large, but for instance, see Henderson, J. V., Storeygard, A., and Weil, D. N. (2012), “Measuring Economic Growth from Outer Space,” American Economic Review, 102(2), 994–1028, on Nighttime Lights. Or also Ezran, I., Morris, S. D., Rama, M., and Riera-Crichton, D. (2023), “Measuring Global Economic Activity Using Air Pollution,” World Bank Policy Research Working Paper No. 10445, on the use of satellite observations of NO₂ to improve the measurement of economic activity, combined with nighttime lights.
[2] Ezran, I., Morris, S. D., Rama, M., & Riera-Crichton, D. (2023). Measuring global economic activity using air pollution (Policy Research Working Paper No. 10445). World Bank.
[3] Guo, Z., Abushama, H., Siddig, K., Kirui, O. K., Abay, K., & You, L. (2024). Monitoring indicators of economic activities in Sudan amidst ongoing conflict using satellite data. Defence and Peace Economics, 35(8), 992-1008.
[4] Copernicus Sentinel-5P is a European Union satellite that monitors the atmosphere worldwide, providing frequent measurements of air pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide; https://www.copernicus.eu/en

articles.title: View from the markets: The earnings season has been good, but is it good enough?
articles.text:
FRONT OF MIND | ARTICLE – 2 min read
View from the markets: The earnings season has been good, but is it good enough?

By
DANIEL MORRIS 30.10.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
Sector drivers

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

At first blush, there is little to complain about regarding the third-quarter earnings results so far (about half of the companies in the S&P 500 and MSCI Europe have reported). Compared to the third quarter in 2025, profits have risen by 26% for the S&P 500 and by 40%(!) for Europe, with double-digit figures for other major indices, based on data from FactSet (see Exhibit 1). This is well above historical norms.

The worry is that those values are not far off what was expected by analysts, and in one case it was below. Earnings have come in only 2% better than expected for the S&P 500. Typically, earnings surprises (how much better or worse results are versus consensus) run in the 3-4% range. Over the previous few quarters, they were even higher. This quarter few indices have matched that.

The chart shows clearly what the source of the disappointment has been: technology. The surprise for the Nasdaq 100 index is -3% and for emerging market (EM) tech stocks it is -8%. The disappointments in emerging markets were almost entirely driven by tech stocks; results for the other sectors were 1% better.

There are two questions: Are these disappointments surprising and how much do they matter?

Given not only how high expectations have been for technology stocks, and how rapidly the artificial intelligence theme is developing, it is not surprising that companies have reported results that are further off the mark than is typically the case.

Though there has been some disappointment in the short term (which will drive the short-term performance of the stock), the more important consideration for investors is the medium-term outlook (which will determine the stock’s medium-term path).

It is worth recalling that consensus estimates for Nasdaq 100 earnings growth in 2027 is 35% and for emerging market technology stocks it is 39%. Even if actual results are a few percentage points lower, and if valuations do not change significantly, indices would typically appreciate in line with earnings.

Sector drivers

It is not only the tech sector that has boosted EPS (earnings-per-share) growth rates. Higher energy prices have contributed to strong results for indices like MSCI Europe and Russell Value. Excluding the energy sector, earnings growth for MSCI Europe is a (still good) 17%. But even setting aside the gains from tech and higher oil prices, results across other sectors are robust. The automobile industry continues to be a drag on the consumer discretionary sector, but most of the others are seeing high single or double-digit earnings growth (see Exhibit 2).

Whether this broadening in earnings continues, or even accelerates, will partly depend on the rate of adoption of AI technologies. There is already significant anecdotal evidence of companies finding meaningful productivity improvements through AI. One example is insurance companies reducing their claims review times and credit losses by using micro-expression recognition technology.

Stories of CFOs becoming alarmed by high AI bills also suggests adoption is accelerating. This will be critical not only for the future rate of non-tech company earnings growth, but also for the hyperscalers, as they look for the return on their massive capital expenditure.

articles.title: Staying Invested: After The Worst Day, The Best Day May Come Quickly
articles.text:
Staying Invested: After The Worst Day, The Best Day May Come Quickly

The S&P 500’s worst day and the best day that followed
have something in common: you can’t predict either one.

October 2026

The S&P 500’s worst day and the best day that followed have something in common: you can’t predict either one. The table below underscores the risk of stepping out of the market during periods of heightened volatility. While selling after a sharp decline may feel like a way to avoid further losses, some of the market’s biggest gains have historically occurred soon after its biggest drops. For example, in 2020 and 2025, the S&P 500’s best day after the year’s worst came just six and three trading days later, respectively.
Not every major downturn is followed by a quick rebound — some recoveries take much longer. In 2018, the best day came more than ten months after February’s big drop. The real takeaway is that investors rarely know when a rebound will come, which makes timing an exit and re-entry very difficult. Successfully avoiding the worst day and re-entering at the ideal moment means being right twice. Staying invested helps ensure participation in the recovery, which can be critical to long-term returns.

articles.title: Anti-Corruption After The Plenum
articles.text:
Anti-Corruption After The Plenum

Andrew Batson

Gavekal Dragonomics | 30 Oct 2026

2026 has been another extraordinarily busy year for the Communist Party’s anti-corruption investigators. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection is still churning through tens of thousands of cases every month, including those of high-ranking current and former officials—underscoring once again that no one is safe from its reach. All this effort is aimed not only at rooting out financial impropriety but also at building a system for enforcing compliance with central directives, which top leader Xi Jinping sees as a widespread problem. He has devoted the Party’s Fifth Plenum, which concluded Thursday in Beijing, to “advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance,” meaning how the Party selects, manages and disciplines officials.The most important issue for Xi is the effective top-down transmission of orders. “Implementing the major decisions and plans of the Party Central Committee is a basic requirement of the Party’s political discipline and political rules,” Xi said in a speech to the CCDI in January, which was published in full shortly before the plenum. “We cannot merely shout slogans, still less say one thing and do another. Anyone who violates these requirements must be held accountable.” The transformation of anti-corruption into a system of political supervision, already well advanced, was confirmed by the plenum, which agreed to “integrate conduct improvement and discipline enforcement with anti-corruption measures.”
