articles.title: International Law Enforcement Seizes Virtualine Bulletproof Hosting
articles.text:
Summary
The FBI Washington Field Office, working with international law enforcement partners, seized the domain virtualine.net, which, according to the Justice Department, was used to facilitate prolific criminal activity.
Virtualine, a “bulletproof” hosting provider that openly advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums, hosted infrastructure tied to ransomware operators, infostealers, carding and credential-theft forums, scam operations, and the distribution of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), according to the government.
According to the Justice Department, Virtualine accepted direct, unhosted bitcoin payments from criminal customers and laundered the proceeds to conceal their origin, the government says.
On October 27, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia and the FBI Washington Field Office announced the court-authorized seizure of virtualine.net, the primary web domain of Virtualine, a bulletproof hosting (BPH) provider that enabled a wide range of global cybercrime. The investigation was conducted with assistance from Germany’s Polizei Hessen, the Netherlands’ Politie Midden-Nederland, and the U.K.’s National Crime Agency.The private sector also supported the investigation, and in collaboration with OverRIPE, a coalition of independent security researchers and professionals focused on malicious hosting threats, Chainalysis provided intelligence support to international law enforcement in the disruption of Virtualine’s infrastructure.What is bulletproof hosting?Bulletproof hosting (BPH) providers are web and server hosting services that deliberately ignore abuse complaints, DMCA takedown notices, and law enforcement requests. By offering offshore infrastructure that resists disruption, BPH providers enable persistent criminal operations, including ransomware command-and-control servers, phishing kits, malware distribution, carding shops, infostealer logs, and illicit marketplaces.Virtualine (also known as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech) openly advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums like Exploit.in and HackForums. In one September 2024 post on Exploit.in, Virtualine told a user: “You can use Virtualine for all illegal/black hat activities (including phishing, carding, email spam, port scanning and all others) except for child contents and terrorism activities.” In June 2025 on HackForums, the provider boasted that “Virtualine ignored more abuse than your last three therapists.”In March 2026, Virtualine began marketing an “additional protection plan” that promised, upon receipt of a law enforcement request, to migrate a customer’s criminal infrastructure to a shell company unaffiliated with Virtualine before reactivating the server.Despite publicly disclaiming the hosting of child sexual abuse material, prosecutors accuse Virtualine of knowingly hosting a criminal online forum that sold access to, sexually suggestive, and sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults, and promoted a hack-for-hire service to illicitly obtain intimate content from victims’ accounts.On-chain exposure to the global cybercrime ecosystemVirtualine accepted direct Bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses — a setup that allowed criminal customers to pay without triggering compliance checks at hosted exchanges. According to the Justice Department, Virtualine then laundered the proceeds to obscure their origin.As the Chainalysis Reactor graph below shows, Virtualine’s on-chain footprint has direct exposure to a broad cross-section of the cybercrime ecosystem, including ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, and scam and phishing addresses.The above activity illustrates the systemic role BPH providers play in sustaining the cybercrime economy: a single piece of infrastructure can simultaneously support ransomware extortion, credential theft, fraud, and CSAM distribution, with crypto serving as the common settlement layer.What this means for compliance teamsToday’s action underscores that bulletproof hosting providers are foundational infrastructure that allows ransomware, infostealers, and online fraud to scale. For crypto compliance teams, exposure to BPH payment addresses can be an early signal of broader downstream risk, as those same wallets frequently touch ransomware proceeds, scam infrastructure, and cybercrime marketplace flows. Chainalysis has labeled the relevant cryptocurrency addresses associated with Virtualine in our product suite.FAQsWhat is Virtualine?Virtualine is an offshore bulletproof hosting (BPH) provider — also known as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech — that offered web, cloud, and server hosting services while openly ignoring abuse complaints and law enforcement requests. It advertised its services directly to criminals on forums like Exploit.in and HackForums.What role did cryptocurrency play?Virtualine accepted direct bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without flagging their funds through hosted exchange compliance programs. Virtualine then laundered those proceeds to conceal their origin. On-chain analysis shows Virtualine’s addresses were connected to ransomware strains, infostealers, cybercrime forums, and scam infrastructure.What is bulletproof hosting?Bulletproof hosting is a category of web and server hosting that deliberately ignores abuse reports, DMCA notices, and law enforcement requests, providing persistent infrastructure for criminal operations such as ransomware, phishing, malware distribution, and illicit marketplaces.What should compliance teams do?Compliance teams should treat exposure to known bulletproof hosting payment addresses as a meaningful risk signal, given these services’ direct ties to ransomware, infostealers, and fraud infrastructure. Chainalysis has labeled the relevant addresses in its product suite. articles.title: How the World Bank supports projects with global benefits
articles.text:
Consulting Report

28 Oct 2026

How the World Bank supports projects with global benefits

Commissioned by the German Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ)

How can countries be encouraged to invest in projects that benefit the wider world? The World Bank’s Framework for Financial Incentives (FFI) offers an innovative approach by making financing more attractive for projects addressing climate change, biodiversity loss and other global challenges. This independent assessment, funded by BMZ and implemented by GIZ, finds encouraging early progress and identifies practical ways to strengthen the framework’s reach and effectiveness.

Building on Oxford Economics’ expertise in financing global public goods, this assessment examines the FFI’s early progress. Drawing on project data and consultations with project teams and experts, it explores how projects are selected, how financial support is allocated and where the framework can add the most value.The FFI helps countries invest in projects that deliver benefits both at home and across borders. For projects financed by the World Bank’s International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), it offers additional borrowing capacity, longer repayment periods and financial support that reduces borrowing costs.

Across its first five funding rounds, the framework received 48 applications and approved 33, covering all seven World Bank regions. Climate change was the most commonly addressed challenge. Approved projects generally scored more highly on expected cross-border benefits than rejected projects, suggesting that support is reaching projects with greater potential global benefits.

Feedback from project teams and technical experts is encouraging. They report that incentives have helped ease funding constraints, increase project scale and support more ambitious designs. The framework has also encouraged teams to consider cross-border benefits more systematically and opened discussions with borrowing countries about investments whose wider value might otherwise receive less attention.

The findings also highlight opportunities for further development. Many initial applications involved projects already well advanced in planning, limiting the framework’s scope to strengthen their cross-border benefits from the outset. Earlier engagement, better tools for measuring these benefits and clearer assessments of financing needs could help target incentives more effectively.

articles.title: What is a 401(k)? Understanding retirement plans | BlackRock should work!
articles.text:
What is a 401(k) plan?

A 401(k) plan is an investment account offered by employers to help employees save for retirement. Typically, you have to be working full-time and be employed a year somewhere to be eligible. The contribution limit is $23,500 in 2025, with an additional $7,500 “catch-up” if you’re 50 or older. Traditional 401(k) plans use pre-tax dollars, while Roth 401(k) plans use after-tax dollars.

Key takeaways

01

Understand the rules around eligibility and contributions
Eligibility typically requires being at least 21 years old, working full-time and having a year of service. The contribution limit for 2025 is $23,500, with an additional $7,500 for those 50 or older.

02

Know the differences between traditional and Roth 401(k)s
Traditional 401(k) plans use pre-tax dollars, while Roth 401(k) plans use after-tax dollars. Traditional plans require taxes to be paid upon withdrawal, whereas Roth plans offer tax-free withdrawals under certain conditions.

03

Look into your employer’s matching and vesting policies
Employers often contribute to employees' 401(k) accounts through matching contributions. The specifics of matching and vesting rules vary by employer, and employees should consider these provisions before changing jobs to avoid missing out on extra savings.

401(k) plans

What is a 401(k) plan and who is eligible?

A 401(k) plan is an investment account offered by your employer that allows you to save for retirement. If your company offers a 401(k) plan, it may have certain eligibility requirements. While these requirements vary by company, some employees may be excluded from participating if they are not at least 21 years of age or have not completed a year of service with the company.
If you’re considering a job offer, be sure to ask about the company’s retirement plan, including any waiting period.
How much can I contribute to a 401(k) plan?
401(k) plan accounts have higher contribution limits than individual retirement accounts (IRAs). As of 2025 you are able to set aside up to $23,500 across your 401(k) plan accounts.
To boost your contributions even further, you might consider catch-up contributions. If you are 50 or older, you can contribute an extra $7,500 (up to $31,000 total in 2025) to your 401(k) account. This increased limit can help boost your savings as you near the retirement finish line. But you don’t actually have to be “behind” in your savings to take advantage of catch-up contributions.
What is the difference between a traditional and Roth 401(k) plan?
There are two common kinds of 401(k) plans: traditional and Roth. These plans have some similarities: They are subject to the same annual contribution limit and may offer the same investment options. However, traditional and Roth 401(k) plans differ in terms of the tax benefits they offer.

Traditional

Roth

Contributions

Made on a pre-tax basis

Made on an after-tax basis

Withdrawals

Subject to income tax

Tax-free after age 59 ½*

*Only if the distribution satisfies certain conditions, for example that it has been at least five years since the first Roth contribution, or that the participant is disabled. IRS.gov. Data as of Jul. 2024.
A traditional 401(k) plan is sometimes referred to as a pre-tax 401(k) plan. You contribute to the plan with before-tax dollars. Because you don’t pay taxes on the money you put into the plan, you must pay taxes (both federal and most state income taxes) when you withdraw it. This structure could be an advantage if you’re in a high tax bracket today but expect to be in a lower one when retired.
With a Roth 401(k) plan, the opposite is true. You save after-tax dollars in the account. Because you’ve already paid taxes on what you’re saving, your withdrawals are considered qualified distributions and won’t be taxed as long as you meet both of the following criteria:

You’ve had the account for at least five years.
You begin to make withdrawals either after you’ve turned 59½ or due to disability.

How does 401(k) plan matching work?
One major benefit of 401(k) plans is that employers often contribute to your account and “match” what you save. Each employer has its own methods and rules for how it makes matching 401(k) plan contributions. Importantly, a match does not necessarily mean that an employer matches your contributions dollar for dollar. Instead, employers typically match up to a certain percentage of your salary or your contribution. For instance, the average employer 401(k) match is 4.6% of an employee’s salary, according to the 2024 How America Saves Report.
If your company offers a match, be sure to consider taking advantage of this benefit. It could be a simple and effective way to boost your retirement savings.
One important note: Employers often require you to wait for a certain amount of time before their contributions to your account “vest,” meaning they become yours to keep. Consider this provision before changing jobs so that you don’t inadvertently miss out on extra savings for your retirement.
When can I withdraw from my 401(k) plan?
You can start to withdraw your savings penalty-free when you reach age 59 ½. Taking out your savings before that time could cost you an extra 10% on top of what you’d normally pay in state and federal taxes.
When it’s time to start using your savings, be sure to consider the tax implications. In addition, once you turn 73, you typically have to withdraw a minimum amount annually to comply with distribution requirements.
401(k) plans can be very useful tools in saving for retirement, particularly if you take advantage of features that your plan may offer to help maximize your savings. And the sooner you start saving in your 401(k) plan, the longer any investment earnings have to produce earnings of their own.

Wrap up

Top questions about 401(k)s

First, you don’t have to actually be “behind” in your savings to take advantage of this benefit. If you are 50 or older, you can contribute an extra $7,500 (up to $31,000 total) to your 401(k) account which can help boost your savings as you near retirement.

Because you don’t pay taxes on the money you put into the plan, you must pay taxes (both federal and most state income taxes) when you withdraw it. Note that once you turn 73, you typically have to withdraw a minimum amount annually to comply with distribution requirements.

Employers often require you to wait for a certain amount of time before their contributions to your account “vest,” meaning they become yours to keep. Consider this provision before changing jobs so that you don’t inadvertently miss out on extra savings for your retirement.

Because you’ve already paid taxes on what you’re saving, your withdrawals are considered qualified distributions and won’t be taxed as long as you meet both of the following criteria:

You’ve had the account for at least five years.
You begin to make withdrawals either after you’ve turned 59½ or due to disability.

Saving for retirement can be complicated – but it doesn’t have to be. Arm yourself with the information you need to make the best decisions for your financial future.

articles.title: What’s the Difference Between a 20% Chance and a 0% Chance?
articles.text:
Insights / Research / What’s the Difference Between a 20% Chance and a 0% Chance?

Written by:

Zack Pokorny
Research Associate

Topics

Prediction Markets

research • October 30, 2026

What’s the Difference Between a 20% Chance and a 0% Chance?

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. Prediction market skeptics are crowing (again) after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva upset Flávio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s runoff election on Oct. 25. Heading into the election, prediction markets had Bolsonaro holding a 75% to 80% chance of winning the election to Lula’s 11% to 20% probability after Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil’s presidential election on Oct. 4. Lula ended up winning the runoff and remains Brazil’s president, and Bolsonaro fled to the United States. Traditional polls had shown a statistical dead heat. The polling firm Datafolha had the two candidates tied at 50% each, while AtlasIntel/Bloomberg had Bolsonaro ahead 51.1% to 48.9% and an average compiled by The Rio Times put Bolsonaro at 50.9% to Lula’s 49.1%. Lula ultimately won with 51.8% of valid votes to Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, so most polls leaned slightly toward Bolsonaro and understated Lula’s share by one to four points. Even so, the polls never suggested Bolsonaro was a heavy favorite. Prediction markets offered a far more opinionated stance on the outcome of the election compared to polls that, when compensating for margin of error, offered no tangible takeaway. This setup was similar to that of the 2024 U.S. presidential election, where polls showed an ultra-close race with Kamala Harris barely in the lead while Polymarket gave Trump roughly a 60% chance of winning, a figure that stood at 62% on Election Day. The difference was the ultimate outcome. In 2024, the markets’ bet that polls were understating the Republican candidate’s chances paid off, while in Brazil the equivalent bet failed. This gap is where critics point to an inaccuracy and apparent lack of efficacy in prediction markets’ implied odds. OUR TAKE The picture is not as black and white as the skeptics make it out to be. The take that prediction markets failed in this setting breaks down when taking into consideration what these markets actually tell you: predictions on probabilities. What the detractors miss here is that implied odds are not an implied prophecy. A prediction market price is a statement about frequency, not a guarantee that something will or won’t happen (e.g. a probability >50% does not imply the event must always happen just because the market suggests it is more likely than not). A contract trading at 80% is saying that if you could replay this event many times, the outcome would occur about four times in five, and fail the fifth. A 20% chance is expected to happen one time in five, not never. Lula winning at roughly 11% to 20% was a longshot, not an impossibility, and one longshot landing tells you very little about whether the price was wrong. Human brains struggle to cope with this idea when looking at probabilities. Psychologists have documented for decades that people judge probability with mental shortcuts, and that these shortcuts lead to systematic and predictable errors (see Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in Science, 1974). The problem shows up in elections specifically. In a Journal of Politics study, Sean J. Westwood, Solomon Messing, and Yphtach Lelkes found through experiments that probabilistic forecasts increase certainty about an outcome and confuse many readers. When one candidate is ahead, win probabilities convey substantially more confidence than vote share estimates do. The authors tied this observation to 2016, when forecasts gave Hillary Clinton a 70% to 99% chance of winning and left voters thinking the race was far less competitive than it was. A 60/40 or 80/20 market reads to many people as a verdict, when it is still a description of uncertainty. This misconception turns Bolsonaro’s 75% to 80% probability into “the markets said Bolsonaro would win,” and a Lula victory into a breakdown in market efficacy, when an 80/20 market is still just a description of some uncertainty. Historically, over many markets, prediction platforms’ prices hold up. Kalshi Research tested more than 2.2 million resolved markets, and found prices generally behave like genuine probabilities, with a contract at 70 cents resolving “Yes” about 70% of the time. The calibration plots below show this. Each dot groups markets by their price (horizontal axis) and shows how often those markets actually resolved “Yes” (vertical axis). The dashed diagonal is perfect calibration, where a 70% price means a 70% hit rate. The dots hug that line, and they sit closest to it in the panels measured one week and one day before resolution, which is the window most relevant to the Brazil runoff. Prices are also more accurate as resolution nears, with Brier scores (a standard error measure where lower is better) falling from roughly 0.08 to 0.09 at three months out to about 0.02 at close. This shows that even in the markets that were well calibrated, the favorite didn’t always win. For elections, the favored outcome came in about 90% of the time across most horizons, which means roughly one favorite in 10 lost. The authors also note that in a race with more than two viable candidates, a favorite priced at 60 cents should win only about 60% of the time, and that near-perfect hit rates would point to underpriced favorites rather than better forecasting.

Source: Kalshi Research (https://kalshi.com/research/kalshi-research-calibration.pdf) Brazil’s stock market made a similar bet to that of prediction market odds. After Bolsonaro won the first round, the Ibovespa index jumped almost 8% on Oct. 5, from 192,138 to 206,912, and peaked at a close of 209,067 on Oct. 9. It chopped around this level until after the runoff, when it fell 13.9% in a single session, from 205,083 to 176,608, and kept sliding. As of Oct. 29, it was trading below 170,000 which is about 17% below its pre-runoff close and below where it stood before the first round of the election. The Brazilian Real also lost more than 8% after an election result the market seemingly did not expect. Equity investors didn’t have a secret read on Lula that the prediction markets missed. Everyone seemed to price Bolsonaro as the favorite. Taking this into consideration, prediction markets worked as a viable hedge. A trader long Brazilian stocks could have bought Lula “Yes” contracts as insurance. A contract priced near 20 cents paid five times the stake, so the Lula position would have paid out many multiples as the Brazilian stock market entered a free fall. A 20% price was never a claim that Lula couldn’t win. It was the market rate for protection against this outcome. The data suggests prediction markets were not wrong in the way their doubters are claiming. A price of 75% to 80% means the favorite loses one time in four or five, and Kalshi illustrated this is roughly the case in aggregate. Then again, if the election was stolen, as Bolsonaro has claimed, maybe the markets were wrong, at least about the ultimate outcome (even if they were right about his popularity).

articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Video: Why China's equity markets have lagged (6 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Why bank stocks are falling amid rising rates (6 mins)Video: The AI Show |The AI trade's two-sided test (4 mins)Thought of the dayRisk sentiment improved this week ahead of the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision due today and megacap tech companies’ September-quarter results. Investors found solace in recent data confirming the strength of underlying AI demand. The S&P 500 has risen 1.3% over the past two sessions, while the 10-year US Treasury yield edged up to just above 5%.The Fed is widely expected to keep rates unchanged at 3.75-4% today, following recent comments from several officials that supported a gradual approach. Still, investors will watch how Chair Kevin Warsh explains the central bank’s rationale after data for September showed a reacceleration in inflation. Current fed funds futures indicate three additional 25-basis-point rate hikes over the next 12 months.Our view is that current market pricing of Fed tightening is too hawkish, and the backdrop for equities, fixed income, and gold remains constructive.Robust earnings growth should outweigh monetary tightening for equities. The upcoming tech earnings should provide more evidence on the sustainability and monetization of AI demand, while recent results have been in line with our view that AI should continue to be a key driver of profit growth. Additionally, we expect cyclical segments of the market to see robust earnings growth as manufacturing activity remains in expansion, while healthy aggregate consumption should offer another pillar of support. We therefore expect the S&P 500 to continue to move higher over the next six to 12 months as the Fed tightens modestly. In fact, the average gain in the S&P 500 one year after the first Fed hike was 10.8% over the past 16 hiking cycles since 1954.Quality bonds offer appealing income and diversification benefits. US Treasury yields may continue to face upward pressure amid uncertain geopolitical situations, persistent inflation, additional debt supply from hyperscalers, and ongoing fiscal concerns. But we think what’s more important for investors is that current yields offer sufficient income to compensate for the risk of further volatility. Starting yields have historically been a good indicator of subsequent total returns, and we think a potential Fed repricing could lead to a decline in Treasury yields, leaving scope for capital gains in bonds. The recent performance of Treasuries also suggests that quality fixed income is being perceived as a “haven asset” again, offering diversification and stability in a portfolio.Gold remains a strategic portfolio diversifier amid structural support. While gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded net outflows last week, longer-term fundamentals for bullion remain solid, and we think structural demand should support higher prices. Central bank purchases continue to be strong, Chinese buying is robust, and concerns about rising public debt levels and debt-servicing costs have not abated. With structural dip buyers likely establishing a floor around the current USD 4,000/oz level, we think gold prices have limited downside from here and maintain our view that further pullbacks offer opportunities to add exposure.So, while more Fed hikes remain in store in the coming months, we think the current backdrop remains favorable. We do not believe a measured tightening cycle will derail the US economy, and investors should maintain diversified equity exposure and use the rise in yields to add selectively to quality bonds. We also believe gold remains an effective portfolio diversifier.

articles.title: Daily: Build resilience as tech volatility rises
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, interest rates (4 mins)Video: Why China's equity markets have lagged (6 mins)Thought of the dayMarket sentiment came under pressure on Friday as tech earnings raised fresh concerns about capital expenditure. Stocks in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan fell after a tech-led selloff on Wall Street, while Nasdaq futures were pointing 2% lower ahead of the US market open on Friday. Signs that the US may resume military strikes against Iran also pushed oil prices higher, with Brent crude trading at around USD 117/bbl at the time of writing.But further volatility does not make retreating from markets an effective way to protect portfolios from potential drawdowns, in our view. We continue to see scope for equity gains overall and believe investors should focus on building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech.AI demand remains robust, but we see a rising risk of mid-cycle capex indigestion. Weaker-than-expected growth in megacap tech companies’ core businesses was at the center of investors’ concerns, as markets questioned how the next phase of AI capex would be funded amid continued signals of higher spending from hyperscalers. We are seeing a shift in the funding mix for AI investment after four years of relying on hyperscalers’ cash flows, with incremental capex increasingly drawing on debt, equity, leases, and supplier-backed financing. In our view, the health of underlying demand remains a key metric to watch. Latest results showing accelerating cloud revenue growth and expanding advanced orders for cloud computing capacity point to still-robust demand for AI infrastructure, but we acknowledge the rising risk of mid-cycle capex indigestion, as financing and execution risks are emerging in the more capital-intensive areas of the AI buildout.Resilient growth underpins opportunities beyond US tech. The US economy expanded at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, ahead of the 3.1% estimate and up from 2.2% in the second quarter. This growth has helped keep inflation elevated, but the economy’s resilience also supports the outlook for sectors beyond tech. In fact, the equal-weighted S&P 500 has outperformed its market capitalization-weighted counterpart year to date, suggesting that an improving cyclical backdrop, healthy consumer spending, and structural trends—such as the growing longevity industry—are also supporting market performance. Outside the US, robust earnings growth across the Eurozone and Asia gives investors a broader range of opportunities to participate in potential further equity gains.Quality bonds can help stabilize portfolios. As equities have come under pressure, bonds have rallied, with the 10-year US Treasury yield falling by 37 basis points in October. This shows that quality fixed income is once again serving as a portfolio stabilizer, and we believe still-elevated yields provide sufficient income to compensate for the risk of potential yield volatility. Bonds could also benefit if inflation moderates or economic growth weakens, adding valuable diversification to portfolios.So, with cash unlikely to overcome the combined portfolio challenges of inflation, taxes, longer lifespans, and withdrawals, staying invested remains critical for the long term. Within tech, we continue to like leading megacaps, defensive names in payment networks and consumer electronics, as well as quality semis and hardware companies. But those with an outsized allocation to US tech should diversify across sectors and regions. We also believe investors should maintain a well-diversified portfolio that includes exposure to quality fixed income. Those willing and able to tolerate relevant risks can consider broad commodities and hedge funds to access additional return drivers.

Investment Objective
Our U.S. Broad Market High Yield Strategy seeks to maximize excess returns versus the Bloomberg High Yield 1% Issuer Capped Index over the long term.1

Investment Philosophy
In our Broad Market High Yield Strategy, we seek to earn 125 bps of alpha with a tracking error budget of 200 bps versus the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. High-Yield 1% Issuer Capped Index.
We expect tracking error based on historical volatility measured over a long term period to occur from holding position sizes in portfolios that differ from the issuer’s weighting in the benchmark and from holding positions in issuers that are not in the benchmark.
PGIM believes that actively managed high yield bond portfolios, constructed from the bottom up using methodical, research-based subsector and security selection, can lead to consistent outperformance versus the broad high yield index with a high information ratio.
PGIM attempts to achieve this through well-diversified portfolios of performing credits that are carefully researched. Intensive fundamental research is conducted by a large and experienced internal credit research staff to identify strong and improving credits.
The size and experience of the research organization permit us to apply intense focus on individual securities identified from a broad pool of investment opportunities.
Portfolios are then actively managed to capture the best opportunities and minimize credit losses, within an environment of disciplined risk management oversight.
We use a sector based approach, whereby portfolio managers specialize on certain industries (typically 4 to 6 each). As a result of not having to cover the entire universe of industries, our sector PMs can (a) more deeply understand the issuers and trading levels in their sectors to better evaluate relative value and more quickly respond to market opportunities and (b) can have more frequent dialogue with, and as a result get more favorable treatment from, traders at brokers/dealers for secondary trades and also from capital markets/syndicates individuals at underwriters for new issues.
We inherently think long term and are typically patient investors. Also, our institutional client base tends to be more stable (less flows). These two attributes enable us to take advantage of market opportunities because, on a relative basis versus peers, we tend to be liquidity providers as opposed to liquidity takers. In a world of less liquidity, we can take advantage of available market inefficiencies.

articles.title: A unique vantage point − speech by Nathanaël Benjamin
articles.text:
A unique vantage point − speech by Nathanaël Benjamin

Given at the ISDA Derivatives Trading and Treasury Forum

Published on
01 October 2026

Nat Benjamin sets out how the Bank of England has a unique vantage point from which to understand the UK’s ever more complex and interconnected financial system, and how such surveillance can be used to strengthen its stability. He then illustrates this with gilt repo market resilience as one policy area that has benefited from that mindset.

Speech
Why surveillance matters more than ever
Good afternoon, and my thanks to ISDA for inviting me to speak at this year’s London Derivatives Trading and Treasury Forum. It is a pleasure to be here.
ISDA has played a key role in shaping the modern derivatives market through its work on legal standards, market infrastructure, data, and risk management. At a time when markets are becoming more interconnected and increasingly vital for the provision of financial services to the real economy, that contribution matters more than ever.
The nature of risks to financial stability has changed a lot over the last two decades.
Before the global financial crisis, the attention of authorities was often focused primarily on individual banks. The resilience of individual institutions is still fundamental today, of course. But many of the vulnerabilities that matter today emerge not within a single bank, but from interactions across non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), markets, and funding structures.
Recent episodes have demonstrated that stress can originate in one part of the financial system and propagate rapidly through funding markets, collateral demands, margin calls, and leveraged positions. And the actions taken by individual market players can, even when rational from their own perspective, combine to amplify stress across the system. We have talked about these risks on numerous occasions – including in this forum.
As the risks have changed, so has our financial stability perspective, adopting a resolutely system-wide lens that can observe their complex interconnections and interactions.
That scrutinising lens, how surveillance is evolving, and what it can help us achieve, is the first thing I’m going to talk about today. And then I will turn to one policy area which has benefited from that mindset: the resilience of gilt repo markets.
A unique vantage point
Over the past decade, the post-crisis reform agenda has transformed the information available to authorities.
One of the shortcomings identified following the global financial crisis was the lack of visibility into activity in important financial markets, and into the interconnections between market participants. Transaction-level reporting was introduced in response, allowing authorities to better understand how markets function and how market participants interact.
Today we can draw on transaction-level reporting across derivatives, securities financing, and trading activity, together with fund-level reporting and supervisory data. We've been using these insights for years to better understand how markets function, how risks propagate, and where vulnerabilities may be building across the financial system. They have informed our analysis during episodes such as the “dash for cash” that followed the outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic, the stresses in energy markets following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, or the 2022 gilt market disruption. Yet as the nature of vulnerabilities changes, the way we use this data has changed too. Having access to millions of transaction records is not the same as being able identify how shocks might propagate through a complex web of funding relationships, collateral chains, and leveraged investors.
No single reporting regime was designed to provide a complete view of the financial system. Each dataset offers a different lens. As the UK’s central bank with macro- and micro-prudential authority, we have a unique vantage point that allows us to bring multiple sources of data together, building out a picture of chain reactions that would otherwise be unforeseeable.
Our institutional set-up makes us particularly well placed to do so for UK markets. As a participant in these core markets ourselves, and through the gathering of market intelligence from that position, we obtain invaluable insight that brings colour and context to reporting data. And through close collaboration with our colleagues at the Financial Conduct Authority, we can bring together information from derivatives markets, securities-financing markets, trading activity, fund reporting, and prudential supervision within a shared analytical framework.
This allows us to answer questions that would have been much harder to address in the past. We are increasingly able to identify where leverage resides, how it is financed, who is providing that financing, and how funding and liquidity shocks might propagate through the financial system. These capabilities are helping us to understand the behaviour of leveraged market participants and to evaluate how changes in market structure, such as greater central clearing, broader clearing access, or minimum haircut frameworks, could affect the resilience of core funding markets.
To show what a system-wide perspective can do, let's turn to a sector where these insights have been invaluable: hedge funds.
Data, and the case of hedge fund leverage
Increasingly, hedge funds contribute to liquidity, price discovery, and risk-bearing capacity across important financial markets. The financial stability question for us is not the fact that they use leverage to support their activities – that is a commercial matter entirely up to them, and indeed well-managed leverage is a positive thing for the economy. The question is rather about where that leverage resides, how concentrated it is, how it is financed, and how it interacts with the rest of the financial system.
Those questions cannot be answered using any single dataset, or by looking at hedge funds in isolation. They require combining transaction-level data, fund-level reporting, supervisory intelligence, market engagement, and deep market expertise.
Doing so has already generated insights that would have been difficult to obtain in the past. For example, in our July 2026 Financial Stability Report (FSR) we showed that, over the past four years, hedge funds have shifted from being net cash lenders to net cash borrowers in repo markets across a range of currencies, reflecting the important role of the banks as by far the major providers of leverage.footnote [1] We were also able to show that growth in hedge funds' gilt repo borrowing has coincided with increasing futures open interest, consistent with an expansion in basis trading activity. We were able to spot and track the growth of the cash-futures basis trade in the UK over the last 18 months – which was corroborated by our market intelligence.footnote [2] These insights help us understand where leverage is being created, how it is financed, and which transmission channels may matter during periods of stress.
That said, transaction data can only tell us part of the story. They help us understand positions and interconnections. They do not necessarily tell us how firms will behave if conditions deteriorate. To understand that, we complement our datasets with analysis of behaviours and reaction functions.
That is why we have started to run system-wide scenario exercises in collaboration with the industry. Our first one, two years ago, focussed on core sterling markets. During that exercise, many hedge funds originally assumed that additional repo financing would be available if needed. But it was clear from dealer banks that this would not necessarily be forthcoming. So we shared that feedback with hedge funds and asked how they would respond if banks reduced the amount of gilt repo financing available. Many reported that they would need to unwind positions financed through repo, illustrating how pressures on dealer balance sheets could be transmitted to leveraged investors and potentially amplify market moves.footnote [3]
Hedge funds play an important role in supporting market functioning, including in government bond markets, by warehousing risk and providing liquidity. But they are also generally more responsive to changes in market conditions and financing costs. As a result, the unwinding of leveraged and often crowded positions can have a disproportionate impact on market liquidity and may amplify stress during periods of market turbulence.
This is precisely why a system-wide perspective matters. A hedge fund can observe its own financing relationships. A dealer can observe its own clients. However, only the authorities can bring these perspectives together, helping identify vulnerabilities and interconnections that may not be visible to any single firm. Publishing analysis through our Financial Stability Reports, Staff Working Papers, and other publications allows market participants to benchmark their own exposures against broader market developments, improve risk management playbooks, understand which avenues would or wouldn’t be open to them in a stress, and identify vulnerabilities earlier.
As a concrete example of this, in our Financial Stability Report we have started to publish regularly aggregated data and charts that can help market participants understand wider developments and aid their own risk management. Examples of this in our latest FSR include how the preferred maturities of the gilt investor base have changed over the past decade, investor positioning in gilt repo, and breakdowns of the term and collateral maturity of those transactions.footnote [4] As part of our ongoing market engagement we look to understand which other areas might benefit from increased transparency, such as deep dives into specific market segments like retail investors in gilt markets and transparency on basis trade dynamics.
So please do take a look at our FSRs! I am not sure all the market participants who might find this information helpful actually clocked that we had very deliberately started to publish it. So far the feedback from hedge funds about its usefulness has been positive, and our message is: please put your thinking caps on and let us know what other aggregate data you would find helpful to see for your risk management. If we have it and can share it, we will.
At its best, surveillance is not just about helping authorities understand the system, it is also about helping the system understand itself better. Equipped with better information, market participants can be a more effective first line of defence, and the market as a whole is better able to self-stabilise when shocks hit – reducing the need for us to intervene.
And because we’re better placed than anyone else to see the overall picture, assembling it and sharing it back is an increasingly important policy tool in our toolbox.
But in addition to allowing market transparency to play out more effectively and do its work, surveillance also helps us identify in a discerning way the select few areas where the structure of markets does need to evolve to enhance resilience. Which brings me to a market where we have been asking such questions: the government bond repo market.
Leverage and funding in core markets
Like much of the financial system's infrastructure, the repo market is probably most visible only if it stops working properly. But its day-to-day role is essential – it keeps cash and collateral flowing through the financial system, supports liquidity in government bond markets, and facilitates the transmission of monetary policy.
Our first system-wide exploratory scenario (SWES) several years ago illustrated the crucial role that this market plays. Its resilience has improved, as was demonstrated by the fact that it has withstood successfully all the recent shocks in a heightened global risk environment. But that improved resilience isn’t yet locked permanently into its fundamental structure – it can still not be taken for granted.
Specifically, a key issue on our radar is how leveraged positions that are extremely large, concentrated, or correlated with respect to the size of the market have the potential to amplify shocks if they are unwound abruptly. Market corrections as a result of economic fundamentals are natural and healthy. What we want to avoid is such corrections getting amplified by structural features, as happened in the 2022 LDI crisis. That does not mean eliminating risk, though. Quite the opposite. The repo market performs crucial economic functions precisely because participants take and manage risk, often in the form of leverage. In principle leverage supports market liquidity and efficient risk transfer. Margin protects counterparties. Intermediation connects investors with different funding and investment needs.
Our intention is not to reduce leverage financed through the repo market. It is to ensure that the way it is provided and accessed supports market liquidity, efficient risk transfer, and the allocation of capital in all environments – not just when the sun shines. That might require limiting the particular forms of risk-taking that make the system more fragile.
So well-managed and well-understood leverage is welcome. Out-of-control leverage is unwelcome.
The challenge for policymakers is therefore to identify the combination of measures that best strengthen the resilience and efficiency of the system as a whole, in both normal and stress times. These properties depend on the ability of the financial system to supply liquidity when it is most needed. And they depend on limiting the build-up of vulnerabilities that can generate sudden and disruptive demand for liquidity during periods of stress.
On the supply side, greater central clearing has the potential not only to reduce counterparty credit risk, but also to strengthen the resilience of the market structure itself. The benefits for risk management are well understood, including more transparent and risk-sensitive margining practices. Less often appreciated are the market-wide benefits arising from greater netting efficiencies, lower balance sheet usage and a greater capacity for intermediaries to absorb positions, warehouse risk, and supply liquidity during periods of stress. Bank of England researchers have estimated that greater central clearing could have reduced gilt repo exposures on UK bank dealers' balance sheets during the “dash for cash” by between 40% and 60%.footnote [5] So this could free up a lot of capacity.
Experiences in other jurisdictions suggest that greater use of central clearing can encourage innovation in market structure and access models. In the United States Treasury repo market, for examplefootnote [6], market structures are evolving alongside clearing reforms, with new intermediation models and broader clearing access arrangements developing over time.
This is why access models matter. Different access arrangements can broaden participation in central clearing while preserving the diversity of participants that supports market liquidity. In the indirect model, clients access the central counterparty (CCP) via a clearing member. Sponsored access allows eligible firms to become direct participants of the CCP with support from a sponsoring clearing member, typically a dealer bank. Such support might include managing the connectivity to the CCP; managing collateral and settlement processes; and funding default fund requirements. In some ‘guaranteed’ sponsored models, direct access can be extended to an even wider range of participants, supported by greater obligations of the sponsor, for example to step in and make margin payments on behalf of the sponsored member. Arrangements can therefore sit at different points along a spectrum. By allocating responsibilities differently between clients, clearing members, and the CCP, they create different trade-offs between market access, balance sheet efficiency, incentives to provide intermediation, and overall market resilience.
Improvements in access to client clearing may themselves encourage greater use of clearing and catalyse the evolution of markets over time.
The measures I have discussed so far operate primarily through the liquidity supply channel. But recent episodes have demonstrated that liquidity stress is often driven not simply by a shortage of liquidity supply, but by sudden increases in liquidity demand.
This is where margining and haircut practices become important, reducing the build-up of extreme and unmanageable leverage, strengthening counterparty risk management, and lowering the likelihood of abrupt position liquidations.
In some circumstances, zero or near-zero haircuts can be justified by risk-reducing features such as netting and portfolio margining arrangements, which lower the overall exposure of the lender of leverage to its counterparty by recognising offsetting positions across different portfolios. However, while these arrangements can explain an important share of observed near-zero haircuts, we found that competitive considerations also play a role in the setting of very low haircuts – whereby the haircut is not set on risk grounds, but to avoid losing the client to competitors.footnote [7] This matters because near-zero or negative haircuts that are not directly linked to underlying risk can facilitate the build-up of unmanageable levels of leverage at little cost, and increase vulnerabilities in periods of market stress. More broadly, these findings support ongoing efforts by policymakers to strengthen the resilience of core funding markets and reduce vulnerabilities associated with extreme leverage in non-bank financial institutions.
Considering policy across these areas inevitably involves trade-offs. Poorly calibrated measures could reduce market-making capacity, shift activity elsewhere, or create unintended incentives. Margin and collateral arrangements that limit netting opportunities or prevent the recognition of genuine risk offsets can increase funding pressures precisely when market participants are already under stress.
From a financial stability perspective, the objective is not simply to demand more collateral from market participants. It is to ensure that collateral and margin requirements reflect underlying risks while avoiding unnecessary demands on liquidity during periods of stress.
This raises an important question: can the same level of risk protection be achieved while reducing unnecessary liquidity demands? This is one reason why appropriately designed cross-margining arrangements are attracting increasing interest, as they can improve collateral efficiency and reduce unnecessary liquidity demands where genuine risk offsets exist. However, cross-margining is not a free good. The scope for recognising offsets has to be determined by genuine offsets in the risks, noting asset correlations that appear stable in normal times may become less reliable during periods of stress. Realising the benefits of cross-margining also requires effective legal and operational arrangements and close cooperation across infrastructures and jurisdictions.
No single measure is likely to be a silver bullet for the resilience of gilt repo markets.
Measures that promote the appropriate pricing and management of leverage, support clearing adoption, broaden access to central clearing, and improve collateral efficiency should be viewed as complementary rather than substitutes. Considered together, they may offset some of the costs or limitations that would arise if any individual measure were implemented in isolation.
As it happens, and thankfully, that is what system-wide surveillance is helping us understand. It will certainly inform which policy package we put forward.footnote [8] As we said in the past, doing nothing is not an option.footnote [9] We intend to publish a comprehensive update on this, including potential policy proposals, in early 2027.
Many of these issues are inherently cross-border, and we continue to work closely with international partners through the Financial Stability Board and other fora to strengthen the resilience of market-based finance globally, where surveillance is high on the agenda. We are strong supporters of initiatives such as the FSB’s Nonbank Data Taskforce to break down barriers to transparency in these inherently global markets. The changes we see to the UK’s financial system are also being seen by our fellow regulators around the world, so we are far from alone in investigating these issues.
Conclusion
Of course the challenge of interpreting vast quantities of data to make sense of complex, interconnected systems is not unique to financial regulation. Let me conclude with a famous example of system-wide thinking from history. Often, the deployment of newly invented radar technology is credited with winning the Battle of Britain. But it was not one innovation that won out: not superior radar, better guns, or faster pilots. RAF fighter command understood that it was getting the right data where it needed to go that would win the battle. It was in setting up the famous Dowding System in the 1930s – a central command that could filter thousands of data points from radar systems, civilian spotters, and reconnaissance planes, turn those observations into system-wide insight, and relay them back out to gunners and fighter squadrons, giving them the information they needed to make front line decisions – that made British air defence so effective.
They had a system-wide mindset. And that mindset is bound to be powerful as we adapt to a new era of complexity and interconnectedness in the financial system. As central banks and regulators we have a unique vantage point over the whole system. Post-crisis reforms gave us more data than ever before. But our objective is not more and more data for its own sake. It is to draw from it genuinely system-wide insight. And then to share that aggregate data and insight back with the financial system to support its enduring ability to self-stabilise autonomously.
The more reliably it does that, the more selective we can be with policy interventions.
Thank you.
I would like to thank Gerardo Ferrara, Emily Evans, Nicholas Butt, Shefalika, Waris Panjwani, Michael Wood, Bradley Hudd, Julia Giese, David Bailey, and Sasha Mills for their comments and help in the preparation of these remarks.

articles.title: The top Latin American cities in 2026
articles.text:
Blog

30 Oct 2026

The top Latin American cities in 2026

Liam Sides
Associate Director, Cities & Regions

Discussion of the world’s major cities often overlooks the role and dynamics of Latin America. Yet, to ignore the region would be to ignore around a quarter of the world’s land mass and almost a 10th of its population.

In the 2026 edition of the Global Cities Index, Latin American cities are at the forefront of our analysis. Not only has the region seen some the largest increases in their ranking relative to last year, but we have also introduced a new ‘Cities to Watch’ section for the region allowing our analysts to highlight the top five city-economies they are most excited about and think investors should take notice of. The five we covered—Brasília, Lima, Medellín, Monterrey, and Santiago—are a group of cities with diverse drivers, united by their productivity-led expansion as they progress up the value chain.

In terms of the overall rankings for the region, Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina, takes top spot in the region and 138th overall (Chart 1). The city has the region’s second largest economy and has a deep skills base centred around strong universities and the many corporate headquarters. Second up is Chile’s Santiago, boasting similar credentials but higher housing costs and weaker Environmental scores cost it the top spot. Rounding off the top three is rapidly developing Lima as a combination of rural-urban migration, infrastructure investment, and rising trade volumes positions Peru’s capital as a key regional leader.

Major capital cities lead the index in Latin America

The megacities of São Paulo and Mexico City also rank highly, supported by their large GDP size and elevated scores in the Human Capital category. In fact, the Human Capital category is an area of relative outperformance across the region, with cities benefitting from good universities and high levels of educational attainment. The strength of Human Capital in driving Latin American cities’ performance in the index is perhaps best illustrated by the fact that nine of the 10 cities topping the overall rank for the region also top the Human Capital score, with only Medellín breaking into the top, as Costa Rica’s San José falls out.

The region’s poorest-performing category is Quality of Life, which may sound odd when one thinks of the golden beaches of Rio de Janeiro or the cosmopolitan streets of Santiago and Buenos Aires. However, the region has high levels of inequality, severe poverty, and some of the highest crime rates in the world (Chart 3). Cities as far afield as Port-au-Prince in Haiti, Guatemala City, and Fortaleza in Brazil are emblematic of this reality.

While it would be easy to say that reducing crime will shoot Latin American cities up the rankings, it is much more nuanced than that. This is because of the strong link crime has with other socioeconomic factors, like poverty and inequality, explaining the poor performance of Latin American cities across each of these metrics. Instead, the region needs broad-based interventions to stem to the drivers of crime, which in turn means stronger economic performance as much as it does stronger law enforcement.

Peru’s major cities will continue their strong momentum

Looking ahead, the region is set to see several of its cities climb the rankings and become more prominent in the index. Chief among them is Lima. GDP growth in the city will significantly outpace all other major Latin American cities and, over the next decade, will average 3.2% per annum, more than double the rate of São Paulo and rivalling the growth expected in some of Europe’s and the Middle East’s most dynamic cities. Moreover, this will open up substantial consumer market opportunities—having already surpassed Rio de Janeiro in 2021, Lima is projected to have higher average disposable income than both São Paulo and Bogotá by 2050—despite having a level just 82% and 93%, respectively, of the two today.

Slightly further south, Arequipa, Peru’s second-largest city and one of the world’s leading copper producers, is also set to rise in the rankings. Industry accounts for close to two-fifths of the city’s output, and this specialisation has supported one of the fastest rates of economic expansion among Latin American cities over the past two decades, averaging 5.1% per year. Supported by a strong investment pipeline and sustained demand for copper as electrification advances, we expect Arequipa’s largest gains to come in its Economic score, lifting it into the top 10 Latin American cities in our index over the next decade.

Panama City and Georgetown (Guyana) are also set to climb the rankings, reflecting their roles as both capital city economies and centres of national economic activity. Panama City will remain among Latin America’s top-performing cities, supported by deep human capital, high income per person, and its strategic location at the Pacific mouth of the Panama Canal. Georgetown, by contrast, stands out more for its vast natural resources. It is already Latin America’s fastest-growing city economy, with average annual growth of 12.6% over the past two decades. Offshore oil discoveries and rising infrastructure spending are at the centre of this, driving strong employment growth and higher incomes. These dynamics should support further progress over the coming decade, even if income disparities remain among the highest in our Global Cities Index.

Weaker momentum across some of the region’s more established urban centres will see them lose ground in our index over the coming decade. Rio de Janeiro is one such example, with growth set to remain subpar and substantially weaker than in other vital cultural epicentres, such as Buenos Aires and Santiago. A mature urban economy, softer demographic trends, and limited productivity gains are likely to constrain its performance. A similarly weak outlook applies to Cancún, where the same tourism reliance that drives its global appeal also leaves the city with a less stable economic footing than its more diversified city peers.

Subscribe: Spotify / Apple Podcasts / YouTube
Download TranscriptKey takeaways:

Precautionary physical buying: Physical buyers are bidding up available crude amid growing downside risks to supply.
Portfolio hedging: Bond and equity prices are unusually sensitive to oil prices, prompting institutional investors to buy crude to hedge their portfolios.
Supply challenges for refined products: Persian Gulf exports of refined products like diesel and gasoline are still only at around 40% of their 2025 average levels amid damage to refineries and underinvestment in manufacturing.
Metal prices may also rise: Struyven expects copper prices to increase another 10% by the end of 2027. He says gold may climb amid central bank demand for the yellow metal.

Transcript:
Allison Nathan: Oil flows from the Middle East have rebounded sharply, but prices remain high and rising. So what's keeping the market on edge? I'm Allison Nathan, and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges. Joining me is Daan Struyven, co-head of Global Commodities Research and head of Oil Research at Goldman Sachs.
Daan, thanks for joining us again. You've been on this show a lot, but look, oil has been very topical, so thanks for joining us again.
Daan Struyven: Thanks.
Allison Nathan: As I mentioned at the start, crude oil flows from the Middle East have substantially rebounded. If I'm not mistaken, they are at or at least close to 2025 averages at this point.
But I'm looking at my screen, oil prices have surged in recent days, again, deep into triple digits. So, what's driving that price move?
Daan Struyven: So, Brent crude oil prices have risen sharply to now around $112, per barrel because growing tensions in the Middle East and growing downside risks to supply are leading buyers to bid up barrels, both in the physical market and also on the financial side. Physical buyers such as refiners are seeing growing downside risks to supply because of an intensification of shipping attacks in the Middle East and because of some strikes on infrastructure by the Houthis.
And because inventories are low, refiners, physical buyers are trying to get their hands on barrels while they're available because they see a high probability of a sharp drop in supply. And on the financial side, because bonds and equity prices are unusually sensitive to oil prices, there's also a significant bid from investors to hedge their portfolios against energy price upside.
Allison Nathan: Interesting. So, in some ways, what we're seeing here is precautionary buying by the consumers of crude oil, which makes me think that on the other side of it, that could have price implications. When you think about price risk from here, given these very high levels today, and that they're now technically building inventory what are you expecting and where are the risks skewed?
Daan Struyven: So, following the sharp rise in prices, we see the risk to market prices as increasingly symmetrical. Although the risks to our base case price forecast, which sees Brent at the end of this year at $90 and in 2027 annual average at $80, the risks to our forecasts are clearly skewed to the upside.
The key upside risks are an intensification of shipping attacks that could lead to a sharp draw in exports. Second, damage to oil infrastructure or perhaps a stickier risk premium. Now, there's also significant downside risks, especially a potential drop in the risk premium that we estimate at roughly $27 per barrel for Brent at the moment.
But for the risk premium to come off quickly, you would probably need to see a diplomatic solution that market participants see as sustainable. Now, if we don't get significant escalation after the midterms, I think it's reasonable to assume that the risk premium does moderate somewhat.
Allison Nathan: Right. And again, just to be perfectly clear, you said the risk premium is $27 per barrel, so it's a lot of what we have seen in terms of the rise in prices. So, if we did see things improving on the war front, a lot of that could come out.
Daan Struyven: That's right. We think the oil market was balanced last month with oil output equaling demand. And our fair value estimate of Brent, which is $85 per barrel, does take into account the inventory levels. And we do think that essentially all of the increase in prices over the last few weeks is driven by an increase in the risk premium rather than an increase in the fair value of Brent. But it's understandable given the growing downside risk to supply.
Allison Nathan: Right. But it's a different story on the refined product side. We are seeing more physical tightness there. Tell me about that and what are the implications for product prices that we all consume?
Daan Struyven: Yes. So we do estimate that while crude oil exports out of the Persian Gulf are at 110% of 2025 average levels over the last couple of weeks, for refined oil products such as diesel, it's only 40% of 2025 average levels. That's in part because of damage to refineries in the Middle East, and also because it's harder to organize these ship-to-ship transfers for refined products than for crude because the products are more inflammable.
We do think that some of the strength in refined oil product prices, such as diesel, is not related to the Middle East. You had some significant structural tightness as a result of underinvestment before the war started, and Russian refineries have significantly curtailed their output of diesel because of the drone attack from Ukraine.
And so even if you were to see a resolution in the Middle East and a significant moderation in crude prices, we would expect in such a scenario to see diesel prices still well above their historical averages.
Allison Nathan: And what about gasoline prices, though very much in focus here in the US as we look at very high prices at the pump, and we are heading into midterm elections. What's the outlook there?
Daan Struyven: So the double negative supply shock from Russia and the Middle East was initially mostly a diesel shock because the Middle East and Russia specialize in refining diesel, and they produce heavy barrels that are diesel rich. But the tightness in diesel markets is now causing tightness in gasoline markets because when refiners look at the very high diesel margins, they are deciding to switch their output away from gasoline to the higher margin products such as diesel and jet.
And as a result, the gasoline market is tightening very quickly, and there's more room for price upside on the gasoline side, given the lower starting point for prices and the switching behavior by refiners.
Allison Nathan: More room for upside, Daan, that's not good news. But, okay, thanks very much for that. The other area that we are seeing substantial price increases is in freight rates in parts of the energy complex. Why is that happening? Talk us through it.
Daan Struyven: So the global average crude freight rate has surged by $20 per barrel over the last year, with about three-quarters of that increase related to the costs from reorganizing the supply chain to get crude out of the Middle East, both because of a risk premium to compensate the shippers for the higher risk of strikes, but also because we're tying up a lot of tankers in an inefficient way via the ship-to-ship transfers and because the Iranian tankers are also tied up because of the US blockade.
The remaining one quarter of the $20 year-over-year price increase reflects higher marine fuel costs. The implications are twofold. It means greater differences in crude prices across regions. In places like the Americas, US, Canada, where crude producers are close to refiners, it means cheaper crude prices.
In places like Asia, where the refiners are very far away from their crude producers, for instance, the Middle East, they have to pay up the high freight rates, and it's putting upward pressure on crude prices and ultimately product prices. And the second implication is that ultimately these high freight costs have to be paid mostly by the consumers.
And so it's another reason why product prices at the pump, especially in places like Asia are very elevated.
Allison Nathan: Right. And that's not impacting though freight broadly because it's a very different type of tanker that ships oil, correct?
Daan Struyven: That's right. So, the tightness in crude oil tankers is creating some tightness into refined product tankers because you can shift a tanker from a product tanker to a crude tanker. But there are no significant spillovers to broader cargo freight rates for other goods outside of the oil sector.
Allison Nathan: Let's talk for a moment about European natural gas, because LNG, liquefied natural gas, is also being impacted by the war in the Middle East. If the shipments of LNG remain depressed, as I think they are today, but please give us the lay of the land there, and we have a cold winter in Europe, what are the implications for European energy prices this winter?
Daan Struyven: A significant upside to energy prices. And while we characterize the risk to market prices for crude as fairly symmetrical, we do see net upside risks to European natural gas prices. Basically, three reasons. Inventories are very low. It's much harder to store natural gas than it is to store crude.
Second, to your point, estimated exports of LNG from the Middle East are only at around one-third of 2025 average levels. And in addition to middle supply, the second big swing factor is weather. And so, if we were to see a significant improvement in LNG exports from Qatar, TTF European natural gas prices could decline from roughly €90 at the moment to €70.
However, if exports stay at currently low levels, we would see TTF prices in triple digit territory with a potential 70% increase to a €150 per megawatt hour. If you both get stagnation, low flows from the Middle East and a one standard deviation colder than average winter.
Moreover, this would also spill over into power prices. And so we see significant upside risks to European energy prices
Allison Nathan: Just for a little bit more perspective, how does that scenario compare to what we saw in the European energy crisis post the invasion of Ukraine?
Daan Struyven: So while the size of the shock is roughly comparable, the loss of Russian supply is roughly equal to the loss of Middle East supply today. We would not expect European natural gas prices to rise above €300 per megawatt-hour, which was the peak in 2022 for a few reasons.
We have lost about 20% of European natural gas demand. And on the supply side, supply outside of the Middle East, including in the US, has risen significantly. So net upside, but not quite the extreme upside from 2022.
Allison Nathan: Okay, understood. And beyond energy, there are other commodity markets in focus that are tightening. Your focused in particular on copper. What's going on there and why do you see more tightness ahead?
Daan Struyven: So copper prices are up 35% year over year. We see another 10% of upside by the end of next year to $15,600. Essentially because the US and China, and this is a broader theme across commodity markets, are competing for a limited amount of metal.
The US is importing and stockpiling a lot of copper because of an expectation that there could be US import tariffs on copper, and so traders want to be ahead of the potential tariff, get the tariff, get the metal in now. And on the Chinese side, there is a big increase in demand for refined copper because of weakness in terms of recycling supply, the supply of recycled scrap copper.
So, if the two superpowers are pulling on the metal, inventories outside of the US are low. And as those two forces continue to play out, we would expect further tightening and further price upside
Allison Nathan: And remind us, Daan, what industries consume copper? Who will be feeling the most pain from this upside?
Daan Struyven: Data centers and tech companies, defense companies, electrical equipment companies, car producers, and also producers of solar panels. So, it's a fairly widely used commodity, especially for everything related to power, which is precisely a sector where we're seeing a lot of tightness because of the data center power demand.
Allison Nathan: Right. So more reason for some cost inflation there. The other commodity I wanted to ask you about Daan to close out is gold. Generally, we see downward pressure on gold when interest rates are elevated. We know that we have been in a higher rate environment in the recent period, but you're still pretty bullish on gold.
So, talk us through why you think gold has some resilience here.
Daan Struyven: I think the structural bull factor for the gold outlook has not changed. If you, for instance, look at the last three months, central banks have been buying at a pace that's 5X the pre-2022 average when Russia's reserves got frozen. Now, on the cyclical side, the increase in rates does pose a challenge to investor gold demand and to gold prices.
But in the base case of our economists, the Fed is done hiking after a last hike in December. And because some of the rate hikes are priced in we do see a significant upside to gold prices in our base case because of central bank buying and an improvement in the rates environment.
Allison Nathan: Thanks again for joining us, Daan. Appreciate it.
Daan Struyven: Thank you, Allison.
Allison Nathan: This episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Thursday, October 22nd, 2026. If you enjoyed the show, we hope you'll subscribe to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts, and leave us a rating and comment. I'm Allison Nathan. Thanks for listening.
