articles.title: Fix education to make AI work across Europe and Central Asia
articles.text:
Published on
Let's Talk Development

Fix education to make AI work across Europe and Central Asia

Ivailo Izvorski

Aparnaa Somanathan

October 28, 2026

This page in:

English

English

ECA can use AI to offset demographic decline, if schools teach young people to think with it. | © Shutterstock.com

The countries of Europe and Central Asia (ECA) cannot afford to miss the opportunity that artificial intelligence (AI) offers, but they will not seize it without the right skills. This is the one of the main messages of the latest World Bank Economic Update on Europe and Central Asia.
Few developing regions have as much to gain from AI as ECA. Productivity and business dynamism have been slowing for two decades. The working-age population has already shrunk in most countries and is on track to fall sharply across much of the region by 2060. On top of that, the quality of education has declined in most ECA countries over the last decade.
At present, AI's potential in ECA far outpaces the region’s ability to use it. Fewer than one in ten firms report using AI in their operations, roughly half the average in the EU. Worker exposure to AI is equally modest. When firms are asked what holds them back from adopting AI, people and skills top the list. Catching up with peers at similar levels of development, let alone with leading countries, depends less on computer chips or access to advanced models than on people.

What makes AI work
Most firms in the region use AI in shallow ways that rarely translate into real productivity gains. The exceptions — banks screening loan applications, retailers managing stock across suppliers, energy producers optimizing inputs — have something in common: they invested in skills and data systems, and their managers focused on results, not on adopting AI for its own sake.
Four ingredients stand out:

Workers with solid foundations. A sizable part of ECA's workforce lacks the foundational reading, numeracy, and reasoning skills that AI adoption requires.

Vocational education that delivers. About 45 percent of upper-secondary students in ECA are enrolled in vocational programs, more than twice the global average of 22 percent, and above 70 percent in some countries.

Managers who can redesign production processes. Managerial quality is among the strongest predictors of technology adoption. Research suggests that about a quarter of productivity gaps between and within countries reflect management practices. Someone must identify where AI adds value, redesign workflows, and guide staff through the change.

Workers who keep learning. Lifelong learning supported by employers and governments and a willingness to experiment are essential for staying relevant in a shifting labor market.

The report’s conclusion is clear: education and training systems in ECA need serious reform.

What PISA 2025 tells us
The 2025 OECD Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results show that learning quality in ECA has slipped further, especially on the very skills that AI demands: critical understanding, creativity, and judgment.
ECA’s average score across math, reading, and science fell from about 421 points in 2018 to about 406 in 2025, roughly equivalent to losing a full almost a year of schooling. The gap with the EU did narrow, from about three and a half years of learning to two and a half. But this is mostly because EU scores fell by more than ECA scores - not a reason to feel better.
The more worrying picture is how many students are left behind. In most ECA countries, at least half of 15-year-olds score below the minimum proficiency level compared with about one-third in the EU. In Kosovo, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan, the share is four in five or more. At the top end, 4.4 percent of EU students reach the highest proficiency levels. In ECA, only Türkiye comes close; in most countries the share is below 1.5 percent.
Student attitudes are also moving in a troubling direction. The share of students who find learning new things interesting fell in every ECA country between 2022 and 2025 in every ECA country. Students who skip school also score much lower – up to two years of learning behind in some countries.

Why weak education holds AI adoption and adaptation
Today’s 15-year-olds are the workers, managers, and entrepreneurs who will need to make AI work in the 2030s. If most of them lack foundational skills, AI use in the region will stay shallow.
AI rewards people who can critically assess its outputs, not just accept them. PISA 2025 illustrates this clearly: students who check sources and apply critical thinking when using AI score far higher than those who take AI outputs at face value. The gap is about three years of schooling. Yet only 29 percent of ECA students who use AI take that careful approach, compared with 45 percent in the EU. Using AI simply to summarize texts brings no measurable learning benefit.
The risk is a two-speed region. A small, well-educated elite would capture most of AI's gains, while the majority, whose jobs are least exposed today, fall behind as AI spreads into more types of work. This is a problem that no amount of spending later can fully fix.

Fixing education today is the priority
The good news is that the decline is reversible. Türkiye, Montenegro, Georgia, and Uzbekistan are among the six countries with the largest PISA improvements worldwide. Türkiye paired digital infrastructure investment with a curriculum shift away from memorization toward real-world problem solving. Uzbekistan set a national target of reaching the PISA top 30, reformed its curriculum and teacher training, banned phones in schools, and expanded early childhood education coverage from 30 to 75 percent.
These priorities emerge for ECA countries:

Secure foundational learning early. Scale up proven, cost-effective interventions in early childhood education so fewer children fall below the minimum learning threshold.

Teach students to question AI, not just use it blindly. Embed source-checking and evidence-based reasoning across curricula. Students need the skills to tackle challenging topics themselves, rather than offload their thinking to AI tools.

Reduce digital distraction. Set clear school-level rules on device use to protect face-to-face lesson time and maintain students’ focus.

Cultivate curiosity and perseverance. Active, student-centered teaching develops self-directed learners who can adapt as AI reshapes the labor market.

Retrain today's workers and managers. Upskilling programs should target foundational, digital, and managerial skills for AI-complementary work.

The main risk for ECA over the next decade is too little AI adoption, not too much. Compute, data, and investment matter greatly, and countries have to make progress on all three. But education is decisive. It needs to equip young people with the skills to use AI as a tool that amplifies their thinking, not a substitute for it. Without fixing education, countries across ECA will keep using AI in shallow ways, missing its real potential to raise productivity and offset, at least in part, the region’s demographic challenges.

articles.title: Education and urbanization alone may not end global extreme poverty
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Education and urbanization alone may not end global extreme poverty

Minh Cong Nguyen

Nishant Yonzan

Ben Brunckhorst

Sotaire Kwizera

Christoph Lakner

Gabriel Lara Ibarra

Henry Stemmler

October 28, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated in fewer places, where gains in education and urbanization have been associated with much smaller reductions in poverty. Picture, a homeless person in Venice, Italy. / Image: Shutterstock

Counting the number of people living in extreme poverty — on less than $3 a day — is only part of the picture. We also need to understand who they are, where they live, and how their circumstances have changed.
A new paper using household surveys from 154 economies, covering 96 percent of the world’s population, examines the characteristics of people living in extreme poverty from 2003 to 2024. Although extreme poverty has declined worldwide, it is increasingly concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, fragile economies, rural communities, younger populations, and people with limited education. Advances in urbanization and education — both strongly associated with poverty reduction in East and South Asia—have produced much smaller gains in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Global extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated
The world has made substantial progress in reducing extreme poverty, but that progress has slowed over the past decade.
As the number of people living in extreme poverty has declined, those who remain are increasingly concentrated in rural areas, among younger people and those without formal education, and across clusters of neighboring high-poverty regions. Extreme poverty is therefore becoming more entrenched in fewer places, which are also the places where progress in reducing poverty has mostly stalled over the last decade. Figure 1 shows this growing geographic concentration and the limited progress in poverty reduction in many of these areas.

Figure 1. Extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated in fewer subnational regions

Source: Global Subnational Atlas of Poverty (GSAP) data, September 2026 vintage.
Note: The figure shows subnational regions with high (>30%) or low (<30%) extreme poverty in 2013 and 2024. High-High reports regions that had greater than 30% poverty in both years and low-low implies they had less than 30% poverty in both years.

Education and urbanization no longer are strongly correlated with poverty reduction
The link between poverty reduction and broader social change varies considerably across periods and regions.
From 2003 to 2013, countries that became more urban raised their education levels and reduced the number of dependents relative to working-age adults. These factors generally cut extreme poverty faster. East Asia drove much of this pattern: on average, each percentage-point increase in the share of people with more than primary education or in the urban population was associated with about a 10-percentage-point decline in extreme poverty (Figure 2). In South Asia, this relationship strengthened after 2013. From 2013 to 2024, each percentage-point increase in education or urbanization was associated, on average, with a decline in poverty of more than 10 percentage points.
Sub-Saharan Africa made comparable gains in education and urbanization to those in South Asia, yet poverty declined very little. In the region, each percentage-point increase in educational attainment or urbanization was associated with a poverty reduction of less than one percentage point in the first period and only slightly above one percentage point in the second. Education and urban residence remain linked to higher living standards, but progress in these areas alone does not automatically reduce poverty.

Figure 2. Poverty has responded less to education and urbanization in Sub-Saharan Africa

What this means
The global decline in extreme poverty over the past two decades is a major achievement, yet the remaining challenge is increasingly concentrated and difficult to overcome.
Many of the world’s poorest people now live in places where limited education, rural isolation, weak economic opportunities, fragility, and environmental risks overlap. Moreover, factors traditionally associated with poverty reduction are only weakly linked to progress in the areas where poverty is most concentrated.
It is important therefore to understand not only whether education and cities have expanded, but whether these changes have created productive jobs and broadly shared gains in household well-being.
The findings presented here, and in the paper, show associations and do not establish that any single factor causes poverty to rise or fall. Nevertheless, they reveal sharp differences within countries and identify clusters of neighboring areas where poverty remains persistently high. Considered alongside evidence on economic growth, the distribution of its benefits, productivity, employment, and workers’ movement across sectors, the results help identify where broader economic and social progress has not reached the poorest people. Policies should therefore pair investments in people and places with stronger economic opportunities, target persistent high-poverty clusters and communities facing multiple risks, and improve data collection to better understand why poverty trends are diverging. Further insights and a more comprehensive analysis of global poverty and prosperity can be found in the Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report (3PR).

We gratefully acknowledge financial support from the UK Government through the Data and Evidence for Tackling Extreme Poverty (DEEP) Research Program.

articles.text:
PERSPECTIVES Special

Asian banks: Contrasting drivers, contrasting prospects

Ready to talk?

×

Prof. Dr. Jacky Tang, Chief Investment Officer, Emerging Markets; Wolf Kisker, Senior Investment Strategist
October 27, 2026

Share

Share on Facebook

Share on LinkedIn

Share by Email

Contrasting conditions across the region ensure that the prospects for Asian banks are a function of more than economic growth alone. This PERSPECTIVES Special examines how rates, credit demand, investment cycles and valuations are shaping contrasting opportunities across Asia.

Key takeaways
Rate paths, deposit competition and credit costs determine how economic growth can be translated into bank profits. Japanese banks are benefiting from monetary normalisation, Indian banks are experiencing a combination of strong demand and an emerging margin recovery, and Singaporean banks’ fee-generating businesses are helping to offset the pressure on margins.Economic growth alone is not enough. Banks benefit most where the current investment cycle creates external financing needs. Cash-rich technology exporters can fund much of their spending internally, while sustained demand may generate subsequent lending and service opportunities through capacity expansion and infrastructure investment along the AI value chain.Valuations call for selectivity. Indian banks combine the strongest expected 2027 EPS growth with a discount of more than 30% to their historical valuation. In contrast, all other regional banking sectors are trading above their own 10-year averages, with Singaporean banks commanding the largest premium of more than 40%. Earnings delivery and sustainable distributions are therefore essential, while China’s modest growth and credit risks support a neutral stance.

articles.title: Transitioning to mid-cycle – Market Outlook
articles.text:
30 October 2026
Global Market Outlook

Download Report

Transitioningto mid-cycle
We now favour a more balanced stance between stocks and bonds. Near-term event risks and high earnings expectations prompt us to trim equities to a Core holding. The US and Asia ex-Japan (AxJ) remain our preferred regions. We upgrade India to Overweight.

Higher bond yields are improving the outlook for future returns and offering increasingly attractive income opportunities. We are Overweight Emerging Market (EM) USD bonds and favour corporate over sovereign debt, but limit duration to 3-7 years.

We remain Overweight gold. Prices are likely to grind higher as near-term headwinds from higher bond yields are offset by EM central bank demand.

Where are the tactical opportunities?

Are central banks likely to continue hiking rates?

Are quantitative models still bullish on equities?

Strategy
Investment strategy and key themes

Steve Brice

Global Chief Investment Officer

Manpreet Gill

Chief Investment Officer, AMEE

Raymond Cheng, CFA, CPA

Chief Investment Officer, North Asia

12m Foundation Overweights:

Gold
US, Asia ex-Japan equities
Emerging Market USD bonds

Opportunistic ideas – Equities

Global: High dividend
US: Healthcare^
Euro area (EA): Banks, MSCI Switzerland^
Asia: Japan banks

Top Global Sectors:

US: Technology, healthcare^, financials, materials
EA: Financials
Asia: Japan financials

Opportunistic ideas – Bonds

US: Treasury Inflation-protected Securities (TIPS), AAA-rated collateralised loan obligations (CLOs), US High-yield (HY)
Others: AUD corporates

^New

Transitioning to mid-cycle

We now favour a more balanced stance between stocks and bonds. Near-term event risks and high earnings expectations prompt us to trim equities to a Core holding. The US and Asia ex-Japan (AxJ) remain our preferred regions. Within AxJ, we upgrade India to Overweight.
Higher bond yields are improving the outlook for future returns and offering increasingly attractive income opportunities. We are Overweight Emerging Market (EM) USD bonds and favour corporate over government bonds, but limit duration to 3-7 years.
We remain Overweight gold. Prices are likely to grind higher as near-term headwinds from higher bond yields are offset by EM central bank demand.

Great expectations
Individual risk events, high earnings expectations and a higher cost of capital point to a more moderate return environment ahead. In the very near term, financial markets must navigate key event risks, such as (i) the US mid-term elections, which have historically been associated with elevated market volatility and (ii) renewed geopolitical tensions, with several reports suggesting the US is considering renewed strikes on Iran. These concerns have pushed the Brent oil price well above USD 110/bbl despite significant ongoing crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Higher bond yields combined with high earnings expectations raise the risk of an expectations reset. The US Q3 earnings season is attracting significant attention given high earnings expectations, particularly for the AI sector. However, higher US bond yields may start to bite as debt-financed capex takes on a greater share of total capex over the coming year. This, combined with already-high expectations, raises the risk of disappointment and a near-term repricing of expected earnings growth pace.
Despite the current challenges, healthy growth continues to underpin the economic backdrop. The US economic outlook remains well supported, and the absolute level of year-ahead earnings expectations is high. We do not expect Fed rate hikes to result in overly restrictive policy. Our caution, thus, stems from the risk of an expectations repricing rather than an outright economic slowdown.

Fig. 1 Our quant model score has fallen to levels associated with flat-to-modestly-negative equity returns
Our quantitative stock-bond model

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

A more balanced stock-bond mix
We trim global equities to a Core holding, leaving us Neutral on both equities and bonds and Overweight gold. The concerns laid out earlier point to near-term volatility risks and a somewhat lower long-term growth trajectory for equities. Our quant model also reflects this cautious outlook, having downgraded equities to a level usually associated with flat-to-modestly-negative returns.
From a relative perspective, though, the higher yields on offer from bonds also raise the bar by presenting an increasingly compelling return outlook after several years of very low yields. We believe this argues for portfolios that are increasingly balanced between equities and bonds.
Ways to diversify equity exposure
We continue to favour global equity market diversification, with a preference for US and AxJ equities. We remain Overweight US and AxJ equities, expecting them to outperform other major regions. Earnings growth remains the main driver of this view – while growth rates could decelerate somewhat, we still expect them to remain higher than those of other major regions.
Japan and Euro area equities remain attractive as regional diversifiers. Our positive view on both markets’ financial sectors supports our Core holding view on them.
Within Asia, we are Overweight Taiwan and India. Indian equities have lagged the region this year, in part due to limited listed AI-related exposure. However, we believe this is increasingly likely to become an advantage as investors seek greater diversification away from excessive concentration in the AI theme. This comes at a time when the economic and earnings growth outlook for Indian equities is starting to improve. We retain a more Neutral view on Chinese equities amid a still-challenging growth outlook.
We also favour greater sector diversification. In the US, we favour diversifying across our Overweight sectors of technology, financials, materials and healthcare. We also favour financials in Japan and the Euro area.

Fig. 2 Negative gold-USD correlation has held back gold amid USD strength. This is unlikely to persist
Gold and USD correlations over the last 15 years

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Changes to our equity opportunistic ideas also reflect a more defensive stance. In recent weeks, we have closed our global semiconductors, MSCI Taiwan, US communication services and global power & electrification ideas and have opened new ideas on US healthcare and MSCI Switzerland.
Riding the yield train
We believe bond markets offer an attractive opportunity to lock in yields. The 10-year US government bond yield is now in a range last witnessed in 2007. While the process of rising yields results in lower bond prices – as painfully experienced in recent months – the yield level itself starts to significantly improve the outlook for future returns.
Favour corporate over government bonds, but check your duration. Still-high credit quality means that we continue to favour taking on credit risk to earn a higher yield (EM USD bonds are preferred, but we also see investment-grade (IG) and high-yield (HY) bonds as Core holdings). However, limiting duration to 3-7 years remains key to avoiding excessive exposure to any inflation surprises.
Changes to our bond opportunistic ideas also reflect a more balanced stance. We close our EU bank contingent convertible bonds (CoCos2 – please refer page 27) and US utilities corporate hybrids ideas. We also close our opportunistic idea on US 10-year government bonds following the recent pullback in yields, locking in gains.
Alternatives and gold to remain relevant
Alternatives are an effective tool for portfolio risk management. Hedge funds and private markets provide a differentiated return stream, while rotating into alternatives helps reduce equity beta exposure. We examine downside capture and how beta is reduced via hedge fund sub-strategies and private markets in our asset allocation section.
Gold remains a key Overweight. We trim our three- and 12-month forecasts modestly, but see gold forming a strong base above USD 4,000/oz. Rising bond yields and the USD were recent headwinds, but we expect a softer USD and continued EM central bank demand to result in 12-month gains.

Foundation asset allocation models
The Foundation and Foundation+ models are allocations that you can use as the starting point for building a diversified investment portfolio. The Foundation model showcases a set of allocations focusing on traditional asset classes that are accessible to most investors, while the Foundation+ model includes allocations to private assets that may be accessible to investors in some jurisdictions, but not others.
Fig. 3 Foundation asset allocation for a balanced risk profile

Fig. 4 Foundation+ asset allocation for a balanced risk profile

Fig. 5 Multi-asset income allocation for a moderate risk profile

Source: Standard CharteredNotes: (i) Developed Market (DM) IG Bonds is an aggregate of DM IG Government and DM IG Corporate Bonds; (ii) EM Bonds is an aggregate of EM USD and EM Local Ccy Government Bonds
Foundation: Our tactical asset allocation views

Fig. 6 Performance of our Foundation Allocations*

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered; *12-month performance data from 28 October 2025 to 28 October 2026, Six-month performance from 28 April 2026 to 28 October 2026, Three-month performance from 28 July 2026 to 28 October 2026
Fig. 7 Opportunistic ideas performance

Macro overview – at a glance

Rajat Bhattacharya

Senior Investment Strategist

Key themes
Core scenario (soft landing, 45% probability): An economic soft landing remains our core scenario, with the global economy overcoming this year’s oil price shock thanks to a surge in AI investment in the US and Asia. Record wealth generation driven by the stock market rally is supporting US consumption. Fiscal easing in the US, Germany and Japan is supporting growth. Meanwhile, inflation has reaccelerated due to a rebound in fuel prices as the Middle East conflict drags on. Against this backdrop, the Fed, ECB and BoJ all hiked rates in the same month (in September) for the first time. Although all three subsequently paused in October, we expect the Fed to hike twice more, the ECB once more and the BoJ thrice more by June 2027. Nevertheless, we expect the energy and tariff effects on inflation to fade by H2 2027, enabling the Fed and the ECB to cut rates by Q3 2027. Meanwhile, China is likely to target credit easing and accelerate fiscal spending in H1 2027 to revive domestic growth.

Upside risk (no landing, 30% probability): We maintain the probability at 30% as AI-driven investment growth continues. There is a reasonable chance that lower oil prices next year, the AI-fuelled wealth boom and fiscal easing in Germany and Japan will boost ‘animal spirits’. A potential global defence spending boom, led by the US and Europe, could also lift global growth.
Downside risk (25% probability): We raised the risk of a recession to 15%, especially if central banks are forced to accelerate the pace of rate hikes to douse rising inflation. A stock market downturn negating the wealth effect or a bond sell-off due to fiscal concerns are other tail risks. We cut stagflation probability to 10% as we see low risk of oil prices sustaining above USD 120/bbl.
Key chart

The US-led AI-focused investment boom has lifted business confidence. The resulting equity market rally has boosted US household wealth, supporting consumption

Fig. 8 Robust business confidence amid AI boom; equity rally lifts US household net worth

Purchasing managers indices; US household net worth as percentage of personal disposable income

Policy rates watch
We expect the Fed to hike twice more by Q2 2027, then ease in H2 2027, as AI-led expansion continues. The US economy remains firmly in expansion. In Q3, annualised GDP growth accelerated to 3.4%, led by AI investments and consumption. In October, the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) remained strong at 57.6. Since our last monthly report, the consensus estimate for 2026 GDP growth has been nudged up to 2.3% from 2.1%, and the 2027 estimate has risen to 2.2%. That matches the Fed’s upgraded growth projection of 2.3% for 2026, but remains below the Fed’s 2.4% estimate for 2027. AI investment, fiscal support and household wealth are the main growth drivers, although consumer activity lags business spending. Higher bond yields and elevated oil prices are headwinds, but recession risks look contained. Our core scenario remains a ‘soft landing’, at 45%, with a meaningful 30% chance of a ‘no-landing’ upside.

Rising gasoline and diesel prices pushed US core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation to 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, matching estimates. Consensus sees core PCE inflation slowing from 3.2% in Q4 2026 to 2.4% by Q4 2027 as energy and tariff effects fade. Underlying price momentum is softening, and recent PCE methodology revisions have lowered core inflation. However, fuel costs passed on to wider consumers and AI-driven chip shortages remain upside risks.
In October, the Fed held rates at 4.0%, after hiking in September for the first time since 2023. We expect the Fed to hike rates by 25bps in December and 25bps more in H1 2027 due to elevated near-term energy inflation. It is likely to follow with a 25bps cut to 4.25% in Q3 2027 as disinflation returns. This aligns with the Fed’s projected policy path, although it implies a more dovish trajectory than money markets, which are pricing another 56bps of hikes over the next 12 months. Political uncertainty after the mid-term election is a key risk.

ECB to hike once more in December, then pause. The Euro area recovery is firming. GDP grew 1.2% y/y in Q2 2026, up from 0.6% in Q1, and the manufacturing PMI stayed robust at 52.4 in October. Consensus 2026 growth has been raised to 1.0% from 0.9%, and 2027 is unchanged at 1.3%. The main supports are resilient exports and German infrastructure and defence spending. However, cautious consumers and soft private investment limit the recovery, and energy costs are squeezing household incomes and business margins. Recession is not the central expectation. French fiscal stress and sustained high energy costs remain the key risks.
Higher energy prices pushed Euro area headline inflation up to 3.8% y/y in September from 3.2% y/y in August, while core inflation rose to 2.5% y/y. Consensus expects headline and core inflation to ease to 2% y/y and 2.4% y/y by Q4 2027, respectively. Encouragingly, energy has had limited impact on core prices, and longer-term inflation expectations remain stable at around 2.1%. Together, these should allow inflation to moderate in 2027. The main risk is that energy, and especially gas, prices stay high for longer than expected.
The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5% in October after raising it by 50bps this year. Inflation data continue to favour an additional hike in December. We expect an ECB rate hold in H1 2027, followed by a cut by Q3 2027 as disinflation returns. This policy path is more dovish than money markets, which are pricing more than 60bps of hikes over the next 12 months.
China to provide targeted support to defend growth floor. China’s growth momentum recovered in September. Both the manufacturing PMI (50.1) and the non-manufacturing PMI (50.2) moved back into expansion. The construction PMI rose above 50 for the first time this year as infrastructure spending started to take effect. Exports grew 36.3% y/y, pushing the trade surplus to a record USD 133.5bn. We expect growth in 2026 to meet the lower end of the 4.5-5.0% target. Growth is increasingly bifurcated, though, with technology firms and exporters doing well, while household demand stays weak.
Prices are rising again, but only narrowly. Consumer inflation edged up to 0.9% y/y in September, and producer inflation surged to 5% y/y, its highest since 2022, driven by energy and metals prices and concentrated in upstream sectors. With domestic demand weak and a high comparison base next year, the boost from energy prices is likely to fade in 2027.

domestic demand weak and a high comparison base next year, the boost from energy prices is likely to fade in 2027.
Policy is in ‘targeted easing’ mode. We expect a modest fiscal package to defend the growth floor rather than a large stimulus. The PBoC cut a key rate by 25bps to 1.5% to fund ‘Six Networks’ infrastructure projects and raised its relending quotas. A new interest subsidy on first-home mortgages provides limited support to demand. We expect no policy rate cut this year. There is still room to speed up fiscal spending, including by using CNY 500bn of unused local-government debt quota. If the PBoC switches to an overnight reverse repo rate as its policy rate, that would imply a de facto rate cut as the overnight rate is lower than the 7-day official policy rate.
BoJ to hike at a quarterly pace until Q2 2027. Japan’s economy remains solid. Wages are growing above 4%, and the labour market is tight. The main headwind is high energy prices, which is slowing growth. Fiscal spending gives some support: the FY27 draft budget includes ambitious spending plans, alongside a proposed two-year cut to the consumption tax on food and a new five-year defence programme. However, this extra spending raises questions about fiscal sustainability. The BoJ unveiled plans to triple the pace of ETF sales from January 2027, potentially funding the tax cut.
Price pressures now look firmly established. Headline and core inflation rose above 2% for the first time this year, and core-core inflation (ex-fresh food and energy) jumped to 2.4% and is expected to rise towards 3% in Q1 2027. Breakeven inflation rates have stayed above 2% most of this year. Real interest rates remain negative, hurting savers and pensioners.
The BoJ held its policy rate at 1.25% in October, after raising it in September, only three months after its previous hike. This points to an accelerated quarterly hiking pace. We expect the quarterly pace of hikes to continue, taking the rate to 2% by June 2027. Money markets have caught up with our hawkish view in recent months. The BoJ noted for the first time that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, marking a shift from creating inflation to containing it. Politics could slow the hiking cycle in H2 2027. Two government-appointed board members voted against the September hike, and the two most hawkish members are due to leave in July 2027.

Fig. 9 Inflation is likely to ease globally by H2 2027
Consensus inflation estimates across major economies

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

Fig. 10 We expect limited central bank hikes over 12m
Our estimates of key central bank policy rates over 12 months

Asset classes
Fixed Income – at a glance

Jonathan Liang, CFA

CIO, Fixed Income & FX

Cedric Lam

Senior Investment Strategist

Ray Heung

Senior Investment Strategist

Anthony Naab, CFA

Investment Strategist

Our view
Foundation: Bond yields remain near multi-year highs, offering an attractive entry point. We view fixed income as a Core holding (ie, a Neutral allocation) in our multi-asset portfolios. Within the asset class, we maintain an Overweight stance on EM USD government bonds, given their attractive risk-reward. We hold an Underweight view on Developed Market (DM) government bonds due to the tail risks associated with term premia.
The Fed’s decision to hold rates at 3.75-4.00% in October amid still-elevated energy prices suggests that every Fed meeting from here is ‘live’, with a rate change possible on incoming data. With US inflation still running hot and the labour market tight, we expect two more 25bps hikes (one by year-end and one in H1 2027), bringing the Fed’s target range for the federal funds rate to 4.25-4.5%. We continue to favour the 3-7-year part of the US government bond yield curve as the best hedge against any risk-off move driven by AI-related growth fears. As inflation pressures ease in H2 2027, we see room for the Fed to consider a rate cut, which should pull nominal yields lower. Solid corporate fundamentals and supportive technicals should keep spreads tight, but there is limited room for them to tighten further. We still favour EM USD over local-currency (LCY) government bonds.
Opportunistic ideas: We are bullish on US TIPS, AAA-rated CLOs, broad US HYs and Australian dollar (AUD) corporate bonds.
Key charts
Fig. 11 Rate forecasts and our view of bond classes

DM rates – Underweight
We remain Underweight DM government bonds. In the US, government bond yields have retraced meaningfully after a sharp bear steepening through September and early October. We expect real yields to stay elevated over the next six months as AI capex and productivity growth continue to drive above-trend economic growth. We expect two more 25bps rate hikes by June 2027.
Over the next few months, we expect US government bond yields to remain rangebound. The near-term path hinges on five factors: 1) the 3 November US mid-term election, where a ‘Democratic sweep’ would likely be bond-supportive by constraining US President Trump’s fiscal spending agenda, while a ‘Republican sweep’ would likely weigh on bonds as markets price in further fiscal expansion and a higher term premium; 2) Fed communication at upcoming policy meetings;

3) the US Treasury’s quarterly refunding announcement on 4 November, where any signal of reduced long-end issuance would likely compress long-end yields; 4) softening auction demand and repatriation by foreign investors, which add uncertainty around demand for US government bonds; and 5) the fluid geopolitical situation in the Middle East, which is keeping oil prices elevated, with a risk of further upside.
Going into H2 2027, we expect moderating oil prices and the fading inflationary impact of tariffs to give the Fed room to consider rate cuts. The US 30-year yield, however, is likely to stay elevated as fiscal deficit remains substantial next year.
We expect a final ECB hike to 2.75% by December 2026, then a pause in H1 2027, followed by a 25bps cut in Q3 2027. In Japan, we expect quarterly pace of BoJ hikes, with one hike that takes the policy rate to 1.50% by December 2026 and two more in H1 2027, reaching 2.00% before pausing at mid-year.

DM corporates – Core holding
We maintain a Neutral allocation to both DM IG and DM HY corporate bonds, with a tactical bias to add exposure on episodic weakness, as carry continues to dominate total returns across DM credit. Credit spreads have widened from their lows but remain close to historical tights, while yields are still attractive, reinforcing a carry-led stance. This tight-spread regime is anchored by robust issuer fundamentals, strong profitability and resilient balance sheets, despite a visible moderation in rating upgrades over the past quarter.
Technical supply dynamics are reshaping sector dispersion, especially in the IG space, where heavy AI-related issuance is weighing on the long end of the curve. AI-driven supply is surpassing USD 250bn in 2026 and making up a growing share of US IG gross issuance, but there are growing signs that hyperscalers are turning to private markets for funding, which should help ease public bond market supply pressures.
We remain selective at the long end of the yield curve and favour a duration of 3-7 years, where risk-adjusted carry remains most durable. Issuance-driven concessions in sectors with strong capex cycles (notably technology, capital goods and basic industries) present opportunities for investors who can stomach near-term volatility.
Fig. 12 DM IG spreads have widened from their lows, but remain near historically tight levels
Bloomberg Global Aggregate Corp Index, option-adjusted spread (OAS)

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

DM HY spreads have widened to roughly a six-month high. Persistent doubts about whether hyperscalers can generate adequate returns on massive AI capex investments triggered a broad risk asset sell-off. The CCC tier has become the focal point of genuine credit concern, with yields hovering near the high-15% range and spreads near a four-year high. Market focus has shifted to the funding pressures facing AI-related neocloud companies. We view this as idiosyncratic for now and see a limited impact on the broader HY universe. The underlying credit picture is mixed. Leverage is elevated and interest coverage is thin, but the broad market has not yet shown signs of systemic stress. The US HY default rate remains below trend in 2026.

HY offers an attractive income proposition, with all-in yields of over 8%. Its shorter-duration profile, combined with its lower sensitivity to changes in the term premium and rate volatility, make it an attractive sleeve in the current phase of the cycle. We remain attentive to evolving credit rating migration trends and sector-specific supply pressures, particularly as upgrades slow and new issuance clusters around key themes. However, healthy issuer fundamentals and stable credit metrics continue to support it as a Core holding allocation.
Fig. 13 DM HY spreads are off the tights
Bloomberg Global HY Aggregate Corporate Index, OAS

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

EM government bonds – Overweight USD/Core holding for LCY
We are Overweight EM USD government bonds and retain EM LCY government bonds as a Core holding, reflecting a balanced perspective across both regional performance and currency dynamics. In EM USD sovereign debt, the recent spread widening offered an attractive entry point to gain exposure to areas benefiting from resilient global growth and stable external conditions. Technicals remain favourable, with supply being front-loaded and investor positioning remaining relatively light compared with historical levels.
Many EM central banks having tightened earlier and more aggressively post-pandemic, preserving credibility and maintaining positive real rates. External balances have improved, reserve buffers have increased and greater reliance on domestic funding reduces external vulnerability. Lula’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential election raises political risk. The country’s fiscal trajectory under the incoming administration is a key risk to monitor. Fiscal slippage could trigger a broader repricing of LATAM risk. In Asia, higher-rated issuers continue to offer a valuable buffer during bouts of global rate volatility, while select frontier exposures in EMEA remain more sensitive to liquidity shifts and changes in risk appetite. Index composition also shapes resilience: the EM USD benchmark is less exposed to oil price shocks, as countries that are not oil importers account for a larger share of the benchmark than in the LCY benchmark. We expect returns to be primarily driven by carry rather than further spread compression.

Fig. 14 EM USD government bonds offer a yield pick-up of nearly 3ppt over DM peers
Bloomberg EM USD Government Bond Index, yield to worst

Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

EM LCY debt faces additional headwinds, especially as elevated US real yields and an appreciating USD dampen demand from foreign investors and reduce the comparative attractiveness of broad-based duration strategies. However, real yields remain comparatively supportive in several markets, and current valuations signal selective opportunities, especially given the restrictive monetary policy stances prevalent across many EM economies. Accordingly, EM LCY bonds retain their Core holding status, with portfolio emphasis

placed on country selection and measured duration exposure, reflecting the differentiated currency dynamics at play.
Key risks to both the USD and LCY segments include a potential escalation of the Middle East conflict, higher oil prices, renewed hawkishness from the Fed that could support further USD strength and weather-related disruptions, such as the effects of El Niño. Climate risks could prolong inflation pressures and hinder disinflation in vulnerable EM regions.
Asia USD bonds – Core holding
We retain a Neutral allocation to Asia USD bonds, an asset class that continues to reward investors with attractive nominal yields, favourable supply-demand technicals and robust credit fundamentals. Healthy corporate cash flows, low leverage and a high share of sovereign-linked issuers lend the segment a defensive quality relative to broader credit.
The resilience has been evident year to date (YTD). Asia USD bonds have outperformed both DM government and DM IG corporate bonds on a total-return basis. We expect this relative strength to persist. The combination of carry and credit quality (over 60% of issues are sovereign or sovereign-related) anchors our conviction in the asset class, even as we maintain a Neutral stance.

Equity – at a glance

Sundeep Gantori, CFA, CAIA

Chief Investment Officer, Equities

Fook Hien Yap

Senior Investment Strategist

Cindy Lam, CFA

Senior Investment Strategist

Our view
We downgrade global equities from Overweight to a Core allocation as we expect higher volatility in the near term. We expect this volatility to arise as equity market leadership broadens during the transition to a mid-cycle bull market. Equity returns will likely moderate from the 15-20% annualised range of the last few years but remain positive. We remain Overweight US and AxJ equities, which are expected to deliver the highest earnings growth in 2027 among the major regions.
Within AxJ, we remain Overweight Taiwan, given structural AI-driven growth, and upgrade India to Overweight, for diversified non-AI growth exposure. South Korea is a Core holding, with attractive valuations but extreme volatility. China is also a Core holding, with attractive valuations but lacking a positive catalyst. We are Underweight ASEAN, which has a weaker growth profile.
We maintain Japan as a Core holding as nominal growth supports broad-based earnings revisions. We also maintain a Core allocation to Europe ex-UK, which is enjoying an earnings recovery. We remain Underweight UK equities, given the market’s limited exposure to growth sectors.
Key chart

Earnings growth is driving gains in equities

Fig. 15 Broad-based earnings strength is supporting global equities. Our Overweight views on AxJ and US equities are supported by robust earnings growth

Shifting to a mid-cycle bull market

The last few years have seen strong annual returns of 15-20% for global equities, consistent with the early cycle of a bull market, driven in large part by a rapid AI buildout. As the AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly debt funded – we estimate 40% of AI capex in 2027 would be debt-financed – the market is increasingly concerned about the quality of this growth and execution risks. We remain positive on the structural AI theme, but we expect investor focus to shift from rapid buildout to monetisation. During this transition, we expect market leadership to broaden beyond technology. We believe this shift will also be accompanied by higher near-term volatility and a moderation in global equity returns, consistent with a transition to a mid-cycle bull market.
Fig. 16 Projected 16% earnings growth for global equities in 2027 provides a strong tailwind for positive equity returns
2026 and 2027 consensus earnings growth estimates for MSCI AC World sectors

Source: FactSet, Bloomberg, Standard Chartered

US equities – Overweight
US equity valuations have declined this year, with the 12-month forward P/E falling to 19x from 22x at the start of the year. This reflects higher rates, a valuation headwind, and worries about the quality of growth, which is increasingly debt-funded. As market leadership broadens and the US mid-term election nears, we expect higher near-term volatility in the US market. Nonetheless, US equities have broad-based strength, with the ongoing Q3 earnings season pointing to a robust economy. In a world of rising geopolitical risks, the US is also relatively insulated by its domestically driven growth.
AxJ equities – Overweight
AxJ has the strongest earnings growth among major markets, as its technology sector remains a key beneficiary of the AI capex cycle. AxJ’s P/E valuations have also dropped to attractive trough levels, the lowest among major regions. Within AxJ, we are Overweight Taiwan, which benefits from clear visibility on AI-driven growth and dominance in manufacturing advanced AI chips. We also upgrade India to

Overweight due to its resilient domestically driven earnings, providing diversification beyond AI-related growth. India offers the highest exposure to defensive sectors (healthcare, consumer staples and utilities) within AxJ. Both Taiwan and India offer attractive returns on equity.
South Korea equities remain a Core holding. We are positive on long-term agreements that improve earnings visibility for memory chipmakers. Valuations are attractive (the lowest in AxJ), with supportive corporate governance reforms. Still, extreme volatility remains the key overhang. China remains a Core holding, given inexpensive valuations, but re-rating potential appears delayed amid AI monetisation struggles, lingering regulatory risks and weak domestic demand. We remain Underweight ASEAN, as Indonesia’s downgrade warning, oil shocks and a well-supported USD could weigh on the region, although Singapore offers defensive growth.

Japan equities – Core holding

Europe ex-UK equities – Core holding
Europe ex-UK is seeing an earnings recovery after three stagnant years, and we expect to see a continuation of this narrative with Q3 results. UK equities – Underweight
The UK lacks exposure to growth sectors, with relatively muted earnings growth. We expect this to weigh on the UK, making it lag the performance of other markets over the next 12 months, although UK equities tend to hold up better during bouts of volatility.

Gold outlook: We remain constructive over 6-12 months, viewing the latest pullback as liquidity-driven rather than a deterioration in fundamentals. USD strength is a headwind, but gold’s sensitivity to real yields has eased amid continued central bank buying, led by China, and resilient investor demand. Oil outlook: Crude prices remain elevated as shipping disruptions drive freight costs to multi-year highs, sustaining a geopolitical risk premium. While Middle East exports have proven resilient, threats to production infrastructure are mounting. Refined products, especially diesel, face the greatest supply pressure amid depleting inventories and constrained refining capacity. With limited emergency supply buffers, oil markets remain vulnerable to prolonged disruption.

USD view
USD consolidation with limited upside: Our three-month US Dollar Index (DXY) forecast stands at 101, revised upwards from 100.20 last month, reflecting a higher expected Fed rate path. With the October Fed rate pause and a potential December rate hike largely priced in, further tightening would offer limited additional USD support. Persistent inflation, elevated US government bond yields and resilient business activity continue to underpin the USD’s interest-rate advantage. However, in September, payroll growth slowed sharply to 29,000 (from 133,000 in August), the unemployment rate rose to 4.2% from 4.1%, annual wage growth eased to 3.0% from 3.1% and housing starts fell 5.2% m/m. These signs of cooling demand temper expectations of more aggressive Fed tightening. We expect DXY to remain rangebound between 101 and 103, with our three-month forecast at 101.00.

Peaking Fed rates and narrowing rate differentials favour gradual USD weakness: We maintain our 12-month DXY forecast at 98.50. We expect a Fed rate hike in December 2026 and another in H1 2027, taking the federal funds target range to a peak of 4.25-4.50%, before easing in H2 2027. Further BoJ normalisation and the ECB’s relatively restrictive policy stance should progressively narrow the USD’s rate advantage. Persistent fiscal and current account deficits increase reliance on foreign capital inflows, adding to medium-term pressure on the USD. Resilient US growth, AI-related capital inflows and elevated US government bond yields remain important offsets, supporting DXY’s gradual decline towards 98.50.

Summary
Our stock-bond model (3-6 months) is at -2 (minimum: -5) in October, signalling a modest Underweight (UW) in global equities. Historically, a decline in the model score to -2 has been associated with flat to slightly negative returns. The shift was driven by stretched valuations in both global and Asian equities, weaker fundamentals and deteriorating market technicals. On fundamentals, market risk aversion has risen sharply, while PMI new orders have declined over the past three months, pointing to a slowdown in the pace of industrial expansion. On technicals, the share of equity markets trading above their 200-day moving averages, a key gauge of long-term support, has fallen below 60% for the first time since January 2025. The model rebalances in the middle of each month and has generated 11bps of alpha from the equity Underweight initiated on 15 October 2026, lifting YTD alpha vs. the 60/40 equity-bond benchmark to 4.0%.
Our 1-3-month equity market regime model indicates contained bear market risks across US and global equities. Estimated bear market probabilities are 4.2% for the S&P500 and 7.7% for the MSCI AC World, compared with 0.9% and 6.4% respectively in the September outlook. Across both models, volatility measures are the main factors keeping probabilities low, supported by momentum signals. Together, these outweigh modest upward contributions from macro and cross-market factors, leaving little evidence of a bear market regime over the next 1-3 months.
Our market diversity indicator flags reversal risk in MSCI Europe Real Estate and MSCI China Industrials, which are down over 12% and 19% respectively from their August peaks. US equity and USD positioning remain broadly neutral.

articles.title: Making your wealth last longer in retirement
articles.text:
Retirement

Making your wealth last longer in retirement

October 27, 2026

Not everything in retirement is predictable, but many decisions are within your control. Vanguard’s Principles for Retirement Income outlines how your choices, such as managing debt and timing your withdrawals, can significantly extend how long your wealth lasts and help ensure your money goes where you want it to.

Tackle high-interest debt first

With income often less flexible in retirement, reducing debt can go a long way toward making your savings last. Retirees who feel dissatisfied with their retirement are nearly three times more likely to report feeling burdened by unmanageable debt compared with those who feel satisfied.
Retirement savers looking to pay down debt should start with high-interest obligations like credit cards and unsecured loans. Investments rarely earn returns higher than these interest rates, so paying off these obligations can free up cash in the present while increasing flexibility and wealth in the future. Once high-interest debts are paid, you can address moderate-interest obligations like car loans.
While we recommend paying off high-interest debt first because it is the most cost-effective approach, some retirement savers may wish to pay off the smallest balance debt first if it provides them with peace of mind.

Sequence your withdrawals strategically—and tax-efficiently

The order in which you tap your savings matters. Many retirees can reduce their lifetime tax burden by withdrawing from taxable accounts first, then from tax-deferred accounts like traditional IRAs and 401(k)s, and leaving Roth accounts for last. This approach takes advantage of the fact that long-term capital gains rates are often lower than income tax rates early in retirement while income tax on traditional accounts are being deferred.1 In one hypothetical scenario, following this tax-efficient sequence reduced cumulative taxes paid by age 100 by about 14%.
The best withdrawal sequence for you can vary based on your current and expected future tax situation, required minimum distributions (RMDs), and estate planning goals, so consider speaking with an advisor if picking the right approach feels complex.

Time Roth conversions carefully

The years between retiring and when you need to begin taking RMDs from your retirement accounts—age 73 or age 75 for those born in 1960 or later—are often some of the lowest-income years of your retirement. That may put you in a lower tax bracket, which is an ideal time for Roth conversions, in which you pay income tax now to secure tax-free growth later. Vanguard research has found that more than 80% of investors can benefit meaningfully from including Roth conversions in their retirement income plan.2
By gradually converting assets to Roth IRAs during lower-income years, you can:

Smooth out your tax bill;

Reduce future RMDs that might push you into a higher tax bracket; and

Help a surviving spouse avoid steeper single-filer tax rates.

Roth assets can also be passed on to heirs free of income tax, as long as the account has been open for five years.

A Roth conversion strategy can help reduce lifetime tax payments and increase wealth

a. Cumulative tax payments with and without a Roth conversion strategy

b. After-tax wealth with and without a Roth conversion strategy

Notes: The figures assume a 62-year-old female investor with $1,500,000 in a traditional IRA and $500,000 in a taxable account, invested in a static allocation of 50% equities (60% U.S. and 40% international) and 50% bonds (70% U.S. and 30% international). The investor retires and claims Social Security at full retirement age (FRA), with an initial benefit amount of $1,900 per month; FRA is age 67 for those born in 1960 or later, and 66 years and 10 months for those born between 1955 and 1959. The investor has a static annual spending target of $65,000 in real terms. The strategy modeled includes threshold-based Roth conversions starting at age 62 and continuing until the long-term capital gains tax rate on taxable assets reaches 15%. Distribution of return outcomes from the VCMM are derived from 10,000 simulations for each modeled asset class. Simulations are as of February 28, 2026. Results from the model will vary with each use and over time. For more information, please see the Notes section below.

Flex your spending with market conditions

Dynamic spending—adjusting how much you withdraw based on portfolio performance—can help you avoid selling during downturns and enjoy more during strong markets. Rather than taking the same amount every year, you might set guardrails such as boosting withdrawals by up to 5% when your portfolio performs well and trimming withdrawals by up to 2.5% when it underperforms. This approach can help preserve your savings when markets are weak and reduce the risk of needing to make steep spending cuts later in life. Setting guardrails in advance can keep adjustments manageable while helping to make your money last through changing conditions.

Notes: The analysis assumes a 67-year-old female retiree with $800,000 in a traditional 401(k) and $200,000 in a taxable account invested in a static allocation of 50% equities (60% U.S. and 40% international) and 50% bonds (70% U.S. and 30% international). The investor receives $21,080 in annual Social Security benefits. Her real annual spending target includes $50,000 in essential expenses and $15,000 in discretionary expenses. Without dynamic spending, the investor maintains a fixed real spending target adjusted only for inflation. With dynamic spending, the investor’s spending target adjusts based on historical portfolio performance, with annual increases capped at 5% and decreases capped at 2.5%. All results shown are in today’s dollars. Outcomes are generated using the VFAM, which incorporates long-term capital market and inflation projections from VCMM simulations run on February 28, 2026. These results are hypothetical, do not reflect actual investment performance, and are not guarantees of future outcomes.
Sources: Vanguard, using data from the Society of Actuaries.

Protect what you’ve built

Establishing a financial power of attorney (POA) while you’re fully able to make decisions can help ensure your wishes are protected if you experience cognitive decline or are unable to manage your financial affairs for another reason. Choose someone you trust to have access to and oversight of your finances, and consider which type of POA fits your situation:

A durable power of attorney, which takes effect immediately.

A springing power of attorney, which activates only when needed.

For estate planning, how much your heirs receive can be affected by proper account titling and beneficiary designations. Adding someone as a co-owner on your investment account might simplify the transfer but could eliminate the step-up in cost basis, leading to higher taxes if the co-owner sells. Federal estate taxes as of 2026 only apply above $15 million per person or $30 million per couple. If you’re near or over that threshold, estate tax planning will become a priority and may influence your approach to retirement income, gifting, and charitable strategies.
While not everything in retirement is within your control, managing debt, sequencing withdrawals, timing Roth conversions, flexing spending, and protecting assets can help put meaningful financial decisions in your hands. Together, they can help make your wealth last and give you greater confidence in how it’s managed during your life and after.

articles.title: Active Fixed Income Perspectives Q4 2026: Looking through the fog
articles.text:
Active fixed income

Active Fixed Income Perspectives Q4 2026: Looking through the fog

October 23, 2026

Despite ongoing uncertainty around inflation, deficits, geopolitics, and interest rates, the case for fixed income has strengthened. Higher yields provide attractive income and have materially improved prospective returns. Investors have taken notice: Recent strong demand reflects growing recognition that today’s yield environment offers compelling value across a range of potential outcomes.

Vanguard Active Fixed Income Perspectives Q4 2026 (15-page PDF) is our in-depth quarterly commentary on the bond markets, with sector-by-sector analysis and a summary of how those views are reflected in Vanguard’s actively managed bond funds.

Key takeaways

Performance recap

The U.S. economy remained resilient in the third quarter, supported by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Solid growth, elevated energy prices, and a stable labor market led the Federal Reserve to raise rates in September, lifting Treasury yields across the curve. Credit markets remained well supported by healthy fundamentals and strong investor demand. Higher volatility led mortgage-backed securities (MBS) to underperform, while record municipal issuance overwhelmed demand and lifted tax-exempt yields to their highest levels since 2008.

The big picture

Looking forward, the case for owning fixed income has become more compelling. Elevated yields provide investors with attractive income and a larger cushion against uncertainty, even as policy and geopolitical risks remain in focus. Importantly, the recent rise in yields has been driven more by resilient growth and higher real yields than by higher long-term inflation expectations. With global bond yields near their highest levels in roughly two decades, we believe fixed income offers value across a range of potential economic outcomes.

Our approach

Higher yields and greater dispersion across fixed income markets have expanded the opportunity set for active investors. We are focusing on areas where valuations have improved and security selection offers a greater advantage. As a result, we remain underweight sovereign risk in favor of sectors we view as providing more attractive risk-adjusted return potential. At the fund level, we are neutral on U.S. duration and the curve relative to benchmarks. We see attractive opportunities in MBS following the recent repricing and remain constructive on investment-grade credit and securitized assets, where yields continue to offer compelling income potential. In global rates markets, we favor select relative value opportunities, including an overweight to German bunds versus U.S. Treasuries and short duration and curve flattening exposures in Japan. In municipals, elevated yields and attractive structures have created meaningful value in high-grade bonds further out on the curve.

articles.title: Low-key UK Budget kicks the can into 2027
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

28 Oct 2026

Low-key UK Budget kicks the can into 2027

The UK Budget presented recently was a low-key event aimed at keeping markets onside ahead of a more comprehensive overhaul of fiscal policy in 2027. The package of temporary cost-of-living measures will provide a small additional near-term boost to growth, however, we’d already planned to raise our forecast for 2027 due to the recent sustained strength of AI-intensive sectors.

The decision to run with lower headroom looks like a sensible compromise given the uncertainty over whether high gilt yields will persist and the likelihood that fiscal policy will be reshaped next year. We think markets will be comfortable with this decision, though we still have major doubts that the planned tax rises will deliver the scale of deficit reduction that the government hopes over the next few years.

A combination of limited detail, unaddressed challenges, and the length of time for any upside to show means that the devolution announcements will not lead us to revising our regional forecasts.

articles.text:
Back to InsightsGlobal Investment ResearchFuture consumerDemographicsFuture citiesGeneral Research InsightsHong Kong Northern Metropolis: Turning a vision into realityBy Michelle Kwok, Head of Asia Real Estate and Hong Kong Equity Research26 October 2026ArticleArticleShare via EmailShare on FacebookShare on LinkedInShare on TwitterMore than five times the size of Manhattan, the Northern Metropolis will reshape Hong Kong’s economy over the next 20 years. We explore the investment opportunities.
Imagine it’s 2035. You are riding in a robotaxi in Hong Kong’s northern New Territories, surrounded by research and technology laboratories, clusters of data centres, and university campuses.

You are at the heart of the Northern Metropolis, the most ambitious infrastructure project in the city’s history. Unveiled in 2021, the plan will centre around four economic hubs focused on commerce, professional services, technology, and eco-tourism. The Northern Metropolis is seen as a key part of the Greater Bay Area, the network of 11 cities in the Pearl River Delta.
HKD3trnestimated to cost according to CSCI over the lifetime of the project300km²Total land coverage of the Northern Metropolis projectThe numbers tell the story of the project’s vast ambition. According to CSCI, the Northern Metropolis is estimated to cost HKD3trn over the lifetime of the project. It will cover 30,000 hectares, or 300 square kilometres – that’s one third of Hong Kong’s land area and more than five times the size of Manhattan. It will have the capacity to house about 2.5m residents, a third of the current population, supported by half a million new homes and jobs.

Closely connected with Shenzhen and the wider Greater Bay Area, the Northern Metropolis will reshape Hong Kong’s economy and transform the city’s innovation and technology landscape. The project is supported at the highest level. Under mainland China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (FYP), Hong Kong will become a “proactive contributor” to the national strategy via its “super connector” role. At the same time, the Northern Metropolis is going to be a key part of the city’s first FYP – the government has already cut red tape to streamline approvals on multiple fronts.

Some parts of the plan are already taking shape: By mid-2026, more than 90 enterprises had signed up for the Hetao Hong Kong Park, a high-tech ecosystem. Lenovo and China Resources moved in this summer. The University of Hong Kong is considering setting up a bond programme to fund its expansion in University Town, a network of campuses. In August 2026, first large-scale tender was awarded, with JD the anchor tenant. There is also tangible progress on transport and real estate, and data centre investment is on the way.

This is an unprecedented undertaking. The government and private stakeholders face complex challenges in relation to the capital outlay, and the need to attract private sector investment. Our report discusses the implications for macro-economics, demographics and sustainability, and identifies eight cross-sector opportunities.

articles.text:

What’s on upstream leaders’ minds?
Investing in the portfolio for the 2030s and beyond

23 October 2026
4 minute read

Email

View Simon Flowers's full profile

Upstream has a new lease of life. Meetings with industry leaders, investors and bankers in London last week revealed a confidence that’s been hard to detect for a decade or more.
The massive financial windfall from global conflict is certainly part of it. Upstream and integrated companies will collectively reap at least US$700 billion of additional free cash flow in 2026 on our calculations. A rare trifecta of high oil and LNG prices and astonishing refining margins kicked in, Brent averaging US$100/bbl compared with the notional US$60/bbl anticipated pre-Iran war. The windfall is timely as IOCs and NOCs look to invest in building portfolios for the future, but it’s by no means the only factor. Here’s our take on what’s on the industry’s minds.
1. Macro – this is the new normal
Shocks and uncertainty are here to stay, the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz won’t be the last disruption to energy flows. Perspectives on longer-term oil prices haven’t changed much, the industry still considers US$70-75/bbl Brent (real) will be needed to incentivise investment in new projects to offset natural decline. Near-term price forecasting, though, is well-nigh impossible. Volatility is the one certainty for both oil and gas pricing.
2. Global upstream outlook the most upbeat for a decade
The belief that oil and gas demand will be resilient into the 2030s and perhaps beyond has grown in recent years, boosted even by the war in Iran which has been a reminder of the energy system’s present reliance on molecules. Sustained investment is required to fill the supply gap as producing fields decline (we estimate 20 million b/d of new oil supply must be brought onstream by 2035). Importing governments’ desire for supply diversity supports investment in legacy, emerging and new upstream provinces. We have seen reinvigorated interest in a number of regions not experienced since the pre-2015 era.
3. Supply chain is a risk
After a decade of incessant cost pressure from operators, service companies have had little appetite to invest in new capacity as old assets are retired. Bottlenecks loom as upstream invests to meet future demand, not least in deepwater. Refurbishment of old rigs may be a stop gap, but deepwater drilling rigs will become scarce and day rates could soar. Operators will need to reinvent their relationship with the supply chain to secure equipment (largely rigs and heavy lift vessels) at reasonable prices. This is familiar ground for industry; in future closer collaboration with the supply chain will be paramount.
4. Shaping the upstream portfolio
Resilience of portfolio and balance sheet are the guiding lights to minimise risk in a world of heightened uncertainty. After a rocky decade (including dividend cuts for some European majors) bigger IOCs want an all-weather portfolio that can pay the dividend even at the low point of the cycle. Strategies for building a balanced upstream portfolio vary by company size and region, but the general framework for investment is strict hurdle rates, diversification (geographical, oil/gas/LNG production), trading and risk management. Refining’s value in integrated companies’ portfolios has been amply demonstrated through the crisis.
5. Upstream deal-making is back on
There are presently more buyers than sellers, as companies look to strengthen portfolios and future production profiles. Recent transactions show that sellers and buyers can, if the will is there, reach agreement on value even with current extreme price uncertainty. Deals that have completed are typically structured on a base case of Brent US$65-75/bbl but with an oil price-linked payment over a set period. But there’s no free pass for buyers – investors will always have to be persuaded on value, portfolio fit and the impact on the balance sheet. Banks are busy, incoming calls as frequent as outgoing, more deals may flow after the US mid-term elections.
6. M&A, exploration, DROs all on the table
Bigger companies will look at all options to strengthen portfolios, including asset/corporate acquisitions and organic investment. Exploration is unashamedly back, high impact deepwater acreage reloading in particular for the big IOCs and NOCs with its potential to deliver volume at scale. West Africa, Latin America and SE Asia are among the hot spots. The crisis in the Middle East is laying the foundations for access to more Discovered Resource Opportunities in the region, potentially including Saudi Arabia, where until now upstream has been off limits to IOCs. US IOCs, perhaps even Chinese NOCs, with strong G-to-G relationships, look well positioned.

articles.title: Market update - October 30th 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Market update - October 30th, 20264 min readDataBitcoin held its ground through a Fed hold and a nervous pre-election weekBitcoin spent most of the week consolidating with admirable discipline, quickly recovering a brief dip below US$77k on Thursday. Investors are positioned defensively, the premium traders pay to hold leveraged bets on rising prices has shrunk, and there is little appetite to chase risk ahead of the US elections. Yet despite that rather flat surface, Bitcoin has held up better than much of the broader crypto market and many more volatile assets. It does not feel like a market suddenly overcome with optimism, more one becoming increasingly selective about where it is prepared to take risk.A hold, not an all-clearRates were left unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00%, which surprised nobody, while Fed Chair Kevin Warsh was less hawkish than many had feared.¹ His view was that September’s hike is beginning to have an effect, financial conditions have tightened and the Committee can now afford the luxury of waiting for more evidence. He was careful not to imply that tightening is over, but equally avoided commentary that would have sent short-dated yields sharply higher. The relief therefore came less from any sense that the Fed is finished than from the absence of any signal that it intends to go beyond the further hike already pencilled in for this year. The official statement still described inflation as elevated and economic activity as expanding at a strong pace.¹The data behind that caution are not encouraging. September CPI, published earlier in the month, ran at 3.7% year-on-year,² and last Friday’s flash PMI offered little consolation. The composite remained firmly expansionary, while selling-price inflation accelerated to its fastest pace since August 2022.³ The Fed is therefore stuck with a particularly awkward combination: growth that refuses to roll over politely and inflation that refuses to disappear on cue.Alphabet’s earnings have added another wrinkle.⁴ Revenue was not the problem. The concern is that markets have become rather less willing than they were a few months ago to reward anything wearing an AI badge, and the bar for a convincing earnings beat has risen sharply. Disappointment is being punished accordingly. Bitcoin has been caught in some of that volatility, but has again behaved with rather more composure than many of its neighbours.Wall Street moves onto crypto railsOne development this week deserves rather more attention than it has received. trade[XYZ] and ICE, the owner of the New York Stock Exchange, plan to bring 24/7 perpetual futures (futures contracts with no expiry date that trade around the clock) to US investors, built on Hyperliquid, a blockchain-based trading venue. The launch remains subject to CFTC approval.⁵ For Hyperliquid, this is a significant endorsement. It suggests the technology is beginning to move beyond crypto-native experimentation and into the architecture of regulated traditional markets, precisely the sort of crossover we have expected as tokenisation (issuing conventional assets on a blockchain) and 24/7 trading mature.Elections and oilPolymarket implies a 93% probability that Democrats take the House and a 68% probability that they also take the Senate.⁶ Divided government may initially be read as negative for crypto, but we would be wary of pushing that conclusion too far. Stablecoin and digital asset policy has become increasingly bipartisan. Stablecoins, digital dollars backed largely by short-dated US Treasuries, are also a new source of demand for government debt, and that appeal is unlikely to disappear simply because Congress changes colour.Israel’s election has produced no clear majority,⁷ while renewed Middle East tensions continue to push energy prices higher. If that persists, the consequences are fairly mechanical: higher oil, firmer inflation expectations and a Fed with even less room to soften. It remains one of the cleaner channels through which geopolitics can still feed directly into Bitcoin.Waiting, without a tantrumSo the market waits. For the elections, for the next inflation print, for the Fed, and perhaps for somebody else to blink first geopolitically. Bitcoin is not breaking higher, but neither has it been willing to break lower despite tighter policy expectations, volatile equities and elevated geopolitical risk. In a market this uncertain, its refusal to have a tantrum is probably the most constructive signal on offer.SourcesFederal Reserve, FOMC statement and Chair Warsh press conference transcript (preliminary), 28 Oct 2026US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index, September 2026, released 14 Oct 2026S&P Global, Flash US PMI, October 2026, released 23 Oct 2026Alphabet, Q3 2026 earnings release, 28 Oct 2026trade[XYZ], announcement of planned US perpetual futures market with ICE, 29 Oct 2026Polymarket, US 2026 midterm election markets, accessed 29 Oct 2026Associated Press, Israeli election results and coalition outlook, 27–28 Oct 2026Published onOct 30th, 2026WriterJames ButterfillHead of ResearchFormer Head of Research at ETF Securities, James leads CoinShares' Research department with deep expertise in equity and fund management.

articles.title: US Economy Continues To Roar, While The Fed Waits For More
articles.text: The FOMC voted 10-2 on Wednesday to hold the federal funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%, with the two dissenters favoring a 25bps hike. Yet Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's assessment of the US economy sounded decidedly hawkish. Economic growth is robust and broadening, the labor market is in good shape, inflation remains above the Fed's 2.0% y/y target, and financial conditions are hardly tight. So why did the Fed stand pat?Warsh argued that September's hike was already tightening financial conditions, inflation expectations remained anchored, and stronger productivity growth was allowing the economy to expand without overheating.
