articles.title: New Insurer Start-up Unit
articles.text:
New Insurer Start-up Unit

The New Insurer Start-up Unit provides information and support for those thinking of setting up a new insurer in the UK.

Thinking of becoming an insurerBeing an insurer means undertaking the regulated activities of effecting or carrying out contracts of insurance. Any firm that wants to be an insurer must be authorised to undertake these activities by the PRA with consent from the FCA. Before going through the new insurer authorisation process, firms will need to consider what functions they will carry out as an insurer and submit a regulatory business plan to outline their strategy and how it meets our threshold conditions. When you are ready to start the process, you should contact the NISU team by emailing NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk. Upon receipt of an enquiry with the regulatory business plan, we will arrange a meeting with you to get started with the pre-application and application phases. The NISU team are ready to help you become a UK authorised insurer, and please expand the headings below to find out more.

From a regulatory perspective, an insurer is a firm with a ‘Part 4A permission’ that includes the activities of effecting contracts of insurance or carrying out contracts of insurance. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 sets out a list of relevant regulated activities (see Chapter III Insurance) but does not attempt an exhaustive definition of a contract of insurance. Potential applicants should refer to section 6 of the FCA’s Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG 6 - FCA Handbook Opens in a new window) for Guidance on the identification of contracts of insurance. The section Guidance on insurance mediation activities in section 5 may also be helpful (PERG 5 - FCA Handbook Opens in a new window).
The UK insurance market covers various lines of business, to list a few:
Non-life class of business:
• Accident and sickness
• Motor vehicle liability and other motor vehicle insurance
• Fire and other damage to property
• Marine, aviation and railway rolling sock
• General Liability
• Credit and suretyship
• Other classes
Life class of business:
• Life and annuity
• Marriage and birth
• Linked long term
• Permanent health
• Capital redemption
• Pension fund management
• Collective insurance
Depending on the area of the insurance market you plan to enter, there may be alternatives which allow you to offer similar products through another insurer without becoming a direct insurer yourself. For example, if you are interested in working in a niche area of the market or perhaps prefer to test your product first, operating as an intermediary under some form of delegated authority from an existing insurer e.g. as a managing general agent (MGA) may be more appropriate. There are a range of intermediaries, and the most appropriate route will depend on a number of factors, e.g. through which sales channels the insurance will be sold. Information on how to apply for intermediary activities can be accessed via the following link to the FCA website: apply to become a consumer investments firm Opens in a new window.
A firm wanting to sell regulated products but not wishing to become directly authorised can also agree with a PRA and/or FCA authorised firm to become its appointed representative (AR). Insurance mediation activities that an appointed representative can carry out are set out in the FCA handbook Opens in a new window, however, the AR is limited to only carrying out the regulated activities the authorised firm has permission to undertake. A prospective AR will undergo fitness and propriety checks and will have to follow the rules and procedures as set by the authorised firm. Rules relating to appointed representatives are set out in SUP 12 of the FCA Handbook and applicants can also get further information about the application process via the following link to the FCA website: become an appointed representative Opens in a new window.
Will my firm be subject to the Solvency II Directive?
Within the United Kingdom, newly authorised insurers and reinsurers will be subject to the Solvency II regime if they meet all the conditions stated in PRA Rulebook. Insurance General Application | Prudential Regulation Authority Handbook & Rulebook Opens in a new window.
Firms that are not subject to the Solvency II regime are known as ‘Non-Directive Firms Opens in a new window’ and are subject to different rules around key areas such as capital requirements, governance requirements, and reporting requirements. Applicants should consider whether their firm will be subject to the Solvency II regime when preparing any application and plan accordingly.
What business will your insurer carry out?
Before contacting us, you should familiarise yourself with the PRA’s expectations around key topics such as governance and financial resources. Further information on financial planning may be found in SS4/18 Opens in a new window, while the PRA’s expectations regarding governance are detailed in SS5/16 Opens in a new window. The full range of PRA publications containing guidance on a broad range of topics may be found at Prudential regulation publications Opens in a new window.
It is important that you consider the following key areas, as these are things we will initially want to focus on in our review.
• Regulatory business plan
• Senior management, the board and governance
• Financial resources
• IT strategy
• Reinsurance
• Resolution
• Outsourcing
What if your firm is already authorised?
If your firm is already authorised by the FCA, e.g. as an intermediary, you will need to apply to the PRA and FCA to vary your permissions to add insurance activities. While this is legally a different regulatory transaction to a new authorisation, you will need to follow the same process as a new firm applying to be an insurer (because of the substantive change to your business model) and we encourage you to start pre-application with us as normal to help the process of varying your permissions run smoothly.
When can I call myself an Insurer?
A firm cannot call itself an insurer until it has been authorised. The use of certain sensitive words such as ‘Insurance’ and ‘Insurer’, ‘reassurer, ‘reinsurance’, ‘reassurance’, ’reinsurer’, ‘underwriter’ and ‘underwriting’ in registered company names is controlled by legislation in order to prevent the public from being misled. You should seek the FCA’s consent before using domain names that include sensitive words, checking the guidance found at sensitive business names Opens in a new window.
What are the next steps?
As mentioned earlier, when you are ready to start the process, you should contact the NISU team by emailing NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk to discuss your application and we will arrange an initial pre-application meeting. The NISU team are ready to help you become a UK authorised insurer.

The pre-application stage helps the firm to:

Meet the NISU team
Understand how the authorisation process works
Understand regulatory expectations of the firm, in particular, the PRA and FCA Threshold Conditions
Submit an application that is as complete as possible when the firm is ready to formally apply for authorisation
Identify any particular concerns that we might have early on and help you to decide whether you want to spend time and money on an application that may not progress further

It helps the NISU Team to:

Meet the firm and understand their business proposal
Identify any concerns, which will be communicated quickly to the firm and gives the firm the opportunity to resolve them before submitting an application
Deal with the firm’s application quickly once it has been submitted

The table below outlines what we expect from firms during the pre-application process and what you can expect from the NISU team.

Firm’s Responsibilities

NISU Team’s Responsibilities

Be open, honest and collaborate with us.

Be open, honest and give clear feedback on your proposals.

Develop your plans, complete the necessary work, prepare and send materials in good time for meetings with us.

The PRA and FCA will attend all meetings unless we advise you otherwise.

Ensure key individuals at your firm who will drive the proposition forward are involved throughout the process and attend the pre-application meetings.

Ensure the pre-application meeting is productive, and the authorisation process is clearly explained.

Provide all information that you think we should be aware of. Be ready, willing and organised.

Hold the appropriate number of meetings for your application (maximum of 3) giving due consideration to the proposals in the business plan.

Address and incorporate any feedback provided by us into your Business Plan before moving to the next stage.

Ensure feedback letter is sent to the Firm within a maximum of 10 working days after each meeting.

Please note that the NISU team do not provide a consultancy service or legal advice.
We offer a maximum of three meetings for standard applications. However, additional meetings may be arranged if a firm’s proposal involves innovative or particularly complex IT systems. These meetings include the initial meeting, feedback meeting, and challenge session. Established firms, such as those seeking to open new branches or subsidiaries in the UK, may require fewer meetings.

Initial meeting
The initial meeting is held after the submission of a high-level business plan summarising your plans. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 10 working days before we meet. Once you have sent us your materials, we will arrange the meeting at a mutually convenient time and agree on the agenda for the meeting.

The business plan should not be a ‘sales pitch’ as the regulators will have a different focus, and you should aim to provide an explanation of why you want to be an insurer and your business strategy including:

Business plan – products, target market, customer types
Sources of funding – how will the business be funded and details of any investors and/or funding in place
Project plan – an overview and timeline of your plan to set up the new insurer. (This is particularly important if new IT systems are required)
Owner and controllers – details of proposed owners and controllers
Corporate governance – details of structure, board, senior management and governance arrangements

The initial meeting provides an opportunity for firms to discuss their plans with us and ask questions about the authorisation process. It provides the NISU team with the opportunity to raise any concerns with the proposed business at an early stage.

The NISU team will then provide written feedback to the firm within 10 working days of the meeting to enable the firm to respond to and resolve any issues. You should continue to develop your business proposition and incorporate responses to our feedback into the next version

Feedback meeting
The feedback meeting will be held after the firm has submitted, and we have reviewed, a more detailed business plan, which includes the firm’s response to the feedback from the initial meeting. This meeting provides an opportunity to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the firm’s proposed business model. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 10 working days before we meet. After the meeting, the NISU team will provide written feedback to the firm which we expect the firm to address in their subsequent business plan.

At the end of the feedback meeting, we will discuss the actions you will need to complete if you want to progress to the next stage. Within 10 working days of the meeting, we will send you our formal feedback in a letter. You should continue to develop your business plan and incorporate responses to our feedback into the next version.

Challenge session
The challenge session are the culmination of the pre-application application process. This final meeting is held just before a firm submits an application. The aim of the meeting is to discuss your proposals in depth and provide detailed challenge on the content of the final business plan. At this stage, your business plan should be fully developed and will form the basis of the discussion at the challenge session where we will offer an honest and open assessment of your plans. You need to send us materials for discussion a minimum of 15 working days before we meet. Once you have sent us your materials, we will arrange the meetings at a mutually convenient time.

Firms can expect rigorous challenge on their proposed business model. The aim is to identify any remaining issues that need to be addressed before you submit your application. The challenge session will be attended by your case officers along with senior representatives and specialists from both regulators. We expect several of your executives and, where possible, non-executives to attend. You should expect the meeting to last about two hours.

At the end of the challenge session, we will discuss next steps and actions with you and within 10 working days of the meeting, we will send you our formal feedback in a letter. If you go on to submit an application, you should finalise your business plan and incorporate responses to our feedback from the challenge session.

The meetings will typically be held at the PRA’s office in London. The meetings can be held in person or virtual. We will send you an agenda before all meetings which will centre on your explanation of the materials that you have sent us and the attendees from each regulator.

Our aim is that the pre-application process will give the firm a clearer understanding of our regulatory expectations, and the opportunity to resolve any potential problems before an application is submitted. Once the application is submitted, it is expected to be of sufficiently high quality to enable the NISU team to reach a decision more quickly.

Pre-application timeframes
The pace at which a firm progresses through the pre-application stage is up to the firm. Please read through the application forms and supporting notes as you may find them helpful when preparing for the meetings.

The NISU team expect to be kept up to date on your progress and will endeavour to hold pre-application meetings in a timely manner. If, however, we do not hear from a firm for six months after a meeting we will assume that you do not want to proceed with your application and close our file.

Please contact the NISU inbox at NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk and submit a high-level regulatory business plan along with your request for a pre-application meeting. We will then organise the meeting with you. The firm’s advisors or consultants are welcome to attend the pre-application meetings, but we do not expect them to speak on the firm’s behalf.

Please note that the pre-application stage is optional. If you choose not to use it, you can send your application directly to the NISU inbox at NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk. We will then use our statutory powers as set out in FSMA to reach a decision on your application. If you have any questions about the pre-application process, please contact the NISU team, and we will be happy to assist.

Your Business Plan should cover the following points as a minimum:

business plan – details of products, delivery channels and target market
business viability – competitive advantage, market research and how your firm will make money
financial resources – financial projections (for three years), capital management strategy (as appropriate)
sources of funding – proposed funding model
owners and controllers – proposed owners and controllers
corporate governance – structure, board, senior management and governance arrangements
risk management – risk management and control framework
customer journey – products, pricing, complaint handling and on-boarding arrangements (including Anti-Money Laundering/Know Your Customer processes)
outsourcing - details of key outsourcing arrangements
IT infrastructure and systems and timescales for implementation and testing recovery and resolution plans (if appropriate)
policies and procedures – operational and regulatory policies and procedures
business continuity – business continuity plans (if appropriate)
scope of permissions – details of the regulated activities you wish to undertake reinsurance arrangements
project plan – project plan for setting up the insurer

Background to NISUThe New Insurer Start-Up Unit (NISU) is a joint initiative by the UK’s financial regulators, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), set up in 2018.NISU is a team of experts across the PRA and FCA that provides necessary information and support to prospective insurers, aiding their progression to become authorised UK insurers. Our joint assessment process ensures any firm wishing to be an insurer is authorised by both the PRA and FCA.NISU’s objective is to guide firms through the authorisation process by leading efficient pre-application engagement and formalising the application process. We frequently explore initiatives to improve our process and contribute to the PRA’s and FCA’s secondary competitiveness objectives.This NISU guidance serves as a reference tool covering key supervisory topics. While it provides valuable information, it is not exhaustive and does not encompass all applicable UK laws and regulations. Prospective firms should use this webpage to aid their business planning and ensure compliance with all relevant regulatory requirements in the UK. Before commencing the new insurer authorisation process, firms should also consider whether setting up an insurer is right for them and what functions they will carry out. The regulatory business plan (RBP) they develop must outline their strategy and how they will meet and comply with PRA and FCA threshold conditions.We also encourage prospective UK insurers to take advantage of our PRA and FCA pre-application meetings as they can be extremely beneficial for all parties.

Authorisation process and regulatory expectationsTo achieve their objective of setting up an insurer, firms should be ready, willing and organised. It is important for firms to understand the authorisation process and regulatory expectations before submitting an application to us. This will ensure that the application submitted is of high-quality and as complete as possible. Read the New insurer authorisation process and regulatory expectations.
This section clarifies why submitting a complete application is important and gives an indication of what happens during our assessment process, including decision timelines.
Please be aware that authorisation is only the start of a new insurer’s journey to being established. In our guidance below, we have outlined some of our key regulatory expectations, but firms are responsible for considering in detail and complying with all the applicable laws, rules and regulatory policies.Mobilisation regime for new insurersThe PRA created a ‘mobilisation’ regime, effective from 31 December 2024, to facilitate new insurer expansion and entry into the UK market. We welcome discussions with potential new applicants who are applying for authorisation and considering using this new mobilisation phase.

The regime offers an optional stage, beginning at the point of authorisation, during which a new firm can operate with business restrictions while it completes the final development aspects of its insurer. These newly authorised insurers-in-mobilisation are given a period up of 12 months to finish building out their business, including securing additional funding, if required, while operating with business restrictions and proportionate regulatory requirements, as well as adhering to lower minimum capital requirements. Read the mobilisation regime for insurers webpage for further information.For more details on the mobilisation framework for new insurers, refer to:
CP12/23 - Review of Solvency II: Adapting to the UK insurance market
PS2/24 – Review of Solvency II: Adapting to the UK insurance market

Other pathwaysAs well as the formal new insurer authorisations process guidance above, there are other pathways available for firms to consider.

Insurance special purpose vehicles (ISPVs)As part of our amendments to allow the UK non-life insurance sector to play a bigger role in the global ILS market, we have created an accelerated pathway for ISPVs that meet certain defined criteria to gain approval. In such cases, the PRA will undertake rapid assessment of applications and, where satisfied, issue approvals within 10 working days of a 'complete' application submission.We recommend early engagement with the NISU team at the PRA, to assist with ensuring completeness of your ISPV application. Email us at ISPVMailbox@bankofengland.co.uk if you are interested in this accelerated route.The specific criteria for the accelerated 10 working day ISPV process can be found here: PRA's approach to authorising and supervising UK Insurance Special Purpose Vehicles Opens in a new window.For more information, visit insurance special purpose vehicles (ISPVs) Opens in a new window, where you can also find applicable application forms for ISPVs, to be submitted to ISPVMailbox@bankofengland.co.uk.

Wholesale insurance accelerated authorisation pathwayThrough the Wholesale Insurance Accelerated Authorisation Pathway (The Pathway), developed jointly by the PRA and FCA, we aim to provide an accelerated route to authorisation for a sub-set of London Market wholesale applicants.Read our wholesale insurance accelerated authorisation pathway Opens in a new window webpage for more information.

Submitting an applicationThis section lists the relevant application forms and provides details about applicable fees once you are ready to submit an application.

Application feesThe PRA and the FCA Regulatory Transaction fees for applications for new authorisations are payable in accordance with the PRA Rulebook Opens in a new window and the FCA Handbook Opens in a new window. It is your responsibility to cross-check the fees against the PRA Rulebook and FCA guidelines before making any payment. If you are unsure what fees are applicable to your firm, please email us at NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.The preferred method for payment is via BACS to the FCA who will provide a single invoice covering both the PRA and FCA fees.Please make the payment to the FCA using the details below:Account name: FCA Collection account
Bank name: Lloyds Bank
Account number: 00828179
Sort code: 30-00-02
Swift code: LOYD GB 2LCTY
Iban code: GB68 LOYD 3000 0200 8281 79.When you make the payment, please reference it with the following: Title: ‘New authorisation application’ and the ‘firm name’ (name of the firm applying for authorisation).Please then email your remittance advice and payment details to:fcafees@fca.org.uk and NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.If you cannot make payment to the FCA using BACS. Please contact NewInsurerStartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk for instructions on how to pay by cheque.

Applications forms

Full authorisation application form (DOCX) Opens in a new window

Authorisation with restriction (mobilisation) application form (DOCX) Opens in a new window
Branch application/re-domiciliation form (DOCX) Opens in a new window
Supplement for Lloyd's managing agents - notes (DOC) Opens in a new window
Supplement for Lloyd's managing agents (DOC) Opens in a new window

Corporate controller form (docx) Opens in a new window
Partnership controller form (docx) Opens in a new window
Individual controller form (docx) Opens in a new window
Trust controller form (docx) Opens in a new window

IT self-assessment questionnaire: insurers (xlsm)
Detailed IT controls form: insurers (xlsm)

Waivers and modifications applications (pdf)
Application form: Solvency II approval (pdf)

Form A – Long: Application to perform controlled functions (long) (pdf) Opens in a new window
Form A – Short: Application to perform controlled functions (short) (pdf) Opens in a new window
SOR: Statement of responsibilities (pdf) Opens in a new window
Form M: Notification of non-executive director or key function holder (pdf) Opens in a new window

Being an authorised insurerAuthorisation is only the start of the journey to becoming an established insurer. Insurers must continue to meet our threshold conditions at all times, as well as ongoing regulatory requirements under both PRA and FCA Supervision.

Insurers must submit regular financial, risk, and conduct reports, and ensure frameworks and policies are continually reviewed to align with risks and business growth.

As supervision evolves over time, the PRA and FCA adopt a risk-based approach, adjusting oversight based on an insurer’s size, complexity and risk profile. As staying informed is essential, the PRA and FCA provide ongoing industry guidance, thematic reviews, and policy updates that insurers must follow to ensure compliance.

Read Being an authorised insurer for further information.

FAQsVisit our Frequently asked questions page for common queries regarding the application process.

Authorised insurersVisit Which firms does the PRA regulate? for a list of authorised insurers regulated by the PRA.

Contact usIf you have any queries about becoming a new insurer, email us:NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk.The NISU is part of the regulators’ ongoing work to improve the authorisation process for prospective new insurers in the UK. We want the process, information and materials to be helpful for potential applicants so that we can have an effective and efficient way of working together, and lead to an improved quality of application when the time comes. It’s really important that we hear from you, the users of the NISU, about what is working well and what we can improve.As our consideration of further developments relating to the authorisation of new insurers continues, we are also interested to hear views on challengers faced by the firm in the insurance industry and possible measures to address them. Please email NewInsurerStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk with your feedback and input.

articles.text:

Take Two: Market performance diverges

By
BNP PARIBAS ASSET MANAGEMENT 26.10.2026

In this article
What do you need to know?Around the worldFigure in focus: 18%Chart of the weekWords of wisdom: Small AI What’s coming up?

What do you need to know?

Stocks endured further volatility over the past week, as concerns over corporate spending on artificial intelligence and rising oil prices weighed on sentiment. The MSCI World NR and the US blue-chip S&P 500 indices each fell by 1% in the week to Thursday’s close, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped by a steeper 3%.* Elsewhere, the Dow Jones was up 1% while Europe’s Stoxx 600 was flat. Meanwhile, eurozone fixed income underperformed as US Treasuries rallied. The yield on French government bonds surpassed 5% for the first time since 2002 on uncertainty over the country’s finances – yields move inversely to prices.

*In US dollar terms. Source: FactSet, as of 22 October 2026

Around the world

China’s economy expanded at a faster pace than expected in the third quarter of this year. GDP grew by 4.5% on an annualised basis, up from Q2’s three-year low of 4.3%. Growth was boosted by artificial intelligence-related exports, despite domestic demand remaining subdued and an ongoing downturn in the property market. The quarterly data puts China on track to meet the lower end of the government’s official 4.5%-5% growth target for the year, analysts said.

Figure in focus: 18%

Greenhouse emissions must reduce by 18% by the end of the decade to limit global warming to 1.5°C, the United Nations warned. Current levels of emissions reductions show that under the “lowest possible” overshoot scenario, peak warming will reach 1.7°C to 1.8°C around the middle of the century. To meet the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C target, “immediate and aggressive cuts” to emissions are needed, of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, the UN said. If action is taken, including carbon capture and storage, global warming could return to below 1.5°C by 2100, it added.

Chart of the week

Technology hardware is dominant in driving corporate earnings growth and equity price appreciation. The information technology sector accounted for almost two-thirds of global earnings growth in the third quarter, at 60%, followed by energy at 20%. Expectations are high for technology companies globally, with the sector forecast to see a doubling of earnings compared to the same quarter a year ago, according to the market consensus. Earnings growth in other sectors of global stock markets is relatively low. Investors are keeping a sharp eye on earnings trends, reflecting concerns that stock markets may be overly dependent on the tech sector.

Words of wisdom: Small AI

Task-specific AI models which need less computing power and energy to run. The World Bank launched a new digital strategy to help developing countries improve digital access and services and create more jobs. It emphasised the potential benefits of small AI: tools that are adapted to specific tasks and local conditions, such as helping farmers identify crop disease, supporting health workers, or helping businesses manage inventory. However, substantial barriers remain, with only 23% of people in low-income countries using the internet, the World Bank said.

What’s coming up?

Central banks take centre stage this week. On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of Canada each meet to make their respective interest rate decisions. The European Central Bank follows on Thursday with its own rate-setting meeting while the Bank of Japan convenes on Friday. Elsewhere, the UK unveils its Autumn Budget on Wednesday. On Thursday, the US publishes its Q3 GDP growth rate, followed by the eurozone which reports Q3 growth data on Friday.

Higher Yields And Corporate Profits

Tan Kai Xian

Gavekal Research | 22 Oct 2026

Equity investors were served a morsel of optimism Wednesday, as Meta’s chairman Mark Zuckerberg claimed the company’s AI investments “are paying off,” and raised guidance for total 2026 capital expenditure after third-quarter earnings beat estimates. Corporate Law and Transformation

Group reorganizations and transformations come in many forms, domestic or cross-border, transaction-driven or strategic. EY Corporate Law and Transformation teams help businesses design and provide legally robust, commercially efficient structures, combining corporate law knowledge with multidisciplinary delivery to achieve value-added and integrated transformation outcomes.

Complex and fragmented group structures that are difficult to manage and tough to align with business strategyTransaction-driven change requiring pre-deal business separation or post-deal integration, often involving mixed business units in cross-border structures and tight timelinesEvolving regulatory, legal and tax expectations across multiple jurisdictions driving changes to group structuresInefficient group structures with redundant or duplicative entities, often the legacy of deal activityThe need to simplify operating and legal entity models ahead of significant events such as ERP implementation or new go-to-market strategies

Our Corporate Law and Transformation lawyers regularly advise on complex, high-value, multinational carve-out transactions and are consistently recognized by leading legal directories, with many practitioners receiving individual market accolades. With more than 3,000 lawyers and legal professionals across 75+ countries, supported by legal managed service delivery centers, we bring a coordinated global approach to international transformations. News Release
US data centre additions return to growth in Q2 2026 as developers push construction and pipeline continues to expand
54 GW added to Q2 pipeline, up 29% from year-ago and 5% from Q1 2026

28 October 2026
3 minute read

Email
Share by email

54 gigawatts (GW) of new data centre capacity was added to the US pipeline in Q2 2026, up 29% year-over-year, according to a new analysis from Wood Mackenzie.
Cumulative US disclosed data centre pipeline now totals more than 430 GW, of which approximately 59% is under active development. Projects totaling nearly 80 GW are currently under construction, up from 44 GW at the end of Q1, according to Wood Mackenzie’s US data center pipeline Q3 report.
This activity takes place against the backdrop of increased scrutiny and local opposition against data centres, which has triggered more than 400 data centre moratoriums since January 2026 from state and local lawmakers, affecting 18% of tracked data centre sites, representing more than 100 GW of planned capacity.
“The latest data reveals projects are steadily advancing from early development to permitting and construction phases,” said Caitlin Connelly, senior analyst, Wood Mackenzie. “However, power availability and local opposition will remain key constraints to near-term buildout.”
Development concentrates geographically…and among developers
Development is concentrating geographically, with PJM and ERCOT accounting for nearly half of all capacity under development. PJM has pushed ahead of ERCOT in total development capacity, with ~20 GW of new projects entering active development in H1 2026 alone. ERCOT's pipeline, meanwhile, appears to be the most mature, with more than 40% of its development capacity already under construction.
The top five developers account for a quarter of both planned and development capacity, and the pipeline is dominated by a relatively small number of large, sophisticated players. Capital concentration is even more pronounced, as total disclosed planned capex exceeds US$2.3 trillion nationally.
Utility Commitments Plateau
High confidence utility commitments levelled off at ~300 GW in Q2 2026, as a handful of utilities downgraded their reported pipelines to weed out speculative projects. Within that total, committed capacity with signed electricity service or construction agreements expanded to 201 GW, indicating that projects are progressing from advanced discussion phases to signed agreements. PJM remains most exposed to supply risk, with Wood Mackenzie’s risked supply view through 2036 running short of the market's high confidence load commitments.
Local Opposition Emerges as a Structural Constraint
Of the 400 data center moratoriums now spanning 42 states, the most significant single action is the September 2026 pause on new data centre permits in Texas and audit of the existing pipeline, which puts more than 60 GW of planned projects in Wood Mackenzie’s tracker under scrutiny.
Despite the increase in activity, which included just 45 such actions across 2023-2025, the picture is more nuanced than it appears, as 92% of moratoriums target land use or zoning approvals, with average durations of six to twelve months.
“We will likely continue to see local opposition, but the current moratoriums suggest that lawmakers are seeking time to develop stronger frameworks rather than moving to impose outright bans,” said Connelly.
Editor’s note:Q1 2026 additions have been revised upward to 52GW from the 36 GW reported at the time of our previous release, reflecting lags in disclosure tracking as project activity from that period continued to be captured. This revision is consistent with how pipeline data matures across reporting cycles, and does not alter the overall trend.

articles.title: Israel’s deadlocked election could force a new vote in 2027 | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Israel’s deadlocked election could force a new vote in 2027

William A. Galston

William A. Galston

Senior Fellow
- Governance Studies, Center for Effective Public Management (CEPM),

Ezra K. Zilkha Chair in Governance Studies

October 30, 2026

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc lost its majority, but the Jewish opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot barely gained ground, while Arab parties nearly doubled their representation in the Knesset.
Neither side has an easy path to a governing majority; Eisenkot has ruled out Arab parties as partners, and those parties won’t back Netanyahu, making another election in early 2027 the most likely outcome.
If coalition talks fail, Netanyahu would stay on as caretaker prime minister, leaving Israel without a stable government as a possible renewed war with Iran and growing U.S. and European pressure loom.

JERUSALEM, ISRAEL - OCTOBER 28: Small notes are left all over the floor at the conclusion of the Likud Party election-night event at the Teddy Hall, International Convention Center on Oct. 28, 2026, in Jerusalem, Israel. Votes are being counted to elect 120 members of the Knesset, which will determine the make-up of the government that succeeds incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition. The legislative elections were the first to be held since the Hamas-led attacks against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. (Photo by Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images)

10 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

What happened
For several months prior to the 2026 Israeli election, the contest had been characterized as among the most important in the country’s history. It offered the voters their first opportunity to pass judgment on a government that had presided over the Hamas massacre of more than 800 civilians on Oct. 7, 2023, launched a retaliatory campaign that killed nearly 75,000 Palestinians, civilians as well as combatants, and reduced much of Gaza to rubble. Under the leadership of Benjamin Netanyahu, who has served as prime minister for 19 of the past 30 years, Israel reversed its longstanding security doctrine, creating new security perimeters in Lebanon and Syria. In collaboration with the United States, Mr. Netanyahu launched two attacks against Iran to fulfill his long-held aim of overthrowing the clerical regime, which could achieve the capacity to build nuclear weapons and launch a war of extermination against Israel. Led by extreme right-wing nationalists Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, to whom the prime minister had turned to form his majority, Israel authorized increased settlement activity in the West Bank and allowed attacks against Palestinian civilians to go virtually unchecked. In the wake of these developments, Israel lost public support in the United States, Europe, and around the world.
All this and more was on the table as Israelis streamed to the polls on Oct. 27. The turnout of nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, seemed to presage a major shift in the political balance of power. But with nearly all of the vote counted, the contours of the final results have become clear. Although the government’s 68-seat majority was reduced to a minority of around 53, Netanyahu’s Likud remained the single largest party, and the Jewish opposition failed to score significant gains, increasing its seat total from 46 to just 48. By contrast, the Arab parties mobilized their electorates against the extreme right and nearly doubled their representation in the Knesset, moving from 10 to 19 seats.
The failure of the Jewish opposition to gain ground came as a major disappointment to the Israelis (and foreign observers) who had hoped for a solid anti-Netanyahu majority among Israel’s Jewish citizens. In Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition seemed to have found the perfect leader—a former army chief of staff widely respected as steady, blunt, and honest, a father who had lost a son and two nephews in battle after Oct. 7.
Moreover, Eisenkot is the child of Moroccan immigrants, a part of the community of Jews who had been forced to leave their ancestral lands in the Middle East and North Africa after Israel’s founding in 1948. These Jews, having experienced what they regarded as discrimination and disrespect at the hands of the European Jews who dominated the parties of the center and left, moved into the ranks of right-wing parties, fueling Menachem Begin’s rise to power in the 1970s. The opposition hoped that Eisenkot would be able to attract a larger share of these pivotal voters, which he did to some extent. Shas, a religious party that represents much of the Mizrahi community, fell from 11 seats to just six.
But the gain was not nearly enough. Although Eisenkot’s Yashar party ended up as, by far, the largest in the opposition, several other center-left parties lost ground. At the same time, the small parties of the left, which failed to unite in 2022, did so this year and doubled their representation in the Knesset. Overall, the 2026 election did more to rearrange the opposition than to expand it.
What comes next
In the United States, the party in power either wins or loses. But under Israeli law, a third outcome is possible—the political equivalent of a hung jury—which may well be the outcome this time. At the least, Israel now faces an extended period of uncertainty.
Once the final vote totals are officially announced on Nov. 4, President Isaac Herzog will consult the leaders of the parties elected to serve in the new Knesset. He will then give the lawmaker of his choice—who will not necessarily be a member of the party receiving the most votes—the first chance to form a winning coalition. The first designee will have 28 days to form a government, which the president may extend by up to 14 days. If that effort fails, a second designee would have up to 28 days. If that effort also falls short, the Knesset will have 21 days during which a majority of 61 members of the Knesset (MKs) can ask the president to designate a lawmaker of their choice, who would then have 14 days to form a government. While a new government typically receives the support of at least 61 MKs, the law does not require an absolute majority, allowing a minority government to take office with plurality support.
Although President Herzog has vowed to exert maximum pressure on the contending forces to generate the compromises needed to form a new government, his efforts are time-limited. If the government formation process fails, the Knesset would be dissolved, and new elections would be held within 90 days. Crucially, Prime Minister Netanyahu would remain in office as the head of a caretaker government until these elections take place.
It will be very difficult for either the prime minister or the opposition to achieve even a plurality victory. Netanyahu reportedly is pressing for a grand coalition with Eisenkot that would allow him to govern without the far-right parties. But it is hard to imagine that Eisenkot would enter into such an arrangement without an explicit agreement ruling out the possibility that Netanyahu would serve as prime minister again during the life of the new government. It is just as hard to imagine the prime minister acceding to such an agreement, and there is no evidence that enough members of Likud would break ranks to allow it to go forward. As for the Arab parties: They will not support Netanyahu, even tacitly.
The opposition’s prospects of forming a government are not much brighter. During the campaign, Eisenkot stated that he would accept only “Zionist” parties—ones that recognize Israel as a Jewish and democratic state—as coalition partners, and he made it clear that no Arab party meets this test. It is barely possible that he could form a government representing a minority of the Jewish vote with the tacit support of the Arab parties, although recent reports suggest that support for this course within at least one of the Arab parties is limited. Even if a minority government did form, its inherent fragility would probably doom it to a short life.
The Democrats, Israel’s only remaining party of the left, strongly favor a coalition with the Arab parties. So do left-leaning American Jewish organizations. A principled case can be made that the exclusion of Arab parties from any share of government power violates the letter and spirit of Israel’s Declaration of Independence. And there is a practical argument as well: Excluding parties that now command one-sixth of the Knesset seats is a formula for permanent instability.
Still, Eisenkot would pay a huge price for going back on his word, just as Naftali Bennett did in 2021 by including Ra’am in the governing coalition, which he said during the election that he would not do. And Eisenkot’s declaration that neither Arab party meets his “Zionist” criteria is well-founded. If the Arab parties seized the moment to accept Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, they would remove the principal obstacle to their inclusion in a majority coalition. It would be interesting to see what would happen if Eisenkot publicly asked them to take this step. If they agreed, Israeli politics could be transformed. But until they do, the dysfunctional status quo will persist.
This is not to say that no changes are in the offing. When the new Knesset is seated in November, the anti-Netanyahu majority will have the power to elect a new speaker and pass legislation calling for a nonpartisan commission of inquiry into the events of Oct. 7, as Israel has done in the past after major policy failures. Still, the most likely outcome of the 2026 election is another election in early 2027.
Why this matters
This is a fraught moment for Israel to experience an extended period of uncertainty and instability. Multiple reports suggest that Prime Minister Netanyahu and President Trump are planning to resume an all-out war with Iran in the near future. It remains to be seen whether this is a venture that an Israeli leader who has lost his majority can undertake without triggering a profound internal crisis.
Even without such a war, Israel faces a sea of difficulties. The government’s failure to restrain settler violence has generated an international agreement on financial and travel sanctions, and the British government is placing new restrictions on arms exports to Israel. In the United States, the potential Democratic takeover of the House of Representatives (and possibly the Senate as well) will likely change the tone and substance of U.S.-Israeli relations. A phaseout of U.S. financial aid is all but certain, and frustrated Democrats will probably push for much tougher restraints on the export of key weapons systems to Israel. Beyond this, congressional pressure on Israel to change course in the West Bank could intensify, and a weakened Trump administration may not resist this shift as strongly as Israel’s right-wing U.S. supporters would want. Remarks from key figures such as U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Thomas Barrack, who also serves as a special envoy to several Middle Eastern countries, suggest that the administration may be reevaluating its security arrangements throughout the region.
In short, this is the worst possible time for Israel to experience an extended period without a strong, stable government. But the results of the election make it hard to see how Israeli leaders can form such a government anytime soon—unless all sides are willing to retreat from long-held demands and heavily defended red lines.

Strategic Asset Allocation Market Strategy
NDR’s cross‑asset strategic allocation applies decades of quantitative research to guide investors over long‑term horizons.

NDR’s cross-asset strategic asset allocation service leverages NDR’s quantitative methodology and forty-five years of market analysis to help investors navigate a long-term investment horizon. Underpinned by NDR’s 10-year LTCMA analysis, the SAA team provides positioning optimized to a 3-5 year investment horizon across two distribution channels: Financial Advisor model portfolios (six risk-mapped models from Very Conservative to Very Aggressive) and Institutional policy portfolios (optimized relative to policy benchmarks within a tracking error budget). Grounded by a robust, academically supported, methodology and simulation, the service provides long-term coverage of individual asset classes, relative positioning between TAA and SAA portfolios, dynamic allocation bands, and opportunities for consultative advice including investment committee participation (dependent on service level). articles.title: Sustainability as a driver of long-term investment outcomes
articles.text:
PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | PODCAST – 12:06 MIN
Sustainability as a driver of long-term investment outcomes

By
JANE AMBACHTSHEER 29.10.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

How can investors navigate a world reshaped by environmental pressures, technological disruption and geopolitical uncertainty? For BNP Paribas Asset Management, sustainability is central to answering that question.

Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer, discusses BNPP AM’s updated Global Sustainability Strategy, which sets out its priorities through to 2030. Building on the recent merger with AXA Investment Managers, the strategy embeds sustainability expertise across asset classes, using ESG research, due diligence and stewardship to achieve better-informed investment decisions.

Jane explains how integrating sustainability considerations with financial analysis can help investors identify material risks and opportunities, while recognising that clients have different objectives and preferences. From net zero alignment and carbon footprint reduction to positive contributions towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the approach aims to deliver tailored solutions and better client outcomes. “Our underlying ambition is to connect sustainable investment practices with long-term returns to help clients navigate a rapidly changing world.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into solutions across many asset classes can help investors achieve their sustainability ambitions.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Andrew Craig: Hello and welcome to this week’s BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis through the lens of sustainability on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing our new revised edition of the Global Sustainability Strategy. This provides the framework for action on the environmental, social and governance considerations that are embedded in our investment processes and are grounded in the conviction that traditional financial analysis alone is insufficient to capture all the risks and opportunities in today’s global economy.

I’m Andy Craig, Co-Head of the Investment Insights Centre, and I’m joined today by Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management. Welcome, Jane. Thank you for joining me today.

Jane Ambachtsheer: Thanks, Andy. It’s a pleasure to be here.

AC: Can you explain why we need [a] Global Sustainability Strategy?

JA: Well, sustainability, is a core part of how we invest and how we operate as an entity, so it’s important to have a strategy which really articulates how we go about doing that and what our objectives are.

Our previous sustainability strategy took us to 2026, so it was time for us to launch our new one, which we’ve recently done, which takes us out to 2030. The other important component of our new strategy is that it reflects our new entity having evolved and completed the integration of AXA Investment Managers, which now results in BNP Paribas Asset Management being one of the world’s 10 largest investors, with over €1.7 trillion in AUM (assets under management) across liquid and alternative asset classes and a local presence in 35 countries.

So given our new size and scale, it was also certainly time for an evolved approach to our global sustainability strategy.

AC: How does the sustainability strategy fit with the new corporate strategy for the combined entity? What are the key components and how has it evolved?

JA: When we launched at the beginning of 2026 ‘AMplify 2030’, the overall strategy for the new entity, we identified sustainability as one of the core enablers of how we’ll achieve that strategy. That then opened the door for us to publish this new specialised strategy really focused on sustainability.

As a long-term investor, we believe our client outcomes and real economy outcomes are closely connected. Resilient companies, well-functioning markets and sustainable economic growth are really fundamental to the long-term returns our clients seek.

Our strategy sets out our forward-looking priorities and milestones through [to] 2030 and is organised around the pillars of how we achieve that. So, a focus on the future and identifying system level risks around how we do ESG research and due diligence stewardship. Our approach around articulating responsible business conduct expectations which can lead to different exclusions. Our approach to sustainable products and solutions and also around leading by example – our approach to our own culture, sustainability education and the corporate responsibility practices that we’re adopting for our own entity.

AC: How does this new strategy enable us to deliver the best outcomes for our clients?

JA: That’s at the core of everything we do. Our strategy is built for clients, informed by our clients’ expectations and what we believe best practice to be in the global market.

The first [thing] is around making sure we’re helping our clients navigate a changing world. We know that the world is being reshaped by a number of powerful forces:

Environmental pressures: reshaping industries, supply chains, capital allocation, presenting both risks and opportunities

Technology and innovation: creating new technologies, disrupting business models, creating different opportunities

Demographic shifts: transforming labour markets, changes to inequality around the world, consumption patterns and ageing

Geopolitical developments: influencing trade, energy security, energy systems, our approach to climate in nature and access to resources around the world in this changing geopolitical framework.

These megatrends are inter-connected and we try and take a forward-looking lens to help our clients navigate them through understanding the risks and the opportunities that they present. So that’s the broader macro perspective.

We also believe that by integrating ESG considerations alongside financial analysis from a bottom-up asset class perspective, we can have better insights and make better decisions on behalf of our clients.

So sustainability is not a separate investment decision. It’s an important component of informed decision-making from an asset class basis. One of the new evolutions in terms of our overall framework is that we now embed sustainability expertise across the different asset classes.

We have a central team which I lead, which is really responsible for driving the overall strategy and ambition, with our global leadership team overseeing stewardship, supporting our clients, supporting our overall external commitments and reporting stewardship and CSR (corporate social responsibility).

Then we have a number of sustainability experts embedded across the organisation within the different asset classes, reporting up to the different CIOs to make sure we have best quality ESG data, tools, research capabilities embedded into our investment decisions.

That takes me to this final point – the fact that the strategy is built for clients. We have clients from all around the world. They have different objectives, regulatory environments and sustainability preferences. To be able to cater to those different clients, we offer a range of investment approaches and have the opportunity to build structured, custom[ised] sustainability portfolios for our clients.

We have clients optimising around their own preferences or the preferences of their beneficiaries, whether that’s measuring a positive contribution to some of the specific sustainable development goals, achieving certain net zero alignment outcomes, measuring and achieving a certain carbon footprint reduction target.

Different clients have different preferences. A big part of our strategy and our new size and scale is that we have the ability to bring the firm in terms of helping our clients to achieve the best outcomes for them, tapping into the resources across BNP Paribas Asset Management, but also often working in partnership with our colleagues and the broader resources across BNP Paribas Group.

AC: Of course, there are implications for us, BNP Paribas Asset Management as a firm and our own practices. Can you talk us through those?

JA: At the end of the day, we’re a people business. Our people, the intellectual capital that they bring, their relationships with clients, are the greatest opportunity for embedding sustainability into who we are, how we deliver investment outcomes and how we’re operating as an entity.

So we have a strong focus on integrating sustainability into our culture and our own corporate practices. This is one of the unique differentiators for the way we’re approaching sustainability as an organisation.

In terms of our own corporate reporting, we seek to meet and exceed the standards and expectations we’re setting for the companies we’re investing in. That’s really important to our credibility as an asset manager – to live up to those expectations where we’re asking others to do the same.

We have a strong focus on sustainability education and we’ve developed different training pathways for different portions of our population, depending on their existing levels of expertise and focus areas – whether it’s investment teams or legal teams or client-facing teams – to make sure they have the right opportunities around internal training, but also the opportunity to pursue external certifications or training programmes.

We also have a strong focus on being active in the communities where we’re operating –volunteering, philanthropy and developing partnerships with organisations in different communities. Also our annual Community Impact Week, where we have a volunteering fair that we set up around our offices around the world, which is really a chance to engage in some of those organisations, but also to further enhance our internal community, give employees an opportunity to spend time together and spend time giving back.

So there’s a rich ecosystem of things we’re doing internally around creating awareness, providing educational opportunities and volunteering engagement opportunities for colleagues across the different offices around the world in BNP Paribas Asset Management.

AC: Can you talk [to] us about the key upcoming milestones and how you’ll be measuring success as we go forward?

JA: The first and most important measure of success is that we’re able to deliver the outcomes that our clients are engaging us to deliver. That’s front and centre for what we’re doing around our overall sustainability strategy.

But we will also continue to provide our annual sustainability report, which includes progress across all of the different six pillars of our sustainability strategy, including stewardship, which is an area of significant interest for many of our clients. We’re happy to be able to continue to evolve the level of detail around our different approaches for stewardship, be it statistics across the whole platform, a rich range of different examples of company engagement, as well as public policy advocacy.

Later this year, we’ll also be updating our new Net Zero commitment as a combined entity. That’s something we’ve committed to publish and we’ll be sharing in the coming months. We’ll also be introducing our new progress monitor in our next annual report, where we share a number of key indicators that [we] will be measuring and reporting on every year.

We view communication on sustainability as an ongoing opportunity, both at a portfolio and at a firm level, and it’s something that we’ll continue to share updates on with clients as we go.

AC: Jane, thank you. We’ll be looking forward to joining you to talk about those updates as the months go by. Thank you very much for joining me today.

JA: Thanks so much for having me. It was a pleasure to be here.

AC: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you’d like to learn more about our Global Sustainability Strategy, please reach out to your BNP Paribas Asset Management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings you commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Andy Craig and Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

Please do join us again next time. Until then, take care.

articles.title: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
articles.text:
Finance and Economics Discussion Series (FEDS)

Twitter

Share

RSS

October 2026

Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
Aditya Aladangady, Ricardo Duque Gabriel, and Carlo Wix

Abstract: We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely track traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level, capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level, and reproducing the impulse response of official consumption measures to identified monetary policy shocks. We then use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find suggestive evidence that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.
Keywords: Measurement and Data, Consumption, Credit Card Spending

articles.title: Switching The Policy Rate
articles.text:
Switching The Policy Rate

Wei He

Gavekal Dragonomics | 27 Oct 2026

The People’s Bank of China has not cut policy interest rates in more than a year, but some market participants claim that a stealth cut is now underway. On October 19, PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng announced that the central bank would change its main policy rate from the seven-day reverse repo to the overnight reverse repo. The PBOC has reportedly set its overnight rate 15 bp lower than the seven-day tenor, leading to the claims of a de facto cut.The switch will indeed have some effects similar to a rate cut, such as cheaper funding for commercial banks and lower bond yields. But it will not lead to lower rates for most borrowers, and a stealth monetary easing is not the PBOC’s intent: it is switching the policy rate primarily to bring its monetary-policy framework into line with other major central banks. It will continue to keep rates—and in turn bond yields—relatively low and steady in order to facilitate government bond issuance, but is likely to materially lower the policy rate only if economic growth slows further.
