articles.title: The Fed Is Off Its Own Reaction Function. It Should Tell Us Why.
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

The Fed Is Off Its Own Reaction Function. It Should Tell Us Why.

Jason Furman (PIIE)

Date
October 27, 2026 2:45 PM

Photo Credit: PIIE/Jeremey Tripp

This blog post was originally published on PIIE senior fellow Jason Furman's Econvitals.org(link is external) website and republished here with permission. Furman wrote the blog post with assistance from AI (see his website(link is external) for details).

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
Welcome to the first occasional post from me, Jason, a human. Almost everything on Econvitals is an automated briefing, but these posts will all be written by me, as are the chart(s) of the day and the opening paragraph of the Morning Note. I'm not sure how often I'll write these posts (thus the nonspecific "occasional"). My plan is to make them always data oriented but divided between the descriptive and the explanatory with a touch of opinion. This will not be the place for my broader thoughts on issues ranging from the California wealth tax to the latest proposals from President Trump—you can find me opining on those elsewhere. Also, full disclosure: these posts are all copyedited and fact-checked by AI, and all the data analysis is done interactively with AI. Oh, and I suck at titles, so the AI may do those as well.
And now to substance. Four times a year the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) releases a Summary of Economic Projections(link is external) (SEP) with its participants' expectations for growth, unemployment, inflation and—most notably—the federal funds rate (the so-called dots(link is external)). The projections and the Fed's actual policy moves have gotten criticism in equal measure for the ways in which policy and the economy deviate from what the Fed sets out, raising questions about the value of forecasts that are often wrong and actions that often differ from what people interpret as the Fed's plans.
The Fed's forecasts[1] have, however, actually been a very good guide to its reaction function. It often ends up raising rates by less than the dots said it would—but in most of those cases that was the "correct" response to inflation coming in lower than it expected or unemployment higher. And the reverse when it raises rates by more than the dots said. At least this is what it did until the last few years, when the Fed has deviated from its implied reaction function by more than at almost any time since it started publishing interest rate projections in 2012(link is external) (pandemic excluded). That raises a question: is the Fed badly off course, or is there something different, and more obviously transitory, about this inflation? I actually think the Fed has a good answer to why it is so far off its reaction function—but it should be more explicit about giving us that answer.
Now, more numerical detail on all of this.
The Fed's Economic Projections as a Reaction Function
The Fed is not a particularly accurate predictor of its own interest rate moves. Since 2012 it has published 51 sets of projections that can be scored against the set published a year later. Of those, the Fed ended up with higher-than-projected rates 15 times and lower-than-projected rates 21 times (the other 15 were mostly the zero-rate years, when the plan was no change and that is what happened). Some of the misses have been quite large: in December 2021 it projected three quarter-point hikes for 2022 and delivered 4.25 percentage points, and in December 2018 it projected two hikes for 2019 and delivered three cuts.
The question is not whether the Fed knows what it will do in the future, but whether it knows how it will react when the data depart from the expectations on which those future moves were conditioned. The Fed's forecasts of what will happen to the economy are at least as good(link is external) if not a bit better than others'(link is external) but very far from omniscient. So you can think of the projections not as a plan for its actions but as setting out a reaction function(link is external) along the lines of "here is how much we expect to change interest rates, but if unemployment or inflation turn out different from our forecast we will adjust accordingly."
Take two examples:

In December 2018(link is external) the median FOMC projection showed a 0.5 percentage point increase in the federal funds rate over the next year—two quarter-point hikes. The Fed ended up cutting three times, by 0.75 percentage point, a swing of about 1.25 percentage points relative to its plan. That swing was fully consistent with its implicit reaction function. By December 2019(link is external) the Fed's own estimate of 2019 core PCE inflation was 0.4 percentage point lower than it had forecast a year earlier (1.6 percent instead of 2.0), and the unemployment rate 0.1 point higher (3.6 instead of 3.5)—on top of which it had marked down its estimate of the natural rate of unemployment by 0.3 point and its estimate of the neutral federal funds rate by 0.3 point. Run through the original Taylor rule(link is external)—1.5 times the inflation miss, plus 1 times the miss in the unemployment gap, plus the change in the neutral rate—that is 0.6 + 0.4 + 0.3 = 1.3 percentage points, the adjustment the Fed made, to within rounding.
In December 2021(link is external) the Fed projected it would raise rates by 0.75 percentage point over the next year—three quarter-point hikes. It ended up raising them by 4.25 percentage points. Most of the 3.5 percentage point overage was the Taylor rule adjustment: by December 2022(link is external) the Fed's estimate of 2022 core PCE inflation was 2.1 percentage points above its forecast (4.8 percent instead of 2.7), which calls for 1.5 × 2.1 = 3.15 percentage points of extra tightening, slightly offset by unemployment coming in 0.2 point higher than forecast (3.7 instead of 3.5). Net, the rule accounts for about 3 percentage points of the 3.5 point overage.

These two examples are typical. Figure 1 shows, for every set of projections since 2012 paired with the set twelve months later, how much a Taylor rule(link is external) reaction function said the Fed should adjust its planned year-end rate given how its forecasts changed (horizontal axis), and how much it actually adjusted it (vertical axis). (The rule-implied adjustment also includes the Fed's revisions to its estimates of the longer-run unemployment rate and the neutral interest rate.) The line is the Taylor rule itself: on it, the Fed did exactly what the rule implies. The points cluster around it. If the weights are estimated freely, the best fit puts a coefficient of 1.57 on the core inflation revision and 0.99 on the unemployment revision, as compared with 1.5 and 1 in the Taylor rule. The fit excludes the pandemic rounds and the years when the federal funds rate was stuck at zero, when the Fed might well have wanted a lower rate if that were possible.

Figure 1. The FOMC's dots against the Taylor rule, 12 months. Each point pairs one set of FOMC projections with the set twelve months later, January 2012 to September 2026. Horizontal axis: the change in the year-end federal funds rate that the Taylor (1993) rule implies from the committee's own revisions to its core PCE inflation and unemployment projections for that year-end, plus the change in its longer-run funds rate. Vertical axis: how much the committee actually moved its median dot for that year-end. December rounds are labeled by the year-end scored; the latest pair, September 2025 to September 2026, is in orange. Source: Federal Reserve Board, Summary of Economic Projections; Econvitals calculations.

It turns out this reaction function—a Taylor rule in changes, applied to the Fed's own forecast revisions—fits the Fed's behavior better than any empirical Taylor rule estimated over the same period (some details and comparisons are in a Claude-written, Jason-edited online appendix(link is external) to this post). And it fits reasonably well: the rule explains about three-quarters of the variation in how the Fed moves its year-end rate projections (an R² of 0.77), with a typical miss of 0.66 percentage point.[2]
Which brings us to the present.
The Federal Funds Rate Is Currently Well Below What the Fed's Implicit Reaction Function Calls For
In December 2025(link is external) the FOMC expected to cut rates by about 25 basis points over the following year. The economy did not turn out as expected. The Fed had expected the unemployment rate(link is external) to end 2026 at 4.4 percent; its most recent projection, from September(link is external), is 4.1 percent, enough under a Taylor reaction function to eliminate the planned cut.
The bigger, and less pleasant, surprise has been inflation: in December the Fed expected core PCE inflation(link is external) of 2.5 percent in 2026, and its September projection is 3.4 percent. Under a Taylor rule reaction function that revision alone would justify a 1.35 percentage point hike in the federal funds rate (and the Fed's upward revision to its estimate of the longer-run neutral rate, from 3.0 to 3.2 percent, adds another 0.2). That is way more than the 0.25 percentage point hike delivered so far, or even the 0.5 percentage point cumulative increase for 2026 that the market is currently pricing in(link is external). (For what it's worth, my own unemployment forecast is slightly higher than the Fed's September one and my core PCE forecast slightly lower, so under my own forecast I would get a somewhat smaller increase.)
Overall, using the full method behind Figure 1, the Fed's December 2025 projections treated as a reaction function say it should have raised its planned end-2026 rate by 1.85 percentage points, to about 5.25 percent. It raised it by 0.7 relative to its original plans, to 4.1 percent—roughly where the market is too. That shortfall of 1.15 percentage points is unusually large. Of the 37 comparable twelve-month readings since the Fed began publishing its rate projections in 2012 (leaving aside the pandemic and the zero-rate years), only five have been more dovish, and all five came in the past three years.
Moreover, this is not an artifact of one forecast. The Fed has published projections for the end-2026 federal funds rate in 13 rounds, starting in September 2023. Treat each of the twelve earlier ones as a reaction function, apply the Taylor coefficients to how its forecasts have changed since, and nearly all of them imply a substantially higher rate—on average about 1.3 percentage points above the Fed's own current projection of 4.1 percent for the end of this year, as shown in Figure 2. (The exception is the June 2026 round, by which time most of the inflation revision had already happened.) A live version of Figure 2 is maintained on the Econvitals Taylor Rule page(link is external).

Figure 2. Fed funds rate minus Taylor rule adjustment for the end-2026 funds rate, from each earlier set of projections. Each point: how much the FOMC raised its median end-2026 federal funds rate projection between that round and September 2026, minus what the Taylor (1993) rule implies from its own revisions to 2026 core PCE inflation and unemployment and to its longer-run funds rate. Negative means the Fed raised its path by less than the rule says. Source: Federal Reserve Board, Summary of Economic Projections; Econvitals calculations.

This is not just about the current Chair, Kevin Warsh. Use the March 2026(link is external) projections, the last produced under Chair Powell, as the anchor and the gap is smaller but still substantial: the rule says the Fed should have raised its end-2026 projection by 1.45 percentage points since March, and it raised it by 0.7, a shortfall of 0.75 percentage point.
The Fed Being Off Its Reaction Function May Be More a Sign of Wisdom Than Folly
One perspective is that the Fed's implicit reaction function is the right way to think about policy. The economy has been served well by Taylor-type rules, and years like 2021, when the Fed ended up far off its rule, ended up imperiling the U.S. economy. From this perspective, a deviation that ranks among the half dozen most dovish readings of the Fed's own record since 2012 is a flashing warning sign.
Another interpretation is that the Fed is wiser than the formula. It understands, for example, that some of the inflation is the transitory result of tariffs and the Iran conflict—and that, at worst, these will raise the price level once(link is external) and then stop adding to inflation. The Fed probably should not react to the inflation that results from an increase in a value-added tax(link is external); from that perspective, it should not react to tariff-induced inflation either.[3]
Which is it, folly or wisdom? Quantification can shed some light. Using the Fed's December 2025 forecast as the anchor, we can ask what forecast revisions would be consistent with its switching from a 25 basis point cut to the 50 basis points of hikes the market now expects this year. The answer: an unemployment rate of 4.2 percent combined with core PCE inflation of about 2.7 percent. That is roughly half a point below a reasonable current forecast of year-end core PCE inflation (about 3.2 percent)—a gap that could reasonably be attributed to transitory factors like tariffs and the Iran conflict. And if the part of the inflation surprise that shows up in core PCE but not in the trimmed-mean or median measures is treated as noise, the Fed is roughly on its reaction function (the appendix shows the arithmetic).
I confess, I began this exercise thinking the Fed was way off base—but after quantifying it I end up more sympathetic to its approach.
The Bottom Line: Reaction Functions Are a Useful Communications Device—and the Fed Should Explain Its Deviations From Them
I would like to see the Fed publish the Taylor rule recommendation at every one of its rate-setting meetings instead of just twice a year in its semiannual Monetary Policy Report(link is external), ideally picking one as its main reference rule. I like a Taylor-style reaction function even better where the Fed articulates a path and explains that it will deviate from it based on how inflation and unemployment deviate from its forecast. The latter works better when the levels change over time, although it also risks perpetuating and compounding errors over time.
In either case, however, the people on the FOMC—and the staff who support them—know a lot more than the formula knows, and they should use that information in setting policy. But they should also clearly convey it. In the current situation that could take the form: "We were planning one 25 basis point rate cut this year; instead we are now on track for two increases. This is because the unemployment rate has been lower than we expected and inflation higher. Normally we would have raised rates by more based on an inflation forecast error of this size, but we are discounting about half a percentage point of it as due to transitory factors that we expect to unwind or reverse over the coming year. If we are wrong in that expectation we will make up for it with further rate hikes."
Appendix by Claude (Directed and Edited by Jason)
The reaction function in this post differs from a textbook Taylor rule in two ways: it is written in changes rather than levels, and it is run on the Fed's own forecasts rather than on the realized data. This appendix compares it with the familiar alternatives over the same period—January 2012, the first set of projections with dots, through September 2026—leaving out the pandemic rounds and the meetings at which the federal funds rate was stuck at zero (2012–15 and 2020–21), since no rule could be followed downward then. The underlying work is written up in an Econvitals research note, Fed minus rule, rolling(link is external), which gives the full method, the real-time data vintages and the longer history behind the Econvitals Taylor Rule page(link is external).
Table A1 asks the same question of each version: when the Fed moved, did the rule say it would? The forecast-revision rule explains about three-quarters of the variation in how the committee moves its year-end rate projection over twelve months, with a typical miss of 0.66 percentage point, against 1.22 for assuming the projection never moves. Giving unemployment the balanced-approach weight of 2 instead of 1 fits worse on every sample.
The same rule in changes run on the realized data—the change over twelve months in core PCE inflation and in the unemployment rate, as published at the time or as revised since—explains nothing over this period: its miss is larger than assuming the funds rate never changes. That is not because the Fed ignored the data. Policy since 2012 has been about levels: lifting off from zero on a schedule in 2015–18, catching up by more than four points in 2022–23 while trailing core inflation was already falling, then normalizing from a restrictive level. In 2022–23, for example, the Fed raised rates by one to four and a half points over twelve-month windows in which trailing core inflation was already falling and a rule in changes was asking for cuts; in 2016–17 it hiked on a schedule while the rule asked for a quarter point or less. Leave out the catch-up pairs and the realized-data rule explains about 30 percent of the Fed's moves, which load on the change in unemployment rather than on trailing inflation.

Table A2 asks the level question instead: meeting by meeting, how far has the funds rate sat from where each rule says it should be? Every Taylor-type level rule has put the rate below the rule at the great majority of meetings since 2012, by 1.3 to 2.7 percentage points on average, depending mostly on which neutral real rate is used—Taylor's original 2 percent gives the largest gaps, the committee's own longer-run estimate and a real-time Laubach–Williams estimate the smallest—and only a fifth to a half of meetings fall within a point of any of them. A freely fitted level rule over the period (the funds rate regressed on core inflation and the unemployment gap) explains only about a third of the variation, with weights of roughly 0.6 on each, far from Taylor's. The two rules that do track the rate, the Board's inertial and first-difference rules(link is external), do so by construction: each starts from the current rate and moves a little, so they describe the rate's persistence rather than its level. By any of these level measures today's rate is below the rule by about as much as is normal for the period (the Taylor (1993) gap of 1.5 points is the 38th percentile of meetings since 1990), which is why this post's claim is about the Fed's own reaction function rather than about the Taylor rule in levels.

Table A4 varies the inflation measure. Notes
1. This post uses the shorthand "the Fed's forecasts" when all we actually see is the median of the FOMC participants' projections. The median for one variable can come from a different participant than the median for another, and the participants change over time. Still, I'll keep the language simple.
2. My preferred specification is core PCE inflation as a measure of the underlying inflation the Fed appears to react to, looking through the supply shocks to food and energy that make overall PCE inflation diverge from core PCE inflation. And, core PCE is more accurate in this exercise with a typical miss of 0.66 percentage point as compared to a typical miss of 0.81 when overall PCE inflation is used in the reaction function.
3. One rationalization of the Fed's recent actions is that it is looking through supply shocks, as it has generally done in the past, but is adopting a wider concept of them than just food and energy. The trimmed mean PCE inflation rate, a measure that excludes large positive and negative moves, has fallen by about 0.7 percentage point over the last year, to 2.2 percent, and the Cleveland Fed's median PCE inflation rate by about 0.9 point, to 2.6 percent, even as 12-month core PCE inflation rose about 0.2 point, to 3.0 percent, and the Fed's projection for 2026 core PCE inflation rose 0.9 point. Treat the widening gap between core and these measures as noise and the Fed is roughly on its reaction function; the appendix has the arithmetic.

articles.title: Daily: Strengthen portfolio defenses as volatility rises
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioPodcast: AI demand remains the signal amid neocloud noise, on Apple , Spotify (6 mins)Podcast: Across the Pond: Europe’s bond stress test, on Apple , Spotify (22 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Why bank stocks are falling amid rising rates (6 mins)Video: The AI Show |The AI trade's two-sided test (4 mins)Video: Data with Donovan | The Fed's rate path ahead (5 mins)Thought of the dayBrent crude oil hit USD 112/bbl for the first time since May and is on track for a third consecutive week of price gains as fresh attacks in the Middle East have heightened concerns about further disruptions to energy supplies. Since the start of this month, Brent crude has risen 9.4%.Saudi Arabia reported attacks on an Aramco oil field and an airport in its Eastern Province, while the US ordered diplomats to leave the country amid Houthi strikes. Separately, the New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries had developed specific plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the US midterm elections, which take place on 3 November.With the Russia-Ukraine conflict also continuing, geopolitical risks are unlikely to subside in the near term, keeping inflation concerns elevated and adding to macroeconomic uncertainty.But geopolitics are not the only factor driving market performance. Resilient economic growth, robust corporate earnings, and strong AI demand continue to underpin equity gains. Our view remains that investors should focus less on the possibility of short-term drawdowns associated with geopolitical events and more on ensuring that their portfolios can withstand periods of volatility.History suggests that geopolitical shocks are rarely a sufficient reason to stop investing. Since 1941, the S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after the start of a geopolitical crisis roughly three-quarters of the time. For diversified portfolios, the long-term cost of remaining uninvested has often proved greater than the temporary cost of living through a geopolitical drawdown.The global energy system should continue to adapt to the disruption. While still below its pre-war levels, OPEC crude production rose by 0.92 million barrels per day in September to 25.1 million, or around 85% of February’s output, according to the group’s latest Monthly Market Report. Trade routes are also shifting, while the G7 decision to release additional emergency oil stocks should provide some temporary relief. Together, these developments demonstrate the global oil market’s ability to respond to disrupted supplies. We acknowledge that the physical oil market remains tight and is vulnerable to further supply shocks, but our base case is that a gradual recovery of energy flows and production should allow oil prices to moderate into next year. This means that the impact of higher energy prices on the global economy should remain insufficient to derail growth.Exposure to commodities can help manage volatility. Instead of retreating from markets, investors can use energy exposure to insulate portfolios against such supply-driven volatility and boost diversification. In fact, we think investors should consider broad commodities as a differentiated source of return, especially as rising power demand, AI infrastructure investment, electrification, and constrained supply are supportive of an upcycle. Historically, commodities have exhibited low correlations with traditional asset classes, and we think an actively managed approach can help investors navigate across the commodity complex.So, we retain a constructive market outlook and believe investors should stay invested for further equity gains via broadly diversified exposure across sectors and regions. We also believe investors can strengthen their portfolio resilience by incorporating fixed income, broad commodities, and select alternatives according to their risk tolerance, liquidity needs, and financial objectives.

articles.title: Taiwan ETFs – growing in global stature
articles.text:
Back to InsightsGrowing my BusinessEnable GrowthTaiwan ETFs – growing in global stature28 October 2026ArticleArticleShare via EmailShare on FacebookShare on LinkedInShare on TwitterA buoyant stock market, a supportive policy backdrop, and an investor preference towards ETFs, makes Taiwan a compelling market for international issuers.Taiwan’s stock market is rapidly growing in global stature. And its increased importance is attracting the attention of international asset managers looking to issue products in one of the world’s fastest growing ETF markets1.
All these developments are underpinned by Taiwan’s unique position in the supply chain for advanced semiconductors, as enormous levels of AI-related demand for high-end chips is supporting robust economic growth. The island’s GDP expanded by 8.7% in 2025, creating significant wealth that is invested in the local fund market2.
ETFs are the mainstay for Taiwanese investors, accounting for around two thirds of total fund industry assets, due to the ongoing popularity of both fixed income and equity products3. And over the last year, the range of funds coming to market has become more diverse, with active ETFs, multi-asset ETFs, and cross-border ETFs now all part of the product mix.The rapid development of Taiwan’s ETF market – both in terms of size and sophistication – makes it an increasingly attractive destination for international issuers.Julie Kerr | Global Head of Fund and Trustee Services, HSBCThe positive market sentiment in Taiwan has proved resilient throughout 2026, with the benchmark TAIEX index hitting an all-time-high in October.A widening product shelfThe rise of active ETFs in Taiwan demonstrates how quickly a new product can take in the market. These funds were only approved at the end of 2024, and by May 2025 there were only three products managing NTD8.6 billion (USD266 million). But just one year later, there was a hundredfold increase in AUM to NTD866.4 billion (USD26.7 billion), spread across 25 products4.
In that 12-month period, the range of active ETFs broadened significantly: from products that focused on the equity market as a whole to more specialist funds that invest overseas, focus on the technology sector, or engage in high-dividend strategies. In short, the diversity of active ETFs already provides Taiwanese investors with a wide range of asset allocation options.
There are other products that are new to the market. The first multi-asset ETF was launched in August 2025, though with only three of these passive funds launched as of March, the uptake has been relatively muted compared to the active products5.
The latest product category to be launched are the active covered call ETFs, three of which listed in April6. These funds take a long cash position on equities, while at the same time selling call options. Due to the premium generated by the options, covered call ETFs can be used as part of an income-generating strategy, which aligns with Taiwan's longstanding interest in yield-generating products – such as high-dividend equity ETFs and bond ETFs.Developing Taiwan’s ETF industry is a key part of the island’s ambitious plans to attract new domestic and international investors, while presenting opportunities for global asset management companies to issue products locally.Vincent Lin | Head of Markets and Securities Services, HSBC TaiwanAnd there are signs that it is working: as of the end of April, six of the world’s top ten asset managers have established investment trust offices in Taiwan7.
Kaohsiung is the focal point of an official plan to transform the island into an asset management hub for Asia. One year after the city’s financial zone was launched, asset managers have launched 16 offshore funds with an AUM of NTD3.9 billion8.HSBC – supporting issuers on the groundBuoyant markets, a supportive policy backdrop, and a local investor preference for ETFs makes Taiwan a compelling market for global issuers. They can bring experience and strategies that have proved successful in other markets. Furthermore, their cross-border products will stand out if they have strong trading and research resources in the target market that a Taiwanese competitor might lack.
International issuers have been very active in 2026, with foreign firms behind nine of the 26 ETFs launched in the first seven months of the year9.
As one of the largest international securities services providers in Taiwan, HSBC plays an important role in supporting issuers to launch and manage ETFs on the island covering fund administration and transfer agency, and global custody (via the Hong Kong hub). We’re supporting issuers in Taiwan with multiple ETF deals and a strong pipeline.
In addition to helping issuers, we are providing input, through industry engagement, on proposed changes aimed at improving ETF market efficiency – such as reviewing opportunities to the shorten dividend distribution timeline, assessing mechanisms to facilitate same day primary creation, and secondary-market selling for overseas equity ETFs. As standards are finalised, HSBC will work with clients to align operational processes, service levels and documentation as required.
Our ETF servicing capabilities in Taiwan have been designed to operate seamlessly with the capabilities provided by our global platforms. The platform not only fulfils all current local requirements, but at the same time provides a strong foundation for further enhancements of the operating model to cater to evolving market needs.
HSBC's Taiwan offering has received industry recognition through a number of market awards. Most recently, we were awarded Taiwan's Best for Securities Services by Euromoney and Best Fund Administrator by The Asset for the ninth consecutive year.
As Taiwan's ETF market continues to mature, HSBC is well placed to support the next stage of that growth. We look forward to working closely with both established and new-to-market issuers as they navigate Taiwan's fund landscape and bring new strategies to local investors, backed by the depth of our global securities services platform and our on-the-ground expertise in Taiwan.References

articles.title: Business Checkpoint: Looking into the logistics
articles.text: Taylor Bowley October 2026 Small and mid-sized businesses entered Q3 in relatively solid financial condition, with profitability growth up across both groups, according to Bank of America business account data. Nearly half of estimated tariff payments had been refunded by September, though the share of these refunds relative to revenue has peaked. In Bank of America business payments data, logistics spending growth per client was up four times as much for small than midsized firms. Additionally, distribution and inventory transactions growth per client has outpaced spending since the spring of 2025. Growing transportation bottlenecks are re-emerging ahead of the holiday season. Trucking capacity has tightened as driver availability remains constrained, according to BofA Global Research. This has pushed freight rates higher and driven strong transportation sector payroll growth, particularly among mid-sized businesses, according to Bank of America payments data. Read our full analysis for a more in-depth look at these trends. Business Checkpoint is a new, regular publication from Bank of America Institute. It provides a real-time view of the financial health, opportunities and challenges facing small and mid-sized businesses across the US economy, leveraging the depth and breadth of Bank of America's proprietary data. By analyzing activity among both small and mid-sized firms, Business Checkpoint offers timely insights into business profitability, hiring, investment and spending trends. Such data is not intended to be reflective or indicative of, and should not be relied upon as, the results of operations, financial condition or performance of Bank of America. Operational resilience is the ability of firms and the entire financial sector to prevent, adapt, respond to, recover from and learn from disruptions.
Financial firms and financial market infrastructures (FMIs) must have robust plans to deliver important services, no matter the disruption. This includes man-made threats such as physical and cyberattacks, IT system outages and third-party supplier failure. It also includes natural hazards such as fire, flood, severe weather and pandemic. These can affect firms’ safety and soundness, undermine policyholder protection and, in some cases, affect financial stability.
The Bank of England and our Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) carry out this work with the UK's two other financial authorities: the Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
Our approach assumes that sometimes disruptions that prevent firms from operating as usual will occur and mean they cannot provide their services for a period.

External links

Operational Resilience - Financial Conduct Authority Opens in a new window
The National Cyber Security Centre Opens in a new window

Prudential and Resolution Policy Index related links

Banking - Operational resilience
Insurance - Operational resilience

Strategic outcomes

Build firms' resilience: when severe but plausible disruption occurs, it should not affect financial stability, safety and soundness or policyholder protection. Firms must ensure high standards of IT and cyber resilience, third-party dependency risks.
Build systemic operational resilience: firms and the Bank work to ensure that when systemic operational risks crystallise, they do not impact the UK's financial stability. Third parties must be sufficiently resilient to support this outcome. It is important that firms can contribute to sector-wide incident response and can learn and evolve from failures.
Manage risks: limit the likelihood and impact of losses. Firms must set aside capital so that the crystallisation of risks is unlikely to affect firm safety and soundness.

The following outputs are designed with these outcomes in mind:

Monetary Policy Committee voting history

Firm-level outputs

Operational resilience policy
Our Financial Policy Committee (FPC) looks at the entire system. Our Prudential Regulation Committee (PRC) and Financial Market Infrastructure Committee (FMIC) focus on the firms and FMIs we regulate.
In summary, we ask firms to:

identify important business services: boards and senior management must prioritise services that, if disrupted, would affect our objectives and the public interest;
set impact tolerances: firms must say to what extent they could continue important business services after severe but plausible disruptions; and
make sure they can stay within impact tolerances: firms must map their important business services and test their capacity to continue to the agreed extent – they should address any vulnerabilities they have identified.

The operational resilience policy SS1/21 requires firms to prepare a written operational resilience self-assessment of compliance. The aim is to document a firms’ resilience journey, identifying risks that could prevent them from delivering important business services within tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios. It helps the firms’ boards and senior management make informed investment decisions to address resilience gaps.
We assess the status of a firm’s implementation of our policy. This includes reviewing:

their important business services, impact tolerances and additional metrics
scenario testing details, results and assurance that the firm can remain within impact tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios
firms’ identification of risks, threats, and vulnerabilities through mapping, testing and live incidents
response and recovery actions, remediation plans and timelines

Self-assessments allow us to identify good practices at an individual firm level while also facilitating thematic comparisons, helping us build a clearer picture of the wider systemic operational resilience picture across the industry.
Incident management and reporting
The PRA has published a policy that details requirements for reporting certain operational incidents, and notification and reporting of material third-party arrangements. It sets out expectations for regulatory reporting, which aim to enhance the PRA’s understanding of firm and sector threats and vulnerabilities.

CP17/24 – Operational resilience: Operational incident and outsourcing and third-party reporting

Third-party management
The PRA’s current policy is set out primarily in Supervisory Statement (SS) 2/21: Outsourcing and third party risk management, which was published in March 2021. The Bank has a near-identical set of policies for FMIs, such as clearing houses and payment systems.
Operational risk framework
Our role is to assess whether a firm's operational risk management framework allows them to effectively identify, assess, monitor, report and manage material operational risks to which it is or might be exposed, in line with board-approved strategy and risk appetite.
We are also responsible for assessing whether firms hold sufficient capital to mitigate the impact when operational risks crystallise.
This supports the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Rules, which require us to assess whether firms’ own funds and internal capital is adequate to cover the level of the risks to which it is or might be exposed and is reflective of the firm’s operational risk profile.
Cyber resilience
Firms and FMIs should assess their cyber risk and build adequate resilience capabilities to prepare for, and respond to, potentially disruptive cyber incidents. To maintain the financial sector's cyber resilience and to support our supervisory oversight, we have developed cyber assessment tools. They include CBEST, STAR-FS and CQUEST.
CBEST
This provides a framework for regulators to work with firms using a simulated cyberattack. This allows firms to explore how to counteract an attack on the people, processes and technology of cyber security controls. We base the simulated attacks on present threats.
The aim is to test:

a firm's defences
its threat intelligence capability
its ability to detect and respond to external and internal attackers

Firms use the assessment to plan how they can strengthen their resilience.
An accredited service provider carries out the simulation, acting within legal, ethical and moral constraints. It aims to get through a firm's defences using the cyber kill chain. They also assess if the confidentiality, integrity or availability of systems and processes that deliver a firm's important business services can be compromised.

CBEST Threat Intelligence-Led Assessments

CBEST thematic review
The annual CBEST thematic is intended to inform the sector on the findings and lessons learned from our CBEST programme, which assesses the cyber resilience of key financial institutions through security testing performed in ‘live’ corporate environments.

2023 CBEST thematic findings
2024 CBEST thematic findings
2025 CBEST thematic findings

STAR-FS
STAR-FS (simulated targeted attack and response assessments for financial services) is part of the PRA and FCA supervisory toolkit, to assess the cyber resilience of firms' important business services. This allows regulators and firms to better understand vulnerabilities and take remedial actions, thereby improving their resilience and, by extension, the wider financial system.
It promotes a threat-led penetration testing approach that mimics the actions of actors' intent on compromising an organisation's important business services as well as the technology assets and people supporting them.
An implementation guide and supporting templates are available. If your firm is interested in conducting a STAR-FS please contact your supervisor. It aims to provide:

an outcome-based assessment of financial institutions' protection, detection and response technical capabilities against cyber-attacks;
an approach, conducted through a firm-led delivery model, that can identify cyber resilience vulnerabilities within systems, people and processes;
reduced regulatory and firm effort relative to other supervisory technical assessments such as CBEST;
levels of independent technical assurance beyond those ordinarily included in firms' own penetration testing programmes; and
a testing approach accessible by a larger number of financial institutions to experience and learn from.

CQUEST
We use the CQUEST (Cyber resilience questionnaire) to gauge the cyber risk and resilience capabilities of the sector. Firms can also use it as a self-assessment tool to consider their own cyber risk and resilience maturity. It comprises 50 questions with multiple-choice answers across six domains:

governance and leadership
identify
protect
detect
respond
recover

To achieve a reliable outcome, an organisation should identify and direct a competent party with appropriate knowledge of the business to complete the CQUEST. When it is used to inform regulatory activities, supervisors might provide additional guidance and/or they could request evidence or clarifying information in response to the answers.
The latest version of CQUEST builds upon the previous one, and encompasses lessons learned from good practice frameworks and feedback from supervisors and firms.

Download the CQUEST

System-level outputs

Collective action and incident response
The Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG) leads sector-wide collective action on operational resilience. It comprises about 25 members: firms across retail, wholesale, FMIs, insurance, the financial authorities and the National Cyber Security Centre. Its co-chairs are senior executives of the PRA and UK Finance.
CMORG has three core objectives:

identify risks to the resilience of the financial sector.
develop solutions to improve the operational resilience of the sector.
share knowledge

Industry has developed CMORG-endorsed capabilities (including good practice guidance, response frameworks and contingency tools) to support the operational resilience of the UK's financial sector. The financial authorities support the development of these capabilities and efforts to improve resilience. However, their use is optional and they do not constitute regulatory rules or supervisory expectations. As such, they may not necessarily represent formal endorsement by the authorities.
Specialist subgroups support CMORG. They design, manage and deliver operational resilience improvements for the sector. Their work is voluntary. Their chairs meet regularly to discuss CMORG's activities and identify areas for more collaboration. A project management office (PMO) also supports CMORG. It is jointly resourced by us and UK Finance.

Find out more about CMORG Opens in a new window

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC) is a CMORG-led partnership. It aims to help identify, investigate and co-ordinate the response to incidents that may have consequences for the financial sector. It analyses and distributes information to produce timely outputs for the sector's benefit.

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC)

What happens if there is a disruption?
Firms should get in touch with their usual business or supervisory contacts at the Bank or the FCA. The sector's response is facilitated by the Sector Response Framework (SRF). It sets out how organisations across the sector and government are connected. It also explains how they may respond to incidents when the impact becomes broader than a single firm or FMI and requires co-ordination, information-sharing or collective action.
Its purpose is to:

allow firms, FMIs and the sector to make collective, timely and informed decisions in response to incidents
provide a reference to good practice, contingency tools and plans, which may be invoked as part of a sector response
include decision makers and subject matter experts
be organised on a modular basis, so that components of the SRF can respond
be recognised by the financial authorities as the principal structure by which the sector will respond to incidents
support collaborative engagement between the sector and the UK's financial authorities (see below)
be able to engage with frameworks in other jurisdictions, if required

The UK's three financial authorities are the Bank (including the PRA), the FCA and the Treasury. If disruptions could affect the whole sector, these authorities act together.

Find out about how we co-ordinate our response to the disruption of financial services

Sector exercising
The Bank works with the sector to co-ordinate and deliver exercises to strengthen the operational resilience of the UK's financial system.
The most prominent is SIMEX – a biennial, market-wide simulation conducted through a public-private partnership between industry participants and financial authorities. SIMEX performs a unique role in bringing the sector together to address the most challenging and complex risks that individual firms cannot manage alone.
These sector-wide exercises are based on our collective approach to resilience, working together with industry to identify emerging risks and build capabilities to enhance the system’s overall resilience.

SIMEX 24 – A major market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption
SIMEX 22 – A two-day market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption

Critical third-party oversight
The Bank, the PRA and the FCA (the regulators) are responsible for overseeing critical third parties (CTPs) to the UK's financial sector, following their designation by HMT.
Regulated firms and FMIs are increasingly dependent on a small number of third parties for the delivery of functions and services that are essential to the stability of, or confidence in, the UK's financial system. In some cases, third parties can become so critical that no single firm can adequately monitor or manage the systemic risks they pose.
The aim of oversight is to reduce systemic risks arising from the failure of, or disruption to the systemic services they provide to firms. The regulators will assess CTPs against outcomes-focused rules and expectations with the aim of ensuring the systemic services CTPs provide to the financial sector are resilient and therefore any failure of, or disruption to, those services does not threaten the stability of the UK's financial system.
The CTP regime complements, and does not replace, the existing requirements and expectations for firms on SS1/21 operational resilience and SS2/21 outsourcing and third-party risk management policy.

SS6/24 – Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
PS16/24 – Operational resilience: Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
Approach to the oversight of critical third parties

Find out more about the CTP regime:

Critical Third Parties

Cyber and operational resilience stress test (CORST)
The cyber and operational resilience stress test (formerly the Cyber Stress Test or 'CST') is a key part of the Bank’s toolkit on macroprudential operational resilience. The outcomes of cyber and operational resilience stress testing inform the FPC's monitoring of sector operational resilience and its articulation of its tolerance for disruption to vital services. The objectives of testing are to:

provide insight into sector vulnerabilities and the financial stability impacts and residual risk of severe but plausible operational disruption to vital services
explore firm and sector capabilities to respond to, and recover from operational disruption, and to mitigate its impact on financial stability
share lessons to support firms in maturing their approach to operational resilience and financial stability, including firms' roles as systemic risk managers

We invite firms to participate in CORST on a voluntary basis and they identify their own lessons and remediation actions. Actions that require cross-firm co-operation are often progressed through established collective action forums or voluntary groups.
The test aims, over time to explore all systemically important firms and provide insight into not just the impacts of disruption to the services they provide, but also the impacts to their customer firms and from their third parties. Participation may be direct, indirect through co-operation with a direct participant, or through engagement at cross-firm workshops.
The CST24 thematic letter, which provides thematic findings from the 2024 test, also provides resources to support firms’ role in mitigating potential financial stability impacts of disruption to their services.

Thematic findings from the 2024 cyber stress test
Thematic findings from the 2022 cyber stress test

FPC impact tolerance for financial stability
The FPC updated its impact tolerance for payments and settlements after CST22. This was published in the March 2023 FPC Record:

it expected the financial system to be able to complete critical payments by the end of the value date in severe but plausible scenarios; timely recovery of service delivery was the first best way firms could prevent adverse material economic impacts;
in such instances where restoring services would be harmful for financial stability, or impossible, alternative mitigating actions might be appropriate; firms should, therefore plan, prepare and test for such situations and invest so that their response could effectively mitigate any impact on financial stability until service delivery was restored; and
an example of mitigation may be providing an overdraft to a retail Banking customer, so that they can still make purchases, despite a disruption to the payment systems which may have prevented the normal 'payment' being completed

Financial Policy Summary and Record – March 2023 (see paragraphs 101-108)

In Financial Stability in Focus (FSIF), the FPC noted it would regularly review the operational resilience policy toolkit and will explore ways to continue to build system-wide resilience to operational disruption.
In addition to the tools mentioned above, the FPC does this, for example, through:

assessing potential system-wide gaps in, or risks to, operational resilience which are not adequately covered by firm-level or microprudential policies
considering whether to set impact tolerances for additional vital services beyond payments.

The committee has published its macroprudential approach to operational resilience in FSIF and sets out its priorities twice a year in its Financial Stability Report.

articles.text:
International Finance Discussion Papers (IFDP)

Twitter

Share

RSS

October 2026

When and for Whom Does the Sovereign-Bank Nexus Matter? Evidence from Post-Crisis Europe
Charlotte Hoopes, Pinar Uysal, and Ilknur Zer

Abstract:We study whether sovereign risk continues to affect banks a decade after Europe began reshaping its financial architecture. Combining daily bank and sovereign credit default swap spreads with supervisory data on banks' domestic sovereign portfolios, we show that the sovereign-bank relationship remains economically meaningful but is highly conditional. Banks with larger sovereign holdings respond more sharply to home-sovereign risk, and this amplification is substantially stronger for mark-to-market than amortized-cost exposures, consistent with more immediate recognition of valuation losses. Sovereign-to-bank transmission is stronger for less-capitalized, wholesale-funded, and peripheral banks, during periods of elevated market uncertainty, and when the home sovereign has less fiscal capacity. The policy reforms aimed at weakening the sovereignbank relationship only managed to reduce the extent of the link, but not eliminate it.
Keywords: Sovereign-bank nexus, sovereign exposures, bank risk, fiscal space

DOI: https://doi.org/10.17016/IFDP.2026.1448

articles.title: Annual Outlook 2026 | Economic and Market Outlook
articles.text:
Annual outlook 2026: Investing in tomorrow

In our PERSPECTIVES 2026 publication, we look to the year ahead across our ten key investment themes, identifying opportunities and risks on the horizon.

Get in touch

Click here to activate this content.

Investing in tomorrow – Opportunities and risks

The global economy is in constant flux. Trade flows are shifting, regions are gaining or losing influence, and new technologies are also reshaping the economic map. 2025 has been challenging in some respects, but many local equity indices did deliver very good performance. Given the positive macro environment, we expect 2026 to be another constructive year, albeit with continuing market volatility. Although we anticipate a reduction in some uncertainties, it will definitely not be a time for complacency – especially as global trade relations are far from settled. The continued rise of artificial intelligence (AI) may open up new growth opportunities, which should encourage companies to increase their investment activity, potentially giving fresh impetus to both private and public consumption.

The US administration’s tariffs agenda appears to have now been largely implemented. While the disorientation that followed the declaration of “Liberation Day” in early April still lingers globally and domestically, most US trading partners have managed to significantly reduce initial steep tariff hikes through renegotiation. Overall, markets seem to have priced in the effects of the new environment, with overall tariffs still considerably higher than in January 2025 when the current administration began its tenure.

US growth is likely to be supported by the continuation and introduction of extensive tax relief measures, as well as increased spending on security and defence under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The three interest rate cuts expected from the Federal Reserve by the end of 2026 and planned deregulation in the banking sector should also further improve the investment and consumption environment. What makes these government stimuli remarkable is that they come at a time when the US economy is not in recession but is already growing robustly. The US also appears to be close to full employment. Despite the long-term risks such an environment may pose – including inflationary pressures and rising public debt – we expect fiscal and monetary measures to deliver noticeable economic support in 2026.

We also anticipate that policy will deliver a cyclical impulse in Europe, for example due to Germany’s EUR500bn special fund. Planned investments, particularly in infrastructure and climate neutrality, could trigger a short-term upswing. To achieve sustainably higher growth, however, improving domestic economic flexibility remains crucial to foster entrepreneurial initiatives and create an investment climate that enhances productivity. In my view, urgent action is still needed here.

We maintain a broadly constructive outlook for equity markets in 2026. This will be partly due to strong demand for new AI-based applications, which should continue to drive substantial corporate investment flows. Beneficiaries will not only include US “Big Tech” but also a wide range of sectors – construction (thanks to new data centres), utilities (via higher electricity demand) and industrial and basic materials along the supply chain. Our earnings growth forecasts for companies across all major regions are therefore firmly in double-digit territory.

As outlined in our annual outlook themes, investors should also consider potential risks in equity markets. In the area of highly energy-intensive AI applications, for instance, a global power shortage could dampen investor expectations for progress. Not every stock will be a winner in 2026, and short-term corrections at index level remain possible.

Investors should therefore continue to act with discipline. This means focusing on fundamentals rather than chasing perceived trends, while utilising the broad spectrum of investment opportunities. Diversification remains key. Alongside equities, corporate bonds may be attractive – depending on your risk appetite, both investment-grade and high-yield segments. Gold and some non-traditional investments, such as in private equity or infrastructure, also merit consideration. We explore these in detail in the “Alternative Investments” section of this annual outlook.

Overall, we expect a dynamic year for capital markets in 2026 with numerous compelling opportunities. The central question will be whether constructive forecasts can hold up amid a backdrop of economic and geopolitical challenges. Further disruptions to global trade flows or a renewed escalation of tariff tensions could, for example, temporarily pressure corporate earnings and increase market volatility.

In a complex and uncertain environment, investors would therefore be well advised to actively manage risks. This will enable them to respond to market developments in line with their personal investment strategy. Staying invested with a defined strategic asset allocation will be key, as attempts to perfectly time market entry and exit points can often result in missing the best-performing days and weeks.

I hope you find our annual outlook insightful and full of stimulating ideas for your portfolio. We are always available to review and discuss these ideas and look forward to hearing from you.

Christian Nolting

Global CIO

Start a conversation with us

We’d like to learn more about your ambitions for the future and how can support your investment needs – both day-to-day and for the long term.

Theme #1
Value at risk – Crises and conflicts

Geopolitics, inflation, sovereign debt, tariffs: many risk factors likely to persist in 2026.

Earnings expectations: disappointments could trigger volatility.

AI: more of a structural boom than a bubble.

Theme #2
Politics – Cooperation!

Trade tensions between the US and China set to continue in 2026.

Pragmatism may prevent escalation temporarily.

US midterm elections in November to dominate the domestic US agenda.

Theme #3
Economy – The art of intelligence

Global economy set for robust growth overall in 2026.

US growth still ahead of Europe’s. Outlook for China subdued.

AI to drive structural growth, with monetary and fiscal policy as additional drivers.

Theme #4
Policy – Intervention!

Trend toward greater state intervention expected to continue.

State-directed economic policy in China and the US – but also in Europe.

This can often cause more harm than good: risk of missteps remains.

Theme #5
Dollar – The empire strikes back

articles.title: Inflation remains front and center as the Fed holds
articles.text:
Economics & markets

Inflation remains front and center as the Fed holds

October 29, 2026

Josh Hirt

Vanguard senior U.S. economist

Get Vanguard's insights delivered straight to your inbox. Subscribe now

Get Vanguard's insights delivered straight to your inbox. Subscribe now

The Federal Reserve held its policy rate target steady in a range of 3.75%–4% at its October 28 meeting, a decision that financial markets widely expected. What’s next for the Fed comes down largely to inflation.

Prices that have run hot lately have markets anticipating a second 2026 rate hike in December, a view that Vanguard shares. From there, however, we expect less tightening will be needed than markets expect, owing to shock-driven inflation that is set to moderate by the second half of 2027. The key to whether the Fed remains on hold fully in 2027 will be whether near-term data allow the moderating-inflation path to unfold and enable the Fed to maintain its bias toward patience.

Encouraging signs on underlying inflation

Core inflation today reflects three outsize recent shocks: tariffs, energy prices, and AI-related demand. Excluding these effects, we see underlying inflation as being much closer to the Fed’s 2% target.
Tariffs represent the most immediate driver of disinflation as price increases from early 2025 will roll off precipitously by April and May of 2027. That mechanical effect alone should have core inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, approaching 2.5% by late spring—a meaningful decline from current levels.
Oil prices, which have remained stubbornly elevated around $100 per barrel for much of this year, will take longer to moderate. Absent any new and sustained upward price pressure, however, oil prices’ contributions to inflation will remain limited.
AI’s impact remains less certain in the near term and represents a key watch factor. That said, we expect AI-related inflation to continue to contribute 30 to 40 basis points to year-over-year core inflation through 2027 before moderating in 2028.

An economy the Fed can appreciate

This breakdown offers a different perspective on the evolution of inflation in recent years. While overall inflation has moderated little, its composition has indeed shifted. The underlying economy may be performing largely as the Fed intends, with modest policy adjustments keeping it on track to achieve price stability while maintaining labor market balance.
The challenge for policymakers, and the key risk to our baseline view, is whether underlying inflation reaccelerates before these shocks fade. Recent economic momentum has been noteworthy, and the extraordinary AI buildout risks the need for monetary policy tightening beyond our baseline.
That baseline outlook anticipates core PCE inflation moving toward the Fed’s target, ending 2027 at around 2.5%. Such an evolution would support our forecast for one additional Fed rate increase before year-end 2026, with the Fed well-positioned to remain on hold in 2027. The data over the next several months will test our conviction.

Written by:

Will Owens
Research Analyst

Topics

research • October 30, 2026

NYSE Parent Signs Deal to Bring Compliant Hyperliquid Perps to U.S.

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), parent of the New York Stock Exchange, announced a definitive agreement with Trade[XYZ] to bring the latter’s Hyperliquid perpetual futures to the U.S., pending regulatory approval. As part of this deal, ICE will be the exclusive operator of Trade[XYZ]’s regulated markets and is also making a strategic investment. Notably, Wall Street legend Stan Druckenmiller is investing as well, making his first-ever tweet. HYPE, the native token of Hyperliquid, pumped ~20% on the news, from $78 to $94 at time of writing. Hyperliquid will supply the rails via HIP-3* (note the asterisk), which is not exactly the same thing as HIP-3, the year-old protocol upgrade that allows third-party builders to deploy perps. HIP-3* is the newer, gated version designed for regulated entities. Trade[XYZ] will design and deploy the markets, and ICE will run the exchange and clearing. This partnership will allow for the creation of a KYC-gated venue with its own clearinghouse. It will list perps on equities, crypto, indices, commodities, and foreign exchange, with access through futures commission merchants (remember ICE’s venture with OKX). Trade[XYZ]’s HIP-3 markets have done more than $650b in volume and will stay as they are. What makes this new partnership possible is HIP-3*. Hyperliquid unveiled it recently, and it’s live on testnet. It lets deployers run permissioned perpetual markets through an onchain allowlist. On Oct. 26, Hyperliquid announced that Payward, Kraken’s parent, plans to be the first CFTC-regulated deployer. This is a huge announcement, but it’s not entirely surprising. President Donald Trump mentioned Hyperliquid on Aug. 19, stating that CFTC Chair Michael Selig was working to bring the platform to the United States. Also, ICE CEO Jeffrey Sprecher said he’d met the Hyperliquid team multiple times at investment bank Bernstein’s conference in May. TradFi participants love to cite the oil use case. When ICE’s energy markets close, Hyperliquid keeps trading, which has proven useful in times of geopolitical duress. Our takeU.S. traders will get a separate, permissioned venue with its own clearing. The existing open HIP-3 markets will keep trading 24/7 for everyone else. The liquidity will not be shared, meaning the U.S. venue will start from zero. It will be interesting to see how different books react to a Sunday night geopolitical shock, and how tightly arbitrage keeps the two prices together. The backstop for HyperCore (the trading engine of Hyperliquid) is onchain liquidation and, in the tail, auto-deleveraging, as evidenced by last year’s devastating Oct. 10. Nothing announced so far says whether ICE’s clearinghouse will sit on top of HyperCore’s risk engine or replace part of it. It’s also an open question whether ICE already owns any HYPE. Last month, Hyperliquid Labs, the software development company behind the blockchain, sold 3.75m HYPE OTC to an undisclosed institution. Prominent Hyperliquid onchain analyst MLM found 3.125M of it staked with the Hyperliquid Strategies x Unit validator. He traced the other 625k (through a few hops) to a wallet linked to Trade[XYZ], where it was staked this week. This isn’t fully confirmed, though. It’s also uncertain whether trades on the planned U.S. venue would go through HIP-3 and pay the same protocol fees. It’s a little ironic that ICE spent the spring lobbying against this sort of thing. Shortly before Sprecher’s Bernstein remarks, ICE and fellow trading colossus CME pressed U.S. officials to scrutinize Hyperliquid’s role in offshore, oil-linked trading. This announcement is probably the largest positive catalyst in Hyperliquid’s short history, and it will be exciting to see how competitors in the perps space such as Lighter and Kalshi respond. What once seemed like a Hyperliquid bull’s wildest dream is now reality.
