CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesExchangesGoldman Sachs Chairman and CEO David Solomon on AI: Implementation, Accountability, and JobsOct 27, 2026ShareWith the right “rules of the road,” advancing AI doesn’t have to be a choice between innovation and safety, says David Solomon, chairman and CEO of Goldman Sachs. He also explains why he’s optimistic about AI’s impact on the job market in this episode of the Exchanges podcast.
Subscribe: Spotify / Apple Podcasts / YouTube
Download TranscriptKey takeaways:

The third layer of AI control: In addition to governments and tech providers, responsibility for AI also lies with the companies deploying it.
Learning from the past: Previous scientific and technological innovations can provide a model for implementing AI—as can the risk and control processes of financial firms.
Advice for young knowledge workers: Solomon advises young professionals to adapt to AI and treat it as a key tool to enhance their work.

Transcript:
Allison Nathan: How do we get the societal benefits of AI while guarding against its risks?
In a recent op-ed, today's guest argues that winning in the AI era is not a choice between innovation and safety. I'm Allison Nathan, and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges.
Joining me is David Solomon, Chairman and CEO of Goldman Sachs. We'll talk about how AI can be advanced with discipline, what AI means for jobs, how businesses are using it, and who should set the rules.
We'll also discuss the firm's new commitment to help small businesses adopt AI. David, thanks for joining us.
David Solomon: Thank you. Thanks for having me.
Allison Nathan: It's great to have you here in the studio. You and I usually have a conversation at the start of the year to talk about what lies ahead, but we're sitting down today again to focus on the topic that seems to be on everyone's mind: AI.
So, in your op-ed that was published last Friday, you argued that the AI debate is too focused on a choice between moving fast without guardrails or heavy-handed restrictions that could slow progress. So, what's that debate missing?
David Solomon: Well, I think the debate is missing nuance. Most things that are complex and important aren't so binary.
And so, the narrative that's developed that if for some reason we don't let the innovation be unleashed and run at whatever speed with no guardrails, no protections, no risk and controls, we somehow inhibit our competitive position, so therefore, the choice is to regulate, slow down, and stop and weaken our competitive position.
I just don't think it's a binary choice. I think it's a much more nuanced discussion. I think we absolutely can spur great innovation with this technology, but we have to have rules of the road. There have to be guardrails. There has to ultimately be a structure of accountability around the deployment of this technology into society in a way where we can really hold people accountable for the end result and what happens, and I think we can do that.
I don't think it's different with this technology versus others, but it requires a more thoughtful, nuanced discussion than some of this binary, let it run or let's regulate or control it, stop it, slow it down.
Allison Nathan: You say the responsibility for control first sits with governments, second with the companies that are building these AI models, and third with the businesses using them, and it's really that third area that is getting less attention.
Why are companies deploying AI as important as the other two layers of responsibility?
David Solomon: What I tried to do in the op-ed is I was trying to create a simple framework to enhance the conversation. And so, I think very simply, and this is a simple summary of what's in the op-ed, government needs to play a role and set some rules of the road.
The people that are developing these models and the infrastructure that allow the technology to exist and ultimately be deployed in the economy have to take responsibility for what they're building and that it works and that it doesn't do harm. And then the companies that take those products and embed them in their enterprises and their service have to be responsible for the way they're deployed and the impact that they have.
And the third is not getting as much attention, but it's equally important. Goldman Sachs has been using AI-type models for trading platforms for almost 20 years, but there's human accountability attached to every one of those platforms. I could never imagine someone at Goldman Sachs saying to me, "The trading platform went off and did something awful on its own. We couldn't stop it." We wouldn't deploy it if we didn't feel that we had the control to manage it appropriately, and that there was a human being that was ultimately accountable for anything that goes wrong. That's just one example of what needs to happen, but the enterprises have to be responsible for what they deploy into their businesses.
Allison Nathan: The financial services sector uses risk management principles and tools that could help developers and deployers. Tell us more about that. What approach do you think makes the most sense here?
David Solomon: There's been some talk of replicating certain practices that we've seen develop over time with financial services regulation, but these are different things.
I do think, though, there's a lot that can be learned from the experience that large financial institutions have had, particularly around risk management. Financial institutions, particularly the large financial institutions, have developed great risk and control practices, great audit practices, great testing practices, over a long period of time.
Given some of the experiences 20 years ago in the financial crisis, these institutions have learned how to really build up the right infrastructure to test, control, and earn trust. And ultimately, that needs to happen here. And there are businesses that are going to deploy this technology into their enterprise that have great experience in doing those kinds of things, and there are others that need to learn that it's a new muscle group.
They haven't to have risk and control processes of the same level that are going to be necessary for this technology, and they're going to have to figure that out.
Allison Nathan: So, if we kind of put this all together, David, what does winning in the AI era look like from a safety and innovation perspective?
David Solomon: AI is a tremendous technology that I think is going to have enormous societal benefits. But like with anything else that's new and is creating change, there are going to be risk issues, there are going to be speed bumps, and it's our responsibility as a society to figure out how to implement that and put the proper controls into place.
And if we do that, we'll reap the benefits. And while at times things will go wrong or there'll be friction, we will generally control them. And by the way, that's true with almost any technology that accelerates growth, productivity, economic activity. And so, we can do that successfully. Winning, if you want to use that expression, is that we get the benefits of what this technology can do in terms of solving problems in science and wellness and health, drug discovery, disease.
There are all sorts of things that you can think about where we can reap enormous benefits. Winning is that we get those benefits, but we have built a system where there's trust and there's a belief that we can manage the risks associated with the technologies it's deployed, and I think we can accomplish that. I'm optimistic we can accomplish that.
Allison Nathan: Generally optimistic about the potential for the technology and what it can achieve. Also optimistic in terms of the implications for jobs, which has obviously been very much in focus. You've described two camps among business leaders, those expecting a job apocalypse and those expecting a great leap forward. Where do you lean, and what needs to happen for it to play out?
David Solomon: I'm more in the second camp than the first camp with some caveats. Whenever you create new technology, new technology disrupts and automates, and this technology is going to disrupt and automate, and there's just no question that we're going to see that. The question is at what pace? And the question also that doesn't get enough attention is, because of this technology, what new businesses spring up?
What new jobs are created? So, remember, we have a very, very dynamic economy in the US. We create and destroy on average 30 million jobs every year. We generally create a million more than we destroy on average. A lot of those jobs come from small businesses. By the way, there's a great opportunity for small businesses to use this technology to accelerate their ability to grow, bring the cost down in the context of infrastructure they need to be successful.
And so, broadly speaking, while there'll be disruption, I think there'll also be counterbalances to that. Now, here's a question that I think we've got to watch. If the pace of this change is happening quickly, the bridge between the benefits and the jobs that are created and jobs that are being automated, could be quicker.
We might need some policy actions to soften that disruption. And I also think you have to realize that a lot of what this technology does is it makes smart people more productive. So, when people talk about white-collar jobs, just because the technology makes them more productive, it doesn't mean the job goes away.
It means that the smart people can do more productive things while getting the benefit of the technology in their workflows. So, there's going to be a lot of automation, a lot of workflow change, changes in the things that people do. But by the way, you can look back and notice that this has been going on for decades and decades, and this is the next phase of that evolution.
I think about when I started, how I spent my time as a young analyst, and what the productivity of our young analysts are today. We don't have less of them. They just do different things, and they're much more productive than they were 40 years ago. And so that's a good lens. There are lots of jobs that have gone away because of technology.
And as we do that, we create new jobs in our economy. I'm confident and optimistic that that will happen over the next decade or two. I think one of the things we have to watch carefully is in the short term, is there a little bit more disruption? And does that require some policy actions or some steps to smooth that out?
Allison Nathan: So, what's your message or advice for analysts who might be worried that their job is going to disappear?
David Solomon: I understand that people, when there's change, people are fearful. But my advice is, one, embrace the technology, okay? Because the technology, if you're in a knowledge-type job, the technology is going to be an important tool.
So embrace it, learn how to use it, learn how to make yourself more productive in that context. But the world is always changing. The most successful people adapt. And be prepared to adapt and figure out how your productivity can be enhanced in whatever job you're in. And that's something everybody should be doing all the time.
Allison Nathan: If we bring this conversation to what we're doing here at Goldman Sachs, where is AI changing the work people do, including through AI agents, which have been incredibly in focus this year? And what surprised you most as we have adapted and integrated AI into our workflows so far?
David Solomon: We're really focused, in the most simplistic way, we're focused on automation of processes, and we're focused on enhancing client experience.
And so there are lots of ways we can get at that. We have always been very good at giving our very productive people who face clients technology tools and having them figure out how those technology tools enhance the way they serve clients. And we're on that journey now with this technology. And I think the early signs of the benefits that the client experience is going to get are really quite encouraging.
And by the way, they also allow, technology allows, an individual to see more clients or have a bigger footprint. I think about what my client footprint was 40 years ago based on the tools that were available versus what it would be for somebody that was in a client role today. And that's always enhanced and creates productivity, and that's a super exciting thing.
I think the more complicated thing for all enterprises is how you redo operating processes and automate them in ways where you create real productivity gains and efficiency. And then when you get that productivity and efficiency, what do you do with that? Are you just getting margin or operating leverage, or are you also creating capacity to invest in growth in your business in some place where you'd like more capacity to invest in growth?
We see lots of opportunities to invest in growth in our business, and we're trying to use efficiencies from automating processes to give ourselves more capability to drive investment and growth.
Allison Nathan: On that point, Goldman Sachs, of course, advises and finances companies building and using AI. Where is the firm having the biggest impact in this AI investment cycle that everyone is so focused on?
David Solomon: Well, the firm's an advisor, it's a financier. It also has extraordinary technology capabilities. I think we're deploying all those things to help governments and enterprises really think about how they can use this technology most effectively. And so certainly we're giving a lot of advice to companies, to boards, around how they can think about deploying this and what the benefits can be and how they should think about quantifying the economic benefit of the spend.
But in addition, there's an enormous amount of capital formations that's necessary to build the infrastructure to drive this technology. And through our Capital Solutions Group and our very unique ability to act as an advisor, to have huge sourcing capability, but also have an asset management arm attached to the firm, we're in a very unique position or in the middle of a lot of the financing activity and playing a very significant role.
Allison Nathan: Let's switch gears to conclude and talk about smaller businesses, their role in the AI economy, and of course, the announcement that the firm made last week. Goldman has committed $500 million to launch the Small Business AI Institute with some of the leading AI labs. Why are small businesses so important to the AI economy here?
David Solomon: Small businesses are important to our economy here, period. Small businesses by count are 99% of all the companies in the United States, but small businesses drive between 60% and 65% of the job creation in the United States every year. So small businesses are a vitally important part of our economic ecosystem, a huge part of this service economy.
And so giving these businesses tools that allow entrepreneurs of small businesses to accelerate their growth, pursue their passions more aggressively. That's one of the things about entrepreneurs, they're picking businesses where they have passion. There's an expense to building a business, building a platform, setting it up.
That expense is going down with this technology, so that gives more entrepreneurs the opportunity to start businesses. It's a really positive thing, but they need help. They need coaching. They need understanding. They need people that have more experience with these tools and the deployment of technology into an enterprise, even if it's a small enterprise.
And so the AI Institute, we made a $500 million commitment to really do a couple of things. One, it's a continuation of our broad 10,000 Small Business platform, where at this point over the last, I think, 17 years, we've had 20,000 companies, small businesses, go through the program, this business education program.
But now we're going to make to those businesses and new businesses AI training available so they can really test how AI can be used in their businesses, how they can enhance their customer experience, how they can create efficiency in their businesses.
And we've committed $500 million to do that. We're also making more capital available for small businesses in the program.
Allison Nathan: Let me just ask a last question, David, which is obviously there's been a lot of concern and volatility in the market in the last couple weeks around this AI theme. Are you concerned at all about its durability and sustainability?
David Solomon: With a long-term view, I'm not concerned about its durability and sustainability. I think this is going to be a very important technology that is going to be deployed in an enormous application layer in businesses and enterprise and government in a whole variety of ways. But it's going to take 10, 20, 30 years for us to really appreciate the impact of all this.
In the meantime, there's more demand for compute right now than there is compute, and there is an expectation of a very significant buildout. Whether or not the buildout is going to be as significant as some people are saying, whether we're going to spend $5 trillion on the buildout or $10 trillion on the buildout or more, I don't think anybody really knows.
It will be a journey. It won't be a straight line. There'll be accelerations and pullbacks. And so, I think one of the things that's going on in the market that's creating a little bit of volatility is people really trying to understand what's the right way for this to develop, what will be the pace of the development, where are the best opportunities, a lot of capital flows. Certainly as the cost of capital goes up, it changes people's views. And you have two dynamics there. One, a lot of capital creates competition for capital, cost goes up. Two, interest rates have gone up quite a bit this summer for other reasons. And those things kind of push at some of these business models.
And so, this is going to be a journey, but I'm quite confident if you can look out in the medium or the longer term that the benefits from this are going to be terrific. But we'll probably have a recalibration here in the markets at some point in time as people reevaluate how much demand for compute will there be.
What will be the line of growth of that demand? What kind of infrastructure do we really need? How is new technology coming in that makes the chips faster, cheaper, so it changes our perspective on how much data center capacity is needed? Those are all reasonable questions and things that I think we'll learn a lot more about in the coming years.
Allison Nathan: Thanks so much for joining us, David, for your insights on this very important topic, and I look forward to our conversation early next year.
David Solomon: Thanks so much. It's great to see you, Allison. Thank you.
Allison Nathan: And thank you for listening to this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges, which was recorded on Monday, October 26th. If you enjoyed the show, we hope you'll subscribe to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts, and leave us a rating and comment. I'm Allison Nathan.

Podcast • October 27, 2026
Why Now is the Time to Add and Hold BTC, Anthropic’s S-1, and Solana’s Alpenglow

% buffered00:0050:55

In this episode

In this episode of Galaxy Grid, the hosts unpack a dynamic week for digital assets as Bitcoin clings to the $80K level amid wild swings in ETF flows and mounting macro anxiety. Alex Thorn details his latest research report, explaining why technicals, positioning, and fundamentals show now is a historically strong time to buy and hold Bitcoin.

The conversation then shifts to the recent Anthropic S1 filing, analyzing their explosive revenue growth, significant convertible note revaluations, and the unprecedented existential risk disclosures in the prospectus. Thaddeus Pinakiewicz breaks down the sudden surge in AI-driven cybersecurity threats, specifically discussing the severe PHP vulnerabilities discovered by commercial models and the immediate need for agentic defense systems. Finally, the crew examines Solana’s new Alpenglow update, debating its impact on transaction finality, network consensus, and the chain’s pivot toward capturing institutional TradFi volume beyond meme coins.

CareersThere are many chapters in a career. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesExchangesBrookfield’s Connor Teskey on the Real Bottleneck in the AI BuildoutOct 30, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptThe bottleneck in the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout is neither capital nor demand, but rather the operational capability to develop land, secure a grid connection, and build the power supply, says Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey on Goldman Sachs Exchanges: Great Investors. Indeed, one market misconception is that demand for data centers is somehow “fragile,” he says in this conversation with Alison Mass, chairman of Investment Banking in Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets. Teskey also shares his perspective on long-term investing, Brookfield's approach to building businesses and the evolution of its private credit platform.
Transcript:
Connor Teskey: Demand has become the critical input to growth for every major company in every major country around the world, and there is a scarcity of it.
The growth we're seeing across critical infrastructure assets and the overwhelming need for energy around the world goes so far beyond simply artificial intelligence.
Demand is up here and supply is down here. Even if demand growth was to slow, even if it was to plateau, even if it was to decline, there would still be a huge supply-demand imbalance to the providers.
It is perhaps the greatest capital need in the history of mankind. It's pretty exciting.
Alison Mass: Welcome to Goldman Sachs Exchanges: Great Investors. I'm Alison Mass. Today, I'm sitting down with Connor Teskey, CEO of Brookfield Asset Management. Connor joined Brookfield in 2012 at age 24. 14 years later, he runs the entire asset management business, managing approximately $1.3 trillion dollars across infrastructure, renewable power, real estate, private equity, and credit, while continuing to lead its energy group.
In this episode, we discuss Connor's transition to the CEO seat, Brookfield's AI infrastructure buildout across the US and Europe, and the firm's strategic expansion in credit.
Connor, welcome to Great Investors. It's so fantastic to have you here.
Connor Teskey: Thank you for having us.
Alison Mass: So, across all those asset classes that you play in, is there one that you're most excited about right now?
Connor Teskey: I'm probably a little bit biased. I have spent the last 10 years as part of the energy team, a business that's grown very, very rapidly. I still lead that business today. I think if there was one theme across Brookfield that is quite dominant right now, it's energy and infrastructure.
And a lot of the growth in that space, a portion of it is undoubtedly being driven by AI, and AI infrastructure is a huge theme at Brookfield. But the growth we're seeing across critical infrastructure assets and the overwhelming need for energy around the world goes so far beyond simply artificial intelligence.
And that is one that the capital needs are bigger than at any point in history. It is perhaps the greatest capital need in the history of mankind. And the returns are very attractive, and we see this theme not enduring for quarters or years, but through the end of this decade and beyond. It's pretty exciting.
Alison Mass: Yeah. Must be really fun for the energy team investors to have you sitting at the table.
Connor Teskey: Yes and energy's just a fun place to play right now. You know, in only four or five years, electricity is something that everyone took for granted, and now all of a sudden it is the single biggest bottleneck to growth for the greatest companies around the world and the largest countries around the world.
And being a provider of that is an exciting place to be.
Alison Mass: So let's continue on the theme of AI which you brought up. What's your read on the buildout?
Connor Teskey: If there was one headline or narrative that we hear a lot in the market that is detached from what we're seeing in the fundamentals on the ground, it's that the demand for AI infrastructure and the demand for the energy that supports it is in some way fragile. You know, we've seen the market react quite heavily to certain announcements.
Or a potentially more efficient model comes out, or a large hyperscaler walks away from one of its multiple thousands of data center leases, and the whole market reacts. That seems a little divorced from what we're seeing on the ground. Right now, demand is exceptionally high, and supply is only a small fraction of that demand.
Demand is up here, and supply is down here. And therefore, even if demand growth was to slow, even if it was to plateau, even if it was to decline, there would still be a huge supply-demand imbalance to the providers of those assets and those inputs into that ecosystem. So, obviously a huge amount of discipline is required.
These are huge projects. It's a large sum of capital that's going to go into the ground for multiple decades going forward, but the demand is absolutely overwhelming and that imbalance is not going to be disturbed by small changes. The other thing that we're seeing on the AI side is so much talk goes to the big numbers, cause the numbers are quite frankly --
Alison Mass: Staggering.
Connor Teskey: Staggering. Thank you. That is not the bottleneck. There is no shortage of capital, and there is no shortage of demand. The bottleneck is who can actually pull these projects out of the ground. Who has the capabilities to complete the land development, secure the grid connection, build the power supply, build and operate a large-scale gigafactory, provide the redundancy.
That is the scarce input. It is not capital. It is not demand. And we are increasingly seeing the market flow to not just simply those that can show up with big dollars, but those that can show up with both big dollars and big operating capabilities as well.
Alison Mass: All right, so you've already built significant AI infrastructure in the US, and now you're taking that push into Europe. So what is driving that expansion, and what do you think travels across the Atlantic well and what doesn't?
Connor Teskey: So both are going to see very significant buildouts, but the origins of those buildouts and the demand factors are going to be a little bit different.
We can have a thoughtful debate, but of the 15 greatest technology companies in the world, the vast majority of them are based here in the United States. And those corporates are driving a ton of corporate demand in an organic buildout of the AI infrastructure in this country. And that's really being driven by the large technology companies, the hyperscalers, and all of society in the United States is going to benefit from that.
What's interesting is Europe doesn't have that same concentration of homegrown, large-scale technology companies that can provide that corporate demand. That doesn't mean we're not seeing significant growth, but it's coming from two different places.
One, the large global technology companies. Yes, most of them are American, but they are global, so they are, of course, expanding into Europe as well. But the other demand driver that we think is underappreciated is we're actually seeing sovereigns step in, in places where that corporate demand is not going to be the catalyst for the AI buildout.
We're seeing the nation-states... What is AI? At its core, it's a productivity tool. It's designed to drive efficiency and enable more growth. We're seeing nation-states step in and say, "We don't want our population, our country, to be left behind in having access to those tools and those productivity gains in the future," so they will actually backstop the buildout of AI infrastructure.
And we've signed agreements in France, in Sweden, in Qatar, where the initial off-taker to support the buildout of AI infrastructure is not a hyperscaler, but actually a sovereign, and we call that sovereign AI. And we see that demand much more in places outside of the United States and or APAC where, where you do have those domestic global technology leaders.
Alison Mass: That's an interesting perspective. Sovereign AI.
Connor Teskey: Sovereign AI.
Alison Mass: So the power side of this isn't new territory for you, as you've talked about. It's where you started. You built most of the renewables business that's been long core to Brookfield. But the argument has changed. It used to be a climate case, and now it sounds like more of a commercial one, speed to market, availability, energy security. So has the thesis changed in your view, or has the customer changed? What has changed?
Connor Teskey: A lot has changed in the last five to 10 years. But the one thing I would say about our approach that's been quite helpful, and this existed long before my time, is our approach has always been driven by commercial. We don't take technology bets. We don't ever accept one basis point of return discount because of the decarbonization or energy transition impact of an investment.
We think you can make very attractive risk-adjusted returns that also provide those benefits to society. What has changed is demand has become the critical input to growth for every major company in every major country around the world, and there is a scarcity of it. There is a supply-demand imbalance that started at the end of the last decade, the late twenty-teens.
Interestingly, at that point, it wasn't driven by AI. It was driven by these global trends of reindustrialization and electrification. That created a supply-demand imbalance that in and of itself was going to exist for decades and provide multiple decades of electricity demand growth. And then AI took off and took that supply-demand imbalance and exaggerated it even further.
What we would say that we're seeing in our business is two things. Electrons are a commodity, but there is a lot more sophistication around electrons now. Counterparties don't just phone up and say they want power. They want power that's a certain shape in a certain location from a certain source for a certain duration.
And being able to evolve and meet those ever-evolving customer needs is very, very critical to us, and that's leading to the development of new technologies. I'll tell you, the fastest-growing segment of our energy business right now is energy storage. How do you get the joys of low-cost renewables but offset the issues of intermittency?
You offset it with energy storage and batteries, which is undoubtedly the fastest. That wasn't true five years ago. The other thing that we are seeing is because electricity has become such a critical bottleneck, the largest buyers and users of electricity around the world don't always just go to who can provide it at the lowest cost.
It is a very negative for a hyperscaler if they want to turn on a data center but the power supply isn't available yet. So rather than having 10,000 small suppliers who may or may not get a project delivered on time or on budget, we're increasingly seeing the largest users of electricity increasingly focus on a smaller number of scale providers who have the credibility to work through problems, deliver on time, deliver on budget, and really can be a partner to them in providing what is one of the most critical inputs.
And our business over the last five or 10 years, 10 years ago, we essentially sold power to utilities and governments. Today, we sell the most, majority of our power directly to corporates. And we work very much with those corporates to meet their evolving needs. And our relationships with them go beyond individual contracts to global scale framework agreements that just continue to grow and grow over time.
Alison Mass: That makes sense, certainty and ability to deliver.
Connor Teskey: It's far more value than picking up a penny here or a penny there on power price.
Alison Mass: So everything that you've described gets built with borrowed money, which brings me to credit. And in your story, there's a mix of organic and inorganic.
You've built a lot in-house, but you've also bought a majority stake in Oaktree, Howard Marks' firm back in 2019, and now full ownership, plus stakes in several other managers. So how do you decide what you're going to build versus what you're going to buy?
Connor Teskey: The build versus buy decision is one that we make every time we look to grow at Brookfield. It is always a build versus buy decision. And in general, we prefer to build it ourselves if we think we have the capabilities to do so because it's often less expensive.
And two, you can build it exactly how you want it. Sam Pollock, who's built our infrastructure business over the last 20 years, he's built an incredible market-leading franchise. It does not have a peer. If he wants to launch a new strategy, he's not going to go buy someone else to do it.
He's very likely going to use some internal resources to build the strategy from the ground up. However, from time to time, we see capabilities that we think it would be very difficult to replicate, or it would take us too long to replicate in order to capture what we think is a very large and attractive market opportunity.
And that, that was exactly Oaktree for us in 2019. We had a very large and market-leading equity franchise on the private investment side, but we did feel that credit was becoming a core pillar of private markets going forward. And could we have built a market-leading credit franchise over 10 or 15 years? Absolutely.
But we thought it was worth it to accelerate that process, and in hindsight, we think it was a great decision, and we couldn't be more thrilled with the partnership with Oaktree.
Alison Mass: So, staying on Oaktree for a second, how did that deal start, and how did you end up at the center of it?
Connor Teskey: Like a lot of things, some good fortune. I actually started in the private equity group at Brookfield when I joined the firm in Toronto almost 15 years ago.
One of the first things I was asked to review was actually an investment in another asset manager that was in need for capital, and I didn't really know where to start. I'd never looked at an asset management business before.
And after spinning my wheels for probably a few days, I had this idea, which was, well, if I can understand Brookfield's business model, I can probably use that as a base case to try and understand this other asset manager's model. And from that initial review we began, as part of that process, we simply began to track some of the other publicly traded alternative asset managers, largely to see how Brookfield could be doing better and how are we doing versus our peer set.
And at the beginning of 2018, we felt that Oaktree was not trading appropriately in the market, it was one of the names we tracked, relative to the incredible quality of that franchise and what we thought the long-term's earning potential would be.
And it's funny, I went to Bruce and I said, "Well, maybe we can just buy some shares and make a little bit of money." And Bruce said, "Fine, but, you know, maybe think could we do something a little bit more strategic with them?" And we took that away into our little lab and came up with this idea of privatizing the company but partnering with the founders and the existing management. And that was the transaction we did about 12 months later.
Alison Mass: Yeah, and the rest is history.
Connor Teskey: Yeah, it's been great.
Alison Mass: How would you characterize your approach to making investment decisions in general?
Connor Teskey: We have incredible resources around the world, expertise by asset class, by geography.
I think it is very important to try not to be an expert at everything. On any individual decision, there is probably someone at Brookfield who is more of an expert and more informed than I am, and I think being a great investor is knowing where that information is and pulling all that appropriate information in to make the most informed decision.
That would be point one. The second thing is there are no certainties. There absolutely are no certainties. When you get to a level of confidence where things are extremely likely and largely in your control, that's when you pull the trigger and you invest with conviction.
If you try and remove absolutely every risk and turn every variable into an absolute certainty, you will have a perfect track record, but you will make no investments. And I think it is very important to pass judgment of we are in control of enough of the variables here, and we have certainty over enough of the outcomes that we have a return profile that is downside protected and asymmetric to the upside.
And that's really our investing style. And then the last thing I would say is it's very important to be able to simplify things. We invest in extremely large assets on a scale that few around the world do. These are large businesses. It's always important to understand the very small number of key value drivers and understanding which ones do you have a strong view on, which ones are you in control of.
I think being able to simplify large but amazing businesses is very important to making good investment decisions.
Alison Mass: So, most of our listeners have heard of Brookfield, but fewer appreciate the range or the scale. So, give us the rundown, and one thing to flag for any of our listeners who still file you away as a Canadian company, you're headquartered in New York now. So, tell us a little bit about that journey.
Connor Teskey: Sure. So today, Brookfield is the leading global alternative asset manager focused on real assets. The firm and its predecessors were founded in 1899, and yes, our original origins were Canadian, but as we've become a scaled global financial firm, we operate in 50 countries around the world, and we're increasingly concentrated in the global financial centers with our headquarters here in New York.
Alison Mass: So we’ve seen a lot of transition in the leadership of the alternative asset management space over the last five years. You recently stepped into the CEO seat at the asset management business, taking over from Bruce Flatt, who built it, and who's still running Brookfield Corporation.
So, did you feel ready, and how did that transition happen?
Connor Teskey: So a lot of credit goes to not only Bruce, but the other senior leadership of Brookfield. This has been an incredibly methodical, incremental, continuous transition. Yes, we announced a change in titles earlier this year, but this transition has been happening for three years, and it probably has a number of years still to run.
And I remember, and I think we announced it on a Wednesday. Monday and Friday of that week didn't feel a whole lot different. And I think it really comes down to two things. One, Brookfield has created a culture where there's incredible senior mentorship, and they really coach young talent up from an early age and put people in a position to take on more responsibility early and be in a position to win.
And I was fortunate to have incredible mentors and be some of the beneficiary of that. To your question of whether or not you can feel ready, I always feel that there's a certain healthy level of insecurity is good. It keeps you sharp, it keeps you focused. But the fact that it was such a seamless and incremental transition, made it feel very easy.
Alison Mass: You’re a new leader at a relatively young age, and probably a decade younger than some of your peers who've been put into similar positions. Has that been an advantage?
Connor Teskey: One of the things that Bruce and other members of the senior leadership do feel is very important at Brookfield is mixing excellent experience and tenure and knowledge with young energy.
And that's something we do across all of our businesses. I'm fortunate coming into the role to have the most amazing set of senior partners and mentors who have decades of experience that we can draw on. But we love to continuously inject young energy and young perspective into our leadership, into our decision-making.
We think it's, one, important for having fresh perspectives, but two, it's also important to being relatable to an extremely large workforce of Brookfield employees that many of whom are on the younger side as well.
Alison Mass: So, what was the most useful thing that Bruce told you before you took the job that helped you in your first six months in the job?
Connor Teskey: Undoubtedly the thing, having been fortunate to work with Bruce and the other senior leaders for a number of years now that I find most helpful is just how calm and balanced they are when markets inevitably change. We like to forecast, we like to do due diligence, remove risk, things like that, but markets are always moving.
And one of the things that at the very beginning you almost feel a bit unnerved by it, but then you become accustomed to it. It's just the thoughtful, balanced, moderate approach to adjusting to the evolving environment that we all work and live in every day. When Bruce did tell me for the first time about the succession, the succession plan, your mind goes to a lot of places very, very quickly, and I'm sure he said a lot of things that day.
The one that always sticks out to me, which really grounded me very quickly, is he said, "Don't worry whether or not you're the right person. That was our choice, not yours. We just want to make sure this is what you want, and you're committed to doing it for decades to come." And I remember mind going a lot of different directions, and the second he said that, immediately things slowed down and it all became a bit more digestible.
Alison Mass: Yeah. That's very thoughtful because to your point earlier about we're all a little insecure, it takes your insecurity away because you didn't make the decision, they did.
Connor Teskey: Yeah. I'll be honest, I use Bruce's line now.
Alison Mass: Yeah, no, I think it's a good one. I may have to incorporate it myself. So how are involved are you now in the day-to-day investment decisions?
Connor Teskey: So, I sit on all the investment committees, so, oversee any time around the world that Brookfield deploys capital, but I think it's important to recognize with the scale of our operation, how we deploy capital. And the way Brookfield operates is we source, execute, and operate in an incredibly decentralized manner.
For every region around the world that we want to own or invest in assets, and for every asset class around the world, we have a dedicated local team, and those teams are empowered to know everything about that market, go find... know all the themes, know the value levers that are coming, position the business to capture that value, see the risks that are coming, position the business to mitigate that risk in a very decentralized manner. We actually allocate capital in a quite centralized group. And it's in that way that we can grow fast and be local in so many markets around the world, but we can also consolidate all that knowledge to use that global perspective to allocate capital to where we see the best risk-adjusted returns.
So myself and a number of the members of the senior team sit on that centralized investment committee. I always feel it would be the wrong approach for me to try to be the expert in a specific asset class or region where we've got a dedicated team that does it 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year.
I'm rarely questioning underwriting assumptions. We have experts for that. What we do on that investment committee is think more high level, more strategic in terms of our comments and our feedback.
One of the things your question triggers a little bit is, it seems to us a little bit silly to bet on a competitive advantage of simply being smarter than everyone into perpetuity.
You want to create structural and enduring competitive advantages that allow you to deploy capital very attractive risk-adjusted returns at an incredible scale and consistency that few can match. That is our brand.
So, we spend a lot of time focusing on enhancing those strategic, competitive and enduring competitive advantages such that it's not just making the next good investment, it's putting the firm in a position to make several good investments in the years and decades to come.
And that's things like focusing on changes in global themes, where is capital flowing, do we have the right people and the right expertise in the organization? That's where we spend a lot of time.
Alison Mass: So let's widen it out a little bit to the industry. What kind of growth do you expect in alternatives from here?
Connor Teskey: The growth in the alternatives industry is going to be very significant. I actually think it's very tough to see a scenario where the allocations in either the individual market or the institutional market slow. And very simply, the alternatives industry has grown over the last 20 plus years essentially on institutions beginning to and then increasing their allocation to alternatives.
And that's grown the industry for the last 20 years, and that, in and of itself, growing institutional demand could drive the growth of the industry for the next decade and beyond. But now there is this second additional growth lever, which we call the individual market. That's your, your high net worth or private wealth investor, that's your life insurance policy or annuity holder.
That is your 401k or your retiree market. In that segment of the market, the penetration is very low. If institutional investors are allocated somewhere in the, call it mid-teens range to alternatives and probably going up to 20% or 30% over time, that individual market is 2% or less today.
So, in terms of directional trend line, we don't see it slowing down. And it's not a trend or a fad, it's because of what alternatives can provide to those investors' portfolios that traditional portfolios don't have. Private market investments over the long term do come with a return premium because they are private and there is a slight liquidity premium.
But more importantly, they provide a huge amount of stability in portfolios, especially relative to public markets that are becoming increasingly volatile. Secondly, with many of the leading companies around the world staying private longer and with certain industries much more concentrated in the private markets, it can provide diversity to what they can get in a public portfolio.
And then, the last thing I would say is private capital very simply works better for certain types of investments. Think large infrastructure projects that are going to take two, three, four, five years to build and are going to be non-income producing for that period of time, then they turn on and they produce cash for the next four or five decades.
It's really different after they're producing cash, and that works really well in a quarterly-over-quarter reporting cycle. Those early years of putting dollars, non-income producing dollars in the ground doesn't work great in the public markets. So, whether it's returns, whether it's stability, whether it's diversification or access to some of the biggest growth trends and growth themes around the world, we view it as directionally a pretty strong certainty that the growth will continue to be there going forward.
Will it ebb and flow over that very strong growth trend line? Absolutely. And that will be driven by markets, that will be driven by performance of certain vehicles and things like that, but I think the trend line is pretty definitive.
Alison Mass: And as you say, as long as the asset classes continue to outperform the public market indices over any periods of time you look at, one, three, five, 10 years, the investments will flow in.
Connor Teskey: Absolutely. And they've proven to do that over decades.
Alison Mass: So last one before we go to our lightning round. You were a rower in college, I understand. So what did that teach you about leading?
Connor Teskey: Feels a long time ago. I wasted all my time growing up watching, following, playing sports.
Alison Mass: That's not a waste of time.
Connor Teskey: I still spend a lot of time on ESPN. Rowing is a kind of a funny sport. There's very little that's actually enjoyable about rowing itself. It's very - You get up early in the morning, you go somewhere that's often cold or wet in the dark, and you twist your back and pull as hard as you can 3,000 times in a row.
But it is one of the greatest team environments I think you can get in sports because it really is an environment where a crew is only as good as the weakest link. And it doesn't matter if you're the strongest person in the boat or the weakest person in the boat, if you do a little bit better, the whole boat goes faster.
And I think what it teaches you about discipline, what it teaches you about working really hard, and what it teaches you about teamwork, I'd say that those are some of the things we use every day in a much more different environment that we work in now.
Alison Mass: Okay, we like to end these conversations with sort of a quick answer round. So, what is your greatest strength as an investor?
Connor Teskey: Ability to simplify things.
Alison Mass: And what is the best advice you've ever gotten from outside the business?
Connor Teskey: To always remember that this is a people business. People will always do more deals and do more business that people they enjoy working with. This will always be a people business.
Alison Mass: Yeah, I agree. People want to do business with people they like and people they trust.
How do you spend your time out of the office? And I'm assuming it's not on a boat in crew.
Connor Teskey: No, with my family. I have a very young family, so 100% of my time out of the office is with my wife and kids.
Alison Mass: That sounds fun. Which investor do you admire most?
Connor Teskey: Sam Pollock, built our infrastructure business
Alison Mass: Okay. And what are you most excited about in the world right now?
Connor Teskey: I wear two hats at Brookfield, the asset management business and the energy business. It's very fun waking up in industries and markets where the question is not, "Can you grow?" It's, "How much can you grow, and can you do the right growth?" That is exciting. That makes it easy to get out of bed in the morning.
Alison Mass: Well, Connor, thank you so much for joining. It was a fun discussion, and I hope you enjoyed it as well.
Connor Teskey: Thank you for having us.

articles.title: Phishing and Fraud Awareness Notice
articles.text:
Phishing and Fraud Awareness Notice

Bridgewater Associates, LP (“Bridgewater”) is a premier asset management firm, focused on delivering unique insight and partnership for the most sophisticated global institutional investors. We have recently become aware of an increase in fraudulent schemes in which unauthorized third parties (often operating through fake websites, social-media profiles, unsolicited e-mail or social media messages, text messages, telephone calls, or other communication platforms) misrepresent themselves as employees, agents, or affiliates of Bridgewater. These bad actors may attempt to obtain confidential personal information, solicit investments (including cryptocurrency investments), offer investment advice, induce the transfer of funds under false pretenses, or may target job seekers purporting to offer jobs at Bridgewater. The fraudulent activity is sophisticated, constantly evolving and frequently mimics the look and feel of genuine Bridgewater communications, and may reference accurate-looking logos, executive names, marketing materials, and the official Bridgewater.com website. We issue this notice to alert current and prospective clients, counterparties, vendors, job applicants, and the general public to these unlawful practices. The actions of these unauthorized persons are in no way associated with Bridgewater.Bridgewater communicates only through official channels, including with its clients, counterparties and job applicants. Bridgewater’s official website is: https://www.bridgewater.com, and our email address ends strictly in “@bwater.com”. No other websites or email domains are authorized by Bridgewater. The only social media accounts authorized by Bridgewater are LinkedIn and Meta (Facebook and Instagram). We only use these authorized social media accounts to issue informational postings. Please be aware that Bridgewater does not conduct business activities, financial transactions, solicit investments or provide investment advice through social-media direct messages, personal e-mail domains, encrypted messaging apps, or public chat platforms, such as Telegram, WeChat, or WhatsApp, or other public platforms. Bridgewater does not hire from social media or conduct interviews via text or messaging services, nor will Bridgewater request any form of payment in connection with the hiring process.Some of the warning signs or red flags that may indicate a scam include: (a) phishing websites that have the look and feel of the official Bridgewater website, (b) variations in email domains that appear to have come from a Bridgewater email address, (c) fraudulent mobile device apps which purport to be an official Bridgewater app, and (d) time bound offers which pressure you to invest immediately.If you have any questions about this notice or the legitimacy of any communication purportedly from Bridgewater, please email our Legal Department at LRG_FraudAwareness@bwater.com. If you believe you may have been the victim of internet crime or fraudulent activity, please report it to law enforcement in your jurisdiction.

30 October 2026
Daily Navigator

Download Report

Key highlights
USD stays rangebound despite resilient US growth: The USD index (DXY) fell 0.2% to 102.04 on Thursday. US Q3 GDP grew 3.4% annualised, above expectations, while quarterly core PCE inflation slowed to 2.5% annualised from 3.3% in Q2. September core PCE inflation was 3.1% y/y, in line with forecasts. Weekly jobless claims remained low at 194,000. Markets price around 70% chance of a December Fed hike. A technology-share sell-off boosted demand for US government bonds, pushing the 10-year yield 8.1bps lower to 4.94% and the 2-year yield down 10bps to 4.60%. We expect DXY to remain rangebound between 101.50 and 103.00.
EUR/USD stays rangebound as ECB weighs inflation risks: EUR/USD recovered from an intraday low of 1.1104 to close at 1.1180. The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.50%, warning that higher energy prices pose inflation and growth risks. ECB President Christine Lagarde announced she will step down on 7 February 2027, raising uncertainty over future policy leadership. Markets anticipate two further ECB hikes by H1 2027, while we expect one by year-end followed by a pause. EUR/USD support is at 1.1164, with resistance at 1.1199.
BoJ guidance in focus for USD/JPY: USD/JPY traded near 157.69 ahead of today’s BoJ decision. We expect the bank to hold its policy rate at 1.25%, with a December hike anticipated. Markets will watch for policy dissent and upward revisions to inflation forecasts. We expect both the Fed and BoJ to hike in December, leaving their interest rate differential broadly unchanged. USD/JPY is expected to remain rangebound between 157.50 and 158.00..

articles.title: Who Is Consuming Chinese Tokens?
articles.text:
Who Is Consuming Chinese Tokens?

Laila Khawaja

Gavekal Technologies: Chips | 29 Oct 2026

An unverified claim that over half of China’s domestic tokens are used for video and micro drama generation has sparked a heated online debate. Critics contrast China’s supposed use of scarce compute resources for entertainment with an alleged US focus on coding and productivity. The controversy took place as Chinese AI video models lead global rankings and as Chinese micro dramas and video generation applications rapidly expand their global influence. While the underlying data remain unconfirmed, the debate reveals the potential disconnect between Beijing’s ambitions for economy-wide AI transformation and the commercial realities of Chinese AI companies.

articles.title: Equities update - Week 44 - October 30 2026
articles.text: Equities update - October 30th 202611 min readFinanceDataWeek 44 brought further equity-market volatility as disappointing mega-cap technology updates and the Fed’s hawkish hold weighed on risk appetite. The Fed maintained rates at 3.75–4.00%, while firmer PCE inflation kept the December FOMC meeting a live at 76% odds of a hike down from 85% at the beginning of the week. Higher oil prices, supported by renewed threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, added to inflation concerns. Gold also weakened as expectations of higher interest rates increased the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets, illustrating how inflation risks can complicate its defensive role. Concerns over the cash-flow impact of substantial AI spending added pressure to technology shares and broader equities, increasing scrutiny of the financing assumptions supporting the infrastructure buildout. On the corporate front, ICE’s agreement to bring Hyperliquid-based markets into a regulated US framework, alongside further stablecoin initiatives from Ripple and SBI, demonstrated the continuing integration of blockchain infrastructure with traditional finance. Listed-platform earnings also showed revenues diversifying beyond crypto trading, while the Binance and Polymarket breaches reinforced the importance of custody, governance and the investment vehicle used to access the sector.Week 44 Key Developments in Blockchain Equities:Index Performance: The Index declined -2.6%, compared with a -4.5% fall in Bitcoin, as persistent inflation and renewed pressure on technology shares weighed on risk appetite. The FOMC held interest rates at 3.75–4.00%, although two officials favoured a 25bp increase, keeping the prospect of further tightening in focus. September PCE inflation accelerated to 3.6% year-on-year, with core inflation at 3.1%, reinforcing concerns that price pressures remain above the Fed’s target. Resilient economic growth and higher oil prices amid renewed Middle East tensions further complicated the inflation outlook. Meanwhile, disappointing updates from Alphabet and Amazon added pressure to the technology trade, as investors scrutinised the impact of substantial AI capital expenditure on cash generation and the timing of investment returns. Weakness in these heavily weighted companies also weighed on broader equity indices.Block Index Key Movers: 7-day top performers: Hyperliquid Strategies (+41.6%), Galaxy Digital (+18.6%), AMD (+11.5%) 7-day worst performers: Nu Holdings (-18.2%), GMO Internet (-13.2%), MercadoLibre (-9.0%) ICE announces agreement to bring Hyperliquid-based perpetual futures to the US – ICE, the parent of the New York Stock Exchange, announced an agreement with Trade[XYZ] to establish US-regulated perpetual futures markets built on Hyperliquid. ICE would provide the regulated market and clearing framework, Trade[XYZ] would contribute product design and deployment expertise, and Hyperliquid would supply the underlying blockchain infrastructure, with customer access expected through brokers and futures commission merchants. The agreement marks a significant step in the convergence of traditional finance and crypto infrastructure, with an established exchange operator adopting crypto rails to expand how financial assets are traded. The proposed market would offer around-the-clock exposure across equities, commodities, currencies and crypto, combining onchain trading capabilities with established distribution and regulatory oversight. Subject to approvals, this could open a new retail growth channel operating separately from ICE’s existing institutional franchise.Stanley Druckenmiller’s public backing reinforces the significance of the announcement. He confirmed an investment in Trade[XYZ] and said he looked forward to using its product to enhance his investment process. Separately, Duquesne Family Office reported a holding in index constituent Hyperliquid Strategies (PURR) valued at approximately US$23m as of 30 June 2026. For PURR, the potential benefit comes through its HYPE token treasury and staking operations. Broader adoption of Hyperliquid could increase trading activity and fee generation, potentially supporting HYPE’s economics and the value of PURR’s holdings. The agreement therefore strengthens the commercial adoption thesis behind PURR, although the eventual equity benefit will depend on the scale of adoption and how economic value accrues to HYPE.Binance’s US$6.3bn hack and Polymarket breach reinforce the case for listed blockchain equities - The security incidents at Binance and Polymarket on 29 October reinforce the importance of how investors access the digital-asset ecosystem. Binance estimated the impact at approximately US$6.3bn and pledged to cover losses through its SAFU fund and company resources. Polymarket temporarily halted its international platform following a third-party security breach and also promised reimbursement. Both incidents highlight the operational and counterparty risks that can accompany holding funds directly on trading platforms.Blockchain equities provide a route to participate in the industry’s growth through an established securities framework. Investors can hold shares through regulated brokers and custodians, with applicable client-asset protections, while assessing businesses through published audited financial statements, corporate governance and ongoing disclosure requirements. US domestic issuers, for example, generally must disclose material cybersecurity incidents within four business days of determining materiality. These arrangements provide a framework for scrutiny and accountability without requiring investors to manage private keys or maintain balances on crypto trading platforms.The week’s results also demonstrated how listed businesses are monetising demand across the ecosystem. Coinbase reported prediction-market revenue exceeding US$173m of quarterly event-contract revenue. Visa’s annualised stablecoin settlement volume exceeding US$25bn provided further evidence of adoption within established financial infrastructure. For equity investors, the opportunity is to participate in the revenues and earnings generated by these activities.Earnings Recap – Key Holdings:Coinbase, Standard Chartered, Mastercard, Galaxy Digital – PositiveSamsung Electronics, Strategy Inc, Robinhood – MixedFlow Traders, PayPal - NegativeOther news - Index constituents:SBI Holdings announced several initiatives connecting stablecoins with asset management, banking and cross-border payments. Alongside BlackRock and Startale, it signed an MOU to explore linking tokenised money-market funds with JPYSC, its yen-denominated trust-type stablecoin. SBI also agreed a strategic alliance and preliminary framework for a Japanese joint venture with Cross River Bank’s parent, CRB Group, covering tokenised loans, cross-border payments and agentic commerce, alongside a proposed strategic investment and potential integration of JPYSC. Separately, SBI announced a capital and business alliance with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group to develop services using stablecoins and tokenised assets, and participated in PhotonPay’s US$65bn of annualised platform-wide transaction volume. Together, these developments broaden SBI’s potential role across asset management, distribution and payment infrastructure, although several initiatives remain exploratory or subject to final agreements and regulatory approvals.Circle and ACI announced a collaboration to demonstrate USDC settlement within existing banking and payments infrastructure, initially in Colombia. The work combines Circle’s infrastructure with ACI Connetic and builds around ACI’s role in Bre-B, Colombia’s interoperable instant-payments ecosystem. The opportunity is to embed stablecoins within established financial-institution workflows.Bullish advanced its tokenised securities strategy with the addition of Qube Research & Technologies, Vertalo and zerohash to the Issuer Sponsored Token Coalition strengthens Bullish’s efforts to build an ecosystem spanning tokenised securities issuance, shareholder registration and trading. Co-founded with Equiniti, the coalition is developing standards that connect tokenised shares with official shareholder records, preserving investors’ dividend and voting rights. This supports the strategic rationale behind Bullish’s proposed acquisition of Equiniti: combining issuer relationships and registry capabilities with Bullish’s exchange infrastructure.Galaxy applied to the OCC to establish Galaxy National Bank. If approved, it would bring digital-asset custody, trading, staking and fiduciary investment advisory services under a federal trust framework. A national structure could support broader institutional relationships and simplify the regulatory architecture around these services.IREN and Wingspire Equipment Finance closed US$363m of financing against revenue-generating GPU servers and networking equipment. The six-lender group included commitments from Eldridge Capital Management and Silver Point Capital. The transaction releases capital already invested in deployed infrastructure backed by multi-year customer contracts. Ripple expanded RLUSD distribution across Coinbase Prime, Exchange and the retail app, with support across XRPL, Base and Ethereum. Global Exchange access and collateral functionality are to follow. RLUSD is also live on Robinhood Chain and Bitstamp, with Robinhood app access expected later this year. Robinhood plans to integrate Ripple Treasury, while the partnership also extends institutional financing and market access through Ripple Prime.HIVE’s BUZZ subsidiary agreed approximately US$129m of equipment financing at a fixed 9% rate over three years, with principal and interest amortising during the term. The equipment supports the previously announced three-year Cohere contract. Asset security, limited recourse support and an equity pledge underpin the facility.Soneium backed by Sony Group, outlined plans for an ecosystem token and introduced ipUSD and IP Vault, with access scheduled to open on 28 October. The vault offers eligible users exposure to a US$549m Partners Group royalties fund tokenised by Asseto; this is the underlying fund’s size. The initiative connects financial infrastructure with entertainment and intellectual property, although customer adoption and the contribution to Sony’s earnings remain early considerations.Nu Holdings and MercadoLibre – Brazil election repricing: Lula’s surprise runoff victory triggered a sharp reversal in Brazilian markets, with the Bovespa closing down 13.9% on Monday and the real falling 8.1% against the dollar. For Nu and MercadoLibre, the immediate implications include country risk, FX translation, credit conditions and consumer demand, which can affect group earnings independently of digital-asset initiatives.Other news – Non - Index constituents:Visa reported revenue of US$12.1bn, and adjusted EPS of US$3.48. Management described more than US$25bn of annualised stablecoin settlement volume, over 225 stablecoin-linked card programmes and commercial production for Visa Direct’s stablecoin prefunding. These disclosures demonstrate adoption within an existing distribution network.Aviva Investors launched a tokenised share class of its GBP22bn Sterling Liquidity Fund on XRPL with an initial GBP50m investment. The development extends institutional cash-management applications, with the commercial opportunity resting on distribution, servicing and assets retained in the new share class.BNY and Ripple expanded their collaboration across institutional custody and potential tokenised trade finance. The work aims to connect assets with payments and collateral workflows. For BNY, the commercial question is whether these capabilities deepen custody, servicing and financing relationships sufficiently to generate recurring fees.Published onOct 30th, 2026WritersSatish PatelInvestment AnalystCo-manages the Invesco CoinShares Global Blockchain ETF with expertise in payments and technology.Alex SchmidtIndex Fund ManagerManages the first and largest fund offering exposure to listed blockchain companies.
